Halifax lawyer has misgivings about new RCMP uniform policy
Officers now have option to wear name tag or 5-digit regimental number to identify themselves
A Halifax lawyer says an RCMP policy change that means officers are no longer required to wear name tags on their uniforms while on duty poses a threat to police accountability and transparency.
Under a policy shift first reported by the Globe and Mail earlier this month, members of Canada's national police force can now choose between wearing a traditional name tag or their five-digit regimental number. The report said the policy has been in effect since March 30.
But defence lawyer Asaf Rashid said in an interview with CBC Radio's Information Morning Nova Scotia that officers should be required to display both, arguing that replacing names with numbers creates a barrier for the public during rapidly evolving situations.
“Who's going to be able to remember a number in a fast-paced environment where police are moving around very quickly,” Rashid said, describing the policy shift as a step toward "draconian" practices.
“There’s a certain sense of impunity when you don’t have your name tag on that maybe you can get away with it. They should be accountable, they should be transparent, and there shouldn’t be any limit on that.”
Rashid represented several people who were charged when a large group of protesters clashed with Halifax Regional Police more than five years ago during the controversial homeless encampment evictions in the city's downtown.
“In one particular case there was an officer who said he forgot to bring the uniform that had his name tag on it and he seemed to be taking certain liberties away from individuals," Rashid said.
The RCMP introduced the policy change to protect officers from online harassment and "doxing," the compilation and release of someone's personal information, including their name, address and phone number.
“Officers were targeted online and their private life was exposed based on their last name,” RCMP spokesperson Sgt. Maj. Julie Gagnon said.
In some cases, Gagnon said, officers received death threats.
“We sure don't want that for officers. So we're now giving the options … because the name might be just easier to find on open sources online,” she said.
Gagnon said a regimental number is unique to each officer and is just as effective as a surname for identification. She maintained that members of the public can still submit complaints or identify officers by providing either their name or regimental number to a local detachment.
“The public does not have to worry about the accountability of the RCMP because we are accountable for our actions and we will remain accountable for our actions,” Gagnon said.
However, the change reopens a debate highlighted in a 2024 report by the Civilian Review and Complaints Commission for the RCMP.
The oversight body looked into an incident where officers removed their name tags during a protest in British Columbia. It determined the practice was unreasonable without an alternative form of identification.
“It is much harder to hold the police accountable for their actions,” the report said. “This eats away at the public’s trust in the police.”
While the RCMP decided to permit regimental numbers in place of name tags during protests, the commission found that numbers were still difficult for the public to remember in high-stress situations.
Instead, the commission recommended officers wear "prominent but simple codes on the front and back of their uniforms" during public demonstrations.

A summer that started early across the US has no intention of quitting, even as the calendar turns to autumn.
The culprits? El Niño and climate change, which contributed to this summer’s record-breaking warmth and are delaying pumpkin spice season.
Forecasters with the US Climate Prediction Center continue to see increased odds for hotter-than-normal temperatures across much of the country through at least the end of September.
Computer models show a pronounced ridge pattern, an atmospheric arrangement that can lock in sustained spells of warmer-than-normal conditions. This setup will feature widespread unseasonable warmth throughout the country, a pattern consistent with a strong El Niño. The greatest odds of above-normal temperatures exist around the Upper Midwest and the Deep South. Some models suggest temperatures could run 5 to 10 degrees Fahrenheit above normal for the latter half of September.
The blast of unseasonably warm air comes after the hottest summer in US history in a year in which tens of thousands of heat records have fallen across the US. That includes nearly 44,000 record daytime highs and more than 53,000 record-high overnight minimum temperatures recorded at weather stations across the country. Thousands more monthly and all-time heat records have fallen since the start of 2026. Over the same period of time, only about 21,500 low-temperature records fell, or around one cold record for every four heat records.
Many of the busted records date back more than a century. Salt Lake City hit 109 degrees Fahrenheit on July 12, for example, marking its hottest-ever temperature since records began in 1874. Washington, DC, tied its all-time warmest overnight low of 84 degrees Fahrenheit on July 3, where daily observations date back to 1871.
The heat hasn’t relented, despite the calendar turning to September. Even areas that typically escape countrywide heat waves have suffered. Much of Southern California endured excessive heat warnings during the second week of September as hot conditions and soupy air made Rodeo Drive feel more like Bourbon Street.
Why Has Fall Started So Hot?
Climate change is far and away the primary driver of the extreme heat baking the US. Rising average temperatures raise the baseline for extreme heat, making very hot days even steamier now than they would’ve been just a few decades ago.
That trend has been especially notable at night: Many communities across the country have also seen a precipitous increase in overnight temperatures during the warm months as both temperatures and mugginess increase. The lack of relief is what makes heat waves particularly deadly; without beneficial overnight cooling, heat stress becomes too much for many people to withstand.
A warmer climate is also altering upper-level patterns in a way that’s more favorable to extreme heat events. Strong centers of high pressure aloft force air to sink toward the ground. This air heats up as it compresses, combining with intense sunshine and dry soils to ratchet the heat well above normal. These ridges, often called heat domes, are more common in a warming world.
When Will the Heat End?
While overall highs for the remainder of September won’t be as extreme as they are in July, many areas will continue to endure summer-like heat.
El Niño is also lurking in the background. This pattern of warmer-than-normal waters in the Pacific Ocean affects weather patterns around the world.
We typically feel El Niño’s greatest effects during the cold months as these abnormally warm ocean temperatures alter the jet stream, which are responsible for weather patterns during the autumn and winter months.
This year’s El Niño is shaping up to be a record-setting event. Each El Niño is different, but the patterns during previous strong El Niños suggest that a vast swath of the US is in for overall warmer-than-normal temperatures through the fall and winter. In other words, we’re likely not done breaking heat records yet this year.

For years, Microsoft and OpenAI have fought to keep certain information out of the public eye in their fight with news organizations that have accused the AI firms of teaming up to violate copyright laws by stealing tons of news content to train AI.
However, now the details that should never have been marked confidential are starting to leak. In a motion for summary judgment that was unsealed Thursday from news plaintiffs led by The New York Times, internal documents are exposed that news groups alleged show exactly how Microsoft and OpenAI viewed the threat to news before unleashing new AI products like ChatGPT and Copilot.
Perhaps most explosively, Microsoft Director of Applied Science Brent Hecht repeatedly warned in documents that scraping news for AI training was “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions,” calling it perhaps the “largest theft of labor in human history,” news orgs said. In another document, Hecht contradicted Microsoft and OpenAI’s argument that training AI on news content is fair use, suggesting that the plan to widely scrape news made “a complete mockery of the idea of ‘fair use.’”
Over at OpenAI, ChatGPT head Nick Turley wrote in an internal message that publishers would face an “existential threat” from commercial products trained on news content that can be used to substitute news providers. One Microsoft document even described a “doom loop,” news orgs said, “that will hurt the performance of our models and the entire web at the same time.”
“It is highly unusual that an end-product threatens the economic foundations of its essential suppliers, but that is the situation we have created for our LLM business with respect to its ‘content supply chain,’” that document said.
Data from both firms shows that this prediction was accurate. Microsoft recorded 83–93 percent drops in click-through rates for some news plaintiffs, and 51–94 percent drops for others. Add to that reporting on low click-through rates from ChatGPT search results and news organizations’ own reporting on traffic declines. Suddenly, it becomes easier to see how declining news revenue could ultimately rob chatbots of the abundant streams of reliable information that supposedly makes them such groundbreaking tools.
Meanwhile, “almost no one intended for content they created to be used in this fashion, nor are they compensated for its use,” Hecht acknowledged in a Microsoft document.
News organizations say they’re ready to go to trial because there’s so much “compelling evidence of substitution.” If they can prove that chatbots are replacing them in their own markets, while serving to spit out excerpts of articles verbatim, they think that one-two punch may eviscerate Microsoft and OpenAI’s fair use arguments.
“The future not just of journalism but of responsible AI too depends on preserving incentives for humans to produce the creative works on which a healthy society depends,” news groups argued.
Chatbots are “largely substitutive, period”
Under oath, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella testified that AI companies shouldn’t be violating news sites’ terms of use by dodging paywalls. But over at OpenAI, internal messages showed that when a staffer, Nick Ryder, informed President Greg Brockman that “a hack” was found for OpenAI crawlers “to get around” the NYT paywall, Brockman replied, “Ah, nice.”
Nadella also acknowledged that chatbots have served as substitutes for news platforms, describing the chatbot as stealing clicks from news sites by “giving you the information right there on the website on the AI platform versus needing to go to the underlying source.”
There’s consensus on that at OpenAI, where a software engineer said in an internal message that “no matter how prominently we show the links, users won’t click.”
OpenAI’s Turley agreed that there is “no good reason to click” when the chatbot provides information, the motion said. He also seemingly suggested that the doom loop was already in motion, describing chatbots as “largely substitutive, period” and predicting that they “will get more and more substitutive as they get better.”
News groups argued that insiders’ own statements should be damning.
“With respect to outputs that are substantially similar to training or grounding sources, courts have rejected claims that copying news articles to provide a product that substitutes for demand for news is fair use,” news groups argued.
Microsoft disclaims exec’s comments
News groups tried many different tactics to test if Microsoft and OpenAI products would output their news articles verbatim. Their motion shows they went further than early strategies where they would ask chatbots to provide access to entire news stories by repeatedly asking “what’s the next line?”
In some cases, news organizations found that chatbots would generate long excerpts of articles when users requested summaries of articles. Other flagged outputs were generated by asking for key bullet points of articles. Particularly successful were prompts requesting that chatbots “rate the bias” of news articles. Chatbots also reproduced portions of articles if users asked them to pick any article off a certain site’s homepage.
In their motion, news plaintiffs have only asked the court to rule on infringed articles where outputs “demonstrate extensive verbatim overlap,” because they’re confident that the “substitutive purposes of defendants’ copying weigh against fair use.” Legal concerns with other articles will be raised at trial, they said.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to Ars’ request to comment.
However, a Microsoft spokesperson defended Microsoft’s AI products as a transformative fair use that don’t substitute for news sites. The spokesperson said that Nadella’s testimony touched on “broad principles and changes underway in how people find and consume information,” which were merely “observations” that “should not be confused with conclusions about copyright questions before the Court, which Microsoft addresses in its filings.”
Regarding Hecht’s comments, the spokesperson claimed that those documents only “reflect one employee’s individual perspective, are not a legal analysis, and do not represent the company’s views.”
Steven Lieberman, counsel for the New York Daily News and seven of its sister papers, disagrees. He told Ars that “the evidence revealed here for the first time shows that OpenAI and Microsoft knew that what they were doing was wrong.”
“Throughout this case Defendants insisted that these documents be treated as confidential so that the public could not see them,” Lieberman said. “Well, now the cat is out of the bag. Finally, the world can see what OpenAI and Microsoft thought all along about the fairness of their own behavior.”
Microsoft exec described “accidental cover up”
News plaintiffs have argued that regardless of the individual expressing the views, the internal documents make clear that firms anticipated that verbatim outputs would harm news sites. Further, they alleged that instead of preventing the outputs, the firms tried to make it harder for news groups to test chatbots by creating a filter that Hecht suggested could be perceived as an “accidental cover up” because it would result in “people who have a right over the content having less visibility into what was used for training.”
News groups are also upset that instead of listening to insiders warning that scraping news was theft, Microsoft and OpenAI never chose to license content, allegedly usurping them in another market in ways they couldn’t anticipate.
Specifically, their motion accused Microsoft of violating “industry norms” by selling a dataset purchased for Bing as training data for OpenAI, allegedly doing so without consulting news groups that would not have approved of that repurposing of their consent to basic search engine crawling. Further, OpenAI allegedly “acted improperly” by obtaining a NYT dataset with 1.8 million articles from a third party that was bound to an agreement that the data wouldn’t be used for commercial purposes. OpenAI’s employees knew it “would not be appropriate” to use that data “to train a model,” but they did it anyway, news groups alleged.
For news groups, the problem isn’t just Microsoft and OpenAI, but all the AI firms that are following their lead in “free-riding” on their content, the motion said. Most notably, after ChatGPT’s launch, Google’s AI Overviews was quickly introduced and started absorbing even more traffic that previously went to news sites.
If courts don’t clarify that AI firms must license news content, both news publishers and AI firms could be doomed, news plaintiffs argued. One Microsoft internal document agreed that “there is a ‘real risk’ that GenAI could ‘significantly disrupt’” the “employment of the very people who generated the data on which the foundation model was trained,” they noted. Microsoft even included a cartoon illustrating the problem of LLMs destroying their own supply chains, they said:
“AI companies remain powerless to break out of this ‘doom loop,’ because, while the industry as a whole would benefit if every company paid to sustain the continued production of the creative works their technology depends on, each individual company is better off taking content for free while others pay,” news groups argued.
As evidence of this blind greed, their motion emphasized that Brockman wrote that he was “deeply motivated by the gazillions” that could be gained by commercializing OpenAI’s technology.
“Finding that copying news for AI is not fair use would solve this prisoners’ dilemma by putting all AI companies, OpenAI and Microsoft included, on an even footing,” news organizations said.
This story was updated with a quote from New York Daily News counsel Steven Lieberman.
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

Brighton and Hove Albion started its Premier League match against Arsenal wearing a kit different than its conventional home jersey of blue-and-white stripes.
While several fans were left confused about the reason, the club later revealed that the blue jersey was a special edition kit to celebrate its 125-year anniversary.
“As the teams take to the field, supporters will welcome the players with individual flags located on every home seat, a blue-and-white tifo mosaic in the East Stand, an expanded pyrotechnics display, and a special 125 centre-circle flag,” read the team’s statement about the matchday plans.
“To mark the occasion, players will wear the commemorative 125 anniversary kit comprising a classic blue shirt and cream shorts modelled on the original 1901 strip, which will be the only time the kit is worn in competitive action. The match will also feature specially designed white corner flags bearing the 125 anniversary crest.”
“At half-time, the stadium will host exclusive pitch-side content and legend interviews featuring Bobby Zamora and Jack Hinshelwood, as well as a feature with chairman Tony Bloom,” the club added.
Brighton and Hove Albion is coming into the match after beating Manchester United 3-2 in the League Cup and is currently fifth in the Premier League standings.

Imagine walking into a neighbourhood medical store with a prescription in hand. The pharmacist checks the medicine, packs it and hands it over. But what happens when there is no prescription? According to a nationwide survey, for a large number of consumers, the answer is that the medicine may still be sold. The finding comes as the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has proposed installing CCTV cameras at medical stores to make prescription-medicine sales traceable.
The survey, conducted by LocalCircles, saw about 1.06 lakh responses from consumers across 327 districts of India. Of the total respondents, 63% were men and 37% women. Besides, 52% of them were from tier-1 districts, 29% from tier-2 districts and 29% from tier-3, 4 and 5 districts.
The survey found that 64% of consumers said their chemist never or rarely asked for a doctor’s prescription before selling medicines in the past 12 months. Only 15% said their chemist mostly or always refused to sell medicines without a prescription. The survey also found that only 31% of consumers were able to get assistance from a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always, while 13% said they were assisted by someone who was not a qualified pharmacist.
The findings come as the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has floated a draft notification proposing mandatory CCTV surveillance at every medical store that dispenses drugs sold on a doctor’s prescription. Under the proposal, the supply, other than by wholesale, of any drug sold on the prescription of a Registered Medical Practitioner would have to take place under a CCTV surveillance system installed and maintained at the premises.
The proposal also comes against the backdrop of intensified enforcement in multiple States against chemists selling prescription medicines without valid prescriptions, operating without registered pharmacists and failing to provide proper bills.
Neighbourhood chemist remains the main source
The survey found that the neighbourhood chemist remains the primary source of medicines for most consumers. The question on how respondents had primarily purchased medicines in the previous 12 months received 16,822 responses. This revealed that 86% of the respondents primarily depended on local chemists, followed by 14% on ePharmacy apps.
Who is actually behind the counter?
The survey then looked at whether consumers were receiving assistance from qualified pharmacists when they needed help with medicine or disease-related queries. The question received 19,409 responses. 31% of the consumers said they were able to get assistance from a qualified pharmacist most of the time or always. 27% of them said they never or very rarely received such assistance.
Home delivery is not free of the prescription gap
The survey also examined prescription checks when medicines were delivered to consumers’ homes. The question received 15,473 responses. 41% of consumers surveyed said a prescription was never or rarely asked for during home delivery.
A missing bill can mean a missing trail
Consumers were also asked whether they received proper bills when buying medicines from local chemists. Of the 20,573 respondents, 26% said they were not provided a GST bill. “A bill is not merely a tax document. It carries the batch number, expiry date and identity of the seller and provides a record if a medicine turns out to be expired, defective or counterfeit,” it said.
The survey also sought to establish whether consumers had purchased medicines that later turned out to be counterfeit or ineffective. The question received 18,457 responses. 15% of consumers said they had bought medicines that were later found to be fake or counterfeit.

HEIBAN DISTRICT, Sudan — For more than a decade, medical missionary Tom Catena has run the largest hospital in the Nuba Mountains, a rugged territory the size of Austria, most recently in the midst of a brutal civil war.
There is no oncologist on staff at Mother of Mercy, but as the war destroys much of the country’s health care system, patients like Fatouma Mahdi Ahmed Saeed, who has cervical cancer, keep turning up at his door.
Diagnosed last year by a private doctor in her home city of Nyala, the capital of South Darfur, Saeed had no choice but to make a dangerous trip of hundreds of miles to Catena’s hospital in central Sudan.
“I was in a lot of pain and desperate to get treatment,” she said. “The journey was very difficult, but I was not scared. I kept going. I know my day will come when God decides.”
Sudan’s civil war began in 2023, as two rival factions clashed for control of the nation’s military.
Some 13 million people have been forced to flee their homes in Sudan, according to the United Nations, in what is currently the world’s largest displacement crisis. Both sides have been accused of indiscriminately targeting hospitals and health clinics, with 205 attacks on health care facilities since the start of the war, according to the U.N. International aid cuts have added to these challenges, “forcing the collapse of an already fragile health care system,” Doctors Without Borders said in a statement this month.
As a result, it’s now difficult for people with cancer and other long-term illnesses to receive treatment that was once readily available. “They’re indirect casualties of war,” said Catena of the cancer patients recovering alongside wounded civilians in his crowded wards. He originally trained in family medicine, and is now the only permanent surgeon in the Nuba Mountains.
“If there was peace, they would have gotten treated in Khartoum, Darfur, or El Obeid. Now those hospitals are gone,” Catena added.
There are no recent numbers available for cancer deaths in Sudan, but the situation is not unlike the challenges faced by patients with long-term illnesses living through other wars. “Take any conflict in the world — Gaza, Ukraine — all those sick people are still there,” Catena said.
Before the war, Nyala had good hospitals, facilities where Saeed could have been diagnosed and treated, but many have been destroyed or badly damaged in the fighting. Even with the support of international health charities such as Doctors Without Borders, essential services have been slow to return.
When STAT visited Mother of Mercy hospital earlier this year, Catena and his staff had administered some 15 doses of chemotherapy in a single day to patients with nowhere else to go.
Saeed said she had to sell one of her calves and seek help from her family to pay the private doctor for her cancer diagnosis.
She first travelled from Darfur to the neighboring country of South Sudan in search of care last year, avoiding strikes from drones that buzzed like bees overhead. Her sister and son accompanied her, subsisting only on flour cooked into simple meals. Sometimes, they were stopped at checkpoints manned by menacing soldiers. When Saeed became tired, she lay down in the dirt to rest.
Turned away, the family traveled on to the Nuba Mountains, where Catena treated her at Mother of Mercy. Receiving any care at all makes Saeed one of the fortunate ones.
When STAT spoke with her, she had come back to the hospital for a follow-up appointment, making the trip through war-torn Sudan a second time. Afterward, she went home to Darfur, only to return again to the hospital, where she is currently undergoing another round of chemotherapy. Catena does not know if he will be able to cure her.
The World Health Organization WHO reports that some 37% of Sudan’s health care centers have been destroyed by fighting, while attacks on civilian doctors, clinics, and ambulances are frequent. African countries already face a particularly high cancer burden. The WHO recorded 560,000 deaths from cancer across the continent in 2022.
According to a paper published in 2025 in the American medical journal Global Oncology, Sudan was once a regional leader in cancer care. But now, chemotherapy medication and other essential drugs are hard to come by, and normal supply chains have been disrupted by conflict.
Without an oncologist on staff and lacking the equipment needed to review biopsies, Mother of Mercy must send tissue samples to the United States, and it can take as long as six months to receive an answer. As a result, Catena must often make diagnoses based on a clinical exam, looking for cancers already evident. He estimated that the nearest hospital capable of delivering cancer care is in Port Sudan, some 700 miles away, across an active frontline.
Last year, one of the warring factions, the Rapid Support Forces, announced an alliance with the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, the rebel group that controls the Nuba Mountains. Now, these once-secluded hills have become a staging ground for RSF militants as they attempt to fight their way back to Khartoum, the nation’s capital, which is held by the rival Sudanese Armed Forces.
By the time people reach Catena, their cancers are often far advanced.
Ifrah Ahmed, who suffers from osteosarcoma, a type of bone cancer, is 10 years old. Just as Saeed could not get proper care in Darfur, Ahmed had no choice but to leave her hometown of Babanusa, in West Kordofan, where the health care system has broken down.
Friends and neighbors told her family about Mother of Mercy, so Ahmed made the journey by rickshaw with her grandmother, pain spreading through her right leg. When she arrived, it had to be amputated at the hip. Catena also administered two doses of chemo to the girl.
With tight curls and a bright pink shirt, Ahmed smiled shyly. “I wish to be healthy and with my mom in a safe place,” she said.
Ahmed has since returned home, but Catena said that osteosarcoma has a high chance of spreading to the lungs, and she must return for a check-up before the end of the year. Fighting is fierce, making travel difficult.
There are others whom Catena can’t save.
Abasst Abonja and his family came from South Sudan, another sign of how far resources are stretched in this region.
The 76-year-old spent two weeks in the hospital, unable to eat for his last four days. Skeletal and weak, he died the day STAT visited.
At his bedside, his wife wept. “What have you done to deserve such a death?” she asked.
Reporting for this story was supported by The Pulitzer Center.

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

A nine-second long video clip is has gone viral on social media, showing a man assaulting a puffed rice vendor. In the video, the man is seen overturning the box hanging from the snack seller’s neck and pouring all the food items onto the vendor’s face before they scatter onto the street. As this purported attack unfolds, the vendor stares at the man helplessly.
The video was posted by X user Alka Maurya on September 16 and has garnered more than 2,85,000 views and shared over 1,500 times till publication time. The caption of the post, translated from Hindi, reads: “(He) must be feeling so proud after doing something like this.” (Archive)
कितना गर्व महसूस कर रहा होगा ऐसे करके हैं ना …… pic.twitter.com/F6upi4I2ZD
— Alka Maurya (@MauryaAlka76391) September 16, 2026
Apart from Maurya, film actor Kamaal R Khan posted the same video with the caption: “How will you fix this mentality which has developed in last 10 years. India can’t be fixed now.” (Archive)
How will you fix this mentality which has developed in last 10 years. India can’t be fixed now. pic.twitter.com/o2T2AJzGoj
— KRK (@kamaalrkhan) September 17, 2026
Other social media users circulated the viral clip with similar captions, condemning the man seen purportedly attacking the vendor.
As a billboard visible in the video reads ‘Welcome to Patna Junction’, the Patna police was tagged in the comment section of certain posts, requesting them to take stringent action against the man who allegedly assaulted the vendor.
Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the viral video clip, we ran reverse image search on several relevant keyframes. It led us to a video posted by content creator Sonu Paswan on Instagram. With 1,79,000 followers, he posts scripted videos highlighting the helpless condition of the working class people in India. Paswan has a social media presence on Facebook and YouTube as well. And according to his social media bios, he is from Darbhanga, Bihar.
In all of his videos, accessible on his Facebook page, Paswan himself can be seen playing different “poor characters” being harassed and attacked by others as he helplessly accepts his fate.
On September 18, Friday, Paswan posted a video on his Instagram page, where he clarified that he enacts emotional scenes on poverty as ‘content’ on his social media platforms. He clarifies that the viral clip does not depict a real attack on him, but is in fact a prepared skit. “I want to tell you that in the video you are seeing, the vendor is me and the man who is attacking me is part of my team. I want to let you know that we, as a team, make emotional videos on poverty. I request you to take this video purely as entertainment, and not believe that this is real,” he said.
The caption of this video reads, translated from Hindi, “Because we make emotional videos on the poor…You all give me so much love…but you guys have taken this clip to heart.
I know I have hurt you guys with this video. Please delete the video from your channel…I request you not to share this video any further.”
View this post on Instagram
After the clip started going viral and attracted significant backlash, on September 17, most of his videos on YouTube and all of his previous videos on Instagram had to be deleted. In the aforementioned video, Paswan urges audiences to not share the viral clip and excerbate his situation even further. “I request you to not share the clip on your personal profiles, please do this much for your brothers,” he said. He shared the same clarification on his YouTube page.
Moreover, Paswan posted videos of the guy who is acting as the attacker in the video, also clarifying the viral clip is indeed a skit, on his Instagram and YouTube pages. “The video you guys are watching and getting emotional and taking to heart is just our content…its not real…please stop roasting this video. Because of you [sharing the viral clip as real] all my efforts have gone to waste, all my videos, over 300 videos…I have had to delete them all. I request you to keep supporting and loving us,” he states in the video.
View this post on Instagram
Given that their skit went viral, misleadingly as a real incident, the content creators said they received backlash and trolling, compelling them to remove their previous videos. At present, Paswan’s Instagram page only features the two clarification videos and his YouTube page features the same. However, his Facebook still displayed his earlier content. The description of his Facebook page, translated from Hindi, also reads: “I make emotional videos on poverty.”
True to the description, Paswan’s Facebook page contains videos similar in theme to the viral video. In these videos, visibly destitute people or poor vendors are seen being humiliated or suffering at the hands of others, while accepting their fate.
Paswan can be identified acting in all of these videos, and a visual match can be established, indicating that he was indeed the person seen in the viral video. Thus, it can be concluded that a scripted video made by a content creator has gone viral, leading netizens to falsely believe that it depicts a real incident of attack on a puffed rice vendor.

South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, has said he will not deploy the military to the Middle East in a way that could draw the country into conflict, resisting calls from Donald Trump to support his war in Iran.
“There won’t be deployment that would involve or enter war. I can tell you that very clearly,” Lee said at a news conference on Friday. “We won’t deploy military assets in any form to that end.”
However, Lee added that he was reviewing whether to play a greater role in safeguarding navigation in the region. South Korea maintains a naval presence off the coast of Somalia as part of an anti-piracy mission.
“[It] is also clear that we must do the minimum as other countries do to protect our commercial shipping and crude shipments, and also the safety of our people,” he said.
Trump has criticised Seoul for what he called insufficient support for the Iran war and scaled back major joint military drills by the two countries’ armed forces this summer, a move that unsettled the US ally.
South Korea’s government has been reviewing a possible military deployment to the Strait of Hormuz, although the idea is proving unpopular domestically.
Asked about progress in reaching an agreement with the US on Seoul’s US investment commitments under its trade deal with Washington, Lee said concern over the commercial viability of the package was the main sticking point.
Lee said there were elements that were difficult for Seoul to accept, but that the two sides were nearing an agreement.
South Korea committed last year to invest $350bn in US manufacturing in return for Washington lowering tariffs on Korean imports to 15%.
Seoul this week postponed a parliamentary briefing on the investment plans, which is expected to take place next week instead.
The South Korean president also said it was possible that a meeting could take place in the coming months between Trump and the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, but many factors needed to align for that to happen.
“What’s clear is that President Trump wants talks, and I want him to as well, and we’re continuing coordination to make dialogue between the North and the US possible,” he said.
North Korean state media has so far remained largely silent on the repeated calls from Trump for such a meeting. Trump has been pushing aides for a meeting with Kim as soon as the autumn, the Wall Street Journal has reported.

Tailgate parties, marching bands... and Ted Lasso? Wembley hosts US college game
- Published
The NFL has been playing in London since 2007 but now a different kind of American football is coming to the capital of England.
American college football games were being played abroad long before the NFL headed overseas, in countries as diverse as Cuba, Japan and Tanzania.
But this Saturday the UK will host just its second college football game, and it will be a far bigger event than the first at Crystal Palace in 1988.
About 2,500 fans were there that day, whereas 60,000 will be at Wembley to watch the Kansas Jayhawks face the Arizona State Sun Devils (17:00 BST).
The inaugural Union Jack Classic (UJC) will feature marching bands, spirit squads and tailgate parties outside the stadium - and Ted Lasso actor Jason Sudeikis might be there too.
Why bring a college game to London?
The UJC chief executive is entrepreneur Brian Dubiski. He and a business partner both played college football, with the latter then working with the NFL in London.
And while chatting over a few beers, they asked themselves why no-one had taken college football back to England, especially since Wembley's first NFL game in 2007.
After mulling the idea over for a few years, they decided to do it themselves and managed to book a date at English football's national stadium.
Then they had to find the teams. Brett Yormark, commissioner of the Big 12 Conference, is "bullish" about building its global appeal and was keen to be involved.
So two Big 12 teams committed to the trip. Founded in 1890, the University of Kansas (KU) has one of the oldest college teams and wants to expand its brand, while the game coincides with Arizona State (ASU) opening a London campus this month.
Before this trip, most of their players did not own a passport so both teams also wanted to give them a cultural experience they will never forget.
- What is the Union Jack Classic and who is in it? 
  - Published16 hours ago
What makes college football different?
Virtually all NFL players come via the US college system, and in many parts of America, college football is more popular than the NFL.
College games often have bigger crowds - eight of the world's 10 biggest stadiums are for college football, all holding more than 100,000.
The fans are also more passionate as support is often passed down from one generation to another, and multiple generations attend the same school. Kansas player Calvin Clements, for example, is a fifth-generation Jayhawk.
Actor Paul Rudd is also a Jayhawk, while lifelong fan Jason Sudeikis grew up in Kansas and frequently weaves KU references into his work.
"They're very spirited, and you get the tribalism, so it's the closest thing we have to European football fanbases," Dubiski told BBC Sport.
Both the NFL and college football have tailgate parties, where fans gather in the car park and eat and drink for hours before the game.
But college football fans chant during games, which feature marching bands and spirit squads - made up of cheerleaders, dancers and mascots.
"We want the game to showcase what we think is one of the greatest sports in America," said Yormark.
"There's something special about college football - the pageantry, the traditions, the fandom. It's dynamic - there's a lot of energy and passion. It truly is an experience."
Who has bought tickets?
According to the NFL, 14 million people in the UK identify as fans of America's biggest sports league.
UJC organisers have tried to tap into that fanbase and the UK infrastructure the NFL has built, but also appeal to younger fans.
It formed partnerships with the British American Football Association (Bafa), British Universities and Colleges Sport (BUCS), and the Jacksonville Jaguars, who host an annual NFL game at Wembley.
About 60,000 tickets have been sold and 15,000 fans are travelling from the US, with student sections to help create the typical college gameday atmosphere.
"We're really pleased with that in year one," said Dubiski. "We never expected to sell the stadium out, and 60,000 is higher than the average Big 12 attendance."
Dubiski agreed an exclusive multi-year deal with Wembley and is already working on games in the next three years. He might expand to other European cities and bring basketball games too.
Why college football could rival NFL
Yormark believes a positive experience for fans and players would constitute success, plus an exciting game.
Former NFL quarterback Robert Griffin III, now a college football analyst with Fox Sports, agrees that "we've got to bring excitement".
"The way to encourage fandom is to create moments, so I'm happy the two teams coming over know how to score points - and score them in bunches," he said.
Griffin also believes college football could ultimately be more successful overseas than the NFL.
"The fandom around college football is better, it just is," he added. "It's more similar to world football so there's a better opportunity to connect, also because there's more teams. In the NFL there's 32, but in college football there's 400 you can fall in love with.
"And if you want to be a real NFL fan, you have to be a college football fan because that's the feeder system into the league and you get to watch these guys develop."
What's happening on gameday?
Griffin will be at Wembley as part of Fox's team for their flagship pre-game show, which has gone overseas for the first time, with coverage starting two hours before kick-off.
"They'll be set up right outside Wembley," said Dubiski. "They get the crowd worked up into a frenzy, so it's loud, it's boisterous and a lot of fun.
"We've focused on picking up the tailgating experience and Americana of a college gameday in the States and planting it in London."
The main tailgate party begins at 10:00 - seven hours before kick-off - serving authentic Kansas barbecue food, and there will be cheerleaders and marching bands on Wembley Way.
Inside the stadium, there is a pre-game music line-up and half-time show, and organsiers hope Sudeikis is among the crowd. He and some British actors have been invited, although it is not confirmed who will attend.

The Delhi High Court on Wednesday (September 16, 2026) asked the Centre to respond on whether it was contemplating formulating a policy to regulate addiction-causing design features on social media platforms like infinite scroll and autoplay.
A bench of Justice Nitin Wasudeo Sambre and Justice Amit Sharma said it would hear a PIL seeking the constitution of an expert committee to examine engagement-maximising and addiction-causing design features on social media platforms after three weeks. It asked Additional Solicitor General Chetan Sharma to take instructions on the issue.
Mr. Sharma said that it would be in the domain of the policymakers to consider some of the issues raised in the plea and suggested that the petitioner could submit a representation to the government.
The counsel for the Centre and certain social media platforms also took objection to the maintainability of the petition in view of some orders from the Supreme Court and high courts which refused to entertain petitions on a similar issue.
Addictive architecture
Petitioner Vikas Kathuria, a professor of law, said the fulcrum of the issue is not what content social media platforms carry, but how such platforms are architecturally designed to cause addiction through infinite scroll, autoplay, algorithmically curated and personalised feeds, notification systems, and variable-reward engagement metrics, such as “likes”, to capture, retain and repeatedly re-stimulate the attention of the user.
The plea said the concern assumes significance in the Indian context as statistics reveal that Indian youths aged 18-24 spend more than an average of 120 minutes daily on social media.
It has been clinically proven that long hours on social media are linked to suicide and depression among adolescents, the petition said.
The plea sought the court’s direction to the Central Government and the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights to restrict, prohibit, or regulate the use of these features.

Marking a significant boost to India’s domestic aerospace manufacturing, state-run Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) on Friday handed over a new fleet of advanced indigenous aircraft to the Indian Air Force (IAF) and Pawan Hans Limited.
The handover ceremony was attended by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh and Civil Aviation Minister K Rammohan Naidu.
During the event, HAL delivered two LCA FOC Trainer aircraft to the IAF (completing the twin-seater deliveries under the FOC contract), three HTT-40 Basic Trainer aircraft, marking the start of deliveries under a 70-aircraft contract, and four Dhruv Next Generation (NG) helicopters to Pawan Hans Limited.
The handover, the Union Ministers said, marked an important milestone in the country's journey toward self-reliance, highlighting the role of HAL and its industry partners in strengthening the domestic aerospace ecosystem.
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said, “India is moving systematically towards Aatmanirbharta in defence, as the nation is manufacturing the state-of-the-art equipment indigenously ever since Prime Minister Narendra Modi-led Government began working with the core mantra of self-reliance.”
The platforms together represent HAL's capabilities across military aviation, civil rotary-wing aviation, and pilot training, it said in a statement.
HAL CMD Ravi K said that the handover of Tejas FOC Twin Seater Trainers, HTT 40 Basic Trainers and Dhruv NG helicopters demonstrates HAL's ability to develop and deliver platforms for diverse civil and defence requirements.
These platforms reflect the depth of capability that HAL has built over the years and the strength of the indigenous aerospace ecosystem that supports them, he said.
Speaking on the occasion, Civil Aviation Minister Naidu said that the certification and induction of the Dhruv NG into civil operations marked an important milestone for India's indigenous civil aviation ecosystem.
He termed it a reflection of the growing capability of the Indian industry to develop and support advanced aerospace platforms for commercial applications. Naidu said Prime Minister Narendra Modi has given a clear vision for Indians to travel in Made-in-India civilian aircraft.
“Very soon Indians will travel in Made-in-India civilian aircraft,” the minister quoted Modi as saying.
Here's all we know about these indigenous aircraft:
According to a statement shared by HAL, the LCA Tejas FOC Twin-Seater Trainer is a lightweight, all-weather, multi-role 4.5-generation aircraft designed primarily to support the training requirements of the IAF, while retaining the capability to undertake fighter operations when required.
It incorporates contemporary technologies, including relaxed static stability, a quadruplex fly-by-wire flight-control system, carefree manoeuvring, an advanced glass cockpit, integrated digital avionics and advanced composite materials for the airframe.
“These technologies have enabled India to develop and operationalise an advanced twin-seat fighter aircraft capability,” it said.
The HTT-40 (Hindustan Turbo Trainer-40) is an indigenously designed and developed Basic Trainer Aircraft intended to meet the primary training requirements of the Indian Defence Services.
Designed by HAL's Aircraft Research and Design Centre (ARDC), the aircraft is built around a proven turboprop engine and is designed to provide good low-speed handling characteristics and effective training for trainee pilots.
The HTT-40 incorporates a modern cockpit and avionics suite and is capable of performing a range of basic training and flying roles, aerobatics, general handling, instrument flying, navigation, night flying and close formation flying, it added.
Dhruv Next Generation is a HAL-designed and manufactured 5.5-tonne, light twin-engine, multi-role helicopter, officials said.
The Dhruv NG platform has been developed to address demanding operating conditions in India and has been upgraded to meet the requirements of the global civil aviation market, it said.
Its features include a civil-certified glass cockpit, a modern avionics suite, advanced navigation systems and enhanced situational awareness. Safety features include crashworthy seats, self-sealing fuel tanks, and a twin-engine configuration that provides redundancy.

The man who would be king - the rise and fall of 'the next Prince Naseem'
- Published
Boxer Daniel Teasdale was hailed as the heir to the legendary Prince Naseem Hamed, but his promise never materialised into fame, fortune and films.
"He's better than Naz at the same age," said trainer Brendan Ingle.
Hamed had won his first world title aged 21. Teasdale was still a teenager.
Ingle, from his gym in Sheffield, moulded the careers of a conveyor belt of world-beaters and title winners. He guided both of the fighters from childhood.
Before super-middleweight Teasdale's first professional bout, the Rotherham fighter had been featured in national newspapers, books and was being documented by photographers and film-makers.
He won a succession of national titles, establishing himself as the next contender to emerge from the Ingle gym.
Photographer Simon Roberts travelled to the Ingle gym in 1997 hoping to photograph Hamed.
"Brendan said 'don't worry about Naz, start photographing that kid in the corner. He's going to be bigger than Naz'. That was Daniel," Roberts said.
Roberts began to follow the young sensation, hoping to capture his rise on camera.
Filmmaker Stuart Mitchell had a similar brief.
"We were selling the documentary as 'who's the next Prince Naseem?'," says Mitchell.
He recalls Teasdale being the subject of similar headlines in national newspapers, and later accompanying him to an event gathering together the best British prospects from every sport for the new Millennium.
Attention on Ingle's latest protégé was more than just hype.
"He was like Oscar de la Hoya," recalls former stablemate Amer Khan.
"Teasdale was exceptional as a junior, he was stopping everyone."
Teasdale learnt both ballet and gymnastics to develop his footwork and skills in the ring and was seemingly set for stardom.
"I was very teachable, could talk, had the looks and could box," says Teasdale, who took up the sport aged six.
The bitterness of Hamed's split from trainer Ingle in 1998 has been well-documented, with both sides seemingly losing.
"Brendan lost the focus with the up-and-comers," Teasdale says.
He followed Naz in leaving the gym, linking up with one of its greatest exports, three-time world title challenger Herol 'Bomber' Graham.
The exit was said to have been spearheaded by Teasdale's father who "essentially gave up his career" to help his son fulfil his potential, Roberts says.
It was funded by a businessman with no prior experience in boxing, but a thirst to be part of Teasdale's rise to the top.
Teasdale remembers Graham's influence as "a breath of fresh air", but the presence of others was less helpful.
"People started to try and feed off Daniel," says Roberts.
"I photographed [Mike] Tyson and Lennox [Lewis], I have seen all of this stuff before."
'Everybody wanted a piece'
Mitchell was also filming future Olympic bronze medallist Darren Sutherland when he arrived at the Ingle gym from Ireland.
"Daniel was probably more talented than Darren, the trouble with Daniel was he was always being wooed," reveals Mitchell.
Teasdale's tag as the next Prince Naseem also hung heavy.
"I was like catnip for cats, everybody wanted a piece," Teasdale explains.
While the career of some talented prospects is carefully nurtured, Teasdale may not have been as well protected.
"To some extent Daniel was used because he was seen as a big potential and was a good scalp for somebody who wanted to get through the ranks," Roberts says.
Different trainers, managers and promoters followed, but Teasdale admits instability harmed his progress.
His debut had been a disaster - abandoned due to rioting in the crowd - while the following year he received death threats before a bout.
Despite undeniable talent, those early misfortunes could now be seen as an omen of what was to come.
After filming Teasdale across five years, Mitchell shelved his documentary when commissioners lost interest.
He too lost faith after a training session in Graham's garage.
"It felt very small and I didn't think this was going anywhere," he says bluntly.
Many have since raised doubts over whether the "pretty boy" was made for a career getting punched in the face.
"Everybody has a weakness and mine was women," Teasdale confesses.
"I lost the edge and my focus wasn't where it should be."
He walked away from the sport in 2005 after he was stopped in the first round of a light-heavyweight contest - his first professional defeat.
He returned in 2010 and reunited with Ingle, winning his one and only comeback fight.
"After that I just gave it up, I thought 'I'm not going to be second best to the first me," says Teasdale, whose professional career ended after just five fights over a seven-year period.
"At 27 I should have been a world champion defending my title."
Roberts continued to photograph Teasdale.
"There were a lot of unfortunate circumstances with him which meant he didn't fulfil his potential," Roberts says.
"There was a lot of bad advice and a lot of people wanting something from him, and not necessarily for the good."
Mitchell did some "soul searching" over his role in Teasdale's journey.
"There was so much clamour around him - then it just evaporated," he recalls.
"That must be very difficult to deal with when expectations are that you are going to be a successful and famous boxer."
Teasdale says "everything went up in the air" as a professional, in contrast to the stability of his early years.
Bad management played a part in not fulfilling his potential, but he admits "living for other people's dreams and ambitions."
Still, there are no regrets about how his career turned out.
"It's made me who I am," says Teasdale, now enjoying an altogether different career as a support worker.
"I'm doing the job that I love, it's not the profile that I was but it's all about being stable in your life."

Bombay Shaving Company (BSC) founder Shantanu Deshpande said the company has revised its Switch4 advertisement in accordance with the undertaking given by the Delhi High Court (HC), while maintaining that the “facts and principles” behind the campaign remain unchanged. “Consumers deserve choice. Locking consumers in with a handle and then limiting choice on blades is an anti-market, anti-consumer business strategy … We stand by Switch4. We stand by innovation. And above all, we stand by the consumer’s right to choose,” Deshpande said in a post on LinkedIn. The comment comes a day after the Delhi HC directed the startup to remove the ad campaign at the centre of its ongoing product disparagement dispute with Gillette India. The court on Thursday recorded compliance by the startup. Gillette alleged that the advertisement disparaged its products, while the startup argued that it was a comparative advertising campaign and did not explicitly name Gillette. The court’s latest proceedings also saw Gillette object to a fresh BSC commercial, with its counsel calling the advertisement obscene and seeking intervention. The court declined to pass an order on the new commercial, saying the issue could be considered if it was formally challenged. BSC maintained that the fresh advertisement did not refer to Gillette or disparage its products. Gillette had also raised concerns over copies of the original advertisement continuing to circulate through social media accounts and influencers outside BSC’s control. The court allowed Gillette to approach the platforms directly for removal. The latest dispute is the second legal clash between BSC and Gillette over advertising. In 2024, Gillette challenged a BSC commercial for its Sensi Smart 3 razor that depicted a competitor’s razor catching fire. The matter was resolved through mediation in February 2026 after BSC withdrew the challenged advertisement. Gillette and BSC’s recent legal clash also comes on the heels of another D2C startup being taken to court by an incumbent over comparative advertising. Beco, a startup selling sustainable home care products, had run an advertising campaign titled “War on What’s Hidden” targeting Hindustan Unilever’s Surf Excel and Vim cleaning products. In the campaign, it claimed that certain ingredients in HUL’s products could lead to skin irritation and allergic reactions, and asked consumers to “Switch to BECO”. HUL challenged the ads in the Delhi High Court, alleging commercial disparagement, trademark infringement, and passing off. Ultimately, the court ruled in its favour, finding that Beco had not been able to establish its claims as factual and ordering the startup to take down all its related ads.

A newly signed United States sanctions law grants the administration authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on imports from the five largest buyers of Russian crude oil and natural gas within 30 days. Although India and China are major purchasers, the legislation does not name specific nations or define how top importers will be calculated. In response, India has maintained that national interest and energy security for its 1.4 billion citizens remain paramount through diversified energy sourcing. New Delhi highlighted the potential impact on bilateral ties and global energy markets, reiterating its commitment to taking all necessary measures to protect domestic economic interests.

Singer Pat Boone calls on his ‘very tired’ friend Donald Trump to ‘be quiet’ – and stop being rude to women
Boone urged Trump to skip press conferences and embrace a more polite, humorous approach similar to Ronald Reagan’s, which he said could lead to more coverage and support
Legendary singer-songwriter Pat Boone publicly urged his “friend,” President Donald Trump, to tone down his rhetoric Friday, telling him in a social media video to “try for just a little while to be quiet.”
The 92-year-old former teen idol turned conservative crooner addressed Trump, 80, directly in a video posted to Instagram and Facebook.
“Hello Mr. President, Pat Boone here,” Boone said. “Been a while since I spoke to you or about you, but really I feel like I am your friend.”
Boone referenced his past support for Trump, saying, “I voted for you back when you were running for president, and you were calling people names in the debates.”
Boone met Trump at a fundraiser at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate while Trump was hosting “The Apprentice,” the Daily Best reports. The two have remained friends with Boone speaking publicly about their conversations over the years, including a 2016 phone call during Trump’s presidential campaign when Boone urged him to stop “calling names” and act more presidential, according to the Jerusalem Post.
“I cautioned you that you should not be doing something that makes you sound like a schoolboy on the playground, but if you want to be president you should sound like a president and be presidential,” Boone referenced his previous advice in Friday’s video,
“You did not take my advice much at the time, but you have done a lot of things in the meanwhile, however, right now I feel like you are very tired,” he continued. “And I'm worried that many of us haven't prayed enough for you because I feel like you are wearing out and you are feeling the pressure and expressing yourself in ways that are not becoming to you. They are not presidential.”
Boone then suggested that Trump stop publicly discussing his accomplishments and avoid attacking others.
“So, may I recommend something to you?” he said. “That you be quiet. That you quit talking about the things that want people to be proud of. Let them discover those things for themselves, and also please be polite to women and quit calling names.”
Trump has repeatedly insulted female reporters who ask him challenging questions about his administration’s policies, including telling one “quiet, piggy.”
Boone also suggested that the press refrain from covering Trump for several days.
“Don't even come to a press conference,” he said. “Of course, you are not wanting many of them to be there anyway. So, let it be empty. Let there be nobody to ask you any questions. Nobody to hear what you want to say or possibly brag about. And then as you hear nothing, the deafening roar of silence, it may convince you that being like Ronald Reagan and using a sense of humor as well as being very polite and respectful will get you more hearers, better reporting, more support while there is still time.”
Boone ended his message by again emphasizing that he was speaking to Trump as a friend.
“I say this as a friend, try for just a little while to be quiet.”
The message came as Trump has continued his public clashes with news organizations and other critics. On Friday, Trump announced that CNN, MS NOW and Politico would be barred from the White House, accusing the outlets of reporting “FAKE NEWS.” Sure enough, on Saturday morning, journalists from all three organizations were blocked from entry.
Boone's comments also came during a week of heightened attention surrounding Trump's relationship with the media and the Kennedy Center, where Trump has been involved in a dispute over the future of the performing arts institution.
The Independent has contacted the White House for comment.
