In 2024, Donald Trump’s victory was powered in large part by massive gains with Latino voters. He won 48 percent of those voters that year, up from 36 percent in 2020 and 28 percent in 2016. But now, that support is plummeting; Trump’s approval rating among Latinos who voted for him recently fell from 93 percent to 66 percent, where it was at the beginning of his second term.
Why Trump’s Latino voters are fleeing him
The Latino backlash to Trump is a major bellwether.
Why? It has a lot to do, as with everything these days, with the economy.
It was the same in 2024. During that election, voters were experiencing rising costs and stagnant wages — the same trend that has continued until today. In 2024, though, Joe Biden and his administration — which also meant Vice President Kamala Harris — took the blame from all voters, and particularly Latinos. Today, the blame is falling on Trump.
America, Actually host Astead Herndon caught up with Stephanie Valencia, who co-founded Equis Research, a political research firm that specializes in Latino voters, to unpack some of these recent shifts and explain them.
“I think one important data point to understand about the Latino voter is Latinos make up more of the wage workforce than any other part or any other racial subgroup,” she said on the podcast. “And so what that means is when wages are down and inflation is high, Latinos feel it more.”
That’s why, when the economy is bad, this group is primed to be a “swinging giant” in US politics, Valencia explains — and right now, it appears to be swinging hard against Trump.
Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel.
Equis has called Latinos one of the last great wild cards in American politics. Is that because of some of the double-digit swings that we’ve seen among this voting group over the past few elections?
Yes, it absolutely has to do with that. Latinos often get given the title the “sleeping giant,” which I just want to get rid of from everybody’s vocabulary.
We should be called the “swinging giant” based on how much shift we have seen election to election. A third of Latinos consider themselves kind of independent or apolitical, and that swinging middle really is deciding every single election.
Your playbook gets into messengers and particularly how we reach folks where they are. It makes a Spanish-Spanglish distinction talking about the different types of media that Latino voters consume.
I wanted to ask, in that vein, what’s the single biggest mistake campaigns make in terms of not reaching folks where they are?
Oh man, how long do we have so I can tell you how many mistakes? They’re really simple unforced errors. I’m going to give a very concrete and simple example that I think illustrates that.
Look, I’m Latina. I grew up speaking mostly English, but I listen to Spanish-language radio. I watch a lot of YouTube, and on YouTube I’m watching people like Karol G and Carin León. A lot of people — a lot of Latino swing voters — have the same media consumption habits that I do.
The first problem or challenge that a lot of candidates make is they just simply translate their English ad into Spanish. And that is, to me, one of the biggest mistakes because there are a lot of things that people want to be communicating in Spanish that don’t translate word for word. There are sayings in Spanish that don’t translate directly from English or more direct ways you can communicate.
I’m sure it immediately reads Google Translate rather than an original message for said community.
Exactly. So that’s mistake No. 1. Mistake No. 2 is when they’re deploying that ad digitally, as a proxy for talking to people, they’re going to use Spanish-language browser settings. So they say, “We don’t want people who speak English to see the Spanish-language ad.”
So the way they find that set of voters is just by going to people who have Spanish-language browser settings.
Like I said, I don’t have a Spanish-language browser setting. Everything I consume online is set in English on Chrome, but I still watch a lot of content in Spanish on YouTube.
So you’re missing a voter like me who’s going to see a Spanish language ad from a James Talarico or a Manny Rutinel and be turned on by it because I’m going to say, “Hey, that candidate’s speaking to our community. That candidate has enough respect to develop a Spanish-language ad.”
We did some testing a couple of years ago that showed that over 70 percent of Latinos who see an ad in Spanish think that party or candidate cares more about Latinos. It matters that much.
Let’s stay in 2024 for a second longer. Your research found that Project 2025 and Trump’s mass deportation plans were not top of mind for most people, and that they were thinking about the economy. I wanted to ask about that because I remember the RNC signs at the convention saying, “Mass deportations now.” One number says that 62 percent of Latinos now think that Trump wants to deport undocumented immigrants broadly.
Why did it take till post-election to realize those threats of mass deportation were real considering they were so front and center during his campaign?
I think this is really important for us as avid news consumers to understand the kind of news that the average voter, and especially that voter who’s coming in and out of elections, is consuming.
What they were seeing on mainstream media, perhaps even Fox News at the time, was a focus on people or Trump surrogates who said he was going to focus on serious criminals, securing the border, and violent criminals.
And so that’s what people bought. Fast-forward to 2026; the people who feel most regretful who voted for Trump in 2024 are most regretful because of immigration. They feel like there was a broken promise there.
They were told he was going to focus on the border, which everybody agreed was chaos, and he was going to focus on violent criminals and serious threats, and at the end of the day, he has not complied with that.
And then add that to the litany of broken promises.
I’m hearing a distinction between a focus on the border, which Republicans did try to prioritize rather than the interior deportations that may have been more attributed to Stephen Miller than Donald Trump. But we have certainly seen that be a focus of the administration once they came back into office.
You mentioned the shift that has happened since 2024, and that’s really important, of course. Trump’s approval rating with Latinos is now worse than with non-Latinos, a stunning reversal in 18 months.
You mentioned the factors that have contributed there, but is this really just the economy?
It’s the economy, it’s the war, and it’s immigration. It’s those three things.
One thing that is really interesting to note about Trump’s approval, other than that it’s at basement levels — and he’s very much pulled down the GOP with him broadly and with Latino voters — is that in Trump 1.0, his approval on the economy and the cost of living was actually better than his everyday approval on his total job.
And he has been underwater with Latinos almost this entire term so far on the cost of living and the economy. It’s almost been a complete and total reversal.
Listen, you tell people you’re going to fix egg prices and gas is going to go down, and then you do the opposite, and we’re hearing that story universally across different electorate groups.
You’re saying that’s still the main story when it comes to Latinos also?
Yes, it’s still the main story. I think one important data point to understand about the Latino voter is Latinos make up more of the wage workforce than any other part or any other racial subgroup. What that means is when wages are down and inflation is high, Latinos feel it more.
We have less savings. We have lower rates of home ownership. So the safety nets that other people might have, we just don’t have.
That really has exacerbated the kind of impact that people are feeling right now as they’re trying to make ends meet.
You mentioned the exponential growth in the terms of people who now regret or are disappointed with their vote for Donald Trump. Does that mean a preference for Democrats? How should we think about the binary choice between D and R versus what is a clear story about a backlash to Donald Trump’s actions?
I think it is a huge mistake for Democrats to rest on their laurels and think that because of what people are feeling about Trump and Republicans and the sense of disappointment and promises broken that that is automatically going to translate for them as a party and as a brand.
Right now, the Democratic brand has suffered a repeated set of blows among Latino voters. Twenty years of comprehensive immigration reform hasn’t been delivered. It’s a thing that comes up in almost every focus group.
And part of what the build-up to 2024 was, was not only 20 years of a promise undelivered; it was the chaos at the border, it was feeling like Democrats were focused on everything but Latinos and their families, or everyday Americans and their families, and that they had lost that thread.

LeBron the star as Angola aims to cash in on E1 racing
- Published
It is difficult to imagine an electric powerboat racing series capturing the attention of an Angolan audience for whom football and basketball is king, but the presence of NBA royalty LeBron James certainly helped.
The 41-year-old was among the A-listers in Luanda as the E1 World Championship rolled into southern Africa for the first time at the weekend, having made its debut on the continent last year in Lagos, Nigeria.
"It's not a short trip, but he [LeBron] is here because he believes in what we're doing," E1 chief executive Jamie Copas told BBC Sport Africa in the Angolan capital.
"You can't underestimate the value of it. They [the celebrity owners] come with huge followings."
James, like fellow sport stars Rafa Nadal, Tom Brady, Didier Drogba and Virat Kohli and actor Will Smith, is an E1 team owner after buying into the series.
Similar to Formula E on land, it aims to blend sport with strong messaging around sustainability and green technology.
James said Angola had made his first trip to the country "super welcoming" after visiting the National Museum of Slavery.
"Obviously there is a lot of history here," the new signing for the Philadelphia 76ers told local media.
"A lot of history that not only is here in the country but also [crosses] over to America."
Angola's men are reigning African basketball champions, securing a record-extending 12th continental title on home soil last year, and unsurprisingly spectators of the E1 racing at the Clube Naval de Luanda clamoured for a glimpse of one of basketball's biggest icons.
Journalist Omar Prata, covering the race for the Jornal de Angola, admitted that E1 was not on his radar until Hollywood star Smith, whose Westbrook Racing team is sponsored by Visit Angola, announced in March that a deal had been agreed to race in Luanda for the next three years.
"I see the potential it could bring to project the city at a time when the government is trying to work on tourism," Prata said.
"And of course it means a lot to have LeBron James here. Angolans have seen him on television, they try to emulate him on the street courts, they have his posters."
Boosting Angola long-term
The star power of E1's owners is helping to bring eyeballs to what is a traditionally niche sport where powerboat pilots skim and bounce around tight courses at speeds close to 100kmph.
Yet, on a calendar that features traditional celebrity haunts like Miami, Monaco and Lake Como, Luanda's name seems an outlier.
Among those taking in the action from the fanzone was local resident Edson Cabeta.
"It is the first time I have seen anything like this," he said.
"Today it is foreigners doing this; tomorrow, perhaps we could have an Angolan team."
The aspiration is that hosting an E1 race will help Angola boost visitor numbers, with minister for tourism Marcio de Jesus Lopes Daniel saying enhanced foreign awareness of the country is the "first step" in a long-term plan.
"Our ambition is not simply to make Angola famous," Daniel told the BBC.
"It is to make Angola more desirable to visit, invest in and do business in."
Angola has not been afraid to speculate to accumulate in the past, bringing Lionel Messi's Argentina side to Luanda for a football friendly last November to celebrate 50 years of the nation's independence.
Daniel said it would be "premature" to assess the economic impact of this weekend's race in Luanda.
"An event of this scale generates demand across several sectors and it creates opportunities," he added.
"We want to turn the international attention generated by E1 into future trips, stays, private investment and jobs. That is the real return we are looking for."
Sustainability challenges
Beyond the spectacle and waterfront backdrops, E1 aims to transcend motorsport.
Sustainability has been one cornerstone, and marine conservation efforts around the race in Angola included mangrove restoration.
Putting sustainability front and centre inevitably invites scrutiny - particularly when races have taken place in Saudi Arabia, the United States, Nigeria and now Angola, all major oil-producing nations.
"The world's on a journey," Copas said.
"We're welcomed in places that do have a lot of fossil-fuel infrastructure.
"Each one of those markets is conscious of it and wants to be doing more from a green point of view. If we can help, why wouldn't we?"
Copas told BBC Sport Africa that E1 would only consider air freight as a last resort for transporting its teams and that they aim to showcase their technology on each stop, persuading people that electric charging is a viable alternative to diesel even on water.
But as the global series expanded to 10 teams and seven races in 2025, its own emissions rose from 1,672 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in its first season to 4,049 tonnes in its second, according to E1's own annual sustainability report.
"We need to travel to meet new people, to tell our stories, which we would hope would be of greater benefit than the carbon footprint that we have," Copas explained.
"We work really hard to offset our carbon and to make sure every stage of our logistics journey is done in the most sustainable way.
"It would be crazy for us to say we're not going to travel and we're not going to race, because then we can't do the job that we're here to do."
There is an acknowledgement within E1 that the work is unfinished and that more active reductions are needed.
'Continuing the story'
E1 was due to return to Lagos in October, but Nigeria's race was cancelled earlier this month, perhaps showing how the series is still working to establish itself.
It means its longer-term impact in Africa will take time to judge, but the effect of its celebrity owners was obvious around the paddock in Luanda.
After visiting his pilots, Will Smith stopped for selfies and handshakes with fans, telling the crowd it was "great to be here".
On the water, however, there was no fairytale result as Westbrook Racing's hopes of victory were ended by a mechanical fault, with Team Brady taking the inaugural Luanda title.
Smith could have used the help of Kianda, the mermaid-like Angolan water spirit traditionally regarded as a protector of fishermen.
It will take one of her miraculous interventions if electric powerboat racing is to usurp football or basketball in Angolan affections, but Copas hopes E1 can leave a different legacy.
"I think it's for us to help tell Angola stories, and for Angola to help tell ours.
"We will be back next year, we will be back the year after. It's not just about what we're doing in the few days we're here.
"We'd love to see the journey they're on develop even more, and us playing a part in that."

Millions without power as Cuba hit by latest major blackout
- Published
Millions in Cuba were left without power on Friday as the country was plunged into yet another major blackout.
The country's entire electricity grid suffered "total disconnection" that triggered a nationwide outage, Cuba's energy ministry said.
Power was restored to some priority areas by late evening, including those near hospitals and water pumping stations in the capital Havana, grid operator UNE said.
It is at least the sixth partial or total blackout to hit Cuba this year, where ageing electricity infrastructure and chronic fuel shortages have been placed under further strain by a US blockade on oil shipments to the communist-run nation.
UNE said the outage started just before 14:00 local time on Friday (18:00 GMT) due to a transmission fault coupled with poor weather conditions in central Cuba.
Protocols to begin the "gradual restoration" of power were activated, the operator's national load dispatch director Felix Estrada said, with the process ongoing on Saturday.
Cuba relies heavily on fuel imports, meaning tight US sanctions and an oil blockade since the start of the year have exacerbated existing shortages.
Food and medicine have also become more scarce, with hospitals struggling to function normally and schools and government offices having to close.
"Lately, it's becoming a habit," Havana resident Frank Lorenzo told news agency Reuters on Friday.
"Before it happened less frequently - once a month… just yesterday we were 24 hours without electricity, they turned it on for just an hour and it went down again."
"It's one thing after another: no water, no gas for cooking, no electricity," 36-year-old schoolteacher Lidia Fernandez told news agency AFP. "Honestly, I don't know how we haven't gone crazy."
Francisco Rodriguez, 78, said his home had already gone without power for 28 hours on Friday and feared he would not have light "for several days".
The repeated blackouts have prompted rare protests in Cuba, where unauthorised demonstrations are illegal and those who defy the ban risk being jailed.
Havana has blamed its fuel crisis on the Trump administration and denounced all of its sanctions - including a new round announced in August - which are part of a wider pressure campaign against the Caribbean island's leadership.
Cuba's regional ally Venezuela was believed to have sent it around 35,000 barrels of oil a day - about half of its oil needs - until Venezuela's own supplies were cut off following the US seizure of its President Nicolás Maduro in January.
US President Donald Trump has threatened tariffs on countries shipping oil to Havana, and a number of such shipments have been seized by the US.
Washington meanwhile attributes Cuba's energy crisis to poor internal management and has accused it of posing a "national security threat". Trump has openly discussed toppling its leadership, including threatening a "friendly takeover" in March this year.

Barclays Bank is facing a formal complaint over its financial links to a coal-fired power station near the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and home to millions of people in Bangladesh and India.
Three complainants from the region have submitted a case to the UK government’s Office for Responsible Business Conduct, alleging that the British bank breached international guidelines by underwriting companies involved in the emission-heavy Maitree super thermal power project, also known as the Rampal power plant.
The coal-fired power station is situated near the Sundarbans, a Unesco world heritage site made up of more than 100 tiny islands across a river delta that supports hundreds of plant and animal species, including the Bengal tiger.
Sharif Jamil, an environmental campaigner based in the Bangladeshi capital, Dhaka, who is one of the complainants, said heavy-metal pollution from the plant and the industrial development surrounding it was entering the Sundarbans through its interconnected rivers and canals.
“The Rampal power plant is right on the bank of the Pasur River, which is the lifeline of the Sundarbans,” he said. “The health of the forest is in trouble.”
Last November, a study found elevated levels of mercury and arsenic in water samples taken from the Sundarbans, with the highest concentrations recorded in the Pasur River.
Researchers identified industrial discharge and port-related activities among the sources of heavy-metal contamination and said the Rampal power station posed “a significant environmental threat due to emissions from coal combustion and increased navigation traffic”.
Millions of people live in the Sundarbans, and many depend on the river and forests for food and other resources.
The claimants allege that Barclays failed to conduct sufficient due diligence on the environmental and human rights risks before providing financial services to organisations connected to the project.
Barclays underwrote debt of India’s state-owned NTPC Ltd (formerly the National Thermal Power Corporation), one of the joint-venture partners behind the plant, according to King’s Legal Clinic, which is assisting the complainants. It also says Barclays underwrote bond issues for the Export-Import Bank of India between 2016 and 2019, which provided a loan for the Rampal project.
The complainants argue that emissions from the plant will contribute to global heating, rising sea levels and extreme weather in a region already highly vulnerable to the climate crisis. Mangroves act as a natural barrier against cyclones and other extreme weather.
The power station faced sustained opposition during its planning and construction, including concerns raised by Unesco in a report in 2016, which concluded that “air and water pollution have a high likelihood to irreversibly damage the … World Heritage property”. Some financial institutions, including banks in France, refused to support the project because of its potential environmental and social effects, the complaint says.
Jamil said Barclays’ international standing obliged it to consider the consequences of financing. “The greater your reputation, the greater your responsibility to behave responsibly towards the planet and its people,” he said. “Barclays is a reputed global organisation, and that is why it also has a responsibility.
“Other banks and financial institutions were divesting from, or declining to finance, this project,” he added. “Barclays and other financial organisations should change their policies and examine how their operations can protect the planet from climate catastrophe.”
Jamil also called on banks to direct more funding towards renewable energy rather than imported fossil fuels. “Bangladesh has sunlight throughout the year,” he said. “Why should we expand fossil fuels when there is enormous potential to produce electricity from renewable energy?”
The other complainants include Animesh Mandal, a farmer and politician, and the Dakshinbanga Matsyajibi Forum, a trade union representing fish workers in West Bengal.
They are being assisted by students and lawyers at King’s Human Rights and Environment Clinic, part of King’s College London’s law school.
Sue Willman, a solicitor at the clinic, said: “Rural communities in the Sundarbans are on the frontline of the climate and nature crisis. We hope to persuade banks and financial institutions to think again before financing oil and coal developments that are contributing to that crisis.”
The Office for Responsible Business Conduct, part of the Department for Business and Trade, will assess whether to consider the complaint.
Barclays Bank and BIFPCL (Bangladesh India Friendship Power Company Ltd), the holding company for the Maitree super thermal power project, declined to comment.

AI is resetting assumptions about how quickly professional services firms should move, and consulting clients are getting impatient.
"I am seeing clients ask for our help in delivering outcomes at a more rapid pace" compared to this time last year, Jeanelle Johnson, PwC's managing partner for the Washington DC area, told Business Insider.
"Something that we might have said takes eight to 10 weeks; the expectation is probably half of that. The shelf life is half," Johnson said.
Clients are not necessarily expecting an entire transformation to be completed in a fraction of the time; the expectation is more for pilots and proofs of concepts, she said.
"There's an expectation now that tools should accelerate the work," she added.
Johnson leads more than 2,200 consulting and accounting employees in her role as PwC's DC managing partner. Asked whether those compressed timelines were putting pressure on her consulting teams, she said: "We're working on it."
The Big Four professional services firms — PwC, Deloitte, KPMG, and EY — alongside firms like McKinsey, BCG, and Accenture, are at the center of the AI shift sweeping through workplaces. They have raced to build internal chatbots, train staff, and test AI in client work.
The technology can now assist with, and increasingly perform, early-stage consulting tasks such as market research, due diligence, and brainstorming.
At McKinsey, AI has accelerated the early problem-solving cycle, turning what used to be a team's "week one answer" — the first hypothesis after a week of research and analysis — into an "hour one answer," Kate Smaje, McKinsey's Global Leader for technology and AI, told Business Insider in June.
That frees up consultants to spend more time testing deeper parts of the issue tree rather than waiting days to get oriented, Smaje said.
Amid the rank and file, employees at top firms have told Business Insider they're seeing a difference in delivery times due to AI.
A software engineer at Deloitte US told Business Insider that some coding tasks had fallen from a dayslong process to around five minutes with AI, and an EY-Parthenon consultant in the UK said that due diligence that previously took two weeks of manual work and spreadsheet handling can now be completed in a day with AI.
As well as pressure to deliver faster results, the shift is also raising questions about how the pricing model that has rested on human labor will adapt as more work gets done by AI.
The work is more complex
For Johnson, faster delivery should not be confused with less work.
AI will change how consultants spend their time, freeing capacity for more meaningful or higher-value work rather than simply reducing the number of hours needed on a project, she told Business Insider.
The work itself is also becoming more complex, she added. Clients are navigating geopolitical tensions, wars, tariffs, and macroeconomic uncertainty simultaneously — a broader set of pressures than consultants would often have helped them tackle in the past.
"The confluence of all those things at the same time is something that we used to deal with one or two things at a time," Johnson said.
"Now we're in a world order where we have to deal with 10 plus, plus, plus at a time."

A father and son who built their legacy in hammer throw shared one of the biggest moments of the 
Asian Games
 opening ceremony on Saturday.
Japan’s Shigenobu Murofushi and his son Koji Murofushi jointly lit the cauldron at the 20th Asian Games in Nagoya, bringing the torch relay to a memorable end.
Both Shigenobu and Koji are former Asian Games champions in hammer throw. The duo climbed the stairs to the podium together before lighting the cauldron.
The ceremony featured dance, music and fireworks as the Asian Games officially opened in Aichi-Nagoya.
From Olympic champion to father-son moment
The cauldron lighting was the final part of a relay involving some of Japan’s biggest sporting names.
Women’s wrestler Fujinami Akari brought the torch into the stadium before passing it to four-time Olympic swimming champion Kitajima Kosuke.
The torch then went to Ito Koji, a three-time gold medallist in athletics at the 1998 Bangkok Asian Games. Takahashi Ayaka, the 2016 Rio Olympics badminton women’s doubles champion, was next.
Shigenobu Murofushi and Koji Murofushi (Reuters Photo)
The torch was then handed to Koji Murofushi, the 2004 Athens Olympics hammer throw champion.
The final torchbearer was his father, Shigenobu Murofushi, who won the Asian Games hammer throw title five times in a row.
The two then came together to light the cauldron, which had a metallic design inspired by the shape of a heart.
Who is Shigenobu Murofushi?
Shigenobu Murofushi is one of Japan’s most successful hammer throwers. He competed at three Olympic Games — Munich 1972, Montreal 1976 and Los Angeles 1984.
He also served as Japan’s flag-bearer at the 1984 Olympics.
Murofushi initially tried sumo and shot put before taking up hammer throw. In 1984, he set a Japanese record of 75.96m. That mark remained the national record until his son Koji broke it in 1998.
Shigenobu won the Asian Games hammer throw gold medal in 1970, 1974, 1978, 1982 and 1986. He also won silver in 1966.
His Asian Games medal record includes five gold medals and one silver.
He also won gold at the 1979 and 1981 Asian Championships.
Shigenobu’s Olympic journey
While Shigenobu dominated the Asian Games, an Olympic medal remained out of reach.
He finished eighth at the 1972 Munich Olympics, 11th at Montreal 1976 and 15th at Los Angeles 1984.
His son would later achieve what he could not at the Olympics.
Koji Murofushi followed his father’s footsteps
Koji started hammer throw at the age of 10 under the guidance of his father.
He went on to become one of the leading hammer throwers in the world. Koji won the silver medal at the 2001 World Championships before claiming bronze in 2003.
His biggest Olympic moment came at the 2004 Athens Games, where he won the hammer throw gold medal.
He added an Olympic bronze at the 2012 London Games.
Koji also became world champion in 2011 in Daegu.
Shigenobu Murofushi and Koji Murofushi (Reuters Photo)
Koji’s Asian Games medal record
Koji continued his family’s success at the Asian Games.
He won gold in hammer throw at Bangkok in 1998 and Busan in 2002. He had earlier won silver at Hiroshima in 1994.
His Asian Games record therefore includes two gold medals and one silver.
Koji also won gold at the 2002 Asian Championships and three silver medals at the continental championships in 1993, 1995 and 1998.
A family legacy comes full circle
The Murofushis have now added another special chapter to their long sporting legacy.
Shigenobu dominated the Asian Games in the 1970s and 1980s. Koji followed him into the event and later became an Olympic and world champion.
On Saturday, the father and son stood together at the centre of the Asian Games opening ceremony — not to compete, but to light the flame that officially began the Games.
Glittering opening ceremony
The 20th Asian Games officially began in Nagoya with a two-hour opening ceremony at the Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium. Japan's Emperor Naruhito officially declared the Games open. Empress Masako, members of the Japanese imperial family, Olympic Council of Asia president Sheikh Joaan bin Hamad Al Thani and International Olympic Committee president Kirsty Coventry were also present at the ceremony.
The event started with the Japanese national anthem and the raising of the national flag. Nine members of the Japanese Self-Defence Forces carried the flag to the stage before it was hoisted.
The stadium was then turned dark, with a spotlight focused on the Japanese flag.
The ceremony was followed by the parade of athletes. Teams from 45 nations and regions took part, along with the OCA Refugee Team, taking the total number of participating delegations to 46.

Years ago, I got a call from a friend. "The most amazing thing happened," she gushed, "we got engaged!" She proceeded to tell me about how her boyfriend proposed. They're such a loving and compatible couple, I couldn't have been happier for them. Days later, I saw the picture online, her finger encrusted with an antique diamond ring, an heirloom from her fiancé's grandmother, just like she had told me about over the phone.
Over the years, I would get a message, sometimes out of the blue, from a friend saying something along the lines of, "Let's catch up." Then we'd set up a time to meet, or, if we lived too far apart, have a phone call. At times, the news was joyful, like a pregnancy or a major step in a relationship. Other times, it was somber, a divorce, a job loss, a tragic health condition.
Sometimes I would see my friends post on social media later, after they had already told me. Each time, I felt honored that they had reached out to me directly. I felt special that they wanted to make sure I knew what was going on in their life, and not just that I was within the blast radius of a social media post.
When it was my turn, I prioritized personal connections
The year 2023 was big for me. At the beginning of the year, my boyfriend and I bought a weekend house in the mountains. That spring, he proposed to me at that weekend house, under a starry sky. We were both in our mid-30s and eager to start a family. That summer, we eloped with an intimate ceremony at the same place we had our first date three years earlier. In the fall, we shared the good news with family and friends that we were expecting our first child.
I felt the temptation to share all my good fortunes with pictures broadcasted across the World Wide Web. But instead of a picture, I sent my friends a message. "Let's get together," or "let's have a call," it said.
Instead of posting the quintessential picture of us holding up a set of keys in front of a house, we told our friends about buying a vacation house over drinks. "We can't wait to see it!" they exclaimed, and we clinked our glasses together in celebration. 
When I met up with a friend I hadn't seen in a while, she grabbed my hand mid-hug when the sparkle of the diamond caught her eye. Another friend brought over a housewarming gift. She caught a glimpse of the grainy sonogram picture on the fridge. "I'm so happy for you guys," she said, holding back tears of joy.
Hugs beat out "likes" or heart emojis any day
So much happened in such a short period of time that year. When we caught up with friends we hadn't seen in a couple of months, the answer to "so, what's new with you?" sometimes ended up being "we bought a house, and we got engaged, and now we're married, and we're having a baby!"
Each time I shared the special things going on in my life, I got to experience the joy again, through the other person. Those moments created memories that I would never have had from just posting online. Waiting to share news in person with the people I love, and seeing their reaction, released more endorphins than any number of "likes" to a post.
Technology has helped me stay in touch with my family and friends around the country and the world. I've come to find that sharing life's ups and downs with the people I love, in person when possible, or by call if not, is the best way to stay connected.

Three dead and eight injured in Philippines school shooting
- Published
A 16-year-old gunman has shot two students dead and injured eight others at a Philippine high school, before killing himself.
The two deceased victims were 14-year-old pupils at a school in Banga in the southern province of Mindanao, the local mayor told the BBC.
Albert Palencia said four of the injured were in critical condition.
The education department said in a statement it was "deeply concerned" by the reported incident which took place on Friday afternoon at Banga National High School.
This is the third deadly school shooting in the Philippines since June this year.
"Our immediate priority is the safety and well-being of our learners, teachers and school personnel," the education department said, adding it was coordinating with authorities to verify the incident and provide necessary support.
"We urge everyone to remain calm and refrain from sharing unverified information as authorities continue their investigation."
Palencia told Reuters news agency that during a lunchtime conversation on Friday, the gunman had urged friends to go home "because after lunch, [he would] be executing [his] plan".
"His friends laughed because the shooter was a known joker," Palencia told the news agency.
"After lunch, he started shooting students. He hit 10 students before killing himself."
Classes have been suspended "in all levels in the entire municipality of Banga" due to the shooting, disaster management authorities said in a statement.
The Philippines Red Cross said it was alerted to the incident at 14:00 local time (06:00 GMT) and had dispatched an ambulance with four paramedics to provide life-saving assistance.
Police are at the site investigating the shooting, local media reported.
Gun crime is not uncommon in the Philippines, which has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the region. Broadly speaking, school shootings are rare, but today's incident marks the third deadly campus shooting in the last four months.
In June, three students were killed and more were injured after their peers opened fire at a high school in central Philippines. Investigators believed the deadly shooting had been motivated by a "grudge" over bullying.
In August, a student at a Catholic junior high school in the southern Philippines shot dead a fellow student and later took his own life. In this case, the suspect had fired at the teacher, but missed, then moved to another classroom and shot a student, who later died.
Following the shooting on Friday, Reynaldo Tamayo, the South Cotabato governor, urged adult gun owners to "be responsible in storing firearms" and ensuring that minors do not get access to them.
"We cannot expect a handful of security personnel to monitor thousands of students. We need to work together because otherwise this will be very difficult for us to address," he told Reuters.

Five persons accused in the murder of Bahujan Samaj Party leader K. Armstrong have been granted mandatory bail on the ground that the Central Bureau of Investigation is yet to file a final report, while they have been in prison for more than two years without the trial commencing.
Sources said almost all those arrested and remanded in connection with the case have now been enlarged on bail.
On the evening of July 5, 2024, Armstrong was hacked to death by a gang of nine members. Armstrong was rushed to Apollo Hospital, Greams Road, but died on the way.
Based on a complaint, the Sembium police registered a case and formed special teams. The suspects were arrested in quick succession. A total of 30 people, including three women, were cited as accused. Gangsters Nagendran and Sambav Senthil were among them. Nagendran later died of ill health, while another accused, Thiruvenkadam, was killed in an encounter. Sambav Senthil and his associate Mottai Krishnan remain absconding.
On September 24, 2025, the Madras High Court quashed the charge sheet filed by the Sembium police and transferred the investigation to the CBI, citing concerns over the thoroughness and impartiality of the State police probe. The State government later withdrew its challenge before the Supreme Court.
Meanwhile, more than 15 accused, including Aswathaman, were enlarged on bail. The CBI took over the case and re-registered it as R.C. No. 09/S/2026 on August 6, 2026. Five more accused, including Manna alias Manivannan, subsequently approached the Principal Sessions Court seeking bail.
Long incarceration
The defence counsel, Muthamizh Selvan, submitted that the accused had been in judicial custody for more than two years and that the earlier charge sheet had been quashed. He argued that the CBI had not examined any witness for a considerable period after taking over the probe and that continued incarceration violated the accused’s right to a speedy investigation and trial.
The CBI Special Public Prosecutor opposed the petitions, submitting that the agency was actively investigating the case, including examining and re-examining crucial witnesses and scrutinising electronic records, financial transactions and the roles of untraced co-conspirators. Granting bail at this stage would jeopardise the investigation into the remaining conspiratorial links, the prosecutor submitted.
Allowing the bail petitions, Principal Sessions Judge B. Karthikyan observed that the CBI did not appear to have examined even a single witness during the month preceding the hearing. The judge noted that the earlier investigation had recorded the statements of 237 witnesses and said the extent of the material now before the CBI indicated the enormity of the task facing the agency.
“It does not appear that investigation would be completed in a short time,” the judge observed. The judge also noted that the accused had already spent more than two years in custody and that the investigation remained at the FIR stage after the earlier final report was quashed.

More than 180 writers have signed a letter to Eritrean president Isaias Afwerki calling for proof of life for 12 writers arrested in 2001.
Nobel laureates Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee join prominent writers including Colm Tóibín, Elif Shafak, Isabel Allende, Ben Okri, Yann Martel, Kamila Shamsie and Tsitsi Dangarembga in signing the letter dated 18 September, marking 25 years since a government crackdown on the independent press. “Within days, Eritrea’s free press and the nation’s independent voices were systematically crushed,” opens the letter.
It lists 12 writers who have been held incommunicado since 2001, including the poet Amanuel Asrat and playwright and journalist Dawit Isaak.
“The families of these writers, the Eritrean people and the global literary community have been met with a painful and unlawful silence,” continues the statement. “To withhold all information regarding their health, location, and survival is a violation of international law and an act of cruelty.”
Along with Asrat and Isaak, the other writers named in the letter are Dawit Habtemichael, Fessehaye “Joshua” Yohannes, Mattewos Habteab, Medhanie Haile, Sahle “Wedi-ltay” Tsegazeab, Said Abdelkadir, Said Idris “Abu Are”, Seyoum Tsehaye, Temesgen Ghebreyesus and Yousif Mohammed Ali. Six of the writers were profiled in the Guardian in 2015.
The letter, signed by 188 writers in total, calls for “immediate, verified proof of life for all arbitrarily detained Eritrean writers and critics”.
Other signatories include Andrei Kurkov, Anthony Doerr, Chloe Aridjis, Lauren Groff, Lemn Sissay, Maaza Mengiste, Madeleine Thien, Margaret Busby, Max Porter, Philippe Sands, Preti Taneja, Tice Cin and Viv Groskop.
“Mr President, Eritrea’s future must be built with its brightest minds, not based on their suppression,” the letter adds. “No writer or journalist should be disappeared for peacefully expressing their views.”
Eritrea operates as a repressive dictatorship under Afwerki, with no national elections held since independence in 1993.
“We remain in solidarity with our missing colleagues, and we will not cease our efforts until they are free,” the letter concludes.
PEN International will attempt delivery of the letter at the Eritrean embassy in London at 10am on Friday. Earlier this year, the organisation launched a petition, open to the public, which also calls for proof of life.
“Twenty-five years is an unbearable length of time for any family to live without knowing whether a loved one is alive,”, said Burhan Sönmez, president of PEN International. “These writers have not disappeared from our memory. We will continue to speak their names, and we will continue to demand the truth about what happened to them.”

'It's like a dog set loose on us' - fear over Kenya's crackdown on foreign traders
- Published
For Ndaikech Ali, who has been traversing the streets of the Kenyan capital eking out a living as a tuk-tuk driver for the past nine years, Nairobi's traffic - not xenophobia - has been his biggest concern.
During his time in the East African nation, the Burundian says he has always found Kenyans to be friendly and welcoming - that is until last week, when the president ordered a crackdown on foreigners working as traders or operating small-scale businesses.
"Now they have turned against us," he told the BBC at the Burundian embassy in Nairobi where many have been queuing this week for documents to allow them to travel back home.
"The threats are many… even from children," he said, adding: "It's a like a dog has been set loose upon us. We have been bitten."
President William Ruto made his remarks last week when addressing Kenyan traders gathered at state house - in reference to legislation before parliament that seeks to exclude foreign nationals from petty trade and to mandate the local sourcing of certain materials.
During his speech, he said that all foreign nationals operating small businesses had until 7 September to pack up shop, saying such low-level jobs should be reserved for Kenyans.
Ali, like others, panicked, saying it seemed the president's announcement had been interpreted by some Kenyans as a signal that foreign nationals were no longer welcome in the country.
"We face harassment and can't work," he says. "If our work is stopped, we lose the income that enables us to pay rent and buy food. When those jobs are taken away, the only option left is to return home."
Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees"
Other Burundians and some other foreign nationals have rushed to border crossing points to leave the country, with reports suggesting that a number have ended up stranded there.
Some couples fear they will be forced to separate - and some families have already been divided.
"I have been here from 2019," said a Burundian man, who identified himself only as Prosper and who has a child with a Kenyan woman.
"When I heard the announcement, it was very painful because when I go, I'm forced to leave my family... and I love my family," he told the BBC.
In Nairobi's low-income neighbourhood of Majengo, Kenyan Grace Wamaitha said her Burundian husband had already gone - leaving the day after the president's 3 September directive.
She is distraught as she has been left trying to feed their five children - and has taken on extra work washing clothes.
"Now he's gone, who will help me pay school fees? I don't know what to do. Let them come back," she told the BBC.
In Nairobi and other major towns, migrants from the region can be found working in barber shops and salons, construction, operating motorbike taxis and street vending, as well as selling clothes, food and household goods.
Some have fled conflicts or economic hardship at home, while others have moved to Kenya in search of better opportunities. Within the East African Community (EAC), a regional bloc made up of eight countries, including Burundi and Kenya, the relative free movement of people is allowed - but employment and long-term residence do require permits.
Kenyan law also recognises the right of refugees to work and operate businesses, although they are also required to obtain the appropriate documentation.
Filmon Eyob, a co-ordinator within Nairobi's Eritrean community, agrees with concerns that the crackdown order will be used as pretext to harass foreigners.
He told the BBC that while many Kenyans had been supportive and welcoming, some Eritreans and Ethiopians had closed their businesses and stayed at home over the last week as a precaution.
The president's remarks also sparked a diplomatic row, with the Burundian foreign affairs minister warning that "hate speech against Burundi" could have repercussions for Kenyans abroad.
The authorities in Kenya have struggled to contain the fallout - and as the matter came to a head, Kenyan foreign affairs official Korir Sing'Oei visited and apologised to Burundians at the embassy this week, assuring them of protection from violence.
Critics argue that Ruto's remarks were a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia, although the government has denied this.
Since then, a series of official statements have sought to clarify the directive.
The government has now given a 90-day window for undocumented foreign nationals running small business to register and comply with local laws. During the process, those undergoing registration will be presumed to be living legally in Kenya.
Yet observers and those affected argue that it did not have to be this way.
Academic Hesbon Owilla told the BBC the president's comments were bound to be misinterpreted, especially by people who did not have the right documentation.
He says that while the proposed policy is good for Kenya and in line with global migration protocols, the communication about it ought to have been more diplomatic.
For those not in the audience, Owilla says people interpreted the president words as saying: "We are kicking these guys out."
The president did not stop at small-scale traders. A day later, he ordered India's Tata Chemicals to leave the country, saying the company had not provided sufficient benefits to the local Maasai community in Kajiado county.
Tata has been mining soda ash for years in Lake Magadi, a vast area often covered by a whitish salt crust. The lake's extreme briny environment sustains algae blooms that attract flamboyances of pink flamingos that thrive in the area.
Mining operations began at the lake in 1911 under a British colonial arrangement that is said to have remained largely intact, despite long-running land and resource disputes pitting the company and its predecessors against community and the government.
Economist Odhiambo Ramogi argues that the move to restrict foreign nationals from businesses is too broad - and could do with finessing.
He points out that Kenya hosts hundreds of thousands of refugees as well as other migrants, mostly from the EAC region, as well as other international investors.
Ramogi says that Ruto's intention seemed to go beyond "just protecting jobs for Kenyans".
The president's remarks have prompted a wave of support for foreign nationals, including by civil society groups and ordinary Kenyans who have criticised his approach.
In the wake of the criticism, Ruto, who is up for re-election next year, has sought to counter the backlash.
"Kenya will remain an open, secure and welcoming country, protecting opportunities for its citizens, safeguarding the rights of all persons lawfully within its borders," a statement by his spokesman said.
"Kenya's commitment to the East African Community of the African continent remains firm."
Ramogi says that in the end, it is Kenya that stands to lose when citizens of neighbouring countries are targeted.
He points out that Kenya earned $56m (£41m) in exports to Burundi last year, adding that the country would still benefit by allowing competition, as "locking out aliens simply means you don't want a competitive economy that gets to grow a lot faster".
"Now, if you got $56m out of a country, why are you worried about a hawker who's just trying to make, say, $200 in a month?
"It absolutely makes no sense what the president has done."
For Nairobi resident Lima Kabura, whose husband is Tanzanian, the president's remarks were just too hasty. She says he should have first established those who were in the country illegally.
"When they are forced out, I'm left with no work, no business and no husband," she said.

Allaying apprehensions over the surge in dengue cases in Tamil Nadu, the Directorate of Public Health (DPH) and Preventive Medicine on Wednesday (September 17, 2026) said the spread of dengue this year was neither unusual nor alarming, and urged the public not to panic.
The Directorate issued a statement to allay apprehensions among the public that dengue fever cases have increased significantly in the State during the current year.
It said that this year, the spread of dengue was neither unusual nor occurring at an alarming level. Every year, seasonal variations in dengue cases occur naturally during the monsoon due to changes in climatic conditions.
It said that a comparison of official data from January to September over the past three years provided a clear picture of the current situation. In 2024, a total of 34,339 persons were affected by dengue and 13 deaths were reported. In 2025, 15,688 persons were affected and 13 deaths were reported. In the current year, as of September 16, 16,334 persons were affected and nine deaths were reported, the release said.
However, as per the official data put out by the National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control, there were a total of 27,378 dengue cases in the State in 2024.
The DPH noted that usually, breeding of Aedes mosquitoes that transmit dengue increased during the monsoon. In particular, conditions conducive for increased mosquito breeding may occur from October to December, and hence, dengue cases were being continuously monitored, while preventive and control measures were intensified.
Control measures
Officers were deployed across the State to coordinate dengue prevention and control measures. Fever wards were established to monitor patients with fever and to provide timely treatment. Triaging was undertaken to assess the health condition of patients and provide appropriate treatment on a priority basis based on the severity of the illness.
The directorate said that mosquito control measures, including larval control and source reduction, were being taken up across the State.
DPH urges public to cooperate
Making an appeal to the public, the DPH stressed the need for the public to work along with the government in dengue prevention and control measures. It requested the public to ensure that water does not stagnate in and around their houses and to ensure that there is no water accumulation in unused plastic items, coconut shells, old tyres, flower pots, and other containers. They should identify and immediately remove mosquito breeding sources in and around their houses and extend full cooperation to the mosquito control and dengue prevention measures taken up by the government and local bodies.
If symptoms such as fever occur, they should approach the nearest primary health centre or government hospital to seek medical advice and appropriate treatment without delay. It said that dengue transmission can be controlled more effectively if the public extends cooperation for the preventive measures undertaken by the government.

The Data-Center Debate Is Divorced From the Facts
All those scary numbers aren’t what they seem.
As the build-out of AI data centers has accelerated, the public has tended to focus on every possible downside of these industrial projects. Some wariness—about the developments and the companies behind them—is sensible. As with almost any new industrial development, and depending on where they are built and how they are powered and cooled, data centers pose risks of excessive carbon-dioxide emissions and noise pollution.
But the panic about the harms of these projects has well outpaced the evidence. In my years researching and reporting on AI and the environment, with support from a grant from Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy), I’ve noticed that misconceptions abound. This panic, moreover, is leading communities to forgo massive amounts of tax revenue—largely because of threats that are inflated, confused, and sometimes nonexistent. The trade-offs are real.
In June, a Massachusetts city near where I grew up blocked a data center, in large part out of concern over the amount of water the development would use and pollute. Data centers do need a lot of water to cool their equipment, and—as with most industrial building projects—constructing these developments can introduce chemical additives into the local wastewater. But there are no confirmed cases of this data-center pollution harming people, and this city specifically has abundant fresh water.
Most of the fear about water seems to be the product of misunderstood details from news reports, spread like a game of telephone. The New York Times published a story last year about a Georgia couple whose water taps at home went dry after Meta broke ground on a $750 million data center nearby. The couple suggested that Meta’s construction created a buildup of sediment in the water, which caused water-pressure problems and damaged their well (many homes in the area use well water). Whether the construction actually caused these problems remains unclear, but the story is often read as evidence of the harms of data centers. Yet sediment buildup in groundwater is a standard construction risk, and most places don’t ban large buildings over it. Almost all stories about the harms of data centers cite such construction-related problems.
As for the concern that data centers add toxic “forever chemicals,” known as PFAS, to local water sources, this seems to involve some confusion over how centers use water to cool the machinery. Some systems use fluorinated fluids classified as PFAS to help cool servers and prevent fires, but these are designed as closed loops that stay contained in equipment. There’s always the threat of a leak, but contaminating local waterways is a risk of any major industrial project.
One known exception in which a data center was linked to a water-pollution problem was in Oregon, where Amazon data centers used groundwater that was already contaminated from decades of local agriculture and food processing. Because much of the water used to cool equipment ends up evaporating during the process, the wastewater that left the data center had a higher concentration of nitrates, which exacerbated the contamination problem in the local groundwater. Amazon agreed to settle the matter for $20.5 million without admitting guilt. The company accurately noted that the area had been suffering from polluted water for decades, even if the data center made it worse.
The data-center debate includes plenty of dauntingly large numbers without context, such as that they consume millions of gallons of water a day. This is a significant amount, but also comparable to the water use of other industries. The data center with the highest known water consumption, Google’s development in Council Bluffs, Iowa, consumes about 1.3 billion gallons a year. That sounds massive, but so is the amount of water used to irrigate Iowa’s corn crops. If Google had bought a cornfield four to six times as large as the data center’s plot, or about eight square miles (roughly 0.04 percent of the total area Iowa uses for corn), the company would consume the same amount of water irrigating it. All American data centers together will consume about 1 percent of the water that America uses to irrigate corn. This is not nothing, but hardly horrifying in context.
Another misconception is that data centers consistently raise local electricity prices. There is no clear positive relationship or broad pattern between data centers and household electricity prices, but people are happy to spread misleading claims on the subject. A common statistic that critics bandy about is that electricity costs near data centers have skyrocketed by as much as 267 percent in five years. Senator Elizabeth Warren cited this number in an op-ed earlier this year. But the figure comes from a Bloomberg analysis of wholesale electricity prices at specific nodes on the grid, not the prices that households pay. Although wholesale prices influence residential prices over time, residential prices are largely insulated from wholesale spikes and drops, and American-household bills have not risen anywhere near 267 percent during the data-center build-out. When price hikes have been linked to data centers, the amount looks more like 10 percent.
Perhaps the most pernicious misunderstanding of the facts involves the claim that data centers don’t pay taxes. Early reports about the sales-tax exemptions on machinery and equipment that data centers enjoy in most states have somehow morphed into a sweeping assumption that data centers are actually depriving states and municipalities of tax revenues. The reality is that data centers are a reliable and lucrative source of tax revenue wherever they are built. Real-estate and personal-property taxes ensure that the tax burden on these developments is high, regardless of sales taxes.
For example, Loudoun County, Virginia, which has the largest concentration of data centers in the country, collects $1.3 billion a year in county taxes from these centers—about $2,800 per resident. This represents nearly half of all local tax funding for county government and public schools, despite Virginia’s waiver of sales taxes on related machinery and equipment. Local opposition to new data centers has come to Loudoun too, but residents are unlikely to forgo hundreds of millions of dollars a year to shut down the data centers in operation.
Another common concern is that data centers will “take up all the land” because these facilities consume a lot of space. Yet my own rough estimate puts the combined footprint of all data-center buildings in America at about 25 square miles by 2028—a little over half the size of Disney World and spread across the country. These projects also buy land around the buildings and for future expansion, but the combined landholdings of all new and existing data centers would cover about 1,400 square miles, a little more than three times the land used to grow Christmas trees in the United States.
For a sense of scale, again consider Loudoun County. Data centers take up 3 percent of Loudoun’s land, even as they generate nearly 40 percent of the county’s general-fund revenue. Despite concerns that these centers depress local land values, a 2025 study of home sales in Northern Virginia, including Loudoun, found that homes closer to data centers sold for higher prices, perhaps because the infrastructure that’s valuable for data centers is also valuable for homeowners.
Then there are the conspiracy theories, such as the idea that data centers emit harmful, inaudible low-frequency sounds, known as infrasounds. Such claims sometimes misrepresent the studies they cite. No infrasounds at the levels the data centers emit have been found to be harmful. This is not to say that data centers don’t cause some noise pollution, but the idea that imperceptible infrasounds have some mystical ability to make people unwell is not borne out by the evidence.
As for the underlying anxieties about AI that may be motivating the data-center backlash, slowing down the construction of data centers is not the same as slowing down the capabilities of AI. Yet banning data centers has become shorthand for political candidates who wish to seem tough on AI, when this is a distraction: The wiser and tougher move is to heavily regulate the industry.
No data center is a harmless boon for locals, but the real question is whether their downsides outweigh their benefits. Given the status-quo bias at play—whereby change seems inherently costlier than keeping things the same—I’ve discovered a simple trick to make the trade-off clear. I now ask people, “Would we spend as much tax revenue as the data center will bring in to avoid its downsides?” For example, would the residents of Loudoun County each pay $2,800 a year to reduce some of the county’s air pollution and water use, lower electricity bills by about $6 a month, and make about 3 percent of the county’s land available for something else? Since this is the actual question before communities, I find that spelling it out is handy. In Loudon, and in other jurisdictions around the country, many voters seem, on balance, to prefer the data centers.

Ryanair boss Michael O'Leary apologises over 'high-fare rapists' remarks
- Published
Ryanair chief executive Michael O'Leary has said he is "truly sorry" for describing rival airlines as "high-fare rapists".
He had previously refused to apologise to a rape crisis centre which criticised him for the comments.
O'Leary had made the remark earlier this month while talking to journalists ahead of Ryanair's yearly meeting with shareholders.
Following the comments, the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) wrote to him asking for an apology, in a letter seen by the BBC.
O'Leary had originally said that some people were "desperate to get to Ryanair's low fares because they can't afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe".
He subsequently defended his choice of words when asked by a reporter from the Press Association whether the language was appropriate.
"British Airways, Lufthansa, and everybody else's high fares, I'll happily offend them on a regular basis," he had added.
Asked whether it would offend sexual assault victims, he said rape was "a terrible crime".
In a video posted on Friday, O'Leary said that, over the last ten days, he had had "conversations with family and friends, both inside and outside Ryanair".
"I have come to realise however that the word that I used so carelessly has caused considerable upset and offence to a wide number of people, especially to victims and survivors.
"I want to apologise, sincerely and unreservedly, to those people, especially to the survivors."
O'Leary described his choice of language as "careless", and said "it won't happen again".
"I will try to learn from this mistake, and do better in future."
Following O'Leary's first comments, the DRCC's chief executive Rachel Morrogh had written to O'Leary accusing him of trying to get a headline with his comments.
She said the DRCC had received calls from rape victims who were "upset and distressed because of what you said".
She offered O'Leary training on the impact of sexual violence and urged him to apologise.
"I can't imagine you would ever use the term so flippantly again if you truly understood [what] it was like to survive rape," she wrote.
In response, O'Leary had said: "I am quite clear that no remarks of mine could possibly trivialise the heinous crime of rape."
He added that as he had not "trivialised the heinous crime of rape" he would "not be issuing any apology or accepting your offer of training".
It was not the first time O'Leary had offended people while talking about his business.
In 2004, he reportedly called the owners of Stansted Airport "a bunch of overcharging rapists", external in a row over airport charges.
He has also previously called some of his own staff "lazy bastards" and once said to passengers looking for a refund "we don't want to hear your sob stories".
In June, he said the airline would "reluctantly" stop charging parents to sit next to children after a watchdog investigation was opened, but insisted its previous policy complied with laws.

Cuba once again plunges into complete darkness as blackout hits island
‘The country is in such a sad state, and there are no words for what we’re going through’
Millions of people across Cuba were left without electricity on Friday following a total collapse of the island's power grid.
The Ministry of Energy and Mines confirmed the widespread blackout on its official X account, stating that authorities had initiated "activating service-restoration protocols."
According to Cuban authorities, a failure occurred in transmission lines in the western part of the country, causing the system to collapse there, as far as Matanzas province, and disconnecting the eastern section.
The official newspaper Granma reported that "unstable" weather conditions further aggravated the grid's situation.
By dusk, power had been restored to 5% of users in Havana, which serves about 862,000 customers, according to official data.
Small power-distribution "micro-islands" were being established in Camagüey, Pinar del Río and Granma provinces, while some systems serving hospitals and other emergency facilities were reactivated.
"No one can stand these constant blackouts. There isn’t enough food, there’s no water, there’s no electricity — you have no idea," Mercedes Rodriguez, a 60-year-old worker in Havana, told The Associated Press as she waited for public transportation to return home.
"The country is in such a sad state, and there are no words for what we’re going through."
Power grid collapses have grown increasingly common over the past two years amid a severe economic crisis gripping the island. The shortages have worsened since January, after the United States imposed an energy blockade aimed at forcing a change in Cuba’s political system.
These restrictions prevent Cuba from importing the fuel needed to operate its thermoelectric power plants, as well as replacement parts required to maintain infrastructure that in many cases has become obsolete. Just one fuel delivery has arrived since, brought by a Russian tanker in March.
The two most recent nationwide blackouts occurred in early August, following previous outages in July and March, alongside several regional failures.
Even when the national power grid is working, Cubans endure outages lasting more than 30 consecutive hours.
The blackouts heavily impact the population and, combined with the energy embargo, have caused transportation limitations, reduced work hours and flight cancellations, in addition to serious public health consequences.
The outages also affect basic activities such as cooking, water supply, and internet and telephone service.
Abilén Marrero, a homemaker, sat resignedly at the entrance to her building in central Havana.
"Maybe it’ll come back this afternoon or tomorrow—there’s no way to know. We just have to wait," she said.

A patient enters an operating theatre for a procedure on the right knee. The limb is marked, the scans are available and the surgical team has checked the records. Just before the operation begins, the team stops. A nurse reads out the patient’s identity, the procedure planned, the side of the body to be operated on and the type of anaesthesia. The surgeon, anaesthetist and other members of the team confirm the details. This brief pause, known as ‘timeout’, may take only a few minutes. But it is one of several layers of checks designed to prevent a potentially devastating mistake.
This exercise is an example of what Syed Mohammed Ghouse, consultant robotic and transplant surgeon, Asian Institute of Nephrology and Urology, described as the ‘Swiss cheese mechanism’, in which several layers of checks are put in place so that if one safety barrier fails, another can detect the error before it reaches the patient.
The need for such multiple safeguards is at the heart of World Patient Safety Day, observed on September 17. The World Health Organisation’s theme for 2026 is ‘Safe care for noncommunicable diseases’.
Doctors say patient safety has to be viewed much more broadly than preventing an obvious surgical or medication error. Ranga Reddy Burri, president, Infection Control Academy of India, said the understanding of patient safety has now expanded considerably: the responsibility cannot rest only with doctors and nurses. Policymakers, accreditation agencies, patients, caregivers, families, communities and even housekeeping staff have roles to play. “A hospital just having an accreditation doesn’t actually guarantee the kind of safety that is required,” Dr. Burri said, stressing the need to train all stakeholders involved in a patient’s journey.
Where it begins
Patient safety begins even before treatment starts, notes Dr. Burri. The availability of sophisticated diagnostic equipment has not necessarily solved the problem of ensuring an accurate diagnosis. “The diagnosis quality has actually gone down over a period of time,” he said. He attributed part of the problem to doctors moving away from basic clinical examination, including auscultation, percussion, palpation and physical examination. He described the emerging situation as ‘no touch’ healthcare, where doctors can sometimes begin looking at a computer even before adequately engaging with the patient.
Neurologist Sudhir Kumar of Apollo Hospitals, Hyderabad, also pointed to the importance of ensuring quality of medical education as the number of medical colleges and seats increases. “If we don’t ensure quality services, then it will worsen the patient’s safety because diagnosis may be missed; treatment may not be perfect,” he said.
Medication problems
Medication safety remains another major area of concern. Dr. Kumar said spurious and fake medicines continue to pose a patient-safety risk despite the existence of drug inspectors and regulatory checks.
Dr. Ghouse pointed to another problem of look-alike and sound-alike medicines. With a large number of pharmaceutical companies and medicines available, drugs with similar names can create opportunities for errors, particularly when medicines are handled by someone who is distracted or not sufficiently alert. He said hospitals use measures such as separate labelling and storing look-alike and sound-alike medicines away from each other, along with other quality-control measures.
Technology has reduced some types of prescription errors, but doctors say it has not eliminated them. Dr. Ghouse said typed and printed prescriptions are still not universal, especially at small clinics. Dr. Kumar said prescription errors can also occur when different doctors prescribe medicines under different brand names or when medicines from the same group are inadvertently duplicated. “For example, a patient may end up taking the same medicine twice because different brand names make it difficult to recognise that the drugs are essentially the same.”
Within hospitals
Some patient-safety risks are less dramatic but can still have serious consequences, particularly among older patients. Dr. Burri said falls in hospitals, including falls while patients are going to the bathroom or getting out of bed, can result in major injuries. “Hospitals need to ensure that their physical environments are designed to prevent slipping and other hazards.
Patient safety also extends beyond just their wards or rooms. Dr. Kumar pointed to hospital fires, electrical problems and other infrastructure-related hazards as areas that require greater attention. He said while the number of hospitals was increasing, some facilities are decades old, raising questions about who regularly audits their wiring and electrical connections.
For Dr. Burri, infection prevention and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) remain central to the patient-safety conversation. Unnecessary antibiotic administration, delayed diagnosis, unhygienic environments and non-adherence to infection-prevention and control guidelines can all contribute to the problem, he said.
These risks can become particularly important for patients with chronic diseases, who may require repeated interactions with healthcare facilities. Dr. Burri said patients with conditions such as chronic kidney disease, lung diseases and cancer may have vulnerabilities that make infection prevention an important component of safe care. “Healthcare workers and administrators therefore have a central role in ensuring that infection-control practices are followed,” he added.
Data and AI
As healthcare becomes increasingly digital, patient safety is also becoming connected to data privacy. Dr. Kumar said medical information is private, but increasing digitisation has created new risks around cybersecurity and access to medical records. He pointed to instances of hospital data breaches and leaks and said multiple categories of hospital staff may have access to digital systems for operational reasons.
Artificial intelligence is increasingly entering healthcare, but Dr. Kumar said it should remain a tool rather than become a substitute for clinical reasoning. He said there was a risk that medical students and young doctors could begin relying on AI tools too early instead of developing their own ability to analyse symptoms and arrive at differential diagnoses.
Centering the patient
For all the technology, protocols and checklists being introduced into hospitals, the doctors point to one element that cannot be removed from the equation, the patient. Dr. Burri said patients, families, caregivers and communities must understand their own role in ensuring safety.

Russia lodges protest with Japan over US Typhoon missile deployment
Russia’s Foreign Ministry says that it has sent a note to Japan over its hosting of U.S. medium-range missile systems
MOSCOW -- Russia’s Foreign Ministry said on Friday that it has made a formal protest to Japan over its decision to host U.S.-made medium-range missile systems that Moscow sees as a threat.
The Foreign Ministry said its note of protest, which was issued earlier this month, warned Tokyo that the deployment of the U.S. Typhon missile systems on the island of Kyushu threatens Russia’s security, regional peace, and stability and urged their removal.
Earlier this week, Russia's Deputy Foreign Minister Andrei Rudenko met with Akira Muto, the Japanese ambassador to Moscow, and urged Tokyo to “treat the contents of the previously sent note with the utmost seriousness,” the ministry said.
The strain follows President Vladimir Putin’s trip last month to the Kuril Islands, the Moscow-controlled Pacific archipelago that is claimed by both countries.
The Soviet Union took the islands from Japan in the final days of World War II and the ongoing dispute has prevented the countries from signing a peace treaty formally ending their hostilities. Moscow has rejected Tokyo's complaints, reaffirming that Russia’s “sovereignty and jurisdiction over the southern Kuril Islands are absolutely unshakable.”

Anamanaguchi, the band consisting of Peter Berkman, James DeVito, Luke Silas, and Ary Warnaar, are most known for their chiptune music. Like me, you might have first heard them in game soundtracks like 2010’s Scott Pilgrim vs. the World: The Game or know of their collaboration with Hatsune Miku (which even made its way into Fortnite). They’ve gone through different eras of breakneck chiptune beats and dance-y pop songs, but their 2025 album Anyway took an indie rock departure — recorded in person at the American Football house and filled with fuzzy guitars.
