If most Albertans don't want to leave Canada, where is the pro-Canada movement?
With a month to go, separatists have way more money and are dominating the online conversation
Over the last year, a steady drumbeat of polling has found again and again that most Albertans oppose separation — but based on fundraising and online chatter, you might not know that.
In a month, Albertans will head to the polls to vote on the future of the province, and the separatists occupy an outsize share of the spotlight, having raised three times the money and dominating the online conversation by as much as eight to one.
The pro-Canada side, meanwhile, remains divided, thanks largely to election finance rules that prevent collaboration, and worries about complacency. More than one federalist organizer has said that the time for persuasion is over. After an emotional and hotly-contested few months, most Albertans have dug in their heels on a position, federalists say.
The challenge now? Getting people to actually vote.
“I think the federalist side in this referendum campaign has hit a point of real unease,” says Avnish Nanda, the spokesperson for Our Alberta Advantage, which launched a new campaign to get out the vote this week. Called 5x for Canada, it features a series of tongue-in-cheek videos designed to equip people to get their friends to cast a ballot. (Slogan: Votemaxxing for Canada.)
“The separatists are just everywhere,” Nanda said.
Polling might cap support for independence at about a quarter of the province, but if a bigger proportion of separatists show up, the math gets dicey, he pointed out.
“Even if they don’t win outright, if the separatists get 30 per cent of the vote, I think Alberta is forever changed.”
Team Canada
Making the case for Canada is a patchwork of groups and individuals, including former deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk, who, along with volunteers, has spent over a year driving a maple leaf-emblazoned RV almost 40,000 kilometres around the province.
There’s a team of academics and former politicians working as a “pop-up think-tank” under the name Lead Not Leave, and Conservatives for Canada, the campaign launched by the federal party to target their own supporters. Polling suggests right-leaning voters are more likely to have separatist sympathies.
In perhaps the strangest case of odd bedfellows, rival ex-premiers Rachel Notley and Jason Kenney have joined forces for a Canadian Chamber of Commerce campaign in support of keeping Alberta in Canada. Kenney in particular has emerged as a vocal anti-separatist, who has argued that, historically, followers of the movement couldn’t “get elected to dog catcher.”
Each group has functioned mostly individually.
“I see them rowing in the same direction,” Lukaszuk said of the other groups. “But in different canoes.”
Rules keep groups separate, leaders say
But unlike the generally cohesive Yes and No campaigns in Quebec, it was never realistic — or allowed — for pro-Canada groups to unite under the same banner, says Jared Wesley, a professor of political science at the University of Alberta and a member of Lead Not Leave.
During Quebec’s referendum, each side was required to more or less co-operate under a national committee. In comparison, Alberta’s rules prevent collaboration. Campaign finance rules say groups — third party advertisers, specifically — can’t work together lest they risk running afoul of spending limits.
“Any conversation among federalists that are a part of these various groups always starts off with, ‘To be clear, we’re not co-ordinating, right?’” Wesley says with a laugh. “I mean, to be frank, the law simply does not allow us to compare notes.”
The separatists are all going to vote. Every one of them will crawl over broken glass to vote.- Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi
That means groups can’t share resources, co-ordinate events or vet each other’s public communications, he said.
In some ways, the splintered nature of the movement is an advantage, he argued.
“I think the notion that everyone should be part of one team on either side of the debate is based on an old way of political communications,” he said.
The media environment right now is very divided, Wesley said, meaning people get their information from a dizzying array of news organizations, websites and social media posts, often based on their own interests and political leanings.
Because the federalist groups are similarly varied, they speak to different parts of the population, he added.
“Some of them are partisan; some aren’t. Some of them are moderate, some are progressive, some are conservative,” he said.
“The way that our public sphere is fractured suggests that’s not a bad strategy.”
Alberta's ad campaign
There are also questions about the role — or lack thereof — of the institutional voices more common in political campaigning. Premier Danielle Smith has repeatedly said she does not want Alberta to separate, but also put the question about separatism on the ballot and has been criticized by both sides for the role she has played in the campaign so far.
This week the Alberta government launched a $4-million advertising campaign on the referendum questions, which urges viewers to “stand up for a strong and sovereign Alberta within a united Canada,” but doesn’t otherwise argue the federal case.
In an emailed statement, Smith's press secretary, Sam Blackett, said the government will use "various channels" to communicate with Albertans about the referendum questions, including online, TV, radio and social media.
"The Premier also travels across Alberta every summer and will continue speaking directly with Albertans through town halls, public events, media interviews and more," he wrote.
The prime minister has been critical of the referendum — calling it a “dangerous bluff” back in May — and recently met with Forever Canadian campaigners, but hasn’t spearheaded a campaign.
In July, Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre appointed Alberta MP Dane Lloyd as the party’s point person on the referendum, writing at the time that Lloyd’s task was “not to scold Albertans” but to “hear” them.
But the party’s third-party advertiser, Conservatives for Canada, was only registered on Sept. 4 and has yet to raise any funds. This is the official entity that allows them to raise money and take a position on the referendum under election financing rules.
In an email, a spokesperson said turnout will be key, so Lloyd had been focused on “doorknocking and roundtable discussions in addition to social media, media appearances and much more.”
The concern about turnout is being echoed across the political spectrum.
Speaking to media this week, Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said his party had been working on getting out the vote all summer, but he remained worried about motivation in the federal camp.
“The thing that worries me the most is I hear every single day, ‘Naheed, why are you so worked up about this? The separatists are never going to win,’” he said.
“The separatists are all going to vote. Every one of them will crawl over broken glass to vote."
And if the other side doesn’t also turn up, that could be a real difference, he added.
Boost in motivation
There are some signs the federalists might be beginning to stir. Vote motivation on the federalist side has had a “significant boost” in recent weeks, according to new polling data from Pollara Strategic Insights.
In order to gauge motivation, Pollara asked people whether they would wait an hour in line to vote, which, with an unprecedented 10 referendum questions on the ballot, may not be a theoretical question come October.
For the first time, their most recent numbers found those voting to stay in Canada were more eager to cast a ballot than their opponents, with 64 per cent saying they were “very motivated” to vote. What the separatists may lack in numbers they make up for in enthusiasm, and their motivation number has hovered around the 60 per cent mark all summer.
“I think that’s a notable swing,” said Dan Arnold, Pollara’s chief strategy officer.
“My sense is that the biggest reason that we’re seeing a growth in motivation among voters who want to stay in Canada is a reaction to what’s going on with Trump,” he added.
In other signs of life, Canadian singer and songwriter Jann Arden is set to headline a free unity concert in Calgary this weekend at The Confluence billed as “for everyone who calls Canada home.”
The event really snowballed in the last three weeks, says event producer Ian Menzies, with both artists and organizers volunteering their labour, the city issuing the permits and Forever Canadian chipping in funding.
“I think there’s a lot of pent up [energy],” he said. “People are feeling like they want to have a way to express their fealty to Canada and their desire for unity.”

Common problems with Google Wallet and how to fix them
What to do when payments and digital IDs don't seem to work.
Google Wallet is one of those apps that you quickly get used to having. Switching actual cards for virtual ones that let you pay for your shopping with your phone means you can ditch your physical wallet (and the clutter you're keeping in it). Once it's set up, you shouldn't really need to think about much else.
Seamless to use, or so it should be. There are problems that can make it difficult to use Google Wallet. Obvious ones, like a card that won't add, are frustrating enough, but there are other common issues you'll need to watch out for. Your phone settings, and even your bank or phone provider, might be a barrier.
Here are some of the problems that you might encounter and, if you do, what you can do to get things working again.
Your phone won't make contactless payments
You'll know if your phone isn't ready to make contactless payments if it doesn't respond when you tap it on a contactless terminal in a store while the phone is unlocked. You can check that your phone is ready to pay by opening Google Wallet, tapping your profile picture, and selecting Payment Setup. Any outstanding issues that need resolving, such as a card that hasn't finished setting up, can be fixed here. Google's built-in guide for this will help you get started.
You'll also need to enable NFC, the tech that lets your phone communicate with payment terminals, by searching for it in your phone's settings and switching it on. On a recent Samsung Galaxy smartphone, it'll be listed under Connections > NFC and contactless payments, and you'll need to make sure this slider is tapped on. You can search for NFC in the Settings app if it isn't listed there.
With your card ready, you should be able to unlock your phone and hold its back against the contactless reader for a few seconds for the contactless payment to complete. One of Google Wallet's advantages over Apple Wallet is that you shouldn't need to open the app at all to get this to work, as it'll use your default card. You can use an alternative card by swiping through to that card in the Wallet app.
Move your phone around slightly if it doesn't work the first time, as the NFC antenna might be in a different place to what you expect. Waving it quickly over the terminal isn't the right method, either: just hold it in place to give it a chance to connect.
Your case is a potential blocking point, too. Thick cases, cases made of metal, and those that include slots to hold physical cards can all block or interrupt a reader. You can always double-check if it'll block payments by simply giving it a go, but you'll probably want to do this in a store that isn't busy. If it doesn't work, remove the case, try again, and you'll know for sure if the case is the problem.
Also, keep an eye for any on-screen checks and instructions. You may need to verify if it's the first payment you've made with a contactless card. If a payment fails unexpectedly, double-check with your bank to see if the issue is separate to your digital card. You can check Google's troubleshooting guidance if you do run into issues, too.
Your bank card won't add or finish verifying
A key problem with digital cards in Google Wallet is an incomplete setup. You can only start making contactless payments if your card is set up and ready to go. Just having a physical bank card isn't a guarantee that it'll translate into support for Google Wallet, though. Not all banks support Google Wallet, and you're also going to need a card or bank account that's eligible, too.
You should check with your bank or card provider in the first instance if setup fails. You can double-check your card's eligibility online but, even if it is eligible, your bank may need to approve it, or require you to go through additional verification. Google will warn you if it couldn't finish the setup process which is usually a sign that your bank isn't accepting the request. It's worth checking if your bank has an Add to GPay option in your banking app or online account, which will give you another (approved) way to set up your card details.
Even if you do everything right, verification might still be the sticking point. You might, for instance, need to wait for a code in a text message from your bank to complete the process. If that doesn't arrive, check in with your bank, and make sure your correct details are on file. This is a common problem for people with decades-old accounts and outdated phone contact details that meant that, when they needed to verify online, they couldn't.
If your details are up-to-date, request another code, making sure to check spam and other folders. Other verification methods might be offered, depending on your bank, with phone calls and bank account code verification listed on Google's website as potential verification methods. Tap Finish Setup within the Wallet app to complete any remaining steps to use your card before you can use it.
Your phone doesn't meet security requirements
There are a couple of security conditions that your phone will need to have in place to be able to make contactless payments using Google Wallet. Google lists a few of them, but a key one is Google Play Protect certification.
You can check if your phone is certified by opening the Play Store, tapping your profile icon, then tapping Settings > About. Under Play Protect certification, you'll see Device is certified appear if you've got it. Without it, Google will block contactless payments entirely to protect your financial data. You might be able to fix this by updating Google Play services and installing any available Android system updates, too.
As a bare minimum, Google is expecting you to use basic security on your phone, such as a screen lock. A pin, pattern or password will do, as will biometrics, but you've got to have something in place so that your phone can't just be unlocked without any security measures. You might also need to unlock your phone the first time you restart to make sure you can make a contactless payment.
It gets trickier if you've tweaked your phone with an unlocked bootloader or a custom Android ROM. These can block the required checks, and you'll need to check the guidance online. For instance, privacy-focused GrapheneOS doesn't support NFC payments using Google Wallet, so you can't make contactless payments with a phone running it.
You can't add your digital ID
Struggling to add an ID pass to your Google Wallet? Your phone will need to support it, and your ID will need to come from a country that has enabled support for it, too. Again, you can find up-to-date eligibility listed on Google's website. Your phone needs to run Android 9 or later, and you'll need NFC and a screen lock enabled. You'll also need to use a personal Gmail account, as a business or custom account won't work.
How you manage this can prove problematic. Your phone needs to cleanly read your passport's NFC chip, so remove your phone case, lay your passport flat and slowly move the back of your phone over its cover or photo page. You'll also need to run through extra verification, like recording your face. This'll only work with one device at a time, so if you've already done this on another phone, you'll need to remove that pass first.
Most problems with Google Wallet only need a quick settings change, but you might need to check with your bank that your card is ready to work with it. Try to keep your physical cards handy, and don't ditch your physical ID, either, as digital IDs aren't accepted everywhere.

On Friday, the president threatened to ban CNN, MS Now, and Politico from the White House. It could have just been another one of his Truth Social fever dreams, but it turns out it’s very real. All three publications were turned away from the White House this morning, NPR reports, marking an escalation in the administration’s war on the First Amendment.
Trump treads further on free speech with new journalist bans
The president’s threat against CNN, MS Now, and Politico was real.
Politico tried to get to the bottom of it, asking why now? It reports that “many senior [White House] staff were surprised by the directive” (what’s new?), and that it was done “while chief of staff Susie Wiles was out of town.” Apparently he’s been talked down from this kind of sweeping move before, but Trump has already banned journalists from the White House. In 2025, he barred AP reporters from the White House and Air Force One; the AP sued and is still in litigation over the matter. He also revoked CNN reporter Jim Acosta’s credentials in his first term, though CNN won them back in court. Clearly, the administration is not too worried about adverse judicial rulings.
This isn’t just about a few publications in the White House. It’s part of a broader attack on journalism and the First Amendment that has exploded during Trump’s second term. The Department of Defense (now the Department of War, though that change was not authorized by Congress), has also pushed reporters out of the Pentagon. Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Friday that he “fully supports” Trump’s ban on CNN, MS Now, and Politico, blithely stating “we are grateful these outlets already chose to self-deport from the Pentagon” and echoing the president’s bullshit about fake news.
And journalism and broadcast organizations have faced repeated attack by Trump’s FCC, which is wielding its immense power against anyone who dares to question the president’s conduct. The president has proved he is willing to use almost any lever at his disposal to curb critical speech of himself and his government, which is the beating heart of the First Amendment.
The newly-banned organizations will surely challenge this measure in court, and unless our constitutional order has completely fallen apart, they’ll likely win. But that doesn’t erase the damage — the distraction, cost, and chaos that this kind of thing will cause.
Here are statements from CNN, MS Now, and Politico on the bans.
CNN:
Early today, CNN journalists were denied access to the White House grounds. CNN’s mission to report on the US government will continue regardless of any attempts to restrict physical access to the White House and other government buildings, or any other attempts to impede our journalism. We have a right under the US Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right.
We will not be deflected from our duty to hold the government and other public bodies to account, and we will continue to report on the actions and processes of this administration without fear or favor.
CNN stands fully behind our White House team.
MS Now:
Earlier this morning, MS NOW journalists were denied access to the White House grounds. The White House belongs to the American people, and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars.
MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy.
We stand firmly behind our anchors, our reporters, and our newsroom.
We will continue to report on the president, the administration, and the issues that impact the American people.
Politico, statement from Global Editor In Chief Jonathan Greenberger:
A few minutes ago, our colleague Cheyenne Haslett attempted to enter the White House to do her job as a POLITICO reporter. Secret Service denied her entry to the complex and confiscated the pass that allows her access to the White House. We stand by her and all reporters here covering the White House. As we said yesterday, we will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights.

Holocaust survivors’ heirs sue California museums for return of Nazi-looted art
‘It's our honor to take on this role on behalf of the community and use most of the proceeds to help these elderly survivors’
Two legal actions have been initiated in California by representatives and heirs of Jewish Holocaust victims seeking the recovery of paintings seized by Nazis that currently reside in renowned institutions in Auschwitz and Los Angeles.
These filings mark the first legal challenges mounted following fresh state and federal legislation designed to bolster claims in the U.S. regarding cultural property taken from Jewish families during World War II.
Filed on Monday in Los Angeles Superior Court, one action brought by the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles alongside its board chair Daniel Gryczman targets the Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena, demanding the return of "Adam and Eve," a pair of 1530 life-size panel paintings by Lucas Cranach the Elder.
A second action, submitted the same day in Los Angeles federal court by the daughters of late Holocaust survivor Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt, a California animator held at Auschwitz, demands the surrender of watercolor portraits.
The artist was coerced into creating these images of fellow captives for Josef Mengele, the Nazi doctor known as the "Angel of Death."
Spokespersons representing the institutions state that the museums retain valid legal title to the paintings and plan to maintain public displays. Specific monetary valuations are not stated in the legal complaints.
Tensions over Nazi-confiscated artwork pit the descendants of Jewish families navigating generational trauma against cultural institutions seeking to preserve material evidence from a dark historical period.
The Nazi regime carried out history's largest plunder between 1933 and 1945, stripping Jewish owners, collectors, and public institutions across Europe of more than 600,000 artistic items.
Decades later, numerous creations remain hanging in international institutions, complicating restitution efforts far beyond basic ownership disputes.
Marei von Saher, sole heir to Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, assigned her legal rights to the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, led by president and CEO Rabbi Noah Farkas.
The pair of panel works had been taken from Goudstikker's holdings by Hermann Goring, Adolf Hitler's second-in-command, before passing through several hands and ultimately being purchased in the 1960s by the Pasadena Museum of Modern Art, later renamed the Norton Simon Museum after its major benefactor.
Farkas stated that the federation intends to direct most net financial recoveries toward providing crucial assistance to approximately 2,500 Holocaust survivors residing throughout the Los Angeles region.
"These are incredibly beautiful European masterpieces stolen from a Jewish family to enrich the Nazi party and fund the war and death machine against the people," Farkas noted.
"It's our honor to take on this role on behalf of the community and use most of the proceeds to help these elderly survivors live out the last years of their lives in dignity, comfort and peace – something their family members were denied during the Holocaust."
In a statement, Marei von Saher expressed appreciation to the organization for championing her family's legal battle.
"This effort represents a meaningful step toward justice for Holocaust survivors and victims of Nazi era atrocities," she stated.
California Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel, D-Woodland Hills, drafted Assembly Bill 2867, which Gov. Gavin Newsom signed in September 2024.
The measure mandates the application of state law in cases brought by state residents or heirs attempting to reclaim art taken during the Holocaust or other persecutions.
Gabriel, co-chair of the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, authored the bill following a federal ruling allowing Madrid's state-owned Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum to retain a valuable impressionist work by Camille Pissarro.
That artwork had been confiscated from the Cassirer family by Nazi authorities in 1939. The lawsuit that catalyzed the statutory revision is scheduled for a federal court hearing in California next month.
Gabriel remarked that public institutions should "do some deep introspection on whether they want to be on the right side of history."
Responding to the suit, the Norton Simon Museum issued a statement highlighting a 2018 federal court ruling that unanimously confirmed the institution's legal ownership of the Cranach works.
The U.S. Supreme Court declined to review lower court decisions in May 2019.
According to the museum, the Cranach panels originally belonged to the Stroganoff family before being offered at an unauthorized 1931 Soviet sale in Berlin, where Goudstikker acquired them.
Following a complex chain of ownership, a Stroganoff descendant sold the works to the institution, which subsequently preserved and restored them.
"For nearly 50 years, they have been on view at the Norton Simon Museum and will continue to be accessible to the public for years to come," the museum stated.
Pawel Sawicki, representing the Auschwitz Memorial, asserted that the watercolors depicting Roma captives—painted under coercion by Gottliebova Babbitt to document Mengele's illicit medical experiments and racial studies— "must remain in the Memorial" as evidence of atrocities.
He argued they should not be categorized as "Nazi-looted art" because the artist created them under duress as an inmate without technical legal ownership.
While acknowledging the family's deep connection, Sawicki emphasized that the portraits of Roma and Sinti victims are rare surviving records of Mengele's horrific experiments and must be safeguarded as historical artifacts specific to Auschwitz.
"While fully respecting the rights of people who created some of the documents here, we are of the opinion that any loss in the collections of the Memorial will constitute irreparable harm," Sawicki said. " … The loss of even the smallest part of the documentation is an irreparable loss and blemish on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz."
Joel Greenberg, founder of Philadelphia-area non-profit Art Ashes, which assists Jewish families in tracking Nazi-stolen property, noted that beyond California's statute, President Donald Trump enacted and refreshed the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025. This legislation permanently eliminated statute-of-limitations deadlines, enabling survivors and heirs to pursue art recovery indefinitely.
Greenberg explained that the federal update allows families up to six years to pursue legal recovery from the point they identify the current possessor of their property.
"These new laws mean that technical defenses will no longer stick in court," he said. "Every case will be heard on its merits."
He added that the revised legal framework guarantees Jewish families procedural fairness and an opportunity to present ownership claims in court.
"It will make sure the stories of what happened to European Jewry is not lost and forgotten," Greenberg remarked. "The art can still be returned to the rightful owner."

Katie Zerbst was doing laundry on a Sunday morning in June when she heard a "guttural" moan. "It was the sound that makes you just drop everything and run," the 45-year-old mother told Business Insider.
Rushing into the kitchen, Zerbst found her 10-year-old daughter, Violet, covered in steaming hot, sparkly goo. Burns seared across her face, and skin from her top lip was flapping down into her mouth. Moments earlier, Violet had popped a squishy toy into the microwave for 30 seconds. She wanted to make the glittery cube more malleable so she could squish it more easily. When she pulled it out, it erupted like a volcano.
Violet ended up in the emergency room, and she isn't the only child to visit the hospital after playing with a squishy.
Business Insider reviewed dozens of incident reports, spoke to parents, and consulted doctors and regulators about the risks behind this year's biggest toy craze. Despite a spike in reports of burns and concerns about toxic exposure, oversight of squishies — slime-filled toys shaped like dumplings, fruit, ice cubes, and other cute characters — falls into a regulatory gray area, and the market is teeming with counterfeits and knockoffs.
What's in a squishy?
Squishies, with their gooey, foamy, or gel-like textures, fall into the category of "sensory toys," like fidget spinners, kinetic sand, and magnetic balls.
In recent years, the toys have gone "from zero to hero," Five Below CEO Winnie Park told investors in June. They're helping the retailer to become "America's greatest little toy store" by driving brick-and-mortar traffic, Park said on September's earnings call. Kohl's also credited the toy with a sales bump, and workers from several retailers have taken to social media with tales of over-eager customers demanding their favorite squishies. Instagram and TikTok are full of satisfying videos of hands squishing toys shaped like a strawberry or a tube of toothpaste.
However, reports from homes and hospitals across the country describe exploding and leaking toys, along with chemical smells. America's Poison Centers told Business Insider that more than half of the 11,500 reports about squishies received by its member organizations since 2024 happened in the first six months of 2026, though only a small portion of the ruptures caused severe injury.
Schylling, which manufactures the most popular squishy brand, NeeDoh, was hit with two lawsuits in July over squishy explosions that plaintiffs say resulted in severe burns. One complaint said that a NeeDoh Nice Cube, left lying on a TV stand near a window, remained cool to the touch but, when squeezed, erupted with a scalding gel that left blisters on the person's leg. Lawyers for the company declined to comment on the allegations.
The US Consumer Product Safety Commission has also seen a spike in squishy-related incident reports from shoppers and hospitals this year. A Business Insider review found about two dozen consumers describing how ruptures — due to microwaves, hot cars, and squeezing — have burned kids this year. Roughly 20 more reported strong smells emanating from the squishy toys. Hospital reports collected by CPSC showed about a dozen explosion cases in 2025, the latest year available.
One parent told the CPSC the toy didn't "just pop"; it "exploded" in February 2024 after their daughter squeezed it on her 10th birthday. This August, another reported that their 8-year-old son was squeezing his squishy normally when it ruptured. "The outer layer of the toy failed without warning, spraying the internal filling directly across my son's face and into his eyes," causing immediate "burning and distress," the report said. A February report to CPSC echoed a common complaint about a squishy that "emitted an extremely powerful and persistent chemical odor, resembling acetone or nail polish remover," which gave its owner a headache.
In response to growing public concern, the CPSC issued guidance in August, warning shoppers of serious burn hazards from intentionally or unintentionally exposing toys to heat. A spokesperson told Business Insider that these toys hit on several longstanding concerns for the agency, including the dangers of water beads and potential exposure to unsafe chemicals. As for the dangers of microwaving them? That's considered improper use, and the agency doesn't typically punish companies when consumers don't follow safety warnings, the spokesperson said.
Underlying these reports is the common frustration that squishy ingredients vary widely and often aren't listed on the packaging. NeeDoh discloses that its products, including the Nice Cube, Dream Drop, and Groovy Glob, use fairly common ingredients such as maltose sugar, cornstarch, and polyvinyl alcohol, the latter of which the brand says is non-toxic and also found in white glue.
While these ingredients are considered chemically safe, the lawsuit in California cites academic research to argue that some of these substances have thermal properties that, along with a soft polymer casing, can make scalding hot gel feel deceptively cool to the touch — until the toy pops.
The market is also rife with knock-offs, and federal safety rules are patchy. US regulations don't require independent testing and certification of toys, unless they're marketed to children under 13.
Manufacturers initially decide how to market and age-grade their products, subject to CPSC oversight. While products clearly intended for young children, such as baby pacifiers or toddler teethers, must meet stricter testing requirements, squishies can plausibly be sold as children's toys, adult stress balls, desk accessories, or collectibles. Many are marketed as products for all ages, and verifying a toy's age classification can involve a lengthy review.
That ambiguity raises a broader question: When an all-ages product becomes wildly popular with children, should it be treated as a children's toy? The CPSC says it considers not just a product's label, but also how it's designed, marketed, and reasonably understood and used by consumers when determining whether it's a children's product. That last part can change over time, and sometimes it shifts faster than regulators can keep up with.
The agency said that reputable brands typically go beyond legal requirements by seeking voluntary safety certification from independent organizations, such as ASTM International or United Laboratories, and include their logos on their packaging. An ASTM spokesperson told Business Insider the organization's standards are periodically reviewed and revised in consultation with a committee of more than 1,000 members to address new products and hazards.
The squishy market is ballooning
The Zerbst family bought their Glitter Super Squeeze at a local toy store in Queensland, Australia. After Violet's injury, they looked into the product and found that it was manufactured in China under the name Smooshos for distribution in Australia by MDI, a toy supplier. The package didn't list ingredients. It included a warning that "microwaving may cause injury to yourself and others," but that doesn't stop young children from encountering social media trends that promote microwaving them.
Our reporting found that some serious injuries happened even when the toys were used as intended, without being heated or frozen — a concern that cropped up in the CPSC complaints, the lawsuits, and in our interviews with parents of injured children.
Jodanna Bevan, a 39-year-old mom of four who lives in Wales, bought discounted dumpling-shaped squishies from Shein. In late July, her son Hudson was squeezing one of them in his playroom when it suddenly popped, spraying a thick, white, sandy substance into the 4-year-old's face. Bevan and her husband quickly washed out his eyes. When Hudson woke up at 6 a.m. the next day, they were so swollen he couldn't open them.
"He was screaming and so scared," Bevan told Business Insider.
At the hospital, Hudson had to be sedated as staff repeatedly rinsed his eyes. "It's like a torture treatment for a child," she added. While his vision doesn't seem to be affected, the experience was emotionally fraught for the family.
"You feel so guilty then as a parent, seeing them go through that," Bevan said.
Bevan threw the toy away before checking for ingredients. She doesn't think it would have helped. "Where you buy the toys in these different corner shops and whatnot, it doesn't say anything on there about what could be in them," she said.
Shein, which has since pulled the product, would not disclose the ingredients. A Shein spokesperson told Business Insider the company requires all third-party sellers to comply with local laws and its product safety standards. The spokesperson also said Shein works with multiple international testing and inspection agencies "to identify and address non-compliant products."
After the BBC covered Bevan's story, Shein emailed Bevan an apology and offered her a full refund for the squishy toys — £10.12 (a little under $14) for four, two-piece sets — plus £20 ($27) in Shein store credit.
The CPSC told Business Insider that the commission and US Customs have intercepted 96 shipments of squishy toys so far this year, preventing more than 640,000 items from entering the country because they violated various safety regulations.
"That's probably just the tip of the iceberg," said Courtney Griffin, director of consumer product safety at the Consumer Federation of America, a research and advocacy nonprofit.
The rise of online marketplaces, where international third parties sell directly to customers in the US and elsewhere, has further complicated regulators' and consumers' ability to know exactly what is in the products.
Trying to catch risky products is like playing whack-a-mole, but the feds have gotten some off the market. In early September, CPSC recalled a brand of squishy dumplings that contained water beads and posed a choking hazard if the toy ruptured. The dumplings, made in China, were distributed via Amazon. In May, the agency recalled a squishy monkey called Orb Funkee — made in China, distributed by a Canadian wholesaler — after tests revealed it may contain asbestos.
"If you are pushing for kids to just buy more, more, more of these, that certainly lends itself to the rise of dupes and counterfeits, fakes, and other unsafe things," Griffin said.
It's back-to-squishy season
Parents are braced for more squishies to enter their homes with the start of the school year. It's become a meme on TikTok — parents picking up random toys, wondering where they came from. Friends? Grandparents? Birthday party gift bags?
But for a small number of families, the fun ends in the emergency room.
"Everything's fine one instant to everything is 100% not fine the next," Kelly McElligott, a burn outreach coordinator at Loyola Medical Center in Illinois, said. "That it is all very overwhelming on top of your kid being hurt and you not knowing what the long-term prognosis is."
McElligott, who's seen around six cases this year, monitors patients for up to two years to make sure they're healing properly, physically and emotionally. Even if the surface skin looks OK, scar tissue can form beneath or cause functional issues if the scarring tightens over joints, she said.
Most squishies don't cause injuries, even when they pop. America's Poison Centers said 85% of exposure cases had no documented signs or symptoms, and 94% of those cases were managed at home or outside a healthcare facility.
"I was just scared of any lasting damage from a cult squishy"Katie Zerbst
The stories of children who have been injured have created a dilemma for parents whose kids are obsessed with them.
Summiah Hafeez's 8-year-old daughter has about 10 to 15 squishies. Two dumplings and a stick of butter are her prized possessions. Initially, Hafeez bought a couple as a reward for reading more books, but soon squishies were turning up everywhere.
"Whenever any other kid comes over, that's what she wants to show them," Hafeez, 31, who lives in Dallas, told Business Insider. "It's definitely a big thing among all kids right now."
Hafeez keeps them out of the car; the Texas heat can easily top 100 degrees in the warmer months. She's taught her daughter to store the toys on a shelf in her room, away from her 2-year-old sister, who Hafeez worries might eat them. She also doesn't allow her daughter to use the microwave for any reason.
Those who've experienced burns are taking a harder line. Bevan has purged all the squishies in the house and is trying to spread the word about their potential dangers. "All our friends have had them for their children," she said. "You've got to be aware that there could actually be some dangerous chemicals in there."
As for Violet, her mom shudders at the memory of rushing her into the shower, letting a stream of cold water run over her face and body. Zerbst said her daughter sat in the shower for 40 minutes, waiting for an ambulance to arrive. The paramedics congratulated Zerbst for her quick thinking in administering first aid.
"It was terrifying to hear Violet whimpering, but she was pretty calm and collected on the whole," the mom said. "I was just scared of any lasting damage from a cult squishy that seemed so harmless and fun."

At 8.37am local time last Wednesday, a huge mass of rock and ice sheared free from a mountain, sliding 1,200 metres to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, about 60km north of the country’s capital, Kathmandu.
Horrifying images and videos soon emerged of a torrent of mud, water and debris that swept down the Lhende Khola valley at speeds approaching 150km/h. Flowing down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers that run between Tibet and Nepal, the flood water swept away homes, roads, bridges and power plants. Along the Trishuli, water levels rose by as much as nine metres in half an hour. As of the time of writing, the death toll of the disaster approached 1,000 people, with more than 4,400 on both sides of the border missing.
As the rescue effort continued – hampered by bad weather, poor access and the threat of further flooding due to two lakes that have formed after the landslide – Nepali prime minister Balendra Shah said the catastrophe was “not an ordinary” event.
Shah said on social media that “the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change … It is now time for us to strongly raise with the international community the issue of the disasters we are experiencing as a result of climate change.”
More on the scale of this disaster and what it tells us about our climate crisis, after this week’s headlines.
In focus
What caused last week’s catastrophe was not immediately clear: initial reports suggested the floods could have been caused by an earthquake in the area that triggered a landslide, while early satellite imagery suggested that a glacial collapse was to blame. Subsequent satellite analysis showed that bedrock underneath a glacier collapsed, with the landslide registering as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
“It seems that a massive rock face with the glacier on top of it has essentially gone,” says Adrian McCallum, a senior lecturer in geotechnical engineering at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Australia. One seismologist called the landslide “one of the largest in the last decade or two in the world”.
As Nepal’s Shah said in his statement, our environmental crisis cannot be separated from this disaster. The Himalayas – spanning Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan – are warming twice as fast as the global average, putting the region at increased risk of avalanches, landslides and floods. The UN said in 2023 that Nepal’s mountains had lost close to one-third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.
While scientists haven’t definitively linked the Lhende Khola landslide to the climate crisis, they have pointed out that rising temperatures mean permanently frozen mountain slopes are at risk of melting and destabilising.
“Increased temperatures result in increased melt, which results in increased water,” McCallum says. “Movement of water into voids within either soil or rock … destabilises what once may have been a more solid rock mass or soil environment.”
With global heating, mountainous areas are also at risk of permafrost degradation, “glacial lake outburst floods” (GLOFs), and increasingly erratic rainfall, raising flood and landslide risk.
Glacial lakes form behind natural dams as a result of glacier melt, and can cause catastrophic outburst floods if their natural dam walls are breached. More than 12,000 deaths have been attributed to such floods globally.
Given the risks to downstream communities in the Himalayas, scientists have pointed to the need for early warning systems, which would require coordinated international monitoring efforts.
“Wherever the glaciers are receding … you have the potential for a GLOF to occur,” McCallum says, such as in the European Alps and the South American Andes. In North America, an outburst flood causes periodic problems in Juneau, the capital of Alaska.
To be clear, there was no GLOF involved in last week’s landslide. But Nepal has more than 2,000 glacial lakes, and 21 of those, according to the UN, are considered potentially dangerous.
As climate academic Bill McGuire wrote for the Guardian this week, global heating will “leave no part of the planet untouched. As the world processes the horror of the events in Nepal and Tibet, it is a lesson that we ignore at our peril.”

Although Ed Sheeran has no more openers on his Loop Tour, at least one artist is coming to his defense after dropping Macklemore over his pro-Palestine remarks.
On Friday, after departing the tour, Aaron Rowe defended Sheeran for his “human f*cking error” in caving to Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft‘s demand that he remove Macklemore from the tour, arguing that instead, people should be “using this opportunity to plaster Robert Kraft’s face everywhere.”
“I’m gonna be honest, I think you are all focusing on the wrong person here. All I keep hearing is Ed Sheeran this, Ed Sheeran that, but you really should be focusing on the likes of Robert Kraft,” he began in the video on Instagram. “You really should be focusing on the zionist lobbies that are trying to silence the voices of people who are shouting about genocide, the genocide that is happening in Palestine right now, by Israel.
Watch on Deadline
“Look, I know Ed’s statement could have been a lot better, and I do think that Macklemore shouldn’t have been pulled off the tour. I fully believe it was panicked stations over there, and they rushed to a decision because they didn’t know what to do, because they were getting it from all angles.”
Rowe continued, “That’s a mistake from a person. And I haven’t had a chance to fucking talk to Ed too much, but I fully believes he knows that was a mistake.”

After calling out the Irish government’s role in the Israel-Hamas conflict, Rowe turned his attention back to Kraft, urging others to do the same.
“In the music industry, within the media, there are people with so much money and fucking power, that they’re able to basically shut down any opinion they don’t agree with. Louisiana firefighters responding to a small house blaze found a wildcat native to sub-Saharan Africa illegally enclosed in the back yard, and an animal welfare agency is now seeking to place the creature in an appropriate environment, according to officials.
Firefighters investigating a report of a minor fire at a home in the suburban New Orleans community of Marrero on Tuesday spotted the cat in question – an African serval – behind the residence in a chain-linked enclosure resembling a cramped baseball batting cage, a spokesperson for the local animal protection services said.
A statement from Jefferson protection and animal welfare services (JPaws) said its director, Michelle Brignac, and humane department supervisor, Victoria Clark, joined firefighters at the scene after they were summoned there. Local laws require an exotic animal permit to legally keep a serval as a pet, and the owner of the home at the center of the case did not have such a document, JPaws spokesperson John McCusker told the Guardian on Thursday.
The statement said Brignac and Clark therefore “subdued the hissing serval and wrangled it” into a transport carrier from its 9ft-by-9ft (7.53-sq-meter) cage that McCusker likened to “a dog kennel”. Brignac and Clark then brought the serval to the JPaws facility in the nearby community of Harvey, according to the statement from the agency, which also shared vivid photographs of the wildcat.
Beside their black spots, svelte physiques and striking facial features, servals are known for their ability to leap as high as about 7ft (2 meters) in the air. So McCusker said JPaws gave the serval an entire room to itself while the agency sought an appropriate refuge for the wildcat, which was born in captivity but whose natural habitat is African grasslands.
Servals share some similarities with domesticated cats that make them immensely popular as pets, including their affinities for grooming themselves, purring, yowling and stalking potential prey.
Nonetheless, they are not easily sustained pets, JPaws’ statement maintained. Servals in captivity do not have the physical space and stimulation needed to engage in normal, healthy behaviors, and they endure chronic stress as a result, the agency’s statement said.
They mark their territory, become aggressive as they mature, cannot be fully house-trained and destroy furniture, and they have been known to barge through walls and doors, according to JPaws. Experts also say servals require a diet and specialized care beyond what house cats need, making them a major responsibility.
JPaws’ statement said the agency would explore having the serval held temporarily at New Orleans’ Audubon zoo. A zoo spokesperson, however, said the institution did not plan to take the serval in and understood JPaws was looking into another arrangement, the details of which were not immediately available on Thursday.
The Marrero serval was the latest of several indicators of the wildcats’ growing popularity, a boom driven in part by social media content creators showing them in videos online.
Cases involving servals have also tended to generate widely read news headlines in North America.
That happened in Ohio in 2023, when officials in the Cincinnati area captured an African serval named Amiry that was spotted in a Cincinnati neighborhood tree and later tested positive for cocaine.
In late 2025, a search for an African serval that escaped a Pennsylvania wildlife center culminated in heartbreak after a motorist fatally struck the wildcat, as Philadelphia’s NBC News affiliated reported.
And the news outlet People reported on authorities in the Canadian city of Vancouver returning an African serval to its owners after it escaped and nestled under a neighbor’s porch in June.
The British Columbia province to which Vancouver belongs had just banned keeping exotic cats such as African servals as pets. But, People reported, the owners of such cats were given until the beginning of May 2027 to apply for permits to legally possess them.

First there was a moment of stunned silence. Then, in the Sala Grande, the main screening hall of the Venice film festival within the Palazzo del Cinema, the audience stood almost as one and turned to applaud the film-makers for 25 minutes.
The film the audience had watched for 80 harrowing minutes was the Gaza documentary NAZA, which has been produced by the Guardian.
The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to the civilians expected to be killed in a military attack.
Unfolding against the background of Tel Aviv at night, the participants – intelligence officers and other soldiers – describe a series of systems, some powered by AI, that select the thousands who should die in strikes, often at night and surrounded by their families.
Perhaps most challenging for Israel’s political elite is that it is a story told exclusively in Hebrew by 24 anonymised Israeli military insiders, many of them from elite units.
The documentary depicts a wide variety of viewpoints that all lead to the same conclusion: participation in a programme of mass killing where there were few boundaries between combatant and civilian, in a war where more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed. Some describe being shamed by their experience. Some are neutral. Others describe excitement, and a sense of “fun” as they justify their actions.
It will open in US cinemas from 30 September, with international distribution plans to be announced shortly. The ripples of ovation gathered in volume among the few who have seen the film before its New York premiere, but in Israel the film provoked a very different response.
Rightwing political figures have rushed to accuse its directors – the Oscar-winning Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor – of “treason”. The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has long harboured an antipathy to critical media, declared on Wednesday he would seek new laws to strip citizenship from people who he said “smear” Israeli soldiers.
Demonstrators and members of far-right groups went further still, calling for violence against the pair and the demolition of their homes. Outside Szor’s parents’ house in central Israel, protesters called for the “death penalty for traitors”.
An editorial in the left-leaning newspaper Haaretz warned that their lives were credibly endangered. Dozens of human rights and peace organisations in Israel rallied to defend the film-makers, as did international press freedom organisations.
The whiplash ferocity of the response, even in the midst of a febrile election campaign where Israeli attitudes to the war in Gaza are a central issue, has surprised even those in the Israeli leftwing and human rights community who have long been on the receiving end of such denunciations.
The pushback to the documentary is both a testament to its power and evidence of how the Israeli right is exploiting a film, as yet unseen by most, to craft its own version of what it says it represents.
Critics in Israel seized on the longstanding idea that Israelis should not criticise their country in front of foreign audiences.
Ofer Winter, a controversial former rightwing army officer turned politician, told an election rally for his People of Israel in Rishon LeZion: “An Israeli citizen, a Jew, receives thunderous applause for going out and smearing and defaming his own people.
“I understand that you are afraid to return to Israel,” he taunted the directors. “You are right. You have nothing to return to. It is a disgrace and a shame to return after you spat in the faces of your own people.”
The rightwing journalist Yehuda Schlesinger of Channel 14, a station regarded as being a mouthpiece for Netanyahu, went further still, saying Abraham and Szor should be “pursued” and “hunted”, prevented from returning to Israel, and describing the ovation in Venice as “25 minutes of antisemitic applause”.
By Wednesday, Netanyahu had decided to weigh in, announcing he would promote two bills to legislate against the “defamation” of Israeli soldiers and the state of Israel.
“We will revoke citizenship for anyone who defames IDF soldiers around the world – he will be deeply hurt in his pocket.”
At points, the threats of violence have been realised.
On Wednesday, the journalist Haggai Matar, a director of the left-leaning independent +972 Magazine and Sicha Mekomit (Local Call), where Abraham’s first reporting on the allegations appeared in collaboration with the Guardian, said their offices had been broken into by rightwing activists who had filmed the intrusion.
“The discussion about NAZA has been a million times more prominent than the UK sanctions announcement,” said Dahlia Scheindlin, an Israeli political and polling expert who writes a column for Haaretz, adding that the right was exploiting the current inability of Israelis to see the film and make their own judgment.
“While it is unseen, it can be turned into something electorally potent that at present Israelis aren’t able to demystify.”
The film has also arrived in the midst of a markedly worsening atmosphere towards dissenting views, acute since Hamas’s deadly attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, with the film challenging a long-held expectation that Israel’s media self-censor in times of conflict.
As Israel has become increasingly isolated internationally over both Gaza, where an independent UN inquiry found Israel continues to commit genocide, and growing settler violence in the occupied West Bank, the film also appears to have touched a more complex nerve in Israel’s collective psyche.
Israel’s forthcoming elections in October have acted as an accelerant for the country’s rightwing parties, whose language has become more hardline and extreme under Netanyahu’s far-right coalition.
Human rights activists, critical journalists, the left more broadly and even the notion of an independent judiciary have long been presented as an enemy within by the far right, who appear to be seeking to weaponise the film against a wider community of critics of Israel and its military.
The extreme response from Netanyahu and his allies has itself been condemned.
The Yedioth Ahronoth columnist Nahum Barnea described the calls to strip the film-makers of their citizenship as “delusional”.
The former editor-in-chief of the Jerusalem Post, Yaakov Katz, wrote: “Not only does such a move not make Israel look stronger, but it creates the impression that we have something to hide and are afraid of criticism. It makes it seem like we fear to stand up for our truth and what we believe in.”
And for Haaretz’s Etan Nechin, who saw the film at a press screening in New York earlier this week, the reaction to NAZA is a symptom of a serious malaise.
“In a healthy democracy, NAZA would be shown on the evening news, its allegations would cause a public outrage and the state would promise a thorough investigation,” he wrote. “Instead, following the film’s Venice premiere, Abraham and Szor have effectively been pushed into exile.”

European governments have discussed imposing a bloc-wide windfall tax on energy companies, as near-record fuel and gas prices pile pressure on leaders desperate to contain mounting public discontent and the challenge of the far right.
With elections due next year in eight EU countries including France, Italy, Spain and Poland, leaders are scrambling to head off the potential fallout from what analysts have warned could be one of the continent’s biggest energy shocks in decades.
Germany’s finance minister, Lars Klingbeil, called on the European Commission at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday to propose possible ways to tax what he described as the excessive profits of oil companies.
“Several member states have been calling for models for a long time,” Klingbeil said, demanding proposals by next month. “People can see how oil companies are exploiting the situation, overcharging and significantly increasing their profits.”
Oil futures have climbed back above $100 a barrel, about 50% higher than before the Iran war, as escalating attacks across the Middle East threaten more supply routes. Derivatives markets suggest traders do not expect a near-term drop in prices.
Pump prices have already reached all-time highs across Europe. In Germany, diesel prices surged to a record average of €2.45 a litre on Wednesday, while petrol hit a fresh high of €2.31 a litre, according to Europe’s largest motoring association, ADAC.
Prices are even higher in the Netherlands, where petrol eclipsed last week’s record high to reach €2.73 a litre on Wednesday, with diesel at an average €2.78 a litre. Prices have risen higher still for petrol in Denmark and for diesel in Finland.
Across the EU, petrol prices are 24% higher than a year earlier, while diesel is up 38% and jet fuel costs more than 100% more. Benchmark gas is trading at €81 a megawatt hour, up 150% on a year earlier, with analysts suggesting it could hit €100.
The EU’s economic commissioner, Valdis Dombrovskis, has said the commission has no plans “at this stage” for an EU-wide taxing mechanism, but stressed it was “ready to engage in discussion” and member states were free to impose their own taxes.
Sky-high fuel prices are already a major domestic political issue in France and Italy, both of which next year face crunch elections in which voters’ concerns are likely to be dominated by the soaring cost of living, driven largely by high energy prices.
In Italy, Giorgia Meloni’s ruling rightwing coalition, trailing rivals in the polls, said this week it would scrap road tax for 14.5m cars and motorbikes from next year at a cost of over €2bn, on top of a cut to diesel duty that has already cost €2.8bn.
“We have chosen to redirect a portion of the resources used to address rising fuel prices into a simple, structural measure designed especially for those who use cars and motorcycles every day to work, take their children, or get around,” Meloni said.
France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, told ministers he wanted the government’s “full mobilisation” on fuel supply and prices, including efforts to secure supplies internationally by working toward the “peaceful reopening” of the strait of Hormuz.
In the latest of a wave of protests, French fishers blocked access to two ports and a fuel depot in southern France on Thursday over soaring diesel prices that this week rose to €2.37 a litre, just below their record of €2.38.
The fisheries minister, Catherine Chabaud, said the fishers had agreed after six hours of talks to lift the blockades after a promise that those with cashflow issues would be granted zero-interest loans and support measures would to be tied to fuel price changes.
The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, this week extended emergency fuel subsidies until the end of the year for the agriculture, fishing and construction sectors. But the government is reluctant to step in to cut fuel prices for all.
“Blanket measures that affect everyone – including those who don’t need them – are a false economy,” the country’s finance minister, Roland Lescure, told journalists earlier in the week. “Why? Because ultimately, we’ll have to fund them.”
In August, Spain doubled its diesel tax discount to €0.20 a litre from 1 September after diesel prices jumped by 15.7% in July, while in Germany, the embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz, announced a fuel tax cut late on Friday.
Taxes on petrol and diesel would be cut by by €0.17 from 1 October until the end of the year, the government said, as well as holding talks with the oil industry with the aim of introducing a cap on fuel prices by 1 January 2027 at the latest.
“Anyone who relies on their car every day is reaching breaking point,” Merz said in a statement. “We are showing that we are resilient in the face of the crisis and are helping our citizens,” he added.
Merz’s centre-right CDU was this month heavily defeated in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt by the far-right AfD, and two more state elections this weekend are likely to bring further gains for the far-right party, which has campaigned on a platform of a return to the cheap Russian gas imports Europe largely abandoned after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Syrian regime planned American journalist's kidnapping for weeks
American journalist Austin Tice, who disappeared in Syria in 2012, was kidnapped in a calculated operation that was undertaken over several weeks, according to new reporting from the BBC and NPR.
A member of the group that detained Tice has also claimed the abduction was sanctioned by Syria's leader at the time, President Bashar al-Assad.
Tice was last seen outside of captivity in August of 2012, by rebel fighters, getting into a car with a driver he knew and trusted. For years, many assumed the car had simply stumbled upon a government checkpoint, and that the abduction of the journalist was opportunistic.
New evidence uncovered by reporters Joshua Baker and Sara Obeidat, and included in the podcast series Where is Austin Tice?, from BBC Radio 4 and NPR's Embedded, shows Tice's disappearance was anything but chance.
Baker and Obeidat spoke to members of the Assad regime about Tice's detention, and reviewed recordings of a discussion about his abduction involving a senior regime officer.
One of the people they spoke to, a man named Abu Ali who served in the National Defense Force (NDF), a militia loyal to Assad, said the operation to abduct the journalist began with Tice's driver — a man Tice appeared to have trusted but who had been passing information to the regime. According to Ali, the driver told senior NDF member Sakr Rustom that an American journalist was moving through rebel-held areas and reporting on the opposition.
Tice had pushed into areas of Syria that few journalists had gone to and his reporting was published on the front page of the Washington Post. The Assad regime, meanwhile, was cracking down on anyone revealing its human rights abuses.
Rustom was not just any NDF militia contact — he was the nephew of Bassam al-Hassan, head of the NDF and one of Assad's most trusted security figures. Hassan was also a major general in the Republican Guard.
According to Ali, the information on Tice was passed up to Hassan, who, in turn, shared it with Assad.
And Assad replied: "Bring him to us," Ali said in an interview.
Ali says he was subsequently called into Hassan's office and told the president had approved the operation.
Tice, a student at Georgetown Law who earlier had served as a captain in the U.S. Marines, traveled to Syria in 2012 to become a freelance war reporter.
When Assad's government fell a dozen years later, Tice's friends and family hoped he would emerge from the regime's prisons.
Where is Austin Tice? tells the story of a multi-year investigation by Baker and Obeidat into the disappearance of the American freelance reporter. His case has been followed closely by international media and cited by successive U.S. presidents.
Shortly after the Assad government collapsed in 2024, the BBC uncovered secret Syrian intelligence files on Tice — hundreds of pages of internal records that provided definitive proof the regime once held the journalist.
But what was less clear was how exactly Tice had been taken in the first place, and who was responsible for his abduction.
Tice was living and traveling with rebel Syrian fighters in the days before his disappearance. According to several people interviewed in Where is Austin Tice?, including Syrian officials and a fellow journalist, Tice sometimes shared his Marine Corps training in weapons and tactics with the rebels.
Several former members of the Syrian regime have told Baker and Obeidat that Tice's activity and his profile as a former Marine caused Syrian authorities to suspect the American was not a journalist, but some type of operative for the CIA or another agency. American officials deny this.
On Aug. 11, 2012, Tice celebrated his 31st birthday at a rebel safehouse in Daraya, a suburb on the western edge of Damascus, just a few miles from Assad's presidential palace. In a tweet posted that same day, he described celebrating in a swimming pool, with rebel fighters, Taylor Swift music and whiskey. "Hands down, best birthday ever," Tice wrote.
According to Ali, when Tice's driver came to pick him up, the driver took Tice to a government facility in Tahouneh, on the outskirts of Damascus, where Hassan had an office. Ali says the driver told him that as they pulled up to the facility's gates, he pulled a gun on Tice.
For years, the identity of the driver remained a mystery in Tice's case. The BBC and NPR spoke to more than 20 people following leads and eventually the trail led to the Syrian city of Homs, and the family of a man named Hamid Abu Obeid.
Multiple members of Abu Obeid's family confirmed he was the man who drove Tice away and was involved in his abduction, an account also supported by multiple former members of the NDF militia. But by the time Baker and Obeidat identified him, Abu Obeid had disappeared. Members of his family say they do not know where he is and fear for his safety.
But they did offer a possible hint at his motivation. The Abu Obeid family are Palestinian refugees from Gaza, living in relative poverty in Syria, and according to Hamid's brother, he had been promised a passport, Syrian citizenship, a house, and a weapon in return for delivering Tice. But after the abduction, the family says all he got was a Glock pistol. The family says they were not aware of Hamid's intention to kidnap Tice and learned about it afterward.
After Assad's regime fell, Abu Obeid's wife says he received a phone call from a man who knew about his involvement in Tice's case and was threatening to tell the U.S. embassy, hoping it might help the caller secure asylum. She says Abu Obeid urged him not to. He then took some money, told his wife he was going shopping, and she says she has not seen Hamid since.
A few days later, his wife said, masked men — some dressed in military clothes — came to the family's home and took a number of Abu Obeid's possessions, including his laptop and other electronic devices. She said she does not know if her husband is in hiding, or something worse.

Japan’s welfare ministry has begun considering a plan to raise nursing care insurance premiums for high-income earners age 65 or older from fiscal 2027.
The proposal was submitted to a subcommittee of the Social Security Council, which advises the welfare minister, on Friday. The review comes as higher public pension payments burden low-income earners with higher nursing care insurance premiums.
Premiums for those age 65 or older are calculated by multiplying a base figure set by local governments and by a rate determined by their incomes. In fiscal 2024 to fiscal 2026, the nationwide average of the base figure stood at ¥6,225 per month.
There are 13 rates, ranging from 0.285 to 2.4, with lower rates applying to people with lower incomes. Increases in pension payments, reflecting inflation, are causing low-income earners to qualify for higher rates, resulting in higher premiums.
Under the latest proposal, the ministry plans to raise the highest rate, applied to people with annual incomes of ¥7.2 million or more. It also plans to divide lower-income brackets into smaller categories to curb sharp increases in premiums when people move into a higher rate bracket.
The subcommittee is expected to discuss the plans and reach a decision by the end of the year.

For a long time, fungal infections have meant itchy skin, discoloured nails and sometimes hair loss.
These symptoms are collectively called dermatophytosis and are caused by a group of fungi called dermatophytes.
‘’Unfortunately, immunocompromised patients can get lesions all over their body. The itchiness and the lesions can get so severe that people even get suicidal thoughts,” said Shivaprakash Rudramurthy, professor of medical mycology at the Postgraduate Institute of Medical Education and Research (PGIMER), Chandigarh.
Global warming
Dermatophytes are molds: fungi that grow in long strands. The other common category of fungi is yeast, which are single, oval-shaped cells. Among the yeasts, Candida auris is rapidly emerging as a multidrug resistant pathogen in ICU facilities. It enters the blood stream and causes severe infections, most of which are untreatable by the available antifungals. According to Prof. Rudramurthy, those infected suffer a 30-40% mortality rate.
C. auris has become a menace only in the last two decades. The first report was in 2009 in Japan. Several other fungal species have become more pathogenic only in recent times. The cause of this rise remains unresolved but scientists and medical doctors have some ideas.
Fungi grow best in damp places below 30° C, so they can grow on our skin, especially in moist areas of the body, like armpits and the genital area. However, bloodstream infections in humans were rare because they could not survive in the body’s 37° C temperature.
“Fungal infections are common in cold-blooded animals with lower body temperatures,” Sriram Varahan, a mycologist at CSIR-Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, Hyderabad, said.
“But global warming puts a selective pressure on fungi such that only the more heat-tolerant ones survive. These ones can survive inside our bodies too, if they gain access to it. This is called the fungal infection — mammalian selection hypothesis.”
Clinical samples
Today, roughly 20% of infections reported in hospitals are fungal in nature — yet most hospitals in India lack the capabilities and infrastructure to identify fungal pathogens, Prof Rudramurthy said.
This prompted PGIMER to begin storing fungal pathogens some 25 years ago. Today, the institute holds a stock of 15,000 clinical fungal isolates across India and helps other medical centres and clinicians identify and culture them for study, free of cost.
The C. auris isolates from PGIMER’s repository have come handy for Kaustuv Sanyal and his research associate Aswathy Narayanan, both at the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research, Bengaluru. They study how fungal pathogens divide and their genomes evolve.
In a recent study published in Nature Communications, they characterised the clinical isolates of C. auris found across India. Their focus was the pathogen’s ability to resist antifungals. They were able to establish their findings in patient samples and go beyond earlier studies in model systems.
“More than 90% clinical isolates of C. auris are resistant to common azole-based antifungals, such as fluconazole,” Prof. Sanyal said. Some “30% of them are resistant to another class of antifungals called the polyenes. They mostly respond to a different class of antifungals called the echinocandins.”
A drug may not work on a pathogen for many reasons, including the drug’s target becoming mutated or the drug’s effect being negated by the pathogen’s own biomolecules. Dr. Narayanan and her collaborators at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Thiruvananthapuram, found significant changes in drug-resistant C. auris genomes that could explain why Indian clinical isolates were able to resist azoles and echinocandins.
Susceptibility tests
A fungal cell has two protective layers surrounding it. The outermost is the cell wall and the inner one is the cell membrane. Azole and polyene antifungals target a fat called ergosterol that is enriched in the cell membrane. Echinocandins target the cell wall.
“When we grow C. auris isolates in the presence of fluconazole, the pathogen fights back by making extra copies of the Erg 11 gene. This in turn helps in higher production of ergosterol, thereby eliminating the effect of the azole drug,” Dr Narayanan said.
The study found parts in the C. auris genome where additional copies of the Erg11 gene were present.
With echinocandin drugs such as caspofungin, the team found mutations in the Fks1 gene that allowed the pathogen to resist the drug’s action. The team also found genetic changes promoting higher tolerance of echinocandins.
“Fks1 mutations can enable C. auris to survive even caspofungin doses up to 16 ug/ml. That means a patient with such a pathogen will need the drug at a concentration higher than 16 ug/ml,” Prof. Sanyal said. “Today, clinicians would not know that because they test the pathogen’s ability to survive only until 2 µg/mL of caspofungin — as defined by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and followed globally.”
The logical thing for clinicians would be to look for mutations like in the Fks1 gene and decide the limits for tests to decide the antifungal dose for patients. But due to associated costs, a more practical way is to increase the limits of susceptibility tests for caspofungin to higher than 16 ug/ml, Prof. Sanyal added.
C. auris, without any specific gene mutation or gene duplication, still responds to high concentrations of caspofungin in unexpected ways. While the pathogen dies at lower concentrations of the drug, at exceptionally high ones, it survives. This is paradoxical.
“This is because caspofungin at high doses activates compensatory pathways in the fungus,” Prof. Sanyal explained. “The fungus starts producing chitin, the raw material of the fungal cell wall, in large quantities. Any damage that caspofungin brings about on the cell wall is compensated by the extra chitin production. And thus the cell wall remains intact despite the antifungal.”
Such examples of paradoxical growth are called the Eagle effect, named for the U.S. pathologist Harry Eagle.
Beyond the arms race
The studies underline the importance of clinicians conducting more nuanced susceptibility tests to decide the antifungal doses. They show that fungi are protected from antifungals by genetic mutations as well as by making more copies of protective genes.
Prof. Sanyal also stressed on the need for a combination of therapies to target cellular compensatory pathways, keeping the major antifungals effective against drug-tolerant species.
However, Dr. Varahan said he believed scientists and doctors need to think of gentler alternatives: “When we target [a molecule] without which an organism cannot live at all, evolution ensures that its population survives with a changed molecule. So instead of participating in an arms race, it is perhaps better to target the less critical molecular pathways, inhibition of which will allow the pathogen to still survive but not cause a disease.”
It seems the idea of dousing fungal pathogens with antifungals is nearing its end. The next-generation of antifungals will need more planning.
Somdatta Karak heads science communication at CSIR-CCMB.

Why is Kishore Kumar biography classified as 'best cinema book'? HC asks Centre
A Patna-based petitioner has reportedly challenged the ‘Best Book on Cinema’ award to singer Kishore Kumar's biography in the High Court.
Two years after a biography on legendary Indian musician Kishore Kumar was awarded the ‘Best Book on Cinema’ at the National Film Awards, a petition has challenged the title in Patna High Court.
‘Kishore Kumar: The Ultimate Biography’, authored by Anirudha Bhattacharjee and Parthiv Dhar, and published by HarperCollins, was given the Best Book on Cinema title at the 70th National Film Awards on August 16, 2024.
According to an Indian Express report, a Patna-based petitioner has now challenged the honour in the High Court, alleging that the eligibility criteria for choosing the pick for the title was not followed.
Justice Ajit Kumar heard the petition on Thursday and issued notices to the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting and the National Film Development Corporation (NFDC).
Both bodies have been asked to explain how the biography was chosen as the Best Book on Indian cinema.

Who filed the petition?
The petition was reportedly filed by Anant Prasad Sinha, a Hindi writer and literary critic. He has sought to quash the honour given to the Kishore Kumar book which was presented at New Delhi’s Vigyan Bhawan on October 8, 2024.
His petitions says that a notification published on August 7, 20204, just days before the award for the Kishore Kumar biography were announced had guidelines to choose the best book for nomination in the 70th National Film Awards.
He alleges that those guidelines were violated.
Based on the plea, the high court issued notices to the MIB and NFDC. “At this stage, Senior Panel Counsel for the Union of India seeks three weeks’ time to file a specific counter-affidavit addressing the grievances raised by this petitioner,” the bench was quoted as saying by IE.
