I found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and I want others to do the same
- Published
Mary Timby was fed up with dating apps when she booked a trip to Ireland on a whim last summer - from the comfort of her Colorado couch.
The spur-of-the-moment trip was unlike her: Timby, 39, is a self-described "total planner".
But she'd always wanted to visit Ireland, and she found herself exhausted by the local dating scene while navigating a career transition. And then she remembered a few throwaway lines from a comedy series about a matchmaking festival in Ireland.
So she looked it up - and not only was the Lisdoonvarna Matchmaking Festival real, it was also taking place during the entire month of September, when she was scheduled to visit.
Now, a little more than a year later, Timby is reaping the benefits of that uncharacteristic last-minute decision: She's become a viral star. She's found love with an Irishman she met at a pub called The Matchmaker. And she's even started a new business venture - bringing others to Lisdoonvarna who hope to follow in her footsteps.
"It's really about enjoying County Clare, enjoying the festival, and, if you meet someone, you do - and that's what happened with us," says Timby, smiling at her partner, Jason Mangan, sitting beside her.
They're speaking from the windswept coastal cottage they rented together for the summer in his native County Clare - about 20 miles (32 km) southwest of Lisdoonvarna, the site of their first fortuitous meeting.
'Mary, your video is going viral'
From the outset, Timby's inaugural Ireland trip seemed to take on a life of its own.
She filmed a short video on the plane before her flight took off, telling her approximately 300 TikTok followers that she was heading on an off-the-cuff trip to an Irish matchmaking festival - and didn't "know what's going to happen".
Timby then "turned my phone on airplane mode, then spent about eight hours on the flight (and) woke up at Shannon Airport," she says.
When she turned on her phone, "it was blowing up".
A group of friends had texted her. "They said, 'Mary, your video is going viral,'" she says. "I didn't even have notifications on for social media."
She rented a manual transmission car - horrified to find the gear stick on the left side of the driver's seat - and set off through County Clare to her accommodation at an Irish family's home.
Then she headed to Lisdoonvarna, where she saw firsthand that the festival is a whole-town, month-long celebration of conversation and dancing, rather than a line of singles waiting to be set up by a sage local matchmaker.
That's changed since the festival's origins 170 years ago, when bachelor farmers and moneyed visitors would flock to the spa town of Lisdoonvarna to bathe in its mineral-rich waters and socialise. Generations of matchmakers would ply their trade to set up successful marriages, and word spread. Now, while the town's year-round residents number fewer than 1,000, that number swells up to 80,000 each September as revellers descend upon Lisdoonvarna from around the world.
Third-generation matchmaker Willie Daly still holds court at his nearby home and at festival events, and Timby even visited him during her trip - when he put her on the phone to random men whose accents she struggled to understand.
But the real magic of contemporary Lisdoonvarna lies in the town's overflowing streets and pubs - as Timby soon found out.
Her first night in town was "a little slow," she admits - and Timby was tired and jet-lagged. She retired to her room and spent the next day sightseeing, but the Irish woman running her accommodation convinced her to try Lisdoonvarna again that night.
"My AirBnB host said, 'You should go back tonight, because I heard that the younger folks come out at night,'" laughs Timby.
So she did - and found herself dancing and drinking pints at The Matchmaker Bar in the centre of town. That's when a "handsome Irishman" approached her.
'Conversation just flowed'
"I went over and introduced myself, and... conversation just flowed," says Mangan, 38, from Ennis, County Clare, about 22 miles southeast of Lisdoonvarna. He'd been to the festival before and was well-acquainted with its cultural significance, remembering his grandparents making the journey decades earlier for the dancing.
"Unfortunately, I didn't have much time on my hands, because I was turning back to Ennis," says Mangan, designated driver that night for a group of friends. "So I got her name, and I said, 'Oh, sure, I might see you around.'
"It was a very short interaction, to be honest with you."
He didn't leave it at that, though; Mangan found Timby on Instagram and followed up with a message inviting her out.
"It was short and sweet, and it was really genuine, too," says Timby - and she took him up on the offer.
What followed was a series of whirlwind dates - lunches, dinners, sightseeing and shopping trips. Timby extended her time in Ireland and documented much of it for her newfound following - but she didn't reveal anything about her new beau. They wanted to save the burgeoning romance for themselves.
When Timby eventually had to fly home, there were "tears at the airport" - but they decided to keep the relationship going.
"It was very tough to say goodbye," Timby says. "It was very tough to start a long-distance relationship, but it ended up being a really good opportunity for us to sort of slow things down a bit."
They kept talking daily, Mangan impatiently waiting for Timby to wake up seven hours behind him in Colorado. She flew back to Ireland again, then he made his first trip to America for Thanksgiving 2025. Timby returned to Ireland at Christmas and met his family, and after that, they decided to make her boyfriend's big social media reveal.
"We thought, this is something we already know we want to invest in... we were ready to share," Timby says. "So New Year's Eve, we shared a photo of him, and people were just over-the-moon excited."
The pair watched their following grow, drawing interest from Irish cafes and tourist destinations to the local Gaelic sports club in Colorado. Their story also caught the attention of Lisdoonvarna locals, who approached Timby - a communications consultant - about being an ambassador for the festival.
"So I said: Sign me up," Timby laughs. "I love the festival. It brought me Jay."
Timby's been inundated with messages from lovelorn followers hoping to replicate her matchmaking success.
"I heard from many of my followers... groups of people wanting to go to the festival but not having anyone to go with" or "not knowing what to do," Timby says. "I really listened to that, and I also wanted to be mindful of the fact that I love Ireland.
"I'm so excited to showcase County Clare and all the amazing things that the west coast of Ireland has, but I'm also not a tour operator."
So she partnered with a company called Met Through Friends, which organises and encourages real-life meetups for people looking for love. They released an interest form for a trip, expecting "80 to 100 responses." They received 560.
The first group of eight will make the trip later this month, with Timby's Irish boyfriend consulting on the itinerary.
"You can go on all these apps, swipe left, swipe right, but it's not actually going out and making a connection with someone and experiencing a small little town in Ireland, experiencing the culture," says Mangan.
"It's a once-in-a-lifetime experience... you never know."
Timby, smiling at her boyfriend of one year, agrees.
"I echo everything Jay just said," she says. "Put your phone down and put yourselves out there, and good things will come."

Sikh truck driver survives stabbing attack in rest stop bathroom
The attack came after deadly crashes involving Sikh truck drivers led to debate about commercial driver's licensing requirements
A violent attack against a truck driver at a rest stop in remote Wyoming has left the Sikh community on edge amid rising anti-immigrant vitriol against the community and its truck drivers in particular.
The Sikh victim was attacked from behind while in a restroom along the Interstate 80 Bitter Creek rest stop, midway between Cheyenne and Salt Lake City, according to court documents.
He suffered stabs to the neck and chest and over a dozen other cuts but survived.
Police were still investigating what prompted the Wyoming attack by a man who left the rest area driving a truck-trailer combination, Sweetwater County Sheriff's Department spokesperson Jeff Sheaman said.
“We have zero motive,” Sheaman said.
While police say the motive is unknown, the attack came after deadly crashes involving Sikh truck drivers led to debate about commercial driver's licensing requirements — sparking hatred toward Sikhs as a group, community leaders said.
Anti-Sikh sentiment has been especially severe on truck-driving forums, said one Sikh in the trucking industry, Harsimran Singh, CEO of Gillson Trucking in Stockton, California.
"I’ve been here for the last 25-plus years," Singh said. "I never felt this kind of hate before.”
The victim allegedly told police he was trying to use the restroom when he was attacked from behind. He pushed the attacker, he said, and didn't see the knife at first, according to the police affidavit filed in the case.
Within hours, police arrested Andrew Kris Bzdak in nearby Carbon County, Wyoming.
A family at the rest area who heard the attack allegedly followed Bzdak's truck back onto the highway and tipped off police to help find him, according to the affidavit.
Video taken from a truck at the rest area showed the victim walk casually into the restroom, followed by a man police said was Bzdak.
Soon after, Bzdak allegedly was recorded running from the restroom, followed by the stumbling, wounded victim who fell at least once, according to the affidavit.
Bzdak remained jailed on $1 million bond Friday in Rock Springs, on suspicion of attempted murder, a crime punishable in Wyoming by up to life in prison. An initial appearance was scheduled for Thursday.
A phone message left at an address for Bzdak in Catawissa, Pennsylvania, wasn't immediately returned, nor was a phone message for him at the jail and for his Wyoming public defender, Gary Arnell.
Despite no evident motive, the attack was unnerving for Sikhs, who number around 750,000 in the U.S. Many live in California.
Sikh men wear beards, uncut hair and turbans, and many work as truck drivers. Advocacy groups estimate that at least 150,000 Sikh truck drivers work in the U.S.
In August 2025, authorities said a Sikh truck driver's U-turn on a Florida turnpike caused a crash that killed three people. The crash prompted investigations as well as reports about Sikh truck drivers being harassed.
Then last October, a Sikh truck driver accused of being under the influence of drugs caused a fiery crash that killed three people, authorities said.
Both drivers were in the U.S. illegally, according to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which Singh, the trucking CEO, blamed for stirring anti-immigrant hatred with social media posts.
One such post, since taken down, showed a dark-skinned man with a beard that read, “Get off our roads, you don’t know how to drive Mr. Singh.” DHS officials have said the post referred specifically to the driver in the Florida crash. But Sikh community representatives pointed out that a large number of Sikhs — well over 100,000 in the U.S. and millions worldwide — have the last name Singh.
No matter what motivated the attack, the crime is difficult to separate from racism toward Sikhs, said Jasjit Singh, legal services director for the Sikh community group Jakara Movement and a representative of the victim.
“We were making noise about this,” Jasjit Singh said. “That is how the community feels. Until something really bad happens to us, nothing is going to really happen.”
The victim was headed home Friday after five days in a Casper hospital and hopes to drive his truck across Wyoming again, Jasjit Singh said.
But Harsimran Singh, the trucking CEO, also remained apprehensive.
“We are probably going to see more of this,” Harsimran Singh said. “I'm not surprised that it has happened.”

When she finally claimed her semifinal match in the women’s teqball singles competition at the Asian Games on Saturday morning, Indonesia’s Sumaya fell to her knees and performed the sajdah in celebration. On the other side of the table, Quimcy Dsouza was bent over too, her hands on her knees as the result sank in.
Quimcy had won the first game comfortably, 12-7. She had led in the second. In the decider, she was up 7-3 before an extraordinary comeback saw the Indonesian win nine straight points to seal the tie. The 24-year-old from Mumbai had been within touching distance of a place in the final and of assuring India its first medal at Nagoya. Just like that, the chance was gone.
Quimcy might still medal on Sunday, when she competes for bronze in the women’s singles and mixed doubles. But what a difference a medal on Saturday, in the hours before the official opening ceremony of the Games, would have made. On Sunday, as the Games kick off in earnest, the sports cycle will move on to better-known sports and athletes at venues across town.
For nearly an hour at the Nagoya City Higashi Sports Center on Saturday, though, all eyes were on a sport making its Games debut and the Bengaluru-based engineer chasing an unlikely dream.
The stands at the Higashi centre were full of people, many curious about a sport that is a weird but fun cousin of table tennis, football and sepak takraw. They might have started out curious, but there was admiration for the athleticism on display. Dr. Dinshaw Pardiwala, knee specialist to some of India’s greatest sportspersons and Chief Medical Officer of the Indian contingent, was there. “Let’s go, Quimcy!” he yelled in encouragement from the stands.
Ultimately, though, it was not to be. You could see what the loss meant to Quimcy. She took time to compose herself before explaining how she felt.
“I’m feeling so bad I couldn’t make it to the finals but I’m happy that I even made it this far. I came here without a coach, without guidance or support. I just want India to know I gave it my all. I want India to know what teqball is,” she would say later.
Long-time dream
As a child growing up in Mumbai, Quimcy always dreamed she’d wear an India jersey. The daughter of a State-level footballer and hockey player, she initially thought that ambition would be fulfilled on the athletics track.
“I used to watch the Asian Games as a child and think I’d be running for India some day. I didn’t even know about teqball then,” she says.
The sport was still in its infancy in India when it came into Quimcy’s life by accident. She had moved from athletics to football, even representing Maharashtra at the nationals, when she suffered a ligament injury four years ago. As she lay in bed scrolling aimlessly on Instagram, she came across a video of Brazilian football legend Ronaldinho playing on a table.
That’s how the sport got its start.
“It came about as a way for footballers to have a less strenuous workout while still working on their ball handling ability,” says Nihar Shah, technical director of Teqball India.
Quimcy was instantly smitten.
“I knew I had to do this. The logo for teqball is in the shape of a ‘Q’. I thought right then that I was meant to play this game. I found out that there was a club in Mumbai where there was actually a place where there was a table,” she says.
The sport was still being figured out by players in India. Quimcy’s football background helped her pick it up faster, as it has for many of the players at these Asian Games. Sumaya, too, has a sepak takraw background, 12 years of it, which made overhead kicks against Quimcy easy to execute.
But Sumaya had another advantage: Indonesia had invested in teqball since its inclusion in the Asian Games programme.
“For the last two years I’ve been only playing and training teqball morning, afternoon and night,” she told reporters after her win.
That’s not the case for Quimcy. Like every other member of the Indian team here and like the 180-odd athletes registered as teqball players in India, she’s entirely self-funded.
“Everything that we make goes into the sport,” says Quimcy, who currently works as a test engineer at Decathlon in Bengaluru.
She’s largely self-taught too, learning simply through observation.
“Right from the start, when I’d go to international competitions, I’d look at what the other players were doing. I’d look at what new things they had introduced and how they performed. When we came back, we’d look at their videos, and train and adapt it to our style,” she says.
It’s all this that made the chance to compete in Nagoya so meaningful. Being part of an actual Indian team wasn’t just the fulfilment of a childhood dream but also the legitimising of her choice of sport and the struggles of her compatriots who played it.
“Until now we have paid money from own pockets in order to compete. This (Asian Games) is the first time everything was sponsored by IOA and team. That’s why it was so important. I only dreamed about this day. There’s so much joy because I’m not just carrying my dreams but the dreams of all my teammates as well,” she says.
She had nearly managed to make those dreams come true, winning both her group-stage matches against Japan and Cambodia before falling just short against the Indonesian in the semifinal.
But Quimcy isn’t ready to give up on her dreams just yet. She has already beaten Japan’s Yuina Sakamoto, whom she plays for bronze, in the group stage.
“I have two more chances for a medal. The goal still remains to take a medal for India. The fire still burns as much as it was before today’s match,” she says.

A four-minute warning isn't enough: Russia's new relentless missile tactics exhaust Kyiv residents
- Published
For much of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Daria was not afraid of the shelling.
Even on nights of heavy bombardment, the 27-year-old could sleep through the explosions in her apartment in Kyiv. Like many Ukrainians, she relied on the "two-wall rule": staying safe by keeping two walls between herself and the outside world.
But this year that has changed.
In recent months, Russia has scaled up the intensity and frequency of its attacks against the Ukrainian capital.
In the first 10 days of July alone, the Russians launched dozens of ballistic missiles in three major attacks, killing nearly 60 civilians, according to official figures. Similar large scale attacks took place in August and September.
A BBC Verify analysis of government figures found Kyiv is now suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
It was during an attack one night in May that Daria realised she no longer felt safe in her home.
She and her boyfriend were in the corridor of their ninth-floor apartment, watching a boxing match, as explosions went off around them, the blast waves causing the windows to repeatedly slam open and shut.
When the fight ended, "there was no longer anything to distract me," Daria says. "That's when I realised I was really scared."
At first, she thought she would start using a nearby bomb shelter during attacks.
But in June, when a young mother was killed running to a shelter in Kyiv, Daria decided she needed to leave the city altogether.
She returned to her family's country house, 30km (18.6 miles) away in Romankiv, and now spends a total of four hours a day commuting to and from Kyiv, where she works in the defence sector.
Daria's experience is far from unique.
Residents in Kyiv who say they had got used to Russia's missile and drone strikes have told the BBC World Service the renewed intensity of the attacks is making them rethink how they live their lives.
Previously, Ukraine's air-defence network and military intelligence gave residents a degree of predictability. Large-scale attacks could often be detected in advance, allowing people to spend the night in shelters, leave the city or take other precautions. But since the summer, Russia has changed its tactics.
It has relied less on aircraft, whose movements can be spotted ahead of time, and more on ballistic missiles that travel at tremendous speed and provide little warning. Air-raid alerts sometimes begin only moments before impact, or even simultaneously with the first explosions.
Daria can see her nearest shelter from the window of her apartment, which she still rents. Even so, it takes around 10 minutes to reach it. During a ballistic attack, she might have just four minutes' warning or less, she says.
She decided to leave Kyiv in June after holidaying abroad this summer and seeing people living "normal" lives. Since then, she has only spent one night in Kyiv.
Yet, for many, leaving is not an option.
Sixty-two-year-old Olha Vlasova lives on the seventh floor of a high-rise apartment block with her 98-year-old mother, Nadia Tsybina.
Despite her age, Nadia remains intensely engaged with the world.
From her bed she follows events in Ukraine and abroad, discussing everything from US President Donald Trump's policies, to anti-corruption protests in Kyiv, and the Epstein files.
She's also learned that she can often tell, simply by listening, whether a Russian missile or drone has been intercepted or has reached its target.
This summer, she says she has heard fewer interceptions.
"It's upsetting when there's nothing to shoot them down with," Nadia says. "I can hear them firing with whatever they've got, rifles, machine guns."
With Nadia confined to her bed, she and Olha cannot go to a shelter, however serious an attack is. Instead, as soon as an air-raid siren sounds, Olha covers her mother with a blanket, pushes a mattress into their window frame, and then hides in a wardrobe which puts two walls between her and outside.
Nadia places a pillow over her head to protect her face from flying glass.
Once in her wardrobe, Olha will often stay awake watching the news all night.
"They come in, they bomb us," Nadia says. "You haven't even had time to fall asleep, and there's another alert. They come again, they shoot them down again. And it goes on all night.
"People don't sleep, and then they walk around like zombies."
An increase in daytime attacks means life in Kyiv is now interrupted by air raid sirens day and night.
At the beginning of September, when children returned to school after the summer break, there were dozens of air raid alerts, followed by explosions and fires.
According to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko, two children were injured in attacks on 31 August.
As a result, many children stayed at home, while others spent hours in the basements of schools and kindergartens.
When the sirens sound, it also affects businesses and transport. Shopping centres close and above-ground metro stations suspend operations, often severing public transport links between Kyiv's Left and Right Banks, on either side of the Dnieper River, for hours at a time.
New metro operating rules during air raid alerts are being introduced in an attempt to improve the situation.
For Olha, it has meant seeing less of her eight-year-old granddaughter, who lives on the other side of the city.
She knows if her granddaughter comes to visit, she risks struggling to return home. When metro services stop running, expensive cab journeys are Olha's only option. Crossing the river can cost as much as 1,000 hryvnias ($22, £16.6), she says, just under one-eighth of Ukraine's monthly minimum wage.
The experience has left her frustrated with what she sees as hesitation by some of Ukraine's foreign partners to provide additional air-defence missiles.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly appealed to allies for additional air-defence systems and interceptor missiles.
"They [Ukraine's allies] wait, thinking: 'What if we get attacked?'" Olha says. "It's like refusing to give medicine to a cancer patient because you're saying, 'What if I get sick one day?' Well, maybe you won't. Give it away before it expires."
In another part of the city, mother-of-two Natalia Bushkovska each night rehearses three different plans.
Plan A is to spread bedding in the hallway behind two interior walls; Plan B is to move the family into the building's shared corridor; and Plan C is to head for the basement.
Even there, she admits, she does not feel entirely safe.
"I keep a backpack with essential items," says Natalia, 37. "There's a tourniquet for severe bleeding. I also keep a whistle, just in case.
"If the worst happens, rescuers will be able to find us under the rubble."
Her nine-year-old daughter has her own emergency bag containing toys, lip balm and a tourniquet. Like her 12-year-old brother, she learned how to use a tourniquet through first-aid training.
Natalia says the constant attacks are exhausting.
While her son often sleeps through them, she and her daughter wake up almost every time.
"Because of the attacks, I don't get enough sleep," she says. "Now, in the fifth year of the war, I find it increasingly difficult to bounce back after nights like these."
The growing intensity of the strikes, she says, is taking a psychological toll across the city.
"People are exhausted. They don't have enough time to recover."
On Thursday 17 September, Russia launched a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. According to Mayor Vitali Klitschko, 20 people were injured in the attack. Among the wounded were two children, aged 10 and 12.

Ratcliffe also said the UK had “a bit of a green eye towards wealth at the moment”, “encouraging” the wealthiest to relocate.
He told the podcast: “In America, they applaud people who create wealth.
“And the good thing about those people who create wealth is that they then spend that wealth in the economy in which they’re resident. And, unfortunately, with the things that they’ve been doing, they’ve been encouraging the people who have created wealth to leave the UK because it’s just become uncomfortable for them for tax reasons or whatever.
While the UK’s tax burden has risen to its highest level since the second world war at about 35.3% of GDP, the Office for Budget Responsibility says it remains well below the average of 14 western European economies.
Ratcliffe has also been at odds with Manchester United fans over the summer after the club embarked on a major ticket-touting crackdown that ultimately revoked 685 season tickets, prompting protests from United supporter groups such as the 1958.
The businessman was already fiercely unpopular among the Old Trafford faithful, ever since he decided to increase ticket prices and sack 450 club employees.
The billionaire also took aim at the government’s decision not to invest further in North Sea resources by granting licences for the Jackdaw and Rosebank oil and gasfields, which he said amounted to “insanity”, and warned the UK’s reliance on energy imports meant the country could “run out of gas” if there was a cold spell this winter.
He said: “The risk you’ve got this winter is that we run out of gas. If we have a really sharp cold spell, then there is conceivably the possibility that we’ll run out of gas and have to switch the industry off.”
In response to the billionaire’s criticism, the government said it was working to deliver growth and that business investment had increased in the last two years.
A spokesperson told the BBC that they did not foresee any problems with gas supply: “We have a diverse energy mix and are confident in our security of supply.”
Asked if he was planning on returning to the UK, Ratcliffe said: “Not at the moment, no. I don’t see growth being tackled.
“Two things: we need politicians who are tough enough to deal with some very difficult problems, and we know what the problems are.
“And we need politicians who will make decisions which are good for the country, not good for themselves and their party. And we haven’t had one of those for a long time.”

Trump signs sweeping Russia sanctions bill
- Published
US President Donald Trump has signed a sweeping sanctions bill, taking aim at Russia's economy by punishing major purchasers of its oil and gas.
The bill, passed by the US House of Representatives earlier this week, gives Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.
At Trump's behest, the bill also extends to Iran's energy and weapons sectors.
The bill is named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, one of Ukraine's staunchest defenders in Washington before his death on 11 July.
The 48-page bill, formally titled the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, includes exceptions for countries that import less than 15% of their natural gas from Russia and are working to lessen their dependency.
Additionally, the bill includes sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior figures within the Russian government as well as banks and other financial institutions and Russia's "shadow fleet" of tankers used to circumvent existing sanctions.
Senator Richard Blumenthal, a New York Democrat, previously described the legislation as "scorching sanctions" which would "throttle Putin's war machine".
Data from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, or CREA, shows that China accounted for 50% of Russian crude exports between December 2022 and August 2026, followed by India at 37%.
Turkey and the European Union each accounted for 5% during the same time period, although Russian energy exports to the EU have been decreasing.
Senator Graham had long sought to push the Trump administration to do more to punish Russia for the war that followed its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
The bill also received the support of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who thanked Trump for signing the "critically important legislation".
"The best way to honour Lindsey's memory will be to implement the provisions of this law fully and swiftly," he wrote on social media.
"Senator Graham never doubted for a second that America has enough strength to stand up to dictators and achieve results if it acts the right way."
Graham, 71, died on 11 July of an "aortic dissection" caused by cardiovascular disease shortly after returning from a trip to Kyiv.
"He died doing the work he was born to do," Trump said at the time.
Prior to his death, he was widely considered one of Ukraine's fiercest allies on Capitol Hill, at a time when Republicans were bitterly divided over the extent of US involvement abroad and the amount of aid being given to Ukraine.

15 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న ఉత్తర అరేబియా సముద్రంలో భారత్, పాకిస్తాన్ నావికాదళాలకు చెందిన యుద్ధనౌకలు ఒకదానికొకటి ఢీకొన్నాయి. తమ నౌక సాధారణ నిఘా విధుల్లో ఉండగా పాకిస్తాన్ నౌక వేగంగా, ప్రమాదకరంగా దూసుకొచ్చిందని భారత్ పేర్కొంది. దీనిపై నిరసన తెలుపుతూ సెప్టెంబర్ 16న పాకిస్తాన్ దౌత్యాధికారికి భారత్ సమన్లు జారీ చేసింది. అయితే, పాకిస్తాన్ మాత్రం ఇందుకు భిన్నమైన వాదన వినిపించింది. తమ ‘SEASPARK-26’ నావికా విన్యాసాల్లో ఈ ఘటన జరిగిందని, భారత నౌక ఉద్దేశపూర్వకంగా తమ నౌక సమీపంలోకి వచ్చిందని ఆరోపించింది.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, భారత, పాకిస్తాన్ యుద్ధనౌకలు ఢీకొన్న దృశ్యాలంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: 15 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న భారత్, పాకిస్తాన్ యుద్ధనౌకలు ఒకదానికొకటి ఢీకొన్న దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియో 15 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న భారత్, పాకిస్తాన్ యుద్ధనౌకలు ఢీకొన్న ఘటనకు సంబంధించినది కాదు. వాణిజ్య నౌక ‘ఎంవీ సూయజ్’కు భద్రతగా వెళ్తున్న సమయంలో 2011లో పాకిస్థాన్ నౌక పీఎన్ఎస్ బాబర్, భారత నౌక ఐఎన్ఎస్ గోదావరిని ఢీకొన్న పాత సంఘటనకు సంబంధించిన వీడియో ఇది. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియోని 16 అక్టోబర్ 2014న “mix” అనే యూట్యూబ్ ఛానెల్లో అప్లోడ్ (ఆర్కైవ్) చేసినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ వీడియోలో పాకిస్తాన్ నౌక బాబర్ భారత నౌకతో పోటీ పడుతుందని పేర్కొనబడింది. ఏడెన్ అఖాతంలో (Gulf of Aden) ‘ఎంవీ సూయజ్’ అనే వాణిజ్య నౌకను రక్షించే సమయంలో తీసిన భారత, పాకిస్తాన్ నౌకల దృశ్యాలను ఈ వీడియో చూపుతుందని వివరణలో రాసి ఉంది. దీన్ని బట్టి, వైరల్ వీడియో సెప్టెంబర్ 2026 నాటి ఘటనకు సంబంధించినది కాదని, అది దశాబ్దానికి పైగా పాతదని స్పష్టమవుతుంది.
దీనికి సంబంధించిన మరింత సమాచారం కోసం ఇంటర్నెట్లో వెతకగా, ఇదే ఘటన గురించి చెప్తున్నా 2011 నాటి NDTV వార్తా కథనం లభించింది. ఈ కథనం ప్రకారం, ఈ ఘటన 16 జూన్ 2011న జరిగింది. వాణిజ్య నౌక ‘ఎంవీ సూయజ్’కు భద్రతగా వెళ్తున్న సమయంలో, భారత నావికాదళానికి చెందిన ‘ఐఎన్ఎస్ గోదావరి’ నౌకను దాటి వెళ్లే ప్రయత్నంలో పాకిస్తాన్ యుద్ధనౌక ‘పీఎన్ఎస్ బాబర్’ దాని వెనుక భాగాన్ని ఢీకొట్టింది. సముద్రం అల్లకల్లోలంగా ఉన్న సమయంలో ఐఎన్ఎస్ గోదావరికి అతి సమీపంలోకి వచ్చిన పీఎన్ఎస్ బాబర్ రాసుకుంటూ వెళ్లిందని, దీనివల్ల భారత నౌకలోని హెలికాప్టర్ డెక్కు నష్టం వాటిల్లిందని ఆ కథనం పేర్కొంది. నౌకలు ఢీకొన్న తర్వాత పాకిస్తాన్ నౌక సిబ్బంది సంబరాలు చేసుకుంటున్న దృశ్యాలను కూడా ఆ కథనం చూపించింది.
18 జూన్ 2011న భారత విదేశీ వ్యవహారాల మంత్రిత్వ శాఖ ఒక పత్రికా ప్రకటన విడుదల చేసి పాకిస్తాన్ తీరుపై నిరసన వ్యక్తం చేసింది. పీఎన్ఎస్ బాబర్ చేసిన ప్రమాదకరమైన విన్యాసాలు ఐఎన్ఎస్ గోదావరి నౌక, దాని సిబ్బంది భద్రతను ప్రమాదంలో పడేశాయని అందులో పేర్కొంది. అంతేకాకుండా, పాకిస్తాన్ చర్యలు అంతర్జాతీయ సముద్ర భద్రతా నిబంధనలను, అలాగే సైనిక విన్యాసాలకు ముందస్తు సమాచారం ఇవ్వాలనే 1991 నాటి ఇండో-పాక్ ఒప్పందాన్ని ఉల్లంఘించాయని భారత్ స్పష్టం చేసింది.
చివరిగా, వైరల్ వీడియో 2011లో భారత్, పాకిస్థాన్ నౌకలు ఢీకొన్న పాత ఘటనకు సంబంధించినది.

The world’s busiest railway station, located at the heart of Tokyo in Japan, is testing whether mobile robotic rubbish bins can ease the workload of sanitation workers, a rail operator representative said on Friday.
Shinjuku Station is a sprawling transport complex with multiple rail firms that serve more than 2.7 million passengers every day, and holds the Guinness World Record for the world’s busiest rail station.
In a part of the station operated by East Japan Railway, the bins are emptied manually more than 10 times a day — though the number of wastebaskets has been reduced in recent years for cleanliness and security reasons.
JR East is testing three automated bins, each standing just over one metre (three feet) tall and moving at a cautious 20 centimeters per second.
“We wanted to test how well something like this can operate automatically and safely in an environment like Shinjuku Station,” Shinya Kawamichi, a JR East research official, said.
“We want to see how much of a difference mobile trash bins that collect garbage make, and whether people are actually willing to throw their trash into them,” he said.
The trial project, which runs until late November, will put the robots up against the station’s always-hectic underground concourse, where they are meant to bring trash to human workers.
Kawamichi said the robots are designed to be “slow so that people can put trash in them and so (they) can stop at any moment.”
The company also wanted to test if the robots can navigate busy crowds and be accepted by commuters — with an eye to expanding the future uses of this technology.
The bulky, googly-eyed devices have become a hit among tourists, many of whom stopped to snap photos.
“The eyes are very cute,” said German train driver Chris Genseliein, 30, adding that he had a tough time finding bins in Japanese train stations.
Despite being an enormous complex with two above-ground floors and a massive underground section, JR East’s section of Shinjuku Station only has seven sets of bins and recycling boxes.
Some Japanese passengers said stations are kept clean because people take their trash home.
But others welcomed the added convenience.
“It’s just easier if you could throw things away while walking,” said university student Ryunosuke Noguchi, 22.

The Asian Games are open with more athletes than the Summer Olympics and some unfamiliar sports
The opening ceremony of the Asian Games has marked the official start of the 16-day event
NAGOYA, Japan -- The opening ceremony of the Asian Games on Saturday marked the official start of the 16-day event — but in name only.
Facing a packed schedule, competition in basketball started on Sept. 10 — more than a week ago. The semifinals in men's basketball were on Friday, a day before the official opening.
Soccer has been going on for almost as long. The Summer Olympics typically start a few days early, but this multi-sport event pushes the envelope.
Welcome to the Asian Games, which feature at least 11,000 athletes. The 2024 Summer Olympics in Paris had about 10,700. The last Asian Games in Hangzhou, China, in 2023 had roughly 12,000.
Japanese organizers have yet to release an official athlete total from the 45 countries and regions contesting 43 sports. But it seems likely to reach the total in China of three years ago. Maybe more with a few new sports added.
The games feature the old-standby Olympic disciplines like track and field, swimming and soccer. But there are some Asian specialties, too: kurash, kabaddi, and sepaktakraw to name three.
Kurash is an ancient form of wrestling that originated in Uzbekistan. Kabaddi looks like a game of team tag with a physical edge. And sepaktakraw is a mix of volleyball and soccer.
Games organizers have also added mixed martial arts, padel and teqball to the menu — with esports also on the schedule — hence the time crunch.
Host Japan has the largest delegation with 933 athletes and China came with just over 800. China won 201 gold medals in the last games, followed by Japan (52) and South Korea (42). That pattern is expected to be repeated.
Emperor Naruhito and Empress Masako headed the list of dignitaries. The president of the Olympic Council of Asia, Sheikh Joaan bin Hamad Al Thani, elected earlier this year, was alongside.
“Tonight the eyes of Asia, and much of the world, turn to Japan,” Sheikh Joaan said in his address, which was followed by the Emperor officially opening the games.
The president of the International Olympic Committee, Kirsty Coventry, was also present.
The theme of the opening ceremony was the “Harmonic Heart Beat,” and the stage on the infield at the Nagoya City Stadium was in the shape of a large heart.
Afghanistan led off the traditional parade of athletes with Japan coming in last and, of course, receiving thunderous applause.
The Asian Games have been dotted with controversies in the leadup to the opening ceremony. This also happens in the rush to get ready for most Olympics.
First, there’s the issue of housing for athletes. Japanese organizers decided against building a dedicated athletes village. They opted instead to house an estimated 17,000 athletes and officials on a massive cruise ship, in hotels, and in wooden containers converted to lodging.
Japan officially spent $13 billion on the Tokyo Olympics, delayed until 2021 by the pandemic. A government audit suggested the figure was likely twice that large. So lavish spending was out this time.
Athletes have complained the beds and rooms are too small, some have reported the wooden huts have leaks, and logistics could be an issue with venues spread out around Nagoya.
This is Japan’s third largest metropolitan area with a population of about 9.5 million and located about 200 miles (350 kilometers) south of Tokyo.
Then the inevitable politics. On Friday, the day before the official opening, two incidents made headlines.
Organizers played the North Korean national anthem at a field hockey game between South Korea and Bangladesh. South Korea players stood at attention, bewildered the North Korean anthem was playing.
Many South Koreans are, in fact, unfamiliar with North Korea's anthem and did not know what they were hearing.
At about the same time, Taiwanese sports minister Lee Yang — a two-time Olympic gold medalist in badminton — was temporarily barred from a welcoming ceremony involving Taiwan, and other countries including North Korea, Palestine and India.
The Olympic Council of Asia attributed it to a misunderstanding but did not entirely clarify. Yang was eventually allowed to participate.
Taiwan competes in the Asian Games and the Olympics under the name of Chinese Taipei and without their flag due to China’s claim on the island off its east coast.

When my son moved to New York City after college graduation, I couldn't have been prouder. He had landed a great job, found an apartment, made friends, and embraced everything the city had to offer. Two years after my daughter finished college, we packed up a U-Haul and drove her more than 700 miles to Chicago to start her new chapter.
Watching both of my children confidently step into adulthood was everything I'd hoped for when they were little. Watching them leave was also one of the hardest things I've ever done.
I raised my kids to be independent
As parents, we spend years preparing our children to become independent. We celebrate every milestone that gets them closer to adulthood. The first day of school. Learning to ride a bike. Driving a car. Going away to college. Landing that first job. Every accomplishment feels like proof we're doing something right.
No one tells you that one day those same accomplishments will leave your house quiet.
These days, my son has favorite restaurants in New York I've never been to. He has his own routines, friends, and a new life with his fiancé. My daughter has created a life in Chicago that fits her perfectly. She knows the neighborhoods, has favorite places to shop and eat, and has built her own community. They don't call to ask how to do laundry anymore or need me to remind them about doctor's appointments. They're living exactly the lives I raised them to have.
And somehow, that's where the grief begins.
It hurts every time I say goodbye to them
It's a strange kind of grief because nothing bad has happened. They're healthy. They're happy. They're successful. They call, they visit, and we have wonderful relationships. In many ways, this is the dream every parent hopes for. Yet every time I hug them goodbye after visiting with them, I ache to the core and cry the entire way home.
I realized what I was mourning wasn't my children. It was that version of motherhood that had come to an end.
For twenty-two years, my life revolved around school schedules, sports, family dinners, and helping them become capable adults. Then, almost without noticing, my role changed. They still wanted me in their lives, but they no longer needed me every day. That's exactly what I had worked so hard to accomplish.
The irony wasn't lost on me. My greatest success as a parent also felt like one of my greatest losses.
I wondered if something was wrong with me. Shouldn't I simply be happy? Why did I feel so emotional when this was exactly what I'd wanted for them? It wasn't until I shared my feelings in TikTok videos that I realized I wasn't alone.
In one video, I wrote, "One day your daughter has her own city, her own routines, her own life... and you realize she's become the woman you hoped she'd be."
More than 65,000 people watched it, and more than 2,200 shared it. The comments said everything.
Again and again, parents described the same impossible contradiction: How can I be so incredibly proud and miss them this much at the same time?
It's pride and loss existing side by side.
When I visit my son in New York City or my daughter in Chicago, I love seeing them in their own worlds. I love that they have careers they're passionate about, apartments they've made their own, and lives full of people they love. Seeing them so confident and living fully fills me with pride.
Then I go home.
I miss the ordinary moments
That's when I miss the little things. Shoes in the mudroom. Messy bedrooms. Knowing everyone would be home for dinner. The ordinary moments you never realize you're living for the last time.
I don't think we talk enough about this stage of parenthood. We prepare parents for diapers, teenage years, and college drop-offs. We don't prepare them for the emotional whiplash of watching your children become exactly who you hoped they'd be while quietly grieving the life you shared before they flew.
The goal was never to keep them forever. It was to give them the confidence to build lives they loved, even if those lives took them hundreds of miles away. I spent 22 years raising my children to leave me.
Seeing them thrive tells me I succeeded. Missing them every day reminds me how much I loved the years when they needed me.

An Islamic State group member was sentenced on Wednesday to 20 years in prison for aiding the terrorist organization that took credit for a suicide bombing that killed 13 US service members and about 160 Afghans at the Kabul airport five years ago during the US military’s chaotic withdrawal from the country.
A federal jury in Virginia had convicted Mohammad Sharifullah in April of providing material support to the IS affiliate known as Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP). But jurors could not agree whether he bore some responsibility for the airport bombing on 26 August 2021.
US troops were conducting an evacuation operation at the airport when a suicide bomber detonated an improvised explosive device near an entry point known as Abbey Gate. Sharifullah’s role in the attack was scouting a route to Hamid Karzai international airport, prosecutors said.
Sharifullah, 28, received the maximum sentence for his one-count conviction in an international terrorism case that Donald Trump heralded last year during a speech to a joint session of Congress.
Sharifullah did not testify at his trial and declined to address the court before the US district judge Anthony Trenga imposed the sentence. The judge said the defendant was a “dedicated terrorist” who expressed no remorse for the “unfathomable” grief and suffering that he had caused.
Trenga heard victim impact statements from several parents of US service members. From a podium only a few feet from where Sharifullah sat, they took turns paying tribute to their children’s sacrifices and describing how the attack has shattered their families.
Mark Schmitz of Missouri asked Sharifullah to turn and look at him as he spoke about the life and death of his 20-year-old son, Marine Corps L/Cpl Jared Schmitz.
“They may have taken his life, but they’ll never take his legacy,” Mark Schmitz said. “A bomb killed my son. It did not kill what he stood for.”
Paula Knauss-Selph, whose son, army SSgt Ryan Knauss, was killed in the Abbey Gate bombing, said the family was “forever changed” by the attack.
“No justice will ever be enough to mend my broken heart,” she said.
Sharifullah requested a 17-year prison sentence, while prosecutors sought 20 years. His lawyers said he was never an ISKP leader and had not been convicted of any conduct related to the airport suicide bombing.
“He was brought here because the government believed he participated in the Abbey Gate attack, a theory which it was unable to prove at trial,” defense attorneys wrote.
Prosecutors said in their sentencing memo that “from his teenage years, when he pledged an oath of allegiance to [ISKP], Sharifullah’s carnage was driven by hate. Hate towards Americans.”
Jurors convicted Sharifullah of providing material support to ISKP. They deadlocked on whether any deaths at the airport “resulted from” that conspiracy. Sharifullah could have faced a possible life sentence if the jury had unanimously decided that question.
According to prosecutors, Sharifullah told a journalist that he wanted to “catch and kill the crusaders” from the United States for invading his country after the attacks of September 11. They said Sharifullah was involved in dozens of other attacks, including a March 2024 assault on a Moscow concert hall that killed roughly 140 people.
Defense lawyers argued that prosecutors failed to present any evidence tying Sharifullah to the Kabul bombing besides his own words during hours of FBI questioning. His team said Sharifullah told FBI agents what he thought they wanted to hear, possibly because he was afraid of being tortured in Pakistani custody before he was brought to the US.
A review by US Central Command found that the Abbey Gate bomber was Abdul Rahman al-Logari, an IS member who had been released from an Afghan prison by the Taliban. According to an FBI affidavit, Sharifullah recognized the alleged bomber as an operative he had known while incarcerated.

Dozens of suspected illegal miners die in Nigerian custody
- Published
Thirty-seven people accused of illegal mining in north-central Nigeria have died in custody, local officials said.
Police have set up an investigation into the deaths, which the Nigerian Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) blamed on an apparent disease outbreak.
However, an intelligence report shared with AFP news agency suggested the group died because of overcrowding and poor ventilation inside the detention facility in the Nigerian state of Niger.
State governor Mohammed Umaru Bago called the deaths "sad and tragic" during a press conference on Thursday.
An NSCDC commander has been detained following the deaths, Bago added.
He declared three days of mourning and postponed the start of campaigning for elections scheduled for January.
Officials had arrested the group of young men on Tuesday for suspected illegal mining near Borgu, in the mineral-rich state of Niger. The region is known for small-scale gold mining.
Two days later, 37 people detained as part of the suspected unlawful operation were found dead inside the detention centre run by the NSCDC.
The NSCDC had earlier said the detainees were possibly victims of a diphtheria outbreak, a serious bacterial infection that can be fatal.
But the agency's national headquarters later said the cause had not been established and would require medical and laboratory tests.
"The NSCDC wishes to clarify that reports attributing the deaths to any specific disease remain subject to medical and laboratory confirmation," it added in a statement.
A survivor told the Associated Press news agency that about 65 people had been held in an overcrowded and poorly ventilated cell, suggesting the dead may have suffocated.
Some relatives of the deceased have disputed the official explanation of events, claiming to local media that they were deliberately killed.
One father told Nigerian media that his son had appeared healthy when relatives brought him food the day before his death and called for an independent post-mortem examination.
Another relative, whose 17-year-old brother was among those who died, said the family had visited him during his detention and questioned how a disease could have killed so many detainees without apparently affecting their guards.
Post-mortem examinations are expected to help establish what happened.
Niger's police chief ordered an immediate investigation into "the unfortunate death of suspected illegal miners while in the detention facility of the NSCDC", spokesman Wasiu Abiodun wrote in a statement.
The victim's bodies have since been taken to the general hospital in nearby Minna for examination.
The scramble for gold reserves dug up in illegal mines in Niger state has been blamed for fuelling criminal gang violence, according to officials and experts.
Much of the gold in the region is trafficked through global supply chains, a 2024 SwissAid report found.

After wearing it day and night for a week, I found that better health tracking, faster charging, and a simpler interface make Apple’s latest smartwatch noticeably easier to live with.
New Health Sensing System increases frequency and breadth of health metrics. New Readiness score. Audio Intelligence. Faster charging. Cleaner watchOS 27 interface. Beautiful bronze finish, and ceramic is back.
TIRED
Still only 24 hours of battery life. Privacy concerns around Siri Recap and Live Rewind.
On the surface, the Apple Watch Series 12 doesn’t appear to be a major upgrade over last year’s release and, in many ways, it isn’t. But after a week of wearing it day and night, I noticed that the Series 12 feels more intuitive, putting fewer steps between me and the information I need from my everyday smartwatch.
Health tracking is more thorough, thanks to a new Health Sensing System and faster S11 chip. The watchOS 27 update, first announced at WWDC in June and finally available to consumers, gives the Apple Watch a cleaner, streamlined interface that positions Siri AI at the center of the user experience. The most notable addition is perhaps Audio Intelligence, a suite of listening tools powered by Apple Intelligence. Plus, in a fun return, the Series 12 also comes in ceramic, a premium finish Apple discontinued in 2020.
Not everyone needs the upgrade, though. If you’re coming from the Series 8 or older, the Series 12 is a generational leap, with a better display, longer battery life, and newer health features, including sleep apnea and hypertension notifications. Owners of the Series 9 or 10 have fewer reasons to swap, but the battery improvements alone (18 hours to 24 hours) may be compelling. If you already have the Series 11, Audio Intelligence probably isn’t going to be enough to justify replacing a watch that’s already capable of most of the same functions.
Polished, Inside and Out
Visually, Apple isn’t fixing what isn’t broken, and I’m not mad about it. The Series 12 looks nearly identical to its predecessors, but Apple highlights it as its thinnest Apple Watch yet. The aluminum and titanium models measure 9.7 millimeters thick, and the ceramic option is 9.85 millimeters thick. I didn’t notice a difference during everyday wear, but the Apple Watch Series remains one of the most comfortable smartwatches I’ve tested. Aside from the new Hermès collection, there aren’t any new band designs this year, but Apple has added new colors to the existing lineup.
Photograph: Boutayna Chokrane
The new finishes are exciting, particularly the return of ceramic. Apple first offered a ceramic option with the Series 2 in 2016, and it was discontinued in 2020. Today, it’s available in pearl white and night blue, both of which give the Series 12 a softer finish that looks more like an accessory. The ceramic feels more like a fashionable move rather than a functional one, but Apple is following a trend seen across brands like Oura.
I’m testing the aluminum model in the new dark bronze finish, which has become my favorite. It complements most of my wardrobe and gives the watch a more cosmopolitan look than some of Apple’s sportier colorways. Aluminum models are also available in the standard light gold, black, and space gray; titanium comes in natural and a new radiant gold. The aluminum models are now coated with Ceramic Shield 2, which Apple says is 60 percent tougher than the previous Ion-X glass. I haven’t had enough time with the watch to meaningfully test that durability claim, but for someone who tends to knock their smartwatch on doors and countertops, it’s an improvement I’ll happily accept.
Battery life remains rated at 24 hours, which is slightly disappointing when competitors can go longer between charges. The saving grace is faster charging. Fifteen minutes of charging now provides up to 12 hours of battery life, and five minutes gets you up to 10 hours of sleep tracking. This has been the most useful upgrade for me. I can set the watch to charge while I’m getting ready for bed and put it back on for sleep tracking.
Photograph: Boutayna Chokrane
The Series 12 ships with watchOS 27, but most of the software changes will also arrive on compatible older Apple Watches. I particularly love the revamped app layout. Instead of having to hunt through a sea of icons or scroll through an exhaustive list, Apple now surfaces five Siri AI-suggested apps, the Siri app, and a shortcut to the full app grid. The apps I need most are immediately available without cluttering the display.
Apple is also making the watch easier to navigate with one hand, adding a single-tap gesture to Apple’s existing double-tap and wrist-flick controls. Tap your index finger and thumb together to select widgets in Smart Stack; double-tap lets you scroll through them. A wrist flick can return you to the watch face, silence timers, or dismiss notifications. These gestures are particularly handy (ha) when you’re multitasking or if you want to use your watch discreetly.
Better at Reading You
The new S11 chip brings the standard round of faster CPU and GPU performance, along with a more efficient Neural Engine. S11 also powers a remodeled pedometer to improve step counts and distance measurements, particularly during indoor walks and runs. Compared to Series 11, I didn’t notice much difference in numbers. I do, though, appreciate the new Steps complication, which puts my real-time step count on the watch face, so I can check my progress without opening the Activity app.
Video: Boutayna Chokrane
The bigger hardware upgrade is Apple’s new Health Sensing System. The Series 12 has 32 electrodes for improved skin contact during ECG readings, compared with two on the Series 11. The photodiodes have been rearranged in a ring configuration for improved optical sensing, and larger green LEDs have been added for more accurate heart rate readings.
The result, and one of the watch’s biggest selling points, is that it takes more frequent readings. The Series 12 measures heart rate every five seconds, even while you’re moving, whereas the Series 11 takes readings every five minutes when you’re relatively stationary. The Series 12 can also measure heart rate variability (HRV) as often as every five minutes, compared with every two hours on the Series 11, and it measures two variants: recovery HRV and overall HRV. For health-conscious people, the higher sampling frequency gives you a more continuous picture of how your body responds to stressors throughout the day instead of a handful of isolated snapshots. You can see those readings in the Heart Rate app or through the new live heart rate complications.
Video: Boutayna Chokrane
Readiness has at last arrived for anyone who has been anticipating a unified recovery score from Apple. The new Readiness app pulls together activity, sleep, and other health data to estimate how prepared you are for the day ahead. It takes seven days of sleep data before the score becomes available, which is standard for wearables to determine a baseline.
I like having the score as a quick shorthand instead of attempting to contextualize the individual metrics myself, but I stay skeptical of any recovery score that simplifies complicated physiological states using a proprietary algorithm. That said, Readiness is useful as a prompt to pay attention to your body, and I’m glad Apple finally has one.
Apple is also planning a redesigned Health app later this year, including a new Longevity tab and metrics such as Health Age, which compares your health data with that of your demographic. I haven’t been able to test those features yet, but I have a feeling my Health Age will either be oddly gratifying or immediately anxiety-inducing.
A Little Too Attentive
Audio Intelligence may be Apple’s most controversial addition. The suite brings four audio-focused features, including accelerated Shazam and Sound Recognition, the latter of which has been available on the iPhone since 2020. The more intriguing additions are Siri Recap and Live Rewind, which push the Apple Watch into murky waters by using its microphone to capture and process audio. I haven’t been able to test either feature yet; both are slated to arrive later this year.
Siri Recap is Apple’s answer to the AI notetaking boom. When enabled, it can transcribe conversations and generate summaries using Apple Intelligence. I can see the appeal for meetings and classes. During a briefing, I saw Siri Recap turn a PTA meeting into a detailed set of notes and reminders that seemed genuinely useful.
Live Rewind is harder to wrap my head around. The feature maintains a rolling buffer of recent audio so you can ask the watch for a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Double-press the Digital Crown and, in theory, you can recover something you just missed without asking the other person to repeat themselves.
The privacy concerns are justified, and you can read more about them here. Apple says the audio is processed in a protected memory area called the Secure Enclave. The S11 chip has an isolated buffer for sensor data, and Apple says raw audio isn’t accessible to the operating system, apps, the user, or Apple. The company also says these features don’t create or store audio recordings.
That’s somewhat reassuring, but it doesn’t eliminate the always-listening worries. Live Rewind supposedly plays an audible chime when activated to alert people nearby. Whether a beep is sufficient consent is a personal judgment call. I will test these features myself once they roll out and will report back.
Apple has refined the everyday experience, added health metrics people actually want, and resisted the temptation to bury the watch under a pile of new features. It’s a thoughtful update, and that makes the Series 12 the best Apple Watch yet.

Don't be deterred by setbacks: Tata Sons' N Chandrasekaran's message to graduates
At Sai University's convocation in Chennai, N Chandrasekaran urged graduates to embrace setbacks and AI-led change. His message underlined lifelong learning and self-driven progress as India enters a high-growth phase.
Tata Sons Chairman N Chandrasekaran on Saturday told graduating students that they should not be discouraged by setbacks, but treat failures as chances to work harder and set bold goals as they enter the professional world.
Speaking as the chief guest at the third convocation of Sai University in Chennai, he said artificial intelligence and rapid technological change are reshaping the global economy, even as India is entering a phase of growth that could prove "unparalleled" in its history and across the world for decades to come.
Focusing on personal progress and dealing with adversity, Chandrasekaran said, "Prepare continuously for the careers and not be deterred by setbacks. You have got to measure yourself on progress, continuous improvement, push yourself towards what you want to do. View pressure as a privilege rather than being deterred by high-stakes environments or complex problem-solving."
His remarks came days after the Tata Sons board, at its September 17 meeting, voted to give him a fresh five-year term. However, Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata voted against his reappointment.
He urged the graduating class to run "dual races" by balancing short-term achievements that build momentum with long-term career goals. He also said formal education should not be seen as a one-time achievement and stressed the need for lifelong upskilling in a fast-changing job market. "If you are not keeping pace, you will get outdated," Chandrasekaran said.
"The world is full to the brim with possibilities. Five years from now, there will be industries that do not exist today, and we may not even know their terminology today," he added.
On the use of AI in careers, Chandrasekaran said professionals should use such tools for administrative work, complex data processing and routine operations, so they can spend more time on strategic thinking.
"Creativity in business is at a premium," he said, adding that graduates should position themselves as "early adopters" in emerging AI-driven areas instead of resisting technological change.
Drawing from his experience as a marathon runner, he told students to judge themselves by their own progress rather than by others. Quoting marathoner Juma Ikangaa, he said, "the will to win means nothing without the will to prepare."
He said fear of failure holds back progress, and added that every failure is a step forward while every success builds confidence. "You must run your own race. Everyone has their own journey, skills, strengths, weaknesses and targets. Don't get distracted by others, as they may have different goals. Measure yourself against yourself, towards what you want to achieve," he said.
In his address, Chandrasekaran told graduates to keep learning, embrace pressure, use new technology well and stay focused on their own path, while treating setbacks as part of progress.

“DealShare is today an empty vessel with $90 Mn in cash.” That’s how an investor who is aware of the company’s financial status, describes the startup. Once valued at $1.7 Bn, this is what DealShare has been reduced to, and the company is actively looking for a potential acquirer, with many names reportedly close to acquiring it at a 95%-plus haircut. Truemeds is said to be one such suitor but the proposed acquisition is not a done deal yet, according to another investor aware of the development. Active discussions are ongoing, but Truemeds’ existing investors are not necessarily aligned with the deal. DealShare is also in talks with other potential buyers, the investors added. Captain Fresh is another name that had surfaced in connection with a possible acquisition but Inc42 has learnt that the company is not pursuing the transaction. The talks for an acquisition at a distressed valuation come after years of restructuring and attempts to find a viable business model for DealShare, which once enjoyed unicorn status. But as the company’s current situation shows, a lot of that was down to the timing of DealShare’s fundraising spree when VCs were investing at valuations that seemed unsustainable. Questions sent to DealShare, WestBridge and Truemeds didn’t elicit any response at the time of publishing the story. For investors, that raises an old question related to distressed investments but with renewed urgency: what should be done with the roughly $90 Mn still sitting on DealShare’s balance sheet? The DealShare 2.0 Plan Tanks The first few years of DealShare’s existence were all about proving that its hybrid B2B and B2C model would be able to compete with the startups that were making inroads into B2B supply chain as well as ecommerce marketplaces. DealShare was pitched as the ecommerce and supply chain destination for consumers and small retailers or kiranas in Tier II, Tier III and beyond. By January 2022, it already had major investors on board and turned unicorn after raising $165 Mn from AlphaWave, Tiger Global and others. The startup raised its next round in rather quick time and was all set to enter the private label business towards the end of FY23. However, the business struggled to gain traction or show growth in the next year. Much of the money was spent in acquiring customers on both sides and by August 2023, DealShare exited the B2B vertical to focus only on B2C ecommerce operations. The company’s net loss crossed the ₹500 Cr mark in FY23 against a revenue of ₹1,963.5 Cr, despite raising more than $200 Mn in the previous year. After two years of struggle, where the company saw the departure of founders Vineet Rao, Sankar Bora and Sourjyendu Medda, DealShare was a shadow of the unicorn it once was. Towards the end of 2025, there emerged a new plan and a so-called DealShare 2.0 vision. Investors brought in Kamaldeep Singh, a former Big Bazaar executive, to run the company and build the next phase of DealShare. DealShare’s FY25 numbers also showed the strain. Revenue fell 13.4% YoY to ₹432.4 Cr, while net loss narrowed to ₹87.7 Cr from ₹167.7 Cr a year earlier. The idea behind this new DealShare was to return to the B2C value commerce, but with a different delivery model. While DealShare was never a quick commerce platform, with its reinvention it tried to reduce the delivery time to a two hour delivery. DealShare realised in comparison to 10-minute deliveries, standard fulfilment timelines would give the startup more room to curb delivery costs while continuing to serve customers looking for lower priced groceries and everyday products. As per sources the startup already had 40 dark stores and was doing about 25,000 - 30,000 orders a day. It focused primarily in cities such as Jaipur, Ghaziabad, Lucknow and Kolkata. The two-hour delivery timeline was a conscious choice. The startup did not want to spend heavily trying to match the delivery times of Blinkit and Zepto. “The 10-minute delivery model was not sustainable,” a source familiar with the operations at the time said, arguing that the economics of quick commerce made it difficult to generate profits after delivery and fulfilment costs. While DealShare did touch close to 38,000 orders a day at some point, another source added that gross margins in this business were around 5%-6%, leaving little to no margin for the company after subtracting costs. A separate industry source said DealShare’s online business faced high customer acquisition and fulfilment costs. “The new leadership had an offline retail background and lacked the technology, product and marketing know how needed to build an online-first business, which is why the company was forced to change tack again,” one of the sources said. By April 2026, DealShare had started cutting back its online operations, and turned to a physical store network as its next bet. The person familiar with the startup said the online business began going through changes from April onwards. At the same time, DealShare was expanding its physical store network, moving from around eight stores to 22. Sources said around 8-10 stores were profitable and that the offline business began generating revenue soon after opening. DealShare had plans to open more stores, including in markets such as Lucknow and Ajmer. Another industry source said DealShare had around 15-20 stores in Jaipur and was preparing to open another 15 stores in Lucknow and Kanpur. The stores were doing “decently well”, as per the source who has seen the numbers. The shift to offline, however, did not settle the question of what DealShare should become. The company considered several versions of the business, including an offline-only mode, retaining the online operation and an omnichannel setup where stores would fulfil online orders. “Multiple variations of AOPs (annual operating plan) and things were discussed, and nothing was sort of closed on by the board,” sources said. One person familiar with the discussions said the board, which was led by WestBridge and Alpha Wave was unable to agree on which business model to pursue. “The board was not able to decide on which way we should go forward with the organisation,” the person said. Investors Struggle To Agree On DealShare’s Future The majority institutional stakeholder in DealShare, WestBridge holds roughly 18.4% of the company, whereas Alpha Wave owns around 16.39% stake in the startup. For investors, the problem was not simply choosing between online and offline. It was finding a model that could make the remaining capital work. The startup had already spent years and hundreds of millions of dollars trying to build a growing business. This online vertical was struggling with low gross margins and high customer acquisition and fulfilment costs, while the newer offline business was still being tested. The indecision became harder to sustain with roughly $90 Mn, or around ₹800 - ₹900 Cr, still sitting on DealShare’s balance sheet, according to another investor familiar with the startup. One source said investors had been discussing how to salvage the remaining money for the startup. “The plan is to sell the startup off to someone who can take the money which we have in a bank account to fund their operations,” the person said. Sources told Inc42 that the talks between Truemeds and DealShare were primarily driven by WestBridge, which is a mutual investor in both the startups. That is where DealShare’s strategic uncertainty meets its acquisition talks. The strategy changes have also coincided with a steady churn in the organisation. Having come to steady the ship, new CEO Singh himself is on his way out. The person familiar with the startup said Singh is serving his notice period. CFO Ashish Shah is also close to the exit door. Besides this, several key employees have also left the startup. As per sources, the company has not carried out a blanket layoff, with employees leaving of their own accord. At the same time, DealShare’s online business has come to a complete halt. The startup began cutting back its online operations around April 2026 and eventually stopped fulfilment from its warehouses. The physical stores continue to operate, but the online business is now “next to zero,” according to the source. The app remains available and sources said around 30,000 users open the app every month, although many leave without placing an order. Roughly 22 DealShare stores are currently operational, but plans to add more stores in Lucknow and Kanpur have been put on hold. The result is a business that looks very different from the one investors were trying to build less than a year ago. The two hour delivery model has effectively been shut down, offline expansion has stopped and the management team brought in for DealShare 2.0 is changing again. Truemeds Talks Put The Cash In Focus The acquisition discussions with Truemeds come against this backdrop. Truemeds has emerged as the frontrunner, but the potential transaction is still subject to investor alignment, according to a person aware of the development. DealShare is also speaking with other potential parties. The roughly $90 Mn cash balance is likely to be a key part of any transaction, and sets the floor for the deal. But another source put it more bluntly. “Why will Truemeds buy a grocery business? It’s just an acquisition of DealShare’s cash reserves,” the source said. It seems that DealShare’s leftover VC backing will be the only thing worth buying. The same source questions whether investors in the potential buyer would be comfortable with such a transaction, particularly if the deal involves issuing shares and diluting their holdings. That is also why the Truemeds deal cannot yet be treated as a done transaction. There are many moving pieces here that may result in the deal falling through. DealShare’s investors appear to be looking for a way out after years of backing a business that has struggled to find a model that can deliver any meaningful growth or returns. For a startup that has raised $400 Mn in funding and touched a valuation peak of $1.7 Bn just over four years ago, the turn in fortunes is nothing short of astounding.
