73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

As Ennu Ninte Moideen completes 11 years, Parvathy Thiruvothu has revisited one of the most defining performances of her career. The National Award-winning actor played Kanchanamala in R.S. Vimal’s 2015 romantic drama, which brought the real-life love story of Kanchanamala and B.P. Moideen to the screen, with Prithviraj Sukumaran playing Moideen.
Ennu Ninte Moideen turns 11: Parvathy Thiruvothu revisits Kanchanamala and her approach to the role
Based on the lives of Kanchanamala and B.P. Moideen from Mukkam in Kozhikode, Ennu Ninte Moideen went on to become a box-office success. Parvathy’s portrayal of Kanchanamala also earned her the Kerala State Film Award for Best Actress, adding to the significance of the role in her career.
For Parvathy, portraying a real person meant looking beyond the romance at the woman whose life she was bringing to the screen. While preparing for the character, the actor spent time with the real Kanchanamala, choosing to observe and listen to her in order to understand her personality, choices and circumstances.
Reflecting on the process of portraying the character, Parvathy said, “Kanchanamala was someone I was constantly trying to understand. I realised that relatability isn’t required for me to portray a character in the best possible way. What matters is understanding the person, their choices, and the circumstances they come from. What I would not do is judge characters for their choices. And working with Prithvi on the film was also a very special experience because we were both trying to understand these two people and their relationship with honesty.”
The film also marked an important collaboration between Parvathy and Prithviraj Sukumaran. The two actors subsequently reunited for My Story, Koode and I, Nobody, continuing their professional association across different projects.
More than a decade after its release, Kanchanamala remains a notable character in Parvathy’s filmography. Her reflection on the role also offers insight into an approach that focuses on understanding characters through their individual circumstances rather than attempting to make them relatable to the actor.
Parvathy is currently riding high on the success of Pradhama Drishtya Kuttakkar. She will next be seen in Storm, an upcoming thriller from Prime Video and HRX Films.

The cause of death of an Anna University student at the Kilpauk Medical College Hospital (KMCH) on Friday was scrub typhus and not dengue, the Directorate of Public Health and Preventive Medicine clarified on Saturday. Panic over dengue gripped the campus, with scores of students turning up for blood tests.
The 20-year-old hostel inmate came to the Kalaignar Centenary Super Speciality Hospital in Guindy on Thursday (September 17, 2026) with four days of high-grade fever and was referred to the KMCH the same day. He died the next day. “Diagnosis: scrub typhus. No dengue diagnosis. It’s a single reported case,” the department posted on X.
The post came after social media and some television channels reported that there had been a dengue outbreak, which had led to three deaths.
The news triggered alarm on campus and students rushed to a primary health centre for tests. A medical officer said that for the past 15 days, around 80 students had turned up in the mornings and around 50 in the evenings with general presentation of fever and cold. The deceased student reported at the health centre with similar symptoms on September 14 and, as per protocol, a complete blood count (CBC) was done on the third day of fever on September 16. The CBC report recorded a count of 1.38 lakh platelets, which ruled out dengue, but the patient did not turn up to collect his report, the doctor added.
“I do not know what happened between then (September 16) and Friday. Besides, ours is only a primary health centre. We carry out blood tests and refer students as soon as they return with any findings,” the doctor said. In the past few weeks, around five cases of dengue have been detected on campus. “The students were referred immediately. They have since recovered and have been discharged,” he added.
Till about midday on Saturday, around 70 students turned up for screening at the health centre as soon as the news of dengue outbreak broke. The university authorities said they had been allaying fears and have started screening students for scrub typhus as well, along with dengue and leptospirosis.
Screening camp and sanitation drive
The Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC) has set up a special screening camp for hostel inmates, the medical officer informed. In addition, GCC Commissioner G.S. Sameeran inspected intensive sanitation and mosquito-control work being carried out at the Anna University campus in Guindy. A total of 100 workers were engaged in sanitation operations, including the removal of accumulated garbage and waste and the implementation of mosquito-control measures, a press release said.
Dr. Sameeran reviewed the ongoing work and instructed officials to ensure that garden waste and garbage were cleared from the campus, and the premises were kept clean, the release said. He also directed officials to prevent water stagnation to curb mosquito breeding and to carry out mosquito-control fogging operations. Officials were further instructed to continuously monitor students and provide appropriate treatment wherever required, the release added.
According to the release, Dr. Sameeran also instructed officials to undertake similar sanitation measures at all educational institutions across Chennai. He directed officials to conduct regular inspections and monitor the implementation of these measures, the release said.
Anna University Registrar V. Kumaresan, City Health Officer M. Jagadeesan, and other officials were present, the release added.

Aerospace propulsion startup DheyaTech has raised ₹43 Cr (around $5.1 Mn) in a funding round led by Avaana Capital, with participation from Unimech Aerospace and Manufacturing. The Bengaluru-based startup plans to use the fresh capital to scale production, establish an integrated testing facility for its gas turbine engines, and work with domestic and global OEMs to accelerate commercial deployments. DheyaTech is targeting flight trials of its engines in Q4 2026. The startup said it has already secured orders from Indian and global OEMs, without disclosing their names or the value of the contracts. Founded in 2018 by aerospace engineers Gurushankara KC, Abhinav Alva, and Chetan Kumar, DheyaTech develops indigenous small gas turbine engines for advanced aerial platforms and energy systems. Its engine portfolio spans thrust capacities ranging from 20 kgf to 400 kgf. The startup said the engines are now entering the commercial deployment stage after years of research and development. DheyaTech claims to have built the entire product development pipeline in-house, covering engine design, development, assembly, and testing. It has also developed a proprietary adaptive engine control unit (ECU), which manages and adjusts an engine’s operation. The startup claimed that it is the first Indian private company to pursue independent airworthiness certification for its gas turbine engines under the guidance of the Centre for Military Airworthiness and Certification (CEMILAC), a DRDO laboratory. Beyond propulsion, DheyaTech is expanding into hydrogen-based technologies and distributed power-generation systems. In collaboration with the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) Bengaluru, DheyaTech has also developed a hydrogen-based flexi-fuel combustor for its 60-kW turbogenerator. A turbogenerator combines a gas turbine with an electrical generator to produce power. DheyaTech’s fundraise comes amid growing investor interest in Indian aerospace and spacetech startups developing indigenous hardware and propulsion technologies. In January, aerospace propulsion startup D-Propulse raised ₹25 Cr from IAN Alpha Fund to develop indigenous propulsion systems based on rotating detonation engine technology. Meanwhile, spacetech startup InspeCity raised ₹100 Cr in August in a round co-led by Ashish Kacholia and Speciale Invest. It plans to use the capital to fund four in-orbit missions and advance its satellite-servicing and propulsion technologies. Advanced hardware and technology startups, including aerospace, defence, semiconductor, and robotics ventures, raised $365 Mn across 66 deals in the first half of 2026.

Srinagar, Sep 19: Leader of Opposition in the Jammu and Kashmir Assembly Sunil Sharma on Saturday questioned the Omar Abdullah-led government over what he described as its repeated use of “statehood” as a response to basic public grievances, asking why the government was in office if it lacked the authority to address routine issues.
Addressing a public interaction programme in Srinagar, Sharma said people were approaching the government with problems related to water, electricity, roads, schools, hospitals and jobs but were repeatedly being told that the administration lacked the required powers.
“For every issue, whether small or big, the only answer that comes from the government and government machinery is that we have no powers,” Sharma said.
He said the elected government had completed two years but people were still facing frustration and confusion.
“The popular government has completed two years, and throughout these two years, we have brought the poor people to a position of frustration and confusion,” he said.
Sharma said the Opposition had a responsibility to engage with people when the government failed to address their concerns. He said his party's legislative group would take up issues raised by people in the upcoming Assembly session and also pursue matters requiring intervention from the Centre.
He, however, questioned the government's explanation that several problems could not be addressed because Jammu and Kashmir had not yet regained statehood.
“Where pipes had to be connected, where poles and wires were required, where schools needed staff, where hospitals needed doctors and paramedics, where potholes on roads had to be filled, for every issue the same answer was received — statehood is not there,” he said.
Sharma then questioned the purpose of the elected government and the Assembly if statehood was being cited as the answer to basic administrative problems.
“If at the end of two years we say that we need statehood even to install poles, wires and pipes, and we need statehood even to provide staff, then why are we in government? Why are we in the Assembly?” he asked.
He went further and said the government should consider dissolving the present arrangement rather than continue for the full five-year term if it believed it could not function without statehood.
“If after two years we still have the same answer, I feel that after five years the same answer will be repeated,” Sharma said.
He said unemployment, particularly among young people, would be among the major issues for the Opposition during the upcoming Assembly session. Referring to data presented during the interaction, he said people aged between 19 and 29 accounted for more than 32% of Jammu and Kashmir's population.
“This section is the largest in Jammu and Kashmir's population and is currently under stress and depression,” Sharma said, arguing that many young people had no income to support their parents, pay for siblings' education or meet family responsibilities.
He also criticised the government's approach to recruitment and outsourcing, claiming that 25,000 jobs had already been occupied through outsourcing.
“You have occupied 25,000 jobs. I say this with a guarantee that these 25,000 will not be advertised again,” he said.
Sharma said outsourced employees could themselves begin demanding regularisation in the future, adding that workers from different government schemes and departments were already seeking regularisation.
He also accused the government of trying to play the role of the Opposition while retaining the privileges of being in power.
“The unfortunate thing is that the people sitting in government also want to do the work of the Opposition,” Sharma said. “The government also wants to remain in the Opposition, but wants to enjoy all the power.”
On the upcoming Assembly session, Sharma said there were numerous issues to be raised but questioned the limited number of sitting days.
He also contrasted the government's claim that Jammu and Kashmir had more Assembly sittings, on average, than some other states, with the region's specific problems.
“Jammu and Kashmir's issues are different. There are so many issues here on a single platform. So a response like this makes a person ask: where should we go, whom should we speak to?” he said.
Sharma also defended the Opposition's public outreach programme, saying it was intended to hear people's grievances and take them to the appropriate forums.
On statehood, he said the issue should not be used as a blanket explanation for administrative shortcomings.
“I am raising the slogan of statehood only to strengthen my vote bank,” he said, while adding that statehood was not preventing the government from dealing with most of the issues being raised by people.
Sharma's remarks came ahead of the upcoming Assembly session, with the BJP seeking to focus attention on unemployment, recruitment, public services and what it describes as the government's failure to address people's day-to-day grievances.

President Donald Trump said on Saturday that he was creating a new "AI force" to "watch over" AI development, one week after a chorus of AI leaders called for government regulation of the ever-advancing tech.
At the same time, he said he would not heed those leaders' call to slow down AI development.
"We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," the president said on Truth Social, his social media platform. "Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!"
Trump said he would also soon be announcing a new AI "Czar."
Trump's comments on Saturday amount to his most concrete response yet toward calls from leaders of frontier AI labs to slow down and regulate AI development to ensure its safety for humanity.
Trump did not offer further details about the new AI Force in his social media post.
Trump likened calls to slowing AI development to "Hoaxes, all generated by the Radical Left Dumocrats, for purposes of destroying our Country."
He said existing criminal statutes were sufficient to protect against incidents of misalignment — a techie term for when agents do things their human minders didn't intend. Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI have all said in recent weeks that some of their AI agents have gone rogue and escaped testing environments, in some cases hacking into other companies.
Last week, a chorus of leading AI CEOs said AI development should be slowed down until adequate risk-prevention measures could be put in place.
In an essay titled "We Must Pace the Frontier," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed a three-pronged plan that would, in his view, strengthen safeguards to ensure AI remains under the control of human engineers.
One of those prongs included calls for the US government, "for antitrust reasons," to regulate frontier AI labs. Amodei's essay was signal-boosted by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
Not all AI CEOs and influential people are so gung-ho about regulation, however.
Some, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and David Sacks, a presidential advisor on science and tech, said government regulation would put the US at a disadvantage with China and choke the growth of smaller AI companies.
Sacks also said AI labs don't need the government and can coordinate a slowdown among themselves.
Business Insider reported earlier this month that Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg opposed plans for a national AI regulator on a phone call with the president in August.
Trump, for his part, appears to agree.
"AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country's GDP," he said. "We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!"

In a three-day strategic dialogue, Belgium and WHO reviewed progress in their longstanding partnership, and agreed to further boost their collaboration on universal health coverage, health-systems strengthening and equitable access to essential vaccines, medicines and health technologies.
The Belgian delegation – headed by H.E. Christophe Payot, Ambassador of Belgium to the United Nations and other international organizations in Geneva – discussed issues of strategic importance, exchanged views on how to smoothly align WHO strategic directions and Belgium's development cooperation priorities in the context of an evolving global health landscape.
The partners exchanged updates on Belgium's support to global health areas brought in the spotlight during the Belgian presidency of Council of the European Union in 2024. WHO was represented by leadership and technical experts from Headquarters and from the Regional Offices for Africa and for Europe.
"After listening to the leaders and experts of WHO we now better understand how they are navigating these challenging times", said Mr Koen Van Acoleyen, Minister Counselor at the Permanent Representation of Belgium to the UN. "We are honoured that we can walk this road together."
Accelerating equitable access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies
The partners reviewed the current status and the most noticeable results achieved by the Access to Medicines programme funded by Belgium. WHO illustrated its work and challenges with an example of country-level implementation in Senegal. It also explained WHO's policies and work on equitable access and local production. Both parties recognized a shared goal for sustainability of the Access to Medicines initiative, as market shaping is key to ensure long-term success.
Health emergencies and pandemic prevention, preparedness and response
Discussions covered WHO's role in strengthening the global architecture for health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience, including the pandemic agreement negotiations and the One Health approach. WHO's crucial field work on health emergency response was demonstrated by presenting the activities in Gaza. The debate also touched upon threats posed by acceleration of biological risks and zoonoses, along with WHO engagement, in particular, risk mitigation.
Universal Health Coverage (UHC)
Elaborating on progress made on UHC-Partnership, the participants reviewed results achieved by WHO with Belgium support in the period 2021-2024, specifically in Belgium's partner countries. They discussed the way forward, exploring the potential for enhanced collaboration at country level, including eventual alignment between WHO country office programmes and Belgium's country level bilateral cooperation. Examples included a summary of the work and challenges at country level from the Democratic Republic of Congo. The visitors listened to a recap of WHO's policies and work on mental health in the context of primary health care.
The partners also reviewed progress in other areas of collaboration on WHO programmes supported by Belgium, such as Neglected Tropical Diseases and Sexual, Reproductive Health and Rights. The review underpinned the importance of an evidence-based approach in these areas.
WHO appreciates Belgium's commitment and engagement, displayed by the participation of representatives of the country's Federal government as well as the Flemish and Walloon governments. "We thank you for your support, honesty, and strong engagement for global health", said Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General, External Relations and Governing Bodies. "Your efforts in supporting our work in Mozambique and Senegal are clear examples of the crucial work we accomplish together".
Looking into the future
The partners discussed ways forward for the Belgium-WHO collaboration framework and multi-year agreement, including progress towards a renewed WHO-Belgium Country Cooperation Strategy.
The enhanced collaboration between Belgium and WHO will support a strong global health agenda under the WHO 14th General Programme of Work (GPW14). There was a shared vision that UHC and health systems strengthening being at the heart of GPW14 ambitions will be taken as essential scope in WHO's ongoing prioritization work.
"We recognize WHO as a trustworthy partner in global health. We felt proud hearing how crucial our support is to the Organization and how it is having a positive impact at country, regional, and global levels", said Mr Dirk Brems, Director of Thematic and Multilateral Cooperation, Directorate-General Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Aid. "It's important we continue these discussions as we tread uncharted territories, and we look forward to working together for strong and sustained multilateralism".

No fire alarms or sprinklers at Pakistan neonatal unit where fire killed 14, report finds
- Published
An official inquiry into a Pakistan hospital fire that killed 14 babies last month has found the neonatal unit lacked fire alarms and sprinklers, while firefighters reported that escape routes were "locked or obstructed".
One firefighter, who asked to remain anonymous, told the BBC he had heard from other rescue workers that entering the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) hospital in Islamabad was "extremely difficult".
"The doors were locked so they had to break through the windows to enter. Even after getting inside, the doors leading towards the ward were locked."
PIMS has not provided a comment on the report and its findings.
The firefighter said he arrived once the blaze had been put out.
It was "difficult for me to even describe what we saw," he said. "The medical equipment above [the babies] had melted and collapsed onto them."
The report from an investigative committee headed by a retired senior civil servant found "systemic and institutional failure" which meant what began as an electrical spark became a "catastrophe".
- At least 14 babies die in Pakistan hospital fire 
  - Published26 August
- Inside hospital after fire kills 14 babies in Pakistan 
  - Published26 August
For many inside the hospital on the morning of 26 August, the first warnings were shouts.
Abdul Ghafoor was in a nearby ward with his mother, who was a patient, when he heard someone warning that a fire had erupted. He went upstairs to see if he could help.
"The entire ward was filled with smoke, we could not see anything," he told the BBC.
CCTV from the corridor outside shows how quickly the fire spread. According to the report, the first indication that something was wrong came at 06:38 when a nurse can be seen running from the ward to get help, returning 20 seconds later with a security guard.
Another nurse, Razia Noreen, is then seen rushing into the ward, emerging seconds later with one of the babies who turned out to be the only one to survive.
Within a minute, the report says, dense smoke had obscured the camera.
Hivsa Walid, her newborn niece and sister-in-law were in the ward next door. Hours later she told the BBC that they had heard a loud commotion and then realised it was a fire when they saw smoke emerging from the unit where the babies were sleeping.
"In that moment, I couldn't understand what was going on. We just focused on getting downstairs and saving ourselves."
On the day of the fire, authorities suggested the fire had started from a spark in the ward's air conditioner.
The report agrees that this was the most probable source of the fire, due to an overheating electrical supply cable - although it remains unclear what exactly the electrical defect was.
The fire then spread quickly, igniting plastics, equipment and bins.
Several babies in the ward were on oxygen support, but the report says that while oxygen may have intensified the fire, there isn't evidence that it created a pathway for it to spread.
The air conditioning units had undergone maintenance, but the report says this is not the same as a safety check. Back in 2018, the hospital's air conditioning units had been approved to be replaced and upgraded, but eight years later this hadn't happened.
The report states that there was no functioning smoke detection, fire alarms or sprinkler system. It found no evidence that the staff in the unit had been trained or had ever rehearsed how to evacuate the ward of newborns, many of whom were premature or "medically fragile". It also found staff had not been trained on how to isolate the oxygen supply in the case of an emergency.
Several people described chaos and confusion in the hospital.
"There should have been fire extinguishers and protocols, but no one was doing anything," Walid said. "Everyone was just running."
Ghafoor said that he was part of a group of seven or eight who tried to find a way to relieve the thick smoke; they managed to break glass panels at the end of the corridor before firefighters arrived.
The emergency services weren't notified about the fire until 06:54, the report says, nearly 20 minutes after it first began. It says the first rescue workers arrived at 07:01.
Like the firefighter who spoke to the BBC, Ghafoor also said rescue staff struggled to get through some of the hospital's doors.
At the time, the hospital's executive director had told BBC News that the door to the newborns' ward was not locked, but guarded, because of previous incidents of baby abductions from government hospitals.
The report says that while "ordinary access restrictions may be legitimate for security purposes… they cannot render designated emergency routes inaccessible when needed."
The report also found that the hospital had received previous warnings about fire risks. A month before, a fire had broken out at its nursing hostel, raising issues with smoke detection, alarms and general fire preparedness.
It says that the hospital and its senior management "bear the principal institutional responsibility for failing to convert known risks, prior warnings and assigned duties into an effective safety system".
Pakistan's prime minister has directed the inquiry's short-term measures to be implemented within the next three months and ordered fire safety audits of public and private offices and buildings.
He has also suspended eight officials and asked for criminal proceedings to be initiated against them.

Gujarat man kills daughter, keeps body in fridge, dies by suicide; 3 notes found
Police discovered the deaths after Dhanak's wife Manjuben, who had gone to her father's house on September 14, was unable to reach him by phone.
A 40-year-old construction site supervisor allegedly killed his five-year-old daughter before taking his own life in Gujarat's Amreli district, police said on Friday.
Kishore Dhanak allegedly smothered his daughter Himanshi at their home on Wednesday and then placed her body inside a refrigerator before hanging himself, Rajula Deputy Superintendent of Police Nayana Goradiya told news agency PTI.
Police discovered the deaths after Dhanak's wife Manjuben, who had gone to her father's house on September 14, was unable to reach him by phone. She later sent her brother to check on him on Wednesday evening. When there was no response at the house, she broke in and found Dhanak hanging from a ceiling fan.
Three suicide notes found at home
According to the first information report (FIR), Dhanak had left three suicide notes on a bed.

In one note, he said he had taken a personal loan and invested the money in construction work, his wife stated in the FIR. He allegedly said he was due to receive ₹7.25 lakh from his business friends but had not received the money.
"He had to receive ₹7.25 lakh, but they (business friends) had not given him anything. Now he had no money and could not find any solution, and hence, he was committing suicide with his daughter," the FIR stated.
In another note, Dhanak said he had killed his daughter because he did not want her to suffer after his death. In the third, he apologised and disclosed that he had kept the child's body inside the refrigerator.
Room decorated with balloons and candles
Inspector P L Chaudhary said the room showed signs that Dhanak had apparently arranged what appeared to be a final birthday celebration for his daughter.
"There was something unusual about the room," inspector P L Chaudhary told news agency PTI.

He said the room had been decorated with balloons and candles. Dhanak had dressed Himanshi in white clothes, placed a dupatta on her head and kept cushions inside the refrigerator.
Dhanak had also placed 'tulsi' leaves on the child's lips, Chaudhary said.
"It seemed like he wanted to celebrate her birthday one last time. They had also performed a puja with idols in the room, which was decorated with balloons and candles. He also kept chocolates in the room and refrigerator," Chaudhary said.
Although it was not Himanshi's birthday, a paper carrying the words "Happy Birthday Himanshi" had been placed on the refrigerator, he said.
Police have registered a case under section 103(1) (murder) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. Further investigation is underway.

Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers.
The men – one from Egypt and one from Eritrea – were then taken to a prison. About 30 detainees from the US remain trapped at a hotel in the outskirts of the coastal city of Malabo after being deported from the US. Detainees have said they believe the men were beaten for telling the press and human rights advocates about the poor conditions and violence inside the hotel, and that they are haunted by flashbacks and terrified they will be retaliated against next.
Human rights advocates and experts have warned for months that conditions at the Hotel Bamy – a run-down establishment that has served as a detention center for US deportees – are dangerous.
The US has sent at least 66 people from different African countries, Cuba and Brazil to Equatorial Guinea, which has received $7.5m as part of a deal to cooperate with the US deportation program. The Trump administration has pursued dozens of similar deals with countries to take in immigrants that the US cannot deport directly to their home countries, where judges have deemed they would face torture or persecution. In the past, the US government allowed those people to live and work in the US indefinitely.
The Trump administration, however, has sought instead to expel them to third countries where they have no ties, do not speak the local language and have no legal status – trapping them in limbo.
Advocates have been especially concerned for deportees sent to Equatorial Guinea, where the authoritarian government is notorious for human rights abuses, including torture, according to the US state department. Detainees held at Hotel Bamy have told the Guardian that armed guards keep watch over them 24/7, and that they have not been provided any medical care or even fresh clothes since arriving there. One of the detainees, who has a severe stomach hernia that requires visits to the hospital to drain his stomach due excessive fluid build-up, said he has been unable to see a doctor since arriving at Hotel Bamy.
Other detainees have managed to obtain medication for HIV, diabetes and other conditions via human rights lawyers, but remain fearful that access to medications will be arbitrarily cut off.
The two men who were tortured – Ahmed Soliman, 31, of Egypt, and Samson Birhane, 47, of Eritrea – have since been transferred to a prison in Malabo. Multiple witnesses recounted that the police officers shouted, “Where is the phone? Where is the phone!” as they beat the men, who had initially been accused of breaking a mirror at the hotel before they were pulled aside and arrested.
The beating, which occurred on 11 September, followed the release of a video first reported by Reuters showing conditions at the hotel and the violent behavior of the guards. The detainees had been using cellphones to communicate with lawyers and the media about the conditions they were facing.
In the video taken by Soliman, which lawyers shared with the Guardian, authorities are seen pointing guns at the deportees. A Cuban man asked the officer for the return of his confiscated mobile phone so he could contact relatives and a lawyer, but was ignored. When officers noticed Soliman filming the exchange with his mobile phone, multiple officers rushed at him and others standing nearby, pointed their guns, and told Soliman to remain on his knees with his hands up for 10-15 minutes.
In another video, Soliman was able to film authorities forcibly sending US deportees to Ethiopia, where they are likely to face torture. When deportees resisted going with authorities, officials gave them the option to “go back to their home country” or “go to prison”. At least 12 people have been returned by Equatorial Guinea to their home country, where they face persecution.
In May, human rights experts at the United Nations issued a rare public appeal asking Equatorial Guinea to halt plans to return deportees to their home countries and to comply with international human rights standards and avoid refoulement, or the expulsion of people to countries where they face persecution.
“This is a human rights catastrophe,” said Bella Mosselmans, director of the Global Strategic Litigation Council, who represents several of the deportees at Hotel Bamy. The US and Equatorial Guinea “must be held accountable for the atrocities they are committing”, she added.
In the week since Soliman and Birhane were beaten, police have also been searching the other detainees’ hotel rooms for cellphones, and have confiscated them. They have also barred lawyers from seeing the deportees. Authorities have told the 29 US deportees who remain at Hotel Bamy that they may never see Soliman or Birhane again, according to lawyers. One detainee who witnessed the beating said authorities treat them as if they are “blanks” who “don’t even exist”. Another detainee said an officer told her: “You will disappear from the earth. I am the law.”
Witnesses said they feared for the lives of Soliman and Birhane, who came to the US as children.
Soliman is a gay man from Egypt who had lived in Phoenix for most of his life. He had a green card, but lost status after he was convicted of drug possession. He served time for his crimes, and in October, a judge had determined he would face persecution and torture if he were to return to Egypt due to his sexuality.
Birhane had come to the US as a refugee when he was 13, but lost status after a conviction for robbery when he was in high school, in 1988. He was allowed to remain in the US after a judge ruled he faced torture in Eritrea, and had been regularly checking in with Immigration and Customs Enforcement as required.
Lawyers for the deportees shared copies of multiple emails they had sent to the US embassy in Equatorial Guinea alerting them to threats and violence against those detained at Hotel Bamy, but those messages have gone unanswered, they said. In July, amid a lawsuit challenging conditions for deportees, the African Commission issued an urgent interim order instructing the government of Equatorial Guinea to refrain from deporting, transferring, or relocating deportees against their will.
The US Department of Homeland Security did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.
A spokesperson for the state department said: “The US government will use all legal means to remove those with no right to remain in our country.”
The agency did not respond to questions about whether it was aware of how Equatorial Guinea was treating US deportees, nor would it acknowledge whether any measures have been taken to intervene.
“As a general matter, we do not comment on the details of our private diplomatic communications with other governments,” the spokesperson said.

The story so far:
On September 14, 2026, U.S. Air Force secretary Troy Meink said the country has “space control” weapons deployed in Earth’s orbit to defend U.S. forces against “hostile adversary action”. The disclosure drew backlash from Russia and China, among other quarters.
What is a ‘space control’ weapon?
As per the U.S. Space Force, ‘space control’ refers to military activities required to control the space domain. In 2025, the then-Space Force chief, Gen. Chance Saltzman, said such a device could possess both “kinetic and non-kinetic” capabilities and could disrupt or degrade an adversary’s capabilities.
‘Kinetic’ generally refers to physically damaging an object through impact, such as by smashing into it. Non-kinetic methods include electromagnetic interference that can jam or spoof a satellite’s communications, and directed energy systems that interfere with its sensors.
In fact, the current Space Force war-fighting framework recognises three kinds of counter-space operations: orbital, electromagnetic, and cyberspace.
What has the U.S. deployed?
We do not know. We also do not know how many units/instances of the system exist, what they are capable of, which orbits they are in, and whether they are kinetic or non-kinetic. Mr. Meink had said that while disclosing the weapon’s (or weapons’) existence would contribute to deterrence, revealing their operational details would subtract from the deterrence. There is also no indication whether these weapons are the same as the space-based interceptors the U.S. government has planned for the ‘Golden Dome’ missile defence programme. These interceptors are still undergoing tests.
What will the weapons defend against?
Mr. Meink has referred to “hostile adversary action”. Incumbent Space Force chief Gen. Douglas Schiess has also referred to “space-enabled attacks”.
In other instances over the years, U.S. officials have repeatedly singled out Russian and Chinese counter-space capabilities as reasons for their government to develop similar capabilities of its own, to protect its own satellites. Russia and China have also demonstrated sophisticated satellite manoeuvres in orbit.
For example, in 2020, two Russian satellites manoeuvred close to a U.S. government satellite, prompting the Space Command to call the behaviour potentially threatening. In 2022, the Chinese Shijian-21 satellite used a robotic arm to tow a defunct Chinese geostationary satellite into a graveyard orbit.
However, we do not know the circumstances in which the U.S. will use its weapons as the government has not published the rules of engagement for orbital weapons.
Is it legal to have weapons in orbit?
The relevant instrument is the Outer Space Treaty, which entered into force in 1967, during the Cold War and the nuclear arms race between the U.S. and the Soviet Union. It prohibits its party states, which include the U.S., Russia, and China today, from placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit or stationing them elsewhere in outer space. It also obviates states from setting up military bases and conducting weapons tests on the moon and other celestial bodies.
However, the treaty does not prohibit states from placing conventional weapons in orbit. The treaty also says all activities in outer space must comply with international law, which means other bodies of international law governing the use of force and armed conflicts can be applied to military operations in orbit. As the U.S. government has not disclosed what its orbital weapons are capable of, it is not possible to say whether it violates specific treaty conditions.
Can other countries prevent unilateral action?
There is no international body to order the U.S. to remove its weapons from orbit. However, there are various diplomatic and legal avenues through which other countries can seek more information and negotiate restraints. For example, Article IX of the treaty requires states to have “due regard” for the interests of other parties, which a (party) state can invoke if it believes U.S. activities in orbit could harm its own peaceful use of space. States can also endeavour to draft new orbital governance rules through the United Nations process on the Prevention of an Arms Race in Outer Space, whose third substantive session is scheduled for November. Countries can also raise the issue before the UN Security Council or the General Assembly as a threat to international peace and security, under Article 35 of the UN Charter.

Trump says he will appoint a new AI adviser, without providing details
WASHINGTON, Sept 19 : U.S. President Donald Trump said in a social media post on Saturday that he plans to appoint a new artificial intelligence adviser, known as an "AI czar," and create an "AI force," though he did not provide details about either initiative or how they would be implemented.
Fears are growing in Washington among lawmakers about the risks posed by AI technology on humans and property. Earlier this month, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said that "people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI and argued that additional regulation is unnecessary.
"We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry," Trump wrote on Truth Social, his social media platform. "Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows! However, we will also be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System."
If Trump follows through on the pledge, it would be his second AI czar. Venture capitalist David Sacks previously served in the role before stepping down in the spring and moving into an external advisory position.
Sacks has echoed Trump's skepticism of new AI regulation. Speaking at a Politico event on Wednesday, he said AI developers should be responsible for ensuring the safety of their products and could be held liable if problems arise, adding that new federal rules are unnecessary.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trump's post.
Trump's post comes ahead of his scheduled meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday. Washington and Beijing are competing for leadership in artificial intelligence, which both governments view as vital to their economic and military strength. Trump and technology executives have argued that excessive regulation would slow US AI development and undermine American companies' ability to compete with Chinese rivals, a claim that safety advocates often refute.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will meet with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng on Sunday at JPMorgan Chase headquarters in New York to discuss AI security, trade and other economic issues, a person familiar with the planning said on Saturday.

Murder suspect who tried to surrender at police station was turned away by NYPD cop: report
Tiliek Shamel Thompson was later charged with with murder, assault, strangulation, child abandonment, and acting in a manner injurious to a child
A murder suspect accused of beating a New York City mother to death and leaving her body with her 7-year-old daughter allegedly walked out of an NYPD station after trying to surrender, according to his attorney and the New York Post.
Tiliek Shamel Thompson, 41, went to the 33rd Precinct stationhouse in Washington Heights around 5 a.m. on September 11, accompanied by his two cousins, as police investigated the killing of Lovay Williams, 27. However, he was not successfully taken into custody until September 12, when he was charged with murder, assault, strangulation and acting in manner injurious to a child.
Williams was found dead inside her apartment on 156th Street on September 6, suffering trauma to her face and neck, according to the Post. She was pronounced dead at the scene. Her 7-year-old daughter was also inside the apartment but was found unharmed. Williams and Thompson were dating, relatives told the Post.
Days later, Thompson and his cousins went to the station because they understood police were looking for him, his attorney, Neville Onielle Dexter Mitchell, told the Post.
“His two cousins said, ‘You’re looking for him,’” Mitchell said, according to the Post.
The officer working the desk allegedly responded, “I just came back from vacation. Nobody’s here,” Mitchell said.
However, an NYPD spokeswoman disputed that account to the Post after reviewing audio and video from the encounter. She said the family did not tell the officer that police were looking for Thompson and that the officer misunderstood the group’s reason for coming to the station.
The officer reportedly believed the three were members of Williams’ family and relayed that information to a sergeant. The officer's reference to being on vacation was meant to explain that he had been away when Williams was killed, according to the NYPD spokeswoman.
The officer then gave one of Thompson’s cousins a phone number for homicide detectives and allowed the group to leave.
Thompson, who police sources reportedly identified as a person of interest in Williams’ killing, later returned to police and successfully surrendered. He was charged with murder.
The NYPD has acknowledged that the encounter was mishandled, according to the Post.
The Independent has contacted the NYPD for comment.
The alleged handling of Thompson’s attempted surrender has drawn criticism from current and former NYPD officers, who said officers should have detained him or contacted homicide detectives even if investigators were not immediately available.
“If he went there and said he was there to turn himself in, they should have investigated,” a senior police officer told the Post on the condition of anonymity.
“I’d say you should hold the guy and investigate further,” the officer added. “Even if detectives aren’t there, you can call them. I’m sure they’d love to take a homicide collar.”
Former NYPD Detective Michael Alcazar similarly said officers should have contacted detectives working the overnight shift, known as nightwatch.
“You got a homicide suspect turning himself in, so you detain him until the squad gets there,” he said. “I’m not surprised if they turned him away. We’re scraping the bottom of the barrel.”
The incident comes as the NYPD works to increase its ranks after years of recruitment challenges. The department hired 4,056 new officers in 2025, the largest number hired in a single year, according to the Post. The NYPD also lowered some hiring requirements, including reducing the number of college credits required from 60 to 24.

Boks power & All Blacks of old - what did we learn from series?
- Published
South Africa further cemented themselves as the world's best team with a 3-1 victory over New Zealand in the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series.
After losing the opening Test in Johannesburg, the world champions won three straight games, comfortably claiming the series with a 43-28 win in Baltimore.
The fourth Test, played in the United States, came after three Tests in South Africa where the All Blacks continued to show promising signs under Dave Rennie.
With the Rugby World Cup next year, what did we learn from the series, which replaced this year's Rugby Championship and will be played again in 2029?
Power remains Springboks' trump card
New Zealander Tony Brown's arrival as attack coach in 2024 pointed to South Africa's ambition to dominate in all facets of the game.
The former Highlanders head coach, who will join the All Blacks in 2028, is known for creating a cohesive attacking shape built on sharp ball movement.
But having been outscored in terms of tries over the first two Tests, the Springboks flipped their pack-power trump card - pivotal to their back-to-back World Cup successes - to prevent a repeat of New Zealand's victorious 1996 series win in South Africa.
Nothing illustrated that more than a monster maul that started just inside New Zealand's 22 and ended with Malcolm Marx peeling off to score the decisive try under the posts.
That came after a penalty try from a scrum in the first half. In Baltimore, their power again proved too much.
"South Africa have tried to play expansively a couple of times when we have dominance after hurting teams in the maul or scrum," Schalk Brits, a 2019 World Cup winner, told BBC Sport.
"New Zealand didn't have that dominance in the forwards, but people said they played beautiful rugby. I don't care if it is beautiful or not.
"Beauty is in the eye of the beholder and I love a maul and scrum."
Fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, who was injured at the end of May, returned to start all four Tests. He was initially named on the bench for the second match, only for Handre Pollard to withdraw.
Despite improving as the series went on, the 24-year-old lacked his usual flashes of individual brilliance.
It remains to be seen whether South Africa turn back to 32-year-old Pollard, as they did in 2023, on the biggest occasions to close out games.
Rassie Erasmus' experienced back-to-back World Cup winners - Marx (32), Eben Etzebeth (34), Pieter-Steph du Toit (34), Siya Kolisi (35), Damian de Allende (34), Cheslin Kolbe (32) - all remain regular starters.
The world champions have proven they can also play an exciting brand of attacking rugby, but appeasing the masses will not matter if a familiar formula can bring them three straight World Cups.
All Blacks return to what made them great
Scott Robertson's dismissal in January after two years as head coach sunk New Zealand to a new low.
Rennie, not the flashiest appointment, had to hit the ground running, and a stunning Test win over South Africa at Ellis Park was a case of doing just that.
The 33-16 victory injected jeopardy into a series which many had the Springboks winning comfortably, given their home advantage and recent dominance.
Hurricanes half-backs Cam Roigard and Ruben Love, both aged 25, were trusted by Rennie to instil a return to the All Blacks way - the ability to score from transition from anywhere on the field and compound scoreboard pressure.
Four or more tries in each Test in South Africa showed just that, with the third Test all square at half-time.
"Scott Robertson was a good culture coach but maybe not a brilliant technical coach. Dave Rennie is a brilliant technical coach," former England wing Ugo Monye told Rugby Union Weekly.
"After the Nations Championship, you could see the structures and how they want to play. I think the All Blacks' backline is the most skilled in World Rugby."
Love struggled to have the same commanding impact in Tests two and three, with fly-half Richie Mo'unga returning for the Baltimore game, his first Test since the World Cup final.
The 32-year-old Mo'unga, who is back after a stint in Japan, was not at the standard that made him one of the best fly-halves at the 2023 World Cup.
However, getting him back up to speed will be an All Blacks goal over the next 12 months.
Former England scrum-half Danny Care said: "Imagine what New Zealand would do with a platform and some dominance. It is great for the game that they are coming back to be the All Blacks of old, and the next 12 months will be fascinating."
World Cup rivals: France 'can play multiple styles', and be 'careful of Ireland'
South Africa live for must-win games. That is when, according to Brits, the Boks "come alive".
Defeat at Ellis Park cost them their world number one status - which was quickly regained - but also exposed a vulnerability.
South Africa, who lost matches in the pool stages of the past two World Cups, are currently the favourites to win next year's tournament in Australia, bringing a pressure they have not experienced previously.
"We hate being the favourite, we almost have to have our backs against the wall," Brits said.
"We prefer not to have the eyes on us and move under the radar. I think that is the best way for any team."
Back-to-back Six Nations champions France sent a weakened side to Christchurch in July and lost 34-32 to New Zealand.
When matched against the Springboks last November, France were beaten emphatically, 32-17.
Brits believes France are "the most settled" and offer tactical flexibility similar to that of the world champions.
"I feel like South Africa have an advantage as they can play multiple styles, and it feels like most other nations don't have that capability," Brits said.
"The only team that can play multiple styles is France, as they can grind it out with the forwards, play the kicking game and the expansive game as well."
He added that England still need to become what they are "supposed to be" and to keep an eye on Ireland, who are travelling "under the radar" after peaking in previous World Cup cycles prior to the tournament.
"Ireland still have amazing rugby players and coaches – the best coaches out there - and a top-four squad," Brits added. "Be careful of Ireland."

The 18th BRICS Summit was held at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on 12–13 September 2026, with leaders from BRICS member and partner countries in attendance. In this context, a selfie purportedly showing Russian President Vladimir Putin, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa, and former Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi is being widely shared on social media (here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: A real selfie image featuring world leaders at the 2026 BRICS Summit.
Fact: The image is AI-generated. It includes individuals who did not attend the summit. The image also features former Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi, who died in a helicopter crash in May 2024. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.

Brazil was represented by Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira, while Crown Prince Khaled bin Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan represented the UAE. The image also features former Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi, who died in a helicopter crash in May 2024. Therefore, the presence of these individuals in a purported selfie from the 2026 BRICS Summit raises questions about the authenticity of the image.

Pictures of the leaders who participated in the conference can be seen here and here.
To sum up, this AI-generated image is being shared as a real photo of world leaders at the 2026 BRICS summit.

Ever wonder how the Fed's interest rate actually works? We've got answers
It may be the most important tool in the Federal Reserve's toolkit: the interest rate.
And on Wednesday, the Fed wielded it for the first time this year, raising rates by a quarter percentage point in a bid to slow down accelerating inflation. But what does it mean when the Fed raises — or lowers — rates? And how does that affect the economy and all of us?
Here's how to understand it all.
So what does the Fed actually do?
The Fed really has two main jobs. The first is to ensure that prices remain stable, which generally means inflation that is neither too hot, nor too cold.
The second job is to strive for an economy with maximum employment — meaning ensuring the labor market is growing at a healthy pace and people who want jobs can find them.
There are times when things are clicking in the economy and both of the two Fed mandates are at peace with each other. Inflation is just at the right temperature, meaning everyday prices are not rising too much, while the labor market is growing steadily, meaning people who want work can find them.
But more often than not, the Fed finds itself in a situation where it has to focus on one of the two — or worse: Both inflation and the labor market are flashing warning signs and policy makers have to confront the agonizing choice of which one to focus on first.
Loading...
So how does the Fed accomplish its goals?
The Fed has several tools at its disposal to try to influence the economy — but none is more important than the interest rate.
When inflation is running hot, the Fed typically springs into action by raising interest rates — just like it did this week.
Although the Fed doesn't directly control what firms charge for mortgages or credit cards, it's hoping that by raising its own interest rate, it can lead to a domino effect across the economy that can then push up many kinds of borrowing costs across the economy.
It's the equivalent of applying the brakes on the economy. The main goal is to try to cool down prices by trying to get people and businesses to think more carefully about their spending. People might think a little harder about whether to buy a home if mortgage rates are higher — or whether to take that business loan if banks are charging more.
On the flip side, when the Fed is concerned about the labor market and wants to push up economic activity, it cuts interest rates in the hopes that the opposite will happen. It's the equivalent of trying to press on the accelerator for the economy.
Take what happened during the Covid-19 pandemic— the Fed, then led by Jerome Powell, was concerned that the pandemic would lead to massive layoffs.
So Powell and the Fed slashed interest rates to near zero, hoping it would spur financial firms to charge less for loans or mortgages — and thus encourage more spending across the economy. It worked — until inflation began climbing and then the Fed had to do the opposite and start cutting rates.
So why is the Fed raising interest rates now?
As Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said Wednesday, "The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long."
Inflation has run above the Fed's 2% target for five years, and the central bank is not confident it would cool off without higher interest rates.
Warsh also made the case that it's the right moment to act with the economy strong enough to absorb the impact of what is ultimately a modest interest rate hike.
Consumer spending has been growing even as higher prices continue to pinch many households. And the job market appears to be on solid footing to weather higher borrowing costs without triggering a surge in layoffs.
So what happens now in the economy – and our pocketbooks?
The Fed's rate hike is small enough that it shouldn't have a dramatic effect — but it does come as many borrowing costs are already rising, partly in anticipation of higher interest rates.
The average rate for a 30-year fixed rate mortgage jumped to 6.95% this week, almost two-tenths of a percent higher than a week earlier, according to mortgage giant Freddie Mac data out on Thursday.
That's enough to increase the cost of a standard home loan by hundreds of dollars each month and further stall hopes of a recovery for the country's stagnant housing market.
"It's like that Godfather movie," said Kara Ng, senior economist at the real estate company Zillow. "Everytime it tries to break out, something pulls it back in."
A higher interest rate also trickles down to the cost of carrying a balance on a credit card or a Buy Now Pay Later deal, though the moves are not as substantial as with mortgages.
Analysts at LendingTree, an online loan marketplace, estimate that for someone with $7,000 in credit card debt, the Fed's rate hike would cost just a few extra dollars each month.
But these higher borrowing costs come as Americans have already been struggling with the high cost of living. The Fed, though, is hoping that the added near-term pain to households will be worth it if it can eventually help bring down inflation.
So now what?
This depends on how the economy responds to the Fed's rate hike — and on forces beyond the central bank's control, like the war in the Middle East, which is pushing up energy costs such as gas prices.
Any improvement on the cost of living is not likely to happen quickly. In fact, the Fed's rate-setting committee signaled a plan to raise rates once more this year, before holding steady in 2027.
At the end of the day, there are no quick fixes to inflation — and it may be a while before households see any relief from high prices.

Ukraine's soldiers want drones and robots that can handle more of the flying and driving themselves, letting one operator oversee multiple systems instead of manually controlling each one.
Ukraine's rapidly expanding arsenal of aerial drones and ground robots has become central to its fight against Russia's larger military. Defense technology companies say they're increasingly automating certain tasks while keeping humans responsible for decisions about using force.
In practice, that means shifting more routine work from the operator to the drone. Newer systems can increasingly navigate, return to base, and help identify targets independently, allowing operators to focus on other tasks, from target confirmation to swarm control.
Mykyta Rozhkov, the chief business development officer at Ukrainian defense technology company Frontline Robotics, told Business Insider that his company's innovation has come from soldier' requests.
"Our soldiers are coming to us with a request of: 'How can you provide us with the capability to have different robots controlled by one person?' or 'Can we make a shift of our UAV pilots easier?'"
The company responded to these requests by developing software that lets drones handle more of the flight themselves, including traveling to and from an area of interest with minimal input.
"In the new version of a drone that we produce right now and supply, there is an autonomy layer installed in the drone itself," Rozhkov explained. "So it can go autonomously to the area of interest, then come back with basically one button."
A "pilot can bring the system home with a push of a button," and the drone can figure out the shortest way back, he said.
Autonomy is also being built into the company's product updates. The latest version of its Linza drone — the 3.0 released this year — has more onboard autonomy, so it can operate when GPS is unavailable because of Russian electronic warfare.
It puts less "mental demand on a soldier so they can do more stuff." It took eight months to develop, but it offers "a huge upper hand," Rozhkov said.
Frontline's Zoom reconnaissance drone also has AI navigation, so it can work when it loses satellite navigational signals.
These changes, likewise, were driven by soldier feedback, the executive said. Unlike many Western defense firms, Ukrainian companies often work directly with soldiers, even talking to them from the front lines over FaceTime and listening to their insights.
The broader shift toward artificial intelligence and autonomy is also a priority for Ukraine's government. Ukraine's defense ministry said in August that units were using "more than 70 different systems powered by AI and computer vision technologies to strike enemy targets."
And it said that the aim is to eventually have 100% of drones on the front line equipped with computer vision and AI capabilities.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, battlefield technology has moved from one pilot fully manually controlling one drone, to AI helping pilots find targets and providing autopilot capabilities, to now enabling one operator to oversee multiple drones while AI assists with basic tasks, like flying and driving, and helps take over when Russian electronic warfare cuts the connection.
Former defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov predicted last month that "we will reach a stage where autonomous drones will fight autonomous drones."
A host of Ukrainian companies are pursuing that vision, and some are working toward larger swarms of autonomous weapons that can communicate with one another.
Achi, the CEO of Ukrainian defense firm Ark Robotics, told Business Insider that the evolution toward a single pilot controlling many drones is "kind of a prerequisite to be successful in the total drone warfare that is coming to all of us."
The defense technology company is developing a system that allows thousands of aerial drones and ground robots, including those not made by Ark Robotics, to work together with minimal human intervention, and enables an operator to be thousands of kilometers away.
Achi said that to have the advantage on the battlefield, "you need these asymmetrical systems that allow you to work with multiple drones at the same time."
Ukraine's combat systems need to be able to work amid Russia's heavy electronic warfare. Ukraine's Twist Robotics makes hardware and software that allow drones to navigate and track designated targets when Russia disrupts GPS. It does that "by default" because the problem is so common, co-founder Rostyslav Olenchyn told Business Insider.
Most of the company's products have AI assistance, allowing the drone to "accomplish the mission" even if an operator makes a mistake or loses control.
How much autonomy is in use remains somewhat limited by both technical and ethical constraints. Many companies and experts describe what is often portrayed as autonomy as exaggerated in practice, resembling advanced automation rather than independently acting AI.
Ukraine says it has not removed human oversight.
Its defense ministry said last month that "algorithms are now being entrusted with critical combat tasks, ranging from navigation and object identification to autonomous target engagement. However, the final decision on target selection and engagement is made by a human operator."
It said it will keep humans in the loop on principle, and while technology helps to identify a target, "the final decision to engage remains with a human, while the system's level of autonomy is limited based on the potential cost of an error."
Ukraine is rapidly advancing to match Russia's volume and allow its human soldiers to stay farther from the fight. Rozhkov described the general trend as "trying to get people outside of the danger zone."

WHO and Netherlands Strategic Dialogue in The Hague, Netherlands 10 April 2024. Credit: Michel Mees Photography
The WHO and the Netherlands convened in The Hague on 10 April 2024, to discuss joint priorities and alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and WHO’s key strategic goals, marking a new milestone in their longstanding partnership.
Rooted in the Netherlands' unwavering commitment to global health, human rights, and universal access to comprehensive health services, the collaboration between the WHO and the Netherlands is instrumental in addressing global health challenges and fostering health and well-being, worldwide and in the country.
Against the backdrop of ongoing conflicts, disasters, and the escalating impact of climate change, and the interconnectedness of the Dutch public health landscape in the Netherlands with global health challenges, this year’s Strategic Dialogue emerged as a critical platform for reflecting on this partnership’s long-term vision.
“In this Strategic Dialogue, throughout all sessions, WHO and the Netherlands showed a commitment to cooperation and to deepening their partnership based on the strong alignment between their respective priorities and objectives”, said Ms Marjolijn Sonnema, Director General for Public Health at the Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport.
A key outcome of the Strategic Dialogue was the recognition of the alignment between the Dutch Global Health Strategy and the WHO's forthcoming 14th General Programme of Work, paving the way for synergies in areas such as health system strengthening, pandemic preparedness, climate change and health, anti-microbial resistance (AMR) and mental health support.
"At a time when inequity in health and in access to essential health services and financial protection is increasing, disproportionately impacting the poor and most vulnerable, the Netherlands stands as a global health leader and trusted WHO partner. With shared priorities and commitment to sexual and reproductive rights, gender equity, health systems, security, climate resilience, and mental health, we look forward to strengthening our partnership to enhance the health and well-being of all, globally and in the Netherlands", said Dr Bruce Aylward, WHO Assistant Director-General, Universal Health Coverage, Life Course.
WHO acknowledged the Netherlands' global leadership as a flexible donor, with an agreement around the imperative to ensure WHO's financing is more sustainable, through the inaugural WHO Investment Round. This WHO initiative aims to mobilize predictable, sustainable and flexible resources essential for the WHO to respond swiftly and effectively to global health challenges and improve health outcomes, particularly for vulnerable populations.
Addressing contemporary challenges such as geopolitical tensions while seizing opportunities for advancing global health objectives were also on the table during the dialogue. Both parties stressed the importance of sustained collaboration to address pressing health issues comprehensively.
Taking stock of the joint achievements since the previous strategic dialogue in 2022
In 2022, the Strategic Dialogue between the Netherlands and WHO called on both partners to enhance synergies between WHO priorities and the new Dutch Global Health Strategy. Implementing this approach, the Netherlands and WHO:
- Expanded their cooperation to new areas of joint interest, e.g., climate change and health;
- Renewed their longstanding cooperation on Water, Sanitation and Hygiene and Mental Health and Psychosocial Support in health emergencies and humanitarian settings;
- Improved the flexibility and predictability of the Netherlands’ financial support through renewed General Arrangements with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (2022-2025) and the Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport (2024–2028) demonstrating the Netherlands’ commitment to WHO’s sustainable financing;
- Hosted together the 2nd World Local Production Forum in the Netherlands;
- Continued and deepened their technical cooperation through secondments, Junior Professional Officers and the Collaborative Centres.
The outcomes of the 2024 dialogue will inform future collaboration between the Netherlands and the WHO, so that efforts are aligned, and the optimal use of resources is helps achieve improved health outcomes worldwide. The enduring partnership between the Netherlands and the WHO stands as a cornerstone in the global health landscape, reflecting a shared commitment to advancing health and well-being globally.
-----------------
The Netherlands is a key supporter and strategic partner of the WHO.
In 2022- 2023, the Netherlands was one of the top five flexible WHO contributors with nearly US$ 19 million in core voluntary contributions. Overall, the Netherlands contributed more than US$ 106 million to the WHO in 2022 - 2023, of which US$ 93 million, nearly 90%, was voluntary funding.
The Netherlands also supports the WHO's technical expertise through secondments of staff and helps boost young people's careers in public health via the WHO's Junior Professional Officer Programme.
This demonstrates the Netherlands' commitment through its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport to the WHO’s central role in the global health architecture.
Through this support, the Netherlands contributes to crucial activities in the areas of sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care, antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.
