Anthropologists and community leaders from Nagaland, a remote state in north-eastern India bordering Myanmar, have expressed joy and relief that human remains belonging to their ancestors that had been on display in a British museum for nearly a century are finally being returned.
On Monday, the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford announced that 39 pieces of human remains – including parts of skulls, a finger and a piece of skin with hair – belonging to the Naga tribes, will be returned to Nagaland after six years of negotiation between the community and the museum.
For the Nagas, the repatriation is not just about “bones and ancestral remains … It is about memory returning to where it belongs,” the community said in a statement.
“We are at peace,” said A Peihwang Wangsa, an Indigenous Konyak man involved in the repatriation negotiations. “Our forefathers are coming back.”
Wangsa, whose ancestors’ remains are among those being returned, added that the homecoming would be a moment of “mourning and celebration”.
NT Thamlong Phom, a Naga community leader from the Phom sub-tribe, said: “I feel joy, I feel blessed.
“Ever since the announcement was made, my entire community has felt happy,” he said. “Our ancestors’ spirit will have a final resting place.”
Thejao Vihienuo, who is also part of the repatriation discussions and went to Oxford in 2025, said he had been “angry and unhappy” to see the remains of his ancestors, which he said had been “taken in a most dubious manner”.
“It was displayed as if it was a trophy, but they silently spoke of the atrocities the British committed on our people,” he said.
The return caused “mixed feelings”, he said, but added: “We owe it to our ancestors to bring their remains back and put them to peaceful rest. And also to our younger generation to decolonise their minds and show that our children are not inferior to any white man.”
The Nagas are a transnational Indigenous group of tribes living in India’s north-east and parts of Myanmar, once associated with headhunting but now predominantly Christian.
The Pitt Rivers Museum, home to one of the world’s largest ethnological collections, has more than 6,500 Naga objects, 898 of which were on display. Most of the collection was “coercively” acquired by the colonial administrators James Philip Mills and John Henry Hutton.
The human remains were displayed at the museum for 80 years. In 2020, they were put into storage during a revamp aimed at addressing the institution’s colonial past and how exhibiting human remains “reinforced racist and stereotypical thinking” of other cultures.
The museum said in a statement: “Thirty-nine Naga ancestors will soon begin their journey home from Oxford to Nagaland.”
In November, a Naga delegation will visit Oxford for a handover ceremony and the remains are expected to arrive in Nagaland before the end of the year. They will be laid to rest in a traditional community ceremony in the state capital, Kohima.
The repatriation negotiations were led by representatives from all of the Naga tribes.
“It has been a journey of redemption,” said Prof Dolly Kikon, a Naga anthropologist. “This shows that we are no longer victims of colonial violence. We embrace our roles as people who find redemption and healing by giving dignity and honour to a very violent past.”
The negotiations started in 2020, when Kikon wrote to the museum after reading “an article in the Guardian that they were doing an ethical review” of the collection. “They replied within 24 hours,” said Kikon.
That was just the beginning of a lengthy process that soon expanded into a wider community-led campaign.
The Forum for Naga Reconciliation, a community peace group, assembled a team known as Recover, Restore and Decolonise, bringing together Naga volunteers from across the region to work on the repatriation effort.
“They travelled to villages and organised meetings to inform people about the remains,” said Arkotong Longkumer, a Naga anthropologist who worked closely with Kikon to lead the initiative, which he described as “open and transparent”.
“It was an intergenerational journey that brought together students, civil society, tribal leaders and the church,” said Longkumer, who teaches at Edinburgh University.
A Naga delegation, including tribal leaders, visited Oxford in 2025 to officially register a claim to the remains.
“I had never known our ancestral human remains had been taken away like that,” said Wangsa. “I felt angry when I saw them.”
Laura Van Broekhoven, director of the Pitt Rivers Museum and a professor of museum studies and ethics at Oxford University, said the museum was completing paperwork to enable the return of the remains.
“We will then start working towards the ceremonial aspects so we can have everything ready,” she said. “In our experience, handover ceremonies can be very emotional.”

The U.S. is working on rules for pharmaceutical companies investing in China that would likely preserve their ability to strike most licensing deals for Chinese drugs, Reuters reports. This would mark a departure for the Trump administration, which has sought to tighten business ties with China for other industries under new national security legislation, and would be looser than restrictions sought by some lawmakers. The rules, being drafted by the U.S. Treasury Department, are likely to allow U.S. drugmakers to invest in promising new drugs being developed by Chinese companies as long as they are not related to pathogens or biotechnology that could be weaponized.

At least 16 killed after vehicle loaded with explosives rams into Pakistan mosque
- Published
At least 16 people, including five police officers, have been killed after a vehicle loaded with explosives rammed into a mosque in north-western Pakistan, according to a senior police official in Peshawar.
A gun battle is still ongoing between attackers and security forces at the mosque, near police headquarters, in the Kohat district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
One of the assailants has reportedly been killed, an officer says, and a rescue operation is under way.
In a statement, Pakistan's President Asif Ali Zardari expressed "his best wishes for the swift recovery of those injured in the explosion."
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police chief inspector general Zulfikar Hameed described the attack as a "suicide attack", according to Reuters news agency.
There has been no immediate claim of responsibility.
Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif also condemned the blast.
Militancy in Pakistan's border areas has risen sharply in recent months, targeting the military and police.
Islamabad says militants use safe haven in Afghanistan to train and plan attacks in Pakistan. Afghanistan's Taliban government denies the accusation and says militancy is Pakistan's domestic problem.

China-led study reveals ‘Greater Gondwana’ was 80% of Earth’s crust 500m years ago
Research suggests that the land mass that once dominated Earth was larger than previously thought
Fragments of a long-disappeared ancient giant land mass have been discovered buried deep beneath parts of the modern continents that once formed it, according to an international team led by Chinese scientists.
Published this month in the peer-reviewed journal Science Advances, the discovery reveals that Gondwana – a land mass that dominated Earth some 500 million years ago – was much larger than previously believed.
Crucially, the findings show how geological activity related to Gondwana created favourable conditions for the Cambrian explosion.
The study was jointly conducted by researchers from the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences, Australia’s Curtin University, and Zhejiang Lab, a non-profit research institution in eastern China.

The new lines of southern Lebanon
The U.N. peacekeepers' armored vehicle moves slowly along the de facto border in southern Lebanon, not because of the terrain or the threat of shelling and drones, but because every mile means relearning a landscape profoundly transformed by war.
UNIFIL — the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon — has been monitoring this area since 1978, when it was created to verify Israel's troop withdrawal after its first occupation of Lebanon.
The U.N. expanded UNIFIL's mandate 20 years ago to include monitoring adherence to a ceasefire in fighting between Israel and Lebanon's Iran-backed Hezbollah - the militant group created in 1982 to counter a second Israeli invasion.
Almost half a century later, the peacekeeping force's mandate will expire at the end of the year and due to U.S. and Israeli opposition, will not be renewed. There is still no durable ceasefire.
An agreement in June between Israel and Lebanon has brought only a fragile pause to a conflict that the Lebanese government says has killed more than 4,300 people, displaced more than 1.2 million and redrawn the geography of southern Lebanon since it began in March, when Hezbollah fired rockets at Israel. Israel says 39 soldiers and a military contractor, plus two civilians, have been killed in Hezbollah attacks since then. Seven U.N. peacekeepers have also been killed since the war began this year, according to UNIFIL.
The "blue line" — now marked by blue metal barriers — was the demarcation line drawn up by the U.N. for another Israeli withdrawal in 2000, after 18 years of occupation in southern Lebanon. Now marked by blue plastic barriers, it has served as a de facto border between two countries which has never formally agreed on boundaries.
Today, it remains on the map, but no longer fully describes the reality on the ground.
Months of bombardment have blurred the old boundaries. New lines of control and restriction have emerged, changing how people move, work and return home. After months of restrictions, UNIFIL has reopened access to parts of its eastern sector that Israel's military presence had placed off limits.
"Today, for the first time in several months, we are heading into the eastern sector. It is an opportunity for us," says Sgt. Audric of the French UNIFIL battalion. French military policy in Lebanon prohibits identifying soldiers by first names for security reasons. "Since the negotiations began, we have been able to reopen this sector and finally regain our freedom of movement following the ceasefire."
The reopening comes as the implementation of U.N. Security Council Resolution 1701, adopted in 2006 to end the war between Israel and Hezbollah and establish a security framework for southern Lebanon, faces renewed challenges. At the same time, UNIFIL, first deployed in 1978, could come to an end after nearly five decades. Its original mandate was to restore security, oversee Israel's withdrawal and help re-establish Lebanese state authority in the south.
Yellow line
Israel has established what it calls a buffer zone marked by what it refers to as the yellow line, a strip of land five miles wide in some places where Israeli forces continue to occupy Lebanon. It says the purpose of the zone is to prevent Hezbollah from firing rockets into northern Israel. Israel has barred Lebanese civilians from accessing their own land along the border and has demolished civilian homes and infrastructure in many of the border towns.
"The yellow line does not exist for us, but we have to mark it on the map so that we can visualize it," says Lt. Col. Sebastián Dorado Santos, UNIFIL's Spanish public information officer.
"It has disrupted normal life. Many civilians are unable to go to work or carry out their daily activities. The harvest season is approaching, but they cannot access their fields."
Beyond the line, the physical scars of the conflict are visible everywhere. Roads have been reduced to rough tracks, marked by the passage of Israeli tanks. Houses that once sheltered families have been reduced to concrete and rubble. In some places, Israeli flags fly above the ruins.
A succession of emptied and flattened villages marks the route between the sectors: Houla, Odaisseh, Kafr Kila and the open structure of Fatima's Gate, a former crossing between Israel and Lebanon closed by Israeli forces after they withdrew in 2000.
For local civilians, these are not abstract lines on a map. They separate homes from farmland, communities from workplaces and families from the places where they built their lives. The restricted area covers approximately 6% of Lebanon's territory, reviving memories of Israel's 18-year occupation of southern Lebanon, which ended in 2000.
Access remains largely prohibited, although just a few miles from the most heavily destroyed areas, some Christian villages remain inhabited, although isolated and with limited access to basic services.
Humanitarian convoys bring food, medicine and other essential supplies. Their presence, however, carries a symbolic weight.
"When they see us, they know they are not alone," says Father Hani Tawk, coordinator of a network of Catholic organizations.
Many residents remain caught between a border they do not control, a limited state presence and an occupation with no clear end in sight, Tawk adds.
For local authorities, access to farm land is one of the most pressing concerns.
"Agriculture remains the main source of income and an essential driver of local development," says Mari's mayor, Salman Abou al-Ola. Farmers need to reach their fields and harvest their crops."
The restrictions are also cutting communities off from basic services.
After months of suspension because of fighting, UNIFIL has resumed some of its non-military activities, providing basic medical assistance in areas where access remains severely restricted.
"There are no doctors here, and humanitarian assistance is insufficient. We are living like in a prison," says Fayez Al Khaled, a Syrian resident of Ain al-Arab being treated by a visiting Spanish doctor.
The main road to Nabatieh remains closed. When Khaled's mother became ill, he says, there was no adequate medical care available.
"This area is characterized by a lack of employment opportunities and, more recently, intense fires," says Maj. Jesús Fernández Manchado with the Spanish UNIFIL contingent. He says they suspended their activities in March and only recently resumed them.
The Lebanese government has accused Israel of deliberately setting wildfires in forested and agricultural areas to ensure villagers do not return. The Israeli military has refused to comment on the charges.
"The yellow line affects all our activities because it represents a new reality on the ground," Manchado says. "For civilians, it means separating homes from their land. For us, it is neither recognized, marked, nor demarcated."
But the yellow line is not the only development reshaping southern Lebanon's border. A new system of "pilot zones" has also emerged — pinpointing areas where Israeli forces and Hezbollah fighters are meant to withdraw, with Lebanese armed forces replacing them.
In the town of Zawtar al-Gharbieh, the consequences of that shifting geography are visible inside people's homes. Ihsan Yaghi looks over what remains of her house on a visit from Beirut's southern suburbs, where she has been displaced. Yaghi, who has six daughters and a retired husband, returned after hearing that Israeli forces had withdrawn from the village at the end of July. She waited for a week on it's outskirts for clearance from the Lebanese Armed Forces before finally entering.
Inside the town, evidence of the occupation was still visible. A line of Israeli tanks stood positioned behind the houses.
Just a few meters away, another house had been used as a temporary shelter by Israeli soldiers. Cans, water containers, mattresses and crosses - seeming evidence of the home's former Christian occupants — lay scattered across a dirty room. Drawings that included a Star of David covered the walls — apparent traces left by the soldiers who had stayed there.
Mahasen Fakih had been displaced to the Chouf region and returned to Zawtar a few days ago, and returned to find her home destroyed. There is still no electricity or running water in the town.
"The explosions don't stop throughout the night, especially from Ali al-Taher. I can barely sleep," she says, referring to a mountain landmark where Israel has been fighting to dislodge Hezbollah fighters.
Across southern Lebanon, thousands of people are trying to return to homes that no longer exist.
The blue line remains where it was drawn. But on the ground, a new geography has taken shape, marked by the constant hum of drones, restricted zones, abandoned villages, destroyed roads and fields their owners can no longer reach. Daily airstrikes are a reminder that, for those living here, the war is not over.
The map may still show the same border. On the ground, everything has changed.

- The claim that an image shows U.S. President Donald Trump kissing White House aide Natalie Harp on a golf course remains under investigation.
- The rumor stems from two versions of the image shared on social media in mid-September 2026. The higher-resolution version had telltale signs of artificial intelligence, such as hands with too many fingers, as well as a watermark confirming it was created or edited using OpenAI's generative AI tools. The lower-resolution image did not have an OpenAI watermark and was too blurry for telltale anomalies to be apparent.
- The White House declined to provide Snopes with legitimate photos of Trump and Harp golfing that could be compared to the images shared online. A spokesperson said the image was "clearly a fake."
- Hany Farid, co-founder of deepfake detection company GetReal, told Snopes the higher-resolution image was AI-generated and was clearly derived from the lower-quality version. While he said the lower-resolution version's quality itself was "a bit of a red flag," he said he considered its authenticity inconclusive.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces.
In summer 2026, many people scrutinized White House aide Natalie Harp following news reports of what appeared to be an unusually close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump.
In September, following a Trump visit to Ireland during which he took time to golf at his Trump Organization-owned course, people started sharing multiple versions of an image that appeared to show Trump kissing Harp, whose back is turned toward the camera, while on the golf course.
For example, one X post (archived) shared a low-resolution version of the image. Another popular X post (archived) shared a higher resolution version with crisper colors.
Users also widely posted the image on Threads (archived) and Instagram (archived). Snopes readers emailed us to ask whether the image was real.
Snopes could find no credible evidence or source supporting the authenticity of the image, but we were able to find multiple red flags indicating the higher-resolution version was generated or edited with artificial intelligence tools. The lower-resolution version did not have those same red flags, in part because of its poor quality. Therefore, we've left this claim unrated until more evidence comes to light.
We used Google Lens to run a reverse image search on both versions of the image. The oldest example that turned up was a thumbnail image for a Sept. 14 YouTube video uploaded by political commentator Keith Edwards. We've fact-checked images originating from Edwards' thumbnails twice before. In one of those fact checks, Edwards confirmed he had used an AI tool to generate the image.
Snopes reached out to Edwards by email to confirm the origin of the image of Trump kissing Harp. He responded:
My thumbnail team found the image online. We did not create or alter the underlying image, but we also did not independently verify its original source or that the woman pictured is Natalie Harp. Given that only the back of her head is visible, I don't think her identity can be confirmed from this image alone.
Following this, Snopes used the thumbnail to conduct another reverse image search. While it failed to unearth any older versions of the image, the results (archived) included a wider shot of the subjects than any other we could find. That version, which included the "wtf" text on Edwards' thumbnail, linked to the same Edwards video.
None of the reverse image searches turned up links to credible news sources or even less-credible tabloids sharing the image. Considering the reporting already scrutinizing Trump's relationship with Harp, it's unlikely, if the image were real, that not a single credible news source would report on it. The image also did not appear among photos kept by credible photo repositories, such as Getty Images and The Associated Press.
Although there was no photographer, date or location listed for any version of the image, the timing of its spread suggested it was likely meant to depict something that took place while Trump was visiting his golf course in Ireland on Sept. 13, an activity listed on his calendar as "Executive Time." Photos of that golf course and Google Maps satellite view don't show any trees, in contrast to the image of Trump and Harp kissing.
Snopes reached out to the White House by email to ask if any photos of Trump and/or Harp at the golf course over the weekend exist in order to compare what either was wearing in those images with what they supposedly wore in the image of the kiss. The White House did not send or confirm the requested images, but a White House official said the image shared online was "clearly a fake photo."
While many of those who spread the photo presumed the woman was Harp, there's no way to confirm that considering the subject's face isn't visible.
Some people online claimed the image was actually a 2017 photo of Trump exchanging a cheek-kiss with Norwegian golfer Suzann Pettersen as a greeting. This is false. That kiss was not actually on the golf course, Pettersen was in a different outfit than that of the woman in the recent image and Trump was also dressed differently, as shown in images capturing the moment from 2017.
AI evidence
A tool by OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, detected a watermark in the higher-resolution version image consistent with those generated or edited using the company's AI tools. Moreover, the image depicts Harp holding her golf club with six fingers.
The lower-resolution version of the image was too blurry to clearly identify AI tells such as an excessive number of fingers on either person's hands. While OpenAI's tool didn't identify a watermark within the lower-resolution image shared across X and Threads, the tool did detect OpenAI watermarks on the thumbnail for Edwards' video.
Separately, Snopes tested what the tool would find on a real photo where a small portion had then been edited by AI. OpenAI's tool detected the watermark on such an image, even when the photo was cropped to remove the part that had been edited.
Hany Farid, co-founder of deepfake detection company GetReal and a professor at Drexel University, told Snopes over email that "the high-resolution version was clearly derived from the lower-resolution version and has a SynthID watermark. As for the lower-resolution version, there is not a lot to go on here given the quality and resolution."
"While there are no obvious visual anomalies, the low quality/resolution is a bit of a red flag. In particular, given the apparent narrow depth of focus, this does not appear to photographed with a mobile device and is more likely taken with a DSLR that would afford this type of narrow depth of focus," Farid continued. "Assuming this to be the case, I would expect the image quality to be better. At this point, I'd say the authenticity is inconclusive."

A case in this regard has been registered under the relevant sections of law. [KNT]

Uh oh, we got a cute alert! It’s Bezzy, your adorable, cuddly, anthropomorphized server-rack and stuffed-animal friend! Give this soft lil’ doll a squeeze, and it shall sing you its telltale song: the piercing, grinding ambient squeals emitted from a real US data center.
The Bezzy doll is a stuffed plushie made in a satirical collaboration between the New York–based creative studio Basura and Big Data, the musical project of producer Alan Wilkis, best known for the song “Dangerous,” a 2013 collaboration with the band Joywave. The joint project, which is coming out the same day as a new Big Data single, is called Adopt a Data Center. The goal is to present people with a “cuddly introduction to life with a real data center.”
Data Centers are very un-vogue right now. Built out by all the big AI companies to power their increasingly power-hungry AI tools, data centers have spread across thousands of acres of land in the US. They have been heavily criticized for their energy consumption and expansion of gas power. They have also proven to be audibly annoying, stirring up complaints about noise pollution from those nearby.
The Adopt a Data Center stunt aims to make people think differently about how services produced by data centers fit into their lives. That manifests as a plush stuffie that looks like a server rack in a data center, albeit with long arms and legs and googly eyes. It’s cute in the way Don’t Hug Me I’m Scared is cute. Squeeze Bezzy’s torso and the sound bursts out. It’s a screeching few seconds of a recording taken by a neighbor of a data center in Virginia. The tag on the Bezzy plushie reads, “Hug me for ear-piercing forever hum.”
“We picked this recording as it was the clearest and most suitably irritating,” wrote Rajeev Basu, the founder of Basura, in an email to WIRED. In an interview with the person who recorded the audio, Basu says they described the sound as “like a car alarm going off nonstop. It's high-pitched, and it's all you can focus on.”
Basura has worked on other projects like making luxury wear for dogs and a partnership with Yerba Madre that made dirt shoes designed to break apart during a walk to spread wildflower seeds.
Along with Bezzy, the data centers project includes a collection of stickers that say things like “Every data center deserves a forever home” and “Open your heart. And your power grid.” Basu says the project is the result of dozens of interviews with people who live near data centers in the US. The website itself reads, “Adopt a data center: All they ask for is everything.”
Wilkis, whose band Big Data has “It’s giving Black Mirror, but make it music” in its Spotify description, says that the one upside of the data center debate is that the backlash is genuinely bipartisan.
“AI is a proxy for decades of widening wealth inequality in America, and data centers are its physical embodiment,” Wilkis wrote to WIRED. “With roughly 40 percent of the stock market's value riding on a handful of tech companies, the US economy is already a bet on AI's success.”
Sadly, only 20 Bezzy dolls are available for $99 from the Adopt a Data Center website and the Big Data storefront. Basura designed the toys, which are handmade in the US. But the physical toy isn’t the real point. The satire is meant to hook people into looking at the facts for themselves. When you click “adopt now” on the website, you’re taken to a statement with links to research and stories about how data centers fit into the world.
“It’s not about whether AI data centers should exist,” Basu says. “It’s about who gets to decide where they go, what resources they consume, and whether the communities living beside them actually benefit.”

The proposed deals were voluntary land exchanges, meaning they would require the new owners to hand over separate, environmentally sensitive parcels to the National Park Service in return for the land in question. As of this writing, the deals were in the public comment stage of the process and were not finalized.
Rumors that U.S. President Donald Trump's administration was planning to hand over parcels of land from Georgia's federally protected Cumberland Island National Seashore to private owners who could then build mansions on them circulated online in September 2026.
Users on social media platforms claimed it was essentially a done deal and posted images of Trump next to images of the protected land in question, stating the administration was "selling portions of Cumberland Island National Seashore to build mansions, jeopardizing ancient oak forests and endangered sea turtles."
Readers flocked to Snopes, searching the site for the truth behind the rumor.
The claims referred to a parcel exchange proposal put forth by the Department of the Interior. The proposal was similar to another that made headlines in August 2026 — a parcel exchange at Yosemite National Park.
As a result, we've rated the claim true.
A spokesperson for the Department of the Interior told Snopes via email that "the National Park Service is evaluating two proposed voluntary land exchanges to strengthen the long-term protection and management of Cumberland Island National Seashore" but that "no final decision has been made."
The department said the deals trade the land in question for "sensitive private parcels in the heart of the island" that would be incorporated into the national seashore and protected from development. Meanwhile, they said, "any NPS-managed land conveyed into private ownership would remain subject to permanent conservation easements prohibiting subdivision, limiting the location and scale of development, and protecting natural and cultural resources."
The full statement given to Snopes read:
The National Park Service is evaluating two proposed voluntary land exchanges to strengthen the long-term protection and management of Cumberland Island National Seashore. No final decision has been made. If approved, the proposals would bring sensitive private parcels in the heart of the island into the National Park Service system, where they would be protected from commercial development, while any NPS-managed land conveyed into private ownership would remain subject to permanent conservation easements prohibiting subdivision, limiting the location and scale of development, and protecting natural and cultural resources.
Public input is an important part of this review. NPS will evaluate the substance of the comments received, including concerns about environmental effects, development limits, alternatives and proposed safeguards, and may revise the proposals, conduct additional analysis or select the no-action alternative. The number of comments favoring or opposing a proposal does not by itself determine the outcome; the decision must be based on the environmental analysis, substantive public input, applicable law, independent appraisals and the public interest.
Earlier decisions involving Cumberland Island, as well as separate matters involving Yosemite National Park (to which no final decision has been made), do not predetermine this review. Each proposed land exchange must be evaluated independently based on its own facts, legal authority, environmental effects and conservation benefits. Comments on the Cumberland Island proposals will be accepted through Oct. 16.
The Center for Biological Diversity, a nonprofit organization that works "to secure a future for all species, great and small, hovering on the brink of extinction," posted a response to the Cumberland Island proposal. The news release said, "Conservation groups are condemning the proposed land swap, which would trade park land for privately owned land and allow for the development of eight 15,000-square-foot mansions up to three stories high."
The news release quoted Will Harlan, the Southeast director at the organization, as saying: "This is an American national park, not a Monopoly board. A bunch of new mansions don't belong here. … Like Yosemite, Cumberland Island is a national treasure that belongs to every person in this country. These land swaps are an attack on the American people who own this public land."
The group's criticism continued:
The land swap proposal on Cumberland Island comes just a week after the National Park Service approved a new visitor use management plan that greenlights new development on the island's seashore. Structures will be built on the seashore in the critical habitat of nesting sea turtles and endangered shorebirds. The plan also quadruples the number of visitors and allows massive increases in commercial activity and boat traffic, threatening endangered manatees, Atlantic sturgeon and sea turtles. Thousands of comments opposing the plan flooded the National Park Service, but the agency approved the plan anyway.
The Center for Biological Diversity noted there were more than 3,000 comments opposing the proposal, but, as the Department of the Interior noted in its statement above, that doesn't necessarily reflect a projected result. Instead, "the decision must be based on the environmental analysis, substantive public input, applicable law, independent appraisals and the public interest."
What the exchange proposes
The 81-page document outlining the proposal, embedded above, included two different exchange options beginning on Page 6.
In the first exchange, the NPS would receive 10 acres of "unimproved maritime forest" in trade for 20 acres of current NPS land that would go into private ownership, allowing for two single-family residences.
In the second exchange, the NPS would receive two noncontiguous parcels totaling 119 acres of "upland forest, salt marsh, and ocean frontage." In this swap, 60 acres of current NPS land would go to private owners and allow for up to six single-family residences.
In both options, the limitations for the new construction on the formerly public land would still require 80% of the property to "be designated as a conservation area" used for "conservation purposes and non-commercial, non-industrial, and low-impact outdoor recreation in perpetuity" with the remaining 20% "designated as a potential building area and may be used for non-commercial, non-industrial, single-family residential use."
In either scenario, the maximum allotment for a single-family residence would be 15,000 square feet and 35 feet tall, which appeared to qualify as a "mansion," according to Realtor.com.

Srinagar, Sep 19: J&K Legislative Assembly Secretariat has admitted a private member’s resolution moved by MLA Javid Hassan Baig, seeking to put the proposed Baramulla–Uri railway line alignment from Kanispora towards Khanpora/Sheeri in abeyance pending an independent geological, geotechnical and seismic assessment of the corridor, officials said on Saturday.
The officals said the resolution calls for a comprehensive evaluation of slope stability, soil bearing capacity, seismic vulnerability, drainage and landslide susceptibility before finalising the alignment.
"This House expresses serious concern over the proposed alignment of the Baramulla-Uri Railway Line from Kanispora towards Khanpora/Sheeri and resolves to urge the Government of India that its finalisation on the said stretch be kept in abeyance pending a comprehensive and independent geological, geotechnical and seismic assessment of the proposed corridor," According to a communication issued by the Assembly Secretariat.
In view of the concerns highlighted by the resolution, the Secretariat said that the House urged the Government of India to undertake forthwith a comprehensive and independent geological, geotechnical and seismic investigation of the proposed corridor.
Secretariat further urged the govewrnment to "conduct detailed assessment of slope stability, soil bearing capacity, liquefaction potential, seismic vulnerability, drainage conditions and landslide susceptibility along the proposed alignment and finalize the alignment only after the competent technical authorities establish and certify the geological and structural suitability and long-term safety of the proposed corridor”.

The AfD is surging and Berlin is going to the polls. Could the ‘City of Freedom’ fall to the far-right?
After success in Saxony-Anhalt, the far-right AfD has trained its sights on state elections in the German capital of Berlin. In one of the world’s most liberal cities, the party is just four points off the lead in the polls. Alex Croft reports
Germany is facing a far-right surge as the Alternativ fur Deutschland (AfD) gains momentum across the country. Berlin, one of the world’s most liberal cities, could be next when voters go the polls on Sunday.
After success in the state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, the party has set its sights on the capital, as it continues its efforts to modify its brand after being classified by German intelligence as a right-wing extremist organisation.
Strong polling places the AfD just 3.4 per cent behind The Left party and 2.5 per cent behind chancellor Friedrich Merz’s centre-right CDU, according to an average published by dawum.de. It’s a dramatic change from three years ago, when the AfD sat 19.1 per cent behind the leaders in Berlin’s state election.
An AfD victory in Berlin would turn a political shock after the Saxony-Anhalt result into a country-wide earthquake, marking the second far-right state election success since the Second World War - and the second in two weeks.
“The way the AfD is campaigning looks less toxic, less dirty, less smelly, and that matters,” says Grégoire Roos, director of the Europe and Russia and Eurasia Programmes at Chatham House, who has tracked the AfD’s rise for more than a decade.
“The profile of its leaders, the way they’re campaigning, plus the growing concern with where the city is going, makes up a fertile enough ground for the AfD to secure, if not a victory, at least some form of strategic win - in what has traditionally been seen as a safe space,” he says.
The AfD may look to emulate the gameplan of Ulrich Siegmund, Saxony-Anhalt’s successful leader, which saw the party transform its image from a movement of protest against the mainstream parties to one with more confidence in its own radical agenda.
Read more: German minorities defy far-right AfD’s culture of fear after election win
At face value, the nature of the AfD’s programme is largely unchanged in Berlin. Migration is, as usual, a major pillar of its campaign, including explicit demands for “remigration”, a new buzzword for the far-right.
Housing policy has been emphasised, with AfD advocating for preferential treatment for native-born citizens in Germany. Programmes related to anti-discrimination, diversity and gender equality are forcefully opposed.
But the party appears to recognise the need for a wider appeal. Kristen Brinker, the AfD’s leader in Berlin, has a softer public perception than some of the AfD’s better-known national leaders.
Its local programme in the capital has been centred as much around the big city problems - housing, rent, education - as around German national identity.
“Marginalised parties have understood that to conquer part of the urban electorate, there's a kind of moral caution,” says Mr Roos. “You need to behave a certain way. There's a type of behaviour you should avoid, and [the AfD] have somehow successfully done it. They've passed the first screening in a way."
The impact has been clear. The AfD has shot up to third in the polls and looks set to almost double its 2023 vote share to around 18 per cent.
The Left are topping the polls at 21 per cent with the centre-right CDU second at 20.1 per cent, while the centre-left SPD, for decades Berlin’s largest party, could plummet down to 12.2 per cent.
The AfD has been siphoning voters from four key quarters of the German electorate, Mr Roos says, a trend it will look to replicate in Berlin.
CDU voters dismayed by the direction of both party and country have flocked rightwards, in part due to a sense of betrayal over Merz’s circumvention of the debt brake, a legal fiscal rule limiting how much structural debt a government can build up annually. For hardcore party members, this was nothing short of a cardinal sin.
A similar trend has been seen before, such as in the mid-2010s, when former chancellor Angela Merkel allowed around one million refugees into Germany.
Siegmund himself was a former CDU member, as were several of the AfD’s most prominent founders. In Saxony-Anhalt, the swing from 2021 was clear: the AfD gained 23 points as the CDU lost 19.9, while other parties remained within a few percentage points of their result five years ago.
Young, undecided voters form another vital portion of AfD support. In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD won over 170,000 voters who were undecided before the election, after their campaign managed to “appeal to a younger fringe of the electorate by reaching out to them through means of social media”, says Mr Roos.
Other elements include a fringe of voters who are socially right-wing and economically left-wing, along with neo-Nazi voters, many of whom have been loyal to the party since its inception.
Berlin, however, is different to Saxony-Anhalt. Its CDU electorate is not as right wing as in other states, and the so-called ‘firewall’ - the unwritten agreement in which opposition parties work together to keep the far right out of power - is likely to “stand strong”, Mr Roos says.
Young people in Berlin are also more likely to veer towards the left of the spectrum than in some other areas.
A symbolical under-16s election in Berlin last week, in which 40,000 children participated last week, was dominated by the Left (32.8 per cent) and the Greens (20.9 per cent), with the AfD at just 5.8 per cent. Organisers emphasised that it was voluntary and does not perfectly represent all young people in Berlin, but the gap is nonetheless stark.
But neither is Berlin comparable with some of Germany’s wealthier cities, such as Frankfurt and Munich, where support for the AfD is weak.
For 40 years, the capital was split between West Germany and the GDR, the historical communist state between 1949 and 1990.
“It's not a very wealthy city,” Mr Roos adds. “It's a relatively poor city. The east was part of the GDR [communist East Germany], where the AfD remains very popular. So there's also a pattern that makes it consistent with the logic.”
It is a pattern shared across Europe, he adds, where even in the cities, the desire for radical political change has seen many turn hard-right, exemplified by Reform in the UK.
“Even amongst the globalised urban electorate, there is a fatigue of what politics has become,” Mr Roos says.
As a result, he adds, there is “an increasingly clear openness to throw a bomb in the system”.

Teen who piloted Channel boat with 165 migrants jailed
- Published
A teenager who piloted a dinghy carrying a then-record 165 migrants across the English Channel to the UK has been sentenced to two years and three months in prison.
Chan Mathok Atak, 19, from South Sudan, admitted endangering others during a sea crossing on 23 July - the 16th conviction since the new offence was created in January.
Prosecutors at Canterbury Crown Court said Atak created a risk of death or serious personal injury to others on board the boat.
At the time, the so-called "mega dinghy" set a record for the largest number of migrants brought over on a small boat in recent years. That figure has since been surpassed with 230 people on board a vessel in August.
At Canterbury Crown Court on Friday, Judge Sarah Counsell said the offence was so serious "only an immediate custodial sentence can be justified".
She warned Atak that as a foreign national he was liable in principle to automatic deportation once he completed his sentence.
James Harrison, prosecuting, told the court the boat Atak was piloting was 12.8ft (3.9m) wide and 46.9ft (14.3m) long, a similar length to a standard bus.
The boat had travelled between Calais and the UK and was deflating when it was picked up by border force vessels.
The dinghy, which had 31 children on board with the youngest aged 14, had two outboard engines but one was not working, the court heard.
The National Crime Agency (NCA) said the boat was "severely overcrowded", had limited food, drinking water, and medication, and had been at sea for almost 24 hours.
The quality of the lifejackets on board was also "completely inadequate" and the fire risk was "considerable" due to how close batteries were to fuel cans, the NCA added.
Harrison said just before the boat was intercepted, Atak moved away from the engine into another part of the vessel and took off his jacket.
He said this was an attempt to not to be identified as the helmsman.
However, Atak was seen during 90 minutes of aerial footage to be piloting the vessel using its one remaining functioning engine while wearing a black jacket with an "Italia" logo on it, the court heard.
Footage also showed one person "constantly pumping" to try to re-inflate the rigid-hulled inflatable boat.
Harrison said: "There's no evidence to suggest that the defendant had any training or experience of conducting this type of navigation.
"The size of the vessel and the number of people on board presented an obvious danger. The vessel would have been unstable because of it deflating."
Harrison said the risks of the crossing "would have been apparent to Atak".
In an interview, Atak said he paid €200 euros (£172) to a gang for the crossing but denied he was the helmsman.
NCA senior investigating officer John Turner said: "Atak was unimaginably reckless and his actions could have easily resulted in many deaths had this boat not been intercepted.
"Not only did he place the lives of 165 migrants in severe peril, this flimsy vessel was entirely unsuitable for crossing one of the world's busiest shipping lanes."
Endangerment at sea was made a new offence this year to target those alleged to have steered small boats over the Channel.
Anna Turley, Minister for Border Security and Asylum, described Atak as an "evil criminal".
"He joins 16 other pilots sentenced in just three months for endangering lives with flimsy, overcrowded dinghies," she said.
"This is a stark reminder of the ruthless acts used by smuggling gangs to exploit desperate people for profit, but today shows there is nowhere for them to hide."
Defending him, barrister Audrey Mogan said there was "not a single shred of evidence" to suggest Atak had "anything to do with the number of people on the vessel, the state of the dinghy, or the fact that there were no life jackets or that the jackets were inadequate, or the lack of safety equipment or flares".
"The idea that he had anything to do with the state of the boat and its overcrowding just flies in the face of reason," she added.
Mogan described Atak as someone who had "escaped the horrors of South Sudan", where he saw people being shot and having their throats cut, and militia setting fire to a neighbourhood.

Chennai’s commons belong to those who live, work, and depend on them, speakers at Porombokkiyal 2026 held in Mylapore said on Saturday.
Now in its fourth edition, the event seeks to reclaim poromboke (shared communal land) from its derogatory stigma, integrating the commons into discussions on urban spaces, music, and the internet.
In the opening session — The Many Lives of the Road — a fish vendor from Nochikuppam Mullai said the Loop Road had already disrupted accessibility and livelihoods, subsuming 10 villages and leaving children to play on the streets.
Highlighting systemic exclusion, disability rights activist Aiswarya Rao noted how narrow footpaths and debris made parks inaccessible for wheelchair users. Autorickshaw driver Mohana spoke of the lack of women-only autorickshaw stands and public restrooms.
In the second session titled Commons of Care, moderated by Prashanth, wetland researcher Sarath Kumar, founder of Vyasai Thozhargal (Comrades of Vyasarpadi), shared how residents had transformed a neglected dump yard in the area into the Dr. Ambedkar Tuition Centre in just seven days. The tuition centre has achieved a 100% pass rate for 11 years.
The founder of Pagir, Archana Mohan, shared how she left a 20-year corporate career to create accessible community spaces, as she and her co-founder grew tired of searching for affordable places to meet without having to buy expensive coffee.
In the session on Sharing Fairly: Music, Internet & the Ethics of the Commons, singer Bindhu Malini suggested citing musical inspirations like academic research. Rohith Abraham, aka ofRo, founder of Atti Culture, an independent Chennai-based music label, questioned the ownership of music, while advocate M.V. Swaroop explained the distinctions between ideas and expressions under copyright law. Moderator T.M. Krishna pondered whether music’s intangible nature complicates ownership.
The final open-house session, Naa Porombokku! Nee Porombokkaa?, invited attendees to discuss sustainable shared spaces.
For Lily Ann B., who studied political science and is pursuing environmental change and sustainability, the sessions were inspiring. In a world where hyper-individualism and capitalism corroded care, the sessions offered hope by bringing real-world interconnections to light, she said.

Scientists warn India to brace for super El Nino and ecological damage
Earlier this month, the World Meteorological Organisation said the prevailing El Nino conditions were most likely to intensify into "a very strong event" in the coming months and continue through February 2027.
More than 180 scientists and ecologists in India have signed an appeal asking fellow researchers and field practitioners to prepare for an upcoming "super" El Nino event, warning that it could have devastating effects on the country’s natural systems.
In their appeal, the signatories called for stronger research and monitoring to better understand how extreme climate events affect nature and linked social systems.
Earlier this month, the World Meteorological Organisation said the prevailing El Nino conditions were most likely to intensify into "a very strong event" in the coming months and continue through February 2027.
El Nino is marked by the unusual warming of surface waters in the tropical Pacific Ocean. In the Pacific, temperatures have steadily risen above the 0.5 degrees Celsius threshold and crossed 2.6 degrees Celsius in August. Projections have reported possible anomalies of more than 4 degrees Celsius, the highest in the past 1,000 years.
"We call upon fellow ecologists to respond by strengthening and expanding our research and monitoring efforts to better understand the effects of extreme climate events on the natural world and connected social systems," the signatories said in their appeal.
They said an El Nino event of this strength could have severe effects on India, its people and its ecology. These could include widespread coral bleaching and mortality, an increase in wildfires, and the death of large rainforest trees. There is also a high probability of drought and extreme heat conditions, which they said could be catastrophic for India’s farmers, fishermen and shepherds.
"In addition though, more subtle impacts on India’s nature -- including delayed fruit production or changes in animal behaviour -- could be equally important, but may be much less visible unless you are specifically looking for them," the scientists and ecologists said. They urged fellow scientists to use the warning signs and mobilise as a community to document and study the impact of the event on India’s natural systems.
Roxy Mathew Koll, a climate scientist at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology and one of the signatories, said in a statement, "We must document these changes as they unfold, but also safeguard the ecosystems that remain and reduce the pressures already weakening them. What we learn and protect during this El Nino can help India prepare for a warmer and more volatile future." The appeal is a call for researchers to track both the immediate and less visible effects of a stronger El Nino on India’s ecology and the communities linked to it.

You can use DeX on the Galaxy Z Fold 8's inner screen with this trick
Launching a desktop mode on your Galaxy device is now pretty easy.
Samsung DeX has long been a fan-favorite feature. Since 2017, it has quietly lived in the settings of flagship Samsung devices, always ready to save people in a pinch. If you don't know, Samsung DeX is an excellent tool that allows users to easily turn their Galaxy device into a full-on desktop. All you need to do is turn DeX on, connect it to an external display (wired or wirelessly) and you're ready to go. You can even connect peripherals like a USB dock, mouse and keyboard, and they will all work.
When DeX was first released, phone displays were way smaller, so it didn't make sense to try running a desktop interface on the phone itself. But that's no longer the case, especially with devices like the Z Fold 8 that sport a big 7.6-inch inner screen.
Thankfully, you can now use all of the features of DeX right on your Z Fold 8 directly. It's thanks to an app called Gadesk, which is currently available on the Play Store, so no shady websites or sideloading are involved.
As it's not a hack, it doesn't require rooting or other complicated software. Once the app is installed, it takes just a few minutes sorting out the settings before you can start using DeX on your Z Fold 8 alone — no monitor or external display needed.
How to use DeX on your Galaxy Z Fold 8's inner screen
If you haven't already, grab the app from the Play Store. Before going any further, turn off Auto Blocker by heading to Settings > Security and privacy > toggle off Auto Blocker. Leaving it on can disable steps needed to connect the app. Next, enable wireless debugging on your device through Developer options. To enable Developer options, in Settings, go to About phone > Software information > tap Build number seven times > enter your passcode > confirm. Inside Developer options, turn on Wireless debugging. You need to be connected to Wi-Fi, and you'll be prompted to always allow your chosen network for wireless debugging.
Once that's done, launch the app and select "Connect driver" then choose "First-time pairing." Allow notifications when prompted, and it should take you straight to Developer options. If not, go back into Developer options, then Wireless debugging and tap "Pair device with pairing code." Immediately, you'll see a code on your screen, note it down. Open your notifications, you'll see one titled "Pairing screen detected. Enter the code." Click "Enter pairing code" and write the code your device gave you. Once paired, "DeXprobe" should show up in the Wireless debugging menu, confirming the connection.
Finally, go back to the Gadesk app, and click "Allow Driver", then "Allow.". Next, tap "Enable accessibility" then "AGREE AND OPEN SETTINGS"; you'll be taken to your Z Fold 8's accessibility settings. In there tap Installed apps > find the Gadesk app > toggle on > Allow. Now go back to the app then tap "Start desktop."
Behind all the settings and permissions, the app works by tricking your Z Fold 8 into thinking it's connected to an external display using the wireless debugging feature. Then the app intercepts the desk screen output and uses the accessibility permission you granted it to overlay that output onto your Z Fold 8's inner screen.
Gadesk settings you should know
Now that DeX is successfully running on your Z Fold 8's inner screen, there are a bunch of settings you can tweak inside the Gadesk app. One of the first settings you should change is the orientation. By default, Gadesk runs DeX in landscape, but portrait suits the Z Fold 8's aspect ratio better, especially for multitasking.
If, for some reason, you prefer using a virtual trackpad on your newfound Z Fold 8's DeX mode, you can do that too. Plus the trackpad comes with useful functions including copy, paste, zoom in and out and you can easily change the opacity of the trackpad. Another setting you should take a look at is Gesture action. You have three-finger tap and two-finger tap available and by default they set to Home and Back respectively. But with a few clicks you can customize both gestures to your preference or even set them to none if you don't have any use for it.
It must be noted that the Gadesk app is not entirely free. On the free version, each DeX session is limited to 15 minutes and you'll have to deal with ads. Upgrading removes the time limit and gets rid of ads, but it's a one-time fee of $20. If you haven't had enough time to test before taking the plunge, you can extend your DeX sessions by 10 minutes each time by surrendering yourself to promotions.
While Gadesk is suited to the dimensions of the Z Fold 8, the app supports other DeX-capable Galaxy phones (as long as they run One UI 8 or later) and Google Pixel devices via the built-in desktop Android mode.

What triggered the mass migrant crossings into Ceuta?
Over the last 24 hours, the tiny Spanish territory of Ceuta - home to around 83,000 people - has seen an unprecedented surge in migrant arrivals.
An estimated 60,000 people from Morocco are believed to have crossed into the North African enclave that has long been a focal point for migrant attempting to reach Europe.

Charles Spencer, 9th Earl Spencer is now at the centre of renewed attention because of his forthcoming memoir, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister. The book is due to be published on 22 September 2026, and is described by its publisher as an intimate account of Diana's life and death through the memories of her brother. Charles Spencer, 9th Earl Spencer, is the younger brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, and the maternal uncle of Prince William and Prince Harry. Born on 20 May 1964, he grew up at Althorp, the Spencer family estate in Northamptonshire, alongside Diana and their two older sisters, Lady Sarah McCorquodale and Lady Jane Fellowes. Spencer inherited the family title in March 1992, following the death of his father, John Spencer, the eighth Earl Spencer. Before becoming Earl Spencer, he was known by the courtesy title Viscount Althorp. He was educated at Eton College before studying Modern History at Magdalen College, Oxford. His connection to Diana has always been central to his public identity, but Spencer has built a career of his own. He spent a decade working for NBC News as a television reporter and correspondent before moving into writing and historical broadcasting. His books have largely focused on history, including the Spencer family, Althorp and figures and events from Britain's past. Spencer and Diana shared a childhood shaped by the Spencer family's long history and, later, the breakdown of their parents' marriage. His relationship with his sister became particularly visible after her death in 1997. At Diana's funeral at Westminster Abbey, Spencer delivered the eulogy that became one of the most remembered moments of the service. He spoke about his sister's vulnerability and her relationship with the public, while also making a pointed reference to William and Harry and his hope that they would not be overwhelmed by royal duty and tradition. That speech established Spencer as an important voice in the story of Diana's family and her relationship with the royal establishment. The memoir revisits Diana's childhood, her marriage to the then-Prince Charles, motherhood, the intense media attention surrounding her and the aftermath of her death in Paris in August 1997. Some of its most contentious passages concern the days immediately following Diana's death and the arrangements for her funeral. Spencer claims that he objected to William and Harry, then 15 and 12 respectively, walking behind their mother's coffin. He says he believed Diana would not have wanted her young sons placed at the centre of such a public and emotionally difficult procession. He also describes a tense telephone conversation with the then-Prince Charles over the issue. The memoir has attracted particular attention because Spencer makes claims about conversations involving members of the royal family nearly three decades after Diana's death. Among the most disputed is his allegation that Charles said, "we'll forget her soon enough". Buckingham Palace has rejected the account, with its response pointing to the possibility that grief can affect memory and judgement. Spencer has continued to stand by his recollection. The dispute has placed Spencer once again in a familiar position: Diana's brother speaking publicly about events surrounding her life and death, while the royal family faces renewed scrutiny over the events of 1997. For Spencer, however, Swan Song is presented as more than a book about the monarchy. His own description of the project focuses on preserving his memories of Diana and giving readers a picture of his sister beyond the public image that has endured since her death. Mark Carney received a rapturous reception in the European parliament when he gave his speech on Thursday welcoming a proposal for Canada to become the EU’s first-ever associate member.
Politicians queued to shake his hand and take selfies. One MEP leader described the speech as a historic moment. “Europe has extended a hand, and Canada has taken it,” said the German Green MEP Terry Reintke, who borrowed a Canadian ice hockey shirt for the occasion.
One day earlier, in the same debating chamber, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, issued the unprecedented invitation to Canada to become an associate member – an idea quickly derided by Donald Trump, who threatened Europe with “heavy tariffs” if it became a reality.
But the prospect of Canada’s associate membership is uncertain, not least because no one is sure what it means. “I’m not quite sure why she [von der Leyen] used that term because there’s simply no legal definition,” said one senior politician. “This has just raised lots of questions. So people are talking more about what an associate membership means instead of … this unique partnership and alliance for the future that EU-Canada relations should be about.”
The German chancellor Friedrich Merz’s spokesperson welcomed the initiative for a close partnership with Canada and said Germany was “open to discussing new models that reflect the special significance of the relationship” but called for the associate membership label to be “reconsidered”.
Merz himself has floated “associate membership” for Ukraine, as a stepping stone to joining the bloc, but this was quickly dismissed by other member states.
One EU diplomat said von der Leyen “seemed a bit far out in floating this” and that even before Wednesday’s speech member states had worried that she was overpromising on Canada. A second diplomat said it was “an empty phrase” and it would be up to member states to define the substance.
Any new trading and cooperation relationship with a foreign country would need to be approved by the EU’s 27 member states.
There is a lot of common ground: both sides want to deepen cooperation on AI, energy security, critical raw materials, quantum computing and work together in the Arctic – Carney noted that Canada shared an Arctic border with Denmark, referring to the maritime border with Greenland.
But difficulties went unspoken. While Carney described the 2016 EU-Canada comprehensive economic and trade agreement as “one of the world’s most successful trade agreements”, 10 EU member states have yet to ratify it, including France, Italy and Poland. With all three countries heading into an election year, that looks unlikely to change.
While both sides extol the virtues of deeper trade between allies, they are also pursuing policies that appear to contradict that goal. Last year Canada introduced a buy Canadian policy, to ensure Canadian suppliers get priority in public contracts. The EU is debating its own buy European law, known formally as the Industrial Accelerator Act. The IAA, now being debated in the EU, would oblige member states to meet “made in Europe” content requirements when spending public money on green technologies and electric cars.
Associate membership also raises questions about integration into the EU’s tightly guarded single market. Carney proposed “seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services”. But the EU has long insisted that the four freedoms of its internal market – free movement of goods, services, labour and capital – are one package that cannot be split and require alignment with EU rules.
Now the applause has died down, there are plenty of tricky issues to work out, even for the closest of allies.

Why Canadians are ready for closer ties with Europe
- Published
Miriam Levin-Gold likes Prime Minister Mark Carney's idea of Canadians being able to live and work in the European Union under proposed closer ties with the trade bloc.
"I think that's great for young people to explore different parts of the world and work in different places and have different experiences," the commuter told the BBC in Toronto.
Canadians woke up to news of Carney's speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday morning, welcoming the EU's ambition for Canada to become its first "associate member" as he urged closer co-operation on defence and energy.
"We should deepen our people-to-people ties, allowing our youth to live, work and study where they want on either side of the Atlantic," the PM said.
Carney told MEPs that Canada and Europe were "stronger together" in the face of "geopolitical rupture".
But before Canadians start packing their bags, "associate member" status does not currently exist within the EU and could take years to implement, given that all 27 EU member states would have to approve such an arrangement.
Nevertheless, people the BBC spoke to were excited about the potential prospect of working and studying in the EU as news of Carney's speech spread.
Alex Nash, from Montreal, said closer ties would clear away the obstacles of work visas and permits.
"It would certainly be really nice for that to be easier, more convenient and to be able to visit more easily," she said.
Canadian social media has lit up with the topic.
One person on a Facebook group, A Canadian Outlook, said they would love the opportunity for their grandchildren to study at European universities for better rates. Another woman said it would make it much easier for the home she already owns in France.
"Snow birds are going to love it," another person said, referring to Canadians who head to warmer locations for winter.
The sentiments hint at dissatisfaction in Canada over bilateral tensions with the US.
Growing up in Canada, David Jardine thought of the US as not just a neighbour, but an epicentre of culture and cool.
"I remember wanting to go and visit New York all the time," he told the BBC after finishing his overnight shift, not far from one of Toronto's most iconic buildings, the CN tower.
But he's become a lot more sceptical in the light of US President Donald Trump's trade war with Canada and rhetoric about annexation.
"I would say I think not only does it make more sense to associate closely with Europe, it's a place that I would rather be associating with given the way things are these days," he said.
Maggie Stainton, who manages local pub C'est What in Toronto's St Lawrence Market district, became emotional when she spoke about Canada's frayed ties with the US.
"It's too volatile with the United States," she said. "I feel that there's some stability in Europe."
For decades, America has been a cultural centre of gravity that is difficult to avoid, with many Canadian actors working in Hollywood and Canadian radio stations playing US music.
"I think we're forced to feel more American simply by the influences that we have," Stainton added.
"However, I think deep down, I definitely I lean towards feeling more European in my ideas and ideals."
These views were echoed by many other people the BBC spoke to in the centre of Canada's biggest city.
Carney, who used to lead Canada and Britain's central banks, was elected on a promise that he would not only take a tough stance against Trump, but broaden Canada's economic horizons.
Up to 72% of Canadian exports are to the US, and the ongoing trade tensions have spurred Ottawa to seek closer ties with other nations.
The EU, in many ways, would seem a natural fit. Over half of Canada's population reported having European origins, according to the last census, which was taken in 2021.
A recent Abacus Data survey conducted before Carney's speech found that 80% of Canadians say the country should deepen strategic cooperation with the EU, and over half feel closer to Europe than America.
However, details of Carney's proposed plans for greater ties with the EU are scarce.
A pair of opposition Conservative MPs have called on him to elaborate on what he and the bloc plan to work towards.
"It could be a concrete, meaningful proposal. Or it could be just words and vibes," said Adam Chambers, MP for Simcoe North in Ontario, during an interview with the BBC on the eve of Carney's speech on Thursday.
Chambers alluded to the existing Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) between the EU and Canada, highlighting that it still awaits ratification by multiple EU nations.
And while deepening ties with Europe would be welcomed by many Canadians, there is still a sense that the country's relationship with the US - however strained - must not crumble.
"I grew up here. I've been here 40 years in Canada, in Ontario, and America's always been the neighbour," says Ahmed Khalil.
Building bridges with Europe makes sense, he said: "I think it brings in more money for Canada and more culture, brings Europeans over, probably solves a lot of problems."
But Canada shouldn't forget its southern neighbour, added Khalil.
"I think both are equally valuable to us," he said. "Both are equally valid."

The story so far:
U.S. President Donald Trump has signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, 2026, which could see tariffs of up to 100% being levied on imports from India if it continues to import oil from Russia. This Act, therefore, has significant implications for India with regard to its export ambitions and energy security. The Indian government’s concerns over the tariffs have so far gone unheeded.
Why did the U.S. introduce this law?
The initial purpose of the Act — proposed by the late Senator Lindsey O. Graham and named after him — was to cut off financing for Russia so as to choke its funding of its war with Ukraine. To this end, the Act provides for sanctions to be levied on Russia’s top leadership and its biggest energy customers.
Recently, the ‘and Iran’ part of the title was added to the Act to convey that such measures are also aimed at Iran. The text was amended to say that sanctions on Iran would be levied for another five years until 2031.
What does the Act say about tariffs?
For India, the most crucial aspect of the Act is what it says about countries that import Russian oil. Thirty days after its enactment, the Act allows the U.S. to impose a 100% tariff on goods originating in a country that meets one of two broad criteria. The first is a country that was among the five largest importers, by total volume, of crude oil or natural gas from Russia during the 12 months preceding the Act’s enactment, and that continues to import oil or gas from Russia after the 30-day period.
This is the criterion that will likely impact India. China and India are the top two importers of Russian crude oil. Russian crude oil has accounted for a rising share of India’s oil imports since February 2026, when the U.S. Supreme Court struck down Mr. Trump’s tariff regime, including the 25% punitive tariff he had imposed on India for its Russian oil imports.
According to the latest data, Russia accounted for more than 51% of India's crude oil imports in July 2026. Scaling this back drastically within 30 days, at a time when passage through the Strait of Hormuz is still constrained, will likely be impossible for India.
The second criterion for imposition of tariffs is whether a country was among the top five nations “facilitating Russian oil sanctions evasion during the 12 months preceding the date of the enactment of the Act”. India runs a much lower risk of qualifying for tariffs under this criterion, as Indian oil marketing companies have repeatedly said that all their purchases have been made without violating sanctions.
Will these be the total tariffs on imports from India?
No. The law clearly states that an import tariff imposed under this Act “shall be in addition to any other duty” levied on any good. This includes tariffs imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the United States Trade Representative to investigate and retaliate against foreign trade practices that harm American commerce, and Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, which authorises the U.S. President to restrict imports or impose tariffs if an investigation finds that foreign goods threaten national security.
These two other Acts are important because India is among the countries that already face tariffs under them. That is, the U.S. Trade Representative used Section 301 to investigate American trade partners to determine whether they had done enough to stop the import of goods made using forced labour. Based on its findings, it imposed a tariff of 10% on imports from India. In addition, Mr. Trump had widened existing tariffs under Section 232 to include steel, aluminium, copper, and related derivative products, and hiked the rate to 50%. Since this applied to all countries equally, it placed India on a level playing field with its competitors.
A potential 100% tariff on top of that will severely dent India’s competitiveness in these sectors.
Will these tariffs come into force immediately?
No. A period of 30 days has to elapse before the U.S. can determine whether countries are still importing oil and gas from Russia. It is only after this period that the U.S. can levy the tariffs under the law. Further, the text of the Act says that the U.S. Trade Representative, in consultation with the Secretary of State and the Secretary of Energy would, within 180 days after the initial imposition of tariffs, again review the countries that are the five largest importers of crude oil and natural gas from Russia based on the most recent 12-month period.
What is the potential impact on India’s economy?
The impact on India’s economy has to be looked at in terms of two eventualities. The first is if India continues to buy large quantities of Russian oil and bears the tariffs. The second is if India cuts back on Russian oil imports and manages to have the potential tariffs removed.
In the event that India continues to buy Russian oil and bears the tariffs, we can look at what happened during the period when the 50% tariffs were in force, between August 2025 and February 2026, to gauge the likely impact.
The April to August 2025 period saw merchandise exports to the U.S. grow nearly 18% compared with the same period the previous year. While some of this was due to front-loaded exports in anticipation of future tariffs, it nevertheless highlighted the strong momentum of exports from India to the U.S. However, over the longer April 2025 to February 2026 period, exports to the U.S. grew at a much slower 3.8%, showing a substantial slowdown in exports after August, when the tariffs came into effect.
Conversations with exporters at the time showed that many of them were sharing the cost of the higher tariffs with their U.S. customers in order to retain them. At the rate of 50%, this was already a body blow to most of them. These exporters will not be in a position to share a 100% tariff.
Historical data, however, show that India has chosen to comply with U.S. pressure to reduce oil imports from countries such as Venezuela, Iran, and Russia. If India again cuts down on Russian oil imports, this could have serious ramifications for the supply and price of fuel within India. At a time when the Strait of Hormuz is constrained, and oil prices are again comfortably above $100 a barrel, India will likely find it very expensive to look for newer sources of oil. For Indian citizens, this could translate into more fuel price hikes. For the government, such hikes would be politically unpalatable since there are several key State elections next year.
Is there a third way out?
The Act includes a provision for a waiver of tariffs. The U.S. President can waive the tariffs once he has submitted to Congress a certification in writing that the waiver “is in the national interests of the U.S.” and a report explaining the basis for the certification.
The other way out is if Russia signs “a peace agreement that is accepted by the free and independent Government of Ukraine” and ceases “all military hostilities against and any activities to overthrow, dismantle, and subvert the Government of Ukraine”.
