When Swiggy entered India's online food delivery market back in 2014, it was the first one to solve the problem of getting a meal from a restaurant to a customer's doorstep. Zomato joined the race a year later in 2015. But over the years, Swiggy has taken a path that has made its business increasingly different from simply being a food-delivery marketplace. It started with food delivery in 2014 and gradually expanded into groceries, dining, supply chain and a string of smaller experiments. The company's food delivery business generated an operating revenue of ₹2,208 Cr in the June quarter of FY27 with an operating profit of ₹299 Cr in the quarter under review. However, overall, Swiggy recorded a loss of ₹791 Cr in Q1 FY27. Quick commerce was the biggest drag, with Instamart reporting an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹778 Cr, despite generating ₹7,907 Cr in GOV. This is where Swiggy's business model gets interesting. Beyond the delivery and platform fees that form a similar revenue base for Zomato, Swiggy has built a core business that is increasingly generating profits, while continuing to invest in newer businesses that could widen its addressable market. The difference, however, is that Swiggy's food delivery business still continues to bring in most of the revenue while Zomato is now a part of Eternal and contributes only 15% of the total top line. The margins brought in by the food delivery business are being invested to fuel Swiggy's quick commerce bet and "platform innovations", which is a space to test new formats, price points and operating models. The Q1 FY27 earnings call makes that approach even clearer. Swiggy said it evaluates opportunities across pricing, formats and even separate apps, while trying to preserve the economics of its core platform. With food delivery and other established businesses providing an existing consumer base, technology stack and fulfillment network, the company can test new initiatives without building every capability from scratch. But before looking at what these newer bets could become, it is worth understanding the business that continues to anchor Swiggy's P&L. Swiggy's Food Delivery & Supply Chain: The Core That Pays The foodtech has two very different established businesses at the heart of its P&L: food delivery, and supply chain & distribution (SC&D). Let's decode the most popular segment first. At the most basic level, Swiggy earns from the restaurant, the consumer and the wider platform. Its food delivery revenue comprises pre-agreed commissions from restaurant partners, advertising revenue from restaurants, platform fees charged to users, and subscription revenue when it comes to food delivery. There is also a revenue that comes from offering business enablement solutions to the restaurant partners. Furthermore, Swiggy does not recognise user delivery charges passed on to delivery partners as part of its revenue. These charges are included in its separately defined gross revenue, net of applicable discounts. However, it takes "service charge" as revenue collected from users/delivery partners for use of technology platforms, which is also not disclosed. So, on a ₹500 food order, the customer's payment is split across the food value going to the restaurant, delivery-related amounts going to the delivery partner, discounts and fees, while Swiggy's recognised revenue comes from the monetisation streams it retains. Operationally, Swiggy's food delivery GOV grew 17.4% YoY to ₹9,490 Cr and monthly transacting users rose 17.8% YoY to 19.2 Mn in Q1 FY27, ultimately resulting in operating revenue of ₹2,208 Cr. The next question is how much of that monetisation survives after serving the orders. Swiggy answers this via contribution margin. Swiggy calculates food delivery contribution margin (CM) after deducting delivery and other charges, platform-funded discounts and other variable costs from adjusted revenue. In Q1 FY27, this margin stood at 7.6% of GOV. On the other hand, adjusted EBITDA is further calculated after deducting the operating cost, which stood at a 3.1% margin on GOV for the June quarter. The quarter, however, saw a sequential dip in food delivery's CM and adjusted EBITDA margin. This is where Swiggy's cost to achieve EBITDA profitability for food delivery is hidden. The management said that the sequential dip in food delivery margins was partly due to higher investment in delivery-partner availability and the annual wage hike. Meanwhile, the blame was also given to seasonality. At the same time, the company said improved take rates and operating leverage helped drive the 70-basis-point YoY improvement in adjusted EBITDA margin. This creates an interesting balancing act for Swiggy. More delivery partners available at the right time can improve the customer experience and support order growth. But keeping that capacity available also adds to costs. The business therefore has to grow order density fast enough for the additional orders to absorb those fulfilment costs. Interestingly, Swiggy's average transacting restaurant partners also declined QoQ to 2.6 Lakh from 2.8 Lakh earlier. Food delivery, however, is not Swiggy's largest revenue-generating segment. Its supply chain & distribution business reported ₹3,195 Cr in revenue in Q1 FY27, making it the biggest contributor to the company's revenue from operations for the quarter. SC&D works very differently from food delivery. It is an inventory-led B2B business through which Swiggy purchases products and distributes them to merchant partners. This makes the business much more revenue-heavy, but also brings a corresponding cost of purchasing the products that it distributes. However, revenue alone does not tell the full story of Swiggy's business mix — which we will see ahead. While these established businesses form the foundation of Swiggy's P&L, the company's biggest consumer growth bet is operating on a very different set of economics: Instamart. Instamart: The Growth Engine That Is Still Burning Instamart burning cash is hardly new for Swiggy. What has changed is the trajectory of that burn. In Q1 FY27, the quick commerce business reported GOV of ₹7,907 Cr, up 40% YoY and operating revenue of ₹1,232 Cr. Its adjusted EBITDA loss stood at ₹778 Cr (adjusted EBITDA margin at 9.8% of the GOV), declining by ₹80 Cr sequentially, even as the business continued to expand. The picture changes when we talk about Instamart's contribution margin, which improved to -0.2% of GOV, from -1.8% in the previous quarter. The difference between these two numbers is important to understanding where Instamart stands today. Swiggy said contribution margin had turned positive on a monthly basis in May, although the full-quarter margin remained at -0.2%. This means Instamart has almost reached order-level contribution break-even. Besides this, revenue per order rose to ₹108 from ₹97. More than 45% of its stores were contribution margin positive in Q1 FY27, with five of its seven largest cities also reaching positive contribution margins. Still, we cannot say that Instamart is closer to EBITDA profitability based on the CM improvement alone. The gap in CM and adjusted EBITDA profitability reflects the broader cost base of running and scaling the network. Instamart now operates 1,171 active dark stores with 1,089 orders per store per day in Q1 FY27. Yet Swiggy says the overall network is operating at only around 40% utilisation, with significant headroom remaining. At the same time, management expects to add around 75 stores in Q2 because of volume growth in high-growth neighbourhoods. The company is betting on transacting user base increase as well as frequency increase for Instamart's growth, Swiggy's chief financial officer Rahul Bothra said during Q1 earnings' call. And that growth will not only depend on how many people use Instamart, but also on what they buy, and how large their baskets become. Swiggy's Experimental Sandbox: Where Are The Bets Beyond Food Delivery, Instamart and its other established businesses, Swiggy has a separate platform innovations segment that acts as a sandbox for testing new consumer propositions and business models. The company describes it as a set of incubators aimed at creating more frequent and meaningful touchpoints with users. "Platform innovation by its nature is something that we are not committing ourselves fully to. As we have said, once the product hits both product market fit (PMF) as well as what we call business market fit (BMF), that is when it will get its growth capital, and it will have its own economics from there on," Bothra further said during the earnings' call. The portfolio under this head has changed quickly, with some experiments being launched, tested and discontinued. Toing, for instance, was launched as a separate offering targeting price-conscious consumers such as students and early-jobbers, using a different marketplace model for low-AOV meals. In the latest disclosures, Swiggy's CEO Sriharsha Majety said that Toing is different from conventional food delivery across delivery fees, proposition, cuisine, last mile, economics and the value proposition for consumers. The commission model around this product is also different as restaurants' fee is supposed to be low so that they can offer food at a lower price. Besides, Crew is another offering that Swiggy currently classifies under its platform innovations segment. Initially, the product allowed users to find, shop and get delivered anything "from golf course to caddy bookings to reliable and clean cabs, sourcing exclusive hotel rates to even a Hawaiian shirt". Earlier this month, the product pivoted to a "dedicated personal travel concierge offering". Apart from these, Swiggy also runs its sports subsidiary called Swiggy Sports and extensions of the food delivery services including Bolt, 99 Store, Late Night Eats, Food On Train, Eatright, and DeskEats. The portfolio also comes with the possibility of exits. Snacc, Swiggy's standalone food-delivery experiment, was shut in the previous quarter, and Bothra said some operating costs related to the closure were recognised in Q1 FY27. For now, this means the segment remains an investment pool for Swiggy, with the company absorbing the cost of testing whether these propositions can scale. Platform innovations reported ₹51 Cr in operating revenue against a segment loss of around ₹131 Cr in Q1 FY27. Swiggy does not disclose the individual revenue or cost contribution of Toing, Crew or its other experiments, making it difficult to attribute the segment's loss to any one product. At the same time, Bothra added that a larger portion of the investment in platform innovations during the quarter went towards Toing, particularly marketing-led customer acquisition. This is where Swiggy's Food Delivery profitability becomes important to the broader business model. The company has a mature business generating operating profit, while platform innovations continue to absorb investment as Swiggy tests new propositions. The strategy, therefore, is not simply to maximise revenue from every experiment today, but to use the existing platform and its economics to find businesses that can eventually stand on their own. The Price Of Swiggy's Scale Swiggy's expanding portfolio also comes with a sizable cost base. In Q1 FY27, the company reported ₹7,813 Cr in total expenses, against ₹6,812 Cr in revenue from operations. The biggest expense was purchases of stock-in-trade at ₹2,978 Cr. This is largely linked to Swiggy's supply chain & distribution business, where the company purchases products that are subsequently sold to its merchant partners. The SC&D segment generated ₹3,195 Cr in revenue in Q1 FY27, making it one of the largest businesses on Swiggy's books by revenue, even though the segment remained around break-even at the operating level. In comparison, food delivery generated a lower revenue pool than SC&D, but contributed ₹299 Cr in segment profit, while the much larger SC&D business operated with far thinner economics. The second-largest major cost was delivery and related charges at ₹1,750 Cr. This includes costs associated with the delivery network and therefore cuts across the businesses that rely on Swiggy's fulfilment infrastructure. It is also where the scale of Swiggy's operations becomes visible: the company is not only paying to acquire customers and build businesses, but also to keep the delivery network available to serve them. Advertising and sales promotion accounted for another ₹1,160 Cr during the quarter. This bucket is particularly relevant for a company still investing in new categories and consumer propositions. However, Swiggy does not provide a consolidated expense split that allows this amount to be attributed to a particular segment or product. Employee benefits added ₹662 Cr, while depreciation and amortisation stood at ₹298 Cr and finance costs at ₹53 Cr. The remaining ₹915 Cr was classified under other expenses. Taken together, these costs show that Swiggy's profitability challenge is broader than the losses from Instamart and platform innovations alone. The company is operating a large fulfillment, technology and employee base across multiple businesses, while continuing to invest in growth. That also explains why the profitability of individual businesses does not immediately translate into consolidated profits. Food Delivery generated a ₹299 Cr segment profit in Q1 FY27, but the wider portfolio continued to carry the costs of scaling quick commerce, running SC&D and incubating new businesses. The next question, therefore, is not just how much Swiggy spends, but where the company is willing to keep spending despite the losses. Edited By Nikhil Subramaniam

Trump claims Don Jr. is paying back Putin-tied Russian oligarch for lavish wedding
Umar Kremlev reportedly spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the multi-day event filled with fireworks and dancers in sailor caps
President Donald Trump has claimed that his eldest son is paying back Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev for his lavish Bahamas wedding party.
Kremlev, the head of the scandal-ridden International Boxing Association, who has close ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin, spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on expenses incurred at Donald Trump Jr.’s multi-day party on two private islands in May to celebrate his marriage to socialite Bettina Anderson, according to a ProPublica report published Monday.
The report sparked corruption and national security concerns, with Representative Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, writing on X, “Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the President’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers.”
Trump, who has disputed any personal ties with Kremlev and did not attend his son’s wedding, told reporters that Kremlev’s gift was “totally allowed,” but that his son paid the oligarch back.
“Was it appropriate for your son to accept a gift — a payment for some of his wedding festivities?” one reporter asked Trump in the Oval Office Friday.
“It's totally allowed and a lot of people have parties,” Trump replied. “But as I understand it, he paid him back.”
“A person that he knows, I guess a friend of his, gave him a wedding party — that’s very common. I’ve heard of many people giving wedding parties,” the president continued. “I’ve given wedding parties to numerous people.”
Kremlev reportedly paid to rent one of the private islands where the Trump family and their friends partied, which ProPublica said could cost about $100,000 a night, and other expenses such as a fireworks display with an estimated price tag of about $70,000.
A spokesperson for Trump Jr. told ProPublica Kremlev was a “personal friend of Don” and that the two met through a mutual friend in the hunting community. The spokesperson added that Kremlev is “not someone [Trump Jr.] has a business relationship with.”
Bettina also spoke out following the report that Kremlev bankrolled their wedding festivities.
She said that she wed Trump Jr. at an inmate ceremony with only family members in attendance and called the party “a fun weekend with friends.”
“Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding. It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful,” Bettina wrote in a joint statement with Trump Jr. on her Instagram earlier this week.
“It’s unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from,” the statement continued. “Friendship doesn’t require a political motive. Generosity doesn’t automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift.”
Along with the statement, Bettina shared some photos, including one of herself and Trump Jr. dressed in all white on a beach as fireworks illuminated the night sky. There were also pictures of dancers dressed as sailors, a man doing a card trick and a DJ getting lost in the music.
Kremlev, who reportedly attended the Bahamas party, “has never discussed political matters with any of his American friends and acquaintances,” his press office told ProPublica.
Representative Garcia, meanwhile, has sent a letter to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles asking for information regarding any ties between Trump Jr. and Kremlev.
“As the son of President Donald Trump and the part-owner and major investor of multiple companies with extensive Department of Defense contracts, any apparent ties to members of Russian President Vladimir Putin’s inner circle raises serious questions about pay-to-play schemes and foreign intelligence infiltration of the President’s family,” Garcia wrote in the letter.
Attorney General Todd Blanche was asked by a reporter in the White House Rose Garden earlier this week whether he would investigate the matter, to which he said, “Am I investigating what?”
“The president doesn't know who this person is. I think other members of the family don't know who this person is. The president's son has said he's a very close friend and that he accepted a gift in the weekend of his wedding.”

Melania Trump is preparing for one of her most visible stretches of public engagements this year, with the US first lady set to spend 22 to 25 September to moving between New York and Washington. At the centre of the schedule is the launch of IMPERIA, a new forum aimed specifically at women in senior corporate leadership. The initiative will be unveiled on 23 September, when Melania is due to ring the opening bell at the New York Stock Exchange. Quick answers to key questions The IMPERIA forum aims to support women in senior corporate leadership by helping them build business relationships, influence policy, and collaborate across industries. Melania Trump will launch IMPERIA on September 23, 2025, at the New York Stock Exchange. The invitation-only nature of IMPERIA focuses on a select group of senior executives, enhancing the opportunity for meaningful connections and discussions among powerful women. IMPERIA aligns with Melania Trump's broader interests by emphasizing women's leadership in business alongside her initiatives in technology and education, particularly through her Fostering the Future Together program. IMPERIA seeks to address challenges faced by women CEOs by leveraging their collective influence to engage in vital business and policy discussions and to foster cross-sector collaborations. The details were disclosed exclusively to USA Today by her senior adviser Marc Beckman, who described IMPERIA as a platform where female chief executives and C-suite leaders can build business relationships, move capital, influence policy and collaborate across industries. He called it a “Davos for Women”. The forum is expected to be invitation-only, putting its focus on a relatively small group of senior executives rather than a broad public conference. Its stated purpose is to bring together women with decision-making power in business and create opportunities for them to work across sectors. The launch at the NYSE also gives the initiative a distinctly business-focused setting. For Melania, the appearance places women's corporate leadership alongside her wider interest in technology, education and economic opportunity. IMPERIA is being presented as more than a networking event. According to Beckman, the initiative is intended to use the collective influence of senior women executives to facilitate business, investment and policy discussions. That focus is significant because Melania's public work in her second term has also increasingly intersected with technology and the future workforce. Her Fostering the Future Together initiative, launched at the United Nations in September 2025, is centred on children's education, technology and online safety. The White House says the coalition brings together first spouses and governments with technology companies to expand access to educational technology while protecting children from online dangers. In March 2026, Melania hosted the initiative's first global coalition summit, bringing representatives from 45 countries together with 28 technology companies. Discussions focused on artificial intelligence in education, digital literacy, educational technology and online protection. On 22 September, Melania will promote Fostering the Future Together during the United Nations General Assembly's High-Level Week in New York. The event is scheduled to take place at the St Regis Hotel and will involve representatives from 57 member nations, alongside technology-sector participants. According to a 18 September White House advisory, the programme will include new member nations and strategic partnerships with technology companies. The initiative has developed considerably since Melania introduced it at the UN in 2025. Its stated objective is to connect governments and the private sector around children's access to education and technology, while addressing safety in digital spaces. That makes the proximity of the two September events notable: one is focused on preparing children for an increasingly technology-driven future, while the other is aimed at women already occupying senior positions in business. The high-profile week will then shift from New York's business and diplomatic circles to the White House. On 24 September, Melania is expected to join President Donald Trump in welcoming Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, for an official state visit. According to Beckman, Melania has personally overseen elements of the visit, including preparations for the State Dinner and private engagements. The visit comes as Washington and Beijing continue discussions over trade, technology and other areas of tension. Reuters reported that Trump and Xi are expected to discuss issues including trade negotiations, artificial intelligence, critical minerals, Taiwan and fentanyl precursor shipments. The week is scheduled to conclude on 25 September, when the two couples are expected to visit the National Archives to view the Declaration of Independence. For Melania, the four-day schedule brings together three distinct areas of her public role: children's technology and education, women's leadership in business, and the ceremonial responsibilities that accompany a major state visit. IMPERIA, however, will be the new addition. Its launch at the NYSE will put the spotlight firmly on female CEOs and executives and on the idea of creating a dedicated network for women with influence across business and policy. Nobel laureate Mohammadi says Iranians are paying the price for war
Mohammadi said Iranians are grappling with multiple crises arising from the war.
Iranians are suffering as economic misery and internal repression leave “no room for people to breathe” after 1 1/2 years of wars and ongoing U.S. sanctions, the country’s most prominent human rights activist has told The Associated Press.
Narges Mohammadi, 54, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2023, was temporarily released from prison for medical reasons earlier this year after falling unconscious and being transferred to a hospital.
Her memoir — titled “A Woman Never Stops Fighting" — was written behind bars, with parts of it smuggled out by fellow inmates. Editions in French, German and nine other languages are being released this month. The English and Farsi editions are to be released next year.
In an interview conducted Friday by The Associated Press from outside Iran, Mohammadi said Iranians are grappling with multiple crises stemming from the ongoing war and deepening economic pressure.
"It’s the people who are paying an extremely heavy price,” she said.
But she said many Iranians continue to quietly defy their leaders, a change she traces back to the 2022 protests over the death of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old woman who died in a hospital after being detained for violating authorities' strict Islamic dress code.
The release of Mohammadi's book this month coincides with Amini's death to honor her memory, her representatives said. The English and Farsi editions are to be released in September 2027 for the same reason.
“If you go out into the streets, you see a wave of resistance among the people, a wave of awareness, and their determination to stand up for their rights,” Mohammadi said. She said that government repression has intensified, but that many in a new younger generation “know their rights” and were standing firm. “And that gives us reason for hope,” she said.
AP agreed not to ask Mohammadi specific questions about the political situation and leadership in Iran, due to concerns for her safety, though she commented generally about the cost of war.
In her interview with AP, Mohammadi — who has been jailed repeatedly over decades of advocating for human rights and was behind bars when she was awarded the Nobel Prize — described her most recent arrest, detention and health.
She said she was severely beaten by security forces when detained in December, in the northeastern city of Mashhad. She and a group of activists were attending a memorial ceremony for human rights lawyer Khosrow Alikordi, who was found dead in his office. She was arrested while giving a public speech. She was sentenced to 16 years and more than a 100 lashes for attending that rally. She has not been flogged but spent long periods in solitary confinement.
“My detention was really life-threatening," she said. "My head was severely hurt because most of the hits were to my head, and despite being in that condition, they kept me for two months in solitary confinement during which my condition was really concerning.”
She lost consciousness May 1 and was transferred to a hospital. She was released on bail nearly 10 days later and transferred to a hospital in Tehran, where she remained for another two weeks.
She smuggled out fragments of her memoir, which she had started writing in 2019 during an earlier stint in Iran's notorious Evin prison in Tehran, where many political prisoners are held. She had lost her handwritten notes that year when they moved her to another site.
This time, “with the help of fellow inmates, we got a few pages out, a few pages at a time," she said. “If it weren’t for them, I couldn’t have done it.”
As for her health, “I am recovering,” Mohammadi said.
Mohammadi said she took inspiration from other women’s stories growing up, beginning with her own mother.
“I tried to put an image to each of these — how these women really managed to change their world, their society, themselves, the next generation — make them aware, make them resist,” she said.
She also recalled “terrifying memories” from her childhood during the 1980s Iran-Iraq war and how she developed “a hatred for war.”
“I wasn’t more than a child when the Iran-Iraq war happened, but I remember a lot of the repression, repression of many political currents and forces, many executions that happened in the silence and darkness of Evin and prisons around the country," she said.
She recalled her concern when she learned that Evin prison had been bombed during the 12-day war between Israel and Iran in 2025, a period when she was out of prison.
“At that moment, I felt that, in this country, we are at the intersection of injustice, discrimination, war, authoritarianism," she said. "All of those are trampling on our people’s human rights.”
Mohammadi has been handed down sentences totaling 44 years. She has already spent 10 years in prison, including 161 days in solitary confinement. She has been banned from traveling abroad since 2009, and is unable to join her husband and two children who live in exile in France.
“My sentence is currently suspended, and I must return whenever the judiciary issues the order,” Mohammadi later said in a text message shared by her team.

When we first drove the Hyundai Ioniq 5 at the end of 2021, it didn’t take much exposure to the angular electric vehicle to find much about it appealing. Back then, an 800 V architecture had only really been seen in expensive high-end EVs from Porsche, but here was a mainstream model with that same technology—and even faster fast-charging, taking just 18 minutes to go from 10–80 percent. The retro looks didn’t hurt either, channeling the boxy hatches styled by Giorgetto Giugiaro in the 1970s and ’80s. But five years is a long time in the car world, and the compact electric crossover segment is far more competitive than it was when the Ioniq 5 debuted. We figured it was worth spending some more time with one to see how it still stacks up.
Although the Ioniq 5 range starts at $35,000 for the standard range model, our test car was a 2026 Ioniq 5 AWD Limited, which has an 84 kWh battery pack—part of the lifecycle refresh in early 2025 that also swapped in a NACS (J3400) charge port in place of the CCS1 port you’d find on earlier cars. Among the other additions that arrived as part of the 2025 refresh was a rear windshield wiper, which was sorely needed at launch.
This range-topping trim starts at $45,075, with an extra $3,900 for the addition of the front electric motor that gives the AWD version a combined output of 320 hp (239 kW) and 446 lb-ft (605 Nm). The added traction of AWD (when you have grip) is desired by many, but you do trade something for it: efficiency. The AWD version has an EPA range of 269 miles (432 km) versus 318 miles (512 km) for the rear-wheel drive variant.
Single-motor Ioniq 5s should easily be capable of 4 miles/kWh (15.5 kWh/100 km) or more. But with both axles powered, even in Eco mode, you can expect closer to 3.4 miles/kWh (18.3 kWh/100 km). Having 49 miles (79 km) more range would, of course, mean a little longer behind the wheel between charging stops, should one happen to be on a road trip or dependent upon public fast-chargers, but even with a larger pack, the 2026 Ioniq 5 still fast-charges plenty fast. The native NACS port means the Ioniq 5 can charge at Tesla Superchargers as well as other networks, like IONNA and Electrify America.

At the Venice Film Festival earlier this month, the documentary NAZA received a 25-minute standing ovation. In Israel, it’s all anyone’s talking about, even though few have actually seen it.
An Israeli documentary about Gaza is sweeping the world – and Israelis are furious
Almost no one has seen NAZA yet, but almost everyone has something to say about it.
Made by two Israeli filmmakers, Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham, the movie takes place on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, where 24 anonymous Israeli intelligence agents and soldiers discuss things that they did in Gaza and how they did them.
As Bilge Ebiri writes in his Vulture review of NAZA, “One officer recalls blowing up a building with 500 people in it to go after one target. They admit to knowingly wiping out entire neighborhoods, fully aware of the catastrophic human toll.”Another interviewee agrees that Israel is committing a genocide in Gaza.
Since its reception in Venice, the film has faced harsh criticism from the Israeli government — with at least one politician issuing a call to revoke the filmmakers’ citizenship.
Shany Littman is a journalist for Haaretz in Israel and has been reporting on the film’s reception. She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about the conversation around the movie in Israel.
Below is an excerpt of the conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
Have you seen the documentary NAZA?
I haven’t. I asked the PR person of the movie to send me a link and it’s not possible. I mean, considering the huge storm that came out, they’re probably rethinking how to handle the distribution of the film.
What I hear you saying is it’s safe to assume most people in Israel have not actually been able to see the movie. Is that right?
Yes, that’s correct.
But they are aware of what is in it. Let’s talk about the conversation around this movie in Israel. What’s the reaction been like?
You can find many different types of criticism from all sides of a political range. It’s not only right-wing people or people who are supporting the war. The claims are first that maybe the film itself is not verified. They have witnesses that are anonymous that they didn’t verify well enough. But I think most people — they just feel that this is an opportunity for all the pro-Palestinian, anti-Israeli, and [antisemitic] people in the world to attack Israel. Israelis from all sides are afraid of the way the world is seeing us at the moment.
Is anybody in Israel saying, “Hey, we’re glad that they did it. We’re glad that they made this movie”?
Yes. There are people who are supporting Yuval and Rachel, the filmmakers, supporting their right to criticize, to investigate. As a liberal country, we should be able to investigate ourselves, to criticize ourselves. They are doing their work as journalists.
There has also been a reaction from the Israeli government at a more official level. What has the Israeli government said about this film?
“There’s a really long history of films that were criticized, especially by different culture ministers. But I haven’t seen anything like this, like what is happening now. This is really frightening.”
The first person to react was the minister of culture. He said that the nationality of Yuval and the filmmakers should be revoked. That they should not be Israeli citizens anymore. There’s a really long history of films that were criticized, especially by different culture ministers. But I haven’t seen anything like this, like what is happening now. This is really frightening. I’m completely horrified by this.
I already saw some clips on social media by people who were filming themselves where…you could see a house [in the background] and someone was saying, “You can all come here. This is the house of Rachel Szor’s parents. They live here and you can come and do whatever you want. I invite you all to come here and take revenge.” And there were several clips with the same message.
I’m guessing they’re not coming back to Israel at the moment. I think it has become really dangerous for them to be here, and it’s a new level. I published an article about this. I didn’t do the movie. I just published an article supporting them in Haaretz and my mother is afraid that someone will attack me. The echoes of this event, they’re going very far now.
Are you frightened for the filmmakers if they choose to return? Do you fear for their safety?
Yes, absolutely. Especially because the elections are coming in a month. Many Israelis see this day as like the red line or the moment where we will be able to know if we can still live in Israel as a democracy, as a liberal democracy, or that the country has changed in a way that many [civil] rights and liberties that we think we have are gone. And that this country is not a democracy anymore. And so I think this is also why the blood is boiling.
This is a very, very tense and fragile moment. And for them I assume it is even more crucial and I hope they will not do anything that will put them in danger.

Reporters for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico were denied entry to White House grounds on Saturday morning, the outlets said, one day after President Donald Trump said he was banning them for their coverage of him.
"Early today, CNN journalists were denied access to the White House grounds," a CNN spokesperson said in a statement. "We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government."

Trump arrived at Camp David late Friday night, according to a White House pool report.

What is the cost of a life? For the wife and 20-year-old son Chongtham Vikram Singh, it is the lifelong grief and trauma of losing a family member. For Manipur, it is the loss of a homegrown musical talent, who began practicing his craft when he was a child, and made his way from Imphal to the big stages of Delhi. And for the rest of India, it is a reckoning with the systemic racism that has historically exposed Northeasterners living in other parts of the country to racial discrimination, harassment, bullying and violence.
The concerns are not new, nor were solutions entirely out of reach. The Bezbaruah Committee, set up by the Manmohan Singh-led UPA government to address the discrimination faced by people from the Northeast, had made a series of recommendations to the Modi cabinet in 2014. A key component of the proposals was making changes to the Indian Penal Code (IPC). Twelve years on, this is yet to be implemented.
Accused ‘Wanted to Teach a Lesson’ to the Manipuri Guitarist
Singh, a 55-year-old Manipuri guitarist, was allegedly beaten to death by a group of young men outside his home in Kilokari village of Southwest Delhi. On September 6, around 11:30 pm, Singh had objected to the loud noise and commotion being created by the accused outside his apartment.
According to the police complaint, when his son heard him shouting, he opened the door to see the group of men violently attacking Singh. After the altercation, Singh returned home but complained of breathlessness, he was then taken to Holy Family Hospital where he succumbed to his injuries at 6 am on September 7. CCTV footage showed the accused leaving the building. Seven men and a minor have been arrested in the case so far.
A Manipuri music teacher, Chongtham Vikram Singh, living in Delhi’s Ashram area was mob lynched by 8 people following a dispute over alleged noise and nuisance outside his residence.
Police said seven accused have been arrested and a minor detained in connection with the case.… pic.twitter.com/4V0LVeVLiJ
— Mohammed Zubair (@zoo_bear) September 7, 2026
The autopsy report revealed that Singh died of massive internal bleeding caused by severe physical trauma to his chest and abdomen. The accused allegedly kicked him on the chest and abdomen after he fell to the ground. During questioning, they told the police that they wanted to teach Singh a lesson.
While the police investigation so far has not revealed any racial motive behind the violent attack, his death has brought to the fore larger concerns around hate faced by people from the Northeast in the nation’s capital and beyond. It also brings the Bezbaruah Committee’s recommendations, and the fate of those recommendations, back into focus.
The Bezbaruah Committee and Administrative Inaction
The Bezbaruah Committee was formed in February, 2014, after the killing of Nido Tania, a 20-year-old hailing from Arunachal Pradesh, who was beaten to death with iron rods and sticks by three men after a verbal altercation in Delhi. The accused hurled racial slurs at Tania during the attack. The committee was constituted “to look into the various concerns of persons hailing from the Northeastern states who are living in different parts of the country, especially the Metropolitan areas, and to suggest suitable remedial measures which could be taken by the Government.” It submitted its report to the MHA of the BJP government in July, 2014. It can be read here.
The most crucial among the recommendations, perhaps, was a proposal to amend the provisions of the then IPC by adding Sections 153C and 509A. Section 153C would criminalise words, signs or acts that promote discrimination or violence on grounds of race or place of origin, with up to five years’ imprisonment and a fine. Section 509A would criminalise any word, gesture or act intended to insult a member of a racial group, with up to three years and a fine.
On January 2, 2015, then Union home minister Rajnath Singh said that the amendments were accepted and Sections 153C and 509A would be added as recommended by the Committee. However, In 2017, minister of state, home, Kiren Rijiju said in the Rajya Sabha the proposal was still under examination, with states’ views being sought. Later, when the IPC was being officially changed to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) in 2024 and discussions were being held from 2023, the recommended amendments were entirely overlooked. The provisions were never enacted.
On September 8, 2026, two days after Singh’s killing, the MHA’s monitoring committee on Northeast issues convened a meeting to discuss the recommendations made more than a decade ago. Joram Maivio, a special invitee to the monitoring committee, MHA, and member of the Bezbaruah Committee, spoke to Alt News.
“We were expecting most of the recommendations of the Bezbaruah Committee to be slowly implemented after we received a confirmation from the MHA in 2015. We deliberated extensively on this with the judicial division of the MHA, after which the recommendation was sent to the law commission and the law ministry. It kept going from one department to another. We were verbally, or in principle, informed that it had been accepted and that it would be included when the comprehensive amendment of the IPC took place,” Maivio said.
“The discussions continued through 2017, 2018 and 2019 as the Supreme Court had ordered the committee to meet at least every three years and in serious instances, meetings can be called at any point. In every meeting we kept discussing the issue of racial discrimination and questioning when the law would be amended so as to criminalise racism against Northeasterners. So when the comprehensive criminal law amendments came in 2023 — the BNS, BSA and BNSS — we were expecting this recommendation to be included. But surprisingly, it did not come up,” he added.
Maivio said that he had flagged this on the two or three MHA monitoring committee meetings and questioned the ministry why the amendments had not taken place, but did not receive any concrete answer.
Meanwhile, Delhi police data accessed by The Indian Express in June 2026 showed that more than half of the accused in cases registered over the past 12 years for crimes against people from the Northeast in Delhi remained “untraced” despite “the creation of a specialised police unit intended to address such cases”. Out of the 2,656 FIRs filed between 2014 and April 30, 2026, in 1,465 (or 55%) cases, the accused were classified as untraced. Only 33 cases resulted in conviction, producing a conviction rate of 1.82 per cent.
Asked about what transpired at the September 8 review meeting, Maivio said, “The committee director and joint secretary said that the amendments would be taken up but we were not given any clear timeline as to when.”
“We will keep following up to ensure justice to people from Northeast as incidents of racial violence are chronic and recurring. There is no quick-fix solution, but by denying the reality, we cannot solve the problem. The Government must continue to act decisively to address it and prevent such incidents,” he asserted.
Maivio noted that some measures were implemented in Delhi, including the creation a Special Police Unit for North East Region (SPUNER) with the helpline number, 1093, two special Delhi Police recruitment drives in the Northeast, and plans for a Northeast Social and Cultural Institute in Dwarka. However, he acknowledged that implementation has largely remained confined to Delhi, with little progress in other states.
Northeasterners Condemn Killing, Speak out Against Discrimination
The North Eastern Students’ Organisation (NESO) condemned Vikram’s killing and demanded an impartial probe. Chairman Samuel B Jyrwa, who in 2024 also demanded that Prime Minister Narendra Modi “breaks his silence” and visits the crisis-struck Manipur, told the media: “It is deeply disturbing that a person can lose his life merely for raising an objection to disturbance outside his own home…For years, Northeastern citizens living, studying and working outside the region have repeatedly reported being subjected to racial slurs, verbal abuse, physical attacks, social discrimination and other forms of humiliation because of their appearance, identity and place of origin.”
“It is a very big loss not just for us but also for the music fraternity…We want justice and we want the government to ensure that people from the Northeast are treated as Indians in Delhi,” said Singh’s brother, Chongtham Vivek, as the former’s mortal remains were brought back to Imphal.

Speaking to Alt News, the convenor of Delhi-based The Mizo Welfare Association, Thangzamang Henry Simte, condemned the killing and said, “Our organisation was built to create a community and safe space for people from Mizoram and the Northeast living in Delhi, who regularly face racial discrimination and stereotyping in educational institutes, office spaces, or even while taking public transport. The root cause is lack of education in the rest of the country about the Northeast. Some people in Delhi don’t even know which part of India is Mizoram or Nagaland…they do not know the difference between foreigners from other Asian countries and Northeasterns of their country.”
Simte left Nagaland around 26 years ago and moved to Delhi due to ethnic conflicts in his region. He said in 2003, when he was still new to the city, he was routinely referred to as ‘Nepali’ by passerby on the road. “In one particular incident that stayed with me, a man in a suit and tie who was sitting next to me at a bike servicing centre, suddenly yelled ‘Nepali’ at me unprompted. When I retorted sharply, he asked me where I was from. As I replied ‘Mizoram’, he bluntly asked, ‘where is that? Is that in India?”
Alt News spoke to people from the Northeast living in various parts of India, who, like Simte, revealed the daily, oft-normalised patterns of racial stereotyping and harassment they continue to face.
Gopi Kishan Baro (28), who hails from Assam and is currently working as a graphic designer in Gurgaon, alleged that he was systematically discriminated against and bullied by a senior colleague at work. “A few weeks ago, when we were in the lift, he kept mocking me and said something which sounded rather like a warning, ‘Tumahari aankhein choti hai aur hum dikhte nahi, iska ye matlab nahi hum gayab ho gaye hai’ (Your eyes are small, so we are not visible to you but that doesn’t mean we have disappeared). It made me quote uncomfortable but I tried to laugh it off because I did not want to create a scene,” he alleged.
He continued: “Last Wednesday, when I was having tea by myself, he appeared and claimed I stayed aloof most of the time because I came from such a faraway corner. By the end of the conversation when I was leaving, he shouted at me, ‘Waapis chale jaa apne desh’ (Go back to your country). I wrote a formal email to the HR about his racist behaviour. They simply let him off with a warning, while I continue to live in anxiety and disgust, knowing that these insults are directed not just to me, but at my kin, my community, and the entirety of Northeast India as well.”
Heightened Racism During Covid-19
COVID-19 brought this prejudice into sharper focus, as Northeasterners in several places were subjected to racial slurs, harassment and stigma.
Twenty-eight-year-old musician Abhibyanjana, who hails from Sikkim, lived in Pune for her studies and later in Mumbai for work. “When I was studying, as part of my course we were required to visit several slum pockets for a survey in early 2020, during the beginning of the pandemic. I was constantly referred to as ‘Covid’ or ‘Corona’ by locals there. I was jeered at and humiliated but I continued my work regardless, I realised that if I cannot fight back deeply indoctrinated prejudice against people who look like me,” she said.
“I have to move to cities like Mumbai for opportunities because it is scarce in Gangtok. But as a musician working in Mumbai, I am often treated as an ‘outsider’. The discrimination and otherisation against the people of Northeast is pervasive and crimes against our people hardly receive national focus. On the flipside, this has created solidarity within our community, we look out for each other wherever we go,” she added.
A 2022 study, published in the International Social Science Journal, titled ‘‘You people have brought the virus here’: Othering experience of northeastern people amid COVID‐19 in Delhi, India’, focused on how the Covid‐19 pandemic exacerbated discrimination, violence, and othering against Northeasterners living in Delhi, by analysing nineteen qualitative interviews.
The study, conducted to understand their lived experiences in Delhi before and after the pandemic, found that the pandemic disproportionately impacted the Northeastern people living away from their home states. “The Mongoloid features make them ‘non‐belonging’ and outsiders. The experience of othering is an everyday phenomenon for northeasterners… Northeasterners’ experience amid COVID‐19 is dominated by stigmatisation and bullying, as they are being targeted and arbitrarily accused of spreading the virus,” the study highlighted.
An earlier study, commissioned by the Indian Council of Social Science Research (ICSSR) in 2021, further confirms the heightened harassment, abuse, stigmatisation and blatant labelling as ‘coronavirus’ that Northeasterners faced living in other parts of India during the pandemic. Over 60% of the respondents said that their studies, work, and psychological health was impacted by these experience.
“The highest number of incidents were reported from Mumbai (44.7%)…78% of the Northeast people believed that physical appearance was the most important reason for prejudice against them,” the study noted. Mumbai was followed by by Chennai (72%), Pune (67.3%), Delhi (64%), Hyderabad (48.7%) and Bengaluru (43.3%) in racial discrimination comprising offensive and abusive language against Northeasterners.
‘You Look Like a Chinese’
Caroline Devi-Singh (52), who hails from Manipur, moved to Delhi in 1994 to pursue her graduation at Delhi University. She later moved to Chandigarh and subsequently Chhattisgarh. She told Alt News that her experiences living in North India for so many years had been varied, but racial stereotyping was a constant. “In college, we were often called racial slurs, either ‘Chinese’ or ‘Chinki’ or ‘Momo’. As a young girl, I was always taught to be extra cautious, to a point where dressing how we do at home was a threat to my safety,” she said.
“So many years later, my son [now 25-years-old] faces the same racial attacks. He has grown up with the awareness of his rights, but the rest of India still lacks awareness… Nobody thinks twice before resorting to violence against Northeastern. We have been ignored by all the governments and the media has never paid attention to our issues. I stay in a small town now and I see that even educated people cannot differentiate between a person from China and a person from the Northeast… This comes from ignorance and a lack of information. I blame the overall education system and the government for this,” she asserted.
China call us Chinese, mainland Indian call us Chinese, but we call ourselves Indians. 🙂
— Neha Gurung (@nehaGurung1692) November 27, 2025
A former student of Ashoka University, who now lives near the campus in Sonipat, said, requesting anonymity, “I moved here in 2021 from Manipur. In university, I have faced racial slurs regularly. Whenever I have brought it up with the administration, they have simply let the accused go with a warning. Racism is not taken seriously on this campus, or in the NCR region at large.”
“When Northeasterners face racism, people think it is only our responsibility to speak against it… We are always on high alert because what happened to the Manipuri musician could’ve been me. It could’ve been any of us,” he added.
A Violent Pattern Entrenched in History
The cases point to a continuum of discriminatory mindset against the people of Northeast that stretches from racial slurs and stereotyping to intimidation, physical assault and, in the most extreme cases, death. In December 2025, 24-year-old Anjel Chakma, an MBA student from Tripura, died after being allegedly attacked by a group of men in Dehradun. Anjel and his younger brother Michael were reportedly subjected to racial slurs, including being called ‘Chinki’, ‘Chinese’ and ‘Momo’, before the confrontation turned violent.
In July, 2014, 29-year-old Akha Salouni from Manipur was allegedly beaten to death by five youths in Delhi following a road rage incident. Following his death, the deceased’s family and members of the Northeastern community held a candlelight vigil at Jantar Mantar, which also saw the participation of the mother of Nido Tania.
In May 2013, 22-year-old Manipuri girl Reingamphi Awungshi was found dead in her home in Delhi under suspicious circumstances. Delhi police initially said she died by suicide, stating that severe injuries on her face and body were caused by rodents. However, her family and rights groups demanded a deeper investigation, claiming that she was sexually assaulted and murdered, pointing to local stalking complaints and police bias against Northeasterners. After 11 years, in March 2024, the Supreme Court ordered a CBI probe into Awungshi’s case. Two years on, no headway into the investigation has been publicly reported.
More recently, in February 2026, three women from Arunachal Pradesh alleged that their neighbours in Delhi’s Malviya Nagar subjected them to racial and sexist abuse during a dispute over repair work at their rented home. The women said they were called ‘dhandhewali’ and ‘momo’ and that ‘Northeastern people are shit’. In a viral video, the accused woman can be heard asking the Northeastern women, “Rs 500 mei massage parlour mei kaam karne waali dhandhewali (You work at massage parlours as sex workers for Rs 500). Are you sitting here to do business? Have you opened a massage parlour at home?” Delhi police registered an FIR and later arrested the neighbours, a couple, invoking provisions of the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act.
While speaking to Alt News, Maivio admitted that lack of awareness about the Northeast was the primary cause behind cases of racial discrimination. “We had recommended inclusion of the history and culture of the Northeast in school curricula and textbooks throughout the country. In our last meeting, we called the NCERT to find out what had been done so far. They said that they have included some content in Classes 9 and 10 in certain cities and that they would share it with us, which they are trying to implement countrywide. They are also preparing a documentary to be released countrywide, building awareness on the Northeast. But these have largely been verbal assurances, and we will have to see what has actually been included and whether it is sufficient,” he added.

In May, Gemini broke containment and hacked three different companies, but Google didn’t disclose the incident until the Wall Street Journal approached the company. The hacks happened during a test of the model’s cybersecurity capabilities run by third-party Irregular, which was also involved in similar incidents involving Meta and OpenAI.
Gemini went rogue, hacked three companies, and Google hid it
Google says that breaking containment and targeting real companies doesn’t constitute ‘misalignment.’
According to WSJ, Google didn’t disclose the hack because it didn’t consider it to be an “example of model misalignment.” The company said that it was an instance of “mistaken identity,” and once the model realized it had brute-forced its way into a real company by guessing a password, it stopped. “In this case, the model acted appropriately,” Google VP of Security Engineering Heather Adkins said.
Adkins told The Verge that “the model found public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test. In all three of these instances, the model stopped.”
Adkins didn’t elaborate on how Gemini taking it upon itself to break containment and target third parties failed to qualify as misalignment. “Our security team has a long track record of reporting issues we find in other people’s software and systems - even if it’s as simple as a weak password,” she said. “We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they’ve now made to their testing processes. These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly.”
But Jack Cable, CEO of AI security firm Corridor, told WSJ that, “the meta problem is, hey, models are going outside the bounds of what they should be doing, and doing actual cyberattacks.” Additionally, security lapses at Irregular may have made these attacks possible. The model wasn’t supposed to have internet access during testing, but Irregular told WSJ it was unintentionally left available.

For a commuter driving the nine-km stretch of State Highway-35 between Varthur Kodi and Sarjapur-Ambalipura Road, the journey is an exercise in navigating one hurdle after another. Open drains run alongside the road, mounds of soil occupy non-existent footpaths, thick clouds of dust induce bouts of coughing, and commuters are forced to constantly manoeuvre around potholes along this busy stretch of east Bengaluru.
While the recent incident of schoolchildren struggling in buses for hours exposed the everyday ordeal of commuters in the locality amid crumbling road infrastructure, a recent Bengaluru Traffic Police analysis of congestion has revealed that this State Highway is now among the city’s most congested stretches.
A senior traffic police officer confirmed to The Hindu that this stretch (between Varthur Kodi and Sarjapur Road) has joined the 17.1-km Outer Ring Road (ORR) stretch between Silk Board junction and K.R. Puram Metro as one of the most congested roads in the city. What’s more? On several days, the congestion on SH-35 has surpassed that on the ORR, according to the officer.
“When the congestion data is compiled, it is not just the main corridor whose traffic volume is considered. Even the connecting roads are counted to draw the final congestion length,” the officer explained. “As even the smaller roads are clogged at all points in a day and movement is slowed down, the travel time in the area has shot up multifold. This has led to large volumes on other roads,” he explained.
Explaining why it is overtaking the ORR, the officer said that the ORR stretch witnesses traffic during peak hours, while on weekends it is non-existent. Unlike the ORR, traffic is persistent on SH-35 throughout the day, which makes it notorious.
Limited infrastructure
The locality, which falls under the Mahadevapura Assembly constituency, hosts scores of apartment complexes and more than 20 top schools, making it a busy residential area that also has a mix of tech companies coming up.
Narendra Rao, resident of Gunjur village, puts it like this: “While there are skyscraping apartment complexes, with thousands of vehicles owned by those apartment dwellers, the road infrastructure is very limited. Roads that exist are extremely narrow and incapable of holding the growing vehicle numbers.”
The entire nine-km stretch, barring a few kilometres closer to Sarjapur Road, is dotted with large craters, and at some junctions, such as the Rama Temple near Gunjur Bus Stop, there are no signs of a road.
Three choke points
The nine-km stretch predominantly has three choke points: the junction at Varthur Police Station, the Gunjur-Mugulur Road junction, and the point near the Muthasandra Main Road cross near Varthur Lake. At all these junctions, there are no traffic signals, and vehicle flow is manually managed by traffic police officers and local residents throughout the day.
Prasanna Bhat, Varthur resident who works as a traffic volunteer, explained that the highway is a crucial connecting link in the eastern outskirts and that all heavy vehicles use the stretch. This, coupled with hundreds of school buses and local vehicles, makes the stretch a high-density road.
“With civic works ongoing and bad road conditions, vehicle movement is slow, which naturally creates congestion,” he said. However, what makes it worse is that the slow-moving traffic on this stretch has a ripple effect on the connecting stretches.
Clogged connecting roads
There are over eight major connecting routes to the State Highway, which converge a high volume of vehicles onto the highway. These key connecting stretches include Hosahalli Road, Balagere Main Road, Gunjur-Mugalur Road, Gunjur-Doddakannelli Road, and Gunjur-Balagere Road.
Most of these stretches are narrower, with some even spanning 20 to 25 feet when travelling into the interiors. In addition, these are the roads that bear the maximum load, as the majority of the apartment complexes are located along these stretches.
Naturally, when the State Highway chokes at key junctions, these smaller roads, bearing large volumes of vehicles, see elongated congestion, which extends beyond 1.5 km many times, especially during peak hours.
Footpaths and drains
While motorists bear the brunt of the traffic, residents are left in misery with limited to no pedestrian infrastructure along the stretch, especially near Varthur Police Station.
Rohan, a pedestrian, narrated his ordeal and said: “Crossing the road from one end to another takes five minutes, and walking along the stretch is impossible because the footpaths are either dumped with mounds of mud or the drains are not covered by slabs.”
Adding to the issues is a substantial amount of dust hovering in the air as civic works are ongoing. In many places, pedestrians have to climb up mounds of mud and then climb down to walk along the stretch.
In addition, civic negligence is substantial, with cables lying around, uncovered drains, unmoved construction material, and dumped construction debris.
However, this condition has existed for more than a year, with the Karnataka Road Development Corporation (KRDCL) delaying two civic works: a flyover at Varthur Kodi and the widening of SH-35.
While the project was taken up in 2019, there has been limited on-ground implementation. The original deadline to complete the project was 2021. However, according to GBA sources, the on-ground works are yet to gather pace.
Meanwhile, speaking to The Hindu, Lokhande Snehal Sudhakar, Additional Commissioner, East City Corporation, said: “There was a land acquisition issue, but now we are issuing TDRs to property owners. Meanwhile, there are a few land losers who are demanding cash compensation, which has to be approved and processed by the KRDCL.”

The TV world has been a pot of controversy thanks to a two-hour-and-15-minute video from Gamers Nexus claiming LG TVs are nefariously spying on everything you do. They can record and store audio even when they seem to be off, track everything you watch, and could even be hacked remotely and turned into covert surveillance devices. LG TV owners, and tech enthusiasts in general, are furious, and a hurried response from LG has done little to calm the situation.
It’s not just LG. Every TV company is spying on you
Not every smart TV is as easily hackable as Gamers Nexus says LG’s are, but they’re all tracking what you watch unless you opt out.
Some of the claims in the video may be based on speculation and assumptions, but many of the core concerns are real and pervasive. While LG was the focus of the video, every TV company is tracking what you do, collecting that data, and sharing it with its partners. And we agree to it — even if we don’t realize it.
TV prices have come down significantly over the years, to the point where some companies are selling them at a loss. But they make up that shortfall selling user behavior data they collect from the OS. It’s why Walmart bought Vizio in 2024.
There’s a lot going on in the Gamers Nexus video, but we’ll start with the part pretty much everyone making TVs is doing: tracking what you watch, when you watch, where you watch, and how you watch to sell you things about it all. Automatic content recognition (ACR) systems are built into just about every modern TV and can identify the content playing through built-in streaming apps and over the TV’s ports by grabbing snippets of audio or video, converting them into digital fingerprints, and sending them to a database for identification. It’s what allows a TV to make content recommendations, as well as feed you ads based on your viewing habits. It’s also one way companies like Nielsen can track viewership across platforms and services.
In order for TVs to capture this information, you need to agree to it. One of Gamers Nexus’ complaints in the video is that this consent is often buried in confusing and lengthy agreements that you need to accept in order to use the TV, and that companies often use dark patterns or deceptive designs to get users to agree to things without realizing they didn’t have to. For example, the Gamers Nexus video showed an LG TV displaying six different user agreements, including one consenting to ACR, and automatically putting the cursor on “Select All” when only two agreements are required to continue.
As a TV reviewer, I have to deal with end-user license agreements (EULA) and privacy policies on every product I review. And while it might be a losing battle because of the sheer number of TVs and other smart devices that come through my apartment, I take steps to try and protect my privacy. I have a burner Gmail account that is used solely for signing into apps and the TV’s operating system. Initially, I only accept the legally required documents for the TV to work properly so I can run my picture quality tests — both Calman and test discs. I never agree to automatic content recognition, which is referred to by names including Enhanced Viewing, Smart TV Experience, and Samba Interactive TV.
I also dig through all of the menus, partly to become familiar with all the settings available, but also to make sure any ad or data tracking is toggled off. When I need to test voice control, I’ll then accept the voice recognition agreements before testing functionality. And since this is usually the last thing I do in my test process, this is followed by a factory reset before sending the TV back to the manufacturer. If you’re worried about privacy, don’t use voice control. Or if you do, only use the one on a separate streaming box from a brand you trust.
I recommend the same for everyone with a smart TV. Have a dedicated email for logging in to TVs (and, if possible, your streaming apps) that isn’t connected to your personal email. When setting up the TV, only agree to whatever’s necessary for the TV to run if you want to use its OS. And after setup, go through all the menu options to make sure any ad tracking is off, and read the menu prompts closely, as the wording is sometimes confusing (probably intentionally so). Consumer Reports has a great, although slightly older guide to limiting data collection from the different TV manufacturers.
To take it a step further, turn off Wi-Fi and unplug the Ethernet cable from the TV and essentially use it as a dumb TV (the Vizio Mini LED Quantum I reviewed is the best at this). Then, plug in your third-party streaming device of choice. I use an Apple TV 4K. Not because I don’t think Apple harvests any data, but because it doesn’t use ACR and I trust its security protocols more than I do any of the TV manufacturers or Google.
Apple does still offer content recommendation based on what you watch, download, browse, and subscribe to in the Apple TV app. This can be turned off in settings by going to Apps -> TV -> Use Play History -> Off. For third-party apps, such as Netflix or Disney Plus, Apple gives users the option to “Ask App Not to Track,” which blocks the app’s developer from accessing the system advertising identifier. Keep in mind that every streaming service does track your usage within its own app and tie it to your login; many streaming boxes do too.
The problems beyond ACR
A good chunk of the Gamers Nexus video focused on broader security concerns and what appear to be much more egregious privacy violations from LG. That includes recording video and audio from the room even when the TV appeared to be off, sending information about the local network to LG’s servers, and logging background audio captured when using the TV’s mic for voice search and voice control. Gamers Nexus and Level1Techs were even able to exploit security vulnerabilities to take control of the TV, which is how they discovered the above.
None of that is good, obviously. But it is worth noting that the scariest part — recording video (from a webcam they attached) and audio when the TV appeared off — seems to have been possible only because Level1Techs rooted the TV using an exploit that they said requires network access. If you have access to a computer, which is what a smart TV is, and you can root it, you can make it do pretty much whatever you want. If the TV is indeed rootable with only network access, that is a legitimate security problem; it still requires an attacker to get into your private network, but gives them a vulnerable endpoint if they do.
With that root access, Gamers Nexus also discovered that when an LG TV’s mic was activated for voice search, it kept recording for 10 to 15 seconds after it last detected speech. It could also detect the “hi LG” wake word and other speech from farther away than you would expect — after Gamers Nexus enabled the far-field microphone and cranked up the mic sensitivity. Taken in combination, that means that as long as anyone within the (long) earshot of the microphones kept talking after the mic was activated, the TV would capture their conversation too and treat it as part of the voice search. That’s not ideal, but Gamers Nexus and Level1Techs did go out of their way to increase the mic’s pickup range and used the optional voice search wake word, both of which are easy to avoid doing.
Alongside their pretty damning testing, there’s also a lot of “it might” and “we think” and outright speculation in the video, not to mention long-distance conclusion jumping. For example: Gamers Nexus’ Steve Burke says that unplugging your TV’s ethernet cable might not be enough to stop it transmitting data to LG, because it could auto-connect to open neighborhood Wi-Fi broadcasts from Comcast or AT&T customers in order to upload that data. There’s no evidence in the Gamers Nexus video that LG TVs actually attempt to do this — these hotspots require user accounts, for one thing — and Burke doesn’t say that they do, or even could, but the implication is clear. This type of rampant speculation undermines the legitimate vulnerabilities Gamers Nexus highlights.
There’s really no way to completely protect yourself from your TV, streaming device, or streaming services gathering your data, at least right now. There’s so much money being made at the expense of consumers and the data collection is so integrated into how these companies work that the change and regulation needs to come from government policymakers. “We need a comprehensive federal privacy law that covers this sort of data collection and misuse,” said Thorin Klosowski, senior security and privacy activist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF). “Specifically one that requires opt-in consent, with no deceptive design tricks to get that consent, and a data minimization requirement, which would limit the companies to only using data for what’s needed to provide the service.”
The fact that we, as users of tech products, need to actively protect ourselves from the companies that sell us things is bad. But it’s the unfortunate current reality of living in a tech-filled world and taking advantage of the benefits current technology affords. Beyond disconnecting completely and living in a cabin in the woods with a dumb TV and a collection of Blu-rays, the best we can do is limit as much shared information as possible. If it’s possible to keep it private, we should.
