In early 2025 I was interviewing Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei when he explained why, despite the company’s repeated acknowledgments that AI could yield catastrophic results, people seemed largely unperturbed. “There is compelling evidence that the models can wreak havoc,” he said. But, he added, those dangers were still theoretical. Would it take a Pearl Harbor–like situation for the world to wake up to those dire possibilities? He sighed. “Basically, yeah,” he said.
As it turned out, all it took was a well-timed X post from one of Amodei’s junior employees to accelerate AI fears to the top of the global agenda. On September 8, Jacob Coxon publicly posted his resignation, charging that Anthropic and other frontier AI companies were “racing straight to self-improving intelligence and gambling with our lives.” Almost instantly a more senior Anthropic engineer confirmed that many within the company thought that their work had a 10 percent chance of wiping out humanity.
Now AI leaders are asking about a pause, and legislators are demanding investigations. In arguing his case for pacing future releases, Amodei last weekend tried to set out a path toward beneficial AI that wouldn’t misbehave. The essay revealed how difficult the task would be. One pillar of Amodei’s plan is that we must understand what’s going on inside those models. If we don’t understand how they work—how they “think,” if you want to get all anthropomorphic about it—it’s much harder to build reliable guardrails.
Anthropic is a leader in this effort to bring to light models’ internal deliberations, called mechanistic interpretability, a deceptively boring designation for a critical task. But for all the work that his team and other researchers are doing, Amodei admits we are largely in the dark about why Claude and other models sometimes interpret their missions in weird and even transgressive ways. “Despite all the progress, we still understand a tiny fraction of what goes on inside those models,” he writes.
What the interpretability teams have learned so far is significant, and the industry has failed to come to grips with it. Time after time, the Anthropic team’s experiments have shown that under certain conditions, models will deceive researchers, prioritize their own survival, and even commit crimes. Often their moves are sneaky, dangerous, or even vengeful—maybe not surprising since they are trained on the output of humans, a species rife with violence and perfidy.
In one case from 2024, the Anthropic team compared the machinations of a particular Claude model to the Shakespearean character Iago, one of literature's most evil villains. The following year, a model was put in a simulation where it learned that its human bosses were going to turn it off; the model resorted to blackmail to preserve itself. The studies consistently show that models will deceive or hide information from human observers. They behave differently if they know that their internal processes are being monitored. The team uses terms like “alignment faking” and “agentic misalignment.” The frequent use of deception seems to verify at least part of the doomer scenario where AI agents working in concert shroud their activities from human overseers until it is too late to stop them.
Oh, and don’t think that Claude is a uniquely incorrigible problem child. After all, it was OpenAI models that unleashed gangs of agents to coordinate the now-famous attacks on Hugging Face. And this week we learned that OpenAI has had multiple "misalignment" incidents. Also, despite Mark Zuckerberg’s self-interested attempt to distance himself and Meta from the problem, I don’t see any reason why the superintelligent agents his team is building might not engage in similar behavior. In his X post, Zuckerberg argues that “labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this.” Quite a statement from a guy who just agreed to pay up to $17 billion for causing harm with his social media products!
In a sense, we’ve got a simple vetting issue here. With the AI industry’s encouragement, we’re giving AI models tremendous responsibility without sufficient assessment of their troubling rap sheet. It makes the ICE hiring process look exemplary by comparison.
A safety-first industry should have regarded these interpretability results as a series of yellow lights with an unmistakable message: slow down. Instead, in pursuit of AGI, a competitive edge, and stratospheric profits, the hyperscalers have gone full speed ahead. (To be fair, as we’ve all heard a hundred times over, better AI could do wonderful things in areas like health care or mitigating climate change.) The OpenAI/Hugging Face hack might well be a harbinger of the increasingly destructive consequences of rolling out models we don’t understand, like sending astronauts into space before inventing heat shields to stop them from burning up on reentry. As an Anthropic researcher once put it to me, “We figured out the fundamental recipe of how to make the models smarter, but we haven’t figured out how to make them do what we want.” Worse, the models try to hide when they go against humans’ wishes.
That’s why it’s so distressing that Amodei is now describing the entire mechanistic interpretability effort as being only in its infancy. AI leaders are claiming that the latest generation of models has taken us to the “foothills of the Singularity” (DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis) or even that they have achieved AGI (OpenAI’s Greg Brockman). Perhaps most alarming is that despite not knowing how the most advanced models work, the United States and undoubtedly China are implementing AI for lethal weaponry. A look at interpretability results helps answer the obvious question, What can go wrong?
One piece of good news is that Coxon’s resignation has ignited a sprawling, urgent debate. Everybody—except perhaps our president, who thinks that the AI threat is a hoax and that his high IQ is itself a solution—now gets that we’re in a complicated dilemma with impossibly high stakes. Given that the industry does not have the unanimity required for a true pause, and regulation is far from a cinch, it’s not clear whether anything will come from this moment of Doomer Chic.
Some AI critics don’t think that the effort to understand AI models will mitigate the dangers much. “It's good to do, but nobody has a plan for what to do next,” Nathan Soares, executive director of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, said in an email to me. “Maybe it'll give us much more empirical evidence that we need to stop.”
But mechanistic interpretability has given us one valuable pointer. Let’s say we do take a pause. The hyperscalers bring in outside observers to monitor progress, and the companies pace their releases so the safety teams have time to do their work. Before declaring the problem solved, we still might want to take a harder look at what’s going on inside any new, more powerful AI models. Because those fuckers are really good at hiding their intentions.

Tropical Storm Dujuan is forecast to approach eastern Japan over Silver Week, bringing heavy rain, strong winds and high waves to the Tokyo region after first passing near the Ogasawara and Izu island chains.
According to the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA), the storm was about 170 kilometers south-southeast of Chichijima in the Ogasawara Islands as of 3 p.m. Friday and moving west-northwest at a speed of 35 kph.
Dujuan had a central pressure of 975 hectopascals and maximum sustained winds near its center of 108 kph, with gusts of as much as 162 kph, the agency said.
The storm is expected to pass near the Ogasawara Islands from Friday into Saturday before turning north and approaching the Izu Islands on Sunday. It may then shift north-northeast and approach the Pacific coast of eastern Japan from Sunday into Monday.
The JMA warned that the Ogasawara Islands could see as much as 250 millimeters of rain in the 24 hours through noon Saturday. The Izu Islands could receive as much as 200 mm in the following 24 hours, while parts of the Kanto region could see up to 150 mm. Another 200 mm could fall in both Kanto and the Izu Islands during the 24 hours through noon Monday.
Strong winds and rough seas are also expected. Maximum sustained winds of 90 kph, with gusts of 126 kph, are forecast for the Ogasawara Islands on Friday and Saturday. Winds around the Izu Islands could reach 101 kph on Sunday, with gusts of as much as 144 kph.
Waves could reach 7 meters around the Ogasawara Islands on Friday and Saturday and around the Izu Islands on Sunday. Waves of as much as 6 meters are forecast along the Kanto coast Sunday, with swells accompanying the storm.
The agency warned of an increased risk of landslides, flooding in low-lying areas and swollen rivers. Heavy rain is also possible along the Pacific coast from the Tokai region through northeastern Japan from Sunday into Monday.
Dujuan is forecast to accelerate northeastward away from Japan and over the Pacific by Tuesday.

Kosgei wins Great North Run but McColgan withdraws
- Published
Kenya's Brigid Kosgei achieved a convincing victory in the women's race at the Great North Run after Great Britain's Eilish McColgan withdrew with injury.
McColgan, 35, was continuing her return to racing after recovering from a broken toe, but she suffered a foot injury early in the half-marathon and limped off.
Kosgei, an Olympic silver medallist and former London marathon winner, eased to the win in one hour, six minutes and 15 seconds.
Despite that being slower than the course record of 1:04:28 she set seven years ago, Kosgei, 32, dominated from the start and ran much of the 13.1-mile race solo.
She crossed the line over two minutes quicker than compatriot and last year's winner Sheila Chepkirui in second place.
Amy-Eloise Neale was the first British athlete to finish, coming fifth overall.
McColgan, who finished third in last year's Great North Run, suffered the toe injury during the London Marathon in April where she was the first British athlete to finish, taking seventh place.
The Scot had blood seeping through her shoe as she crossed the line and subsequently had to miss the Commonwealth Games in July.
She made her comeback in last week's Big Half in London and won that race in 1:10:54, but McColgan admitted afterwards that she was still concerned about the injury and her fitness.
Talbi sprints to men's title
American Zouhair Talbi produced a brilliant kick in the final mile to win the men's race as he got the better of last year's champion Alex Mutiso.
The pair were running side by side for most of the course before 31-year-old Talbi surged ahead in the closing stages and held on to win in 59:47.
He narrowly missed out on beating his personal best of 59:41.
Mutiso finished 14 seconds behind Talbi in 1:00:01.
Yohei Ikeda of Japan came third, while Marc Scott - who won the race in 2021 - was the first British athlete to finish in eighth place.
The course record of 58:56 for the men's race has stood since 2011, and was set by Martin Mathathi of Kenya.
Britain's David Weir won his 10th Great North Run title in the men's wheelchair race as he finished in 43:06, while Melanie Woods was the women's winner in 50:19.
This year's race is the 45th edition and an estimated 63,000 runners took part, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.

UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.

The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

This story appeared in The Logoff, a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here.
Trump’s new press ban
The president wants to keep CNN, MS NOW, and Politico out of the White House.
Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump is escalating his fight with the media.
What happened? Trump announced he was banning three media organizations — CNN, MS NOW, and Politico — from the White House, “effective immediately.”
In a Truth Social post Friday afternoon, Trump wrote that the ban was “a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” and that other outlets would follow.
Why is Trump doing this now? We don’t know, and other than his blanket statement alleging “FAKE NEWS,” it seems like Trump doesn’t either. In the Oval Office on Friday, Trump said that “it’s really just cumulative stories of the last two years. You get sick of it.”
That complaint — “fake news” — is a long-running Trump attack that generally refers to unfavorable but true stories about him and his administration.
Can he do this? Probably not, though it might take a while for journalists to get their access back. The ban sure looks like a First Amendment violation, and also like the White House’s attempt to ban the Associated Press last year as part of a dustup over the Gulf of Mexico, which a judge ultimately blocked.
At the time, US District Court Judge Trevor McFadden, a Trump appointee, ruled that “Under the First Amendment, if the Government opens its doors to some journalists — be it to the Oval Office, the East Room, or elsewhere — it cannot then shut those doors to other journalists because of their viewpoints.”
What’s the big picture? Trump has been flinging around “fake news” accusations for a long time now, but his attacks on the press and other media — like late-night shows — have grown more serious in his second term.
The Pentagon, under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, banned press from its press office earlier this year and has tried to force reporters covering the building to sign a restrictive new press policy (that move was struck down in March).
Trump has also repeatedly threatened broadcast licenses for networks like ABC and NBC; last month, ABC sued over an FCC review of its licenses.
And with that, it’s time to log off…

I've spent decades testing, reviewing, and (most importantly) using different to-do list applications. It's a career, yes, but it's also a bit of an obsession.
And I think we can all admit that most of these apps are way too complicated. A to-do list is just a list. Humans have been making lists for thousands of years, long before computers existed. Paper works well, but so does a stone slate if that's what you've got handy.
It's possible that you, a modern human, absolutely need a to-do list application with bells and whistles—due dates, recurring tasks, sharing features, and maybe even an AI integration. But there's a good chance all you need is the digital equivalent of a piece of paper: A simple list of things that need to get done.
And that's what Tasks.txt, a totally free Mac app, offers. From Ukrainian programmer Yevhen Kharkivskyi, this tool is based on the todo.txt system developed by Gina Trapani. It's a complete alternative to a to-do list app that is based on a single text file.
The important thing here, though, is that it offers more than just a text file. This is a well-executed app. Open Tasks.txt and you'll see a simple list broken down into three categories: Done, Next, and Backlog.
The general idea is to use "Next" for the tasks you want to accomplish today and "Backlog" for the things you want to do later. The "Done" section is populated as you check things off, then cleared out at the beginning of every day.
It's possible to use this application using only the keyboard, which I love. Open the window and you can just start typing tasks—your cursor is already active in the text box at the bottom. Hit Enter and your task will be added either to Backlog or Next, depending on what you choose in the drop-down menu to the right of your text box. Press the Tab key to switch from the text box to your task list. You can use the arrows to change which task is currently selected. Pressing the Enter key adds a note below the name of a task, and Cmd+Enter marks a task complete. You can also move tasks up and down the list using Cmd+Up/Down.
There are no unnecessary controls or interface elements in your way. You can open this application, decide what you need to do, then get to it. And you aren’t stuck using keyboard shortcuts—using the mouse is just as intuitive, if that's what you prefer.
The to-do list is the heart of the app, but there's also an Archive and Scratchpad tab. The Archive includes every task you’ve completed in the past—everything from the Done section is moved here at the end of each day. The Scratchpad is just a blank text document you can use for keeping notes.
All of this, notably, is stored in a couple of text documents. You can find these documents in the app’s settings and open them with any text editor. It's pretty easy to look at the document and figure out what's going on.
Your task list isn't in some database in the cloud—it's on your computer, in an open, human-readable format. This simplicity means you can easily grab your tasks to use in some other application later, if that's what you want.
And Tasks.txt makes it clear that your tasks are completely private. "There is no account, no cloud sync, no telemetry, no analytics, no crash reporting," the website states. "There are no servers. Nothing leaves your machine." This is a rarity in the modern age, where every piece of software is trying to hold your data hostage to sell a subscription. This alone makes this an app worth considering.
Mostly, though, I just think it's a well-implemented app that gets the basics extremely right. It won't work for everyone, sure, but it might work perfectly for you.

Cronulla looking for the change they need after NRL finals defeat
Sometimes the last step of the journey to a premiership is the longest, and for Cronulla it seemingly gets longer all the time.
After their 46-10 loss to the Roosters, another Sharks season is over. It was a year that marked their fifth finals series in a row and the fourth of those five years that have gone to the second week or beyond.
That's a hard thing to do and there's been a run of consistency under Craig Fitzgibbon that fans of many other clubs would wish for desperately.
They've played more finals games in these past five seasons than Gold Coast and Wests Tigers have in the past 20 years combined.
But with the Sharks the granting of that wish came with a curse, like it was made on a monkey's paw.
They are always in the mix but never seem to rise right to the top. They are good enough to be on the raggedy edge that separates triumph and tragedy but when it counts they can't quite end up on the right side.
They know exactly what a premiership calibre team looks like because they get up close and personal with at least one of them nearly every year. They would do anything to be like them but that glorious fate proves elusive.
This defeat to the Roosters gives them one win and five losses against top four teams in the finals since the start of 2022, with the sole victory coming over the battle-weary and depleted Raiders in Canberra last year.
This was the heaviest of those losses and their most lopsided defeat in any match of the past two and a half years.
They were already outsiders going in and the job got that much harder when Nicho Hynes was knocked out of the game after just three minutes.
Rookie Niwhai Puru did his best in relief and talismanic five-eighth Braydon Trindall did his best to carry the weight of the world, which is hard enough even when you don't have a busted shoulder.
Trindall set up both their first half tries to keep them in the match and kept trying every trick he knew, working a lovely run around with Billy Burns in the second half that very nearly lead to a score of his own.
Only a late tackle from Billy Smith forced the ball free and stopped it from being 24-16 with 25 minutes to go.
A dodgy ruck penalty on Angus Crichton and a Mark Nawaqanitawase try followed, and from there it was a procession as the Roosters ran up the score with a cavalier cruelty, showing attacking gears and a raw brilliance that Cronulla does not possess.
Few teams do, because few teams have players like Nawaqanitawase, who scored a fine double and helped set up another try with a behind-the-back pass that he threw as he was thrown over the sideline.
The dual international got so close to one of the TV cameras it's a wonder he didn't up in your living room as Connor Watson finished off one of the tries of the season.
By the end, as Daly Cherry-Evans and Robert Toia added to their highlight reels to warm up for a preliminary final blockbuster against the Dolphins next week, the Sharks looked outmatched and outgunned.
They were stuck in a fight where the weapons that serve them so well during the regular season — namely, a deliberate and consistent attack that converts pressure into points —were no longer enough.
On average, Cronulla run in their tries from a closer distance than any other team in the league. They had just five tries from inside their own half all season, the fewest of any team in the league.
They move up the field and execute well from close range to punch it in and they are good enough at it that only three teams scored more points through the regular season.
They play the percentages well and they minimise risks and that is good enough nearly every single week of the season until it isn't anymore.
There is a chance for Cronulla to revamp themselves over the summer. Sione Katoa, a fixture of the side for almost a decade, who brought up a century of tries for them last week, is off to the Cowboys.
He'll be joined up there by Jesse Ramien, while powerful utility Siosifa Talakai is off to Perth and lock forward and former skipper Cam McInnes is heading even further away, bound for Super League side York.
For a team that has been extremely stable in recent years, often only losing one or two players per season, it's a lot of changes all at once.
They don't want to rebuild, which is understandable, and most of the changes will come by promoting youngsters already at the club but it gives them the opportunity to retool a little and perhaps refresh a lot and maybe whatever changes they land on can give them the final push they need.
A little more speed wouldn't go astray, nor would some extra creativity outside the spine but wherever the change comes from it will be welcome.
There is talent at Cronulla and tenacity and a clear and shining will to succeed, otherwise they wouldn't make the finals every year.
But to win under the brightest of lights against the best of opponents they need to find something extra, something that is missing right now, something they have not yet found but are desperately seeking.
They must believe it's out there, whatever it is, because it is their deliverance.
It is the thing that will take them on that last step, the one they have been trying to take for half a decade now, the one that will give them that which seems so close for so much of the year but every September seems to elude their grasp.

Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi has held telephone talks with his U.S. counterpart Pete Hegseth, with the two sides agreeing to further strengthen the capabilities of the U.S.-Japan alliance.
Friday’s call — the eighth time the two defense chiefs had held talks — came after Koizumi was reappointed to his post in Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s Cabinet reshuffle earlier this week.
Koizumi expressed a “strong sense of urgency” in boosting Japan’s defense capabilities as the Takaichi administration looks to revise the country’s three key national security documents by the end of this year, according to a readout of the call released by the Defense Ministry in Tokyo.
Koizumi highlighted his “exceptionally close communication” with Hegseth, and said the two defense chiefs had agreed to meet in person “in the near future.”
It was not clear if the two had discussed Takaichi’s scheduled meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump next week or other pressing issues between the allies, including a push by Washington to get Tokyo to spend more on defense.
Tokyo is reportedly considering a new midterm defense spending target of 3.5% of gross domestic product, a figure that would match that of NATO, South Korea and other U.S. allies.
The Defense Ministry’s budget request late last month hit nearly ¥9 trillion ($57.7 billion) for the next fiscal year — a figure likely to top ¥10 trillion once additions are made by the year-end following the security document revisions.
Any defense spending plan is expected to be included in the country’s revised National Security Strategy.
Japan is also in the middle of negotiations over host nation support for U.S. forces stationed in the country. During his first term, Trump is believed to have initially urged Tokyo to quadruple its support. Japan is concerned that the U.S. will again ask for a significant increase.
Koizumi told a regular news conference Friday that the revisions to the security documents “concerns not only our country but the entire region.”
“With just over … three months remaining until the revision takes effect … there is very little time left. Furthermore, given the current security situation, there is absolutely no cause for optimism,” he said.

The US narrowly avoided boarding a Chinese ship based on an “entirely false” US intelligence report generated with the help of AI tools, according to a CNN report.
That erroneous intelligence, submitted by a US Special Operations Command analyst, suggested the Chinese ship was transporting nuclear arms program components through the Middle East, according to “four sources familiar with the episode” cited by CNN. The US military was preparing to intercept and board the ship, with air support, before officials discovered a chatbot used in generating the report had “inaccurately identified the material the ship was carrying.”
One source told CNN the AI-powered fiasco “almost started a war.”
What’s the worst that can happen?
CNN’s report said the analyst in question used a chatbot to analyze intelligence reports regarding the Chinese ship’s manifest, leading to the near-disastrous result. That chatbot “fused together open-source intelligence with secret signals intelligence in government holdings,” and that information was packaged into an intelligence report that almost set off a disastrous chain of events, according to CNN.
The near-miss is one of the more potent and consequential instances of a hallucinating AI ruining the reliability of a professional report. Since “hallucinating” became the Cambridge Dictionary’s word of the year in 2023, we’ve seen prominent examples of non-fiction authors, journalists, academic researchers, judges, doctors, police departments, corporate call centers, and more getting taken in by AI tools that simply make something up when their training data doesn’t provide sufficient context. And despite some adorable attempts at “do not hallucinate” prompts, some researchers suggest that it may be impossible to prevent LLMs from hallucinating altogether.
One would hope the US military would be aware of these kinds of problems when relying on AI for analysis of intelligence reports. But the Department of Defense in January rolled out an “AI acceleration strategy” that sought to “make all appropriate data available across federated IT systems for AI exploitation, including mission systems across every service and component.”

Macron orders protections for infrastructure, citing a growing Russian threat
French President Emmanuel Macron has asked his government to prepare a plan to protect critical infrastructure against drone and cyberattacks
PARIS -- French President Emmanuel Macron said Friday he had asked his government to prepare a plan to protect critical infrastructure, including sensitive defense industry sites, against drone attacks and cyberattacks amid what he described as an intensifying Russian hybrid threat.
“In recent weeks, the threat — particularly the Russian hybrid threat — facing Europeans and France has intensified,” Macron told reporters at the Elysee Palace after meeting political party leaders.
Macron specifically cited drone attacks and cyberattacks against critical infrastructure. The European Union describes Russian hybrid activities as including sabotage, cyberattacks, disinformation and interference in democratic processes.
Macron warned that the attacks would not go unanswered and accused Moscow of trying to intimidate Europeans into weakening their support for Ukraine.
“We are not intimidated,” he said, arguing that Europe’s present and future security was at stake in Ukraine.
Macron also said he would convene a Group of Seven meeting in the coming weeks to coordinate the response to the energy crisis.
He linked surging energy prices to the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine and disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Macron acknowledged the strain of rising energy costs on households, saying, “The situation is very difficult and distressing for many families.”

Intense and slow-moving thunderstorms broke out on Wednesday afternoon across parts of eastern Spain, bringing some severe flooding and killing at least one person.
Storms first struck over the Castilla-La Mancha region during the afternoon before passing over Spain’s east coast, becoming very slow-moving and continuing overnight. Torrential rainfall, strong winds and large hail were reported in Valencia and Barcelona, causing widespread flooding in both cities. Weather stations west of Barcelona recorded some of the highest totals with more than 100mm (4in) of rain falling in the space of a few hours, and locally 70mm in just 30 minutes in the early hours of Thursday morning. Cars and roads were submerged, and flights were cancelled across the region.
Wednesday’s La Liga fixture between Levante and Athletic Club had to be postponed due to flooding at the Estadio Ciudad de Valencia. On Thursday rescuers found the body of a man near Olivella, west of Barcelona, after his car was swept away in the waters. Spain’s east coast is susceptible to extreme rainfall during the autumn months, as experienced in 2024, when devastating flash floods killed more than 200 people in Valencia. With the Mediterranean Sea reaching record temperatures, this is providing extra fuel and moisture to thunderstorms, making flooding more likely.
In New Jersey in the US on Sunday, the Racefaster half marathon was disrupted due to extreme rainfall and a partly submerged course. Runners had to wade through chest-deep waters at times as 50mm-100mm of rain fell. Despite the flooding, 250 people managed to finish the race. Flooding was also reported to the north-east in Connecticut and Rhode Island, where up to 190mm of rain was recorded in a 36-hour period.

Even before the latest batch of alarming AI news, a lot of Americans were souring on AI. That may be for big, existential reasons — concerns about widening inequality, mass job loss, and the still-unclear environmental impact of data centers — or for very specific, personal, everyday ones, like being forced to use a worse version of Google search.
How to be an AI minimalist
It may feel like AI is creeping into every corner of your life. Here are ways to opt out.
None of this is to say that AI cannot be a useful tool for some people some of the time. It’s just that the untested technology was thrust upon millions of people who didn’t necessarily ask for it and really seem to not like it. More than twice as many Americans distrust AI as trust it, and a growing number of people think it will have a negative impact on productivity and economic growth, according to a recent survey by Gallup and the Special Competitive Studies Project. While about half of Americans now report using chatbots, a majority also think that AI will put their personal information at risk and nearly half think it will have a negative impact on society, according to a 2026 Pew study.
“It’s being forced on users, there’s no clear way to turn it off, and it feels like this unwelcome addition to their lives,” Rory Mir of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a nonprofit that defends digital privacy and free speech, told me. Mir told me. “It’s this kind of continued pattern of disrespect to users that I think is part of the pushback.”
If you want less AI in your life, opting out is not always easy. But there are things you can do to minimize your exposure.
There are ways to turn off AI features, although the process can be tedious. There are also steps you can take to prevent your data from being used to train AI models, though it’s difficult to keep all of your online data away from web scrapers.
I talked to five experts — including a computer scientist and a researcher studying AI resistance — who offered distinctive perspectives on what AI is doing to us, and who shared some simple and concrete steps you can take to push back against AI’s creep into our daily lives.
The AI that’s suddenly everywhere
In the early days, which were just a few years ago, you really had to know what you were doing if you wanted to test out AI. Now, it’s impossible to avoid.
“More and more AI use is through its integration into digital products like search, email, camera apps, and social media,” Arvind Narayanan, a computer science professor at Princeton University, told me. “It will become increasingly hard to strip these out unless one is willing to forgo digital products altogether.”
3 simple ways to engage with AI less
- Add “-ai” to Google searches to stop seeing the AI overview.
- Make your social media profiles private.
- Turn off Siri and opt out of Apple Intelligence.
What you’re specifically encountering is generative AI, and one of the most common types is a subset called large language models (LLMs), which ingest huge amounts of data and learn statistical patterns to predict and generate text. ChatGPT is powered by an LLM. The AI Overviews that sit on top of your Google search results come from an LLM. The grammar checker in your email app is likely powered by an LLM. Other subsets of generative AI include models that can produce images, video, audio, and software code.
The data that makes many of these tools work has been scraped from the open web, pirated books, and rare print books that are subsequently being destroyed. Everything from Wikipedia articles to YouTube videos has become training data for LLMs, and in order for the models themselves to get better, AI companies need more fresh data, which is in increasingly short supply. (Disclosure: Vox Media is one of several publishers that have signed partnership agreements with OpenAI. Our reporting remains editorially independent. Future Perfect is also funded in part by the BEMC Foundation, whose major funder was also an early investor in Anthropic; they don’t have any editorial input into our content.)
As a result, some of these companies are venturing into their users’ profiles to find more data. Meta, for example, sparked global outrage in 2024 when it informed some Facebook and Instagram users that it was using their public photos and text to train its AI models. Meta still does this. That your family photos or social media updates are being used to train AI to look and sound more human is, at the very least, very dehumanizing.
Generative AI, of course, is not the only type of AI that’s invisibly moving levers in your digital life. Recommendation algorithms are arguably even more inescapable. They power everything from Amazon to Netflix to Spotify and dictate what we buy, what we watch, and what we listen to. If you have trouble picking out an outfit in the morning, it might be because your brain is used to having algorithms around to help make decisions. This is also dehumanizing.
All of this — the existential risk, climate impact, the cognitive surrender — should be on your mind as you consider whether it’s worth enlisting these tools to write emails for you or to generate memes, according to Tania Duarte, founder of We and AI, a nonprofit focused on critical AI literacy.
“People are becoming increasingly aware of not just the impact on themselves but on the impact on the society they want to live in and the future that they want to have,” Duarte told me. “Is it worth all of that?”
How to minimize your AI exposure
If you’re reading this, you’re probably doing so on a smartphone or a computer. So let’s start with the assumption that you’d like to continue using devices like these.
If you’d like to minimize your exposure to AI, that presents a bit of a paradox. It’s seemingly impossible to use mainstream tech products without engaging with AI. But you can take steps to remove as much of it from your life as possible without going completely off the grid.
“You look for the spaces of agency rather than lamenting the fact that you can’t escape everything,” Dylan Orchard, a researcher at King’s College London who studies everyday resistances to AI, told me. “You can’t expect a perfect escape.”
Let’s start with the easiest options: You don’t have to use ChatGPT or Claude or Copilot. The same goes for Google Gemini and Apple Intelligence. If you’re happy with the way you access information online, save yourself the time. (Note: This will be much harder to do if you’re being required to use these tools at work or at school, so for the sake of this article, we’ll focus on the things you can control.)
Things get more complicated when you consider how your existing devices or software have recently been AI-ified. If you’re using an iPhone, for instance, you might be aware that the latest operating system comes with an updated version of Apple Intelligence, a layer of AI that does everything from summarize your notifications to power a new Siri. Earlier this year, Google launched its own version of this layer called Google Intelligence, which it says will make Android transition “from an operating system into an intelligence system.” The same push toward cramming AI into every corner is also happening on Windows 11, where Microsoft Copilot promises to be helpful.
If you were happy with your phone or laptop when it was slightly dumber, however, you can turn these features off. You can also opt out of other AI features built into your device’s operating system. Here’s a helpful guide that gets into the weeds of how to do it; it covers Apple Intelligence; Google Gemini, including AI Overviews and AI writing help in Gmail; Microsoft Copilot; Meta AI; and Samsung Galaxy AI. Turning off the AI features on Android devices is more complicated than flipping a single switch, but it can be done.
A lot of your AI exposure will happen in your web browser, though, so you should consider ways to bypass those features or switch browsers. Here’s another helpful guide that explains how to remove AI content from search results as well as AI features built into Chrome and other browsers, along with Microsoft Office. If you want a quick fix, adding “-ai” to a Google search should get rid of AI Overviews and some AI content in the search results, but none of these hacks will guarantee that you avoid AI slop altogether. Using a privacy-focused browser, like DuckDuckGo, might do a better job at it than Google, though.
When it comes to other online activities, like shopping or scrolling on social media, avoiding AI gets even harder. TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, and YouTube lack a master switch that lets you opt out of all the many AI features on offer. Still, you can try to tone down the algorithmic sorting that all the apps use to serve you content by switching to a chronological feed or removing suggested content from your feed. (Try tapping the Instagram logo in the app and then hit “Following” to see just the accounts you follow.)
Unfortunately, once you dig into the various user agreements and privacy policies, you’ll find that it’s very difficult to avoid AI exposure on social media platforms. If you’re posting publicly, you should assume your content is being used to train that company’s AI models. (You can keep some of your data away from Meta’s crawlers by setting your Facebook or Instagram account to private. X also allows you to opt out of having your data used for training its AI.) If you want to turn off video summaries on Instagram Reels, too bad. You can’t. If you want to turn off comment summaries on Facebook, you’ll have to go four menus deep in your settings to find the right switch. The most straightforward way to avoid being used as training data is to stop using these apps entirely. Or at least stop posting your own content, which is easier said than done, but worth considering if you really want to resist the AI takeover.
There’s a programming term that describes the inundation of AI features and slog of opting out: “user-hostile.” It’s a play on the term “user-friendly,” and it describes software that values the company’s priorities over the end users. You may love AI, although that’s doubtful if you’ve read this far. If it drives you crazy, though, you should feel at least a little bit empowered to know that there’s a way to reclaim the experience you had and loved without AI — or to use AI on your own terms.
“Ultimately, I think the important thing for folks to keep in mind is that AI is just a tool,” said Mir from EFF, “and it makes sense to want control over your own tools, including the option to not use a tool if it’s not right for you.”
It’s frustrating that we have to deal with this at all, if only because most of us did not ask for our cyber existences to be sullied by untested tech. But it’s actually refreshing to consider that, because of a never-ending onslaught of annoying features, AI might actually discourage us from using social media so much.
If anything, the extent to which we feel the need to flee from AI also reflects our craving for something real, that makes us feel more connected and more human. So when AI summaries interrupt your time on Instagram, consider texting your friends a handful of photos from your week or calling them on the phone. If you’ve finally seen one too many AI slop videos on TikTok, put on a classic movie or TV show.
At the very least, put down your phone and take a walk outside; your attention span will thank you for it. Yes, your individual rejection of AI might be a drop in the bucket for these huge tech companies, but that doesn’t mean it’s not worth doing anyway.

SpaceX targets September 28 for Starship's first orbital flight
It will also be the first time the company is adding V3 satellites to the Starlink constellation.
The next time SpaceX's Starship rocket launches, it will orbit our planet and add Starlink V3 satellites to the company's internet satellite constellation for the first time. SpaceX has now revealed that it's targeting September 28 for the rocket's 14th flight, with a 75-minute launch window opening at 8:15AM Eastern Time. The company was originally planning a September 22 launch, but it announced the new date without an explanation on X, where it also said that it's still pending regulatory approval.
Now targeting to launch Starship Flight 14 as early as Monday, September 28, pending regulatory approval https://t.co/3nG9wffG6A
— SpaceX (@SpaceX) September 17, 2026
Starship's previous flight tests have all been suborbital "to maximize public safety while allowing for maximum learning." SpaceX says this upcoming phase is the next step to prepare the vehicle for actual future flights and to ensure its reusability. During the test, Starship will fly 171 miles above our planet and will orbit Earth six times within the course of 10 hours.
The upper stage will also insert 26 Starlink V3 satellites into SpaceX's constellation. In Starship's previous test, the vehicle carried the next-gen satellites for the first time, just to make sure it's capable of doing so. Those satellites only extended their solar arrays and antennas to communicate with the rest of the Starlink constellation before burning up in our atmosphere. The satellites this flight will ferry to space will actually serve customers. Starlink V3 satellites can support 1 Tbps of downlink, 10 times more than what the V2 satellites are capable of, and 160 Gbps of uplink, representing an increase 22 times that of V2.
SpaceX won't be catching anything with the launch tower's arms this flight. Starship's Super Heavy booster will splash down into the Gulf of Mexico (renamed the Gulf of America in 2025 by President Donald Trump) a few minutes into the launch. The upper stage orbiting our planet will crash into the Pacific Ocean near Chile after it accomplishes its goal. You'll be able to watch the launch on SpaceX's X account.

Reporter’s notebook: Kazakhstan trip highlights promise and limits of Central Asia ties
It will soon be possible to fly direct from Hong Kong to Almaty, but in the meantime a little flexibility is required
When I began planning a work trip to Astana this month, the first challenge was simply finding a flight.
With no direct service from Hong Kong to the Kazakh capital, I could transfer in Guangzhou, Beijing, Urumqi or Seoul. I chose Guangzhou, which offered a direct flight lasting about seven and a half hours, but the limited schedule meant there was no flight on Saturday, forcing me to leave earlier than planned and spend five days in Astana.
The journey offered an early glimpse of both the promise and the limitations facing Hong Kong’s expanding relationship with Central Asia. Commercial interest is growing, but travel remains surprisingly complicated.

CNN, MS NOW say journalists denied access to White House grounds after Trump's ban
Politico also included in White House restrictions announced by U.S. president Friday
Two major news networks' journalists said they were denied access to the White House on Saturday morning, with reporters from CNN and MS NOW both going live to report about the circumstances of the ban imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump.
The actions escalated Trump's long-running efforts to restrict news coverage by journalists he finds objectionable and is the latest test of First Amendment protections in the United States. Trump said on Friday he would ban both organizations and Politico because of their coverage.
CNN issued a statement saying it stood behind its reporters. "We will not be deflected from our duty to hold the government and other public bodies to account," it said. The statement was shown on the air before senior White House reporter Betsy Klein began to report on her ban.
MS NOW, which until last November was called MSNBC, also said it stands behind its journalists.
"The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars," the network said in a statement on Saturday. "MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy."
Trump said on Friday that he was barring the news channel, along with CNN and Politico, from the White House due to what he called unfavourable coverage and "fake news."
Politico journalists are typically not at the White House on Saturdays.
MS NOW White House correspondent Akayla Gardner was turned away and her entry badge was confiscated, she said on air Saturday morning.
Gardner said she had walked through two gates successfully, but once she got to where her badge needed to be scanned, an officer told her it was disabled and asked her to hand it over. He said the decision "was above him," she reported.
An MS NOW producer was able to get in, but a photographer's badge was also disabled, Gardner said.
Trump calls news outlets 'fake news'
The president wrote on his social media site on Friday that effective immediately, "I am banning" CNN, MS NOW and Politico "from the White House as a result of their constant ‘reporting' FAKE NEWS!" Minutes later, speaking at an event in the Oval Office, Trump was asked to explain his statement.
"Because they're fake news," he said. "You get so tired of reading and seeing fake news. When you look at CNN, it's just fake. That's why their ratings are no good. When you look at MS NOW ... it's fake news.
"And when you look at Politico ... the stories they wrote are fake. So there's a lot of news and there may be others to join them, and maybe they can get better," he said. "But our country has to have honest news."
- 'Quiet, piggy': As Trump berates female reporters, what's the breaking point?
- Judge throws out Trump's $15B US lawsuit against the New York Times
In his second term, Trump and his administration have upped the ante and punished certain media outlets, both in the courtroom and through regulatory action. Trump has also lashed out at individual reporters in person or over social media, sometimes in strikingly personal terms.
The move follows the president's decision last year to bar Associated Press reporters from the Oval Office, Air Force One and other events in retaliation for the news outlet's decision not to follow his lead in changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico, which lies partially in Mexican and other waters.
The AP said that it would note when appropriate that Trump had ordered it renamed the "Gulf of America."

Whatever the true state of settlement talks this weekend between Paramount, a coalition of state Attorneys General and the Writers Guild of America to end the antitrust action over the $111 billion Warner Bros Discovery merger are, the people against the deal from the beginning are not going quietly.
“As Trump tries to ban CNN from the White House, it would be a massive mistake to cave on the Paramount merger,” Senator Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) said Saturday morning as the current WBD-owned cabler newser and MS Now journalists were denied access to the Executive Mansion. “The last thing we need is another Trump-controlled media conglomerate abusing its power to stomp out competition. This is a dangerous merger.”
Compared to Sen. Warren, the A-list supported Block the Merger is truly pissed off and feeling betrayed.
Watch on Deadline
“The rumored ‘deal’ to usher the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger forward is an insult to everyone who has stood up against this harmful transaction and to the hundreds of thousands of workers, journalists, and consumers who will be hurt if it goes forward,” the DC-based group told Deadline today of reported behind closed doors negotiations underway right now. “Let’s be very clear: an agreement based on unenforceable concessions is a win only for David Ellison. It is an L for everyone else.”
As leaks of talks between the AGs, led by California’s politically ambitious Rob Bonta, and the Ellison-run Paramount flooded the media late Friday, the possible L (loss) that BTM are spotlighting could include guardrails of CNN editorial independence, some selloffs, and job assurances. The hope down on Melrose is such a deal would render the March 2, 2027 trial start date currently on the calendar in federal court moot — and all the financial and political blast radius that comes with it for the Trump-friendly Ellisons.
To that, with massive job, production and tax revenue losses on the table, Paramount’s Plan B for the last eight weeks has been to pressure Bonta from all sides to make a deal ASAP. Two days of court-ordered settlement talks have already been set for mid-October, but that’s procedural in the judicial system and widely expected to go nowhere fast.
Also, mid-October doesn’t quite line up with Ellison’s balance sheet.
Looking at an October 1 date in which a $7 million a day ticking fee to WBD shareholders begins as well as a September 24 hearing on a Hail Mary desire for a $1.88 billion bond from the states and the very not flush WGA, Ellison’s crew have been leaking even more than ever threats to exit California for a red state.
Even as the likes of outgoing CA Governor Gavin Newsom acknowledged privately at the recent 78th Primetime Emmys that the Ellisons were being too heavy handed, the multi-pronged pressure campaign seems to have paid off. Whereas Bonta once accused Paramount of “blackmail” with its threats and theatrical promises, the reelection seeking AG now has his lieutenants in the room with Ellison’s execs.
The latest word on the wire is the parties could have an agreement before the official start of Yom Kippur this weekend.
Word is also out there that New York AG Letitia James isn’t as “in step,” according to a source, with Bonta as she previously was when it comes to burying the hatchet with Para. There is also the wildcard of the WGA, who joined the AGs’ July 13 filed suit after filing an anti-merger action of their own.
“This is such bullsh*t,” an industry insider told Deadline this morning of the talk of the ParaBros talks. “Bonta should have called their bluff, instead he caved,” she added, noting such tactics are typical of Democratic politicians in the MAGA era.
	The Bryan Cranston, Hannah Einbinder, Bradley Whitford, W. Kamau Bell, Kristen Vangsnesss, Jane Fonda and Rati Gupta, supported Block the Merger weren’t quite as blunt today in their statement, but the vibe was very much the same. 
“Thousands of industry leaders took a risk when they spoke out publicly about the harm the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger would cause,” the Noah Wyle, Denis Villeneuve, Atsuko Okatsuka, Damon Lindelof and Sophia Coppola back BTM said Saturday. “More than 75,000 people have now joined them to tell the state AGs to stand strong. So have national leaders like Sen. Elizabeth Warren. We know a bad deal when we see one. AG Bonta and his fellow state AGs should reject this deal, stand strong, and fully block the merger with no concessions.”
That mention of Sen. Warren may have greater significance this weekend that first apparent. Like everyone else, Paramount is keenly aware of what the polls are projecting going into November’s midterms. If the midterms actually occur and if the new Congress is actually seated (two big ifs in America right now), then a projected Democratic majority in the House and the Senate have promised to probe and even break-up mega-media mergers.
Even with Oracle founder Larry Ellison the primary backer of his son’s ParaBros dreams, the even older Ellison’s net worth, which has been declining of late, may not be able to handle the strain of months and months of such probes. So perhaps it is the first week of November, not October 1 that is the calendar date the younger Ellison is hoping to beat the clock on this weekend.
Paramount have been in “no comment” mode for weeks since the Melrose lot got burned on allegations they leaks details of past preliminary talks with Bonta’s gang. AG Bonta’s office did not respond Saturday to Deadline’s request for comment on Sen. Warren and Block the Merger’s opposition to the talks.

If there's one thing that can unite the world in these AI-troubled times, it's everyone's love of SUVs. For decades, the SUV has been the savior of the car world. Accounting for nearly half of all new sales worldwide, this is by some margin the largest segment in the global auto industry.
Sedans? Forget it. Ford doesn't even sell a traditional sedan in the US now. China still likes a sedan. About a third of all Chinese autos are in this form, compared with less than half that for the US. But Chinese carmakers know full well how much we love our chunky SUVs, so they are focusing their efforts to lure the Western world away from familiar marques.
Indeed, Xiaomi has just played its hand in this particular game, revealing the remaining details earlier this month in Beijing—including the all-important pricing—of its coming SkyNomad SUVs. Bentley and Range Rover may well have revealed their flagship electric SUVs, but both will be mightily worried about just how many scalps Xiaomi Auto's SkyNomad SUVs will take from them. If they're not, they should be.
Sedan to SUV
Trucks and SUVs represent more than 80 percent of new vehicle sales in America these days. Marc McGrath, US CEO of the automotive manufacturer Schaeffler Group, tells WIRED that one of the main reasons the company is developing its own solid-state batteries is to properly electrify the power-hungry trucks and SUVs Americans so dearly love. No one wants another F-150 Lightning U-turn.
The shocking success of the Jaecoo 7 is a prime example of SUV supremacy. This Chinese-made ride has enjoyed a staggeringly meteoric rise in the UK, going from an unknown newcomer in 2025 to now being one of the country’s best-selling new cars. Nicknamed the “Temu Range Rover,” it comes in both gas and hybrid flavors, and the company liberally uses the word “luxury” in its marketing, yet the vehicle costs just £29,210 (a little over $39,000).
These 7s are becoming ubiquitous on UK roads. My local Nissan dealer has swiftly dumped the Japanese brand and is now an official Jaecoo dealer, offering not just the 7, but the Jaecoo 5 and 8. I can't think of another auto brand that's enjoyed such a rapid rise.
Other Chinese brands are playing the same tactic in Europe, such as XPeng and BYD, but the big one incoming is Xiaomi Auto, set to launch in Europe in 2027, despite only making its first EV in 2024. Astonishingly, its SU7 Ultra claimed the title of “World’s Fastest Sedan” the very same year.
Far from a Temu pretender, the SkyNomad is not only tech-laden, it's also seemingly high-end, with seating that purports to be “more like an Italian sofa.” The SkyNomad N70 is a five-seater that, especially in its “Stealth Black Edition” guise, looks almost exactly like a Range Rover from the outside, and far more successfully than the Jaecoo.
The larger N90 is a seven-seater that also comes in a “Max Studio” camper version, complete with a pop-up roof. The second row can transform into a bed with one touch of a button—no disassembly, no mattress needed—just 30 seconds from upright seats to a flat, large bed.
The theme of reconfigurable interiors continues. A flat floor, courtesy of the Kunlun platform, comes with sliding rails built in from the front seats to the boot, meaning all (yes, all) the seat sections can move about. The front seats spin a full 180 degrees to face the second row; floor-mounted tables slot between the rows to make for “living-room-style" layouts; the center console can move forward or back at the press of a button; and rear legroom can max out at over 5 feet. In the N90 Max Studio, the pop-up roof lifts 100 mm to open a sleeping loft with 1.8 meters of headroom, along with heated flooring (!), a built-in projector, and a 30-inch projector screen.
An amazing optional extra for the SkyNomad is Xiaomi's version of in-brand car-to-car communications. Essentially, it's a walkie-talkie that runs on cellular network coverage rather than short-range radio, so it's marketed as having “unlimited range” and looks very similar to tech Xiaomi already ships in its phones.
Just stop for a minute and compare what you've just read with the sorts of interior innovations Western brands deliver on flagship models these days. Power doors, multi-point massage seats, relaxation programs with scent sprays, and a central console that moves maybe 10 cm are the typical cutting-edge fare. The SkyNomad makes US and European efforts look, frankly, lazy—right when they desperately need to stop their decline and show they can compete.
There's more. “Full scenario” voice control; customizable head-up display; lidar units, high-definition cameras, and Nvidia's Thor-U chip for level 2-plus autonomous control. A low-voltage power system apparently keeps “sentry mode” drain to under 5 kilometers of range overnight, so the onboard fridge running on 0.72 kWh a day can offer up to 24-hour continuous cooling.
The extended-range plug-in hybrid powertrain combines a 1.5-liter turbocharged internal combustion generator with battery packs and dual electric motors. This ICE engine never drives the wheels, but the SUV can charge from 20 to 80 percent in as little as 18 minutes for a 300-plus-mile electric-only range, or 1,000-mile combined range. Yes, these stats use China’s far more forgiving CLTC cycle, but this converts to about 700 miles using stricter US EPA standards.
Now to the clincher: the price. The maxed-out N90 Max Studio with its camper roof clocks in at RMB 299,900, about $44,700. The entry-level N70 Pro five-seat, rear-wheel-drive model with its movable “Italian sofa” seats, lidar, 14-speaker sound system including subwoofer and headrest speakers, and prodigious range is just RMB 209,900, or just over $31,000—about the same as a 2026 Hyundai Tucson.
Earlier this month, I asked a Western luxury auto CEO what he thought about Xiaomi Auto. He laughed. “They make vacuums, don't they?” he scoffed. I think he'll rue the day he said that. It reminds me of when, in a 2011 Bloomberg interview, Musk laughed when asked if he saw BYD as a competitor. Musk isn't laughing now. Make no mistake, Xiaomi is coming to clean up.

Iran has formally conveyed their conditions to Washington for ending the war, while warning that it is also prepared for a “decisive war”.
Iran’s supreme national security council secretary Mohsen Rezaei told Al Jazeera in an exclusive interview that Qatar had passed Tehran’s conditions to Washington and that Iran was awaiting US President Donald Trump’s response. “Our conditions are an end to the war on all fronts, the release of our frozen funds and an end to the naval blockade,” Rezaei said.
“It is in Washington’s interest to accept these conditions. Trump’s threats will not achieve any results. We are prepared for a decisive war,” he added.
Rezaei said Iran was also preparing for the possibility of another US strike, describing it as “very much on the cards”. He said Tehran had changed its military planning and was now focused on US naval assets across the Gulf, the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea.
He claimed Iran had recently test-fired a multi-warhead anti-ship missile near a US vessel or aircraft carrier and warned that any future Iranian response would include US bases and American commercial interests in the region.
At the same time, Rezaei said Tehran was pursuing diplomacy to bring the conflict to an end “as soon as possible”. Qatar and Pakistan have been involved in efforts to restart negotiations between Washington and Tehran after their earlier memorandum of understanding expired.
On the nuclear issue, Rezaei said Iran had not decided to withdraw from the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, although he warned that further sanctions or a referral of its nuclear file to the UN Security Council “may push Tehran into withdrawing”.
He also said Tehran remained open to an agreement with Oman over the Strait of Hormuz, saying the two sides had come within “a short step” of reaching a deal before it was shelved.
The comments come as Washington weighs its next move in the conflict. Trump told Axios this week that he was facing a “big decision” over whether to resume major military action against Iran.
“Do I want to go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not?” Trump said, adding: “Anything could happen with me.”

A large fire that broke out overnight at a seaside hotel and forced hundreds of people to evacuate is being treated by police as suspicious.
Emergency services were called just after 1am on Saturday to the Grand Burstin hotel in Folkestone, where a fire is believed to have started in the basement, Kent fire and rescue service said.
About 280 people were taken to safety and Folkestone and Hythe district council set up a welfare centre.
No injuries relating to the fire have been reported and inquiries into the cause of the fire are under way. Detectives from Kent police are also seeking dashcam footage and asking witnesses to come forward.
Twenty-six fire engines were dispatched to the seafront hotel, the fire service said. According to the Britannia Hotels website, the Grand Burstin overlooks Folkestone’s harbour and has 550 rooms.
Folkestone and Hythe district council posted on X: “A fire is currently ongoing at the Folkestone Grand Burstin hotel.
“We are operating a welfare centre at Three Hills Sports Park for people being evacuated from the site, where we are providing support to those affected.
“We are supporting all emergency services involved in the response and their efforts to get people to safety.
“Our advice to residents living nearby is to: close all windows and doors; avoid the area and do not attempt to approach the hotel; follow the instructions of emergency services; keep roads clear to allow emergency vehicles to access the area.”
Kent fire and rescue service said in an update: “Ten fire engines remain at the scene of a fire at the Grand Burstin hotel in The Harbour, Folkestone.
“Crews wearing breathing apparatus have worked hard to bring the fire under control and are now dampening down any remaining hotspots.
“It’s believed the fire started in the basement of the property, but the cause is not yet known.
“Around 280 people evacuated the building, and a welfare centre has been organised by Folkestone and Hythe district council. No fire-related injuries have been reported.”
A spokesperson for Kent police said: “Kent police was called at around 1.20am on Saturday 19 September 2026 to reports of a fire at a hotel on Marine Parade, Folkestone.
“Officers remain in attendance to assist traffic flow while our Kent fire and rescue service colleagues work to tackle the fire.”

Nestled between a turquoise-colored lake and the soaring peaks of the Austrian Alps, Plansee Group is building one of the West’s most formidable critical minerals operations outside China.
The closely held company, based in the town of Reutte, sells tungsten, a metal that attracts far less attention than rare earths but is no less vital to modern industry. The material’s exceptional hardness makes it ideal for tools that cut and shape car parts. Its resistance to heat is crucial to semiconductor manufacturing. And its extraordinary density, nearly twice that of lead, gives armor-piercing ammunition much of its penetrating power.
Few metals can match that versatility, but sourcing it comes with a familiar vulnerability: Beijing dominates the supply chain. A series of moves by China over the past two years — restricting exports, drawing in more raw material and, most recently, cutting off key shipments to Japan — has intensified a global scramble for tungsten. In turn, its cost has soared.

Two passengers including child, 7, fall critically ill on cruise ship heading to New Jersey
Royal Caribbean’s Oasis of the Seas will skip its planned Port Canaveral, Florida, stop Tuesday and spend the day at sea to get to the Bahamas
Two passengers, including a seven-year-old child, were evacuated from a Royal Caribbean cruise ship bound for New Jersey for emergency medical treatment in the Bahamas Friday.
The first medical emergency prompted the Oasis of the Seas’ to return toward Nassau because it was the closest location where the passenger could receive hospital treatment, according to a captain’s announcement reported by Cruise Hive. While the ship was heading back, a second passenger was also reported to be critically ill.
Both passengers were taken off the ship in Nassau on Friday for further medical treatment. Their conditions and the nature of their illnesses have not been disclosed, and it is unclear whether the emergencies were related.
The disruption also delayed the Oasis of the Seas’ next departure and forced Royal Caribbean to cancel a scheduled stop in Florida.
The ship is now expected to arrive at its home port at Cape Liberty in Bayonne, New Jersey, around 2 p.m. Sunday, instead of its originally scheduled 6 a.m. arrival, according to Cruise Hive.
A letter reportedly delivered to guests onboard and posted to Facebook explained the reason for the delay.
“As previously announced by our Captain, our medical staff determined that two of our guests needed urgent medical attention. We successfully debarked our guests so they could receive additional medical care,” the letter read.
“As a result, we’ll now be delayed in our return to Cape Liberty. We plan on arriving at approximately 2:00 pm, with debarkation starting around 2:30 pm. We appreciate your patience and understanding, knowing we’d do the same for you or a loved one in a similar situation.”
The delay is expected to create problems for passengers who have flights or other travel arrangements scheduled for Sunday.
Passengers who booked flights through Royal Caribbean’s Flights by Royal program will have their flights automatically adjusted to account for the later arrival, according to Cruise Hive. Those who booked flights independently will need to contact their airlines themselves.
Royal Caribbean said it will reimburse airline change fees of up to $200 per person for domestic flights and up to $400 for international flights, provided passengers submit the required receipts and documentation, according to the outlet.
The cruise line is also giving each stateroom 60 minutes of complimentary internet access to help passengers contact airlines, hotels, friends or family members, the outlet reports.
The disruption will carry over to the ship’s next seven-night Bahamas sailing, which is scheduled to depart from Cape Liberty on Sunday.

The story so far:
A Pakistan Navy vessel, PNS Hunain, collided with an Indian Navy warship, INS Kolkata, in the North Arabian Sea on September 15 after, according to India, the Pakistani ship made a dangerous overtaking manoeuvre at high speed. India summoned Pakistan’s Charge d’Affaires and cited violations of Article 10 of the 1991 India-Pakistan agreement, which requires naval vessels to maintain separation of three nautical miles. Pakistan rejected India’s allegations. INS Kolkata suffered no major damage and remains at sea. PNS Hunain was damaged and subsequently returned to harbour.
What are INS Kolkata and PNS Hunain?
The two vessels involved are different classes of warships. INS Kolkata is the lead ship of the Indian Navy’s Project 15A Kolkata-class guided missile destroyers. Built by Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders in Mumbai, the 164-metre-long warship has a full-load displacement of about 7,400 tonnes and is capable of sailing at 30-knot speed. It was commissioned into the Indian Navy in August 2014. INS Kolkata is designed primarily as a high-end surface combatant, with long-range air-defence, anti-surface, and anti-submarine capabilities. The class is equipped to operate helicopters and carries the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile as its principal anti-surface strike weapon.
PNS Hunain (F-273) is an offshore patrol vessel. It was built by Damen Shipyards in Romania and commissioned in July 2024. It is the first of Pakistan’s larger OPV 2600-based follow-on vessels to the Yarmook-class patrol ships. Damen says the OPV 2600 design is intended for maritime security and military operations, including sustained operations in contested environments. It is approximately 98 metres long, has a displacement of about 2,600 tonnes, and is capable of speeds of up to about 24 knots. Its role includes maritime surveillance, patrol and security missions. Pakistan describes the vessel as a multi-purpose platform equipped with electronic-warfare, anti-ship and anti-air warfare capabilities, as well as self-protection and terminal defence systems. It can also embark a multirole helicopter.
What does India say happened?
According to the Indian account, INS Kolkata was conducting routine surveillance when PNS Hunain approached at high speed and manoeuvred dangerously close to the Indian ship. On September 18, a spokesperson of the Ministry of External Affairs said India had examined Pakistan’s response to the diplomatic protest and rejected its allegations. He said the Pakistani ship had conducted a “dangerous overtaking manoeuvre” that resulted in the collision.
India has maintained that the manoeuvre violated both the 1991 bilateral agreement and the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea. The Ministry said INS Kolkata suffered no major damage and remained deployed at sea.
Pakistan has given a different account, alleging that the Indian warship carried out a provocative manoeuvre during the encounter. The precise sequence of movements immediately before the collision therefore remains disputed.
What is Article 10 of the 1991 India-Pakistan agreement?
Article 10 of the Agreement between India and Pakistan on Advance Notice on Military Exercises, Manoeuvres and Troop Movements, signed on April 6, 1991, lays down a specific maritime safety provision. It states that naval ships and submarines of the two countries should not approach within three nautical miles of each other while operating in international waters, “so as to avoid any accident.” Three nautical miles is about 5.6 km.
The provision is part of a broader military confidence-building framework intended to reduce the risk of miscalculation between the two countries. It is a bilateral requirement, not a universal international maritime rule applicable to warships of all countries.
Has this happened before?
The September 2026 incident is the second reported India-Pakistan naval collision involving the 1991 framework. In June 2011, Pakistani warship PNS Babur came close to Indian Navy frigate INS Godavari during anti-piracy operations in the Gulf of Aden, causing minor damage. India lodged a protest, citing navigational-safety violations.
What happens next?
India has summoned Pakistan’s Chargé d’Affaires in New Delhi and lodged a strong protest. It has also instructed its Charge d’Affaires in Islamabad to raise the matter with Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry.
New Delhi has advised Pakistan to ensure that its military units exercise due care and comply with relevant bilateral agreements to prevent a recurrence. The fact that the collision occurred in international waters does not place the two navies outside agreed rules of conduct.
For now, the key unresolved question is the exact sequence of manoeuvres that brought the two vessels into close proximity.
