Attackers sought Mahendra Karma before killing him
One witness said the attackers repeatedly asked, “Where is Karma?” Karma eventually surrendered and identified himself. According to the order, he was taken towards the hill, shot and attacked with sharp-edged weapons. Medical evidence corroborated injuries to his body.
The evidence also showed that Patel and his son Dinesh were taken towards the hill after Patel identified himself as the state Congress president, and subsequently killed. The court rejected the defence argument that the accused had assisted Maoists out of fear. It held they had actively participated in the conspiracy.

Investigation launched after beheaded sea lion is found along San Francisco shore
Tampering with the carcass of a dead marine mammal is a federal crime carrying penalties of up to $36,000 in fines and a year in prison
Police are investigating after a sea lion was found beheaded on San Francisco’s Ocean Beach, according to local reports.
Wildlife experts believe the animal was decapitated after it had already died.
"Maybe the person who did this didn't know that it was illegal, or maybe they did," Sue Pemberton of the California Academy of Sciences told ABC 7 San Francisco.
She said that sometimes the “legality of it doesn’t really stop people.”
“I don't really know what this person was thinking, but people might collect them for the novelty of having a trophy of some sort," she said.
It's not the first time something like this has happened. Another sea lion was found without its head further down the coast on a beach in Pacific Grove last year, according to SFist.
The individual involved in that incident reportedly tried to carry the head away in a Ziploc bag.
Officials said that interfering with the carcasses of marine mammals is a federal offense carrying serious penalties.
Under the Marine Mammal Protection Act, taking parts from a sea lion carcass is illegal and can be punished with up to $36,000 in fines and a year in prison.
Beachgoers who encounter a dead or stranded marine mammal are urged to leave it alone and report the sighting to local wildlife officials or the Marine Mammal Stranding Network.

Oil tankers crossing the Strait of Hormuz are now earning even more than $1 million a day, as the Iran war has increased the risks and the urgency of moving crude through the key shipping chokepoint. The cost of hiring a large crude carrier to transport oil from the Persian Gulf to China, which must pass through the Strait of Hormuz, reached $1.035 million per day this week, according to Baltic Exchange data cited by Fortune. In fact, for the first time, the rate has crossed the $1 million mark. Before the war, a similar transportation cost about $208,000 per day, based on the Platts VLCC index. The price pressure comes as commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has significantly decreased, with the US-Iran war now in its seventh month. Meanwhile, the need to move oil out of the Gulf has increased as restricted supplies have pushed crude prices above $100 a barrel again. “It’s all about risk,” said Ioannis Papadimitriou, principal freight analyst at Vortexa, told Fortune. This risk factor has become a major reason for the rise in the shipping bill. On Friday, two tankers were hit by projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz, underscoring that commercial vessels remain the primary targets of attacks. Insurance costs have also surged. Premiums for vessels have risen to about 10% of the assets aboard, compared with around 0.5% to 1% before the war, Papadimitriou told Fortune. These higher costs are now being passed on to the charterers. Fewer vessels willing to cross the more disrupted eastern side of the strait have further tightened shipping capacity. At the same time, some maritime companies are expanding their fleets to secure cargo deliveries and strengthen their position in the supply chain. The higher freight bill is ultimately being felt by refiners. They face not only more expensive shipping but also higher crude costs, while alternative routes can take longer. The pressure on refinery margins can then feed through to consumers. Fortune cited diesel prices crossing $6 for the first time, about 60% higher than before the war in Iran. Shipping companies, meanwhile, are benefiting from the extraordinary rates. Jagtar Singh Johal granted bail nine years after being detained in India
- Published
A Scottish Sikh activist who has been locked up in India for almost nine years without conviction has been granted bail.
Jagtar Singh Johal, from Dumbarton, was arrested and detained in 2017 in connection with alleged terror offences.
The Indian authorities have accused him of having a role in a series of targeted killings of religious and political figures.
His family said they were still waiting for the details of what will happen next but are "relieved" by the Indian court's decision.
Court documents show Johal was granted bail at Delhi High Court.
As part of his bail conditions, he has to surrender his passport and is barred from speaking to the media about the case.
He must pay a personal bond of 500,000 rupees (£3,907) and is only allowed to access one phone.
The 39-year-old was acquitted last year in a case in which he was accused of financially supporting terror group the Khalistan Liberation Force (KLF), which has carried out attacks in the Punjab region.
But he still faces federal charges lodged by the Indian authorities.
Johal's imprisonment was recognised by a UN panel as arbitrary detention in 2022 and he has claimed to have been tortured.
Indian authorities have previously denied the torture claim and have repeatedly maintained due process is being followed.
He was arrested in the Punjab region just weeks after his wedding in the country.
His supporters say he was targeted for blogging about alleged human rights abuses against the Sikh community in India and was coerced into signing a false confession to participation in the killings.
His brother Gurpreet Singh Johal has lobbied successive governments calling for his brother's release.
"It is a really important milestone for Jagtar's campaign," Gurpreet told the BBC's Radio Scotland Breakfast programme.
"It has been a long haul and an expensive rollercoaster but the community and the public have kept me going to campaign to bring Jagtar home.
"This will be a huge relief for him."
He added that while it is a major step and the family are relieved Jagtar can be at liberty, more work will be required to bring his brother back to Dumbarton.
"It is a momentous moment for the family, his wife has been crying since this morning," Gurpreet added.
"Everyone was joyful, my kids went to school saying they cannot wait to see their uncle coming home.
"It is just a first step, but it is a step in the right direction."
Gupreet previously urged the UK government to provide "diplomatic representation" to bring his activist brother home.
He described his last meeting, with then-Foreign secretary Yvette Cooper in December, as "disappointing".
At the time, a spokesperson for the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office said concerns about Johal's "prolonged detention" were raised with the Indian government at every appropriate opportunity.
Johal was previously denied bail in 2024.
Johal's family have insisted that no concrete evidence has been presented against him.
They say the case was built on the testimony of unreliable witnesses, some of whom have given statements against him only for them to be later recanted in court.
'Flawed proceedings'
First Minister John Swinney said it was a "significant and positive development".
"I hope to see Mr Johal released from custody as soon as the necessary procedures are completed and continue to underline the importance of a fair, transparent and timely judicial process," he added.
Johal is represented in the UK by the legal charities Redress and Reprieve, which have welcomed the judgement.
Reprieve's deputy executive director Dan Dolan said the news was welcome but Johal still faces the death penalty for "trumped up charges".
He said: "We must now watch closely to ensure this order is actually implemented and not obstructed in any way.
"The conditions attached are likely to be onerous."
Redress senior legal advisor Chris Esdaile said granting bail "can't undo the intolerable suffering caused by nine years of arbitrary detention".
He added: "The need for accountability for the allegations of torture and the deeply flawed proceedings against Jagtar remains urgent."

If you haven't booked your holiday flights yet, you may want to brace your wallet: Airlines are cutting options and potentially raising fares as oil prices reach new highs.
After surging in the spring following the start of the war in Iran, oil prices surged yet again this summer and surpassed $100 a barrel this month; jet fuel is $4.53 a gallon as of Thursday. Data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics' latest consumer price index show airfares rose more than 23% year-over-year in August.
Speaking at Morgan Stanley's Laguna Conference on Wednesday, major airline executives said they are cutting flights planned this holiday season and are likely to raise fares to offset oil spikes.
Mike Leskinen, CFO of United Airlines, said the company is seeing strong demand and that its customers are "incredibly, incredibly resilient," but United has already cut some routes that are on the low end of profitability and "don't make sense in a higher fuel environment."
"As you look into the fourth quarter, there'll be some flights in December that we won't fly that we thought we were going to fly," Leskinen said. "If fuel remains high, we'll make some adjustments into the first quarter and beyond into 2027."
Southwest Airlines CFO Tom Doxey and American Airlines CFO Devon May similarly said demand is strong and that if high fuel prices persist, they would trim capacity and raise fares in response.
However, the airline CFOs said it takes time for those increases to show up: "Jet fuel price gets passed through with a lag," Leskinen said. "Period."
Doxey said that "both from the booking curve and just kind of a natural lag, it takes a while for that to come," but Southwest has the "ability to recover a good portion" of those added costs.
Sally French, a travel analyst at NerdWallet, said that, beyond high airfares, airlines have also increased checked-bag and seat-selection fees. "The true cost of flying is higher than ever," she said.
What flight cuts could mean for travelers
It's unclear which specific flights and routes will be axed and how the airlines will rebook those affected. When trimming schedules, airlines have historically looked for markets that are already oversaturated, flights on less-busy travel days like Saturday, and flights that depart at less desirable times and may have lower demand.
Considering the record demand for premium travel, it's also possible airlines will focus resources on more business-heavy markets with strong corporate demand, especially long-haul international routes.
Several airlines are banking on their affluent customers continuing to book as they have grown desensitized to the volatility.
Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian said in an April earnings call that "as difficult as it is to see what's going on with the conflict in the Middle East, I'm not sure that our premium customers are feeling affected by that."
Another wrinkle for travelers looking for affordable flights is that this year marks the first holiday season without Spirit Airlines, which shut down in May, taking its famously low fares off the table.
"Generally speaking, booking now to lock in a good price is best practice, particularly if we're talking winter travel," French said. "That sweet spot window for booking domestic travel is 1-3 months in advance, or 2-8 months for international travel."
She added that booking refundable fares that you can cancel and rebook if prices drop is also a smart move.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

White House tries to take credit for Wendy’s switching back to a classic look
Wendy’s has revived its iconic yellow fry boxes and Frosty cups as customers yearn for the comforts of their 90s childhood
The White House has tried to take credit for Wendy’s switching back to a classic look, but social media users aren’t buying it.
Wendy’s announced this week that it was kicking it old school with its iconic yellow packaging, tapping into a wave of 90s nostalgia as millennials and Gen Z seek childhood comforts.
When the fast-food joint first opened in Columbus, Ohio, in 1969, it used yellow cups and boxes to serve nuggets, fries and its signature Frostys. Over time, Wendy’s got rid of the yellow packaging for its now-familiar red and white boxes and cups.
Now, the yellow packaging is back at Wendy’s for a limited time, and if you ask the White House, it’s all thanks to President Donald Trump, a known lover of rival fast-food joint McDonald's.
In response to an X post about Wendy’s yellow packaging comeback, the White House account wrote on Thursday, “Thank you, President Trump!!!!!”
But people in the comment section either couldn’t see how Trump could have a hand in the decision or mocked him for claiming a fast-food refresh as one of his accomplishments.
“Trump has nothing to do with that. What are you smoking? You should say ‘Thank you, [Wendy’s founder] Dave [Thomas]’ and thank the customers who demanded it back,” one X user said.
Another wrote: “The level of delusion actually scares me.”
“Imagine having so few actual wins that you have to fabricate fake ones about fast food,” a third posted.
Wendy’s, meanwhile, said the reason for the switch-up was that its customers have been begging for it.
“Fans have been asking for its return for years, making it one of the most requested comebacks in Wendy’s history,” a company spokesperson told TODAY.com. “Yellow has been part of Wendy’s since the very beginning and is something many fans instantly recognize.”
The yellow packaging will return on September 28 and continue into 2027, Wendy’s told USA TODAY.
When asked by The Independent to clarify what it meant by its comment thanking Trump for the yellow packaging revival, the White House just said: “America is back!”
People on X also took issue with White House’s post, given that Americans are struggling to afford basic necessities, with even something once considered cheap, like fast food, hitting their wallets hard.
The cost of food was up 2.7 percent in August from the year before, according to the federal government’s Consumer Price Index. The cost of energy has skyrocketed during Trump’s Iran war, rising 16.3 percent in August from the previous year.
“Nobody can afford it, but thank you President Trump!” one person wrote.
Another said: “Anything on gas, grocery, rent or electricity prices there President Trump?”
“Hey we want affordable gas and groceries, not iconic fast food,” one person wrote.
Wendy’s move to bring back its nostalgic yellow packaging came after one of its largest franchise operators filed for bankruptcy.
Meritage Hospitality Group Inc., a major restaurant operator based in Grand Rapids, Michigan, that runs more than 300 Wendy’s restaurants, announced the decision Thursday.
“The filing follows a candid assessment of the financial pressures facing the Company, including the sustained system-wide headwinds affecting the broader Wendy’s brand over the past few years,” the company wrote in a news release. “The Company has a high level of confidence in the opportunity for a brand turnaround.”

6 people injured after vehicle strikes pedestrians at Festival Western de Saint-Tite
A criminal investigation is underway
Quebec provincial police are investigating after six people were injured after they were struck by a vehicle on the site of the Festival Western de Saint-Tite early Saturday morning.
Police say a collision between a vehicle and pedestrians took place on Saint-Joseph Boulevard in Saint-Tite, about 200 kilometres northeast of Montreal.
Witnesses say police arrived on scene around 4:30 a.m.
The vehicle fled the scene, according to the Sûreté du Québec. It was later found in the Quebec City region around 5:30 a.m.
A man in his 20s was arrested by police and is being questioned by investigators.
The victims were transported to hospital with various injuries, none of which were life threatening, police confirmed later Saturday.
The town is hosting the popular Festival Western de St-Tite and three Quebec political leaders are expected on site today as part of their respective campaigns.
Festival officials say Saturday's activities will go ahead as planned.
"An isolated incident beyond our control occurred early this morning on Saint-Joseph Boulevard. Our thoughts are with those involved and their families. We wish them a speedy recovery," the organizers said in a statement.
"The safety of our festival-goers, volunteers, and staff remains our top priority. The Festival is a festive event where everyone should feel safe. That's why every effort is being made to ensure this."
Police say Saint-Joseph Boulevard will remain closed to vehicle traffic between Du Couvent and Moulin Streets for most of Saturday as investigators and technicians work on the scene.
Quebec leaders react
The early morning incident took place as three Quebec party leaders were expected to attend the festival. The Quebec Liberals (PLQ), Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) and the Parti Québécois (PQ) all had stops planned for Saturday.
CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette posted her condolences to the victims on X.
“My thoughts are with the victims, their loved ones, and all those affected by the events that took place at the Western Festival in St-Tite. The ongoing investigation will determine the causes of this act,” Fréchette said.
PQ Leader Pierre St-Pierre Plamondon also offered his condolences.
“My thoughts are with the injured individuals, their loved ones, and all those who witnessed the distressing scene in Saint-Tite.,” St-Pierre Plamondon wrote on X.
"Thank you to the first responders who acted quickly. Quebecers should be able to enjoy places where they can gather and celebrate safely."

US and Denmark reach deal over Greenland's security
- Published
The US and Denmark have announced a deal on Greenland's security and say the agreement will be signed next week.
US President Donald Trump said the agreement would grant the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs".
Denmark's Prime Minister said the deal "strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" but did not address specifics in the agreement that Trump mentioned in a social media post.
The deal comes after months of threats by Trump to "take" Greenland over national security concerns, citing its strategic location for defence purposes and its mineral wealth.
Trump, in a post on Truth Social, said the deal comes with "no cost to the United States" and will grant the US the ability to "to do what is necessary" to "secure and defend the security of Greenland".
He said the deal includes a rule that no US adversary can maintain a military presence in Greenland or "make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval".
Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen confirmed that the agreement will be signed at the United Nations General Assembly next week.
He said the agreement "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also "at the same time recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination".
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called it a "historic deal" and a "huge win for the United States and the American people".
"This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland," he told Fox News.

Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) ordered the state government to take steps that could empower local communities to have a larger say in data center development and slow down approvals in a state that is already home to the data center capital of the world.
Virginia governor creates an AI task force and moves to restrain data centers
Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D) signed an executive order addressing data canters and AI risks.
Executive Order 22 bans executive branch officials from signing non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) for data center projects, requires expedited noise regulations, and a review of backup-generation operations used by data centers, among other requirements. The order also establishes an AI task force responsible for evaluating how the state government can address risks to Virginians like workforce displacement and data privacy issues, and determining how existing law can be applied to AI harms.
The order represents the latest signal that states are taking data center and AI policy into their own hands as Congress and President Donald Trump have been slow or resistant to sweeping changes. Also on Friday, California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) issued an executive order convening experts to tackle AI safety issues, and earlier, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) have both taken executive action to rein in rapid data center development.
In addition to Virginia’s new executive order, Spanberger unveiled a new “Data Center Accountability Framework” for the state, which lays out additional priorities. These include eliminating “by-right approval,” like the kind that existed in Loudoun County for many years allowing developers to build on certain land without additional approvals, removing some state subsidies, establishing environmental guardrails, and safeguarding residents against increased energy prices that are associated with data centers.
A press release for the actions includes many statements from environmental groups praising Spanberger’s approach, but others reportedly wish she’d gone even further. Piedmont Environment Council (PEC), for example, is a nonprofit that has advocated for a moratorium on new development to deal with existing concerns, and PEC president Chris Miller said in a statement that “It largely addresses standards on new data centers and does not deal with what’s already built and in the pipeline, along with the ongoing impacts piling up in communities now.”

Gurugram-based test-prep major Aakash Educational Services Ltd (AESL) managed to narrow its net loss for the financial year FY26 by 15.5% to ₹186.5 Cr from ₹220.8 Cr loss incurred in the previous fiscal. The improvement in the bottom line came despite flat top line performance in the fiscal. Operating revenue rose marginally by 0.4% to ₹2,040.5 Cr in FY26 from ₹2,032.1 Cr in the previous year. While coaching revenue — the core business — inched up 0.3% YoY to ₹1,956.2 Cr, franchisee revenue grew 4% to ₹84.4 Cr. The real swing factor came with revenue registered from non-operating income, with other income more than doubled to ₹113.7 Cr. This was driven largely by a ₹76.1 Cr write-back of provisions or liabilities alongside a ₹19.7 Cr gain from remeasurement of lease liabilities. Including other income, total income rose 3.3% to ₹2,154.3 Cr in the year under review from ₹2,085.1 Cr in FY25. Aakash is one of India's largest test-prep brands for engineering and medical entrance exams and has been operating under the ownership of BYJU’S parent Think & Learn since its 2021 acquisition — a deal that has since been entangled in the broader financial and legal troubles at the BYJU’S group. As of September, Byju Raveendran proposed relinquishing his claimed beneficial interest in 17.89 Mn shares of Aakash Educational Services to settle Qatar Holding’s arbitration claim of more than $235 Mn against him. The latest proposal further places Aakash at the centre of overlapping disputes over ownership, creditor recoveries, and the future of BYJU’S, which once commanded a valuation of $22 Bn. Creditors have been separately exploring a broader settlement centred around Aakash as it remains the most valuable surviving asset within the collapsing edtech. Global TLB lenders, represented by GLAS Trust, are said to be in advanced talks to acquire a 30% stake in Aakash Educational Services, valuing the coaching chain at around $2 Bn. Zooming Into Aakash's FY26 Expenses Total expenses were largely flat, up almost 1% to ₹2,397.8 Cr in FY26 from ₹2,378 Cr in the previous year. As a result, loss before exceptional items and tax narrowed nearly 17% YoY to ₹243.5 Cr from ₹292.9 Cr. However, a ₹23.3 Cr exceptional charge widened this to a pre-tax loss of ₹266.8 Cr — still 8.9% narrower than FY25's ₹292.9 Cr. A deferred tax credit gain of ₹80.3 Cr brought the final loss after tax down to ₹186.5 Cr. Here is a more closer look at where AESL spent the most in the reported year: Employee Benefits Expense: Aakash’s single largest expense declined 2.4% to ₹1,299.6 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹1,331.5 Cr in FY25. Depreciation And Amortisation Expense: Spending under this head declined 4.4% to ₹234.8 Cr in FY26 from ₹245.6 Cr a year ago. Advertisement And Publicity: The company’s promotional expenses fell 6.9% to ₹145.7 Cr in the year under review from ₹156.5 Cr in FY25.

SIT probes fake freedom fighter certificates used for MBBS admissions in Uttarakhand
Dehradun police's SIT has begun probing fake freedom fighter dependent certificates used in Uttarakhand MBBS admissions. The case has raised wider questions over domicile and quota documents as counselling continues.
A Special Investigation Team of the Dehradun police has begun investigating the alleged use of fake freedom fighter dependent certificates for MBBS admissions in Uttarakhand, with cases also registered at two police stations.
The matter has gained urgency as the medical admission and counselling process is currently underway in the state, and Medical Education Minister Subodh Uniyal has asked the Dehradun district magistrate to submit an inquiry report within a week.
The issue was raised by journalist Pradeep Bahuguna, who has now sought a wider investigation into permanent residence, domicile and other certificates used in medical admissions. He has submitted a list of around 350 candidates for verification, while the administration has also sealed four CSC centres and seized some computers and laptops after irregularities were found.
SP (Rural) Jaya Baluni said documents related to the admissions where the alleged use of fake freedom fighter dependent certificates came to light have been sought from the officials and departments concerned. Asked whether an organised gang could be involved, she said the investigation is at an early stage and it would be "premature to draw any such conclusion".
On demands for a probe into alleged fake domicile certificates, she said the two FIRs currently registered relate to the alleged fraud involving freedom fighter dependent certificates and the admissions secured through them, and that the SIT is investigating this specific aspect.
Bahuguna said that during scrutiny of certificates for dependents of freedom fighters, questions also emerged over the domicile documents of some candidates. He alleged that while FIRs had been registered in connection with the freedom fighter dependent certificates, no separate investigation or action had been taken over the alleged use of fake domicile certificates.
He said domicile is a key requirement for MBBS seats under the state quota, and benefits under reserved categories and sub-categories are available only when the required eligibility conditions are met.
Citing another case, Bahuguna alleged that a candidate named Saumya was first allotted a seat under the SC-Orphaned category at Doon Medical College in Dehradun.
According to him, her admission there could not go through after her caste certificate was later cancelled at the Doiwala tehsil level, and she was subsequently allotted a seat under the General-Orphaned category in Haldwani.
Questioning both the allotment process and the candidate's eligibility, he demanded an inquiry into the case.
Bahuguna met Uniyal on Friday and submitted a list of about 350 candidates, seeking detailed verification of their certificates.
He said he was not claiming that all the certificates on the list were fake, but that the available records and admission-related information raised enough suspicion to require official scrutiny.
Uniyal said the government was taking the matter seriously and, suspecting the involvement of a major racket, had directed the district magistrate to carry out an inquiry and file a report within a week.
The minister also said instructions had been issued to complete the investigation quickly so that the status of suspicious cases could be clarified before the admission process ends.
Explaining why he sought scrutiny of 350 candidates, Bahuguna said many of them had completed their high school and intermediate education outside Uttarakhand, while some had even taken the NEET examination in Bihar, West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh. He added, however, that studying in another state or taking NEET elsewhere does not by itself prove a certificate is forged.
"I am not saying that the certificates of all these individuals are fake. But an investigation into their documents is essential. I have identified around 350 names, and it is possible that the actual number of such cases is higher," he said. He also called for an inquiry into whether permanent residence and other certificates used to claim state quota or special category status were issued according to the rules.
Bahuguna further claimed that in one case, the online application status showed as pending even though the candidate had already been allotted a medical seat. These claims have not yet been independently verified.
He said his initial inquiry had raised questions over four dependent-of-a-freedom-fighter certificates linked to the same family, and that after a complaint, officials verified them and cancelled the certificates after finding them forged.
He said the investigation should not remain limited to a few reported cases and should be expanded, including examining the possibility of an organised network.
On the district magistrate's instructions, authorities sealed four CSC centres after irregularities were detected and seized some computers and laptops. According to the administration, the action followed findings related to the centres' functioning and compliance with rules.
Rohit Negi, a CSC operator in Dehradun, told PTI that a CSC's role is generally limited to filling in online applications and uploading documents to the portal. After that, he said, the application moves through the government system and, in cases such as permanent residence certificates, the document is issued only after verification at the tehsil level or by revenue officials or the patwari, and with the approval of the competent authority.
In the wake of the complaints, the role of officials responsible for verification and approval is also being questioned.
Uniyal said the matter came to his notice while he was in Australia and that he issued directions from there to the concerned district magistrate to investigate it. According to him, the initial inquiry found that some certificates were fake, and complaints about permanent residence certificates had also been received.
At present, the SIT is examining the alleged fake freedom fighter dependent certificates, while demands for a wider probe into other documents used in medical admissions continue.

Trump says he is banning media outlets CNN, MS NOW, Politico from White House

In late summer 2026, social media posts claimed that new laws had gone into effect requiring all car drivers and passengers below a certain height to use a booster seat, regardless of their age.
The details changed from post to post (archived), and varied from state to state, but the most common version of the rumor suggested the law applies to anyone under 5 feet, 2 inches in height.
(Facebook)
Snopes readers contacted us looking for more information about the variety of claims.
In short, all the similar rumors are false. No such laws have been passed or are set to come into effect anywhere in the United States.
Searches on DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo uncovered no news reports or evidence about the supposed changes. Reputable local news media outlets would have covered such a story if any of them were true.
It was not possible to definitively determine the origin of the claims. They appeared to be part of a series of AI-generated images promoting new, fictitious state laws. AI-generated fake laws have become a relatively common "template" of rumor that circulates on social media. Snopes has debunked several examples over the past year.
However, the posts spreading the booster seat claim include a second type of image — also AI-generated — of an adult woman sitting in a car seat. Investigating those alleged photos revealed numerous signs they were AI-generated.
For example, one image (shown below) includes a strange white artifact in the center of the harness-style buckle 
(Facebook user Kelsey Biggs)
In addition, Facebook, the platform where most examples of the claim were posted, had labeled the above image and several others as AI-generated content. Running the images through other generative AI detection tools supported this. (Let us note: these tools are fallible, and we recommend using them only as supporting evidence).
Investigating the laws around child-safe car seats and booster seats in each U.S. state and territory led to several sites that contain lists of all car seat, booster seat and seatbelt laws, as of this writing. The laws all specifically mention children, and many designate their requirements based on a combination of age, height and weight. When limitations based on height and weight are included, they tend to be set at for children under 80 pounds and shorter than 4 feet, 9 inches, several inches below the limits suggested by the fictitious laws. None of the authentic laws mention adults under 5 feet, 2 inches being mandated to ride or drive in booster seats.

The Union Health Ministry has asked States and Union Territories to ensure that stem cell therapy is offered as standard clinical care only for disease conditions and indications approved by the Ministry, with its use for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) restricted to duly approved clinical trials.
In an advisory issued on September 16, the Ministry reiterated the existing regulatory framework governing stem cell research and therapy. The advisory was issued to States and Union Territories that have adopted the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010, following a January 30, 2026, judgment of the Supreme Court in Yash Charitable Trust & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors.
For ASD, the Ministry said therapeutic use of any type of stem cell must remain confined to duly approved clinical trials in accordance with the National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017, issued by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) and the Department of Biotechnology.
Stem cell interventions that have not been approved for routine clinical use, including those offered for autism, should not be provided as routine, standard or commercial clinical services, the advisory said.
The move comes against the backdrop of the continuing use of stem-cell interventions for autism despite the lack of established evidence supporting them as a standard treatment. An ICMR review has said that available evidence does not support stem cell therapy over behavioural and supportive therapies for ASD and recommended that such therapy be restricted to approved clinical trials.
The Ministry has asked States and Union Territories to disseminate the Supreme Court’s directions to State and district regulatory authorities as well as government and private clinical establishments involved in stem cell research, treatment, promotion or administration.
The advisory also draws attention to the consequences of non-compliance. The Supreme Court, in its January judgment, said violations of the statutory framework could attract consequences including professional misconduct under Regulation 7.22 of the erstwhile Indian Medical Council Regulations, 2002, as well as action under Sections 32 and 40 of the Clinical Establishments Act, including cancellation of registration and penalties.
The National Medical Commission (NMC), in an advisory issued on September 5, has separately reiterated that stem cell therapy may be offered as standard clinical care only for approved indications. It said unauthorised administration, prescription, promotion or advertisement of stem cell therapy beyond approved indications would constitute professional misconduct.
The NMC has asked State Medical Councils to examine allegations of violations and, where professional misconduct by a registered medical practitioner is established after due process, take disciplinary action under the applicable provisions.

Union minister's fiery response to Guna resident goes viral, Congress reacts
NEW DELHI: A video showing Union minister Jyotiraditya M Scindia in a sharp exchange with a resident over a long-pending road in Guna, Madhya Pradesh, has gone viral on social media, with the Congress sharing the clip and accusing the minister of showing “arrogance of power”.The exchange took place after local residents stopped Scindia’s convoy during his visit and raised concerns over the delayed road work. Residents carrying placards also raised the slogan “Road nahi to vote nahi” (No road, no vote), prompting a tense exchange between the minister and one of the residents.In the video, the resident urges Scindia to ensure the road is completed before the next election and warns that people would otherwise not vote.“This is a request that this road should be laid this time. Otherwise, when you come at the time of voting, we will not vote at all. This entire colony,” the resident says.Scindia objected to the manner in which the demand was made, saying, “Do not ever use this language with me. Understood? I am talking to everyone. You come and make a request. It is my responsibility to get the work done. Okay?”
The Congress later shared the video on its official X account, writing, “Look at the arrogance of power.”
The party also alleged that Scindia “flew into a rage”. The party added, “The moment the public demanded a road, 'His Majesty' flew into a rage.” It further quoted Scindia’s response and said, “The public will soon put this arrogance in its place.”
The video comes amid local complaints over the condition and construction of the road. The confrontation was followed by an announcement on the project.At a public programme later, Scindia announced that Rs 3 crore would be sanctioned for road construction from the MLA’s fund, from the quota of Guna MLA Pannalal Shakya. He also directed the district collector to ensure that work is taken up after the monsoon, according to reports.The episode has since shifted attention from the road demand to the exchange itself, with the viral footage prompting renewed discussion on how elected representatives respond to constituents’ grievances.

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Korea have a long-standing partnership spanning over 75 years. As a result of their fruitful collaboration, there has been significant progress in health and development all around the world. The Republic of Korea has gone from being a donor-recipient country to a donor-country and is now a leader in global health and playing a critical role on the world stage.
Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General for External Relations and Governance (WHO) and Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination (Ministry of Health and Welfare, Republic of Korea), together with counterparts from WHO and the Government of the Republic of Korea. © WHO
To further strengthen this partnership and our commitment to working jointly to address global health challenges, WHO and the Republic of Korea convened their second Strategic Dialogue in Seoul from 28 to 29 August 2024. Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Directory-General for External Relations and Governance, led the WHO delegation and was accompanied by an in-person team and colleagues participating virtually from the three levels of the Organization (headquarters, regional, and country offices).
Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination, Ministry of Health, led the Republic of Korea delegation and was joined by senior officials including Dr Young-Mee Jee, Commissioner, Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, as well as senior counterparts from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety.
In addition, in line with WHO's work to enhance collaboration with parliamentarians, the WHO delegation also met with various Members of the National Assembly that are championing the global health agenda.
The recently concluded two-day meeting resulted in an alignment of priorities and paved the way for enhanced collaboration between WHO and the Government of Korea.

Jagtar Singh Johal, a British Sikh man who was arrested in India in 2017 in connection with alleged terrorism offences, has been granted bail by a Delhi court.
Johal, from Scotland, was arrested for his alleged role in funding the Khalistan Liberation Force, which had carried out targeted killings in India’s Punjab region.
His full trial has been repeatedly deferred by the authorities in the federal court but largely similar conspiracy charges were dismissed by a court in Punjab last year. Throughout his detention the prosecution has failed to produce verifiable evidence, leading to the deferred hearings.
Johal, now 39, travelled to India to marry his fiancee in late 2017. On 4 November, three weeks after the wedding, the couple were shopping with a relative in the Punjab city of Jalandhar when a group of men took Johal from his car, placed a black hood over his head and put him in an unmarked vehicle. He claims he was then denied access to a lawyer and tortured in an attempt to extract a confession. A question remains over whether he was arrested following a tip-off from British intelligence services.
Commenting on Friday’s ruling, Johal’s Scotland-based brother Gurpreet Singh Johal said: “The past two years has been an expensive rollercoaster, contesting bails at the supreme court and back to the high court. I had a long, sleepless night knowing that the decision would be made this morning. Now, all I can think about is Jagtar walking out of prison. We have waited so long and fought so hard for this moment.”
He added of previous hearings: “Whenever the evidence against Jagtar is tested in court, judges find what we’ve said all along, which is that there isn’t any.
“How long will this sick joke of a legal process be allowed to continue? We’re obviously delighted that Jagtar will soon be released, but he won’t be truly free until he is back in Dumbarton, with his wife and family.”
Gurpreet Johal, who also lives in Dumbarton, has lobbied a succession of UK foreign secretaries, who have repeatedly admitted the case has dragged on too long, but have been reluctant to call publicly for his release on the grounds that they should not interfere in the judiciary of another country.
The UK government recently appointed Alistair Burt as a special envoy for complex consular cases and he has met Gurpreet Johal in Scotland to discuss the case.
Dan Dolan, the deputy executive director of Reprieve, one of the organisation’s fighting for Johal’s release, said: “While this judgment is welcome as Jagtar should not be in prison a day longer, we must now watch closely to ensure this order is actually implemented and not obstructed in any way. The conditions attached are likely to be onerous. We must also remember that Jagtar will still be facing the death penalty in eight cases against him, despite these cases essentially duplicating trumped-up charges on which he has already been fully acquitted.”
Chris Esdaile, a senior legal adviser to Redress, another organisaiton representing Johal, said granting bail “can’t undo the intolerable suffering caused by nine years of arbitrary detention”.
He added: “The need for accountability for the allegations of torture and the deeply flawed proceedings against Jagtar remains urgent.”
Johal’s lawyers said they were still awaiting the details of what would happen next in relation to posting bail terms. While the judges’ order was that Jagtar should be released on bail, he remained in custody while judges confirmed his bail conditions, which may be stringent. The court must also confirm the sums of money that must be posted as a bond.

Concerns about an AI-induced apocalypse are reaching a fever pitch, from Silicon Valley to Washington, DC.
One of the top theories about how a rogue AI will wipe us out? Biological weapons.
Earlier this summer, AI CEOs called for new laws to control the manufacturing of synthetic DNA. Then last month, researchers at Stanford University and the Arc Institute showed that AI can design new viral genomes. The idea gained steam last week after Anthropic released a report indicating that there had been efforts to use Claude in ways that “could support biological weapons development. “The report authors cite biological misuse as “one of the most serious risks of frontier AI models.” Shortly thereafter, chief executive officer Dario Amodei urged the government to help AI labs “pace the frontier.”
Despite the alarm around an AI-created killer plague, many scientists say the risk is fairly low on the list of the world’s concerns.
David Bellamy, a research scientist at the Institute of Foundation Models in Sunnyvale, California, does not see AI as a fundamentally new threat when it comes to the creation of bioweapons. The scientific community has grappled for decades with the question of whether to publish potentially dangerous biological research—known as the dual-use dilemma.
Before large language models, the internet itself, open-access science journals, and translation services like Google Translate made it easier for people to access biological information, including lab protocols, Bellamy says.
“AI is essentially a tool that can help both good actors, like scientists, and also threat actors to peruse information more quickly and define and source those protocols more quickly,” he adds. “But those capabilities are not really the bottleneck in the production of bioweapons.”
The real bottleneck, he says, is the process of assembling a virus or other biological agent and the raw materials, equipment, and knowledge that would be needed to do so. A bad actor would need to obtain the necessary gene fragments and build a whole genome from scratch, then verify that the virus can infect humans, cause the desired illness, and be transmissible from person to person. Robotic lab assistants can automate some tasks and speed up workflows to a point, but a person would still need the know-how to run those experiments and the resources to carry them out.
Jason Kelly, the CEO of the biotech startup Ginkgo Bioworks, thinks it’s unlikely an artificial general intelligence could commandeer and disseminate existing pathogens, let alone engineer new ones and deploy them. Ginkgo Bioworks specializes in creating autonomous labs and recently ran a project with OpenAI where its GPT-5 model ran a lab.
“The AI could not take over the lab,” he says, in part because the humans who worked inside could simply decline to get the bot whatever substances and equipment it was requesting to physically produce a bioweapon. All those pesky humans acting as checks mean “you’d have to have dramatically more robots all over the place,” he says, for an AGI to be able to deploy machines to do the often-delicate virology work required.
Immunologist Derya Unutmaz likewise says humans would be able to thwart any attempts by AGI to develop a deadly disease. Even if a nefarious super intelligence did somehow manage to unleash a supervirus, he argues that scientists would be able to use other AI systems to swiftly develop a vaccine.
Still, even some people who don’t think that AGI independently siccing a bioweapon on us right now is a real threat are concerned about bad actors using the technology as well as what might happen down the line.
“It is impossible for AI to access a fully autonomous lab and autonomously build a virus today because fully autonomous labs do not exist yet,” says Olivia Scharfman, a biotechnology fellow at the technology think tank Institute for Progress. “But I do think that an AI could pay someone to do it for them.”
She thinks AI-assisted bioterrorism is an immediate threat and that there are some groups that might be nihilistic enough to do so, including “transhumanist AI successionists,” people who buy into a fringe ideology who hope to supplant humans with bots.
Other experts aren’t so worried about an AI bioweapon because they don’t think that biological warfare makes much sense methodologically. “The risks tend to be somewhat misunderstood,” genetic biologist and professor of computational biology Francois Belloux tells WIRED, noting that people tend to “overestimate the value of pathogens as weapons.”
Setting aside the AGI of it all, Belloux says that bioweapons are simply not an especially attractive choice for aspiring genocidaires, especially as it’s difficult to target certain groups and spare others, and mass-producing and distributing pathogens is logistically complicated versus, say, launching a bomb. “If you want to kill people, there are much, much, much better ways to kill them than to try to engineer some virus or bacterium and then release it,” he says—whether you’re the most sophisticated artificial mind ever created or just a regular human.
With AI bringing the threat of bioweapons into focus, Scharfman says this is the right moment to push for better protections against all biological threats, including existing pathogens like H1N1. That could include high-level actions like passing legislation to enhance security protocols around DNA synthesis technology, but she also advocates for changes to mitigate risk from all viruses, like upgrading air purification systems in buildings.
Whether AI demonstrably raises the risk of bioweapon development is a hard question to answer, says Steph Guerra, head of AI and bio at Rand Corporation, a policy think tank. “AI has been shown to be very good at integrating information together and being motivational to people for doing good and bad things,” she says.
Even if the risk is low, Guerra says, there are still ways that society can protect against potential misuse. One is that governments can adopt laws requiring firms that sell synthetic DNA and RNA to screen customers and orders to prevent the misuse of genetic material. Many companies already use software to screen orders for so-called “sequences of concern,” but the practice is not universal or mandated.
Before a bad actor could get to that point, though, most everyone agrees that models should have appropriate safeguards in place so that they don’t provide actionable, dangerous information to people.
Guerra says the risk of an AI-developed biothreat can also be mitigated by strengthening global surveillance systems to detect outbreaks of new diseases and circulating pathogens to researchers as early as possible. She says data-sharing protocols across AI companies, gene synthesis providers, and the government could also help prevent misuse.
“With pretty much almost any biosecurity control, there are going to be ways that they can be circumvented,” she says. “That's why we need layered approaches that provide friction across the entire pathway, from ideation to intention of a bad actor, all the way to the release of a bioweapon.”
Unutmaz says there’s an even more pressing worry: that all the AI doom conversations are diverting attention from how cutting-edge systems can assist humans in vaccine development and other medical breakthroughs.
“We really need to focus on the positive aspect of it,” he says.

Postponement not an option as Kenya races to be ready for Afcon 2027
- Published
African football boss Patrice Motsepe has called for a "heightened sense of urgency" from next year's Africa Cup of Nations co-hosts Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.
The tournament is set to return to East Africa for the first time in 51 years, with the opening match kicking off on 19 June and the final scheduled for 17 July.
Stadiums are supposed to be ready for testing in around three months' time, and Confederation of African Football (Caf) president Motsepe says there is little room for delay.
"Even though we've got nine months, we need to start using those stadiums in January next year to test them and to see what further improvements are required," he told BBC Sport Africa after inspecting preparations in Kenya on Friday.
Motsepe said there had been "very good progress" while also acknowledging that some facilities were still below the required level.
"We've got very high standards in terms of our expectations of the infrastructure, the facilities and the stadiums, the hotels, the roads, the football pitches where training takes place," the South African added.
"We require those facilities to be world class."
Despite delays in certain areas, Motsepe insisted: "There isn't the slightest consideration of a postponement.
"There should be no need because there's a deep amount of commitment."
Kenya to 'accelerate preparations'
Motsepe began his inspection visit for Afcon 2027 in Tanzania before touring Kenya, where he inspected two venues in Nairobi: Kasarani Stadium and the newly constructed 60,000-capacity Talanta Stadium.
BBC Sport Africa understands that one of the main areas of concern in Kenya is the Kasarani and its corresponding training facility.
The stadium is set to host the 2029 World Athletics Championships, which Nairobi was awarded on Tuesday ahead of London and Rome.
When Caf conducted its previous inspection in mid-February, the local organisers were told that stadiums and their associated training facilities should be around 80% ready by August.
However, Kasarani has seen limited progress over the past seven months, with several areas still requiring attention.
One of the biggest challenges is the playing surface, which is yet to be laid. Work is also required on cabling for broadcast and television operations, floodlights and the stadiums' sky boxes.
Motsepe also pointed to the demands created by hosting hundreds of VIPs and heads of state, saying some stadium designs will need to be reconfigured.
"Security issues in relation to where the special guests, particularly the heads of state, will be seated requires a revision of the original plans," the 64-year-old explained.
Kenya's cabinet secretary for sports Salim Mvurya insisted preparations would be completed on time.
"I assure Caf and Kenyans we will accelerate the preparations for Afcon 2027," Mvurya said.
"We will conclude everything by December to be sure we can have test matches in the various facilities."

December is significant because Motsepe is due to return to the region for a final assessment visit in January.
Recent Caf tournaments have regularly been delayed from their original dates.
This year's Women's Africa Cup of Nations was played in July after the planned kick-off in March was postponed with just 12 days' notice.
The 2024 African Nations Championship - the former tournament for home-based players only - in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda was postponed from its intended February 2025 dates to August 2025 to ensure infrastructure and facilities were "at the levels necessary". That decision came 18 days before the tournament was due to start.
Meanwhile, the 2023 Afcon in Ivory Coast was moved to the early months of 2024 because of concerns about the rainy season.
Two years ago Motsepe's former deputy Veron Mosengo-Omba admitted that Caf faced a "scheduling nightmare" to fit its biennial tournaments into the crowded football calendar.
Some pundits claim that is part of the reasoning behind the decision to play the men's Afcon every four years after 2028.
Sporting legacy
Despite previous delays to tournaments and concerns over preparations in East Africa, Motsepe has made it clear the Afcon 2027 timetable will not be reconsidered.
"There's no plan B, there's no plan C," he said.
For Kenya, getting it right this time matters more because Afcon has become part of a bigger sporting project.
"One of the reasons why Kenya won the 2029 World Athletics Championship bid is because we are hosting Afcon. Therefore this is a legacy," Mvurya said.
"Sport is not just entertainment, it is livelihood, it is economic transformation.
"Therefore we are aware the opportunity to host Afcon will be key for our economic inspiration. Our tourism will be a big beneficiary.
"As government, we are confident we will host a successful Afcon."
The next three months are likely to be particularly crucial in making that promise a reality.

The makers of Pehla Pyaar Doosri Baar have unveiled a fun promotional video featuring Anubhav Bassi, Gurleen Pannu and Devesh Dixit, who turn their attention towards the film’s six debutantes. New Delhi, December 1975. It was love at first sight when a Swedish hippy called Lotta von Schedvin sat down to be sketched by an Indian street artist, Pradyumna Kumar Mahanandia, known to everyone as PK. In the 10 minutes it took PK to complete her portrait, everything clicked into place for the pair. They were swept headlong in a whirlwind romance, and PK took Lotta to his village in the east of India to meet his family. But soon after, the time came for Lotta to pack up her VW campervan and head back home with her friends.
Heart-stricken PK promised to follow, but a plane ticket to Sweden was an impossible dream. Determined not to lose the love of his life, PK bought a secondhand Raleigh bike, and with $80 sewn into the waistband of his trousers, set off to cycle 6,000 miles to Lotta. He knew the sun set in the west, so that was the direction he took. His plan was to follow the hippy trail, cycling through India, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran and Turkey, crossing Europe, finally arriving in Sweden.
Actually, he was heading to Switzerland until a fellow backpacker pointed out that Switzerland and Sweden were two different countries. In a new Netflix documentary, The Cycle of Love, PK jokes that his strength was his fuzzy grasp of European geography. Watching the film, you wonder if his superpower might have been his smile – warm and joyous, it lights the room. Either way, he made it to Sweden. The journey took 123 days, and ended up involving a flight or two, and a couple of trains. In May 1977, PK knocked on Lotta’s door in Borås, Sweden. They have been together ever since.
Documentary-maker Orlando von Einsiedel first heard about the story when he gave a talk in Sweden. “At the end, two young people came up and handed me a book,” he says. “They said: ‘This is about our parents’ story. We know your work. Would you be interested in this as a film?’” The book was The Amazing Story of the Man Who Cycled from India to Europe for Love by Swedish journalist Per J Andersson.
The two young people were PK and Lotta’s grownup kids Emilie and Karl. Von Einsiedel politely took the book but didn’t think too much about it. “Normally in my experience, when somebody approaches you and says ‘I’ve got a brilliant story’, it doesn’t work out.”
A couple of months later, Von Einsiedel picked up the book as a holiday read, opening it on the flight out of London. “The moment I started I thought, ‘Oh my God, you idiot Orlando! This is extraordinary.’” It wasn’t just the against-all-odds, 6,000-mile cycle ride, PK’s story was a tale of fate and destiny. When he was born, the astrologer in his village made four predictions about his future wife: she would be a Taurus, born outside India, musical and own a jungle. So naturally the first question he asked Lotta was: “Are you a Taurus?” Her answer was yes. She was also a gifted musician, and – most bonkers of all – her family owned land with a forest in Sweden.
“When you tell people the story, it’s almost too good to be true,” says Von Einsiedel, cheerful and chatty on a video call from New York. The previous night he attended the US premiere of The Cycle of Love with PK and Lotta, who have been happily married for nearly 50 years. The pair have been getting the celebrity treatment wherever they go. “Everybody in the cinema stands up for them, people are weeping when they come on stage.” What do the couple make of the film? He grins. “I know they like it, because whenever they go to a festival, they watch every single screening from beginning to end.” How many times have they seen it? “A lot.”
The film tells their story with enormous warmth. It includes a dramatisation of the epic ride, with PK played by the British-based Indian actor Chirag Lobo, and Mina Dale as Lotta. Everybody else is non-professional, explains Von Einsiedel. “Our producers would go out and street-cast people on the morning of filming.”
What about the script, I ask? There are gorgeous, heartwarming scenes as PK shares his story with people he meets on the road, who in return tell him about their life and loves. How were those scenes scripted? “No script. Everything is improvised. When PK interacts with everyday people he meets along the way, those are just normal conversations about love and hopes and dreams.”
Wasn’t that a bit risky – getting a plane to India with two actors, no script and trusting that deep and meaningful conversations would materialise from conversations with ordinary people? “Massively risky, except I tested if it might work in Lewisham town centre,” Von Einsiedel says, grinning. “I have a friend who’s an actor. We went to Lewisham with a bike.” Armed with a notepad, his friend told people that he was cycling from London to Cape Town for love. “He pretended to draw portraits. What was extraordinary is the first person he sat down to draw turned around and said: ‘I love your story. I’ll buy you a plane ticket immediately.’”
It’s the kindness of strangers that makes the documentary so uplifting. When PK cycles out of Kabul, he stops to help an Austrian backpacker, Linea, who crashed her car, knocking out most of her teeth. He stays with her for several days at hospital, even though it means his visa expiring and further delay. Later, when he arrives in Istanbul and checks his post, there is a train ticket to Vienna – a thank you from Linea for his kindness.
What struck Von Einsiedel when he met the real-life PK was that his story about love went beyond boy-meets-girl. “For me, it’s not just about romantic love. It’s about self-love and love for all the people that we share this planet with.” PK was born into a dalit family, the marginalised group in India formerly known as “untouchables”. At school, he was made to sit outside during lessons and not allowed to play with the other children. Even after he won a scholarship to study fine art in Delhi, he experienced periods of homelessness and isolation.
“From the moment I started talking to PK it became clear what a difficult and traumatic childhood he’d had,” Von Einsiedel says. “He spoke so movingly about being on the journey and how it was the first time that strangers would touch him and hug him. That it was key to him starting to believe in himself and love himself. He said: ‘How can you love anybody if you can’t love yourself?’ I get emotional just saying that.”
PK explained how he felt accepted on the journey, hanging out with hippies and locals in the villages and towns he passed through. People with very little offered him hospitality, a meal or a roof for the night. In the documentary, this warm feeling of togetherness thuds to the ground when PK arrives in Europe, grilled by hostile and overtly racist German border officers. “That was his first experience,” says Von Einsiedel. “He travelled through all these countries, Afghanistan and Iran, and everybody treated him with respect. Then as soon as he got to Europe he immediately experienced racism.”
Von Einsiedel grew up in south London. At university he studied social anthropology and in his 20s was a professional snowboarder. “I learned the craft of film-making making snowboard films,” he says. “When I knew how to do that, I segued into making films about social issues I believed in.” He started working with Al Jazeera, travelling to conflict zones.
In 2015, he was nominated for an Oscar for his first full-length documentary, Virunga, about the battle to save a national park in eastern Congo, home to some of the world’s last mountain gorillas. His documentary short, White Helmets, following Syrian volunteers rescuing civilians, won an Oscar. Next he made Evelyn, an incredibly moving film in which Von Einsiedel turned the camera on his own family. His brother Evelyn took his own life aged 22 over a decade earlier. In the film, Von Einsiedel and his two surviving siblings hiked the routes their brother loved to walk with friends and family. “I was very emotionally closed for a long time after my brother died,” he says. “I used to think being emotionally open was a sign of weakness. I was terrified of my own emotions. I see the opposite now. I think being emotionally open is a sign of strength.”
When it comes to picking a subject for a new documentary, he says he is attracted to people who inspire him. “I’m drawn to stories that show the better side of human beings. That’s a thread that runs through the work I like to make.” The Cycle of Love is by far the sunniest film he has made to date. What’s that all about, I ask? “I wanted to make an optimistic film that’s about joy and human connection. The world is difficult. Love is one of those things that all of us can agree on. This story just felt so important to tell.”
