Editor’s note: This work is part of AI Watchdog, The Atlantic’s ongoing investigation into the generative-AI industry.
Earlier this summer, Tamra Westberry received a Facebook notification that made her heart sink. A fellow author had taken to social media to endorse Westberry’s latest book, Project Erebus, after reading about it in a weekly roundup of the latest paranormal-romance releases. Independent authors like Westberry, who is based in Texas and has published dozens of books under the pen name Tara West, usually welcome an encouraging word and a bit of cross-promotion. But Westberry was dismayed. She had never heard of a book called Project Erebus. And she certainly wasn’t its author.
She looked up her author profile on Amazon, and there it was: Project Erebus, a book that featured character names she’d previously used, with a cover echoing that of her recent work. Translations were available in German, French, Italian, and Spanish. The book was a complete mystery to her, but after she read its sample pages, she suspected it was made by someone who’d used AI tools. (I ran the book’s cover and promotional blurb through Pangram, which suggested that they were completely AI-generated.)
Westberry emailed Amazon and requested that the company delink the unaffiliated books from her profile. Amazon removed the books from the platform within a week or so—but not before some of her fans purchased them, read them, and left reviews. “No real detail, characters remain undeveloped. I almost felt I was reading an essay written by a school child,” one disappointed reader wrote in a two-star review for Project Erebus on Goodreads, a literary social network owned by Amazon that had also attributed the book to West.
Across categories—fantasy, horror, even coloring books—writers say they’re seeing AI-generated listings crop up on their Amazon author pages. Some of these works are in entirely different genres from their usual work—such as a children’s series misattributed to a writer of steamy love stories—whereas others echo the subject matter or jacket designs of preexisting books. One writer reported someone sneaking in a fake edition under the listing of their real book. Because Amazon often sends out emails notifying author-page followers about new listings, these titles are able to leech a writer’s fan base, make ill-gotten revenue, and confuse readers.
AI companies pirated millions of books to train today’s most popular models, as The Atlantic has previously reported. Those models are now being used to churn out books in a matter of minutes and place them alongside books that represent years of hard work. In some cases, people go beyond mass-producing second-rate content or publishing copycats of new releases, using the names of established authors on parasitic works that feed off preexisting brands. Writers feel that they have little recourse regarding what AI models ingest, or spit out. “It’s deeply unsettling, after I spent years crafting stories and building my brand, that some no-talent grifter can bottom-feed off my fan base with AI slop,” Westberry, who’s written more than 50 books that were included in a data set used by the likes of OpenAI, Meta, and Anthropic, told me.
The parasite-creator problem is pervasive. Professors have found AI-generated academic papers published under their names; recent reporting suggests that sneaking AI-generated songs onto artists’ streaming profiles is a relatively simple move. The issue has also become endemic to Amazon, the world’s largest online book retailer, which sells hundreds of millions of books annually in the U.S. alone. The platform groups works with the same byline under a unified profile thanks to a largely automatic system. Authors say that Amazon has failed to make a concerted effort to address the phenomenon, and that the onus falls on them to monitor their pages, in a crazy-making game of whack-a-mole.
An Amazon spokesperson told me that the company does take measures to prevent, detect, and remove content that violates its guidelines, but it did not provide more details about how these systems work. “We are committed to a bookstore that readers love and publishers and authors trust, and work directly with authors to address any issues or errors affecting their accounts,” the spokesperson said.
To some degree, Amazon’s parasite-author problem predates the widespread advent of AI. A decade ago, Stephen King publicly urged the site to stop associating his own works with those of Stephen R. King., another horror author whose name was confusing fans. Such instances, however, were few and far between because of the time and effort it required to publish a title. Now that anyone can use LLMs to churn out a novel, the issue has both grown and mutated. While the sheer number of new books published on the platform might inevitably lead to more authors of the same name, Orna Ross, the founder of the Alliance of Independent Authors, noted that many titles are purposefully designed to blend in with a real author’s catalog. “It needs only to fool the algorithm and a rushed buyer for long enough to skim the sale,” she told me.
Authors told me that Amazon is typically quick to delink books from author pages once they’ve been flagged. But getting them removed from the platform entirely can be trickier, especially if a writer hasn’t trademarked their name. Amazon can treat such incidents as a matter of “name coincidence,” Ross said, and leave books up even after decoupling them from profiles. Writers struggling to receive direct action from Amazon have also escalated cases through the Authors Guild, the largest professional organization for writers in America, whose recent reports have warned of AI books falsely attributed to writers.
For many writers of genre fiction, which relies on high output and familiar tropes, staying afloat means playing a volume game, releasing numerous books a year to make a living. That makes certain genres particularly susceptible to AI dupes, which can blend in with the thousands of real titles released annually. Because producing AI versions is so cheap, even a few sales can be profitable. “The people that are making money selling AI copies are generally doing so by selling one or two or three copies of the thousand different books that they publish,” Julie Trelstad, a publishing consultant, told me.
The identity of the individuals behind these books is a mystery to real authors, and often difficult to track down. Regardless, authors don’t view such books as a major sales threat, given that they tend to be less appealing to buyers than genuine works, with slapdash covers and lackluster page counts. What writers are really concerned about is the potential for long-lasting reputational harm among readers, who typically trust that a book listed on an Amazon author page was, indeed, written by said author.
Last year, Vanessa O’Loughlin, an Irish author who writes crime books under the name Sam Blake, was alerted to a trilogy of “dark romantasy” books on her profile that she suspected were made with AI. She didn’t write them, for one, and the pages she read felt off. The books revolved around a character named Elara Vance, a combination of popular first and last names used by AI models. O’Loughlin managed to get the stories delinked from her profile within a few days, although they remained online with Sam Blake listed as the author for some weeks after, and sold a few copies. “Dang it! I got fooled by this,” one fan wrote after O’Loughlin warned followers about the books on social media. O’Loughlin fears that new readers who accidentally came across the trilogy might never pick up a Sam Blake book again.
In some cases, parasite titles can even latch on to real ones. This past July, Noelle W. Ihli published The Last to Drown, a successful thriller that’s listed at $16 for a paperback on Amazon. But earlier this month, the book’s Amazon page also gave viewers the option to purchase another paperback version that featured the same title and a nearly indistinguishable cover. This edition included a slightly different summary that is 100 percent AI-generated, according to Pangram, and its interior pages appeared to be AI-written as well. It also sold for $5 more. Ihli discovered the title after being alerted by confused readers who had received a suspicious copy in the mail, and it was removed earlier this week, shortly after she filed an intellectual-property-infringement claim with Amazon. “Unless I’m checking obsessively every day, it’s really easy for something like this to slip through the cracks,” Ihli told me.
Amazon has introduced some safeguards in response to the onslaught of AI-generated listings. The company restricts the number of books an author can self-publish to 10 a week per book format, and sometimes requests identity verification for accounts. Even so, authors continue to run into variations of the same issue. A romance author who writes under the name Olivia Sinclair (and who asked to keep her legal name private for work and family reasons) previously got Amazon to remove a number of suspected AI books from her profile and thought the problem had been solved until six children’s books about the adventures of cartoon turtles and foxes were listed on her page in July and August. The books, all of which contained summaries flagged as 100 percent AI-written by Pangram, were delinked from her profile earlier this month, shortly after I notified Amazon of the listings. They still remain online with Sinclair listed as the author, however, in addition to at least two seemingly duplicate copies with yet another author name.
The process of removing these works appears to be primarily complaint-driven: When Amazon does act, it does so reactively, instead of preemptively, according to Ross, the Alliance of Independent Authors’ founder. “Verified authorship at upload would end most of this overnight,” she said. Amazon did not provide a response when asked why it doesn’t verify profile identities across the board. Meanwhile, authors feel largely powerless. For self-published writers in particular, selling books on Amazon is a key aspect of their livelihood. “It’s such a catch-22,” Anna Blakely, a writer who has also run into seemingly AI-generated books on her profile. (Blakely is a pen name; I agreed to withhold the author's real name to protect her privacy.) She predicts that roughly 90 percent of her income comes from sales on the platform. “There’s really no other viable option.”
Other platforms claim to be taking a proactive approach to tackling their own versions of parasite authors. Last year, Spotify announced plans to crack down on songs—AI-generated or otherwise—erroneously appearing on artists’ profiles. The company said it would invest more in its response process for content mismatches, in addition to introducing a new impersonation policy and more recently unveiling a feature for artists to review new music on their profiles. But even these efforts appear to be ineffective: A recent 404 Media report demonstrated how AI-generated songs can still be easily uploaded to real artists’ profiles on streaming services including Spotify and Amazon Music.
Keeping an eye on this flood takes up valuable time and effort that authors could have otherwise put toward writing real books. It also adds insult to injury for writers whose books helped refine the AI tools being used to rip off their work. “It’s a devaluing of words, a devaluing of ideas, a devaluing of the accomplishment and the excitement of literature,” said Ben H. Winters, another author who has found what appears to be AI-generated work released under his name on Amazon. Like the rest of the writers I spoke with, his work surfaced in The Atlantic’s searchable database of copyrighted content that trained AI models. “They’ve assimilated all of this stuff, and now they’re spitting it back at us.”

Rose Friedman, an NPR editor and reporter who shaped the public radio network’s arts & culture coverage and co-created its popular reading guide Books We Love, died of cancer Thursday, September 17, at her home in New York City. She was 38.
Her death was announced on-air by NPR’s Elizabeth Blair, who called Friedman one of the outlet’s finest journalists.
In an obituary and tribute posted on NPR’s website, Blair said, “Rose Friedman was an editor to the end. She said she wanted the second line of her obituary to acknowledge her role as a shop steward for SAG-AFTRA, the union that represents NPR’s editorial workers. She wanted the line to say that her ‘proudest achievement’ was helping convince NPR to increase its paid parental leave.”
Friedman joined NPR as an editorial assistant in her early 20s in 2010. She later served as an editor and reporter, becoming deeply sourced in the publishing industry, editing book reviews and features and writing appreciations of book world personalities such as author Herman Wouk and editor Sonny Mehta.
Watch on Deadline
She co-created what was initially called the Book Concierge, later renamed Books We Love. Reading over hundreds of titles nominated by NPR staff and critics, Friedman narrowed the list to the popular reader’s guide.
“She was voracious,” novelist Meg Wolitzer, who worked with Friedman on a number of NPR reviews and features, said to NPR. “What a gifted, delightful, brilliant, deeply kind person. And I would say a true enthusiast. I got so much working with Rose.”
Raised in Newton, Mass., Friedman is survived by her partner Andrew Anastasi, two children, parents and two sisters.

Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. gave the keynote address Thursday at a conference of an anti-vaccine activist group he once chaired, telling the hundreds in attendance that they had a friend in President Donald Trump's White House.
It was Kennedy's first time appearing at the Children's Health Defense conference since he became secretary. Kennedy took leave from the group when he launched his bid to become president in 2023, but his speech Thursday served as a sort of homecoming, offering him a platform from which to hail the administration's steps to scale back vaccine guidance and reassure the activists in attendance that he was working to turn their priorities into policy.
“Let me be clear: You have a strong and steadfast friend in the White House. We've accomplished in 19 months things that would have seemed unthinkable two years ago,” he said.
The speech, peppered with questions about long established vaccine safety, also highlighted how once fringe views on vaccines have been given a prominent pulpit under the Trump administration.
Kennedy boasted about the administration's moves to downsize the childhood vaccination schedule and reshape a key vaccine advisory board — steps that have since been halted by a judge.
Kennedy lauded Trump for pushing ahead with attempts to overhaul vaccine guidance, including an executive order last month calling for spacing out the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, against medical groups' recommendations.
That executive order and now Kennedy's keynote speech at the Children's Health Defense conference mark a pivot by the White House and the Department of Health and Human Services, who earlier this year had appeared to be moving beyond vaccine efforts and toward a less contentious agenda on healthy food ahead of November’s midterm elections. HHS promoted the speech on its social media channels.
Kennedy, a longtime anti-vaccine activist, chaired Children’s Health Defense for years. He served as the group’s chief legal counsel and expanded it. After becoming health secretary last year, Kennedy moved at a blistering pace to overhaul public health guidance and revamp long-held precedents in vaccine policymaking.
Critics, among them many of the country's top medical associations, have said the moves risk stoking vaccine hesitancy and sowing confusion among Americans who endured a crisis of trust in their public health agencies following the COVID-19 pandemic. That public confidence continues to erode.
“We have not taken vaccines away from anybody. We have preserved access. But we have started asking the questions that you and millions of American parents have been asking for years,” Kennedy told the group.
Mary Holland, the CEO of Children’s Health Defense, referred to Kennedy as “Bobby” and said the group has “gratitude beyond words” to the HHS secretary for “recognizing there are real consequential issues around childhood vaccinations.”
Kennedy's appearance Thursday comes as the country faces its worst year for measles since 1991 and has seen seven reported measles-associated deaths in the last two years — more than the combined total of reported deaths over the previous three decades.
Pennsylvania officials have reported four measles-associated deaths this year. None of the four were vaccinated, according to the state health department. When state officials last month announced the first two of those deaths, it ignited a public feud between Gov. Josh Shapiro and Kennedy.
Shapiro blasted Kennedy's appearance on the social media site X Thursday, saying Kennedy “chose to spend his time today addressing the premier vaccine-denial conference in America.”
Shapiro said the HHS secretary should have encouraged people to get vaccinated for measles, "yet he couldn’t bring himself to do it. Instead, he pushed a narrative that continues to stoke fear and mistrust.”
A representative from the White House did not respond to an Associated Press request for comment on Kennedy’s appearance at the event.
Following Kennedy onstage Thursday was Andrew Wakefield, an author of a since-discredited study that linked the MMR vaccine to autism, which has fueled the anti-vaccine movement even though it was retracted.
Widespread scientific consensus and decades of studies have firmly concluded there is no link between vaccines and autism.
Shaughnessy Naughton, founder of 314 Action, a group that recruits scientists to run for public office, said Kennedy's decision to give a speech at the conference shows “the lack of seriousness he brings to HHS.”
"With a deadly measles outbreak killing people in Pennsylvania, the best thing Kennedy can do for Americans is step aside.”

Soon after the news of Hindutva fanatic Swatantra Bhardwaj getting interim bail for three weeks went out, a 1.16-minute video of him got viral, in which he is with another person who boasts about Bhardwaj’s release and compares him with a lion on the hunt. Bhardwaj then threatens those who had attacked his supporters while he was in detention. He says (in Hindi), “You are like insects.. why did you target my brothers? if they wanted they could have beaten you up.. but for some reason, they followed the law… I will not do anything to you.. tell your father Chandrashekhar Azad (Bhim Army chief whom Bhardwaj compares to Ravana), that this Brahmin lion (referring to himself) will avenge the attack. It is an open challenge…”
Bhardwaj faces criminal charges under Sections 115(2), 126(2) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, along with provisions of the POCSO Act and SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act and an attempt-to-murder charge for an alleged assault on the father of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activist Nishu Azaad. On September 7, he had been sent to 14-day judicial remand.
An X user named Gen-Z of India shared the said video on September 17 and wrote (in Hindi), “As soon as Swatantra Bharadwaj stepped out, he started up again, even though the court had imposed the condition that he would not make any grandstanding statements in the media, but listen to what he is saying.” The post has received close to 1 million views. (Archive)
भारतीय न्याय व्यवस्था एक बार फिर से फ़ैल हो गयी है…
स्वतंत्र भारद्वाज बाहर आते ही फ़िर से शुरू हो गया है, जबकि कोर्ट ने शर्त रखी है कि मीडिया में कोई बयानबाज़ी नहीं करेगा लेकिन यह तो क्या कह रहा है वह सुनिए। pic.twitter.com/pBPNKeQtRs
— Gen-Z of India (@GenZ_of_India_) September 17, 2026
This post was reshared by several influential and verified handles, including Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra, journalist Vir Sanghvi, CJP leader Ratna Singh and others, making it go viral. Others like film writer Darab Farooqi and verified X user @tanmoyofc shared the video as well.
Media outlets Prabhat Khabar and The Mooknayak published reports on the video presenting it as recorded after Bhardwaj’s release on bail in the assault case.
Fact Check
First of all, we found that India Today posted a video on September 17 stating that Bhardwaj came out of Tihar Jail around 9.45 pm on that day (September 17). The caption of India Today’s Instagram post said, “Although he was granted bail two days ago, he was released around 9:45 pm after the remaining procedures were completed. He immediately ran towards a taxi and left without speaking to the media.”
View this post on Instagram
Several other media outlets reported that Bhardwaj walked out of jail late at night on Thursday, September 17, and rushed into a car avoiding media persons.
Next, a reverse image search with some key frames from the viral video led us to a Facebook post and a YouTube video from September 7. This makes it clear that the video was not recorded after Bhardwaj’s release on September 17. Check the screenshots in the gallery below:
By scraping our database of active Right-wing vigilantes, we then identified the other individual in the video as Vaibhaw Kumar alias Vaibhaw Pandey. While going through his Instagram timeline, we found the now-viral video uploaded on June 26.
According to another video posted by Vaibhaw, Bhardwaj was detained on June 22 for threatening CJP leaders at Jantar Mantar.
To sum up, the viral video of Hindutva fanatic and attempt-to-murder accused Swatantra Bhardwaj threatening Chandrashekhar Azad was not recorded after his release on interim bail on September 17. It was shared on social media by another Hindutva vigilante on June 26.

A re-elected Victorian Labor government will create two new Australian-first offences aimed at closing “loopholes” it says have allowed perpetrators of family violence to escape punishment.
On Sunday, the premier, Ben Carroll, will announce an election commitment to legislate a new form of manslaughter covering cases in which a person takes their own life as a result of family violence, as well as a new offence covering perpetrators abandoning a victim in need of medical care.
The latter responds to recommendations made by the coroner after the deaths of Belinda Jones and Narelle Simmons.
Jones, 40, died on the floor of her Maryborough home in July 2023 after her partner left her there overnight and then waited two hours to call an ambulance after waking to find her cold and not breathing.
Jones had succumbed to treatable bacterial infections and sepsis, which a hospital failed to diagnose during an emergency presentation days earlier. Her partner was not charged with any offence in relation to her death.
In her findings published last month, the state coroner, Liberty Sanger, said: “In my view, the act of abandoning a victim of family violence requiring medical attention is an act of family violence, that instils fear in the victim and affirms a perpetrator’s control over the victim.”
Simmons, 42, died in October 2021 after her partner admitted to punching her twice in the face and elbowing her once in the back of the head before leaving her Cranbourne home.
Her body was found nine days later after her daughter requested a welfare check. Sanger was unable to determine whether she died immediately after the assault or hours or days later.
Her partner – whom the coroner said had 18 previous family violence victims – pleaded guilty to common assault and failing to report a reportable death. He was sentenced to five months’ imprisonment and a 12-month community corrections order.
The government’s media release said the two new offences would close “loopholes” that allow perpetrators to “slip through the cracks in the justice system and walk free”.
The government has also committed to increasing the maximum penalty for rape from 25 years to life imprisonment and upping the maximum penalty for every other serious sexual offence by five years. The maximum penalty for persistent breaches of family violence intervention orders would also double from five years’ imprisonment to 10.
It will also make the standard sentence for the murder of a current or former partner 30 years – up from 25.
Labor will amend the Evidence Act to prevent barristers from using humiliating and invasive questioning techniques on victim-survivors in court. Courts would also be able to consider patterns of sexual abuse as evidence at trial.
The announcement follows a week of crime-focused election commitments from Carroll, including creating a new police training facility in Melbourne’s western suburbs and the introduction of Jack’s Law, which would give police and protective services officers the power to stop and search people for knives using handheld metal detectors.
“I’m a tough-on-crime premier – and that means being tough on family and sexual violence,” Carroll said in a statement ahead of Sunday’s announcement.
“We must act on the violence that is killing a Victorian woman every two weeks.”
The Coalition last year committed to Jack’s Law and also have plans to expand adult sentencing for youth offenders, increase police numbers and split the existing court of appeal into two separate entities, if elected in November.

The Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas announced on Saturday that Biometric Aadhaar Authentication (BAA) will be mandatory for domestic LPG customers for them to book refills at regulated selling price with applicable subsidy starting 1 October, 2026.
There are 27.43 crore active consumers, out of which around 89.9 per cent have already completed the process, the ministry said.
Those who have completed the authentication process will not need to take any other action and they will continue to receive refills as before.
For consumers who have not completed BAA, subsidised refill booking at the regulated retail selling price will be enabled once authentication is completed.
1. The person who delivers your LPG cylinder can do the BAA on the spot on the OMC phone application.
2. You can also visit the LPG distributor's office where the authentication process can be carried out.
3. Customers can also opt to do the process themselves. Customers of Indane can use the IndianOil ONE app. Bharatgas customers will have to use the HelloBPCL app, HP PAY is the app for HP Gas customers. If you wish to understand what is the process to complete self e-KYC, there are tutorial videos on the PMUY portal.
If someone is unwilling or unable to complete the BAA, they will continue to receive LPG, but the choice for the same will have to be registered through the digital channels of the OMCs, which include consumer portals, mobile apps, WhatsApp chatbots and IVRS.
These customers, however, will not receive any subsidy, and will have to pay as per market prices when it comes to 5 kg or 10 kg cylinders, subject to local availability, the ministry has said.
The government has said that BAA has become essential in order to ensure subsidised LPG reaches those customers who are genuine and eligible. This will also prevent the diversion of domestic LPG for commercial as well as industrial purposes while removing duplicate or ineligible connections.
The ministry said the implicit subsidy on a 14.2 kg domestic LPG cylinder was around ₹210 in September, compared with ₹721 in June. To keep domestic LPG affordable, the government is providing OMC compensation of ₹30,000 crore during FY 2025-26 and FY 2026-27.
The initial deadline for authentication was set as 30 June, but was extended several times, with the final deadline being 14 September. Now the government has said it will be mandatory beyond 1 October.

How to switch between two phones on CarPlay
It should be easier than this.
CarPlay has been around since 2014 and has been receiving feature updates quite frequently, making it a safer way to interact with your phone while driving. Setting it up is easy and, outside of occasional connection issues, CarPlay tends to work seamlessly without requiring any troubleshooting — well, until you have a passenger with an iPhone that had previously been paired to your car. Though you can set up CarPlay for multiple iPhones in the same vehicle, you can only use one of them with CarPlay at a time.
Let's say two people with CarPlay-paired iPhones get into the same car. If your car automatically connects to the driver's iPhone, there's nothing you need to do, but if it picks the passenger's phone for projecting CarPlay instead, you'll need to manually switch the connection back. Depending on your car manufacturer, the process to pick a different iPhone for CarPlay will vary. Some infotainment systems let you pick a preferred or primary phone that gets priority whenever there are multiple paired iPhones in the vicinity. You should be able to find this under the Bluetooth settings or device management menu on your car's infotainment system.
Some manufacturers, like Hyundai, let you switch CarPlay or Android Auto connections on the go. Your car should remember your preference the next time it detects the same devices. Car infotainment systems are particular, though, so manually turning off Bluetooth and Wi-Fi on the other iPhone is a quick-and-dirty fix. You could also try using a wired CarPlay connection to see if it forces your car to prioritize the iPhone that's physically plugged in over another phone that's connected wirelessly; however, Reddit users have not had much luck with this method.
Using SharePlay in the car
CarPlay's app library actually spans more than just navigation and music apps. There's support for AI chatbots like ChatGPT, fuel price trackers and parking spot finders, but most people are content with having a map and playback controls on the screen. If you were looking to switch CarPlay connections to a passenger's iPhone so they could take over the music, though, there's an elegant workaround that lets them do that.
SharePlay support for CarPlay was introduced with iOS 17, and as long as everyone in the car has an iPhone running iOS 17 or newer, they will be able to join the driver's Apple Music session and add, rearrange or remove tracks using their own device. The passengers don't need to be Apple Music subscribers to use SharePlay in the car — only the host does.
For those who primarily use Spotify instead, the app's Jam feature essentially offers the same functionality and lets everyone in the car join the host's session and contribute to the queue from their own phones. Once again, participants don't need Spotify Premium if they're using the feature in an in-person setting.
Of course, using SharePlay or Spotify Jam only lets the passengers control the music. If they ever need to use navigation or view messages on the car's infotainment screen, they'll need to manually switch CarPlay connections using one of the methods we've mentioned above.

Hitler Could Have Been Stopped
Timothy W. Ryback explains the contemporary lessons of Hitler’s rise.
Does history repeat itself, or merely rhyme? The historian Timothy W. Ryback has thought about this question a lot. Ryback, the director of the Institute for Historical Justice and Reconciliation at The Hague, has written extensively about Adolf Hitler’s Germany, including in books such as Hitler’s Private Library: The Books That Shaped His Life and Hitler’s First Victims: The Quest for Justice.
Ryback’s new book, 53 Days: How Hitler Dismantled a Democracy, which grew out of a series of articles he wrote for The Atlantic, is a straightforward narrative of the period from Monday, January 30, 1933, when Hitler was appointed chancellor, to Thursday, March 23, 1933, when the Reichstag legislative body passed the so-called Enabling Act, which effectively gave the chancellor the power to dissolve the democratic Weimar Republic and inaugurate the Third Reich. As Joseph Goebbels noted at the time, “The big joke on democracy is that it gives its mortal enemies the means of its own destruction.”
Ryback’s 53 Days makes no reference to contemporary politics. And yet certain echoes of the 1930s resonate so loudly that it is impossible not to hear them. To cite just a few: Hitler was obsessed with tariffs. Hitler tried to fire his central banker. Hitler was preoccupied with seizing Greenland. Hitler was intent on adding an expensive new wing to the Reich chancellery, part of his grandiose architectural ambitions for the nation’s capital. He attacked and muzzled the press, attempted to purge the civil service of anyone disloyal to him, had a genius for inflaming the populist grievances of his base, and spurred angry young men to take paramilitary action against perceived enemies.
Reductio ad Hitlerum can have the baleful effect of trivializing the Holocaust, which thankfully has no parallel in the modern American context. Yet closely examining Hitler’s rise can yield useful insights into today’s autocratic moment—and help deepen our understanding of history’s unfolding.
In a conversation I had with Ryback yesterday at The Atlantic Festival, the historian discussed the rhymes and contingencies of history, the uses and misuses of the past, the lessons of 1933, and what a reexamination of Hitler’s rise can teach us about human agency and fate. This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
Scott Stossel: Why this book now?
Timothy W. Ryback: Histories are written for the era. We read about the things that have meaning for us. Read all the great biographies of Adolf Hitler: You’re not going to find a mention of Hitler’s central banker or his tariff policy. But suddenly, these things matter. For me, the most striking are the resonances in the personality type, the positioning. Hitler’s key to success was to never admit defeat, always double down. We’re used to seeing the newsreel footage of Hitler as the raving lunatic, frothing at the mouth. Well, he despised democracy, but he understood it as well as anyone. When Hitler got 37 percent of the vote in the July 1932 election, that was his high-water mark in terms of a completely open, free election. And he said he should be controlling the country. Listen to his logic: 37 percent is 75 percent of 51 percent, meaning the relative majority of the absolute majority. He used that to incredible effect in co-opting, coddling, or crushing his political allies on the far right before he ever turned to the left. And he was always preaching to his base. I mean, his political advisers would come and say, Whoa, cool it with the anti-Semitism. And Hitler would hear nothing of it. He used that formula, that understanding of democratic processes, to get where he got.
Stossel: It has been reported by Trump’s first wife that he kept Mein Kampf by the side of his bed. He denied that and then said No, it was a gift, and it was a collection of Hitler’s speeches. To what extent do you think that Trump is actually looking at Hitler and other fascist leaders of the past for a kind of guidebook for how to take power? And how much of it is just a kind of temperamental instinct for identifying grievances, inflaming them and saying, I will be your solution?
Ryback: This issue of grievance politics was the essence of Hitler’s political posture. And there were a lot of grievances out there. There was the Treaty of Versailles, which forced Germany to accept full responsibility for all the destruction of the First World War. There were massive reparation payments, which strained the economy. The other thing: He gridlocked the legislative processes time and again. He basically paralyzed the Reichstag, made it impossible for any laws to be passed, forcing the government to rule by executive decree, then turned around and said, Look, democracy doesn’t work as a system. Give me a chance. So I think the modalities were very similar. Keep in mind, the grievances that Hitler was playing off of, actually, a lot of it was legitimate.
Stossel: As it is today. You have a chapter in this book titled “Guardrails,” speaking to Hitler’s transgression of guardrails. How do you see, today, the pushing against and possible weakening of guardrails?
Ryback: Historians always look back, which lends these processes a sense of historical inevitability, rather than the reality, which is political contingency—what happens from one moment to the next. And I think in that regard, you begin to see Hitler in a very different context. His first day as chancellor, he wants to rewrite election laws. Turns out that’s too complicated. He then wants to ban the Communist Party. There’s pushback: Do we really have a right to do this? Could it cause social unrest? He said, Well, look, if there’s social unrest, we’ll just call in the army. To which the minister of defense, Werner von Blomberg, stands up and says, Mr. Chancellor, with all due respect, our military is trained to defend the German nation against foreign enemies; it is unthinkable that a German soldier could be ordered to shoot on German citizens in German streets. And this puts Hitler in his place. Hitler realized he’s banged up against about every constitutional guardrail there is. The next day, he issues this official memo to the members of the Nazi Party, and he declares war on his own government.
Stossel: I’m immediately put in mind of Jim Mattis and Mark Milley, and other folks who, in the first term, said, We are here to defend the Constitution, not to execute your will if it’s not in defense of the Constitution. You anticipated my next question, which was: When you look back at historical events, the natural inclination of both historians and lay people is to understand the narrative as kind of predetermined. But with Hitler’s rise to power, there are so many points along the way where a single action could have stopped him. President Hindenburg had already replaced three chancellors before Hitler came to power. He didn’t have to approve Hitler’s press for the Enabling Act. Do you think that Hitler’s rise and the Third Reich and the Holocaust were inevitable?
Ryback: Was the Holocaust inevitable? Big question. Simple answer: no. Look, we’ve got an election coming up in November. You watch Fox News, you get one version of what’s going to happen; watch CNN, The New York Times, you get another. We have no idea yet. One day after the election, you’re going to have every political pundit explaining how this outcome was inevitable. Hitler was going to rallies and saying, I don’t care what the outcome of the election is going to be. I am here to save the German nation. I will not leave the chancellorship. The newspapers at the time said, You know, Mr. Hitler should read the constitution because it’s not up to him to decide whether he stays in office. It’s the president. In some ways, I felt like the book should have been, “How Hitler almost failed to dismantle a democracy.” Forgotten heroes stood up to him: the journalists who were calling him out at every step; the Social Democrats, who were being threatened, and yet pursuing an attempt to save the republic.
Stossel: One key moment in the rise of Hitler and his consolidation of power was obviously the Reichstag fire. Your book comes out before our next election, where we think about October surprises. What worries you, looking ahead to the midterms?
Ryback: This is where there are a lot of resonances with the electoral processes at that time. You had a monolithic right-wing movement. You had a fractured left-wing coalition that was continuing to fragment. You had a center group of undecided voters that was going to tip the election in one direction or another.
Stossel: When Hitler came to power, I think it’s fair to say that people did not expect that the National Socialists would have been able to win as many of the Reichstag seats as they did. In 2016, everyone thought Hillary was going to win. She did not. In 2024, again, it looked for a long time like Trump’s defeat was inevitable. It was not. Looking ahead to two months from now, polling suggests favorable signals for the Democrats. How do you think about November 2026?
Ryback: Hitler said a lot of horrific things. But to my mind, one of the most chilling was when Hitler finally got to power. He said, For the last 12 years, people have been mocking and ridiculing me. No one’s laughing anymore. Hitler did run against Hindenburg in the spring of 1932 for the presidency of Weimar. He lost by 6 million votes. Well, what did he do? He went to court to sue to have the election results overturned amid claims of voter fraud and irregularities by state officials. Where have we heard that before? The judge threw him out on his ear.
In March 1933, the German people went to the polls again. It was a referendum on the Hitler administration. No one knew what was going to happen. The Germans saw everything that Hitler had shown the German people, what he wanted the country to be. It was the largest electoral turnout in the history of parliamentary elections in Germany, going back to the 1870s. And they gave Hitler an overwhelming victory.
What I would say is: Don’t look at March 5, 1933. Look at April 2026, when the Hungarians had to go to the polls. Viktor Orbán had been in power for 15 years. Orbán had compromised the courts, he had suppressed the opposition press, he had driven the Central European University out of the country—and a lot of dissidents left. And yet, two-thirds of Hungarians voted to get him out of office, and did. Had the German people voted in March 1933 the way the Hungarians voted last spring, there would not have been a Third Reich. There would not have been a Holocaust. And Hitler would have been out of office within weeks.

Shooting at high school in the Philippines kills at least 3 young people, injures 6
A shooting at a high school in the southern Philippines has left at least three young people dead and six others injured, including the gunman
MANILA, Philippines -- A shooting at a high school in the southern Philippines on Friday left at least three young people dead and six others injured, including the gunman, a local official said.
Rolly Doane Aquino, a provincial disaster response official in South Cotabato province, said three people were killed and six others were hospitalized after the shooting at Banga National High School in the town of Banga.
The Philippine National Police confirmed in a statement that three people had died and several others had been wounded. The circumstances of the shooting remained under investigation.
South Cotabato Gov. Reynaldo Tamayo said the gunman’s best friend told officials that he was a member of a “true crime community.” Tamayo said authorities would investigate the claim.

An Iranian actress who won the best newcomer award at the Venice film festival has come under severe attack from the country’s authorities and state media after highlighting the plight of women in Iran in her acceptance speech.
Laleh Marzban last Saturday won the best actress award in the Orizzonti sidebar competition for emerging talent, for her role in Mohsen Gharaei’s Falling House, a film revolving around three generations of women who are incarcerated in their own home by the family’s father.
At the awards gala, Marzban dedicated her prize to “the women of my country who have paid the highest price for even the smallest measure of freedom”. Speaking in Farsi, she added that Iranians were experiencing some of the most difficult days of their lives but should not lose hope.
On Thursday, the Supreme Council of the Cultural Revolution, a conservative-dominated government body appointed by Iran’s supreme leader, issued a statement condemning Marzban’s speech as “presenting a one-sided narrative of Iran’s proud society”.
Referring only to “recent statements and behaviour made at the Venice film festival”, it said reducing Iranian women to “the stereotypes desired by western circles […] is not in line with the awareness-raising mission and social commitment of art”.
The statement has come on the back of a raft of similarly worded attacks in state-affiliated Iranian media, some of which called for the actress to be disciplined by the regime.
Zahra Chekhmaghi, a journalist and presenter associated with the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB), called Marzban “a two-faced person, […] self-interested, hypocritical, despicable and miserable”, while another IRIB-affiliated media personality, actress Zhila Sadeghi, criticised Marzban for not dedicating her speech instead to the children killed in a US missile strike on an elementary school in Minab on 28 February.
On state TV IRIB, a Qu’ran expert said the actress had been “deceived by the enemy” and called on the government to not let her work in Iran. Another news agency, Student News Network (SNN), urged the ministry of culture to not let Marzban back into the country.
The Iranian reaction to Gharaei’s film and Marzban’s speech appears to mirror the pushback against another film that premiered on the Lido this year, Guardian-produced documentary NAZA, about Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza.
Prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu said this week he would seek new laws allowing Israel to strip citizenship from people who “smear” Israeli soldiers, escalating a campaign against NAZA’s directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.
Gharaei’s Falling House thematises the collapse of traditional patriarchal family structures in Iran, and men’s efforts to keep them in place by force. Marzban plays twentysomething Ensi, who announces to her family her plans to leave the country and pursue a modelling career in Turkey. In a desperate effort to assert his authority, her father Rashid (Farhad Aslani) locks Ensi and the other female members of the household in their rooms.
Asked after Falling House’s Venice premiere how the film would be received in Iran, Marzban said: “This question is very important for me as an actress, and as all other women in Iran, whether they be doctors, artists, whatever profession women can perform, we can only make one step at the time, one step towards our objective,” she said.
“I have made my small part. I have given my contribution. I really hope many other people can make small steps towards our common objective.”

‘Holy moly!’: Rare shark visit to Bedford Basin inspires shock and awe
Shark expert says basking sharks 'completely harmless'
It’s been a long time since swimming was encouraged in the Bedford Basin, but that didn’t stop one shark from making a rare and lengthy visit on Friday night.
"I have never seen a shark in the Bedford Basin before. That was a first," said Bedford resident John Calder.
Calder had nearly finished his commute home from work when he came across a crowd standing on the Shore Drive Bridge, which overlooks the basin where it meets the Sackville River.
“I got out of my car to see what was happening and lo and behold, there was two giant shark fins that were protruding from the water,” Calder said Saturday. “Right away, I said: 'Holy moly! That's a shark.'"
According to marine biologist and shark researcher Neil Hammerschlag, who reviewed multiple videos of the shark shared on social media, “it’s clearly a basking shark.”
“They pose no risk to humans, they eat little plankton, and they’re called basking sharks because they often spend time near the surface where they look like they’re basking in the sun,” said Hammerschlag, president of Atlantic Shark Expeditions.
The shark's habit of floating near the surface, combined with the fact that it is the second-largest fish in the world, made it easy to spot once it entered the basin.
However, finding one in such a busy waterway — surrounded by dozens of sailboats and densely populated shores — is highly unusual.
“I think this is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to see an animal this large so close to shore,” Hammerschlag said.
Shark spent hours in basin
While Calder watched the shark for only 15 minutes before it swam away, he described it as a moment where time stood still.
“You go about your day, and then all of a sudden there’s a shark, and it’s like everything stops, nothing else is important and you’re just watching mother nature,” he said.
Around 7:30 p.m., Calder's wife, Lisa McCloskey, and his 14-year-old stepdaughter, Audrey Hill, spotted the shark near a dock at the Bedford Basin Yacht Club.
“It seemed kind of surreal,” McCloskey said. “We could almost see our house in the distance, and then we’re watching this massive shark come out of the water and it came near us and almost rolled over so we saw its whole body as well ... it was magical.”
For nearly two hours, a growing crowd watched as the shark surfaced and submerged.
“There were probably like 30 or 40 of us, and people were hugging each other when they saw the shark,” McCloskey said. “It really felt like a community event. Everyone was chatting and it was really lovely.”
Hammerschlag said it remains unclear why the shark ventured into the basin. Basking sharks are far more common in open, plankton-rich waters like the Bay of Fundy.
The shark may have been unwell or disoriented, Hammerschlag said, but “unless it washes up on shore,” there's no way to know for sure.
“Either way, it’s a remarkable encounter, and this is a beautiful animal, completely harmless to people, and whoever had the opportunity to see it should consider themselves lucky.”

Days after the guidelines related to the 0.4% Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on Unified Payments Interface (UPI) payments above ₹2,000 were issued, the traders and associations in Ghaziabad are concerned lot and contemplating action starting October 15.

Arteta vows Arsenal will learn from chastening Brighton defeat
BRIGHTON, England, Sept 19 : There were no excuses from Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta after his side's perfect start to their Premier League title defence came to an ignominious end at Brighton & Hove Albion on Saturday with a stunning 3-0 defeat in which they were out-hustled by their hosts.
Arsenal won their opening four games of the league season, conceding just a single goal, but were undone by a superb Brighton performance that sees them move up to third in the table with 10 points from their five games.
Arsenal dropped to second place on goal difference with 12 points from five games as they suffered their heaviest defeat in all competitions since a 3-0 home loss to Brighton in May 2023.
Brighton took the lead following a superb strike from Pascal Gross as the ball went in off the post. Charalampos Kostoulas then finished from 25 yards and Chema Andres headed home a corner to add a third goal.
“They deserved to win the game, they were the better team, especially in the early stages of the first half. We were not competing on the level that is required,” Arteta said. "We did technical errors in the wrong areas and lost our duels.
“But I have to put into perspective what the team has done since the World Cup. I think it has been exceptional. We will learn from this experience and go again.”
Brighton’s success was built on pressing Arsenal into submission and giving them little time on the ball, denying them control of the game.
Arteta’s side were poor as a result, but that was also due to Brighton’s bravery and in the final third the home side were clinical, taking their Premier League tally to 16 goals in five games this season.
Given that no other side has scored more than 10, free-scoring Brighton have emerged as one of the best teams to watch so far this season.
The visitors were also uncharacteristically poor defending set-pieces and might have lost by a greater margin on another day.
“It was the perfect performance from us,” Andres said. “The team was amazing, the intensity was what we needed to win against this amazing team.
“It was my first Premier League goal and an important moment in the match for us to go 3-0 up. You cannot say it is game over against players of the quality of Arsenal, but the team kept pushing for the win.”

An AI tool is set to start advising air traffic controllers on managing air traffic in the congested airspace above the Washington, DC, area. The expected launch would be the first step toward a planned nationwide rollout covering the 29 million square miles of US national airspace overseen by the Federal Aviation Administration.
The FAA describes the SMART system as using AI models to predict air traffic flows and identify potential conflicts based on operational factors like airline schedules, weather, airport capacity, and airspace conditions. US government and industry officials told The Wall Street Journal that SMART could debut for the three major airports in the Washington, DC, area as soon as Monday, September 21.
The decision to launch SMART in limited scope before going nationwide is the “right call,” said Philip Mann, principal consultant at Vector Strategic Consulting LLC, where he advises on aviation safety and AI governance. Mann previously worked at the FAA in multiple roles for 17 years.
“SMART’s risk was never any single prediction—it is a national-scale system with AI components carrying more unknowns than anything the FAA has fielded,” Mann wrote in an email to Ars. “Every cut in scope shrinks the unknowns.”
The AI-driven forecasts and recommendations are meant to give the FAA, airlines, and aircraft operators the same shared view of operational conditions so that they can agree on the most efficient routes and departure times. The goals of SMART include reducing aircraft fuel burn, improving on-time performance for flights, and speeding up recovery from weather and air traffic congestion events.
However, the airline industry was reportedly confused for weeks about the agency’s plans to deploy the AI tool, according to Politico. Anonymous airline officials told Politico that their concerns only eased after the FAA said the SMART AI tool would not change any procedures for air traffic controllers or airlines, and would instead produce “alternative route information” that is made available through existing FAA systems.

Vijayawada man Sai Krishna beaten to death in police custody, cremated same night: SIT
The SIT officials identified the cement platform No. 16 in the crematorium as the spot where the cremation had taken place
The Special Investigation Team (SIT) of the Andhra Pradesh police probing the mysterious disappearance of 25-year-old Gade Sai Krishna in Vijayawada in May, has confirmed that he was beaten to death by the Krishnalanka police at an abandoned building on May 12, people familiar with the matter said on Saturday.
After confirming that Sai Krishna had died, the police clandestinely took his body to the Swargapuri crematorium near the Krishnalanka police station and cremated it the same night, the SIT authorities told a local court in Vijayawada on Friday.
The SIT officials identified the cement platform No. 16 in the crematorium as the spot where the cremation had taken place. “We collected ash and bone remains from the site for further examination,” the SIT informed the court.
The SIT, headed by inspector general of police M Ravi Prakash and comprised West Godavari superintendent of police Adnan Naveen Asmi, Alluri Sitarama Raju SP Amit Bardar and Bapatla additional SP L Sudhakar as members, was constituted on June 21, after the missing of Sai Krishna triggered a state-wide outrage.
On June 23, the SIT arrested Krishnalanka inspector of police SSV Nagaraju and on June 29, two head constables, Potharlanka Ashok Kumar and Jangam Nani, surrendered before the SIT authorities. All the three were suspended pending investigation.
On Friday, the SIT produced the fourth accused Gulivundala Suresh, a close associate of Nagaraju, before the Second Additional Judicial Magistrate Court, Vijayawada.
The SIT charged Suresh, a real estate broker, with helping Nagaraju and the head constables in shifting Sai Krishna’s body to the crematorium and later bringing pressure on the deceased’s family members to withdraw the complaint as part of a compromise formula.
In the remand report presented before the court, which was reviewed by HT, Nagaraju and the two head constables confined Sai Krishna and subjected him to torture in an abandoned building at Ranigarithota, near the Varadhi area of Vijayawada.
The remand report stated that Suresh had allegedly witnessed Sai Krishna being questioned at the Krishnalanka police station on May 7 by then inspector Nagaraju and head constables Ashok and Nani. Suresh subsequently travelled to Nepal with his friends and returned to Vijayawada on May 11.
“On May 12 at around 10.30 am, Suresh went to the police station to meet Nagaraju. He was allegedly taken by Ashok Kumar to an abandoned building at Ranigarithota, where he found Sai Krishna in a severely weakened condition. The deceased told Suresh that he had been beaten every day since being brought to the building with the intention of killing him,” the SIT said.
Subsequently, Sai Krishna reportedly collapsed and became unconscious and on checking his pulse, the police realised that he had died. “On the night of May 12, the two head constables shifted the body to the crematorium on a motor bike, while Suresh accompanied them. They remained at the crematorium until the body was completely burnt,” the SIT report said.
After Sai Krishna’s family filed a habeas corpus petition in the Andhra Pradesh high court in June, Suresh acting on behalf of Nagaraju, allegedly approached Sai Krishna’s maternal uncle Navarang and pressured him to withdraw the petition.
“After Nagaraju was arrested and two head constables surrendered, Suresh went absconding and on the advice of his lawyers, he surrendered to the SIT on Thursday evening,” the report added.

In March this year, the American College of Cardiology (ACC) and the American Heart Association (AHA), both globally recognised premier organisations in cardiovascular medicine, handed down their newest dyslipidemia guideline, and gave universal Lipoprotein(a) screening in every adult a ‘Class I’ recommendation -- the strongest tier there is. The High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein (hsCRP) test got a lighter endorsement: checked selectively, alongside coronary calcium scoring, to sharpen risk estimates when they’re uncertain. These two long-debated biomarkers, were both freshly blessed by the field’s governing societies.
Then arrived the irony. On July 31, pharma major Novo Nordisk’s ziltivekimab — a drug built to block the inflammatory pathway behind elevated C-Reactive Protein (CRP) — fully hit its target in a Phase 3 clinical trial and still didn’t move the needle on heart attacks or strokes. Five weeks later, pelacarsenm, a drug that lowers high levels of Lp(a) failed the same way. Within six months of the guideline telling every clinician to start checking these numbers, the two flagship drugs built to act on them came up empty.
It’s a familiar shape for cardiology. Heart disease mortality fell almost every year through the back half of the last century — statins, blood pressure control, smoking cessation, better acute care — and that decline has visibly slowed this past decade, even as the drug arsenal has never been more sophisticated. LDL (’bad cholesterol’) is already driven remarkably low in anyone on a serious statin; medicine needed a new lever, and reached for the two candidates the guidelines had just endorsed. Neither has delivered yet.
What actually happened
On September 4, Novartis announced pelacarsen missed the primary endpoint of Lp(a)HORIZON, the first cardiovascular outcomes trial ever run for a drug built to lower lipoprotein(a). Pelacarsen is an antisense drug — a short, lab-made strand of genetic material injected monthly, designed to intercept the liver’s instructions for building Lp(a) before it’s ever made, rather than mopping up what’s already circulating. In 8,323 patients with established heart disease, it cut Lp(a) by roughly 80%. And yet, there was no reduction in heart attacks or stroke.
What we were taught
Lp(a) was drilled into me in medical school as one of the ‘unfair’ risk factors — a number you’re essentially born with, indifferent to diet or willpower, and loaded disproportionately onto South Asian patients, who as a population carry some of the highest mean Lp(a) levels of any group studied. It helped explain a pattern every cardiology rotation eventually shows you: South Asian patients with premature, multi-vessel disease and normal LDL numbers. That teaching isn’t wrong, and this trial doesn’t overturn it — Lp(a) is a real, heritable, biologically active risk factor. What it disputes is narrower: whether lowering it, this late and this fast, changes what happens next.
What Lp(a) actually is
Here’s the plain version of how a heart attack builds. LDL particles, commonly known as ‘bad cholesterol’ work their way into the artery wall and get stuck there. Once trapped, immune cells chemically alter them and swallow them up, ballooning into fat-filled ‘foam cells.’ Over years, those dying cells pile up into a fatty core, and the artery seals it off with a cap of scar-like tissue. When that cap eventually cracks or wears thin, a blood clot forms on top of it — that’s the heart attack.
Statins, ezetimibe, and the newer PCSK9-inhibitor injections all lower LDL through different mechanisms, but the trial data lines up the same way every time: about a 22% drop in heart attacks and strokes for every 39-point drop in LDL, no matter how you get there.
Lp(a) is an LDL particle with one extra piece stuck to it — a protein called apolipoprotein(a), built from the same molecular parts as the protein your body uses to break up blood clots. But it’s a decoy, not a copy: it fits into the same docking spots on a forming clot, without carrying the working part that actually gets activated into a clot-dissolving enzyme. So instead of helping to break clots down, it crowds out the real thing and makes clots a little harder to clear. That’s what makes Lp(a) different from LDL: it builds plaque the same way LDL does, but it also nudges the body toward clotting rather than away from it. And unlike LDL, your Lp(a) level is almost entirely set by your genes at birth — diet, exercise, and statins barely move it.
Why did the trial fail?
A floor effect: Mean background LDL in the trial was 66 mg/dL as most patients were already on aggressive therapy. Whatever risk Lp(a) adds on top of that may be smaller than older, less-treated cohorts suggested, offering little room for an 80% reduction to matter.
Too late in the game: Every patient entered with 50-plus years of Lp(a) exposure already built into their arteries. Lowering the level for three or four years in someone’s sixties, after a cardiac event, may be too late to undo a lifetime of exposure the genetic data actually measured.
This isn’t cardiology’s first time at this wall. The CANTOS trial suggested a decade ago that quieting the immune system could work, independent of cholesterol reduction. Hitting the biomarkers still doesn’t seem to be enough: Lp(a) may just be writing the newest chapter of the same story.
Back to basics
The interventions with the deepest trial evidence are still the boring ones: eat well, move, don’t smoke, stay lean. LDL, blood pressure, glucose, and tobacco remain the pillars with decades of reproducible data behind them.
Lp(a) will likely still matter — as a flag for who needs those basics enforced hardest, and maybe eventually as a target that is treated decades earlier than this trial tried. But for now, the fanciest number on the panel failed its biggest test, and the oldest advice in medicine didn’t.
No antisense drug, no anti-inflammatory antibody, has found a way around the same wall. In Greek mythology, Icarus didn’t fall because he was foolish — he flew exactly as high as anyone reasonably could, and the sun turned out to be closer than he’d been told. Despite everything medicine can now measure, alter and silence, the quest for a healthy long life perhaps rests on the same principles it has rested on for centuries: eat well, move well, sleep well.
(Dr. Dinesh Arab is director, interventional and structural cardiology, AdventHealth Daytona Beach and clinical assistant professor of medicine, Florida State University. dinarab@yahoo.com)

Yatsushiro, Kumamoto Pref. – A section on the Kyushu Shinkansen bullet train line that had been halted due to the impact of a major earthquake in Kumamoto Prefecture in late July returned to service on Friday.
All sections on the high-speed train line linking Hakata Station in Fukuoka Prefecture and Kagoshima-Chuo Station in Kagoshima Prefecture are now back to operations 52 days after the July 28 temblor, which measured up to 7, the highest level, on Japan’s seismic intensity scale.
Restarted on Friday was the section between Kumamoto and Shin-Minamata stations, both in Kumamoto Prefecture.
Kyushu Railway, or JR Kyushu, the operator of the line, said that trains will travel at a reduced speed of 70 kph on a section of about 10 kilometers near Shin-Yatsushiro Station, located between Kumamoto and Shin-Minamata stations, for the time being to ensure safe operations. The section sustained heavy damage from the earthquake.
Therefore, the number of the trains linking Kagoshima-Chuo and the Sanyo Shinkansen line will be reduced by 10% from the normal level. As the travel time between Kumamoto and Kagoshima-Chuo stations will be about eight minutes longer, the departure time at Kagoshima-Chuo will be moved up by up to nine minutes.
At Shin-Yatsushiro Station on Friday, passengers formed a long line from slightly after 6 a.m., waiting for the day’s first trains.
A 53-year-old male corporate worker from the city of Yatsushiro who commutes to the city of Minamata said: “The reopening (of the section between Kumamoto and Shin-Minamata stations) was earlier than I had expected. I’d like to express gratitude to those who worked hard for the restoration.”
One 17-year-old local student is using the line as an alternative route for commuting to the city of Kumamoto, where his high school is, because a train line he regularly uses is still being halted due to the impact of the quake.
He said that he now leaves his home 30 minutes later than usual. “I’m grateful because I don’t have to wake up early,” he added.
The Kyushu Shinkansen line was halted on all sections after the earthquake.
Services between Hakata and Kumamoto stations were resumed July 31, three days after the quake. The section between Shin-Minamata and Kagoshima-Chuo was reopened Aug. 7 while the number of trains in operation was reduced.
Operations between Kumamoto and Shin-Minamata stations had remained suspended, however, due to damage, including rail distorti.

The Department of Commerce (Aided) of Madras Christian College hosted its Global Alumni Meet on Saturday.

Arun Mammen, Vice-Chairman and Managing Director of MRF Limited, was the guest of honour. He urged alumni to act as a conduit between the corporate sector and academic institutions. Head of the Department Vijayakumari Joseph acknowledged the contributions of founders and senior professors.
A panel discussion involving alumni, faculty members, and students followed the inauguration. Alumni Matthew proposed the establishment of the Mr. Swaminathan Endowment Fund, and Rakesh Stanley reminisced about his college days. The meet concluded with cultural events and the lighting of candles by participants.

Aadhaar-issuing body, the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI), is working on a plan to take Aadhaar global, especially to enable non-resident Indians and overseas citizens of India, a senior official said.
UIDAI CEO Saurabh Vijay said his ambition is to make the Aadhaar infrastructure best in class to facilitate the platform's global expansion.
“I think for Aadhaar, the focus now is on making Aadhaar international. We really want to work on the interoperability part of it — how to make it more possible. So already some PoCs (proof of concept) are happening,” Vijay said during a fireside chat at Global Fintech Fest 2026.
“Our legal framework is also going (in that direction) to make Aadhaar international. We are working on policies to make it (available) for overseas citizens of India (OCIs) so that it brings in more investment.”
Currently, for Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) holding a valid Indian passport, the application process is highly accessible. The standard 182-day residency requirement is waived, allowing NRIs to apply immediately upon arrival.
However, there is no online alternative; applicants must still physically visit an authorised Aadhaar Enrolment Centre in India to complete the biometric verification.
But for the Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) cardholders, applying for Aadhaar is subject to stricter eligibility criteria. Currently classified alongside resident foreign nationals for Aadhaar purposes, OCI cardholders must physically reside in India for at least 182 days within the 12 months immediately preceding their application date.
Once eligible, they must submit their valid OCI card and foreign passport, along with applicable proof of an Indian address, during their in-person enrolment.
In the same event, Chairman Neelkanth Mishra said UIDAI is extensively deploying Artificial Intelligence (AI) to detect and counter fraud, as it seeks to outsmart fraudsters in the “cat-and-mouse game”.
"Fraudsters keep getting smarter, but we are also getting smarter," Mishra said. “UIDAI is using AI extensively for fraud detection.”
"So, in fact, well before it became a buzzword, we had liveness tests on face and thumbprints. It is a 'cat and mouse' game. So basically fraudsters keep getting smarter, but we are also getting smarter," he said.
Emphasising the rapid increase in Aadhaar usage, he said daily authentications had risen “dramatically” from about seven crore when he first wrote his comments for UIDAI's annual report, to 10 crore now.
UIDAI is preparing its infrastructure to handle 25-30 crore Aadhaar authentications a day, he highlighted.

Herpetologists first discovered in 1933 that rattlesnakes are immune to their own venom. Native to the Americas, rattlesnakes are pit vipers, a family of vipers with a heat-sensing pit organ between each nostril and eye.
Venom resistance in snakes comes in two forms: either the targets in their bodies have evolved such that the venom doesn’t attack them, like in cobras, or they possess specific molecules in their bloodstream that serve as “toxin sponges”, like in vipers, Sean B. Carroll, chair of biology at the University of Maryland, U.S., said.
In 1972, Japanese researchers discovered the first example of a so-called toxin sponge — a serum protein dubbed Fetuin-A — from Okinawa habu (Protobothrops flavoviridis), a pit viper endemic to the Ryukyu Islands. Fetuin-A could inhibit metalloproteinases, a class of venom toxins that could cause haemorrhage, damage tissue, and disrupt the coagulation system.
Metalloproteinases are the most abundant toxin family in rattlesnake venoms, and researchers have studied metalloproteinase inhibitors such as Fetuin-A in great detail. However, only recently did they discover that Fetuin-A belongs to a larger family of FETUA proteins.
In a 2022 paper, Dr. Carroll and his team identified four FETUA proteins from the western diamondback rattlesnake (Crotalus atrox).
Curiously, understanding the principles of venom resistance from C. atrox led the researchers to leverage these antitoxins, which had evolved over millions of years, for human benefit.
In a new study in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team at Maryland has shown that specific combinations of C. atrox FETUA proteins can fully neutralise rattlesnake venom lethality in mice, with roughly 10-times the potency of commercial antivenom.
‘String of surprises’
On discovering metalloproteinase-inhibiting FETUA-2, 3, 4, and 5 proteins from C. atrox, the research team studied their antivenom potency. By injecting various protein combinations preincubated with C. atrox venom into experimental mice, they found that some combinations successfully blocked haemorrhaging, while some even staved off death.
“Rattlesnake venoms have 10-15 different kinds of toxins,” Dr. Carroll said. “So it was entirely unexpected that just blocking metalloproteinases would block the lethality of the venom.”
The test results that followed were a “string of surprises”. Encouraged by the success of FETUA proteins against C. atrox venom, the team tried them against the eastern diamondback rattlesnake (Crotalus adamanteus), which proved successful. Then they tested them against two Asian snakes: the Malayan pit viper (Calloselasma rhodostoma) and the Chinese moccasin (Deinagkistrodon acutus). The proteins could protect against those as well.
The team then moved to candidates outside of pit vipers. Of the two true vipers they tested against, the proteins protected significantly against the Sochurek’s saw-scaled viper (Echis carinatus sochureki) — but none against the puff adder (Bitis arietans).
“Our surprises ran out, you could say,” Dr. Carroll said.
According to him, an antivenom needs potency and broad reactivity. And not only could these proteins recognise and neutralise the venom of a spectrum of distant species, when tested against CroFab, a commercial antivenom obtained from animals immunised with four pit viper venoms, including C. atrox, the proteins proved tenfold more potent.
The findings are a “real advance” for antivenom development, according to Kartik Sunagar, an associate professor at the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru; he was not involved in the study. “The paper shows convincingly that a combination of naturally evolved FETUA proteins can fully neutralise rattlesnake venom lethality by inhibiting metalloproteinases alone.”
However, Dr. Sunagar also pointed out that the study did not exactly measure clinical capacity.
“Every efficacy experiment premixed venom and inhibitor before injection,” he said. “So the study measures neutralising capacity, not treatment of an animal already envenomed, which is the clinically relevant scenario.”
Next-generation antivenom
According to Dr. Carroll, unlike lab-made compounds, FETUA proteins have been tested in nature.
“Rattlesnakes have evolved these proteins for 50 million years, with remarkable specificity and potency to inhibit their own venom, which gives me the sense that it is worth exploring,” he said.
Manufacturability and purity are added advantages, he added: “We can make recombinant FETUA proteins in the lab in unlimited quantities — whereas traditional antivenom requires animals to be immunised, and then the obtained antibodies have to be purified.”
Dr. Sunagar also shared the view that the recombinant and defined nature of FETUA proteins will help sidestep the low purity of animal-derived products.
While the study showed that these proteins can protect experimental mice from venom lethality, toxins other than metalloproteinases will have physiological effects on humans, Dr Carroll said: “What we don’t know is what else we will have to use in conjunction with these proteins to make an antivenom” for humans.
“FETUAs do nothing for the neurotoxins that dominate many medically important venoms,” Dr. Sunagar said. “The honest reading is that these proteins form the metalloproteinase-neutralising component of a next-generation antivenom, but it is not yet a standalone therapy.”
Dr. Carroll also said his team has found a new component that could aid human antivenom development, but did not elaborate on ongoing research.
Implications for India
In countries like India, which host both vipers and elapids such as cobras, FETUA proteins alone cannot provide a complete antivenom solution, Dr. Carroll said.
Although the study revealed partial protection against saw-scaled vipers (Echis carinatus sp.), one of India’s ‘Big Four’ and a major cause of death and disability, partial cross-reactivity need not translate into clinical protection, Dr. Sunagar added.
But India’s bigger takeaway is the strategy: “The logical path for India is to identify and test FETUAs from our own vipers rather than relying on rattlesnake versions, and to pair them with agents covering the neurotoxic elapids the FETUAs cannot touch,” according to Dr. Sunagar.

In a first, top European design prize awarded to €20 uniform for China’s delivery drivers
Developed with the assistance of Jack Ma, designers aimed to bestow dignity on the drivers, an ‘important profession’, the lead designer says
Taobao Instant Commerce, Alibaba’s on-demand delivery service that was revamped last year and is known as Taobao Shangou in Chinese, won a top French Design Award prize on Saturday for its delivery worker uniform, marking the first time the prize was awarded for a design for frontline workers.
“We think the [Taobao Shangou] suit design would transform delivery workwear into a recognisable professional uniform, helping reshape how society sees this essential profession,” said Dario Olivero, chair of the award’s organising committee.
For the team that designed the uniform, the idea started with a discussion they had last year with Jack Ma, the founder of Alibaba Group Holding, said Yang Tao, the lead designer of the city rider suits.
“Delivery riders … have become an important profession in China. Chefs wear uniforms, flight attendants wear uniforms – so why wasn’t there a professional uniform designed specifically for riders?” Yang said while accepting the award.

He again tried to interact with the contestants, but his health started deteriorating. In the promo for Sunday's episode, we see Salman in extreme pain, and the contestants tell him to take a break. The promo ends with Salman lying down on stage.
Soon, videos of the episode and the promo went viral on social media, and Salman took to his Instagram Story to clarify that he is fine. The actor wrote, "Nothing is wrong with my health by the grace of God. The Bigg Boss promo should not have been cut like the way it was cut.
