Salman Khan Takes Off His Shirt
While talking about him getting age-shamed and body-shamed, Salman got angry and took off his shirt and showed his body. He also slammed paparazzi for clicking pictures and videos of actresses from behind despite being told not to do so. He also mentioned that the paps clicked his own niece from behind. The actor was very upset about social media trolling and spoke about it for a long time.

As Zach Cregger puts audiences in the player’s POV with Resident Evil, Austin Abrams had to begin with Level One.
The actor admitted he wasn’t familiar with the Resident Evil video games or movies before taking the lead in Cregger’s adaptation, now playing in theaters, explaining the horror gaming genre “really goddamn rocks your nervous system.”
“Not that I was like an anti-fan,” explained Abrams. “The movies, I haven’t seen, and the games were something that just felt too frightening to engage with. I mean that genuinely. I remember playing Dead Space, a very different game, but kind of a similar vibe, and literally just panic playing the beginning of it and being like, ‘I can’t do this.'”
After Cregger recounted filming a stunt that “would’ve killed” Abrams if it had gone wrong, the actor admitted the experience was also “harrowing” for him, running down a snow-covered road as zombies jumped off roofs and splattered on the pavement around him.
Watch on Deadline
Following his work with Cregger on last year’s horror hit Weapons, Abrams was “very grateful” to reunite with the horror auteur and work together to build the role of Brian, an original character that did not appear in the games.
“One, you don’t wanna fuck up the shot,” Abrams said. “Also, you don’t wanna make a wrong move or something goes wrong. So, it’s kind of scary each time.”
“It was definitely doing the best you can to create a person that feels tangible, and they have a gravity to them, and also you understand them,” he said. “So, there was definitely a process there of discovering that, and also just who do you want to see in this situation. Because it was just kind of an avatar that, when I think of that word, I think of like a blank slate almost. That’s not necessarily interesting to see, and so it was, who do you want to see go through this? That was kind of a guiding light a little bit too.”
Read on about Austin Abrams’ starring role in Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil, now in theaters.
DEADLINE: I love seeing you and Zach work on this together after Weapons. What was it like reuniting for Resident Evil?
AUSTIN ABRAMS: It was awesome, man. In a lot of ways, it was really interesting cause it kind of felt like we just picked up where we left off, even though it was a different project, and different character. But dude, I love Zach, I love working with him, I love what he makes. It was great, and [I’m] just very grateful that he would trust me enough to handle this project.
DEADLINE: Were you a fan of the Resident Evil games, or even the movies before?
ABRAMS: No, none of it. Not that I was like an anti-fan. … the movies, I haven’t seen, and the games were something that just felt too frightening to engage with. I mean that genuinely. I remember playing Dead Space, a very different game, but kind of a similar vibe, and literally just panic playing the beginning of it and being like, “I can’t do this.” Cause it really goddamn rocks your nervous system until you get used to it. But no, it was always something that was just like, when you’re a kid and you’re looking at an R-rated movie or something, you’re like, “God, that’s so scary,” and it feels like this big looming thing. That was essentially what this was for me. So, it wasn’t until coming into this project that I started to get familiar with them.
DEADLINE: Tell me about working with Zach to build your character Brian, because I know he said that Brian is kind of an avatar for him and how he would make these decisions. But also tell me about infusing the character with some of your sense of humor and comedic timing.
ABRAMS: Well, you can’t play an avatar, in terms of being a character. That’s just kind of a general idea, so it was definitely doing the best you can to create a person that feels tangible, and they have a gravity to them, and also you understand them. So, there was definitely a process there of discovering that, and also just who do you want to see in this situation. Because it was just kind of an avatar that, when I think of that word, I think of like a blank slate almost. That’s not necessarily interesting to see, and so it was, who do you want to see go through this. That was kind of a guiding light a little bit too.
DEADLINE: Tell me about his relationship with his girlfriend and how this news from her kind of impacts his whole fight for survival.
ABRAMS: He learns that someone he really is in love with, that also is someone that wants to go to the next level of their relationship. And I feel like Brian has been, up until this point, he seems a little bit incapable and scared of that. He essentially has this moment where this possibility of a huge life change where he would really need to step up in a real way, that I think he’s been avoiding up until when you see him. He’s kind of faced with that and terrified of that, and then he starts to go through this actual horror movie. We have all of our little issues in life or things that feel really big, but then when something real happens, when you almost die, when someone you love dies, when it’s actually like, all of this could end—well, all this will end, not could end, it will end, and it could end at any second. It puts everything into perspective. So, I think he gets kind of put into perspective and starts to realize, “What do I actually want?”
DEADLINE: What it was being immersed in Zach’s take on Raccoon City. Did you have a favorite creature that you had to fight?
ABRAMS: Practical sets are always great, so something like the sewer was a really cool practical set. I mean, that that guy in the trailer, the big man in the sewer was really kind of crazy to look at, ’cause he really looked like a real, just humongous dude. I mean, I don’t even know how tall that guy would have been, and then there’s another creature that’s a little funnier, kind of towards the end. It’s kind of hilarious and really kind of surprised me.
DEADLINE: I’m also curious about shooting a lot of these stunts. I know Zach said the one with the falling zombies, if you would have made one wrong step, it could have been disastrous. What was it like for you filming that one?
ABRAMS: I would say, it’s harrowing, man. I mean, if you imagine yourself; I’m gonna run this way, and they’re gonna call action, and I need to do it at a certain pace, so that everything goes well and goes right, and also you need to not slip, and the ground is all wet, with this kind of combination of some real snow, but then the fake snow or whatever, you’re just in sneakers that don’t have any grip, and there’s these things falling. One, you don’t wanna fuck up the shot. Also, you don’t wanna make a wrong move or something goes wrong. So, it’s kind of scary each time.
DEADLINE: It looks awesome though. After doing Whalefall also, do you prefer working in snow or working in a water tank?
ABRAMS: I mean, working in water is pretty fun. A lot of Whalefall was working in like a small amount of water. It wasn’t like a lot. A lot of it wasn’t working directly in water, it was kind of like a little kiddie pool. But when you’re fully in water with the suit on and everything, that’s nice. But also I love the aesthetic of a horror movie with snow, like The Shining. It’s just really something that’s beautiful, that really gives a feeling to me, kind of like, you shouldn’t be outside. You see it, you see the character, and you know where you wanna be. You wanna be inside next to a fire with a cat, watching a movie or reading a book or something. It just adds a whole other element, this person should not be out here doing this right now, that I think is just really enjoyable to watch.
DEADLINE: What do you think about your “scream king” status? It seems like you’ve really solidified that with Tragedy Girls, Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark and Weapons.
ABRAMS: I don’t really have any feelings about that, one way or the other. I guess that’s just kind of an idea and a concept, so nothing really strong comes to mind. You’re just doing the work that feels interesting at the time, especially working with Zach and doing two back-to-back, basically. But no, I don’t have too many thoughts around that. Things will all ebb and flow. It’s not a goal in mind, at least.

Not every red-carpet look can be a winner.
Throughout 2026, we've seen celebrities wear showstopping ensembles at the Met Gala, Oscars, Grammy Awards, and more. Fashion is part of the job.
Unfortunately, some A-listers opted for ill-fitting suits, confusing sets, and overwhelming gowns at such red-carpet events.
Here's what's missed the mark so far this year.
Kate Hudson wore a two-piece set that needed tailoring in January.
She wore the Nina Ricci ensemble for a BAFTA Tea Party hosted in Beverly Hills. It comprised extra-long black trousers, a sheer, long-sleeve turtleneck tucked in, and a tan bralette underneath.
The outfit's color palette suited Hudson, and her see-through shirt was a fun choice. Still, her pants were so oversized that they distracted from the overall look.
Jenna Ortega attended the Golden Globes in a dress that overwhelmed her.
Dilara Findikoglu designed her black Golden Globes gown, which had a high neckline, a floor-length skirt, torso cutouts, and fringe at the shoulders.
While the lower half of the outfit looked chic on Ortega, the top half was too overpowering for her petite frame. A different neckline could have improved the look.
Sombr's outfit at the Grammys had potential, but it ultimately fell flat.
The musician hit the Grammys red carpet in a custom Valentino set. It included skinny, silver trousers covered in sequins and a matching blazer, which he wore open over a lace top.
The latter piece was unique and stood out on the red carpet. Unfortunately, his suit did the same, but for the wrong reasons. It looked more like a costume than a high-fashion ensemble.
Miley Cyrus wore one too many layers at the same event.
The musician, who is known for her daring style, wore Celine in the form of black barrel trousers and a white button-up blouse.
The classic outfit could have worked for Cyrus if she'd gone without her puffy leather jacket. It restricted the neckline of her top and was decorated with too many large gold brooches.
Lauren Sánchez Bezos probably should have picked a different dress for a pre-Oscar dinner.
As Chanel hosted the dinner, Sánchez Bezos wore a Karl Lagerfeld design from the fashion house's spring 1986 collection.
The gown's ruched bodice with a single sleeve and leather belt looked fine, but its matching skirt was too long. Some simple tailoring to make it shorter and give it shape would have improved the look.
It made for one of Sánchez Bezos' worst looks this year.
Kevin O'Leary attended the Oscars in March, and his outfit was odd.
The businessman wore a dramatic Dolce & Gabbana set that featured skinny trousers, a satin shirt, and a robe-style jacket printed with scenes in silver.
The top of his Oscars outfit looked too much like sleepwear, and his main accessory — a graded NBA trading card worn as a necklace — didn't make sense.
Heidi Klum's yellow gown at the Vanity Fair Oscar Party missed the mark.
Chrome Hearts designed the supermodel's gown, which had a halter neckline, a form-fitted bodice, and sheer panels across the chest, hips, and legs.
The latter detailing made the dress look incomplete, and its pale-yellow color washed out Klum.
Chrissy Teigen should have worn a different top when she attended the Fashion Trust US event in April.
She posed on the pink carpet wearing a yellow feathered skirt, neon-orange pumps, and a white structural tank top that sat above her torso rather than against it.
The white piece and her black clutch didn't match the outfit's vibrancy. The same top in a brighter color, maybe the same orange as her shoes, would have made it more cohesive.
Ben Stiller's Met Gala ensemble was lackluster.
For the "Costume Art" gala, where the dress code was "Fashion is Art," Stiller wore a standard suit with a white shirt and an orange tie, a nod to the New York Knicks.
The outfit might have worked at a standard red-carpet event, but it wasn't the right choice for the Met Gala. He missed the theme entirely.
Cardi B might be a Met Gala icon, but her 2026 look didn't work.
She wore a Marc Jacobs gown that was crafted from black lace over tan, pink, purple, and orange fabric.
It hugged most of her body except at the feet and shoulders, where the fabric was gathered into puffy bunches. The outfit had no clear meaning, and it looked strange on the red carpet.
Hudson Williams made his Met Gala debut, but it disappointed.
The "Heated Rivalry" star wore Balenciaga in the form of a baby-blue suit with black velvet detailing and a train attached at the waist.
It seemed like Williams was going for a daring look, especially since he chose to forgo a shirt. Unfortunately, the outfit looked unfinished, and his makeup was too strong.
Drew Barrymore's outfit at the Tony Awards in June didn't suit her.
Balenciaga designed her three-piece ensemble for the Tonys. It featured a baggy white top with a train, high-waisted trousers, and elbow-length white gloves.
Each piece looked a little too big on Barrymore, and the pants made her outfit look too casual. Swapping the latter for a skirt might have made it better.
Shaun Ross should have worn a different coat for the BET Awards.
The model and musician aimed to honor Missy Elliot with his pleather, full-length coat from the Chinese fashion brand Annakiki.
The coat, however, didn't look much like the one she wore in "The Rain (Supa Dupa Fly)" music video, so the meaning was lost on the red carpet.
Its uniquely shaped hood also distracted from the rest of the piece.
Dwight Howard should have made one simple swap for his ESPYS outfit.
The basketball player chose a black satin suit for the awards ceremony, which looked sleek on the red carpet and paired well with his gold jewelry.
Still, the pleated pants he chose, which flared at the ankles, looked a bit too short for his tall frame. Looser-fitting trousers would have suited the outfit better.
Shailene Woodley's outfit for the Emmys was the wrong choice.
She wore a Balenciaga set that comprised embellished gold trousers and a loose-fitting blue halter top with a plunging neckline. The actor also wore a colorful gemstone necklace, an updo hairstyle, and burgundy leather gloves.
While Woodley became an Emmy winner, taking home the outstanding guest actress in a drama series award, her outfit wasn't as successful.
She should have ditched the accessories and worn a more form-fitting top.

NEW DELHI: Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar on Friday announced that Tulu, spoken in the state's Dakshina Kannada and Udupi districts, would be recognised as an additional administrative language in the region, fulfilling a long-standing demand."Today, we have decided to make Tulu applicable to Udupi and Dakshina Kannada districts and declare it the state’s second additional administrative language," Shivakumar told reporters after a marathon cabinet meeting in Mangaluru.According to a cabinet note shared by the chief minister’s office, Tulu would be Karnataka’s "second additional administrative language" in Dakshina Kannada and Udupi.The 2011 national census recorded more than 18 lakh native Tulu speakers in Karnataka, whose population was recorded at over six crore at the time. Kannada is the state's most-widely spoken and its primary official language.This was also the first time a cabinet meeting was held in Mangaluru and not in Bengaluru.
Eye on BJP's coastal bastion
The political significance of Shivakumar taking his cabinet to Mangaluru becomes clearer against the BJP's electoral dominance in the region.Coastal Karnataka, particularly Dakshina Kannada and Udupi, has long been one of the BJP's strongest pockets in the state.
In the 2023 Karnataka assembly election, BJP won 11 of the 13 seats across the two districts, taking all five seats in Udupi and six of the eight in Dakshina Kannada. The Congress won only two constituencies.This was despite Congress sweeping to power across Karnataka with 135 seats, against 66 for the BJP.The BJP's hold remained intact in the 2024 Lok Sabha election. It won both parliamentary seats covering the region, with Brijesh Chowta defeating Congress's Padmaraj R by over 64,000 votes in Dakshina Kannada. Kota Srinivas Poojary won Udupi-Chikkamagaluru by more than 2.5 lakh votes.The BJP responded to the Tulu announcement by alleging that Shivakumar was "peddling soft Hindutva to make a dent in the BJP’s vote bank.""Shivakumar has never made any secret of his firm belief in Hinduism and frequently visits temples, performs rituals publicly and quotes scriptures. He is now peddling soft Hindutva. This was also evident from his rendition of 'Namaste Sada Vatsale' inside the Karnataka assembly," a BJP leader told PTI, referring to an August 2025 incident in which Shivakumar sang a few lines of the RSS anthem.The RSS is the BJP's ideological mentor.But there is a political twist to the Tulu issue itself. The BJP had previously taken up the demand while in power in Karnataka.In January 2023, the then BJP government led by Basavaraj Bommai constituted a committee to examine granting Tulu the status of a second official language in the state, months before the assembly election.
More than just Tulu
Significantly, Shivakumar’s announcements went beyond granting Tulu the status of a second administrative language.The Cabinet meeting in Mangaluru marked the Shivakumar government’s first meeting outside Bengaluru, the state capital. Shivakumar claimed the move was intended to recognise the region’s contribution and address its development needs.
The chief minister added that a draft notification would soon be issued to invite public feedback on renaming the Dakshina Kannada district to Mangaluru district.He also announced a host of policies for the coastal Karnataka region, introducing a dedicated tourism policy for the coastal areas to treats tourism projects as infrastructure initiatives while offering investors special incentives and extended loan repayment windows.Additionally, the government approved the Karnataka Marine Biotechnology Policy, 2026-31, which paves the way for upgrading the existing fisheries college into the Fisheries, Marine and Blue Economy University and expanding its student intake from 60 to 200 seats.Beyond these policies, the administration unveiled new urban development planning, fisheries sector incentives, and major financial allocations totaling around Rs 32,611 crore—split evenly between rural development and regional growth for Mangaluru, Udupi, and the coastal region.The announcements further included plans to hold decentralised Cabinet meetings across 10 to 12 locations in the state over the next 15 months and the sanctioning of a new medical college worth approximately Rs 450 crore for the region.

The average price of rice in Japan fell below ¥3,000 for the first time since early September 2024, the agriculture ministry said Friday.
Across around 1,000 supermarkets, a 5-kilogram bag of rice cost ¥2,971 in the week leading up to Sunday, down ¥32 from a week before and the fifth straight week that prices have dropped.
Rice prices had been rising since the summer of 2024, when a supply shortage triggered what became known as the Reiwa-era rice crisis. In January, the average price of rice was ¥4,416.
But supply-demand conditions have recently eased, reflecting the government’s release of rice from its stockpiles as well as increased production.
Lower rice prices benefit households. But with prices expected to fall further, farmers are concerned that they may fail to cover production costs.
Agriculture minister Kazuo Yana has voiced concern over the issue.
“The situation is becoming extremely difficult and simply unacceptable for farmers trying to stay in business,” Yana said at a news conference on Friday.
The average price of brand rice, which accounts for 85% of total sales volume, fell ¥35 to ¥2,988, while that of relatively cheap blended rice fell ¥34 to ¥2,866.
Rice harvested in 2025 and sold to wholesalers in August fell in price month on month for the first time in two months. The average price for 60 kg of unmilled rice stood at ¥31,556, down ¥930 from the previous month. The figure is the average of transaction prices between wholesalers and rice buyers dealing with farmers.
Rice prices in both retail and business-to-business transactions have been on a downward trend.

Mumbai: A 200-kg iron beam fell from the 13th floor of an under-construction building near the Kanjurmarg police station’s externment department on September 18, narrowly avoiding a major accident. Fortunately, no one was injured in the incident.
Police Book Contractor And Safety Supervisors Over Negligence Allegations
Police have registered a case against KAMS Realtor’s site contractor Mitesh Jain, site engineer Dhanraj Ramchandra Jagtap, and safety supervisors Vikram and Sohel Mirza for allegedly failing to take adequate safety precautions at the construction site.
According to the FIR, Assistant Police Sub-Inspector Vishwas Dashrath Desai, 56, who was posted with the externment department, was on day duty on September 18. The department’s office is located next to the construction site of KAMS Realtor.
Beam Falls Near Office Entrance During Afternoon Hours
Police said that small stones, gravel and iron rods had allegedly fallen near the office from the construction site on several occasions. The contractor had reportedly been warned about the issue by the police.
At around noon, Desai was working on a computer inside the office when he heard a loud noise. On rushing outside, he found a massive iron beam, weighing approximately 200 kg, lying directly in front of the office entrance. The beam had fallen onto a tree and the tin roofing of the office.
Workers at the construction site reportedly told the police that the iron beam had fallen from their site.
No one was injured in the incident, but the impact damaged the office’s tin roofing. Police have registered a case under relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), alleging acts that endangered the lives and personal safety of others. Further investigation is underway.

Cairns man dedicates his life savings to helping local kids thrive
In short:
Cairns man Rob Hodge invested his own money and passion into creating a program to help at-risk youth.
Fresh Start Academy trains young people in mechanics and barbering to set them on a better path for the future.
What's next?
After securing trial funding, Mr Hodge hopes to secure long-term support following a successful first semester of mechanics.
After almost three decades working with at-risk young people through government departments, Rob Hodge found there were limits when working to change things.
He said it felt like there was a philosophy that young people came with risks, and those needed to be contained.
"It was really tough to be able to provide young people opportunities,"
In the Cairns community, he said it was hard convincing people to care.
So, Mr Hodge left his "fairly comfortable government job" and took his own risk, building a program with his own hands, money and family.
He founded Fresh Start Academy, which works with young people, including those considered "at-risk" by the youth justice department.
"My life savings has gone into this," he said.
Participants learn practical trade skills on the job, with the group offering a barbering course initially and now adding mechanics, and 24 young people attending each semester.
"If we get them early and if we provide a learning space for them that invigorates them, that's the real truth to sustainable diversion," Mr Hodge said.
The program has now received $300,000 in funding until January next year through the state government's Kickstarter program.
Half of Mr Hodge's students are kids aged 15-to-17-year-old who are "disengaged" with school or considered at risk of entering the justice system.
Purpose and pride
The latest Queensland Crime Report, released in June, found Far North Queensland had the highest number of serious repeat youth offenders.
They are young people who authorities say often influence other kids to offend.
However, Mr Hodge said his experience taught him while punishment had a place, purpose and pride created lasting change.
"We have young people who have been kicked from pillar to post from the time that they were born," he said.
"They've grown up knowing that they're the have-nots."
In an earlier barbering program, Mr Hodge watched teens change how they viewed themselves after seeing smiles on customers' faces.
"If they don't have physical gifts that can change their position, then it's only temporary," he said.
Inside the workshop
Fresh Start Academy program coordinator, and Mr Hodge's son, Traye, said the program was a "win-win" for community members who donated their cars to get fixed.
"It's a full free service by our fully qualified mechanic here, and our young people are getting a chance to really learn hands-on," he said.
The teenagers attend the program twice a week, obtaining a certificate in Automotive Vocational Preparation, while working directly with cars.
The program also uses the interactions to encourage school-aged students to engage with other forms of education.
Since the first semester, four young people have gone on to apprenticeships, and another four are continuing their studies at TAFE.
Some young people, including 16-year-old Robert Cutmore, join the program, not because they are "at risk" or involved with the justice system, but so they can try learning away from a classroom.
Robert said school "just wasn't really working", and said he struggled to sit still and absorb information from the board.
"It's more of a one-on-one thing for me, hands-on work like here at Fresh Start," he said.
Since starting the program, Robert's mentors said he had become one of their best students.
He has now applied for apprenticeships and said he has found a future in mechanics.
Immeasurable benefits
Youth Advocacy Centre chief executive Katherine Hayes said programs like Mr Hodge's were "exactly what we should be supporting" to address juvenile crime.
She said grassroots, early intervention programs built skills like turning up, accountability and confidence, which were harder to measure but just as important.
"We're dealing with complex human beings here and it's not a conveyor belt of change," she said.
However, stigma remained a major barrier because young offenders were acutely aware of how they were perceived.
"I think it helps contribute to a sort of nihilism in their way of thinking that 'well, I've got nothing to lose'," Ms Hayes said.
She said most young people in the system were not violent offenders, and many had a chance of "coming out better" with support.

When Gloria Steinem’s plane touched down in Bombay in 1957, she could not have known that her stay in India would become what she later called a “pivotal, life-dividing event [that] made me who I am”.
She was 22, with a degree in government from Smith college and was travelling on a Chester Bowles fellowship.
India was “not only a place I’d always wanted to go, but (also) an escape from a very kind and tempting man to whom I was engaged and knew I shouldn’t marry,” Steinem later wrote. The prospect of marrying Blair Chotzinoff, a pilot from a well-connected New York family, depressed her “enormously because marriage meant the end of life to me”.
Funds were short, so she wangled a free airline ticket in exchange for an article “that I still feel guilty to this day because I never wrote”.
While in London waiting for her Indian visa, she discovered she was pregnant and obtained an illegal abortion – an experience that underpinned her conviction that, without control over reproduction, women could not control their own lives.
Steinem, who died this week at the age of 92, arrived in Delhi with romantic expectations of “ageless beauty and jewelled elephants”. They were quickly displaced. Driving from the airport, she had what she called her “first glimpse of Asian poverty”, seeing people sleeping on pavements and doorsteps.
She lived at Miranda House, one of Delhi University’s leading women’s colleges, immersing herself in student life.
“At night in our rooms we have long sessions and are asked everything: the Christians’ conception of God, the intricacies of western lingerie, the dating system, how much milk the American cow gives,” Steinem wrote.
Steinem’s Indian years have been extensively documented by Rashida Shafiq of Southern Methodist University, who drew on her fellowship reports and other archival material for a recently published PhD thesis.
She adopted the sari as everyday dress, writing: “Saris make one stand straighter and walk more slowly and worry less about time and efficiency.”
India was not entirely unfamiliar territory. Her mother and paternal grandmother had been Theosophists, part of a spiritual movement that drew heavily on Hindu and Buddhist ideas such as karma and reincarnation, and at college Steinem had written a paper on the Communist party of India.
When her fellowship money ran out, she supported herself by writing for Indian newspapers, doing advertising work and taking occasional modelling jobs – including posing in saris.
Wider travel in the country brought some of her most important encounters.
She met Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, the former princess and follower of Mahatma Gandhi who became independent India’s first health minister, and spent two hours with Indira Gandhi, whom she described as “shy to uncertainty, gentle and a little whimsical”.
At a Radical Humanist study camp in Mussoorie, followers of the former communist MN Roy debated democracy, individual freedom and political organisation. Steinem later said she learned there that “radical” need not mean violent or extremist, but could mean “going to the root,” and that “the means we choose dictate the ends we achieve”.
But some of her most lasting political education happened on the road.
On a journey from Calcutta to Kerala, Steinem travelled third class in a railway carriage reserved for women, which she later described as “a dormitory on wheels”.
Women settled in with children and food, nursing babies, sharing tiffins and talking. They wanted to know everything about her and conversations ranged across marriage, childbirth, contraception and family life. “Had I been isolated in a car, this talking circle could never have happened,” Steinem wrote later.
Years before American feminist “consciousness-raising” groups brought women together to discover that supposedly private problems were widely shared, Steinem had watched women in India exchange intimate experiences among themselves.
But the experience she regarded as most important came after caste violence erupted in what was then Madras state in 1957.
Steinem joined workers associated with the movement of Vinoba Bhave, a leading disciple of Gandhi, who were walking from village to village trying to counter rumours, discourage revenge and bring people together to talk.
She travelled with little more than “a cup, a comb and the sari I wore”.
In settlements scarred by violence, meetings were held beneath trees and in village courtyards.
“I listened as villagers narrated burnings, murders, thefts and rapes, with fear and trauma needing no translation,” she wrote.
The lesson was to listen before offering solutions. “Ask the people what they want, don’t tell them what they need,” was how Steinem later described it.
She remembered “the ancient and modern magic of groups in which anyone may speak in turn, everyone must listen and consensus is more important than time”.
“If you want to know how people live, you have to go where they live; if you want people to listen to you, you have to listen to them,” she later said. “I believe I learned that in India.”
Steinem returned to the United States in 1958, more than a decade before she became one of the leading figures in the women’s movement.
“I couldn’t integrate into the rest of my life these two very, very crucial years,” she recalled. “It was only after the women’s movement started that links began to be forged.”
She repeatedly connected her later organising methods with India. “The first organising I did was in India, though I didn’t realise it then,” she said.
Her years travelling across America as a feminist activist, she later wrote, were “just a western version of walking in villages”.
And when Ms. magazine, which Steinem co-founded, produced its spring 1972 preview issue, its cover featured an American housewife depicted as the many-armed Hindu goddess Kali, pregnant with her hands clutching a frying pan, duster, telephone, iron and other symbols of the domestic demands placed on women.
Steinem said the image “had come out of my Indian past”.

The latest GTA 6 content leak rabbit hole has taken fans straight back to GTA 5, revealing the unseen dialog from the game’s original Option A ending. Trevor Philips was apparently supposed to meet an even more horrifying fate.
The newly surfaced material comes from the enormous 192 GB batch of scrapped GTA 5 source code files that suggested GTA 6 may get Liberty City DLC. Recently, the enormous batch of files has been circulating publicly, and data miners continue to dig through the years-old development material.

Instead of Trevor crashing into an oil tanker, the leaked dialogue suggests that Rockstar originally considered having him slam into a truck filled with liquid nitrogen. The result would have been brutally fitting for Trevor, as he would freeze before shattering to pieces.

The GTA 5 and GTA 6 content leak goes far beyond these alternate possibilities. The whole archive reportedly contains cut GTA 5 content, early dialogue, vehicles, mission information, Agent Trevor, DLC assets, and possibly early GTA 6 files.
Fans should remember that most of the material originates from Rockstar’s 2022 security breach and was not newly created. The archive also reportedly contains evidence of a planned Liberty City expansion for GTA 5 alongside some low-quality GTA 6 map assets that resemble the areas shown in the game’s trailers.
These discoveries underline just how many ideas, characters, and storylines Rockstar explored before settling on GTA 5’s final form.

Trump Is Betting on the Wrong Europe
The far-right parties the White House favors have a foreign-policy agenda that won’t serve American interests.
Donald Trump says he wants a Europe that is more capable of defending itself. But the nationalist-populist movements he is championing there will not advance this agenda and may put Europe at odds with the United States over China.
Earlier this month, the nationalist-populist Alternative for Germany party came just a few seats short of an outright majority in a regional parliament, its best-ever result. This Sunday, Germans will vote in two more regional elections. The ruling Christian Democrats are behind in both races, and the AfD is expected to do well in one. On Wednesday, Chancellor Friedrich Merz canceled his visit to the United Nations General Assembly next week, sparking speculation that he could soon be forced to resign.
U.S. officials are ebullient. Trump greeted the AfD’s recent electoral victory with a triumphant message on Truth Social that finished with “MGGA” (Make Germany Great Again). Richard Grenell, Trump’s former ambassador to Germany and now a presidential envoy, called the result “a huge win and a new day in Germany.”
The Trump administration has consistently embraced Europe’s nationalist-populist parties as ideological partners, and even launched a State Department fund to support MAGA-aligned European groups. It surely sees the AfD’s ascendance as a sign that politics are moving in its direction. But that is true only if Trump’s real goal is a fragmented Europe that accommodates Russian and Chinese power and is unable to punch its weight. Such an outcome would be catastrophic for U.S. interests.
Some people in the administration insist that the idea is not to weaken Europe but to shift the burden for its conventional defense to the Europeans themselves. Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, for example, reject claims that the administration is soft on Russia and say that they are calling instead for greater European self-sufficiency. Colby advocates for what he calls NATO 3.0, in which Europeans would take on the primary responsibility for their conventional defense.
But the nationalist populists do not share this view. The AfD has called for an end to all arms deliveries to Ukraine and a lifting of all sanctions on Russia. Its co-leaders, Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, boycotted Volodymyr Zelensky’s speech to the Bundestag in 2024, dismissing the Ukrainian president as a “war and beggar president.”
In France, Marine Le Pen, the parliamentary leader of the nationalist-populist party National Rally and the front-runner for next spring’s presidential election, has promised to take France out of NATO’s integrated military command (France would remain a member of the alliance). Such a withdrawal would hardly help the Trump administration shift the burden of NATO’s defense to Europe.
The Trump administration’s affinity for Europe’s nationalist-populist right seems to be almost entirely cultural and civilizational, and based on the notion that Europe’s populists are fighting the same culture wars—including against immigration—as their counterparts in the United States. J. D. Vance explicitly praised then–Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán as an ally in defense of Western civilization at an election rally in Budapest on the eve of the Hungarian elections. And the Trump team seems to see the European populist right’s enemies—the European Union and national political establishments—as versions of its own domestic foes. This commonality appears to take precedence over foreign-policy concerns.
Trump officials have blasted centrist European governments for being too soft on Beijing but have said nothing about the populist right’s position on China. Some of these parties—particularly the AfD and Fidesz, in Hungary—favor much closer ties to the American adversary. The AfD’s Weidel lived in China for six years, speaks Mandarin, and wrote her doctoral dissertation about China’s pension system. Chrupalla, her co-leader, accused the German government of waging “economic war” against China for proposing a tougher trade policy toward Beijing. They have both called for warmer relations with China. Orbán, who was defeated in the Hungarian elections earlier this year, blocked the EU from criticizing Beijing, initiated an “all-weather comprehensive strategic partnership” with China, and welcomed Chinese investment in Hungarian infrastructure.
These largely transactional attitudes toward China and Russia may reflect a broader worldview among the nationalist populists, who praise Trump but are deeply skeptical of American power. In an analysis for the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Jeremy Cliffe argued that the AfD supports a multipolar world order and believes that great powers, such as China and Russia, should possess spheres of influence—a perspective that Trump seems sympathetic toward. The AfD, Cliffe wrote, “may regard Trump as a civilizational ally, but its senior figures have long described the United States as a raumfremd in Europe, a hard to translate German word that means something like ‘territorially alien.’”
If parties with these views take power, they could reduce American influence in Europe while making common European action on Russia and China much more difficult. They will also make Eastern Europeans nervous about German rearmament. In 2011, Radek Sikorski, Poland’s foreign minister, said, “I fear German power less than German inaction.” He recently revisited that remark, telling the German newspaper Handelsblatt, “We want Germany, under democratic leadership and as the largest economy in Europe, to play a strong role in securing our common security. But we remember all too well where a rearmed Germany can lead in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party—and that is exactly what the AfD represents.”
Senior Trump-administration officials say they are building a Europe that will carry its own weight. Maybe they are so beguiled by the nationalist populists’ domestic agenda that they have not yet realized it will come at the expense of NATO 3.0. Or maybe Trump doesn’t care about Europe’s defense, doesn’t see it as a U.S. interest, and doesn’t believe that Europe has any contribution to make to America’s security.
Trump and Vance seem to be laying the foundation for a more divided Europe that is incapable of deterring Russia, ever more dependent on China, and at odds with itself. If the administration continues on this path, it may get the European culture war it wants, but the United States will lose its ally.

MS NOW, CNN journalists denied entry to the White House after Trump’s ban
‘MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy,’ the outlet said
Reporters for MS NOW and CNN said the White House turned them away Saturday morning, a day after President Donald Trump announced plans to block the network and other news outlets from the complex.
“CNN reporter Betsy Klein was denied access at the White House on Saturday morning and her press pass was seized,” the organization said.
This move heightens Trump’s ongoing efforts to limit reporting by media members he opposes, representing a new challenge to First Amendment freedoms in the U.S.
On Friday, Trump announced he was barring the channel, as well as CNN and Politico, from the White House over what he labeled hostile coverage and "fake news."
In a statement, MS NOW said it fully supports its journalists.
"The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars," the network stated in a release Saturday.
"MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy."
On Friday, Trump wrote on Truth Social, “effective immediately,” the president would be “banning Fake News CNN, MSNOW ... and Politico ... from the White House as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS.”
“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America. Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” he added.
It remained uncertain Saturday morning if CNN reporters were likewise prohibited from entering the White House.
Correspondents from that network are normally on site during weekends when the president is located in Washington or at nearby Camp David.
Trump is visiting the Maryland retreat this weekend.
Politico reporters do not typically cover the White House on Saturdays.
It’s unclear what, if anything, specifically led to the president’s outburst, but Trump has had a years-long feud with CNN dating back to his first campaign for the presidency and his first term in the White House. And in an unrelated Oval Office press availability, he doubled down shortly after.
The president does not actually possess the authority to arbitrarily ban entire outlets from the White House based on the content those outlets publish.
Not only does the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution protect the right of journalists to report without government interference, but a 1977 District of Columbia Circuit Court case, Sherill v. Knight, states that “bona fide journalists” cannot be denied access to White House press facilities except in cases when a journalist seeking a press credential to enter the White House “presents a potential source of physical danger to the President and/or his immediate family so serious as to justify his exclusion.”

A man has died after being bitten by a shark off Sorrento beach in Perth’s north.
Emergency services were called to the popular beach at about 10.30am on Friday after reports of a shark-related incident.
Western Australia police said a man had been bitten by a shark while swimming along the coast. He died as a result of his injuries, police said.
Emergency services, including water and air personnel, conducted an extensive search of the area. The swimmer’s body had not been found.
The Alkimos Surf Life Saving Club said Sorrento beach would remain closed until 12pm on Saturday. Locals were urged to stay out of the water until the beach was declared safe for swimming.
The City of Wanneroo closed all other beaches along its coastline until 12pm on Saturday.
The local state MP, Liam Staltari, extended his condolences to the man’s family, friends and loved ones.
“Like all locals and people from across WA, I’m deeply saddened by the tragic death of a man following today’s shark attack at Sorrento beach,” he said.
“Our entire community is thinking of you at this incredibly difficult time.”
A witness, Darrel Haythornthwaite, told 7News that he could not believe the incident had occurred, “especially in a place like this”. He said the man’s friend, who was swimming with him, made it back to shore but was inconsolable.
“He felt bad because he didn’t go back to save his mate and I said, ‘Nah you couldn’t have done that’,” he told the outlet. “There’s nothing that anyone could have done.”
Another witness, Ingrid Mitchell, told 9News she swam at the beach every day and did not expect sharks to attack outside of dawn and dusk.
“There was other swimmers in there … just near the seaweed, and there was one poor girl there who was sun-baking, and she saw the whole lot as well,” she said.
A third witness, Jacqui Rapaic, told the ABC she was walking along the beach with a friend when the incident occurred.
“My friend said, ‘Jac, I think there’s been a shark attack’ and I looked out to the ocean and I could see a pool of blood,” she said.
“I hugged onto my friend … [we] felt rather traumatised at that point. It happened so quickly.”
The fatality followed a shark attack on Monday at the remote Glenfield beach, north of Geraldton on WA’s mid-west coast, which left a surfer with serious injuries.
He was taken to the nearby Geraldton health campus and was in a stable condition.

Can an AI chatbot save lives by answering texts about pregnancy?
It started with an accident.
A network of clinics for pregnant women in Kenya set up an automated text messaging service to send out appointment reminders. But when the moms received the texts, they started to write back.
Some asked if it's safe to eat avocados during pregnancy (you can!). Others asked if certain symptoms they were experiencing, like swelling or headaches, are normal during pregnancy.
"At the time I joined I think we were getting less than 100 questions a day," recalls Jay Patel, director of technology for Jacaranda Health. "Now it's 15,000."
At first, Jacaranda hired nurses to answer questions one by one. But over the years since 2020, developers have created a program that uses artificial intelligence to understand patient's questions, prioritize them and flag when a user may need immediate medical care. It's called PROMPTS — and is used by patients visiting public clinics in 24 Kenyan counties.
For women without a smartphone, cell reception, or easy access to the internet, a text to PROMPTS may be the fastest way to get a question answered. Other times, it's a reliable way to determine if a long trip to a hospital is necessary.
"If a mom in a rural part of Kenya starts bleeding at 2 a.m., she can't just Google it," Patel says. "But this service runs completely over SMS. It's completely free to the user, and it's accessible to anyone who has a basic phone."
About 7% of messages are flagged by the system as potentially urgent. These are routed directly to a nurse.
"It bypasses all AI functionality and gets straight to the help desk, into a special queue," Patel says. "They can pick it up immediately, look at the mom's question history and call her."
That kind of quick response is critical in Kenya, where about 6,000 women die each year from childbirth or pregnancy-related causes. That's 16 women a day. Almost a third of those deaths are believed to be related to delays in seeking care.
Lisa Mushega, a policy expert for HENNET, a Kenyan coalition of health care providers, says PROMPTS helps prevent these delays by giving women a direct line to a health professional. (Jacaranda Health is a member of the coalition).
"It's a referral," Mushega says. "[PROMPTS] is data driven and can improve the quality of care — informed by the voices of mothers themselves."
Mushega says she has met women who used PROMPTS to correctly identify signs of pre-eclampsia, a life-threatening condition that can start with swollen legs. Another new mother used the system when her newborn seemed sick, and she wasn't sure how to calm him.
"She was told to go to the nearest health facility, because her baby was actually having jaundice," Mushega says. "It really comes in handy."
At a time when the use of artificial intelligence is drawing existential concerns and calls for regulation, a program like PROMPTS demonstrates its potential value, says Smisha Agarwal, director of global digital health at Johns Hopkins University.
The AI Edge
Historically, most public health messaging is one-sided: Public service advertisements, billboards or automated messages written by health authorities and disseminated to the public.
"That conversation is really bounded by what a health system decides a mother should know," Agarwal says. Artificial intelligence sets a different course: "What the LLM really changes is the direction of conversation. Because now we can center it on what the mother actually wants to know, and in a private space on her own phone. There is a fundamental change in power."
In Kenya, PROMPTS understands messages in English, Swahili and Sheng — a popular dialect in Nairobi that is a mix of the two languages. Jacaranda has also expanded to parts of Ghana, Nigeria and Tanzania, building versions for speakers of Twi and Hausa.
"There's local context," Patel says. "If there's a question about nutrition in Kenya, and you give the same answer from a question about nutrition in Nigeria, you're going to get laughed out of the room."
Jacaranda Health is also using PROMPTS to help doctors identify areas of need, based on anonymous feedback from some of the estimated 700,000 users each year.
"Lots of mothers are reporting that they're getting blood pressure checks, but very few report getting breast exams," says spokesperson Laura Down. "It gives mums more agency in the health system — as well as a better understanding of their pregnancy history."
In other cases, Down says the questions mothers are asking can help doctors understand what's happening in their own community.
"So for example, we're starting to see correlations between a spike in extreme heat and a spike in mothers reporting issues like headaches or swelling or dehydration," Down says.
Any potential drawbacks?
But there are limits. These interventions work best in places that already have functional healthcare systems, Agarwal says. There's very little margin for error when human medical needs are processed by a machine. The way the system is trained to do a rapid handoff to a human nurse in an emergency becomes a key factor.
"The first thing I want to know is, what happens when the system gets a message wrong?" says Javaid Iqbal Sofi, a researcher focusing on AI policy and governance at Virginian Tech University. "Suppose a woman describes something urgent, but the system treats it as routine. Would someone catch that? How quickly?"
Patient privacy issues and missed opportunities for care are common concerns, as AI platforms are adopted in medical contexts worldwide. Last month, the use of platforms developed by Palantir to automate staff schedules in hospitals in the United States drew protests by a national nursing union. The use of AI by insurance companies to process and deny medical claims — even without a human reviewing them — has led to outrage and calls for regulation.
In contrast, PROMPTS operates as a limited-use program, trained on a relatively narrow set of issues and concerns. Its developers say the human element of the system is the most important part. A team of 18 nurses are employed to monitor, audit, and respond to PROMPTS questions around the clock.
"Humans are responsible for ensuring the quality of messages going out, and we audit the quality of the answers," says Javan Waita, Jacaranda Health's director of programs in Kenya.
Maintaining a significant human component of the program improves accuracy but raises the cost. Right now, it costs about $2 per user to maintain PROMPTS, which is absorbed by the nonprofit. That gets a mom through pregnancy, and stays with her for a year after birth.
Waita says this is an important backstop, especially when mothers might not have an alternative.
"The sooner a mother is able to access care, the sooner doctors will be able to understand the problem," Waita says. "If PROMPTS isn't there, it means more complications for mothers, more complications for newborns."

'This is our company': Nigerians show off oil wealth after share-buying frenzy
- Published
Every Nigerian is now an oil magnate.
At least that is what the social media memes would have you believe as investor fever hits the country.
Nigerians have been eager to have a piece of the energy business that was built up by the country's – and continent's – richest man: Aliko Dangote.
More than four billion shares in his giant oil refinery – representing just over 3% of the company - went on the market on Monday in Africa's biggest-ever sale of its kind.
The minimum purchase was 10 shares for about $4 (£3) and despite this only representing a miniscule portion of the firm, many are now celebrating and joking about their new-found (part-)owner status.
One popular social media video has a Nigerian narrating how he stopped a speeding Dangote company lorry driver, telling him not to be reckless with company property.
Other memes show investors trying to phone up Dangote to discuss business matters.
And the term "Yangote" – a pun in the Hausa language essentially meaning "we all have a share now" - has been trending on social media.
On the first day of the Initial Public Offering (IPO), investment apps crashed as they could not handle the high demand.
Bamboo, which runs one of the most popular investor tools here, later apologised, saying: "We know we let you down."
Public affairs analyst Jamil Ubah said he had rarely seen Nigerians as excited about something as this. He argued that it fed the dream that it could lead to greater riches for a population that is often battling to make ends meet.
"I think the hope for the common man is that his money will grow into something big, and don't forget this is coming at a time when many are struggling as the economy is not doing great," he told the BBC.
Dangote wanted this to be "the people's IPO" with drivers, cooks, cleaners and servants having the chance to be part of something big.
And they took him at his word.
Twenty-five-year-old clothes seller Idris Lawal Musa made his first-ever stock exchange purchase and told the BBC he was happy after investing 21,000 naira ($16; £12) in 40 shares.
"It is no longer Dangote but 'Yangote', the company belongs to us now," he said while laughing.
But he may make a quick sale.
"I am a trader by profession and when I see that the shares have increased in price I will sell," he noted.
The popularity also reflects a growing investment culture among younger Nigerians who have embraced mobile trading platforms, cryptocurrencies and digital savings products.
But fear of missing out may have also pushed some to get into the investment business.
In the build-up to the IPO, social media platforms were awash with financial conversations. People shared subscription guides, debated valuation metrics and encouraged friends and family to participate.
But amid the frenzy, experts have warned that there are risks – shares can go down in value, as well as up, meaning people could lose some, or all, of their investment.
Financial analyst Shuaib Uwais said prospective investors should avoid thinking of the IPO as a guaranteed route to wealth.
He urged people to consider a number of factors that could impact the refinery's future performance, including disruptions to crude oil supply, operational challenges, regulatory changes and fluctuations in demand for refined petroleum products.
"If for any reason the company experiences difficulty in sourcing its raw materials, there could be challenges," he told the BBC.
Nevertheless, the IPO has given people the chance to be part of this home-grown success story.
Dangote's sprawling refinery on the outskirts of Lagos, which began operating two years ago and now processes around 700,000 barrels of crude a day, has transformed the fortunes of Nigeria's oil sector.
Until recently, Africa's largest crude oil producer had no refining capacity and had to import the finished product. Now the Dangote refinery is feeding much of the domestic demand.
But for Dangote, the share offer is about raising cash to fund the growth of the business, something that the country's mini-magnates may now be able to get behind.

Between surviving an illness and returning to regular life, lies a journey of a thousand small victories. Physiotherapy helps people take those victories, one step at a time.
There is a moment after a heart attack or stroke that very few people talk about. It is not the moment the ambulance arrives. It is not the moment the doctors say the patient is out of danger. It is the moment when the hospital doors close behind you, you return home, and everyone expects life to slowly return to normal.
But what does ‘normal’ mean?
For someone who has had a stroke, it may mean learning to walk again, using an arm that suddenly feels unfamiliar, finding their balance, or simply getting out of bed without someone holding their hand. For someone who has survived a heart attack, it may mean taking that first walk outside without constantly wondering whether their heart can handle it.
And sometimes, the hardest part is not the physical limitation. It is the fear. “What if it happens again?” That question can stay with a person long after they have left the hospital. This is where physiotherapy becomes much more than a set of exercises.
What rehabilitation entails
We often imagine rehabilitation as someone working hard in a gym, lifting weights or walking on a treadmill. The reality can be much quieter.
For a stroke survivor, the first goal may simply be to sit upright without support. Then to stand. Then to take a few steps. For the family watching, it may seem like very little. For the person doing it, it may feel like climbing a mountain.
A physiotherapist is there for these moments. Not just to count repetitions or measure strength, but to help someone understand that progress does not always have to be dramatic. Sometimes, progress is one extra step. Sometimes, it is standing for ten seconds longer. Sometimes, it is being able to walk to the bathroom without asking for help. And sometimes, it is simply finding the confidence to try.
What patients go through
Imagine being someone who used to walk to work, play with their children, exercise regularly or climb four flights of stairs without giving it a second thought. Then you have a heart attack. Suddenly, your heartbeat becomes something you constantly notice. You begin questioning every sensation. Is this normal? Am I too tired? Is my heart rate too high? Should I stop?
That fear can lead people to become overly cautious and inactive. Cardiac rehabilitation can help break that cycle. With appropriate medical assessment and supervision, patients can gradually return to physical activity, improve their exercise capacity and learn how to manage their cardiovascular health with greater confidence. The physiotherapist’s role is not simply to say, “Push harder.” It is to say: “Let us understand what your body can safely do today—and build from there.”
Not only for the elderly
A stroke or heart attack is often imagined as something that happens late in life, after the age of 60 or so. But when it happens to a younger person, the shock can be enormous. Someone in their 30s or 40s may suddenly find themselves worrying about things they never expected to question. Will I be able to go back to work? Can I take care of my children? Can I travel? Can I exercise again? Can I return to the sport I love?
They may look perfectly healthy from the outside. But inside, they may be dealing with fatigue, weakness, uncertainty and fear about what comes next. That is why rehabilitation cannot simply be based on a person’s age or diagnosis. A younger patient may need to return to a physically demanding job. A sportsperson may want to return to competition. A parent may simply want enough energy to play with their children. Rehabilitation has to fit the life that person wants to return to.
The patient is not a diagnosis. This may be one of the most important things a physiotherapist learns. A medical report might say stroke. It might say heart attack. It might list numbers, test results and medications. But none of those words explain who the patient is. They do not tell you that the patient loves taking their morning walk. They do not tell you that someone has a child waiting at home. They do not tell you that being able to climb the stairs independently means more to that person than almost anything else. Good rehabilitation starts with a simple question: “What do you want to get back to?” The answer may be different for every person. And that answer becomes an important part of the treatment.
Preventive goals
Physiotherapy is also about preventing the next story. Rehabilitation should not only begin after a crisis. Physiotherapists also have an important role in helping people become more physically active, develop healthier movement habits and reduce preventable health risks. Physical activity is an important part of cardiovascular health, but exercise is not a prescription that can simply be copied from one person to another.
The right type, intensity and amount of activity depend on the individual. For someone recovering from a cardiac event, exercise may require appropriate medical guidance and monitoring of symptoms, heart rate, blood pressure and exercise tolerance. For someone recovering from a stroke, rehabilitation may involve improving balance, strength, coordination, walking and everyday functional activities.
The goal is not to push everyone to do more. The goal is to help each person do what is right for them—safely and consistently. The greatest thing a physiotherapist restores is not movement. It is the part of someone’s life they thought was gone forever.
We often say that physiotherapists help people move. But perhaps that does not quite capture the whole story. Physiotherapists help people return to the things that make life feel like life.
(Shanthi Dass is a sports physiotherapist and managing director of Synergy The Clinic, Chennai. synergytheclinic@gmail.com)

In August 2026, Trump expanded a U.S. beef import quota by roughly 660 million pounds. The European Union did also adopt restrictions on Brazilian beef in summer 2026.
The quota expansion of roughly 660 million pounds was not specifically for Brazilian or JBS beef, according to a presidential proclamation. It was not possible to rule out the prospect that, despite not being mentioned in the proclamation, JBS or Brazilian beef could be the main or sole beneficiaries of the expansion. It is also imprecise to say the imported beef would be tariff-free.
The Wall Street Journal reported that JBS controlling shareholder Joesley Batista asked Trump to lower tariffs on Brazilian beef. It was not possible for Snopes to independently verify this report.
The suggestion appeared to be that the imported products would come from Brazil despite the European restrictions on Brazilian beef, and that JBS would benefit from the reduced tariffs.
One Instagram post (archived) featuring the rumor describes JBS as the "primary beef supplier" for McDonald's, Burger King, Sysco, Walmart's Great Value brand and Kroger private-label products. Its caption reads, in part:
The owner of JBS met privately with Trump in the Oval Office, and discussed lowering the import tax on Brazilian beef.
The next day, Trump opened the border to 660 million pounds of tariff-free imported beef. JBS is the world's largest meat processing company. Their headquarters are in Brazil.
The EU banned Brazilian beef after Brazil couldn't prove their cattle met antibiotic safety rules. China rejected beef from Argentina after it was lab tested to contain a drug linked to cancer.

Trump expanded beef imports in August 2026
On Aug. 26, 2026, Trump signed a proclamation temporarily increasing the amount of lean beef trimmings that could enter the U.S. under an existing tariff-rate quota by 300,000 metric tons. That increase equals roughly 660 million pounds.

The White House said Trump's measure increased the amount of beef eligible for the lower tariff rate rather than eliminating duties for beef altogether.
Moreover, the proclamation did not explicitly say the beef would come from Brazil. Identity and access management startup OTPless has elevated cofounders Satyam Nathani and Tanmay Sagar as CEO and COO, respectively, as incumbent CEO Bhavik Koladiya steps away. Koladiya told Inc42 that he plans to retire but did not comment further on his future plans. Under the new leadership structure, Nathani will lead the startup’s strategy and expansion, while Sagar will oversee its operations and execution. OTPless said the appointments come as it looks to expand its offerings across authentication, identity, and payments. In a LinkedIn post announcing the leadership transition, Koladiya described his entrepreneurial journey as “exhilarating and exhausting”. He also expressed confidence in Nathani and Sagar leading OTPless through its next phase of growth. Before joining OTPless, Koladiya cofounded fintech unicorn BharatPe and later founded VC firm Finix Partners. OTPless was founded in 2021 by Nathani and Sagar, with Koladiya taking charge as CEO in January 2023. Nathani and Sagar were founding members of BharatPe. The Bengaluru-based startup helps consumer internet enterprises offer authentication services through its SDKs and APIs. Its offerings include silent network authentication, WhatsApp authentication, device intelligence, and passkeys. These offerings are aimed at reducing dependence on OTPs, PINs, and passwords while enabling enterprises to identify users, prevent fraud, and improve conversion during sign-ups and transactions. OTPless claims to authenticate more than 300 Mn mobile users and serve enterprises including Meesho, Navi, PhysicsWallah, ShareChat, Shiprocket, ixigo, and Zepto. It said it has reached ₹36 Cr in annualised revenue, representing a 2.5X increase over the previous year. The startup also claimed to have been profitable for the past two quarters. OTPless has raised over $6 Mn to date from Venture Highway, White Venture, FJ Labs, SIDBI , Piper Serica, among others. It last raised $3.5 Mn in a pre-Series A funding round led by SIDBI in May 2024. At the time, OTPless said it would use the capital to expand globally and extend its product suite beyond authentication into authorisation.

A post (here & here) is being shared on social media claiming that a pregnant woman gave birth on the road in Unnao, Uttar Pradesh, after a government hospital refused her admission due to her inability to cover the medical expenses. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals of a woman giving birth on the roadside in Unnao, Uttar Pradesh, after a government hospital denied her admission.
Fact: The visuals are from Rajbiraj, Nepal, where a woman gave birth on the street outside a government Hospital in September 2026 after being denied care over unpaid preliminary test fees. However, a similar incident took place in Uttar Pradesh in April 2026, when a woman delivered her baby on the roadside outside a government hospital in Shamli district after staff allegedly demanded a bribe and refused her admission. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of viral visuals directed us to Nepali news reports (here, here & here) covering the same incident. The event reportedly occurred in the town of Rajbiraj, Nepal. According to these reports, on 10 September 2026, Babita Kumari Paswan, a 30-year-old woman, delivered her baby on the pavement outside the state-owned Gajendra Narayan Singh Hospital in Rajbiraj, Nepal, after her family couldn’t get the money required for preliminary tests.
After a video of the incident went viral, six hospital staff were reportedly suspended pending an investigation. A Google Street View of the hospital’s location matching the area seen in the viral video can be viewed here. However, it is worth noting that in April 2026, a similar incident (here & here) did occur in Uttar Pradesh, where a 30-year-old woman gave birth to a baby boy on the roadside outside the Shamli District Combined Hospital after staff allegedly refused her admission and demanded money. Hospital authorities formed a committee to investigate the matter.
To sum it up, the viral video depicting a woman delivering an infant on the street is from Nepal, not from Uttar Pradesh.

The Liberal Democrats’ leader, Sir Ed Davey, took aim at Nigel Farage’s Reform UK and Elon Musk on the first day of his party’s annual conference, saying that they “won’t give up the fight” to defeat “nasty populism” and the far-right party’s “£72m arsenal of hate and lies”.
Speaking from the main stage at Brighton Centre, Davey called on the assembled delegates not to be deterred in the face of Reform’s hope “that the anger and the hatred and the lies will grind us down until eventually we just give up”, and praised earlier speakers for showing “why we care and why we fight”.
He contrasted this with Reform, which “care about their own bank balance and they fight because two crypto billionaires gave them 72m quid”.
Davey, who entered conference season having to address frustrations over his leadership expressed by some Lib Dem MPs, also used the speech to recall his early political life as a student campaigning successfully for his university college to boycott Barclays, due to its investments in apartheid-era South Africa.

Davey said: “Today – we are back. Fighting again the fight that fired me up at university. The fight to end injustices. In our country and around the world. The fight to defeat the nasty populism of Trump, Le Pen, the AfD and the rest.
