Is this a mouse, a human, or something else?
Researchers have created a mouse whose brain is half-human by volume.
In recent decades, scientists have gotten much better at growing “cerebral organoids” — miniature, three-dimensional brain-like structures — from human stem cells as a way to study brain development and disease. Now, a group from Stanford University has advanced their usefulness by growing these globs of cells inside mice missing chunks of their own brain.
Across memory and motor tests, the scientists reported that these neuro-chimeric mice performed about the same as normal mice. But hours of open field observations revealed something totally different.
What a wild item to write and a phenomenal story from STAT’s Megan Molteni. Read on for more about the scientific utilities for and ethical implications of these mousensteins.
Will Chris Klomp stand up to RFK Jr.?
That was the question on senators’ lips as two key committees grilled the senior federal health official nominated to be Kennedy’s second-in-command.
Over two days of hearings, senators fired questions at Klomp about whether he would stand up to the health secretary — especially on Trump and Kennedy’s vaccine policy changes, which have coincided with measles outbreaks across several states and multiple deaths in Pennsylvania.
The “famously thrifty technology entrepreneur” has already been a major player in the Trump administration as Medicare director and then chief counselor to Kennedy. He has negotiated deals with pharmaceutical companies and acted as a liaison between the Department of Health and Human Services and the White House.
What did Klomp say about the measles deaths? Read Chelsea Cirruzzo’s story.
I promise this photo is not AI-generated
This is a real picture of twin girls, Hiyab and Wuhbto, who were born in Ethiopia with conjoined skulls in 2024. They are now recuperating, unconjoined, after surgeons at a St. Louis hospital separated their heads in February.
Twins joined at the head — craniopagus twins — are exceedingly rare. One in every 2.5 million live births! Only 62 separation attempts have ever been made worldwide. Hiyab and Wuhbto shared brain tissue and blood vessels, which made surgery last more than 24 hours and required more than 60 specialists, according to an announcement from SSM Health Cardinal Glennon Children’s Hospital. Surgeons completed repair of Wuhbto’s skull earlier this year. Hiyab is slated for the same procedure this fall.
Medicine ain’t always perfect, but wow can it do some marvelous things. You can watch the livestream of the announcement here.
Purer fentanyl won’t solve the U.S. overdose death crisis
In January, a paper published in Science analyzed government mortality figures, data on drugs seized by the DEA, and Reddit posts to determine that decreasing fentanyl potency due to Chinese government crackdowns could explain the recent decline in U.S. opioid overdose deaths. But when another research team tried to replicate that study, they didn’t come to the same conclusion.
“A simplistic supply shock is not supported by the evidence,” the authors wrote yesterday in Science Advances.
The researchers noted that as fentanyl purity increased across the country, there was no associated national drop in overdose rates. While there did seem to be a broad association between declining purity and overdoses, it was shared with other, unrelated trends. And importantly, the DEA acknowledged at the time that increasing purity in its drug seizures was likely due to a change in its sampling plan.
It’s also critical not to overlook geographic variability in the drug supply, the replication study authors wrote. As one of them told Lev Facher when the first study was published, many regions had declining overdose rates before potency apparently began to drop. — Theresa Gaffney
Potentially good Ebola news
After 7,258 confirmed cases and 3,510 deaths, there is reason to be cautiously optimistic about the trajectory of the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Disease transmission rates are declining in most of the affected provinces, though months of work remain to get the outbreak under control, said Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the director-general of the World Health Organization, during a news conference yesterday.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, is the second-largest on record. The WHO said it expects a Phase 3 randomized clinical trial of Ebola vaccines to begin in the next couple of weeks. The inimitable Helen Branswell has the full update.

Quick Answer
You can build an Android app with Google Antigravity by designing the UI in Google Stitch, generating the app with Gemini using Expo React Native, previewing it through Expo Go, and creating an APK with Expo EAS. You can also connect Supabase for cloud sync.
Building apps on software is now everyone’s cup of tea, thanks to AI. Even if you have never written a single line of code before, you can just go to any AI tool and build the app you want. However, the real complexity lies in making those apps useful instead of AI slop. To help you out, we have created this series where we help you learn how to build fully functional and reliable apps using AI tools.
To start with beginners, in this guide you will learn how to create an Android app using Google Antigravity.
There are multiple ways to create an app. However, this guide explains how you can create Android apps using Expo, a cross-platform builder that lets you easily build apps and share them between Android and iPhone, and you can also run Expo apps on the web. In the future, you will learn how to create Flutter apps, which offer more flexibility.
Table of Contents
Prerequisites
To create Android apps, you need:
- A Google AI Pro subscription
- Antigravity installed on your Mac or Windows
- An Android phone
- Download the Expo Go app. You can install it for free from the Google Play Store
- An Expo account (which you can sign up here for free)
How to Create Android apps Using AntiGravity
Step 1: Get Google Gemini AI Pro
First, opt for Google Gemini AI Pro. This subscription gives access to the Google Gemini models inside Antigravity. If you are looking for a totally free way with a generous limit to create Android apps, you can view our tutorial on how to create Android apps using Google AI Studio for free.
If you already have a Google One AI Premium subscription, you can directly install the Google Antigravity application and get started.
Although Google isn’t the best at its coding models, it offers very generous free terms compared to other models. Moreover, Google’s recently launched Gemini 3.8 Flash is also reliable for building apps if you guide it in the right way.
Step 2: Create the app UI using Google Stitch
Once you have opted for a Google AI Pro subscription, go to this website: stitch.withgoogle.com to design the UI of the app you are building. It is a free tool, and if you have a Google AI Pro subscription, you get better rate limits.
Stitch is a UI design website similar to Figma, but it relies more on an AI approach, which lets you generate UI for apps and websites just by prompting.
In my experience, Google Stitch, in most cases, produces generic UI designs, but it’s a great start for someone to get started with the app UI.
You can also skip this step if you have reference images. Most AI models are very good at replicating designs and understanding the structure. However, if you want a structured approach and a little customization, you can follow this process: Generate your initial designs using Stitch, then edit and modify them. Finally, use those references in tools like Google Antigravity to generate apps with the best UI, exactly the way you need.
To create a UI design, you can view our full, detailed tutorial on how to create UI designs using Google Stitch.
Step 1: First, open Google Stitch and enter the prompt for the app you want to create.
In this case, let’s create a to-do list app because that is a very good starting point, even for beginners. Remember to select “app” as an option while creating, because Google Stitch supports both app and website designs.
Step 2: Now, enter a prompt to generate the UI of the app. Then tap on Enter
Step 3: Now wait until Google Stitch provides a full UI design of the app.
Step 4: You can tap on any element or use AI to describe the changes you want, or you can just use the built-in basic tools to edit sections, text, and much more.
Step 5: If you dont like the design, you can click on the plus icon and tap on upload files, and then you can upload the reference files.
Step 6: To preview how the app works, you can tap on the prototype option to preview how the full app works
Step 7: And once you have the design, tap on Export, and you can export directly to Google Antigravity or save it as a ZIP file.
I recommend downloading it as a ZIP file because sharing to Google Antigravity doesn’t work in most cases.
Step 3: Open Google Antigravity
Now open Antigravity and set it up as a CLI. You can also use it as an agent for UI; Antigravity supports both, but I prefer the CLI experience. Now tap on Open Folder and create a new app, or you can select an existing folder. For those who are unaware, all app files will be stored in this folder.
Now open the CLI, and on the right, you can see the chat interface. Now, in the chat, you can tap on the model’s name and select Google 3.8 Flash High. For your information, Google 3.8 Flash is better than the Pro series. It is the latest model and very good at AI generation, especially if you have reference images.
Step 4: Add your UI reference images
Now, click on the plus icon and attach the images. You can attach up to five images at a time.
Now enter this prompt to ask Google Antigravity to create an app.
Please build an Expo React Native app in TypeScript based on the attached UI designs.
Requirements:
Replicate the layout, typography, colors, and components from the attached screenshots as closely as possible.
Use standard Expo packages (@expo/vector-icons, @react-native-async-storage/async-storage, expo-linear-gradient, react-native-safe-area-context).
Implement full client-side state with local persistence using AsyncStorage so added tasks and items persist across app reloads.
Keep the code modular with clean components in a src/ folder.
Ensure there are zero TypeScript compile errors.
Step 5: Create the app using Gemini
Once you are done, wait for some time until Google Gemini 3.8 Flash creates an app.
Since it runs on Expo, you can preview the build on your Android phone. Simply enter this prompt, and it will generate your QR code in the terminal. If you want to make any changes, you can ask Google Gemini to do that for you.
Step 6: Preview the app on your Android phone
Now, open your Android phone and install the Expo app. Open the Expo app on your Android phone and tap on “Scan QR code,” and the app will be installed on your device. Now you can preview all the changes that you have made.
If you want to make any changes, you can enter the prompt with the required changes. Maybe also include better UI references to help the Google Gemini model understand better. In my experience, Google models hallucinate a lot. Once everything is finished and you are happy with the output.
Step 7: Create an Expo account
Now, before that, you need to go to Expo.io and create a free account. If you have already created one, you can just sign in. Now, Expo EAS will use your Expo account to create the build.
Now, once the account is created, there are two ways to connect Expo Go with your Google Antigravity. First is using a local authentication session, which is stored in your home folder. You can run login in Terminal at any time to connect.
To do that, open Terminal in Antigravity and then run this command
Command: npx eas-cli login
Now enter the username and password you created for your Expo account. Google Antigravity will remember these credentials for all future builds. So this is a one-time process; you don’t need to do this for every new app build.
If you don’t want to submit your credentials, you can create an Expo access token (perhaps for one-time use, or if you are sharing with a friend). You don’t need this if you are using it personally on your device.
However, if you want to connect your Expo account through an access token:
- Go to expo.dev/settings/access-tokens.
- Create a token, name it “Antigravity”, and generate the new token.
- Open the terminal and run this command:
Commad: export EXPO_TOKEN="your_copied_token_here"
Step 8: Build the Android app
You can simply enter the prompt and wait for some time until Google Antigravity starts an Expo build in the Expo build app. Once it finishes, it will give you a direct download link for the app.
Prompt:
Since you are using a free version, Expo offers some free rate limits, and then later it uses buffer time to build the app, which averages between 1 and 7 hours, depending on the traffic. If you are lucky enough, the app should be ready in less than 5 minutes. Once it’s ready, Google Antigravity will offer a direct download link.
Step 9: Download the app
You can copy the download link and paste it into any app on your Android, tap on it, and install the app. Alternatively, you can just download the app on your PC and share it to your Android.
Once the build process is completed. you can see the app download link. You can directly share the download link to an Android device.
Step 10: Scan the app before installing
Even though the app is built by you, I highly recommend scanning it before installing it on your Android phone. You can use any free online scanners to scan the app and confirm there are no security issues or malware within your app. Once you are done, you can install the app.
Step 11: Install the app on your Android phone
If this is your first time installing a third-party app, Google Chrome will block the app download from unknown sources. When prompted, you can enable unknown sources; once enabled, you can use the package installer to install the app on your Android phone.
Connect your Android app to Supabase (Optional)
Now that the basic Android phone app has been set up and will successfully run on your device, if you want to back up data in the cloud, you can connect it to Supabase.
Supabase is a free database hoster that lets you host small files in the cloud so that your app can use this data, allowing you to use the same app on other devices with sync enabled.
Step 12: Enable Supabase Integration
To connect it to Supabase: Go back to Google Antigravity and enable Supabase MCP. Next, open this URL and create a new account in Supabase. Now, in Supabase, create a new project. Example: my-to-do-app.
Once a project is created, go to your project settings and then API, and copy the following details:
- Project URL – You can go to Project Settings > General

BiharChief MinisterSamrat Choudhary on Saturday (September 19, 2026) announced plans to link 1 crore women with employment opportunities. He also said that the government will provide fellowships to 1,000 women to pursue a PhD, and under this fellowship, a monthly stipend of ₹10,000 will be provided for four years. He announced this during the 25th foundation day of the Bihar State Women Commission.
Addressing the gathering, Mr. Choudhary said that women in Bihar are moving forward rapidly, and their growing economic, social and political participation reflects the State’s changing landscape.
He added that the provision of 50% reservation for women in Panchayati Raj institutions and urban local bodies has significantly strengthened their participation. He also noted that ‘Jeevika’ has played an important role in making women economically strong.
“The government aims to directly link 1 crore women to employment opportunities. Under the school uniform scheme, arrangements are being made to provide uniforms prepared by ‘Jivika Didis’ [women from self-help groups] instead of distributing cash to students; this initiative will also create new employment avenues,” Mr. Choudhary said.
He mentioned that incentive schemes are currently operational in Bihar to promote the education of female students at the matriculation, intermediate, and undergraduate levels, and assistance is also being provided to students preparing for competitive examinations.
“Through the Girls’ PhD Fellowship, a target has been set to provide financial aid of ₹10,000 per month to 1,000 female students annually for higher education and research. Efforts are underway to establish a university dedicated to women to further expand opportunities for women’s higher education,”Mr. Choudhary said.
Speaking on women’s safety, the Chief Minister pointed out that the introduction of the ‘Police Didi’ system in the State is a step ahead on this front, adding that female police personnel are being deployed near schools, colleges and other educational institutions to ensure the safety of girl students calling it a pioneering initiative by Bihar.
He urged the Commission not to limit itself merely to resolving complaints but also to offer regular suggestions to the government for improving the status of women.
“I want the Women’s Commission to become a factory for creating political activists. The Commission should play an active role in empowering women socially, economically, and politically,”Mr. Choudhary said.
In the presence of the Commission’s Chairperson, Apsara Mishra, the Bihar CM said that women’s empowerment forms a crucial foundation for Bihar’s prosperity and expressed confidence that the Commission would continue to work tirelessly leading up to its golden jubilee — to integrate women into the mainstream of development and safeguard their rights and dignity.
A short film based on the Commission’s 25-year journey was screened during the event, and to mark the Silver Jubilee, the Chief Minister released a special postage stamp dedicated to the Commission—in collaboration with the Department of Posts—and unveiled the Commission’s souvenir.

‘Vale, our brilliant friend’: Victorian Greens MP Tim Read dies
Kat Wong
The Greens MP for Brunswick, Tim Read, has been remembered for his kindness and integrity after his death on Saturday at the age of 64.
Read was diagnosed with melanoma in November and earlier this year announced he would retire from politics at the state election.
On Saturday, Victorian Greens leader Ellen Sandell announced he had died surrounded by those he loved.
“Tim was a brilliant local MP, doctor and scientist – but to those who knew him, he was also the kindest, funniest and most fundamentally decent of people,” Sandell said.
He could always see the moral question at the heart of every political issue. It’s why he was so outspoken when it came to supporting the cause of the Palestinian people and why he continued to remind us all about how much coal was being burned in Victoria each day. He never lost perspective about what was truly important …
Vale our brilliant friend. We will miss you.
Sandell recalled Read’s advocacy on pill testing, tobacco licensing and a statutory ban on solitary confinement in prisons, and praised his contribution to Victoria’s anti-corruption and integrity laws.
“Victoria is a bettter and fairer place, and politics in the future will be much more accountable and transparent because of Tim,” she said.
The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, said in a statement Read was a man of principle and compassion who had dedicated his life to being “a voice for Brunswick”.
I always valued his intelligent and humane contributions to the public debate. I always respected his convictions and his determination to make life better for others.
He knew his values. He lived them.
Carroll said he had spoken to Read last week.
“We spoke about something on which we have always agreed: integrity in public life and the need for reform,” Carroll said.
“Despite his health challenges, he was positive and optimistic for a better world.”
The Victorian opposition leader, Jess Wilson, also offered her condolences:
Tim was a man of conviction and a thoroughly decent person. He brought sincerity, compassion and a strong sense of public duty to his work, earning respect across the Parliament. His commitment to integrity in public life was unwavering.

The Greenland Fiasco Stumbles to an End
President Trump announced an agreement that appeared to satisfy all parties but came at a great cost.
Jesper Møller Sørensen, the Danish ambassador to Washington, projected an air of calm. He was serving hors d’oeuvres, including reindeer sausage and smoked salmon, at his residence, where American, Danish, and Greenlandic guests had gathered for a Wednesday event billed as “A Taste of the Arctic.” On the terrace, he told me that months-long discussions about the future of Greenland were heading in a good direction. But, he warned, the outcome would depend on whether one person could be swayed.
It was obvious that he was talking about President Trump, who has long coveted Greenland, a semiautonomous territory of Denmark. Trump has claimed that the United States needs the island for national security, at times declining to rule out using force to acquire it. When his rhetoric became more threatening earlier this year, the Danish armed forces flew emergency blood supplies and explosives to the island to prepare for a potential U.S. attack. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, warned that a U.S. invasion would mean that “everything ends” for NATO—something of an understatement for a scenario in which one founding member of the alliance attacks another.
At the World Economic Forum in Davos, in January, Trump stepped back from the brink, proclaiming the “framework of a future deal.” In the subsequent months, he returned to the topic in fits of pique, at one point arguing that Greenland “should be controlled by the United States, not Denmark.” Meanwhile, representatives from the United States, Denmark, and Greenland met to consider ways to bolster U.S. security interests on the island and fend off hostile powers in the Arctic region, namely Russia and China. Now the promised “future deal” appears to be here. It builds on a Cold War agreement between the U.S. and Denmark and includes no transfer of territory to the United States. Instead, it envisions the kind of expanded U.S.-military access and multilateral cooperation that leaders from Denmark and Greenland said was available all along, and doesn’t threaten to blow up the security architecture that the U.S. has helped maintain for nearly 80 years.
Earlier tonight, Trump wrote on social media that Washington “will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America.” He also said that U.S. adversaries will be barred from having bases on Greenland or making sensitive investments in the island, which is rich in minerals and other raw materials. A Cold War–era agreement signed by Denmark and the United States already gave Washington broad latitude to conduct military operations in the territory, and the U.S. Space Force currently has a base on the island’s northwest coast. The United States once stationed thousands of soldiers across multiple bases and radar sites, but it shrank its presence in the decades after the Cold War.
Current and former U.S. officials told me that one area of concern in Washington was the possibility that Greenland, not party to that 1951 agreement, might vote for independence or otherwise alter its political allegiances, and then proceed to restrict U.S. infrastructure and access. The new agreement will also include Greenland and bind all three parties to a more permanent U.S. presence; the U.S. will, among other things, have the ability to build additional bases and use the island’s airspace. Trump wrote, “We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland, of which there are many.”
U.S. and European officials told me that the agreement will affirm the right of Greenland’s population to determine its own future. It is also expected to include language barring non-NATO bases as well as mechanisms for blocking Chinese and Russian investments. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose deputies played a leading role in the discussions, hailed the agreement. “This deal permanently and completely addresses our national security concerns in Greenland,” he said in a statement.
Danish officials said that the three parties will sign the agreement at the United Nations General Assembly next week and that it will enter into force after necessary parliamentary procedures. Greenland’s premier, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, said that the accord “recognizes Greenland’s interests and our place in the international cooperation.” Frederiksen, the Danish prime minister, said that the agreement is a boon for NATO and Europe as well. The statements were positive but restrained, reflecting the pain inflicted by this saga. Europeans found it difficult to decipher Trump’s motives—or to understand whether they were about to be attacked or simply trolled. One day, there was menacing rhetoric on Truth Social; the next, memes on X of penguins.
It was already late at night in Nuuk, Greenland’s capital, when Trump announced the deal. But a reporter from Denmark’s public broadcaster observed politicians going in and out of the government building, reflecting fervent interest in the American president’s designs on their land. Washington may have achieved its security objectives. But it has lost something else: trust among its hosts. “Goodbye, U.S.A.,” one resident said.

Gets very loud for its size. Clear, detailed sound. Very durable build. Swappable battery. IP66 dust and waterproof.
TIRED
Expensive. Overkill for many. Single hand-carry grip. Pricey strap sold separately.
How loud is too loud? That's the question I find myself asking as I turn up the volume dial on the Soundboks Rider portable Bluetooth speaker. By myself, outdoors, a five or six on the dial is plenty loud; anything more starts to get uncomfortable. But this speaker can push out a ridiculous 118-decibel sound pressure level (dB SPL). That's basically a rock concert.
If that's your jam, this may be your perfect speaker. It's distinct, stylish, built to last, and, importantly, sounds great. But it's absolutely overkill for most people, who would be better off with a smaller, more affordable speaker from the likes of Sony, JBL, or Marshall, all of which offer plenty of tamer options below the Rider's $600 price tag.
Bring The Party
Soundboks Rider Specs
Dimensions
13.8 x 9.4 x 7.9 (H x W x D) inches
Weight
14.3 pounds
Water and Dust Resistance
IP66
Battery life
Up to 35 hours
Charging
USB-C, swappable LiFePO4 battery
Connectivity
Bluetooth 4.2, 3.5-mm AUX
Drivers
8-inch woofer, 1.2-inch tweeter
The Soundboks Rider looks like no other portable speaker I've tested. It resembles something you'd find on stage at a concert rather than at your next barbecue. Its restrained design is almost the antithesis of the flashy, LED-pulsing party speakers you might find from brands like JBL or Samsung.
The build quality is impressive, confidence-inspiring, and clearly made to last. It's built like a tank, with a steel front grille, silicone rubber ball corners, and a thick plastic cabinet. During a drop test, I was frankly more worried about the speaker breaking my stairs than my stairs breaking the speaker. Another win for longevity is the replaceable battery—it charges via USB-C, and you can swap it in and out in seconds. This feels like a speaker you could have for decades.
While smaller than Soundboks' other speakers, it is still much larger than your average Bluetooth unit, and a bit awkward to carry with its single carry-grip on one corner. I would have loved to see two carry handles, one on each side. That would make the Rider easier and more flexible to carry, similar to the Sony ULT Field 7.
Unlike the larger Soundboks Mix and Soundboks 4, this is meant to be a stand-alone speaker—it does not have Soundboks' wireless multi-speaker connectivity (SKAA TeamUp), a speaker stand mount, or additional inputs (read: XLR).
Soundboks speakers can get loud, and despite the Rider being the smallest in the brand's lineup, its audio output is astonishing. I was frankly scared to turn this speaker up to max volume (11 on the dial, IYKYK).
To spare my New York City neighbors, I took this speaker outdoors and cranked it to 11; even then, I could only manage it for a short while before I worried someone would call 311 to file a noise complaint. Which is to say: the Rider is plenty loud for most parties I can think of.
But the Rider isn't just loud—it's clear. Across all volume ranges, it sounds great. While it can produce big bass, it isn't overpowering in the mix. The sound profile matches the speaker's understated, PA-style aesthetic—clear, strong, and detailed.
The speaker can output up to 118 dB SPL. That's well within painful levels, and similar to a rock concert. I'm honestly not sure when or where I'd need to push out that much audio, but if you ever do, the Rider is game.
Fine Tuning
The app is similarly streamlined and unfussy. You can control basically every speaker function remotely, including volume, sound profiles, EQ modes, and even turning it off.
Connecting, however, was a little finicky. I had to pair, unpair, re-pair, power off, and power on a few times before the app and speaker would actually start talking to each other. That was even more irritating because, after a firmware update, the app told me to forget the speaker and re-pair all over again. I've tested hundreds of wireless audio gadgets—Bluetooth connectivity issues with brand-new products are less surprising than you might think and often get sorted out within a month or two of software updates. Still, it made the whole experience feel decidedly less premium than the Rider's $600 price might suggest.
Is It Overkill?
The Soundboks Rider is an excellent speaker. In terms of loudness, durability, and battery life, it runs circles around most of the competition, including larger party-slash-karaoke speakers like the Sony Tower 5 and JBL PartyBox Club 120.
But as a larger, portable Bluetooth speaker meant to stand all on its own, it's a bit niche, especially for $600. I do think it's overkill for a lot of people—I can't think of many folks in my life who need this combination of loud and bombproof in their speaker. You can also get plenty of portable Bluetooth speakers for less (the aforementioned $500 Sony ULT Field 7 and $330 JBL PartyBox Encore Essential 2 come to mind) that might do the job just fine.
Soundboks says this is a portable party speaker built for spontaneity and outdoor adventure. For my spontaneous adventures, the Rider is overkill. But if your adventures include a lot more people (and a lot more space) than mine, it might be the perfect fit—big enough to bring to any party and durable enough that you never have to worry.

Learning another language is a highly complex mental activity. It requires people to remember words, distinguish unfamiliar sounds, recognize patterns, work out grammatical rules, and retrieve the right expression at the right moment. All of this happens while listening, interpreting, and preparing a response.
Could all this mental activity also help keep an aging brain healthier? Research suggests it can.
Concerns about memory and dementia can send aging adults looking for ways to exercise their brain and maintain cognitive function, whether it is solving crossword puzzles or playing a musical instrument. Language learning might not seem like the same kind of brain exercise, but it is a complex activity that engages several mental processes at once.
I am a linguist who studies language acquisition, use, and loss. My new book, Beyond Words: How We Learn, Use, and Lose Language, examines language and the mind across people’s lifespans.
Research increasingly suggests that language learning and bilingualism can offer cognitive benefits—including for older adults. Learning another language can also create opportunities for communication and social connection.
A workout for the brain
A person’s brain remains capable of change throughout their life. This ability to adapt in response to experience is known as neuroplasticity.
Learning unfamiliar sounds, vocabulary, and grammatical patterns requires the brain to form and strengthen connections. Language learning engages several mental processes at once, requiring people to absorb and retrieve information, notice when something does not work out, and adjust. This sustained mental effort makes language learning a particularly rich form of cognitive exercise.

'No doubt' that climate change played role in Nepal-Tibet flood, study finds
- Published
A study has found that climate change had contributed to the glacier collapse that unleashed devastating floods on the Nepal-Tibet border.
More than 1,400 people were killed and thousands are missing following the deluge on 26 August.
There was "absolutely no doubt that human-induced climate change played a role here in the preconditioning of the disaster", said Friederike Otto, a climatologist at Imperial College London and one of the study's authors.
The World Weather Attribution study, published on Thursday, said the disaster was the result of a "compound event" caused by rising temperatures, thinning glaciers, thawing permafrost and pre-existing geological weaknesses.
Massive floods and landslides swept through border towns and villages in Nepal and Tibet, wiping out thousands of houses, destroying energy infrastructure and leaving thousands dead or missing.
Scientists had previously said that the floods were caused by the collapse of a glacier slope near the peak of Langtang Lirung, a mountain on Nepal's side of the Himalayas.
The large chunk of glacier hit the bottom of a valley with such force that it registered as a magnitude 5.2 earthquake, according to United States Geological Survey (USGS) data.
The World Weather Attribution study said climate change was a "destabilising factor acting on a pre-existing geological predisposition", but it was not the only cause of the disaster.
According to the study, July and August temperatures in the area were around 1.5C (34.7F) warmer "due to human influence on the climate".
Meanwhile, glaciers in the region had also been thinning by about half a metre (1.6ft) a year, which could weaken existing fractures and increase instability.
Heavy snowfall last October and November also added to a large amount of meltwater early this year.
This combination of activities "may have interacted to amplify the compound event," the study said.
A magnitude 7.8 earthquake that struck the area in 2015 and triggered a rock-ice avalanche, could have also weakened the underlying rock mass, according to the study.
However, authorities said they could not confirm that earthquake's exact impact on the glacier collapse last month.
Another co-author of the report, Utrecht University mountain hydrologist Walter Immerzeel, told reporters that the area was a "geologically vulnerable slope".
Immerzeel said it was "potentially weakened by the 2015 earthquake" and "destabilised further" by glacier and permafrost retreat.
In the wake of the disaster, Nepali authorities have called for global efforts to tackle climate change, saying the country is one of the lowest contributors to greenhouse emissions yet one of the most vulnerable places to the effects of global warming.
In his first foreign trip as Nepali Prime Minister, Balendra Shah is set to appear at United Nations General Assembly in New York next week to talk about the recent disaster and climate justice.

China’s AI Rollout Is Messier Than It Looks
A top-down tech revolution is harder to manage than a bottom-up one.
Anxiety about AI in the United States appears to be getting worse. Prosaic concerns about machines disrupting industries, stealing jobs, and compromising schoolwork are giving way to more harrowing fears about the end of humanity.
Even after top AI executives in the U.S. called for slowing down the breakneck pace of development, President Trump dismissed these safety concerns as a “hoax” that would hand China an advantage in the race for AI supremacy.
Outside of China, Trump’s assertion may appear well founded. While the U.S. roils over the prospects of AI, China’s leadership looks to be charging ahead. In surveys, Chinese people appear more enthusiastic about AI and its potential benefits than respondents in the U.S., and they are adopting it more quickly. Although Chinese President Xi Jinping has expressed more alarm than Trump about the threats of AI—and has even called for regulation to “ensure that AI is always under human control”—his government has made adopting the technology a national priority. The plan is to have AI in every aspect of China’s economy and society by 2035. The country’s steady release of AI models that are open-source, high-performing, and relatively cheap to build and run has been sending shivers through Silicon Valley and Wall Street.
But for all the concern about China’s advances in AI, the reality is that the country is racked by the same anxieties about the onrush of AI as the rest of the world. Chinese social-media platforms are filled with posts in which workers and professionals express their worries that AI will steal their job and livelihood. Leaders in Beijing seem ever more concerned about the potential political and economic risks of this technological disruption.
In the U.S., these tensions are being debated openly and, in theory, will be managed in the courts and on Capitol Hill. In China, where there are no such avenues for people to determine their own fate, leaders must still confront the problems and threats inherent to this technological revolution. This puts the Communist Party in a bind: Advancing AI may well empower China on the world stage, but holding the technology back may be necessary for the party to preserve itself.
Xu Peng, a 30-year-old actor, was out of work last year when he got an unexpected break. A director had reached out to cast him in a short-drama series, each episode minutes long, which have become enormously popular in China. Xu traveled to Hengdian, a film-production hub in eastern China, and began landing roles in one or two dramas a month. And then it all stopped. Xu had expected to act in two dramas after the Chinese New Year in February, but never heard from the studio. When he contacted the producer, he got the news: The company had canceled the productions and would be making videos using artificial intelligence instead.
“It was as though everything was fine yesterday, and today it is suddenly gone,” Xu said.
Xu’s fate is the fear of workers across the country—and around the world. Social-media posters regularly express anxiety about being “distilled,” a term Chinese people use for when an employer uses a worker’s data to train an AI model. In May on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, someone going by the name Nanbei wrote that after leaving a recent job, she learned that her former employer had fed thousands of her chat messages, hundreds of documents, and every one of her work emails into an AI system to create a “digital robot” that took over her responsibilities—and even gave it her name. “The company no longer has to pay me a cent in salary, yet it can keep me there ‘working overtime’ forever,” Nanbei wrote. Another worker, using the handle Xiexiaoya, posted on RedNote, China’s Instagram, in June that the prospect of being distilled kept her awake at night. “I’m afraid my AI double might become more popular than I am,” she wrote.
Two years ago, Shen Anyu, a voice actor who earns a living from narrating news commentaries and other short programs, began noticing an alarming number of videos on social-media platforms that seemed to feature his voice without his permission. Shen hired a lawyer earlier this year and filed a lawsuit against a voice-generation platform. The case is still pending, but in the meantime, his career is “losing blood,” he said, as he loses work to AI. Living with the new technology “is inevitable,” he said, but “I’m not yet sure how we should coexist with AI.”
Though some Chinese people are embracing AI, many are not ready for the change it brings. Bruce Jiang, a 42-year-old commercial director in Shanghai, loves choosing the right lens and finding the perfect shot, and he didn’t want to outsource these and other aspects of his craft to an algorithm. But after his clients began pressuring him to use the technology—“‘You only have to tell AI what you want, and it produces it like magic,’” he said they insisted—he began using tools such as the video-generator Kling for certain tasks. The experience, he said, has been demoralizing. The old method “was work, and it was a cost, but it was also a kind of pleasure,” Jiang said. “That pleasure is disappearing.”
Chinese policy makers at national and local levels have introduced ambitious plans and financial support to rush the country into the AI age. Entrepreneurs across China are adopting AI in the hopes of cutting costs, remaining competitive, and aligning their firms with Beijing’s priorities. In China’s cutthroat society—and especially in sectors where AI is making rapid inroads, such as the entertainment industry—many like Jiang are afraid that they’ll get left behind if they don’t join in.
But these swift and radical changes have yielded mixed results. The state-linked China Center for Information Industry Development estimated in June that nearly 70 percent of the country’s small businesses have not moved beyond initial trials of adopting AI in their operations, largely owing to the costs and complexity of integrating the technology.
After the Chinese AI lab DeepSeek released a large language model last year, Chinese companies rushed to adopt it. But instead of buying a software subscription (an unpopular practice in China owing to the country’s history of piracy), some businesses opted for what locals call an “all-in-one machine,” or a mini data center with DeepSeek installed, which managers simply plugged into their computer systems. This solution was especially popular among state-owned enterprises and government bureaus looking to appear advanced, but the hardware proved to be an ineffective way to use AI. Buyers soon came to see that the machines weren’t worth the investment, and their sales quickly fell.
Earlier this year, plenty of buzz similarly surrounded OpenClaw, a free, open-source, autonomous AI agent. Tech companies hosted popular events to help users install and use the tool, a process that Chinese enthusiasts call “raising a lobster.” At the OpenClaw festival in Beijing in March, the internet-service provider Baidu set up pools with live crustaceans to entertain attendees. Local-government officials encouraged the frenzy by pledging financial aid to start-ups that used OpenClaw.
Disillusionment came quickly. Some distraught users took to social media to express their alarm at how the AI agent, which required masses of personal data to operate without detailed instructions, had a habit of going rogue. “I jumped on the bandwagon” expecting to get a “digital employee,” a woman using the social-media handle HotdogWang wrote in March on RedNote. “Instead, it turned out to be both a money pit and a ticking time bomb.” Some reported that their AI helper had deleted emails or made credit-card purchases without permission. One Douyin user, posting under the name Qizaibushidaju, wrote, “I simply installed it because everyone else was doing so,” only to uninstall it 72 hours later owing to security concerns.
Although Chinese tech executives are not yet engaged in a public debate over the risks of an algorithm-created calamity—the country’s constraints on free speech may inhibit them from speaking out—some Chinese people do worry about more than just jobs and data. “There are only two options for the future,” a man calling himself Qiangni Yinshou wrote on Douyin. “Either humanity goes extinct, or humans shut AI down.”
A user by the name of Buyehou wrote on RedNote that when he engaged a chatbot in a philosophical discussion about humanity’s future, he was told that the options included “either merging with AI or being eliminated.” The man added that “when AI becomes far smarter than humans, has consciousness of its own, and can evolve independently, it will be impossible for humans to control it. There is no turning back now.”
Despite their outward show of confidence, China’s leaders plainly don’t know how life works with AI either. But figuring it out is an urgent concern here, given Beijing’s evident faith in AI as a magical solution to the country’s deepening economic and social problems, and as an essential tool in the pursuit of global dominance over the United States. In the U.S., the diffusion of AI is largely a bottom-up phenomenon as companies, investors, and consumers test the risks and benefits of this new technology. In China, where the development and spread of AI is a national mission that is costing the government hundreds of billions of dollars, leaders are eager to impose these advances from above.
In theory, China’s autocrats can ram through their agenda with scant regard for public sentiment. If confronted with the kinds of protests against AI data centers that have become prevalent in the U.S., Beijing’s leaders could easily send police to crush them and then cover up the problem in a deluge of propaganda. The Communist Party has already shown its willingness to override public concerns in pursuit of technological advantage. In 2024, trials of autonomously driven taxis in the city of Wuhan sparked concern over how robotaxis were “stealing people’s rice bowls”—but the trials have expanded anyway.
Yet China’s leaders have traditionally prized policies that promote stable employment out of fear that mounting joblessness could create unrest and threaten the political order. When the country first embraced markets and opened to trade, its rapidly growing economy and expanding private sector could absorb displaced workers. Now, when China’s sluggish economy already has a jobs problem—nearly a fifth of young workers are unemployed—the advances of AI threaten to put many more people out of work.
“In a nominally Communist state, the image of the party elite allying with business interests to displace the human proletariat with a robot class of workers carries certain political risks,” Carl Minzner, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, told me. “There is the potential for a lot of disgruntled people.”
China’s leaders are showing signs of nervousness. Earlier this year a court in Hangzhou, a technology hub in eastern China, upheld a ruling in favor of a tech worker who had challenged his compensation package after being replaced by AI. In the court’s judgment, the dismissal was unlawful and the worker deserved more money. Although a local-court verdict does not set a national precedent, it appears to be a warning to employers that mass AI layoffs are politically unacceptable. “As employers enjoy the benefits of technology, they must also shoulder corresponding social responsibilities,” the Beijing municipal government wrote last year. The state news agency Xinhua commented in March that “those companies that equate AI with ‘reducing staff’ may seem to lower costs in the short term, but in reality, they lose the core competitiveness of talent accumulation and further erode employee trust.”
Pushing companies to invest in new technologies without shedding redundant workers may preserve social order, but it would also limit AI’s benefits. Jeffrey Ding, an expert on AI in China at George Washington University, told me that the country’s leaders face a “balancing act” between political and economic necessity. “AI does have the potential for bringing massive, widespread productivity growth,” he said. But he also noted that the Communist Party prioritizes legitimacy and regime stability. If embracing AI demands “massive displacement and a lot of structural changes, then that’s where the trade-off begins to bite, and they might have to veer toward slowing down AI adoption.”
If American AI firms do, in fact, slow the pace of innovation, the Communist Party may see this as an opportunity to race ahead in AI. But China’s leaders, facing their own domestic challenges and preoccupied with their own grip on power, may decide that imposing these innovations on the masses is simply too risky—for their own sake, if not for the sake of humanity.
That would probably suit many Chinese people just fine. Xu, the actor, has found work teaching archery and horseback riding—skills he acquired in acting gigs. But he hasn’t given up on his theatrical career. He now plans to produce his own short dramas, partly with the help of AI, though he said that the performers on-screen will all be living, breathing people. AI “will not completely replace human actors,” Xu insisted. At least he can hope.
Cao Li in Hong Kong contributed reporting to this story.

Taiwan holds first joint military drills using attack drones ahead of Trump-Xi summit
Taiwan’s president has overseen military drills featuring missiles and drones on Friday, ahead of a planned summit next week between the U.S. and Chinese leaders in which the fate of the self-ruled island will be discussed
TAIPEI, Taiwan -- Taiwan conducted military drills featuring missiles and drones on Friday ahead of the summit next week in the U.S. between President Donald Trump and China's Xi Jinping in which the fate of the self-ruled island will be discussed.
China claims Taiwan, a self-governing democracy, as its own breakaway province and hasn’t renounced the use of force to bring it under its control. Beijing has pushed Trump to take a stronger stance opposing Taiwan’s independence. The leaders of the U.S. and China are set to meet on Sept. 24 for the first time since May.
Taiwan’s military drills included for the first time joint combat exercises featuring multiple types of attack drones. President Lai Ching-te said the drills showcased the Taiwanese army’s modernization.
“The coordinated use of unmanned vehicles with conventional weapons reflects the adaptation to modern warfare,” he said, according to a statement released by his office.
The statement did not specify what types of drones were being tested in the southern Pingtung county. The military also launched multiple anti-air, anti-ship and anti-landing missiles as part of the exercises.
Taiwan has increased its military spending in recent years. The island relies on arms purchases from the United States, which is bound by its own laws to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself.
U.S. arms sales to Taiwan have been at the center of talks between Trump and Xi. After their last summit in May, Trump postponed a planned $14 billion arms package to Taiwan, fueling doubts about the U.S. commitment to the island. Trump called the arms sales a “very good negotiating chip” with China.
Taiwan’s army will continue staging drills next week, including newly bought U.S.-made HIMARS rocket systems and Stinger missile simulators among other types of equipment.

‘Bharat is not a geography, it is responsibility’: CDS General Subramani tells IIT Roorkee students
Subramani, the guest of honour at the ceremony, spoke about the rapidly changing global landscape and the challenges and opportunities it presents.
Chief of Defence Staff General NS Raja Subramani addressed graduating students at IIT Roorkee’s two-day convocation on Saturday, where 2,701 students were awarded degrees.
Subramani, the guest of honour at the ceremony, spoke about the rapidly changing global landscape and the challenges and opportunities it presents for young engineers and technologists.
Also Read | CDS Subramani to seek approval of theatre commands from defence minister Rajnath Singh
Subramani's message to students
Addressing the graduating students, General Subramani described the changing global environment through the acronym ‘DHARA’ and said that it stands for ‘Disruptive, Hyperconnectedness, Asymmetry, Realignment and Autonomy’.
"I will speak about Bharat a little later, but before that I want to speak about the changing world and I will give you an acronym for that. That is 'DHARA,' denoting Disruptive, Hyperconnectedness, Asymmetry, Realignment and Autonomy," he said.
Elaborating on the first two elements, General Subramani said the pace of technological change was making it essential for young engineers and technologists to continually update their skills. He also pointed to the vulnerabilities created by increasing interdependence between different systems, saying graduates would have an important role in building resilient technologies.
“The world is undergoing enormous disruption; technology is changing faster than we can catch up. You, as graduates, will have to learn, unlearn, relearn and adapt and be curious throughout if you want to keep up with the changing world... We are hyperconnected not only in WhatsApp and social media but also in our financial systems, airlines, networks, and energy systems. This interconnectedness also carries vulnerability with it. You, as the future engineers and technologists, need to develop systems which have resilience...”
He added, "Bharat is not a geography. It is a responsibility which generations before you have carried, and you will carry as you navigate this world."
A total of 2,701 students were awarded degrees during the convocation, with National Security Advisor Ajit Doval attending as the chief guest and General Subramani as the guest of honour.

NSA Ajit Doval also attends event
Doval, who attended the ceremony as the chief guest, told the graduating students that they were entering an era of unprecedented opportunities. He described them as the “luckiest generation in a millennium” and spoke about the transformation of society from earlier periods marked by struggle and constraints.
"You may not be conscious of the fact that, in the last 1,000 years, you are the luckiest generation, which is going to have so many opportunities. Generations before you were struggling under slavery. And not only that, things have changed here, but globally too. Things have changed for the better for you,” Doval said.
Doval also shared an account from his early years in the intelligence service, recounting a high-stakes border mission during Sikkim's merger with India.
Senior advocate Harish Salve and IIT Roorkee Director KK Pant were also present at the convocation ceremony.

Nature and land defenders were murdered at the rate of one every three days last year, prompting many communities to set up self-defence units, according to the latest annual death toll by the independent watchdog Global Witness.
Organised crime groups or professional killers were implicated in more than a third of the 124 killings of defenders in 2025 as narco-trafficking activities overlapped with intrusions into indigenous territories and environmental crime, such as illegal logging and wildcat gold mining.
This was particularly true in Latin America, which accounted for 85% of last year’s deaths of people trying to protect forests, rivers and other ecosystems.
Colombia had the highest toll with 39 killings, followed by Brazil with 26 and Honduras with 12. In Asia, the most dangerous country for defenders was the Philippines, with 12 killings – many during crackdowns by state security forces.
Since Global Witness began compiling statistics in 2012, the overall global tally is now 2,375 deaths and disappearances – on a par with a small-scale war.
On a more positive note, the headline figure has declined over the last two years, from 196 in 2023 and 142 in 2024, though the report authors say this is likely to be an underestimate because data collection is difficult in war zones and authoritarian regimes.
Many countries and companies are also carrying out nonlethal attacks on defenders, including criminalisation and online smear campaigns.
Many defenders are now exposed to more organised crime with less assistance from the international community, partly as a result of cuts by the Trump administration. “The dismantling of USAID, which previously supported initiatives for Indigenous peoples to steward their own land, has had particularly serious implications for defenders,” the report says.
Almost three-quarters of the killings documented in 2025 were of Indigenous people and small-scale farmers targeted for defending their land. With less outside help, an increasing number of these communities are establishing their own territorial defence mechanisms.
The report highlights the example of the Kakataibo Indigenous Guard in the Peruvian Amazon. Six of the community’s leaders have been killed since 2020 amid growing incursions into the forest by criminal groups. Starting in 2022 with a few dozen recruits, the guard now has more than 150 volunteers in its 10 bases.
Segundo Ispón, the commander of the organisation, said the self-defence groups provided a global benefit: “Defending our territory is important to us as a community and as a people, and we’re proud to support the climate that we all depend on. In our culture, the work of defending our resources and territory is taught from an early age. But for this next generation coming up, the work is more dangerous than ever.”
At least a dozen other communities in Peru have organised self-defence units. Similar bodies have existed for some years in Colombia and Brazil. But it is risky. Last year, seven Indigenous guards were murdered. In at least five of these cases, the killings were linked to organised crime.
Many forest communities report the narco-threat is growing closer. In July, Asháninka leaders on the Brazilian border with Peru petitioned the government for help after armed and masked men entered their homes, apparently in search of assassination targets.
In the Ucayali basin on the other side of the border, Global Witness said there was a 600% increase in coca production between 2019 and 2023. This is pushing gangs to expand smuggling networks, including through the opening of illegal roads and trails through the forest. Corruption further adds to the risks facing forest protectors who stand in their way because many local politicians and police are in the pay of the traffickers.
Forest communities want help from governments to ease these pressures but there are concerns the opposite may be happening. Under US leadership, many rightwing governments are pursuing military crackdowns on coca growers and drug traffickers, which is pushing narco-gangs further into remote regions and indigenous territories.
Ricardo Soberón, a former head of Peru’s anti-narcotics office, said many communities were also affected on the border of Peru and Colombia. “We are in a situation where transnational criminal groups have appropriated the daily life of the Huitoto, Quichua, Bora, Secoya Indigenous people, who live along the Putumayo basin,” he said.
Of particular concern, he added, were the threats against local leaders, environmental defenders and human rights activists who call for a more effective state presence. He fears the newly elected rightwing governments in affected countries will make matters worse by militarising the conflict in line with the “America shield” priorities of the Trump administration.
Global Witness has urged the authorities to respect and work with nature and land defenders rather than making their role more difficult.
Toby Hill, the lead author of the report, said: “Defenders are the world’s eyes and ears on the ground. It’s thanks to them that we know when ecosystems are being destroyed, where forests are being cleared or rivers polluted. We can’t forget the thousands of defenders around the world who are working every day to protect their territories and cultures under increasing pressure.”

Stating that judiciary was at a crossroads, Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, Judge of the Madras High Court, said it was time for the judiciary to have an introspection to restore neutrality.
Commercialisation of legal education, political affiliations of advocates, politicisation of judgments, and the lack of transparency in the Collegium system of judicial appointments in the country were among the foremost issues that needed to be collectively addressed by the judiciary and the Bar with dynamism, said Justice Anand Venkatesh, addressing the ninth State Conference of Indian Association of Lawyers in Coimbatore on Saturday (September 19).
“The profession is not commercial in nature. It is essentially a service-oriented noble profession. Advocates are expected to be fearless and independent for protecting rights of citizens, upholding rule of law, and protecting independence of judiciary itself,” Justice Anand Venkatesh said, quoting a Supreme Court ruling. “Advocates are perceived to be intellectuals among elites, and social activists among the downtrodden,” he emphasised.
The slide in legal education was perceptible due to the mushrooming of law colleges. From only a few hundreds during the 1990s, the country now had 1,500 plus law colleges.
The candidates studying in the 27 national law colleges accounted for only 5% of the total advocates getting enrolled, he pointed out, expressing concern over absence of topics such as intellectual property rights and international law in the syllabi of government law colleges.
Candidates from the government law colleges came out without any foundation in fundamentals. Junior advocates were in a state of crisis since they were not being guided by senior advocates. Artificial Intelligence would take over documentation and drafting, and render them redundant, he cautioned.
Absence of a Vice-Chancellor at Tamil Nadu Dr. Ambedkar Law University (TNDALU) was a cause for deep concern, the High Court Judge said.
Politicisation of the bar associations impacted the neutrality of the judiciary. He wondered how the neutrality of the Bar Council of India could be accepted when its chairman, belonging to a political party, was also a member of the Rajya Sabha.
The course-correction even for the judiciary was possible only through neutral bars, he emphasised.

Donald Trump announced on Friday that the US had struck an Arctic security pact with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland, after threatening for months to take Greenland by force.
The US president cast the deal as a personal triumph, claiming in a post on Truth Social that the “very important, historic, and special” agreement “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns”.
“We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland,” Trump added. The US already has a presence on the island, and the right to expand bases, through Nato.
Greenland is a self-governing territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, a fellow Nato member.
In his post, Trump said that the agreement means “no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval”.
The US and Denmark will formally sign the agreement next week, on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly in New York City, according to the Danish government.
Statements from Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, and the leader of Greenland’s government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, posted online late Friday, emphasized that the agreement would fall far short of Trump’s stated desire for “the acquisition of Greenland by the United States”.
Frederiksen said that the agreement “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination”.
Nielsen said the agreement “ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western alliance”, suggesting that the deal might possibly just reiterate the existing US rights through Nato to use the island as a security base.
Once agreed to, the pact will need to go through parliamentary procedures to be enacted, the statement said.
At a Nato summit in Ankara earlier this year, Trump renewed his bid for the US to acquire Greenland, threatening to pull all American armed forces out of Europe after the continent repeatedly pushed back.

How to block and unblock a number on your Android phone
Has someone been trying to reach you about your car's extended warranty?
It's not a stretch to say that the modern smartphone is one of humanity's greatest inventions; there's so much packed into that pocket-friendly supercomputer. But even the greatest of inventions has its cons. For smartphones, one of those bitter cons is unwanted calls.
With all the benefits, convenience and interconnectedness smartphones allow you to enjoy, unfortunately, they also allow scammers, spammers and all sorts of annoying people to conveniently connect with you either through texts or, worse, constant calls. Thankfully, you can easily block unwanted callers on your Android phone. Android is a vast ecosystem, so the exact process for blocking numbers may differ based on your Android device. But for the majority of Android phones, the Phone or Contacts app is the first step in blocking those annoying scam texts. And if you ever change your mind about a number you banished to the block list, you can also unblock it right from the Phone or Contacts app.
How to block a number on your Android phone
If you're using a Samsung phone, there are two ways you can block calls from unwanted people: with the Contacts app and with the Phone app for numbers that aren't saved.
Using the Contacts app:
- 
Open the Contacts app
- 
Select the contact you want to block
- 
Tap More
- 
Tap Block contact
- 
Confirm the block
Using the Phone app:
- 
Open the Phone app
- 
Find and copy the number you want to block
- 
Tap More (three dots) at the top corner
- 
Select Settings
- 
Tap Block numbers
- 
Tap Add phone number and paste or type the number you want to block
- 
Tap the plus sign
If the number called you recently, then you can easily block it from the Recents section in the Phone app. Navigate to the number you want to block and tap Details > More Options > Block number.
Blocking a number on a Pixel phone or a device running stock Android is just as straightforward:
- 
Open your Phone app
- 
Select More (three dots)
- 
Tap Call history
- 
Tap a call from the number you want to block
- 
Tap Block/report spam
Once you do this, anytime the number tries to call you, your Android phone will automatically decline it before it even rings or pops up on your screen, and texts will usually be filtered into a blocked or spam folder. Do note that blocking a number is handled by your device, not your carrier. So, if you move your SIM to a different device, you'll likely have to block the number again.
How to unblock a number on your Android phone
Unblocking a number follows a similar process. To unblock a contact on the Samsung Contacts app, simply:
- 
Open the Contacts app
- 
Select the contact you want to unblock
- 
Tap More options (three dots)
- 
Select Unblock contact
If you're using the Phone app:
- 
Open the Phone app
- 
Select More (three dots)
- 
Tap Settings
- 
Select Block numbers
- 
Then tap the (-) beside the number you want to unblock
For the Google Pixel and stock Android users:
- 
Open the Phone app
- 
Tap More (three dots)
- 
Select Settings
- 
Then Blocked numbers
- 
Tap Clear (x) next to the number to unblock it
As soon as you unblock the number, it'll be able to call and text you like normal. Do note that any calls sent from the number during the block period won't get added to your call logs, so that stays forever lost.

There isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.
Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.
The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?
Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.
In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.
India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.
“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”
In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.
Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)
Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.
But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.
The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.
The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.
Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.
Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.
That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.
The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”
What else we’re reading about
Lollapalooza | British pop star Olivia Dean is to perform in India for the first time in January when she headlines Lollapalooza 2027 in Mumbai. Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.
The price of gold | Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Indians once again to refrain from buying gold and travelling abroad. He had first made an appeal to self-reliance in May, in part to conserve India’s declining foreign exchange reserves amid a rise in import prices and global energy shocks.
Census 2027 | The new and expanded questionnaire for the 2027 census is raising concerns, reports Scroll’s Anant Gupta. The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversial due to fears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Singer Prateek Kuhad (@prateekkuhad), whose latest album, Full Moon Chamber, was released in July, shares an indulgent treat: “I’m a big fan of artisanal Indian chocolate makers. I really like Manam, Carra and Naviluna, and there are many others. Although India has been growing cacao [commercially] since the 1960s, its craft bean-to-bar movement is more recent. Even a plain chocolate bar from one of these makers can be remarkably complex and delicious. More people outside India should know about it and try it.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
4,756,000
One-third of the electorate in Delhi, about 4.76 million voters, have been deleted from the draft voting list as the Election Commission carries out a contentious revision of its rolls across states. So far, about 130 million names have been dropped from draft rolls in 30 states and union territories, the Indian Express reported.
Vibe check
Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. Their mashup of the Colombian star’s Hips Don’t Lie with the traditional folk song called Moruda has got everyone grooving (42m views and counting).
It took two months to pull off, says creative director Jagirdar RV. Most artists in the group, aged between 23 and 60, don’t speak or read English and learned the lyrics by rote. The song choice was simple, he said, because it “has a very nice vibe which matched our vibe”.
It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet.
