Japan’s central bank has increased interest rates to a fresh 31-year high as it attempts to combat high global inflation linked to the war in Iran.
The Bank of Japan voted to raise its target interest rate from 1% to 1.25%, the highest level since 1995.
The move meant the BoJ joined the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank in tightening monetary policy this month, as central banks attempt to curb the impact of rising prices, linked to the conflict in the Middle East.
The Bank of England on Thursday voted to leave UK interest rates on hold at 3.75% but warned they could soon rise amid the fallout from the Iran war.
The BoJ has been raising rates since 2024, when it lifted its base rate out of negative territory. It has been under pressure to raise borrowing costs as the yen weakened steadily against the dollar this year, to levels that prompted policymakers to intervene to stabilise the currency. The Japanese currency weakened about 0.7% against the dollar on Friday.
The vote to raise rates was not unanimous – with two board members dissenting to the increase.
“The tone of the statement, along with two dissenters for the decision to raise rates, leaves lingering doubts that Japan’s central bank will be cautious in tightening monetary policy further,” Fred Neumann, the chief Asia economist at HSBC, said.
“While back-to-back hikes appear unlikely, investors will look for clues as to whether officials are prepared to raise interest rates again in December.”
The drop in the yen helped the Nikkei stock market index to rise nearly 2%, while the Japanese two-year government bond yields, which are most sensitive to monetary policy expectations, fell four basis points to 1.82%.
European stock futures slipped 0.35%, indicating a lower open.
Prashant Newnaha, a senior rates strategist at TD Securities, said the BOJ reiterated its concerns that underlying inflation could deviate upwards from its 2% target, but “we don’t see a smoking gun supporting a back-to-back hike in October”.
He said: “We stick with our call for rate hikes roughly every quarter with the next 25 basis points hike in December.”
Hopes of alternative ways for oil supply from the Middle East to reach markets pushed Brent crude futures down as much as 1.5% to $103.29 a barrel even as concerns about strikes between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis lingered.

Beebom Score
Video games in the 21st century love sticking to a blueprint. You go from Point A to Point B, face a few obstacles in the middle, unlock new skills, fight bigger and badder enemies, and you save the day and the credits roll. The same formula worked for decades.
But the games that actually stick with you are the ones that take that blueprint and shred it in pieces. Remedy’s entire studio lifeline is built on that formula. Max Payne turned a grieving cop into psychological noir, Alan Wake turned a novelist’s own writing against him, and Control turned a government building into a Kafkaesque fever dream that lived in my head for months after my first playthrough.
I played the original Control extensively and loved it. However, at the same time, I never once felt the urge to replay it from start to finish. So, when Remedy announced Control Resonant as an action-RPG and what they like to call an “open-ended modern world” game, I was curious where the Bureau could possibly go next.
And now 25 hours later, I can confidently say it took me somewhere I did not see coming. Control Resonant is bigger, weirder, more ambitious, and more memorable than its predecessor. It takes the paranormal DNA of the first game and drops you into a warped Manhattan, hands you a new protagonist, reworks the combat from the ground up, and turns the entire city into one enormous puzzle. Somehow, it all resonates.
Story: The Faden Siblings Are Still The Bureau’s Biggest Problem
If you’ve played the original Control, you may be familiar with the name Jesse Faden, who was the protagonist of the title and walked into The Oldest House from an outside world. She’s an outsider stepping into the Federal Bureau of Control (FBC) and its broken world, hunting for her missing brother.
She finds the FBC director dead, inherits the role from The Board, and is handed a Service Weapon, which she uses in the entire game, cleansing the House of the Hiss while trying to save Dylan, who ends the story in a coma.
And this is where Control Resonant begins, where Dylan wakes up with an Aberrant stabbed into his chest. Resonant completely flips the script of Control, to say the least. In the first game, Jesse was the one who walked in from Ordinary into the FBC. Now it’s Dylan’s turn to walk out of the FBC into the corrupted world, while he was locked up as a lab rat named “P6”.
Manhattan is no longer the city anyone remembers. The Hiss, the Mold, and the return of an old paranatural entity have spilled past the Oldest House’s walls, fracturing the city into distinct zones, each full of its nightmarish environment. Dylan isn’t P6 anymore as he embraces his Dylan Faden personality as he finally gets to be the protagonist of his own life.
His mission is simple: find Jesse, deal with the Hiss that corrupted him for years. Getting there is anything but simple.
Resonant is built around five major zones – Downtown, Central, Park, Evacuation Zone, and the West Incursion Zone – plus a couple more I won’t spoil. Remedy markets the game as an “open-ended modern world.” However, I’d call it open-world, just a tightly curated one. Nothing here feels like padding for padding’s sake, as every space feels engineered to have something strange waiting around the corner.
Dylan reports to Emily Pope, now Director of Research, while Zoe is his handler who communicates with him throughout the game over radio and introduces him to music whenever he’s overwhelmed. While it does sound like a small character beat, it isn’t.
Dylan spent years imprisoned and experimented on by the Bureau, and the deeper you go, the more that damage makes sense. For this relationship, I’ll applaud Sean Durrie and Frankie Kevich, who breathe life into Dylan and Zoe’s conversations and dynamic, which makes you want to explore this friendship further as you progress.
Plus, Dylan’s relationship with Jesse is the emotional spine of the whole game, and Remedy has beautifully kept that sentiment intact, alongside flipping how the search-and-rescue dynamic works in mission-based games. Even the side content in Control Resonant stops feeling like filler and starts feeling like actual world texture: fetching a toy for a dog, planting antennas to expand zone coverage, defending a Bureau supply crate from a Hiss swarm- each of these gives you a purpose to explore.
While written down on paper, it sounds ridiculous, but they’re exactly the kind of detour I kept abandoning my main missions for. And that’s the difference between Resonant and the original Control. I’m not saying the first game was all that bad; it was a phenomenal shooter wrapped around an extraordinary setting. Resonant asks what happens when the setting itself becomes the progression system, and the answer is one of the most satisfying action RPGs Remedy has ever built.
But if you’re a fan of the wider Remedy Connected Universe, you’re eating good here. Dr. Darling is back, as charming as ever, but your relationship with him here takes a shift. In Control, his research videos were fascinating; you often wanted to listen more. But here in Resonant, once you learn what he did to Dylan and how he engineered the man Dylan became, that fascination curdles into resentment. And yet the second he’s on screen, you still lean in. That contradiction between your emotions are signal to a brilliant storytelling.
Ahti, the Bureau’s mysterious janitor, also returns in a form that’ll grab anyone who’s played Alan Wake 2. These cameos make Resonant feel like another load-bearing piece of the Remedyverse, even if it leaves plenty of unanswered questions. After all, that’s the most Remedy thing about it.
World: <MANHATTAN//RESONANCE DETECTED>
If Dylan is the protagonist of Control Resonant, then you’re wrong. It’s the corrupted city of Manhattan that is the main character that outshines Dylan at every step. While he’s the catalyst who is moving between zones, taking missions, fighting the Hiss, and hunting for his sister, the city is the one telling the story.
The original Control barely left the Oldest House. Resonant throws open the doors and shows you what the world looks like after everything that happened inside, and it’s not a good look (for Dylan). Each zone in Manhattan has its own visual language, enemy roster, and rules for how reality behaves.
Downtown houses the Oldest House itself; Central looks like recognizable Manhattan until you notice how thoroughly the Hiss has corrupted it. The Evacuation Zone houses the FBC building, which is bending, Park has been swallowed by the Mold, and the West Incursion Zone is where you stop trying to describe things and just start pointing at the screen.
Gravity anomalies let Dylan walk on surfaces that shouldn’t be walkable, as he has four movement abilities to traverse Resonant’s world like it’s a platformer. Float keeps him airborne, Dash moves him forward, Reach yanks him like a magnet towards ledges and surfaces, and Shift realigns his gravity entirely, turning walls and ceilings into viable ground. These tools are proof of a brilliant level design by Remedy, and the entire map is built around the assumption that you’ll eventually break it.
The Sinkhole beneath the Evacuation Zone is a standout example. Dylan takes a diving bell down to plant Signal Probes for the FBC. As he’s done installing them, the bell breaks, and he’s stranded in a descent and has to battle his way through a horde of corrupted Hiss. Once he starts climbing back up, he’s thrown into endless dollhouse-style apartments all around him with flickering light bulbs.
Dylan then navigates through these apartments by bending gravity with every move as he follows a trail of blue light and TVs playing music, on his way to the exit. I mean, it is absolutely mind-bending when you come to play it, and it’s clearly one of the best levels I’ve played in gaming all year.
The West Incursion Zone doubles down on this illusion as well, where buildings duplicate, perspective folds in on itself, and architecture just, well, let’s say, stops behaving like architecture. I replayed several sections purely because I wanted to experience the same space again (the highest compliment you can pay a level designer).
Then there’s an absurd light bulb side quest where Dylan is asked to repair corrupted bulbs for a cartoon maintenance worker who lives inside a projector slide. Once the bulbs are fixed, the character tricks Dylan into being trapped inside the projection as a cartoon, fighting his way back out. This is the design philosophy of Control Resonant in short – take an ordinary object, ask what happens if it’s completely, f***ing bizarre!
But that’s not where the world stops surprising you. There are arcade machines all around where you can interact with and play a game called Shumi, that Dylan and Jesse played as kids. When Dylan interacts with the machine now, he’s thrown into an arcade game mode where you need to survive waves of enemies as a Fortnite-style zone closes in around him, and your time gets logged on the machine.
Similarly, there are Ice Cream trucks scattered around Manhattan, another nod for Dylan to relive those small moments he missed as a kid. These trucks allow you to spend your collected resources and purchase items you need to craft Artifacts, unlock Aberrant forms, and upgrade skills. Together, these elements make the city feel lived-in rather than being essential to the main story.
I remember watching an interview with Control Resonant Creative Director Mikael Kasurinen, who acknowledged the visual overlap between its gravity-warped Manhattan and PRAGMATA’s New York, but in Resonant the concept never feels borrowed. Its warped architecture exists because, in the game, reality is genuinely breaking, not because it looks cool in a trailer.
I only wish there were more reasons to linger in Control Resonant’s Manhattan once the credits roll. After the main story wrapped, I spent an additional six hours wandering, fighting Hiss, chasing side content, and maxing out my build. The world is good enough that I wanted the game to let me squat in it a little longer.
Gameplay: The Board Has Authorized Excessive Violence
Control Resonant often felt like a subtle match between Devil May Cry and Doom. You’re always moving, dodging, swapping weapon forms, using your supernatural abilities around, and turning enemies against each other.
I hate the static cover-shooter combat and absolutely despise QTE-heavy set pieces even more, where the game essentially does the heavy lifting for you, and you just need to press a button for it to play out. I come from a school of thought that believes in “give me a sandbox and let me break it.”
Remedy hands you exactly that sandbox in Control Resonant. The studio widely advertises this as an action RPG, and for the most part that label fits. It gives you the good parts of an RPG (weapons, abilities, builds, progression) without boxing you into inventory Tetris or a skill tree that looks like a conspiracy board.
The Aberrant is Dylan’s weapon that he creates with the help of The Board when Jesse stabs him with it. The weapon itself is unique to the Control franchise as it shifts between six forms. The primary forms are Strike (dual blades, fast, big on crits – my go-to for the entire run), Glaive (a spear with wide AoE reach), and Cleave (balanced, strong back attacks). Secondary forms are Crush (a slow, hard-hitting hammer that also cancels your float into a ground slam), Drill (a motorized spear that charges the longer you hold it), and Extend (a whip that hits multiple targets and can be charged up).
Layer six combo finishers on top, and it becomes a lethal arsenal. Split Pivot – a spinning blade unleashed after four hits- was my finisher of choice. Concussive Beatdown and Spin Edge earn their keep against crowds, but none of it feels mandatory. You experiment with a new build each time, find what clicks, and build Dylan around how you actually want to play.
Jesse plays into Dylan’s growth too. As he moves through Manhattan, Dylan stumbles into Faults tied to Jesse’s visions – pocket spaces where he can interact with a television from the Faden siblings’ childhood bedroom and interact with Jesse. Clearing these Faults unlocks his movement kit.
However, there’s one memory in particular that shapes the precedent of the Control series: in Ordinary, Maine, young Dylan and Jesse discover the Slide Projector and Dylan gets captured by the FBC. This story in particular in Resonant turns into a 2D life-sim arcade-style game that alone deserves an award nomination. It’s proof that Remedy isn’t just thinking about how to tell a story; it’s thinking about how to make playing the story part of the story.
When it comes to abilities, Dylan earns six major ability types by taking down Resonant Entities: Barrage fires projectiles, Inferno stacks burn damage over time (I leaned on this so hard it felt mandatory), Astral Rebuke launches homing spikes to stun and juggle enemies, Push shoves enemies off ledges, Spore Burst fires infecting Mold rounds, and Volatile Anomaly summons a throwable detonatable ally that hits harder the lower its health drops.
You manage all of it inside The Gap – Dylan’s altered mental state where he communes with The Board and handles his character progression. Source is the currency that fuels progression in Control Resonant, and you can get it by clearing zones, taking down Resonant Entities, finishing side content, and generally doing the work yourself. There’s no unlimited free respec, and I actually like that.
When RPG games hand players everything, there’s less reason to explore, fight, and experiment. Resonant builds a loop instead where exploration feeds progression, progression feeds combat, and combat sends you back out to explore. A simple yet engaging loop that works each time if you play games on the daily.
One omission stings apart all this glory, which is the Photo Mode. Sadly, in Control Resonant there’s no Photo Mode at launch, which feels criminal given how good these environments look. Remedy has confirmed that Photo Mode is coming in a post-launch update, and I’m counting down the days.
I’d also kill for a Walkman-style in-world music player. Zoe’s Mixtape is great, but walking Manhattan with Dylan’s favorite tracks playing would’ve sealed the deal – blame Kojima for spoiling me on that front with Death Stranding 2, and I wanted the same rush here. Neither omission is a dealbreaker, but both would make an already excellent world even better to live in.
Bosses: <HISS//MOLD//DEFEAT//REPEAT>
Combat in Control Resonant is satisfying. The original Control gave you the Service Weapon, telekinesis, and the freedom to fling half the environment at enemies. Resonant takes that foundation and stacks melee, supernatural abilities, movement, and weapon forms on top of it. I rarely kept my distance – I wanted to get in close, and the game rewards that instinct constantly.
The first Resonance boss, The Artist, tells you exactly what Remedy is going for: dodge at range, stay airborne, play it careful – or ignore all of that and go straight in for the jugular, which is what I did every time. Combine abilities with Crush, dodge across floating platforms, hunt for crit windows. That became my approach to nearly every boss, and thankfully Resonant never repeats a fight.
There are 23 Hiss enemy types, 11 Hedron types, and 12 Mold types, each bringing its own problems. The Hiss Transporter is one of the most unique Hiss types, which is a corrupted bus that rams the ground and calls in reinforcements.
The Hiss Cluster is yet another enemy type, which is quite annoying, and is a floating orb that fires corrupted beams – dodge it right, and you trigger a slow-motion effect that feels ripped straight out of Max Payne. The Mold Spore Mother flies around, lobbing explosive spores across the arena. Learning enemy weaknesses matters in the game as well: Inferno wrecks Mold, while Drill and Crush do the heavy lifting against Hiss.
The six Resonant Entities are their own combat puzzles. The Factory Resonant in Central hands you Inferno and turns its arena into a lava field where aerial combat becomes essential. The Mold Resonant in Park is a different kind of nightmare – you have to enter a euphoric Mold-induced state before Zoe snaps Dylan out of it with music, then survive a boss built on spores and infection damage. I died to it more than I’d like to admit.
My favorite boss battle in the game is against The Dancer in the Theater. She moves like a contemporary dancer, attacking with sticks on a rhythm built around the Fibonacci sequence. Once you catch the pattern, the fight opens up, but watching the choreography, music, and combat lock into one thing is something else entirely. It’s genuinely beautiful.
I won’t spoil the rest of the Resonants for you because they are surely surprising. What matters is that Control Resonant doesn’t give you six versions of the same fight – every Resonant entity forces you to rethink your loadout and your approach. It hands you an RPG sandbox, and you decide how to break it apart.
Sound and Sight: A Resonance I’d Hear and Look For Each Time
Control Resonant is driven by its soundtrack in a way few games manage. Music was always Remedy’s signature, but here it’s woven into Dylan’s character. Zoe introduces him to music whenever he’s vulnerable or overwhelmed, and those scenes land harder than you’d expect because music is something Dylan lost as a kid and is only now rediscovering as an adult.
There are six original songs accessible through Zoe’s Mixtape menu, and as I mentioned earlier, I wish I could take them with me into the open world. Petri Alanko returns as composer, continuing his long run scoring Remedy’s games, and every zone, boss, and combat beat has its own distinct sound identity.
Then there’s Control Resonant’s graphical allure. I played on an Nvidia RTX 5080 Founders Edition with ray tracing and DLSS 4.5 enabled, and I have to say that this is one of the best-looking games I’ve touched this year.
Remedy is running its proprietary Northlight engine, substantially upgraded to handle the scale of an outdoor Manhattan instead of one contained building, and it shows. Car hoods reflect the city around them, light bounces off wet streets, buildings hold up under scrutiny, and the West Incursion Zone specifically produces genuinely gorgeous Tyndall effects where light leaks between gaps.
Color does a lot of storytelling in Resonant too: Hiss zones drenched in red, Mold environments leaning blue and yellow, and Hedron spaces exploding into kaleidoscopic colors that make the screen look like it’s being peeled apart. With all my settings maxed out, Resonant is Remedy’s most visually ambitious game to date, and nothing comes close to it. The tech makes the world feel physical, which makes it hit that much harder when the world starts bending past recognition.
Performance: The Board Would Like a Word With My GPU
For the most part, Control Resonant runs like it means business. I played at 1080p, everything on Ultra, including ray tracing with path tracing enabled, DLSS 4.5 on for most of the run, on that same RTX 5080. My 180Hz monitor couldn’t even keep up – I saw peaks near 320 FPS, generally hovering between 230 and 240, but the headroom is ridiculous.
My Setup:
CPU: Intel i7 14700K 3.40 GHz
CPU Cooler: CORSAIR H150 RGB 360mm
Motherboard: MSI Z790 Pro Wifi
GPU: Nvidia RTX 5080 Founder’s Edition 16 GB
RAM: Crucial (2x16GB) 5200MHz DDR5
SSD: Kingston 3 TB NVMe SSD
Monitor: 1440p @ 160Hz
I hit a couple of crashes where my PC ran noticeably hot, but between the ambient heat and the settings I was pushing, I wouldn’t call those a pattern rather than a fluke. Outside of that, no meaningful stutter, no tearing, no frustrating frame drops.
Nvidia’s DLSS 4.5 comes with caveats, though. During combat and exploration, it’s close to a must-enable setting, where the neural rendering combined with ray tracing buys you the headroom to run everything maxed. But during cutscenes and character close-ups, the DLSS upscaled visuals occasionally look gimmicky. Emily Pope was the clearest offender, where her face read as overly processed, and hands and fingers occasionally looked like low-poly models.
Switching DLSS off for story beats gave me a cleaner, more intentional-looking image. Playing Control Resonant on PC with my DualSense controller felt like it wanted to use your hardware to the limit and give you the best gaming time you deserve from it.
Verdict: A Resonance That Has Corrupted Me For Other Games
If you’re a through-and-through RPG fan, this isn’t the game for you. But if you want a break from the grind of Onimusha: Way of the Sword or The Blood of Dawnwalker, Remedy has built something wonderfully different.
Resonant is an action RPG that lets you breathe, set inside a strange, open-ended modern world, anchored by an unforgettable story about two siblings separated by a Slide Projector, and driven by combat that never stops asking you to experiment. Most of all, it makes exploration feel like the reward, not the chore between rewards.
New to Remedy games? Then this is a great entry point for you, and you get the story, the spectacle, and the freedom without needing a security clearance for every classified document filed since the original Control was released. Returning players get enough familiar faces and unanswered questions to keep the red string board fully intact.
After 25 hours, I didn’t want to leave Manhattan, and that’s where the Resonance grabbed me. If Remedy announces DLC in the next two months, I already know where my free time is going. With GTA 6 looming over the rest of the year, Control Resonant somehow pulled my attention out of Rockstar’s gravitational field and dragged me back into The Gap.
The Board would probably call that a successful resonance. I call it a problem I’m happy to have.

Parth Jindal elected president of Tamil Nadu Judo Association
Parth Jindal, the founder of JSW Sports, has been elected president of the Tamil Nadu Judo Association (TNJA), taking formal charge after serving as its interim head.
Jindal entered the association through its Thanjavur district unit, where he served as vice-president, before moving into the State body. His election places him at the helm of a programme aimed at expanding judo at the grassroots and creating a stronger pathway for Tamil Nadu’s leading judokas.
Vijaya Mohana Murali, TNJA’s former president and now chief executive officer, said Jindal supported judo for more than a decade before taking a formal role in the association. Murali also said Jindal was a brown belt in the sport.
“He has been supporting judo with zero expectations,” Murali told Sportstar. “He didn’t want to become president or anything. He didn’t have any such expectations.”
Jindal already has an established presence in Indian sport through JSW Sports and the Inspire Institute of Sport (IIS), its high-performance centre in Bellari, Karnataka. Murali said that experience, coupled with Jindal’s personal association with judo, made him a suitable choice to lead the TNJA’s next phase.
The association’s immediate plan is to increase the number of qualified instructors working at the grassroots. Alongside that drive, it intends to identify, assess and further develop promising judokas, with selected athletes training at IIS and, where required, abroad.
The programme will be implemented in six-month phases over the next three years. The opening phase will concentrate on coach development and preparing existing athletes to compete at the international level.
Murali said Jindal had become interim president before the agreement involving JSW, the Tamil Nadu government and the Sports Development Authority of Tamil Nadu was reached. He stressed that the partnership was not the reason for Jindal’s elevation but would support the association’s development plans.
According to the TNJA, the election was conducted by Advocate Elephant Rajendran, the election officer, and overseen by High Court-appointed observer Justice Govindarajan and Tamil Nadu Olympic Association observer Latha.
- Jayantho Sengupta

Mice with human brain cells offer a tool to study disease. Ethicists ask: What's next?
Researchers have developed a new way to install millions of human brain cells into mice, as a way of creating better scientific models for studying neurodegenerative disease.
Using genetic tools, the scientists bred mice that were missing most of their cerebral cortexes – the outermost layer of the brain involved with reasoning, memory and consciousness. Then, they replaced a large part of those missing mouse cells with lab-grown human brain cells, creating mice with human neurons that can be altered to approximate human brain conditions researchers are eager to study.
"For the past two decades, there's been a quest to try to build models of the human brain outside of the human body," says Sergiu Pașca, professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University and senior author on the paper, published in the journal Nature. "This is not going to replace all the models we had before, but it's going to provide us access to other aspects of human brain function that would be very difficult to study otherwise."
Pașca says this research was conducted with strong ethical oversight and pushes research forward. At the same time, outside researchers point out that the development raises significant questions about where it could lead.
"It's really a powerful technology to study human neurons and how human brain circuits can form in a more natural environment" than a petri dish, says Hongkui Zeng, executive vice president and director of brain science at the Allen Institute in Seattle, Washington, who was not affiliated with the study.
But "going forward, there will be some considerations, if not concerns," she added — such as the implications of deploying this technique in larger and longer-living animals.
Making space for human neurons
While it's not the first time human brain cells have been installed in mice, this new effort manages to connect significantly more human cells than before.
Previous attempts were limited by an enduring biological reality: Human brain cells develop at least 20 times slower than those in mice, Pașca says.
That meant that neurons in a regularly developing mouse formed a rapid network, outcompeting the human cells that were dropped in. "By the time the human cells managed to extend a few millimeters, mice cells had already formed most of the connections, and brain development closed," Pașca says.
The team solved for this by breeding genetically engineered mice that were missing specific parts of their brains. "We thought we could provide the human cells more opportunities to connect by removing parts of the nervous system of the mouse in a very precise, very clean way," he says.
To their surprise, the mice they bred were still quite functional: "They actually have quite good locomotion," Pașca says, "They don't do that well in memory tasks…[but] you wouldn't be able to tell when you look at these animals that they're lacking half of the volume of their brain."
This part of the experiment shows the remarkable adaptability of developing brains, says Keng of the Allen Institute. Animals missing their cerebral cortex — which governs higher-order brain function — aren't expected to do well on challenging tasks. These mice, however, developed alternative strategies using the remaining parts of the brain. "Surprisingly, the animal can adapt," she says, "It's incredible to see that."
A more human-ish lab mouse brain
Next, the research team added small clumps of human neurons to the depleted mouse brains.
"We gently place them, through a very quick, simple procedure, right into that vacant space in the nervous system of the mouse," Pașca says. "Within a few days, the cell starts to divide and expand. Within a few weeks to months, they will essentially grow, become vascularized, and largely take up the space that was present."
The mice with filled-out brains were better at memory tasks and interacting with other mice. "Many of the deficits that were present in the [depleted] mice are now not present in this animal," he says, "So it seems that the human cortical cells are perhaps contributing to restoring some of these lost functions."
But there were some key differences between the mice with human brain cells, and regular, unaltered mice, which bode well for research into human brain conditions, Pașca says.
For instance, mice with human brain cells had problems walking properly after their brains were deprived of oxygen. That's not the case for regular mice, which are resilient to low-oxygen conditions. This more human-like reaction suggests the altered mice might be better models for brain conditions linked to low oxygen, such as cerebral palsy, intellectual disability, and epileptic encephalopathies, he says.
"Hopefully, it will be incredibly powerful for tackling questions of disease and developing therapeutics," says Pașca.
As the tech grows more complex, so do the ethics questions
The researchers emphasize that this is not a full brain transplant; in the experiment, they've removed some 14 million mouse neurons and added around 4 million lab-grown human cortical neurons.
The resulting mice still lack other important types of brain cells, which the researchers deliberately didn't add, and their human neurons don't form a typical outer brain. "The cortex is usually beautifully organized into layers. But here, when we put the cells in, they don't know where up and down really is," Pașca says. "They fail to organize on a larger scale."
And the model is best suited for certain diseases that begin in early human development, due to the human-paced growth of the implanted neurons: "It turns out the timing of development is well-conserved…even when we put them in an animal that is developing faster," he says.
Some of these limitations reflect deliberate choices made by the researchers for ethical reasons, says Nita Farahany, professor of law and philosophy at Duke Law, who served as an unpaid member of an external ethics board that helped guide the progression of this work.
For instance, the researchers chose to stop the experiments when the human brain cells reached around six months old — before they could form a connection in the mouse's brain that is considered a hallmark of consciousness by human development researchers. "They're trying to stop the study before the markers of consciousness, or the fact of consciousness, might emerge," Farahany says — a choice she agrees with.
"But that line itself is a line that you might start to wonder about," she adds. "Do you stop a study before an animal develops consciousness, if it has the potential or is on its way to develop consciousness? Does it have different interests or rights that we would assign to it?"
And should the fact that the mouse has human brain cells change how it's treated and considered? "Do we treat it with greater ethical care than we treat traditional mice? I think probably so," says Farahany. "My instinct is to err on the side of caution with research like this rather than to be more permissive."
The ethical considerations will grow as these experiments continue down expected paths, such as attempting a similar procedure on larger animals such as pigs or non-human primates, says Zeng of the Allen Institute. "Because those animals live a lot longer, the human neurons could survive longer and they could form more functionally meaningful circuits – but then I think the ethical issues also become a lot bigger, more serious as well," she says.
These types of concerns come with conducting cutting-edge research, says Farahany. The team has been "incredibly thoughtful" in conducting their work as well and ethically as possible, she says. Still, "this brings us into new gray areas for which there are not clear ethical guidelines or norms," she says.
With this publication, the researchers have presented the public with a next step in this model, she says. Now, it's society's turn to weigh in.

They're not playing our song! North Korean anthem played at South Korean hockey match
South Korean field hockey players were perplexed when the national anthem of North Korea was played instead of their own before a men's field hockey match against Bangladesh at the Asian Games
NAGOYA, Japan -- South Korean field hockey players were perplexed Friday when the national anthem of North Korea was played — instead of their own — before a men’s field hockey match against Bangladesh at the Asian Games.
South Korean players looked on, unsure of how to respond. Many South Korean players stood at attention, some ran their hands through their hair, and some left their right hand over their heart as the music played.
Organizers quickly corrected the problem and played the correct anthem.
South Korea won the match 5-0. The Asian Games open officially on Saturday.
South Korea's Yonhap news agency called the situation an “awkward mishap.”
“Standing with their hands over their hearts in front of the unfurled South Korean flag, the South Korean players could not hide their bewilderment,” Yonhap reported.
“Belatedly realizing the mistake, the organizing committee played Bangladesh's national anthem first before playing South Korea's," Yonhap added. “However, pressed for time ahead of the scheduled match start, the referee instructed players to exchange greetings while the South Korean anthem was still playing, forcing South Korean athletes to start the match without being able to sing the anthem.”
Some matches at the Asian Games have been played before the official opening to accommodate a crowded schedule which features more than 11,000 athletes, more than the Summer Olympics.

On August 17, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) announced its revamped social media team, appointing Deepak Mhaskey as the national social media convenor, and Priti Gandhi, Shivanand Dwivedi, Alok Bhatt and Arun Yadav as co-convenors.
While curiosity grew as to who these newly appointed individuals were and their past work and association with the party, social media users were quick to notice that immediately after the announcement, Gandhi, Dwivedi and Yadav made their X accounts private and there was no trace of Bhatt on the internet.
While all the other IT cell members are back to being active on X, albeit after deleting hundreds of thousands of old posts, Alok Bhatt is the only one in the group whose X handle remains inaccessible or ‘protected’ even a month after the new team was announced.
The only remnants of Bhatt’s online presence are the now-disabled X account, screenshots from his X posts and some articles in Right-wing outlets like OpIndia, Organiser and Swarajya.
Alt News found that in the past, Bhatt had been called out for controversial tweets several times. In archived screenshots of his posts from the past, the BJP functionary can be seen using sexist, Islamophobic, and derogatory language, some of which can be seen below:
Who is Alok Bhatt?
Bhatt, who claims to hail from Dehradun, has worn many hats over the course of his career. According to his LinkedIn profile, he graduated from Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University (HNBGU) in Uttarakhand and went on to work with several organisations, including NIIT University, where he served as financial controller until April 2010.
In 2010, he founded Nature Connect Outdoors — an education and adventure non-profit organisation that deals in outdoor education and skill development, including treks, camping, and rafting expeditions. According to the website’s bio, Bhatt had “shunned his corporate career” to follow his passion, which culminated in the formation of the NGO. The organisation is still functional.
According to details available on Zauba Corp, Bhatt is a Chartered Accountant (CA) and the partner of a firm of CAs called RSAC & CO LLP, incorporated in May 2021.
Bhatt has also served as the economic adviser to former Uttarakhand chief minister Trivendra Singh Rawat. However, it’s not clear when he was appointed and when exactly his tenure ended. He wrote an article for Firstpost defending the ministry of housing and urban affairs over the controversial Central Vista project. The author bio designated him as ‘Economic Advisor’ to Rawat.
In 2020, after a district officer’s press release promoting inter-caste and interfaith marriages drew criticism from social media users, Bhatt had reportedly tweeted: “No one from the government has spoken in support of promoting interfaith marriages. No one in the BJP government in their wildest dreams will support anything that is made out here.”
We sent an email and called up Bhatt several times to know more from him, but he did not respond.
Long-standing Association With BJP
Bhatt’s X handle, @alok_bhatt, was followed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. In fact, Modi quote-tweeted one of Bhatt’s posts in 2024, where he urged people to watch the film Sabarmati Report.
Bhatt was also invited to PM Modi’s swearing-in ceremony in the past. In 2024, Right-wing influencer Vikas Pandey shared an image with Bhatt alongside former BJP spokesperson Nupur Sharma, member of the economic advisory council to the PM, Sanjeev Sanyal, and others, with the caption “First swearing in”.
Pics from first swearing in @amishra77 @NupurSharmaBJP @sanjeevsanyal @alok_bhatt pic.twitter.com/YADSZm1lCT
— Vikas Pandey (Sankrityayan) (@MODIfiedVikas) June 9, 2024
We also found an X post from 2015 where Bhatt can be seen with the Prime Minister.
Matter of pride 4 me when friends meets the man of millenium @narendramodi @alok_bhatt @kaushkrahul @tajinderbagga pic.twitter.com/LG2e1lGsNT
— Vishnu Dhanuka (Modi ka Parivar) (@VishnuDhanuka) July 2, 2015
In April 2022, Right-wing influencer Shefali Vaidya, who has been fact-checked by Alt News several times in the past, posted an image with Bhatt on X saying that she had met the latter and “his lovely family” in Uttarakhand.
No Uttarakhand trip would have been complete without meeting @alok_bhatt and his lovely family! pic.twitter.com/1QHMaJk9OY
— Shefali Vaidya. 🇮🇳 (@ShefVaidya) April 2, 2022
X Handle Suspended for Violating Guidelines
Alt News found at least three instances, in 2018, 2019, and 2020, where X (then Twitter) had initiated action against Bhatt’s handle for violation of community guidelines, and at least two of those three actions were owing to hateful content.
In 2018, Bhatt declared that all the “killers of Pandits, Rapists of Pandits, Terrorists killing in Kashmir, instigators of Godhra, and bombers of Mumbai were all Muslims, and thus Islam was the problem”. His account had then been ‘limited’.
Why is @alok_bhatt blocked by twitter for a week when blue-ticked racist bigots like Audrey Truschke are still on Twitter despite their naked Hinduphobia? @TwitterIndia pic.twitter.com/3qlnNiVWhj
— Shefali Vaidya. 🇮🇳 (@ShefVaidya) April 20, 2018
In 2019, Bhatt declared in a post that “their boys could take on Jihadis” but needed police action for “rumour mongers” like activist Shehla Rashid. “These jihadi accomplices are running a hate campaign aided and abetted by Media…please help our state dispel rumours,” the tweet read. His account was suspended after this. Political analyst and Right-wing influencer Suresh Nakhua took to Twitter to condemn the move.
Just because @alok_bhatt exposed lies of Shehla Liar Rashid, @twitter has suspended the handle.#BringBackAlokBhatt pic.twitter.com/YJpuOAxQjZ
— Suresh Nakhua 🇮🇳 (@SureshNakhua) February 17, 2019
His account was suspended again in 2020.
What’s this @TwitterIndia ? @alok_bhatt has tweeted about Hindu girls being kidnapped, r@ped and forcefully converted to !slam in Pakistan and his account has been suspended, What kind of nonsense is this? Explain!#BringBackAlokBhatt pic.twitter.com/w4T3epRn6t
— संवैधानिक डकैत (@Shivam_h9) May 29, 2020
The Pamphlet-Savitr Analytics-Alok Bhatt Connection
In 2022, Bhatt took on a directorial role at Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation, a company that was incorporated in April 26 that year, with Bhatt and Ashish Nautiyal initially named as directors. According to documents filed with the Union ministry of corporate affairs (MCA), Bhatt holds 9,500 shares, or 95 per cent of the company, while Nautiyal holds the remaining 500 shares, or 5 per cent.
Interestingly, Nautiyal is also the founding editor of the Right-wing media outlet, The Pamphlet.
Savitr Analytics has no website or online presence. We went through its financial records filed with the MCA for the financial years 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25, and found that it was registered as a Section 8 company, i.e., a non-profit. In the 2024-25 financial year, its total revenue from operations was Rs 2.7 crore.
The organisation’s revenue across all three years comes from ‘sale of services’, and the rows for ‘Grants or donations received (relevant for Sec 8 companies)’, present in the 2022-23 and 2023-24 filings, are left blank in 2022-23 and 2023-24. In 2024-25, the row does not exist.
Under ‘Corporate Information’, they state ‘Research and awareness about Indian culture and heritage…’, ‘Promotion of commerce, art, science, sports, education, research, social welfare, religion, charity, and environmental protection…’ and ‘Advancement of education, learning, and skills development…’ as their activities.
There was a category called ‘professional expenses’ in the 2022-23 filing that was later relabeled as ‘content production expenses’. Rs. 41,48,600 was spent in the first year, Rs. 95,36,600 (filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the second year, and Rs. 1,38,53,200 (also filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the third year.
Next, we found that an individual named Ridhika Aggarwal stated on LinkedIn that she worked as a content writer for Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation until August 2023. We went through her X timeline (linked to her LinkedIn profile) and found that she wrote at least three articles for The Pamphlet during her tenure at Savitr. None of the articles are currently available on the website.
Ridhika is also listed as a non-official member of a steering committee formed by the Union ministry of environment, forest and climate change in 2023.
The Pamphlet, previously known as The Indian Affairs, posted for the first time on Facebook in April 2022, which is the same time when Savitr Analytics was incorporated.
ठीक 2 साल पहले देहरादून में आज ही के दिन @Pamphlet_in ऑफिस निर्माण की शुरुआत हो गई थी, उत्तराखण्ड चुनाव निपटने के बाद मैं २० दिन के अपने नैनीताल और लैंसडाउन प्रवास के बाद दून घाटी में उतरा था।
आज ही के दिन साल 2019 में लोकसभा चुनाव का रिजल्ट भी आया था और प्रधानमंत्री… pic.twitter.com/6lAVSW3twN
— V Ashish Nautiyal (@ashu_nauty) May 15, 2024
The Pamphlet claims to “cut through the noise of the modern information ecosystem by offering readers and viewers clarity, depth and perspective on issues that shape India and the world.” Its reports have seem to be echoing pro-BJP narratives. An August 11 video report, for instance, was captioned: “Questions raised in the public domain regarding the credentials of two CJP leaders, Abhijeet Dipke and Saurav Das, have brought up several serious concerns”. It questioned Dipke’s Boston University degree, academic timeline and funding, as well as Das’ property, tenancy, rent, police verification, and electoral records.
During the CJP protests, another report took a swipe at Mohammed Junaid, who had been feeding protesters, with the reporter noting that “such bhaijaans were also seen” at the protest sites in Shaheen Bagh and Farmers’ stir. Thumbnails of these reports carried AI-generated visuals of individuals critical of the Union government, their faces distorted through AI to portray them in a negative light. This is a tactic common across Right-wing outlets and social media troll handles.
More recently, the outlet, alongside Abhijit Iyer-Mitra, Law Beat, The Jaipur Dialogues and The Sunday Guardian, was summoned by the Delhi high court over a Rs 2 crore privacy suit by Cockroach Janta Party spokesperson Saurav Das, who alleged that they had disclosed his home address and other personal details online. The case will be heard on September 14.
The video below depicts a time when the outlet was still called The Indian Affairs, and Nautiyal (in striped shirt) can be seen with his colleagues alongside educator Pawan Gupta.
The Indian Affairs @ForIndiaMatters Coming Soon
Subscribe our Youtube Channel: https://t.co/orjioxscXy #TIA #TheIndianAffairs pic.twitter.com/v1VVtf83XZ
— The Pamphlet (@Pamphlet_in) July 22, 2022
Nautiyal’s last video with The Pamphlet was uploaded in December 2024. In June 2025, Nautiyal was pictured with the OpIndia team. His first video for OpIndia, an interview with Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Dhami, came a month later, in July 2025.
Nautiyal is now the multimedia & digital head and editor at OpIndia, and is no longer listed as a director of Savitr on the MCA website.
It is worth noting that The Pamphlet’s website does not disclose any parent company, ownership, editorial team, funding details or board of directors. Its ‘About Us’ page offers only a description of what it does, while calling itself ‘an independent digital media platform’. The only publicly mentioned funding source we could find was YouTube memberships of The Pamphlet costing Rs. 119 to Rs. 3199 per month.
Nautiyal is not the only link between Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet. An individual named Shiv Kumar Mishra was appointed the director of Savitr Analytics in April 2023. In March 2023, Mishra was announced as the CEO of The Pamphlet.
Please welcome @shivkmishr, Founder & CEO, The Pamphlet https://t.co/U53aK62Fzo
— The Pamphlet (@Pamphlet_in) March 14, 2023
In other words, two of the three directors of Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation have held senior positions at The Pamphlet. And in both cases, the appointments to Savitr and The Pamphlet came in close succession. This raises the question of whether the two entities are formally linked.
We also found that The Pamphlet had an office space from its inception in Dehradun, and it is evident from a photo posted by Nautiyal that it began with a team of at least 20 people. Bhatt, the reader would remember, also claims to be from Dehradun.
While all of this points to a connection between Bhatt and The Pamphlet, there appears to be a concerted effort to keep that relationship under wraps. Hence, we tried to dig more.
Is Bhatt Linked to The Pamphlet? We Asked The Pamphlet
We sent an email to The Pamphlet on September 3 asking them about the relationship between Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet, and whether Alok Bhatt was connected to The Pamphlet, given that he holds a 95% stake in Savitr Analytics, a company whose other directors have held senior positions at The Pamphlet. We also asked them about their funding sources, since nothing is mentioned on the website.
In reply, they asked us to send our queries to another email ID of The Pamphlet and also to Alok Bhatt, Nirwa Mehta, Ashish Nautiyal and Shiv Mishra. Interestingly, they provided us with the email IDs and phone numbers of each of these individuals. This, in itself, might be considered an indicator of some sort of link between The Pamphlet and Bhatt. It is unlikely for an organisation to provide the direct contact details of someone with whom it has no professional association.
We then sent our queries to all of them.
Nautiyal responded to us saying that his reporting manager, OpIndia editor Nupur J Sharma, “suggested” him “not to give (you) any quotes or information as a matter of policy of not engaging with entities that don’t act in good faith”. A day later, he took to X to let the world know that a woman from Alt News “with a Hindu-sounding name” had approached him with some questions.
Pamphlet editor Nirwa Mehta sent us a 1,071-word response, but did not answer any of our questions. Instead, she sent a detailed set of reciprocal questions concerning Alt News’ funding transparency, the outside associations of its founders and editor, and grants received by individuals associated with Alt News, both currently and in the past. She offered to answer Alt News’ questions in writing once Alt News answered hers first.
It is worth noting that The Pamphlet published a video on Alt News on August 16, 2026, without seeking a response from the organisation.
This correspondent responded to Mehta, stating that questions concerning Alt News’ funding should be directed to its editor, while questions concerning any of the founders’ personal assignments should be directed to the person concerned. We also reminded her that a so-called expose on Alt News’ founders had been published by The Pamphlet without either of the concerned persons being approached for a response — a violation of basic journalistic ethics.
In her final response, Mehta did not address the question of ethics. Instead, in a demand that many may find bizarre, she asked this correspondent, “as a responsible employee”, to take her questions to the Alt News directors.
At this point, we felt there was no point continuing the conversation.
We will update our article if The Pamphlet answers Alt News’ questions on whether Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet are connected in any way, and whether Alok Bhatt, BJP’s new IT cell member who continues to remain away from X, holds a position at The Pamphlet.
Social Media Posts Answer the Question
The connection between The Pamphlet and Alok Bhatt is one of internet’s worst kept secrets, it seems. We found several instances on social media where well-known faces from the Right-wing ecosystem tagged Alok Bhatt alongside members of The Pamphlet team — whether to thank them for invitations to Delhi Shabdotsav 2026, where The Pamphlet Panchayat featured on the itinerary, or in connection with other events involving the organisation.
On January 5, 2026, Right-wing influencer Abhijit Iyer-Mitra, who was recently criticised for comparing Newslaundry journalists to prostitutes, thanked The Pamphlet team — including its editor Nirwa Mehta, anchor Shreya Arora, and Bhatt — for inviting him to speak at The Pamphlet Panchayat.
Responding to Iyer-Mitra, Nirwa Mehta and another The Pamphlet employee, Pratibha, thanked him for being a part of the session. The exchange is significant because it can be seen as an acknowledgement by the Pamphlet editor and another employee of Bhatt being a part of the organisation.
Delhi Shabdotsav 2026 was a three-day cultural and literary festival held from January 2 to January 4, 2026, organised by Suruchi Prakashan with the support of the department of art, culture and languages of the Delhi government. The Pamphlet was the digital partner at the event and hosted ‘The Pamphlet Panchayat’ at the fest. The Pamphlet team held and moderated several discussions over the three days, including those with Sanjeev Newar, Vijay Patel, and Subhi Vishwakarma. The subjects of the discussions ranged from ‘Love Jihad: factsheet’ to ‘Bharat’s Hostile Neighbourhood & Need to Regain Shatrubodh’.
We went through the images posted on Shabdotsav’s website and found that Bhatt was present at the event.
The link between Alok Bhatt and The Pamphlet becomes more apparent in another conversation on X in which Iyer-Mitra directly addressed Mehta as Pamphlet and Alok Bhatt’s ‘staff’. Iyer jokingly rebuked Mehta for liking a certain kind of car. Tagging Bhatt, he wrote, “Do @Pamphlet_in and @alok_bhatt @shreya_arora22 approve of these disgusting and extremely hateful statements by their staff?” Mehta responded to Iyer-Mitra’s post, but did not object to the ‘staff’ reference.
On June 1, 2023, a little more than a year after The Pamphlet’s inception, one @saket71 posted a picture with Ashish Nautiyal, who was working at The Pamphlet then, and called him a ‘Media Mughal’. He later tagged Alok Bhatt and Shiv Mishra, praising them for “putting a great team together.”
Such a pleasure to meet the young stars of @Pamphlet_in , @RitikaChandola @himanshi__bisht and the whole team. Such a great young team, full of hope and dreams, and a visible sense of great camaraderie. Kudos to @alok_bhatt and @shivkmishr for putting a great team together. https://t.co/NnmHkA9rQO
— saket साकेत ಸಾಕೇತ್ 🇮🇳 (@saket71) June 1, 2023
Several people have congratulated Alok Bhatt at various points of time upon The Pamphlet reaching certain milestones.
To sum up, what raises serious questions about the BJP’s decision to name Bhatt as its social media co-convenor is not just his past social media conduct, but also the opacity surrounding his professional associations. One organisation he appears to be associated with, The Pamphlet, does not publicly disclose its ownership, editorial team, board or funding sources. Without any apparent source of funding, it starts off as a 20-member organization. Who pays their salary? How are establishment costs met? There are no answers. Again, another corporate entity closely linked to him, Savitr Analytics, has no website or public online presence despite reporting Rs 2.7 crore in operational revenue in 2025.
Things get murkier when one takes into account the desperate efforts by Bhatt’s associates to conceal his association with The Pamphlet, evident in the organisation’s refusal to answer direct questions regarding this.
In other words, a man linked to organisations with questionable records, and whose involvement with a pro-government outlet is abundantly visible in public, but markedly absent from the outlet’s own disclosures, has now been given a formal position in the BJP’s social media cell.

Israel’s president has pardoned a combat medic who shot dead a badly wounded Palestinian attacker who had stabbed a soldier in the occupied West Bank, in a case that divided the country a decade ago.
Elor Azaria’s conviction in 2017 for manslaughter and his release after serving two-thirds of his 18-month sentence drew enormous attention in Israel, where military service is compulsory for most Jewish men.
In his first interview after his release, Azaria said he would “act exactly the same, because that’s how I needed to act”.
Azaria had approached Abdel Fattah al-Sharif as he lay on the ground, unarmed and badly hurt, after stabbing a soldier in the city of Hebron. A mobile phone video captured Azaria shooting al-Sharif in the head.
The office of president Isaac Herzog said in a statement on Saturday that he acted on the recommendation of defence minister Israel Katz. The statement cited the time that had passed, and the spirit of the approaching Yom Kippur, or Day of Atonement, holiday as among the factors in the decision.
Herzog’s office also said that Azaria, who was 20 when he was sentenced, had “expressed his sorrow” in his request. The statement noted that in an earlier request, he called his gunshot an “operational error”.
In a separate statement, Katz called it a “right, humane and fitting decision” and said Azaria had been in a “complex operational mission”.
But the military’s chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, had said in a letter to the defence minister that the pardon should not be granted, Israeli media reported.
The conviction was a rare case of a military court ruling against a soldier for deadly action taken in the field. Top generals had pressed for his prosecution, while many in the Israeli public supported Azaria at a time when there had been a series of stabbings and car-ramming attacks by Palestinians or Israeli Arabs. Some supporters protested outside his trial.
On Saturday, Israel’s hard-line national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said in a statement that “cancelling the criminal record of someone who killed a terrorist makes me emotional and very happy”.
Some Palestinians and human rights groups had described Azaria’s sentence as far too lenient. Prosecutors had sought a sentence of three to five years.
The statement by Herzog’s office on Saturday said that his decision “does not constitute a reassessment of the case”.
The divisions over Azaria’s case led to public polling and political pressure that led the defence minister at the time, Moshe Ya’alon, to resign.
After the verdict, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu called for Azaria to be pardoned.
After the sentencing, the Palestinian government minister in charge of prisoner affairs, Issa Karaka, called it a “joke”.

Aprilia's Jorge Martin made an extraordinary recovery from a chaotic opening-lap battle with championship rival Marc Marquez to win the Austrian Grand Prix sprint from pole position on Saturday (September 19, 2026) and reclaim the MotoGP championship lead.
Martin, who had stormed to pole position ahead of reigning MotoGP champion Marquez earlier on Saturday (September 18), beat the Ducati rider to claim his 20th sprint victory after KTM's Pedro Acosta crashed out while leading in the closing stages.
The 28-year-old Martin, the 2024 MotoGP champion, now has 286 points in the standings, three ahead of Spanish compatriot Marquez, heading into Sunday's Grand Prix at the Red Bull Ring in Spielberg.
Martin's race appeared to unravel in the opening corners when he was forced on to the defensive by seven-time MotoGP champion Marquez, ran wide and dropped to eighth.
Acosta capitalised to take command and built a lead of nearly three seconds, only to crash out with about three laps remaining at KTM's home circuit.
Martin, meanwhile, carved his way back through the pack to secure a remarkable victory.
"I enjoyed the race for sure," Martin said. "I was a bit lucky with Pedro because we thought that I would be second. We started well but then we were on the limit on the first lap, so I thought my chances were over.
"But then, lap by lap, I didn't give up during the race. I was pushing till my maximum, trying to be super concentrated to come from the back and then win. The end was so good.
"I am really happy for my team because they really deserve it. We are ready for tomorrow. I hope that we can continue at this pace."
Marquez had seized the championship lead for the first time this season by winning last weekend's chaotic San Marino Grand Prix. The result had left him level on points with Martin but the 33-year-old moved to the top of the standings by virtue of having won more races this season.
"Today the target was third place in the sprint and I tried not to lose a lot of points against Jorge because it's already in practice that Pedro and Jorge had a better pace," Marquez said.
"Then I found the position where I sat just behind Jorge, and we were a bit lucky with Pedro's mistake. But happy and ready for tomorrow."
Aprilia's Marco Bezzecchi, third in the championship standings, completed the podium.
Trackhouse Aprilia's Ai Ogura finished fourth with Alex Marquez fifth.

Listed NBFC Kissht has secured board approval to raise up ₹832.2 Cr via a preferential issue of equity shares to 34 investors and entities. In a filing with the exchanges, the company said that its board has approved the issuance of 2.6 Cr fully paid-up equity shares to the investors at an issue price of ₹314.11 apiece. The NBFC did not disclose how it plans to utilise the fresh proceeds from the issue. The allotment is still subject to regulatory and shareholder approval. The company has also convened an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders to seek approval for the preferential issue. “Funds raising by way of a preferential issue on a private placement basis of up to 2,64,93,882 fully paid-up equity shares of the company… for cash, at an issue price of ₹314.11 per share… for an amount aggregating to ₹832.19 Cr to identified investors (non-promoters), in accordance with the provisions of… applicable laws….,” read the filing. Among the investing companies, Axis Flexi Cap Fund, Axis Multi Cap Fund and Axis Small Cap Fund together will receive 63.7 Lakh shares worth nearly ₹200 Cr. Massachusetts Institute of Technology, via two entities, will also receive 27.1 Lakh shares totalling ₹85 Cr. Envision Capital will also get 12.7 Lakh shares valued at nearly ₹40 Cr, while PE firm First Bridge will lap up 12.1 Lakh shares for a sum of ₹20 Cr. Kissht will also allot 23.9 Lakh shares to three entities linked to Ashoka WhiteOak Capital for a consideration of nearly ₹75 Cr. Other investors that will receive allotment under the preferential issue include 360 One, Alchemy Capital, Groww, Bandhan Small Cap Fund, Unity Small Finance Bank, among others. In terms of the other individual investors, Ameeta Rajendra Naik will receive 63,671 shares worth ₹2 Cr and Anil Shah will get 1.6 Lakh shares valued at nearly ₹5 Cr. The latest fundraise comes barely four months after the NBFC made a strong debut on the exchanges, listing at a premium of 11.7% on the BSE compared to its issue price of ₹171. Its public issue comprised a fresh issue of shares worth ₹850 Cr and an OFS component totalling ₹76 Cr. Founded in 2015 by Ranvir Singh and Krishnan Vishwanathan, Kissht is a lending tech platform that offers digital personal and business loans of up to ₹5 Lakh. It also offers health-related insurance products and secured loans through loans against property. In July, it also received regulatory approval to begin distribution of mutual funds through its wholly-owned subsidiary Invincible Minds. The NBFC claimed to have 45+ active lending and co-lending partners under its belt at the end of June 2026. It also operated 101 offline branches across eight states and union territories, and managed to more than double YoY its active customer base to 3.49 Mn in Q1 FY27. On the financial front, Kissht’s consolidated net profit zoomed 59% to ₹95.1 Cr in Q1 FY27 as against ₹59.7 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Meanwhile, operating revenue zoomed nearly 45% to ₹669.5 Cr during the quarter under review as against ₹463.1 Cr in Q1 FY26. Shares of the NBFC closed Thursday’s trading session 5.08% higher at ₹359.7 on the BSE.

During the seventh edition of Semicon India today, Odisha’s chief minister (CM) Mohan Charan Majhi shared that the state is planning to set up an ‘Odisha Silicon Valley’ across an 870 acre stretch between Cuttack and Bhubaneswar. The state aims to transform from a mineral-rich region into a high-tech chip-making powerhouse. The CM said that the administration is in conversations with international semiconductor companies based out of countries like Sweden, Japan, and others to discuss potential projects pertaining to semiconductors, AI, and data centres in the state. As of now, construction across the state has begun on two central government-approved projects: Sicsem Pvt Ltd’s first-in-India silicon carbide fab and integrated packaging facility, and 3D Glass Solutions’ glass-substrate packaging facility, the CM announced. Efforts have also begun to launch a Phase 2 project with Sicsem to establish a silicon carbide epitaxy and packaging facility, per CM Majhi. As of now, the Odisha government has approved five additional semiconductor projects worth approximately ₹11,000 Cr, which are estimated to create around 4,500 direct jobs and over 16,000 indirect jobs. While RiR Power Electronics, Sancorn Technology, and ASP Semiconductor have signed MOUs for semiconductor projects, Intel and 3D Glass Solutions have also signed an MOU for a partnership aiming to bring $3.3 Bn (₹30,550 Cr) in investment and over 1,800 direct jobs to the state. To support research and commercialisation, Odisha is also investing ₹125 Cr towards a ₹452 Cr National Industry Co-Development Hub on Integrated Power Electronics alongside IIT Bhubaneswar and the National Research Foundation. The state government has also amended its semiconductor policy and committed up to 25% capex for projects approved under the India Semiconductor Mission, the CM revealed. “With this credit, along with full infrastructure support and incentives, Odisha's offering is very attractive and competitive, ensuring our success,” he said. CM Majhi also highlighted specialised training programmes at the World Skill Center in Bhubaneswar developed in partnership with the Singapore government through which the government is aiming to meet the demand for highly skilled labour from the technology ecosystem. “We are focusing heavily on emerging technologies like semiconductors, AI, and data centres. Beyond the World Skill Center, we have developed key ITIs into Institutes of National Excellence equipped with labs and modern training infrastructure,” he added. He further said the government aims to prioritise skill-based employability over local hiring quotas in order to ensure the youth of Odisha can be integrated into the tech ecosystem.
