Partnership is key to ending AIDS – UK leadership can get us there faster
Ending AIDS as a public health threat is still possible by 2030, writes Courtenay Howe. But we need a renewed commitment to all the things that have helped create the progress we have made over the last few decades
It’s not about one country having all the answers and another having all the questions,” Kirsty McNeill, the minister for international development and Africa, said this week, describing the UK’s approach to partnerships, “but instead, bringing together different strengths to achieve far more than either of us could alone.”
Many of us who work in international development and advocacy will resonate with this framing. Shifting from hierarchical forms of aid to a system based on solidarity and partnership is something that many of us have tirelessly advocated for, and has long been a driving principal of the global HIV response.
Community involvement and leadership have been central to the response and the resulting progress speaks for itself. In 2002, the year the UK co-founded the Global Fund partnership, only 102,000 people had access to HIV treatment, less than 1 per cent of people living with HIV.
New data from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria released this week shows that last year 26.9 million people, in countries where the Global Fund invests, had access to antiretroviral therapy for HIV. The number of AIDS-related deaths in 2025 was 57 per cent lower than in 2010, from 1.3 million to 570,000.
But the current environment in which communities and organisations such as the Global Fund advance efforts towards ending AIDS as a public health threat cannot be overlooked.
In 2025, donor government funding for HIV decreased by $2.1 billion (£1.6bn) compared to 2024, representing a 25 per cent cut. Funding cuts globally have had a significant impact particularly on HIV prevention efforts and women are disproportionately affected. In sub-Saharan Africa women account for 6 out of 10 new acquisitions and adolescent girls and young women (aged 15-24 years) remain at high risk with 3000 new HIV acquisitions per week in 2025.
The UK’s own funding cuts, reducing the ODA budget to 0.3 per cent last year, raises concerns about a step back from international political and financial leadership in global health. The welcome shift in international development towards a new collaborative and solidaristic model still requires the UK’s important commitment to advocating for and supporting partnership and community leadership on the global stage.
The communities that had been at the forefront of the HIV response have been impacted hardest by these funding cuts. For many community-led organisations, their delivery of critical HIV prevention and provision of support to people living with HIV has reduced by 50 per cent. Alongside devastating funding cuts, we also see a rollback on human rights and the criminalisation of marginalised communities increasing for the first time since UNAIDS began tracking these trends.
Ending AIDS as a public health threat is still possible by 2030. But we need a renewed commitment to community leadership and human rights. We need scale-up and rollout of innovations such as the twice-yearly jab for HIV prevention, lenacapavir, and continued partnership to support more sustainable and self-reliant country responses to the HIV response.
We need scientific and medical advances to be accessible to low- and middle-income countries. Over the next few years, UK political leadership and sustainable funding will be critical in determining whether we stay on track to meet this goal.
Courtenay Howe is head of advocacy at STOPAIDS

Flooding around the city of Malda in the Indian state of West Bengal since Thursday has had a devastating effect. A swell caused by Hurricane Marie led to significant beach erosion across Orange county in California on 7 September. The erosion formed a cliff edge on some of the beaches, along with exposing old asphalt, pipes and even pieces of an old pier. The flooding caused by the swell damaged homes and vehicles, as well as flooding streets, leaving behind a layer of sand. The swell has been estimated to be between 8 and 10ft tall. Local people say it is not uncommon to see beach erosion, but this has been one of the most severe cases.

Premium flexible workspace operator Innov8 Workspaces sharply improved its profitability in the fiscal year FY26 while rapidly expanding the network of centres it operates across the country. Innov8's net profit surged nearly 11.8X to ₹13.8 Cr in FY26 from ₹1.2 Cr in FY25, as per its annual report. Important to highlight that the startup's profitability took a 97% hit in FY25 from ₹37.7 Cr in FY24. Meanwhile, operating revenue rose 76% to ₹201.3 Cr from ₹114.5 Cr, while EBITDA net of lease increased 64.6% to ₹49.4 Cr from ₹30 Cr. The company had projected its FY26 I-GAAP EBITDA to double to ₹60 Cr back in September 2025. The sharp improvement in the bottom line was also aided by a notable uptick in non-operating revenue. Innov8 reported ₹38.9 Cr in other income during FY26, more than 12X the ₹3.1 Cr recorded in the previous year. A substantial portion of this came from a ₹36.7 Cr gain on termination of lease contracts. Including other income of ₹38.9 Cr, the total income stood at ₹240.2 Cr in FY26, a 104.4% increase from ₹117.5 Cr in the previous year. Revenue Nearly Doubles In Two Years Innov8's growth has accelerated considerably over the past two years. Operating revenue increased from ₹52.7 Cr in FY24 to ₹114.5 Cr in FY25 and further to ₹201.3 Cr in FY26. In this, rental income remained the company's primary source of revenue, contributing ₹173.6 Cr, or around 86% of operating revenue, in FY26. This was up 59.3% from ₹108.9 Cr in FY25. The company also generated ₹27.6 Cr from other operational income, while revenue from the sale of food and beverages stood at ₹15.5 Lakh. Other operational income rose sharply from ₹5.4 Cr in FY25, indicating that ancillary services are becoming a larger part of the company's revenue mix. The annual report says the growth was driven by expansion of the portfolio, higher occupancy, improved pricing and the scaling of its managed workspace business. Innov8 follows a landlord-led capex model in which landlords fund the fit-outs while Innov8 provides the brand, demand generation, design and operations. This model allows the company to expand without taking on the entire fit-out burden for new centres. Innov8 said this asset-light structure has allowed it to open a new centre roughly every three weeks over the past 15 months. Innov8 ended FY26 with 58 operational centres, adding 16 centres during the year. The expansion continued after the end of the fiscal year. The company added another 14 centres in the three months following March 31, 2026, taking its network to 72 centres as of July 2026. It has set a target of reaching 101 centres during FY27. Importantly, the company plans to expand to 22 cities during FY27, with Kochi, Coimbatore, Kolkata and Jaipur among the cities identified for expansion. It continues to focus on business districts and commercial clusters in cities including Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Chennai. Its stated strategy is to prioritise high-density commercial locations rather than pursue suburban volume. Vatika Acquisition Adds Enterprise Business One of the biggest developments after the close of FY26 was Innov8's acquisition of Vatika Business Centres Private Limited. The company entered into a share purchase agreement on June 8, 2026, to acquire the entire share capital of Vatika Business Centres for ₹27 Cr. The transaction closed on June 18, with 80% of the consideration payable at closing and the remaining 20% due three months later. Innov8 paid ₹10.2 Cr at closing, according to the annual report. The acquisition gives Innov8 an established managed-office platform and is expected to strengthen its enterprise workspace business. The company said Vatika brings marquee enterprise clients on long-term commitments and provides further room for expansion in the managed-office segment. "Our ambition has always been to build premium workspaces that combine thoughtful design, vibrant community, enterprise-grade infrastructure and fully managed services, while giving businesses the flexibility to adapt as their needs evolve... A customer can begin with five seats and grow to five hundred without ever leaving the Innov8 network. Our expansion into managed workspaces, including through the acquisition of Vatika Business Centres Private Limited, completes that ladder," said Rakesh Kumar, director and CFO, Innov8. Breaking Down Innov8’s Expenses The company’s total expenses increased to ₹226.2 Cr in FY26, an uptick of 86% from ₹121.6 Cr in the previous fiscal year. Here is a closer look at the areas where Innov8 spent the most: Depreciation And Amortisation Expense: Constituting 42.7% of the overall expenditure, spending under this head rose 2.3X to ₹96.7 Cr in the year under review, from ₹42.4 Cr in FY25. Finance Costs: Expenses towards interest on lease liabilities, interest on borrowing and bank charges came up to ₹70 Cr in FY26, marking 127.8% increase from ₹30.7 Cr in the previous fiscal. Finance costs contributed to 30.9% of the total expenses. Employee Benefit Expenses: Employee costs, including salaries, wages, bonus, gratuity expense and contribution to PF and other funds rose 75.3% to ₹6.8 Cr in the reported year, from ₹3.9 Cr in FY25.

Amit Shah suffers food poisoning in Karnataka, skips scheduled events
Union Home Minister Amit Shah missed scheduled events in Hubballi and Belagavi after suffering food poisoning. BJP leaders said he later recovered, but the illness disrupted key inaugurations during his Karnataka visit.
Union Home Minister Amit Shah, who was in Karnataka to attend two events on Saturday, suffered from "food poisoning" and is now "perfect", senior BJP leader and Union minister Pralhad Joshi said.
Shah skipped an event in Hubballi earlier in the day and his visit to Belagavi district was cancelled. However, local leaders said he visited the KLE campus in Hubballi in the evening before leaving for Delhi.
Shah was scheduled to inaugurate the new academic building of KLE Jagadguru Gangadhar Mahaswamigalu Moorusavirmath Medical College and the 1,200-bed KLE Hospital and Medical Research Centre at Gabbur in Hubballi.
Earlier in the day, Joshi, Karnataka Medical Education Minister Sharan Prakash Patil, former chief minister Basavaraj Bommai, Belagavi MP Jagadish Shettar and Sri Gurusiddha Rajayogindra Swami of Shri Jagadguru Moorusavirmath inaugurated the KLE campuses in his absence.
At the event, KLE Society Chairman and former Rajya Sabha MP Prabhakar Kore said, "Union Home Minister Amit Shah, who was the main attraction of this historic event, has remained in the hotel on the advice of doctors as he developed health issues. He asked me to convey this message to you."
Shah had arrived in Hubballi late on Friday.
Shah's visit to Examba in Chikkodi taluk of Belagavi district, where he was scheduled to inaugurate the new headquarters building of Sri Beereshwara Cooperative Credit Society, was cancelled.
Speaking to reporters in Examba, Joshi said, "Amit Shah should have come here. He suffered ill health due to food poisoning. Annasaheb Jolle (former BJP MP) had invited me and Shettar (Belagavi MP Jagadish Shettar) for the event, we were supposed to come along with him, but only we have come now."
Joshi later said Shah was "perfect" now. "Naturally, due to vomiting from food poisoning, he had some weakness," he added.

Malaysia’s jailed former Prime Minister Najib Razak, a central figure in the country’s biggest corruption scandal, has been granted a conditional pardon that allows him to serve the remainder of his jail term under house arrest, offering a reprieve for the ex-premier after spending the last four years in prison.
Najib’s house arrest granted by King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar, however, is conditional upon Najib paying a 50 million ringgit ($12.3 million) fine as part of his 1MDB sentence, the Prime Minister’s Department said in a statement on Friday. The house arrest runs through August 2028.
The decision comes after the nation’s Pardons Board, chaired by the king, met for the second time in as many weeks to consider Najib’s bid for a royal pardon. The king deferred a decision on his application, while granting clemency to other prisoners during its Sept. 11 meeting.

Small businesses located near tobacconists are being denied insurance or priced out of coverage as rising arson attacks turn neighbouring shops into collateral damage.
The problem has intensified after a spate of firebombings, which includes a recent Melbourne blaze that destroyed a Richmond tobacco retailer and nearly a dozen neighbouring shops, requiring 80 firefighters to contain.
Crime syndicates have been implicated in more than 200 firebombings of commercial and residential premises in Australia since 2023, according to government data, as rival groups vie for control of the illicit tobacco market.
A Melbourne retailer, who asked not to be identified, told Guardian Australia their insurer refused to renew a policy because they were a “few doors down” from a tobacconist.
“Even if we re-located, which is not really an option for us, who’s to say a tobacconist doesn’t move in next door?” the retailer said.
The retailer said they’d received quotes from other insurers that don’t include fire cover.
Legitimate tobacconists have also reportedly been targeted by syndicates expanding their revenue base, making it difficult for them to secure coverage as well.
Skye Cappuccio, the chief executive of the Council of Small Business Organisations Australia, said accessing or affording insurance for businesses located near tobacconists was becoming problematic.
“Small businesses should not be left carrying the financial consequences of criminal activity that is beyond their control,” Cappuccio said.
“We need a comprehensive effort from governments, law enforcement and regulators to address the illicit tobacco market, alongside broader action to address rising insurance costs and access to affordable cover for small businesses.”
Small businesses close to tobacco market-related firebombings are also affected by loss of foot traffic, revenue and reputation, according to the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission.
While insurers have not disclosed what constitutes “close proximity”, brokers generally consider it to be within about 20 metres of a tobacconist. Tobacco retailers within shopping complexes are seen as a lower risk.
Illicit tobacco accounted for 80% of the cigarettes smoked by Australians in 2025, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, with untaxed packets costing as little as $10 compared with more than $40 for a legal packet.
The surge in demand has sparked a political debate over whether Australia should reduce the tobacco excise to make legal cigarettes cheaper in order to curb illegal sales. Health experts have called for a focus on enforcement, which includes intercepting illegal products that enter the country through Australia’s ports.
A spokesperson at Suncorp said the insurer no longer offered insurance cover for tobacconist retailers, including renewals for existing customers.
The representative said businesses located near tobacconists may still be eligible, with underwriting decisions based on a range of factors, including the nature of the business and location-specific risks.
“As with all commercial insurance, applications are considered on a case-by-case basis,” the spokesperson said.
A QBE spokesperson said decisions were assessed individually.
“Where risk profiles change, this can influence the price, terms or availability of cover,” the spokesperson said.

From near oblivion to Europe - Brighton celebrate 125th anniversary
- Published
It is Thursday, 9 November, 2023. Brighton manager Roberto de Zerbi is addressing his players in the Amsterdam Arena before their Europa League tie with Ajax.
"There's 3,000 Brighton fans in this stadium tonight," said the Italian. "But there's more than twice that number in the city who have travelled over. Remember that when you go on to that pitch."
A long-standing senior Brighton official was in the dressing room that day. A fan first and foremost, but someone who has spent almost three decades working for the club.
"It made the hairs on the back of my neck stand up," he said.
For some clubs, an encounter with Ajax is commonplace. Not Brighton.
"The royalty of European football," says the official. "From where we've come from, to be in that environment. It was a pinch-me moment."
Brighton won 2-0. It was the high point of the first European campaign in the club's history.
Ask Paul Samrah for his single most memorable moment as a Brighton fan and a very different answer comes back, which goes to the heart of why, as they celebrate their 125th birthday around the visit of Arsenal, the Seagulls are almost unique among English clubs.
August 2007. "After the years of campaigning, the days and nights I spent fighting for regime change and then for the stadium, the moment I heard we'd actually got planning permission, that our objectors had decided not to continue their fruitless efforts to stop the stadium," he explained.
"We'd won our battle."
The two stories highlight the before and after reality of Brighton & Hove Albion.
Formed in 1901, Brighton were a Southern League club for almost two decades before they were voted into the Football League. They had experienced only seven seasons in Division Two when they were promoted to the top flight for the first time in 1979.
For years, they were known outside Sussex chiefly for "And Smith must score..." - the BBC radio commentary, delivered by the late Peter Jones, at a critical point during the 1983 FA Cup final, late in extra time. It was the moment when Gordon Smith, clear on goal with a chance to earn Brighton their first major trophy, saw his shot saved by Manchester United goalkeeper Gary Bailey. United won the replay.
But in 1995, chairman Bill Archer sold Brighton's Goldstone Ground, their home since 1902, because of escalating debts that there was no obvious way of paying. Fans were not consulted and no alternative stadium was put in place.
Brighton did not leave until 1997, although their final season at the Goldstone was only confirmed by the property company who owned the stadium, after the final game of the 1995-96 campaign, which had to be abandoned as thousands of furious fans spilled on to the pitch to demonstrate against the ownership. Both crossbars were snapped amid the tumult.
After two seasons playing 70 miles away at Gillingham, and with the idea of a new stadium in the Toad's Hole Valley area of Brighton a non-starter, the club returned to the city in 1999 and started playing at Withdean Stadium, most famous for being the home athletics track of Olympic middle distance gold medallist Steve Ovett.
That brings us back to De Zerbi's pre-match team-talk at Ajax.
Brighton had more than 7,000 fans in Amsterdam that night. When they moved into the Withdean, its capacity was only 6,000. The modern Brighton really is a totally different club to the one that existed before.
"After the 1983 FA Cup final, players were sold, there was no investment, the Goldstone was decaying and the crowds were dipping," said Samrah. "There was no communication between board and fans, directors came and went. There was no continuity, no leadership, no direction. We were just rudderless."
There are some notable figures in the Brighton story.
Former Football Association executive director David Davies got involved, Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott overturned a rejected planning application for Brighton's current stadium in Falmer. Former chairman Dick Knight stabilised a club that in 1997 came within 27 minutes of being relegated out of the Football League.
Without that trio, and many more, it is quite possible Brighton would not exist.
The contemporary Brighton are different.
They began their second European campaign in the Norwegian city of Tromso last month, knowing the Conference League offers the chance of that elusive first trophy.
They play in a magnificent stadium, a short train journey from the city centre, with its new corporate areas, and, generally, inclusive family atmosphere. Their recruitment model, buying players in and selling them on for vast profits, is envied. The new Brighton just beat Manchester United at Old Trafford for the fifth time in six visits. Four games into their 10th consecutive Premier League campaign, they sit fifth.
The contemporary Brighton exist the way they do largely because of the vision and investment of Tony Bloom.
Born in Brighton, Bloom is a lifelong fan. His connection to the club is through his grandfather Harry, a former vice-chairman, and uncle Ray, a director.
Bloom, 56, is an entrepreneur. He made his money in finance and gambling, largely through the use of data. He became chairman in 2009, and masterminded the rise from League One and move into the American Express Stadium. Last season, Brighton's average attendance was more than 31,000.
In their 125-year history, Brighton have never had it so good.
"Anyone walking into Brighton today compared to even 15 years ago would not think it was the same football club," sporting director Mike Cave told BBC Sport.
"The club has been on an unbelievable journey. We've got staff members and many fans who have done that journey. For those of us who weren't here 15 years ago, our responsibility is to ensure what's to come - and I think there's lots - is better than what's happened in the recent or long-distance past."
As for Bloom himself, he has reflected on Brighton's 125th birthday in the programme for the Arsenal game.
"Since 1901, this football club has been part of the fabric of our city and the broader county of Sussex," he said.
"It has connected generations of families and communities. Grandparents have brought their children and grandchildren to matches. Lifelong friendships have been forged on terraces, in stands and on away trips.
"Through good times and bad, Brighton & Hove Albion has provided so many of us with some of the most memorable moments of our lives.
"This club is in my blood. Some of my earliest and most cherished memories are wrapped up in the sights and sounds of the Goldstone.
"When I had the privilege of becoming owner and chairman, it was like being entrusted with something precious to safeguard and help develop for the future.
"Many of you reading these words will remember those difficult years. The loss of the Goldstone. The long journeys to Gillingham. The challenges of the Withdean era.
"What got this football club through was the determination of its fans. The bucket collections. The protests. The refusal to accept the Albion should disappear. This anniversary belongs as much to those supporters as anyone. Quite simply, without them, we would not be here today."
Whether they beat Arsenal or not, Brighton stands tall, for those who fought to preserve something they felt was special, and a man who had a vision - and finance - to build something better.

The Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP) on Saturday (September 19, 2026) bagged three Delhi University Students’ Union (DUSU) central panel posts, while an Independent candidate, earlier associated with National Students’ Union of India (NSUI), won the vice-presidential post.
Like last year, ABVP won the posts of president, secretary and joint secretary. However, this year saw a neck-and-neck battle with NSUI trailing in two posts. ABVP’s total winning margin came down from 23,873 last year to 9,671 this year. The voter turnout increased from 39.5% last year to 40.46% this year.
This year’s student elections took place against the backdrop of Jantar Mantar protests in the city, which saw many Delhi University students participating in it. The polls also happened in the wake of the paying guest building collapse in Satya Niketan area, which has led to student protests for better accommodation facilities.
ABVP’s Yash Dabbas won the president’s post upon receiving 24,576 votes while NSUI’s Vijay Shankar Meena came in second with 22,523 votes.
The vice-president’s post was bagged by Deepanshu Shokeen, an Independent candidate. With 30,615 votes, he won with the highest number of votes, and the widest margin of the four winners. Ishu Maurya from ABVP trailed him with 16,901 votes.
ABVP’s Riya Chhawdi was elected DUSU secretary with 21,650 votes, beating NSUI’s Namrata Chaudhary who finished with 14,869 votes. For the joint secretary post, Lakshay Raj Singh from ABVP won with a slim margin of 813 votes. Vishesh Yadav from Samajwadi Chhatra Sabha (SCS) came in second, while NSUI came in third.
President-elect Mr. Dabas said: “Delhi University’s Gen-Z has given a clear message that it believes in social harmony and nationalism. I will work to transform this trust into responsibility and ensure that the voice of every student is represented strongly through the students’ union.”
The organisation will focus on student safety, better facilities, equal opportunities and a positive academic environment, said Ms. Chhawdi, the Secretary-elect. “We will work to ensure that the concerns of students, particularly women students, receive due attention,” she added.
BJP congratulates ABVP
BJP national president Nitin Nabin on Saturday extended his wishes to the ABVP’s victory in DUSU elections. “Congratulations to all my young friends at Delhi University on ABVP’s historic victory in the DUSU elections! This victory reflects the youth’s continued faith in positive and constructive student politics, rooted in the spirit of Nation First, and their strong resolve to contribute to the vision of a ‘Viksit Bharat’,” he said.
Last year, the presidential candidate from ABVP had won with a margin of 16,196 votes whereas this year it came down to 2,053. Similarly, the joint secretary post was secured by ABVP last year with a margin of 4,445 votes, as opposed to 837 votes this year. The margin for secretary’s post went up this year to 6,781 from 3,234 last year.
Visually-impaired candidate
Aam Aadmi Party’s student body Association of Students for Alternative Politics fielded a visually-impaired candidate for the first time in DUSU elections for the post of secretary. The candidate, Pankaj Kumar Dhingra, received 7,639 votes.
While the joint Left panel with All India Students’ Association (AISA) and Students’ Federation of India (SFI) had hoped to challenge the ABVP-NSUI binary, but their performance was similar to previous years.
While some students pointed out that the Left organisations were active during Jantar Mantar, this did not drastically change their vote share from previous years. Presidential candidate Ananya Raturi got 5,377 votes, coming in third. They came in third in the secretary’s election too, garnering 8,734 votes.
Like last year, many students also opted for the NOTA button. As many as 4,310 students pressed NOTA for president, 4,359 for vice-president, 7,884 for secretary and 7,389 for joint secretary.

AI prescription readers can help decode hard-to-read prescriptions, medicine names, doses, and doctor notes. Tools like August AI, Prescription Reader AI, Docus AI, AI Prescription Reader, and Google Lens/Gemini can simplify medical text, but results should always be verified with a doctor or pharmacist.
I am sure you have been in a situation where you walk out of the clinic, look down at the prescription slip the doctor handed to you, only to find that you cannot understand a single word written on it. It looks less like English and more like something scribbled by a 1-year-old. For decades, deciphering a doctor’s handwriting was a superpower reserved for experienced pharmacists. But that is no longer the case. Thanks to advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and Optical Character Recognition (OCR), the power now rests in your pockets. Here are five AI tools that you can use to your advantage to break down medical jargon and medicine names easily without needing to revisit the doctor.
Table of Contents
Best AI Prescription Readers
August AI Prescription Reader
If you are looking for something that is more than just a simple text translator for your prescriptions, then August AI is the digital health companion that you need to use. Instead of just scanning the document and showing you the raw text, August behaves like a virtual health assistant that you can actually converse with regarding the document that you have uploaded. It has a fully chat-like interface. You take a photo of your prescription (either handwritten or typed) and upload it to the chat. The AI engine then extracts the medication names, dosages, and instructions. But wait, there is more to it.
Instead of spitting raw text, it rewrites those instructions into plain, everyday language. You can then type back your questions to the virtual assistant, like “Can I take this tablet on an empty stomach?” etc., and get personalized answers. Additionally, August AI strips out medically complex jargon and also tells you what the drug will do to your body when taken. Since health data is highly sensitive, August AI uses advanced encryption to ensure medical records aren’t uploaded anywhere. The good thing is that you get this AI tool for free, and it is available for Android and iOS.
Prescription Reader AI: Meds
Another dedicated app that can help you understand what the doctor has written on your prescription is the Prescription Reader AI: Meds app, which is available on Android. This app is built by MS Productions and is arguably the most feature-packed app designed for this purpose. You open the app, point your camera at the prescription, the app takes a scan, and its smart medication recognition engine instantly detects the drug names and formatting. It converts your prescription into readable text, so that you can make informed decisions. Once the app detects a medicine, you don’t have to manually Google its uses, as the Prescription Reader AI app itself shows you the drug’s uses, precautions, and side effects.
Everything that you have searched for remains in your history, so that you can access it quickly. There is a pill reminder and alarm as well, so that you don’t miss your doses. Not only English; it supports multiple languages, supports light and dark modes, and you can also share or save the readable prescription in PDF format. The Prescription Reader AI: Meds app is available for free, but only available on Android.
Download: Android
Docus AI
While you can still apply some workarounds as mentioned above, to read prescriptions, lab reports are still the worst. A blood test report gives you a wall of numbers, acronyms, and reference ranges that are guaranteed to induce anxiety. Some numbers might look too high, while some may look too low, making a normal person confused. Docus AI helps to solve this specific problem. It is built for heavy-duty medical document analysis. You need to upload a PDF, screenshot, or photo of your lab test (blood, urine, swab, etc.). Using Docus AI’s “AI Doctor,” the app will then compare the specific numbers against standard medical guidelines to figure out exactly what is going on inside your body.
Docus AI breaks down hundreds of biomarkers like cholesterol, cortisol, or thyroid levels and lets you understand if the numbers are high or low. It goes a step further and also explains what these numbers actually mean for your health. This way, you can make necessary decisions in your lifestyle. Based on your results, this AI tool may suggest dietary changes, lifestyle adjustments, or prompt you to consult a human specialist immediately. The free version lets you access features like an AI doctor and lab test interpretation, but you can unlock full potential by paying a fee.
AI Prescription Reader
The name says it all. The AI Prescription Reader is a web tool that is good for those who don’t want an AI companion and don’t want to install an app. The AI Prescription Reader is for people who want a fast, free, no-nonsense tool that gets the job done in five seconds. The good thing about this tool is that, apart from being web-based, it is dead simple. All you need to do is upload a document, or you can take a picture with your camera and hit the Analyze button. The AI runs its OCR magic and gives you a clean, formatted text box with the detected medicine, strength, and frequency.
There is a built-in prescription dictionary as well that you can go through to understand the medical terms that doctors have mentioned in the note. You can also export the deciphered text into a PDF and send it to anyone who needs it. The best part about this tool is that it doesn’t ask you to sign up or sign in using any account. You can use it straight away by visiting its website.
Google Lens/Gemini
This list would be incomplete if we do not appreciate the powers Google Lens and now Gemini have brought to our phones. Google Lens wasn’t specifically built for medical prescriptions, but its world-class text recognition engine makes it one of the powerful tools out there. Recently, I also needed some help, and with the help of Google Lens, I was able to decipher what was written in the prescription, get it checked by the doctor, and it was 100% correct. Though this may not be the case with everyone. It is available for Android and iOS, and you probably already have the Google app on your phone.
It pulls out the medical details about the medicine it has detected and shares them with you, such as what the drug looks like, common uses, and side effects. If an elderly member of your household is using it, they can tap the Listen feature so Google Lens reads the prescription aloud.
Be cautious
Yes, AI is advanced, and things are going in the right direction, but it is to be taken with a quick dose of reality. AI is smart, but it is not 100% accurate. A smudge on the paper or rushed handwriting can still cause the AI to incorrectly determine the wrong medicine. It is easy to confuse 10mg with 70mg for two similarly named drugs. It is always important that you get it verified by experienced medical personnel or the doctor themselves and get the right medicine.

Efforts are underway to widen use of an interim storage facility for spent nuclear fuel in Aomori Prefecture, increasing the number of power plant operators that send fuel there from two to four, but authorities have yet to agree to the plan.
The four power plant operators informed the city of Mutsu on Friday of the proposal to have Kansai Electric Power (Kepco) and Tohoku Electric Power also make use of the storage facility, which currently stores spent fuel from plants run by Tokyo Electric Power Company Holdings (Tepco) and Japan Atomic Power.
Tepco and Japan Atomic may not be able to transport the initially planned 5,000 tons of spent fuel from their own plants to the facility, so they have proposed “interoperator cooperation” to allow other power companies to make use of it as well.
But currently the storage facility doesn’t accept waste from plants other than those operated by Tepco and Japan Atomic. Aomori Gov. Soichiro Miyashita has said that the prefecture will not allow fuel from other companies to be stored there, as that was “not envisaged under the agreement” with the local governments that host it.
Japan’s government is hoping to restart as many nuclear reactors as possible, but securing interim storage space for the ever-increasing volume of spent fuel removed from nuclear reactors has become a more urgent issue.
The purpose of the Mutsu Interim Storage Facility is to hold spent nuclear fuel generated by Tepco and Japan Atomic for up to 50 years. After that, the fuel is supposed to be reprocessed for reuse at the Rokkasho Reprocessing Plant, also in the prefecture.
But earlier this year, Miyashita said he would not agree to the storage of more fuel during this fiscal year because plans for the completion and operation of the Rokkasho plant, long delayed, remain vague.
“Regarding the interim storage project, we can’t confirm the environment is suitable (for accepting more fuel). This is primarily due to the fact that the progress of the Rokkasho Reprocessing Plant has become uncertain,” Miyashita said in March.

There might be no economic case for expanding the Port of Churchill, but that may not be the point
Canada might need shipping route as sovereignty insurance policy, even if it pays a premium to do so
Piece by piece, like patches of ice receding from a frigid waterway, Manitoba's plan to expand the Port of Churchill is getting clearer.
Late last week, port owner Arctic Gateway Group attached a price range to the task of upgrading the site and the railway that connects it to the rest of Canada. CEO Chris Avery said it would cost $2 billion to $3 billion to expand the port to allow it to ship higher volumes of commodities and rebuild the Hudson Bay Railway so it can carry heavier loads.
In the context of provincial megaprojects, $3 billion is nowhere near unprecedented. There are two other projects in the works in Manitoba right now that are in the same price range.
The upgrades underway to the largest of Winnipeg's three sewage-treatment plants are expected to cost $3.2 billion once they're finished. The City of Winnipeg has assembled most of the money it needs to complete the job, which is entering its final phase.
The proposed expansion of Manitoba Hydro's gas-burning generating station in Brandon is also expected to cost $3 billion. Pending regulatory approval, the Crown corporation is ready to proceed with buying three new natural gas turbines.
The Port of Churchill expansion, meanwhile, exists in some sort of development limbo. The essential $3-billion work was not the subject of any pitch at Prime Minister Mark Carney's investment summit in Toronto this week.
Rather, the upgrades to the port and railway exist as a precursor to a larger project touted by Premier Wab Kinew — a $79-billion port expansion that includes a liquefied natural gas terminal floating off the shore of Hudson Bay.
The question before Manitobans right now is, why is the province not simply proceeding with a $3-billion port expansion and railway upgrade, if indeed this infrastructure is a prerequisite for other projects that are inevitable?
The answer is that the provincial government still has a choice as to whether it wishes to proceed.
The City of Winnipeg didn't have a choice when it pulled the trigger on upgrades to its North End Water Pollution Control Centre. Without those upgrades, Winnipeg would violate its environmental licence, run out of sewage-treatment capacity and end up unable to approve new residential and industrial development.
Manitoba Hydro, meanwhile, contends it is also in a difficult position. Without three more gas turbines in place in Brandon by 2030, Hydro argues, Manitobans could suffer from mid-winter power shortages.
There is less at stake if Manitoba dawdles on Churchill, as failing to upgrade the port and railway would affect far fewer residents. The town and dozens of other northern Manitoba communities stand to benefit the most from this particular megaproject.
As well, the economic benefits of the port expansion have not been demonstrated. The federal government has thus far refused to publish a Port of Churchill market sounding it commissioned. This raises suspicion international markets are not in love with the idea.
This could be why Kinew appears to be more interested in pursuing a liquefied natural gas moonshot. This week, the premier said this much larger project provides potential backers with a greater potential rate of return.
All of this ignores the primary purpose Canada ought to be interested in expanding the port at this moment in history, when our American friends have proven to be less than friendly.
As some of the world's leading experts in supply chains have stated over the past year, the Port of Churchill is of vital importance to Canada as an insurance policy — that is, an alternative means of getting goods out of the country — as opposed to being a money-maker.
Avery made this point last week, effectively arguing the port must be expanded if Canada ever hopes to divert more exports away from the United States.
"If we want to grow our non-U.S. trade by 10 percentage points, that's the equivalent volume of four times the size of the Port of Vancouver. So that gives you a context of what we're looking at,'" he said in an interview.
To be clear, Avery has never said an expanded Port of Churchill won't make money. But there is an argument to be made that its value as an insurance policy — effectively, the Canadian sovereignty argument — ought to make its potential as an economy-transforming revenue source a secondary concern.
University of British Columbia transportation and logistics professor Trevor Heaver said in 2025 that Canada should expand the Port of Churchill even without a purely economic case to do so.
- 1st phase of Winnipeg's $3.2B North End sewage treatment plant upgrade nearing completion
- Manitoba Hydro critics fuelled by data showing gas plant underperforms during winter cold snaps
"You've got to view these things from a national perspective, and that is present in this route," said Heaver, adding that insurance, by definition, comes at a higher cost.
Higher costs are certain for a route that involves an isolated port operated in frigid conditions on water that requires ice-hardened vessels to navigate for at least seven months out of the year.
"The economics may play out that it doesn't pay financially, commercially. So then, you're left with the issue of how much are you prepared to pay for the resilience, and how much are you prepared to pay for the sovereignty which comes from it?" Heaver said.
“How much are you prepared to pay for the revitalization of northern Manitoba?”
Heaver is not alone. Vidya Mani, a University of Virginia professor who studies global supply chains, said the Port of Churchill offers Canada's international trade partners the clear benefit of a shipping route that's free of geopolitical conflict.
She said the question is not whether Hudson Bay shipping offers Canada more flexibility.
- GraphicsCanada and the EU are getting cosy. These charts show how our economies stack up
- AnalysisThe journey toward an expanded Port of Churchill has only just begun
"It is more a question of, can this flexibility be paid for?" Mani asked. "It will cost, but can you pay for it?"
Right now, no one's lining up to pay that $3-billion bill. The province doesn't have the ability to do so on its own.
While Manitoba Hydro and the City of Winnipeg can rely on utility bills to finance their own $3-billion projects, the province has no self-sustaining revenue source of its own to tap for a Churchill megaproject.
It's also burdened with nearly $40 billion of its own debt.
Documents obtained by CBC News show the Manitoba government sought U.S. advice last year to find private partners to build an artificial intelligence data centre near Winnipeg, as well as a new Nelson River hydro station, without affecting the province's own balance sheet.
While those talks didn't appear to go anywhere, the mere fact Manitoba was looking for private partners to pay for megaprojects is revealing.
Arctic Gateway can't foot the Churchill tab, either. It's owned by First Nations and other northern communities.
This leaves the federal government as the only saviour if Kinew's trip to Toronto this week did not result in big money coming to the Port of Churchill's rescue.

California public health officials are warning of a possible measles exposure spanning multiple counties after an infected and unvaccinated passenger traveled through the state via Amtrak trains and thruway buses.
The warning comes as the US faces its largest measles resurgence in more than three decades, fueled largely by growing vaccine hesitancy.
The California department of public health said the traveler passed through at least six counties – Alameda, Butte, Kern, Los Angeles, Sacramento and San Joaquin – while making multiple transfers.
Officials said the passenger entered California on an Amtrak train that arrived in Los Angeles on 10 September. From there, the traveler continued to Bakersfield before heading through Stockton, Oroville, Sacramento and Emeryville, eventually leaving California for Denver.
Health officials said passengers who were onboard the same trains or buses, as well as people who were inside the stations along the route on the dates involved, have been exposed to measles.
The state said it is working with federal partners and local health departments to identify and notify people who may have been exposed.
“This case, along with previous measles outbreaks in California this year, serve as reminders of the importance of vaccination against measles,” assistant state public health officer Rita Nguyen said in a statement. “The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is safe and provides long-lasting protection against measles. Vaccination protects both our own families and those who are too young to be fully vaccinated.”
Pennsylvania is currently dealing with the country’s worst active measles outbreak. The Pennsylvania health department announced on Wednesday that 731 cases have been confirmed across 38 counties so far this year. At least four people in the state have died from measles-related illness.
Pennsylvania is now seeking emergency assistance from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as the outbreak continues to spread. State officials have warned, however, that the request could be withdrawn unless the CDC publicly recognizes the four measles-associated deaths, something the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, previously instructed the CDC not to do.
And as the death toll from the outbreak continues to rise, Kennedy headlined the Washington DC conference of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense earlier this week, an group he led for nearly a decade.
He only addressed the measles outbreak in Pennsylvania once during his speech, instead peddling unfounded fears about vaccines at a time when health experts are urgently encouraging people to vaccinate against measles.
“In our country we care about rare illnesses and deaths. We care about every child who dies from measles. They get headlines,” he said. “I’d ask you to care about children who are dying or suffering or being injured by vaccine injuries.”
The California warning also follows another recent mass-exposure incident involving Amtrak.
Earlier this week, it was reported that a person infected with measles traveled onboard an Amtrak train from Sedalia, Missouri, to Chicago, Illinois, resulting in more than 250 people being exposed to the virus in Jackson county alone.
This month, it was also revealed that the Trump administration changed how measles deaths are counted during the outbreak. The CDC is now relying on data from the National Center for Health Statistics, which is used to track mortality trends over time. It is unclear why this change was made.

India’s software services exports rose 8.2% year-on-year to $221.4 billion in 2025-26, with the US continuing to account for more than half of the country’s software exports, according to the Reserve Bank of India’s annual survey released on Friday. The RBI’s Survey on Computer Software and Information Technology Enabled Services Exports: 2025-26 showed that software services exports, excluding sales through the overseas commercial presence of Indian companies, increased from $204.7 billion in 2024-25 to $221.4 billion in 2025-26. The survey covered exports by type of activity, delivery mode, destination and mode of supply. Computer services remained the largest component, accounting for 69.3% of total software services exports in 2025-26, up from 67.4% a year earlier. Within computer services, IT services exports rose to $147 billion from $131.3 billion, while software product development exports declined to $6.4 billion from $6.8 billion. IT-enabled services (ITES) exports increased to $68 billion in 2025-26 from $66.6 billion in the previous year. Business process outsourcing (BPO) services continued to dominate ITES, accounting for $56 billion, or 82.4% of ITES exports. Engineering services contributed $12 billion, up from $10.8 billion in 2024-25. The US remained the largest destination for India’s software exports, with its share rising to 54.1% in 2025-26 from 52.9% a year earlier. Software exports to the US stood at $119.7 billion. Europe was the second-largest destination, accounting for 31.8% of exports, with the UK contributing a 15.4% share. The concentration of exports in the US and Europe was accompanied by the continued dominance of the US dollar in invoicing. The dollar accounted for 72.6% of software export invoices in 2025-26, up from 72% in the previous year. The euro accounted for 9.6%, while the rupee’s share declined to 6.3% from 7.1%. The pound sterling accounted for 6%. Software services exports continued to be overwhelmingly delivered through off-site services. Off-site exports rose to $203 billion in 2025-26 and accounted for 91.7% of total software services exports, compared with a 90.7% share in 2024-25. On-site services accounted for the remaining 8.3%. Private limited companies remained the largest organisational category, accounting for 60.8% of software services exports in 2025-26. Their exports increased to $134.6 billion from $123.1 billion a year earlier. Public limited companies accounted for 36.9%, with exports of $81.7 billion. Including services delivered through the overseas commercial presence of Indian companies, total software services exports increased 9.5% during 2025-26 to $239.3 billion from $218.6 billion in the previous year. Cross-border supply, or Mode 1, accounted for $202.7 billion, while commercial presence, or Mode 3, contributed $17.9 billion. The survey also captured the growing role of foreign affiliates of Indian companies. Software business by these affiliates locally increased to $17.9 billion in 2025-26 from $13.9 billion in the previous year, with the US and UK remaining the major destinations. The RBI contacted 7,569 software export companies for the 2025-26 survey, of which 2,363 companies responded. The participating companies accounted for around 89% of total estimated software services exports. Washington – U.S. President Donald Trump has extended an executive order that would impose a fee of $100,000 for H-1B nonimmigrant visas by another year, the White House said on Friday.
U.S. employers seeking to hire skilled foreign workers can use the federal government’s H-1B visa program for a fee, allowing tech and other professionals from abroad to work in the United States for a few years.
Trump, who has pursued an aggressive immigration crackdown, has criticized the program and wants to permanently raise the fee from between $2,000 and $5,000 to at least $100,000, though the attempt has faced legal challenges.
A Boston-based appeals court is reviewing a June decision by a federal judge who deemed the higher fee imposed by the Trump administration illegal and blocked the government from collecting it. Another court is considering whether a judge properly rejected a challenge to the fee by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the largest U.S. business lobbying group.
Trump’s initial order for a fee hike, first released in September 2025, was set to expire this month. It did not apply to visas granted to foreign citizens already in the United States on student visas, who make up a large share of new H-1B recipients, or to renewals of current visas.
Despite criticism that some companies use the visas to hire lower-paid foreign workers instead of Americans, business groups and companies say they help recruit highly skilled professionals and address a lack of qualified U.S. workers in some industries.
The visas, established by Congress in 1990, are especially critical for tech companies seeking to recruit from India and China.
Changes to how potential visa holders are scrutinized and processed have impacted companies’ hiring and expansion plans, with some top H-1B users, such as Google parent company Alphabet, moving to increase operations in India.

Canada's top general loses election to become head of key NATO Military Committee
Gen. Jennie Carignan's German counterpart named chair of influential advisory body
Despite a push from the federal government, Canada's chief of the defence staff has lost a vote to be the next chair of the NATO Military Committee, the alliance's top military authority and a key advisory body for its political leaders.
Gen. Jennie Carignan and her German counterpart, Gen. Carsten Breuer, were vying for the position. Top military commanders from NATO's 32 members ultimately decided on Saturday to go with Breuer in a secret ballot election.
The news was announced on social media by the current chair, Italian Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, who congratulated Breuer on his election.
"Your operational judgement, your deep familiarity with this alliance and your leadership of the German Armed Forces will serve NATO well," Dragone said.
A Canadian has not held this position in almost two decades — the last being retired general Ray Henault between 2005 and 2008. Had she won, Carignan would have been the first woman to lead the Military Committee in the 77-year history of the alliance.
In a statement posted to social media, Carignan congratulated Breuer and said, "it was an honour to stand as a candidate and to engage with my fellow Allied Chiefs of Defence throughout this process."
"There is important work ahead for our Alliance, and I know General Breuer will bring strong leadership to his new role. I deeply value the close relationship we have built and look forward to continuing to work together on our NATO initiatives," Carignan added.
On Friday, Defence Minister David McGuinty said Carignan deserved the job because she's worked very hard and has "enormous credibility."
"She has reached out to her counterparts in all NATO alliance member countries," McGuinty said following a Liberal caucus meeting in Ottawa. "It would be historical and groundbreaking, the first woman chief of defence to chair such a committee."
CBC News has contacted McGuinty's office for comment on the election result.
Potential U.S. obstacles to Carignan appointment
Experts who previously spoke to CBC News said a potential roadblock to Carignan winning would be U.S. President Donald Trump — particularly after Prime Minister Mark Carney formally unveiled his intent to strengthen Canada's ties to the European Union.
"Trump is not going to let a Canadian or a woman be the head of the military committee, if anybody around him has paid attention to it," said Steven Saideman, a defence expert at Carleton University who's written extensively about NATO.
The elected chair, Breuer, is a 61-year-old army officer who earned the nickname "the chancellor's general" after then-German chancellor Olaf Scholz picked him to lead a crisis committee that helped manage the country's response to the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021 and 2022.
He joined the Bundeswehr in an air defence unit in 1984, and later attended the U.S. general staff college in Fort Leavenworth, Kan., as well as German general staff training in Hamburg.
In 2014, Breuer served with NATO's International Security Assistance Force in the Afghan capital Kabul.
Dragone said on social media that Breuer will take office in July 2027.
With files from Murray Brewster, Reuters

The small fee raising big questions for India's payments revolution
- Published
India's decision to introduce a fee on some transactions made through its widely popular digital payments system has sparked a debate over its impact on businesses.
The National Payments Corporation of India said on Tuesday that a 0.4% fee will apply from 15 October to certain UPI (Unified Payments Interface) payments above 2,000 rupees (£15; $21) made to businesses by customers.
Businesses will have to pay the fee and will not be allowed to pass on the cost to consumers, it said.
The government says the new charge will help keep UPI viable in the long run but experts worry it could raise expenses for businesses and discourage them from using the system.
Launched in 2016, UPI allows people to instantly send and receive money through mobile apps. The ease of use has made it integral part of everyday life in India, used by everyone - from small vendors to booming businesses.
Until now, the government, banks and payment companies have largely borne the cost of running and expanding the UPI system.
The new charge - known as the Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) - is expected to help cover some of those costs.
The government has said that MDR is not a tax or a charge collected by the government or NPCI, which operates the UPI system.
The money will be distributed among payment system providers - including banks - to support operations and continued expansion, the finance ministry press release, external stated.
The charge will not apply to all UPI payments.
Person-to-person transfers will remain free, regardless of the amount. Payments of up to 2,000 rupees made to merchants will also remain free. Merchant payments through QR codes in rural and semi-urban areas will not attract MDR either.
The government said "approximately 96% of person-to-merchant transactions will remain unaffected", either because they are below the threshold or because they are covered by the zero-MDR framework for small merchants.
Certain merchant payments above 2,000 rupees, including those for railways, telecom services, insurance, fuel and agricultural inputs, will instead attract a flat charge of five rupees.
For other transactions above 2,000 rupees that are subject to MDR, the fee will be 0.4% and capped at 300 rupees per transaction. The cap applies to transactions of 75,000 rupees or more.
The regulator has said the money will support investment in areas including payment infrastructure, resilience, innovation and cyber security.
The decision has sparked debate in India.
Some social media users have said charging merchants could weaken one of UPI's biggest attractions - that it has been free to use. Others have warned that some merchants could turn to cash for larger transactions rather than absorb a fee they did not previously have to pay.
Krishnamurthy Subramanian, a former chief economic adviser to the Indian government, said the economics of a system such as UPI cannot be "evaluated using private cost versus private benefit".
Speaking to news channel CNN-News18, Indian entrepreneur and former managing director and co-founder of fintech platform BharatPe, Ashneer Grover said that there can be a possibility where "a shopkeeper could simply refuse to accept a UPI payment of 2,000 rupees and ask you to pay entirely in cash. Then you will go back to using cash".
The Retailers Association of India (RAI) has said that the charge could "undo years of progress in digital payment adoption among India's smallest retailers".
"During the festive season, a large share of transactions crosses the 2,000 rupees mark, and the moment a fee attaches itself to digital payment, cash becomes the path of least resistance," Kumar Rajagopalan, the association's CEO said.
Others argue that a fee is needed to help fund and expand the payments system.
"When government funds the subsidies paid for UPI, that amount comes from tax payers' pocket. Moving to market-linked pricing mechanism removes this tax burden and directly links the cost to large businesses which benefit from UPI," said Bipin Preet Singh, CEO of fintech firm MobiKwik.
Since its launch a decade ago, UPI has become a central part of India's digital payments economy. In August, UPI processed a record 24.51 billion transactions worth 29.82 trillion rupees (roughly $311bn), according to NPCI data.
The question now is whether the new charges will change how businesses use UPI, particularly for larger payments.

Security, trade, and the economy understandably dominated much of the conversation around the BRICS Summit 2026. But for a grouping home to nearly half of humanity, another challenge deserves equal attention: the changing health risks facing its people.
The summit has taken an important step in that direction. The launch of the BRICS Mission for Healthy Lifestyle, endorsement of the BRICS Roadmap for the Joint Initiative on Healthy Lifestyle Promotion (2026-2029), and a Compendium of Replicable Best Practices on Healthy Lifestyle signal growing recognition that prevention must move closer to the centre of public policy.
This is significant for India during Poshan Maah. Nutrition is no longer only about whether people have enough to eat. Increasingly, it is also about what people eat, how they live, and the diseases that follow.
A compressed nutrition transition
BRICS countries are at very different stages of development. Ethiopia continues to struggle with food insecurity and undernutrition. India and Indonesia face persistent maternal and child undernutrition even as obesity and non-communicable diseases (NCDs) rise. China and Brazil have substantially reduced traditional forms of undernutrition but confront growing diet-related disease. In the Gulf, obesity and diabetes are major public-health concerns.
Economic growth and urbanisation are rapidly changing how people eat and live. Traditional diets are giving way to more processed and convenience foods. More meals are eaten outside the home or ordered online. Children encounter pervasive food marketing while becoming less physically active.
Yet undernutrition, anaemia, and micronutrient deficiencies have not disappeared. Overweight, obesity, diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease are rising alongside them.
India sits at the heart of this transition
Our nutrition policies have rightly focused on hunger, maternal and child nutrition, anaemia, and the first 1,000 days of a child from conception to two years. These priorities remain fundamental. But they are no longer enough.
A child poorly nourished in the early years may later grow up surrounded by inexpensive foods high in salt, sugar, and fat, with too little physical activity. Undernutrition in childhood and diabetes or hypertension in adulthood can become parts of the same life story.
Much of the West experienced these problems more sequentially: food scarcity and severe nutritional deficiencies declined before obesity and lifestyle diseases became dominant. Emerging economies face a compressed nutrition transition. Yesterday’s problems remain while tomorrow’s diseases have already arrived.
We have to fight both at once.
From food security to healthy living
This changes the question food policy must answer. The great challenge of the last century was: can we produce enough food? The challenge of this century is also: can we enable people to eat and live well enough to remain healthy?
Agriculture, food, nutrition, and health can no longer work in silos. What farmers grow affects what markets sell. What food companies produce and promote shapes what families buy. And what children eat and the habits they acquire influence their health decades later.
The BRICS Mission for Healthy Lifestyle provides an opportunity to build precisely these connections. Its road map places healthy diets, physical activity, traditional food cultures, and evidence-based behavioural change within a common framework. The accompanying compendium of replicable practices can help countries learn from one another rather than repeatedly reinventing solutions.
India should use this opportunity not merely to share programmes, but to demonstrate how healthy living can be embedded across food systems, schools, and communities.
The next 7,000 days
Poshan Maah offers an opportunity to widen our ambition.
The first 1,000 days remain foundational. Nothing should dilute that focus. But India must now pay much greater attention to the next 7,000 days: childhood and adolescence.
These are the years when lifelong habits around food, physical activity, sleep, and wellbeing are formed. They offer perhaps our best opportunity to act before today’s children become tomorrow’s patients.
Schools can therefore become one of India’s most powerful institutions for preventive health.
This does not require another nutrition textbook, subject or examination. Children often already know that vegetables are good, too much sugar is unhealthy, and physical activity matters. Knowing is not the same as doing.
Schools should help children practise healthy living: eating diverse foods, drinking water, limiting foods high in salt, sugar and fat, eating mindfully, staying active, sleeping well, and maintaining hygiene. School meals, food regulation, nutrition literacy, physical activity, and family engagement should become parts of one preventive-health strategy.
India’s fight against hunger and malnutrition is unfinished. But another challenge has arrived alongside it.
The BRICS Summit has provided a useful framework for responding to both. The task now is to turn its Healthy Lifestyle Mission and Roadmap into action.
Poshan must increasingly mean nourishing early, building healthy habits early, and preventing disease early. For India — and much of the BRICS world — the next frontier is not simply enough food. It is enabling people to eat well, live well and remain healthy throughout life.
Pawan Agarwal is a former CEO of the FSSAI and is the founder & CEO of the Food Future Foundation

A city can have one of two levels of rat. There are cities where rats are glimpsed at night, furtively scurrying into a dark corner or among the train tracks. Then there are cities where the rats are so numerous and so brazen that they work out private disputes by brawling midday on a train platform, or they lounge on your front porch, eating fallen fruit. When rats reach that second level, city officials need some answer, any answer, to their rat problem. Washington, D.C., has reached that level, and Mayor Muriel Bowser’s answer involves rat birth control.
Contraception for rodents has become more popular over the past few years because the most commonly used rodenticides kill painfully, as the poisoned rodent internally bleeds to death over a period of days. Not a lot of people love rats or mice, but people don’t love causing that much suffering, either. Many are fond, too, of cats, owls, and hawks, which can be poisoned when they eat poisoned rats. New York City’s Flaco, the beloved Eurasian eagle-owl sprung from a cage in the Central Park Zoo, was found to have high levels of this kind of poison in his system when he died. And to top it off, some rodents are evolving resistance to poisons.
D.C. hopes that rats will lap up a liquid contraceptive called ContraPest from plastic bait stations. It is not the only city to try the approach: Chicago is having luck with rat birth control in Wicker Park; Boston had mixed results in Jamaica Plain. Most of the available research on ContraPest has been done by the staff of the company that makes it, SenesTech, sometimes in collaboration with external researchers. One study at a poultry farm found that a year of continuous baiting with ContraPest led to a 94 percent reduction in rat activity as measured by camera traps. The company says that if the rats continuously eat the bait, they stop having pups, a finding confirmed in a laboratory setting.
But that’s a big if. A prior attempt to use ContraPest in D.C. was inconclusive, according to Andre Pitman, the program manager for the city’s Rodent and Vector Control Division. In rat hot spots such as Adams Morgan, where evening revelers have been known to throw greasy pizza plates on the ground, rats simply had too much other food around for the birth-control liquid to hold much appeal. “We couldn’t get the rats to drink it,” Pitman told me.
So this time, Pitman said, D.C. is making what, to his knowledge, is the most aggressive push against rats in a very long time. First, the city is going to try to kill rats by heaving poison directly down their burrows, which will then be filled in. City workers will return multiple times, looking for burrows that the rats have reopened, adding more poison, then filling them again. The next week, the same procedure will be followed with a different poison, which clings to rat fur and is ingested as they attempt to lick themselves clean. Finally, starting in week three, the city will put out ContraPest for 15 days. All the while, city workers will clean alleys and encourage residents to remove ground cover, containerize trash, and generally boost hygiene levels so that rats are more likely to take the bait. Post-bar snackers are requested to keep things tidy too.
It is understandable that the nation’s capital, facing a high number of resident complaints, has chosen to throw everything it’s got at the rats. But the downside to the guns-blazing approach, from a scientific standpoint, is that if it succeeds, no one will have any idea why. If burrow numbers are down by the new year, no one can say that birth control works—only that the combination of two poisons, ContraPest, hygiene, and other measures works. And Pitman acknowledges as much. “It is not a fertility pilot,” he said. “It is a rodent blitz.”
Fertility control of wildlife, which is used in elephants, wild horses, kangaroos, and pigeons, among other species, does work sometimes, and advocates for this method worry that premature deployment of oral contraceptives for rodents risks making the entire field look bad. Ultimately, no real independent studies show that SenesTech’s products are safe or effective, Lawrence Green, the interim managing director for the Botstiber Institute for Wildlife Fertility Control, told me. (SenesTech CEO Michael Edell responded, “We have been doing this a long time and have case studies and data to back up our claims.”) Assuming ContraPest can work in cities, rats would likely have to take it for longer than 15 days to see lasting results. As people who take birth control generally know, if you miss a dose, it’s less effective, and you have to keep taking it for as long as you want to not have babies. ContraPest is really meant to be used indefinitely: SenesTech even offers a “Subscribe & save” option.
And that familiar e-commerce option points to a larger truth that everyone I spoke with agreed on: There is no end to this war. The quest to control rats is not about winning. It is about nobly devoting oneself to an unwinnable fight. Because rats spread disease, we must struggle against them, clear-eyed in the knowledge that, unless we are dealing with a small island, eradication is not possible.
The reason that rats will never be conquered, at least not in our lifetime, either with poison or with birth control, is easily explained by two facts of rat biology: They have many babies, and they love to explore. You can nuke rats with poison or slowly usher them into a
population crash with contraceptives, but all you will have done is create unoccupied territories for young, exploratory rats to come occupy. D.C.’s current blitz is focused on Adams Morgan, Chinatown, and Eastern Market, but rats live in other places in Washington. They will be happy to move in once those neighborhoods have space.
Niamh Quinn, a human-wildlife-interactions adviser at the University of California Division of Agriculture and Natural Resources, puts it this way: “We live in an infinite sea of rats.” Just beyond the boundaries of any rat-control project lie more rats, waiting to move in. Pitman, a longtime rat expert since before he joined the city, knows this too. “Rodents were here long before humans,” he said. All we can hope is to control them.

President Donald Trump is following through on pledge to ban journalists he doesn’t like from the White House: This morning, MS NOW, formerly MSNBC, announced that its journalists had been denied access to the White House grounds.

Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has announced a 15% increase in the country’s main cash-transfer programme for poor families, as well as free weight-loss jabs, prompting criticism from opponents who say the moves are electorally motivated just two weeks before the presidential election.
On 4 October, the leftwing incumbent will face the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who has been gaining ground in recent weeks.
The rise in the monthly payment, from about £98 to £113, that he announced on Thursday is due to take effect on 19 October, just before the likely runoff vote on 25 October.
The increase is expected to benefit between 15% and 20% of voters in what promises to be one of the closest ever presidential races in Latin America’s largest country.
Lula said it was not really an increase, but an adjustment in line with inflation to “protect the purchasing power of the most vulnerable families”, but his opponents have criticised its timing so close to the election.
Flávio Bolsonaro called it an “act of desperation” after polls showed him gaining ground – although the most recent survey, released on Thursday night, still showed Lula numerically ahead despite the technical tie. The senator added that Lula was trying to “buy the votes of the poor”.
Created in 2003 during his first term as president, the programme, called Bolsa Família, was a flagship cash-transfer policy that helped lift millions of families out of poverty during his first two terms.
Currently, families with an income of up to £32 per person are eligible, covering about 50 million people, or roughly 27 million of voting age.
The programme has long been fiercely criticised by rightwing politicians, including by Jair Bolsonaro, although he kept it in place during his presidency.
On the eve of the 2022 election, Bolsonaro announced a 50% increase in the monthly payment, prompting Lula’s campaign to file a case with the electoral court alleging abuse of political power and electoral use of the state machinery.
The similarities have sparked a debate between those who say Lula is doing the same thing Bolsonaro did four years ago, and others who argue that the two cases are different.
The journalist Miriam Leitão wrote for O Globo that although both Bolsonaro and Lula made the adjustments “out of electoral interest”, the current incumbent’s increase is in fact limited to inflation over the past four years, during which there had been no adjustment.
She also noted that Bolsonaro’s increase had an expiry date – precisely at the end of the electoral period – while Lula’s is permanent.
Victor Escobar, a researcher at the Laboratory of Parties, Elections and Comparative Politics, agreed. He said that although Lula, like his predecessor, is also being criticised for unveiling a package of benefits on the eve of the election – including a promise to distribute weight-loss jabs free of charge through the public health system – Bolsonaro’s measures were “even more irresponsible from a budgetary point of view”.
In addition to increasing benefits for poor families, Bolsonaro introduced temporary monthly payments of up to £727 for two groups that broadly formed part of his support base, taxi drivers and truck drivers, along with a series of other social benefits whose projected impact on the budget was so large that critics dubbed them the “kamikaze” package.
Escobar acknowledged that Lula’s intention was also electoral, but said that, as long as the measures comply with the law, “it’s something entirely expected when we’re talking about an incumbent running for re-election, who will try to use the legal mechanisms available to improve their voting numbers”.
Some electoral law experts have said that an inflation adjustment is not, in principle, prohibited, but another far-right candidate, the influencer Renan Santos, filed a case with the electoral court seeking to suspend the increase until the president-elect takes office. Although critical of the measure, Flávio Bolsonaro has not done the same, reportedly because of concern about the impact such a move could have among voters who benefit from the programme.

Open earbuds are the big new thing in headphone land. Unlike in-ear variants, open earbuds are like tiny speakers that rest on the ear and let outside sound in naturally, so you can fully hear the world around you. Some use a hook style that wraps around the back of your ear, while others are clip-ons that look more like statement-piece earrings. Style aside, they are excellent for anyone who finds traditional earbuds uncomfortable or wants full environmental awareness for activities like running, biking, or even just doing chores around the house.
I've tested dozens of models since 2022, and while I still recommend having a pair of noise-canceling earbuds, I also love open earbuds for specific use cases.
For more headphone recommendations, check out our guides to the Best Wireless Earbuds, Best Workout Headphones, and Best Wireless Headphones.

The Shokz OpenDots 2 are everything I want open earbuds to be. These are truly take-everywhere, do-anything headphones. That's partly thanks to extremely long battery life—10 hours on a single charge, and 40 hours total with the charging case. They also have an IP57 dust and waterproof rating, the same as premium, flagship earbuds like Apple AirPods Pro 3 and Samsung Galaxy Buds4 Pro. I've worn them in the rain, on the beach, and fully submerged them in water multiple times without issue.
They're clip-ons that wrap around the earlobe, with the speaker end resting at the ear canal opening and the other end behind the ear. Importantly, the top of your ear is free for glasses, sunglasses, or hats. Like nearly all open earbuds, they let in sound from your surroundings, so don't expect them to be a great companion for long-haul flights or daily gym sessions.
They are a bit pricey, though. Shokz recently launched the lower-priced Shokz OpenDots Air and Shokz OpenFit Air 2—I may update this recommendation depending on how my testing goes.

The Aeroclip buds are light, comfortable, and stable on your ear, plus they have stellar battery life and strong water and dust resistance (not waterproof). Waniata used them for daily life: walking the dog, strolling with the baby, riding bikes, making dinner, and hanging out at home—any situation where you want your music but also want to be aware or talk to people. The Soundcore app is easy to use and offers plenty of customization for controls, EQ, and multipoint pairing.

Two years later, they are still a solid, if expensive, option. That's mainly because of sound quality—these earbuds have a clearer, more defined sound than most competitors. Another differentiator is physical button controls on each bud, which I find easier to use than touch alternatives, especially when running or biking.
Like the Shokz and Soundcore, they are supremely comfortable, so much so that I sometimes forgot I was wearing them. But they are much pricier by comparison, and only worth it if you want the best sound quality in this clip-on form factor.
