The Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 are more headphones than earbuds—they have a wraparound headband styling, long battery life, great sound quality (for open headphones), and no charging case. They use a combination of bone conduction (think vibrations) and air conduction (think tiny speakers pointed toward your ears) to deliver sound that's clearer than most smaller open earbuds, especially in noisy environments. That combination of technologies is why these are some of my favorite earbuds for outdoor fitness activities like running and biking.
I do wish these headphones were a little cheaper. I'm currently testing the recently released, more affordable Shokz OpenRun Air 2, and hopeful they can be a budget-friendly alternative.
Honorable Mentions
Nothing Ear (Open) for $99: Former WIRED editor Adrienne So loves these earbuds and uses them for almost all her outdoor activities. They are very slim (19-mm wide) and lightweight. They fit slightly inside your ear and, like most Nothing headphones, have a distinct transparent design. The case doesn't clamp shut very firmly, so be careful, but at this price, that's forgivable.
JLab Epic Open Sport for $100: JLab’s Epic Open Sport stands out for its controls: the JLab emblem is a touch sensor, and each earbud also has physical buttons on top, making it a breeze to control. What holds the Epic Open Sport back is audio quality—the sound isn't very detailed, and it's generally boring to listen to.
Other Open Earbuds I’ve Tested
EarFun Clip for $70: For around $70, these are a solid pick for anyone on a budget. Waniata found the overall package punching above its price point, with a snappy, compact case, comfortable fit, push-button controls, and reliable multiple Bluetooth connections. The problem is our budget pick, the Soundpeats PearlClip Pro, is often on sale for less and offers a similar overall experience. Don't dismiss these earbuds if you find them heavily discounted.
Shokz OpenFit Pro for $250: The Shokz OpenFit Pro has a great premise: open earbuds with noise canceling. Hear the world around you as you would without headphones, and turn on noise-canceling when you don't, just like regular earbuds. And while they do cancel some noise, it's not much. The bigger issue is price: for $250, you could get open earbuds and great noise-canceling earbuds that do a better job for each task.
Suunto Wing 2 for $179: These open-ear headphones are designed for endurance athletes—they have a long 12-hour battery life but also come with a wireless power bank you can take on the go. Dock the headphones in the power bank for up to 36 hours of battery life total. There's nothing inherently wrong with these headphones, but I don't see a world where I would recommend them over the Shokz Openrun Pro 2, which retail for the same amount and offer more comfort, a sleeker design, better sound, and a more robust app.
Suunto Spark for $179: The Suunto Spark has a similar story to the Suunto Wing 2: with athletes in mind, it has features that sync with Suunto fitness watches, but it is outclassed in the areas that matter (comfort, sound quality, battery) by the similarly priced Shokz Openfit 2.
What Are Open Earbuds and How Do They Sound?
At a glance, open earbuds seem a lot like typical wireless earbuds. The big difference is that, instead of going inside your ear canal, they rest somewhere on the outside of your ear, leaving it open so you can easily hear the world around you. I use them all the time for outdoor exercise like running or biking, where I want my music but also need to hear other runners, bikers, and cars to stay safe.
Because they leave your ears open and the sound comes from farther away (outside your ear rather than inside), audio performance isn't as clear, intimate, or bassy as regular earbuds. They also typically don't have noise-canceling features, so they are not a great fit for the office or air travel.
When or Where Would I Use Open Earbuds?
Open earbuds are perfect for outdoor activities, or when you want to talk to other people without taking off your headphones. When I run or go for a bike ride, I only use open earbuds so I can hear my surroundings and stay safe. I also like using them around the house when I am cooking or doing laundry.
What About Semi-Open Earbuds?
Semi-open earbuds, like Apple's AirPods, sit inside the ear but don't have eartips that create a sound seal. They can offer better audio quality than other open earbuds because the speakers and microphones are closer to your ear and mouth. Semi-open earbuds are comfortable, but they're usually pretty loose—they can fall out easily and may be a poor option for fitness activities.
How Do I Test Open Earbuds?
I test open earbuds like I test any pair of headphones: in the real world, in my daily life. I wear each pair for at least a few weeks to test comfort, battery life, ease of use, and onboard controls. I listen to podcasts, watch TV shows, jam out to my favorite playlists, and call friends.
With open earbuds in particular, I also wear them on jogs, bike rides, and errand runs to get a better feel for how stable they are on my ears. I do not expect them to cancel any noise, so I don't make a point of testing them on airplanes or loud commutes—they aren't really made for that. My main audio source is Spotify Lossless, but, when possible, I test other formats and codecs as well.

Anthony Page, the prolific British stage, film and TV director who won a Tony Award for his 1997 Broadway production of A Doll’s House and was twice Emmy-nominated for acclaimed TV movies in the 1970s, died September 11 at a London residential care home. He was 90.
Page’s death has been confirmed by press representative Jo Allan to British news outlets.
The director of the 1977 Oscar-nominated film I Never Promised You A Rose Garden starring Kathleen Quinlan as a young woman struggling with schizophrenia, Page was Emmy nominated for his direction of two high-profile TV-movies in the mid-1970s: Pueblo (1973), which chronicled the capture of an American spy ship in North Korea, and 1975’s The Missiles Of October, a drama starring Martin Sheen and William Devane about the 1962 Cuban missile crisis. Both projects won multiple Emmy Awards.
On Broadway, Page is best remembered for directing a string of acclaimed and starry productions during the 1990s and 2000s, beginning with his Tony-nominated A Doll’s House starring Janet McTeer (herself a Tony nominee for the role). In 2003 he directed a revival of Tennessee Williams’ Cat on a Hot Tin Roof starring Ashley Judd, Jason Patric, Ned Beatty and Margo Martindale, and two years later directed a revival of Edward Albee’s Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf that starred Kathleen Turner as Martha opposite Bill Irwin’s George.
Watch on Deadline
Page made his final Broadway appearance in 2009 with a revival of Beckett’s Waiting for Godot, starring Irwin, John Goodman, John Glover and Nathan Lane.
Born Anthony Frederick Montague Page on September 21, 1935, in Bangalore, British India, Page attended Oxford before relocating to New York to study with famed acting teacher Sanford Meisner. By the mid-1960s he had begun a long association with London’s Royal Court Theatre where he directed and, from 1969 to 1972, served as co-artistic director.
Page made his Broadway debut with 1965’s Inadmissible Evidence, a John Osborne play starring, among others, Nicol Williamson. He returned to Broadway in 1983 with a revival of Shaw’s Heartbreak House starring Philip Bosco, Rosemary Harris, Rex Harrison and Amy Irving. Page would not return to Broadway until his string of star-driven revivals began with A Doll’s House in ’97.
For the screen, Page directed, among others, 1979’s The Lady Vanishes starring Cybill Shepherd, Elliott Gould and Angela Lansbury. Television credits include 1981’s The Patricia Neal Story and Bill starring Mickey Rooney as a mentally disabled man; the 1983 sequel Bill: On His Own; 1988’s Scandal In A Small Town starring Raquel Welch; and, in 1994, seven episodes of the British mini-series Middlemarch.
His final credit was the 2008 British TV film My Zinc Bed, written by playwright David Hare and starring Uma Thurman, Jonathan Pryce and Paddy Considine.
Page is survived by his husband and partner of 40 years Kenneth Butler.

'Nothing good was supposed to come out of me'
- Published
A Nigerian man has shared the story of how he rose up out of "abject poverty" as a child, to become one of the leading UK academics in his field.
David Etor, 43, who grew up in Nigeria, only learned to read and write aged 12 and was told as a child that "nothing good will come out of you", but is now a lecturer in electrical and mechanical engineering at the University of Bristol.
He told the BBC how his family was so poor growing up that his mum would pretend to cook food in a kitchen they shared with others, "to protect our integrity" in front of neighbours.
"I didn't see a way out," he said.
'The poor called us poor'
Speaking to John Darvall on BBC Radio Bristol about the publication of his first book, Etor described growing up in a "compound" with several other families, all sharing a single kitchen, toilet and bathroom.
"It was a very poor neighbourhood. We were particularly very poor that the poor neighbours would refer to us as poor," he said.
"I do remember that there was a time where my mum would boil water.
"[She would] go back in and out, lift the lid, stir the water, go back into the room [and] come back as though she was preparing food...
"She would come back in with that pot of water after a couple of hours and it will be as though she's just finished cooking a meal, but it was just water.
"She was trying to protect our integrity."

To solve the problem, he designed and built a kind of "solar oven".
"It worked incredibly well," he said, which led to an award from the state government and a job.
He then completed an undergraduate degree at Newcastle University and a PhD at the University of Durham, before securing his current job in Bristol.

After 20 years with no police force, safety tops voter concerns in this Quebec community
‘It’s a human right to have public security,’ says Long Point First Nation chief
Provincial election signs are up in Chief Steeve Mathias’s community of Long Point First Nation, but he says there’s been silence when it comes to the issue he wants addressed for his community: an independent police force.
The community of 600, located in Winneway, Que., 630 kilometres northwest of Montreal in the Abitibi-Témiscamingue region, has been waiting to get their own police service reinstated for 20 years.
In the meantime, they’ve had to come up with their own solutions while relying on the closest available provincial police station in Ville-Marie, Que., 100 kilometres away — where Mathias says officers can take two to three hours to arrive in an emergency.
“We're trying to take all the different types of measures … through our own means that are very limited," Mathias said.
The long-term impact of the policing desert is contributing to an increase in violence and drugs, he says. He argues the problem wouldn’t be this serious if the community had a consistent police presence.
“We're getting a lot of pressure from our people. They say, ‘do something about the drug dealing … it's getting out of hand, completely out of control,’” he said.
Ahead of the Oct. 5 provincial election, Mathias is speaking out, noting he wants “to see a government that cares.”
“It’s a human right to have public security … and [it] seems like my community is not eligible,” he said.
‘I feel safer now with my door locked,’ says resident
The police force in Winneway was officially dismantled on March 31, 2006, when a tripartite agreement with the federal and provincial governments ended.
A number of issues led to it, including a failure to come to an agreement on matters such as a lack of resources, infrastructure, jurisdiction and the number of police officers, says Mathias.
The band council began incurring a deficit, he says — significant and untenable for a community of its size.
After the police force was dismantled, the provincial police took charge. Over the years, Mathias says they stopped patrolling regularly.
Now, the response time can be lengthy and is contributing to heightened fear.
“I never used to lock my door at night,” said resident Diane Polson. “I feel safer now with my door locked.”
A lifelong resident of Winneway and interim director of the child-care centre, Polson says the question of security and safety is top of mind for her.
Twenty years ago, Polson served as part of a negotiating team in an effort to keep and expand the small police force the community had in the early 2000s.
In 2022, the community signed a collaboration agreement with the province for a temporary police force made up of officers from neighbouring First Nations.
- After years of demands, this Quebec First Nation will finally get its own police force
- First Nation issues state of emergency amid growing violence, asks Quebec police to step up
But Mathias notes one of its conditions stipulated that provincial police still needed to be present for interventions.
“The two First Nation police services cannot come to the community without … the Sûreté du Québec being present,” he said.
“People found that very ridiculous. You know, there was a situation happening in the community and then like our First Nation police, they couldn't intervene.”
The office of Quebec's minister responsible for relations with First Nations and Inuit, Ian Lafrenière, said the situation involves complex challenges that predate its government.
He agreed that the area should have police coverage, but said the government would not negotiate publicly.
Training locals to protect community
For now, the community is mobilizing to find solutions. It's hired a private security firm to train about 15 to 18 locals to help keep residents safe.
With the plan to purchase a vehicle for security agents to patrol the community, Mathias says the community is trying to give a sense of security particularly to elders, women and youth.
Last winter — in response to growing concerns from residents over the presence of drugs and violence in town — the Long Point First Nation held a general assembly where a decision was made to mandate the council to take action. It allowed them to forbid certain individuals from coming into the community.
As part of this resolution, an individual who lives outside the community was banned. Mathias says he's known in the community as a drug dealer.
But the chief notes, without resources to enforce such bans, there are concerns about violence escalating.
“I find that very shameful that the government are not taking these matters more seriously [as] they should,” he said.
“Take accountability… provide the means and the resources.”

Google’s AI models may not be in the lead by most measures right now, but the company does have one key advantage: your data. If you’re deep in the Google ecosystem, Gemini models have a lot of context on you already. Google’s latest Google Labs experiment, known as CC, aims to expand that kind of customization to the whole family.
CC is an evolution of something that Google announced in 2025. The original CC eventually became Gemini’s Daily Brief, which churns through the data in your Google account to offer daily action items and suggestions. The new CC has a similar goal, but it’s designed to be a shared resource for up to six users in a family.
Google says that CC has its own Google account, allowing each family member to interact with it (or not) as they choose. For example, CC only sees emails from its connected users if they are explicitly shared. You can do that by designating certain addresses as always available to the agent—something like school scheduling emails. You can also send content to CC via email or Google Chat. The agent can even monitor a shared Google Drive folder, into which you can dump invitations, documents, and other content.
One of CC’s main functions is, unsurprisingly, a lot like Daily Brief. Each morning, all the registered users will get a shared “Your Day Ahead” email that pulls together the day’s events and updates on previous tasks. It can also add items to shared calendars, remind you about important tasks, and create documents based on your instructions that are accessible to all CC users.

Mbappe, Vini and Konate obscure Real's Ceuta message
- Published
Kylian Mbappe, Vinicius Junior and Ibrahima Konate rolled up their pre-game T-shirts ahead of Real Madrid's match at Elche on Tuesday to obscure the message of support for the people of Ceuta.
Ceuta is a Spanish autonomous city on the North African coast, bordering Morocco and separated from mainland Spain by the Strait of Gibraltar.
Players from both sides walked on to the pitch at Elche's ground, Martinez Valero, wearing white T-shirts carrying the message "Todos somos caballas" – translated as "We are all Ceutans" – along with references to the Spanish autonomous city.
While most of the players wore the shirts fully, Mbappe, Vinicius and Konate had theirs rolled up to around chest height, obscuring some of the slogan.
Mbappe and Vinicius then removed their shirts before the pre-match handshake, while Konate kept his on for longer. Their team-mates and the Elche players continued to wear the shirts through the pre-match formalities.
This is not the first time Real Madrid have shown support for Ceuta. Before their Champions League meeting with Inter Milan at the Santiago Bernabeu on 8 September, supporters in the south stand displayed cards featuring the coat of arms of the autonomous city, while the rest of the stadium joined the tribute with a round of applause.
The initiative was part of a wider show of support for Ceuta, following a major migration crisis in the Spanish territory after thousands of people entered from Morocco.
At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.
Although most returned, as many as 5,000 remain in makeshift camps or are sleeping on the city's streets and beaches, leading to unrest in the autonomous Spanish city in North Africa.
Locals have expressed safety concerns and some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.
The representatives of the players have been asked for comment.
The episode came shortly before a dramatic night for Real Madrid, who recovered from surrendering a two-goal lead to beat Elche 3-2, with Carlos Espi scoring the winner in stoppage time.
Mbappe was among Madrid's scorers, while Vinicius started the game.
The pre-match gesture also highlighted the differing approaches among players and clubs to the Ceuta campaign.
Barcelona did not take part in the initiative, while players at other La Liga fixtures had worn the shirts as intended.

Professional cyclists can top 100 km/h. But safety has not kept pace — and people are dying
GPS trackers will be used at UCI Road World Championships in Montreal
As the world's top cyclists descend upon Montreal for the UCI Road World Championships, there's a spectre looming over the event.
At least 11 of their compatriots have died in professional races and training rides this year, adding to a growing tally of injuries and deaths in the elite sport.
Though safety gear is being developed alongside the evolution of bicycles that can move faster than ever before, an underlying conflict remains in the sport: at what point must safety trump speed?
Right now, the average speed of the Tour de France winner is 43.3 km/h, set in 2026 — exactly 19 km/h faster than the average speed set by the winner 100 years ago. On the descents, riders now reach upwards of 100 km/h.
Safety technology that might slow riders down, such as wider handlebars, are being considered by the governing body, Union Cycliste Internationale (UCI), and SafeR, an international safety taskforce. Other measures being floated include choosing safer courses, tracking riders in real-time and adopting protective equipment like airbags.
But it has divided riders, some of whom argue that slowing bikes down goes against the spirit of professional cycling — and even those within SafeR, like Adam Hansen, have doubts.
"It's hard to get my head around this, because that's the whole purpose of the sport, is to go as fast as possible," said Hansen, a former professional Australian cyclist and current president of the pro cyclists' union.
Others, like Canada's Michael Woods — who estimates he has endured between 30 and 40 crashes — says changes are critical to prevent future fatalities.
"The bike that I'm on now versus the bike that I first started racing on [in 2010] is night and day," said Woods, whose professional racing career took him across Europe, including winning a stage of the 2023 Tour de France.
"The speeds that you can hit are far higher. But the rules … haven't caught up and that's made the sport far more dangerous."
GPS trackers
Woods and Hansen believe that GPS trackers, which will be used in Montreal, should be mandatory in all races. The trackers will sit underneath the bike's saddle and can transmit real-time data to a central location so that rescuers can respond immediately in the case of a crash.
Earlier this month, against the backdrop of the Aug. 14 death of 19-year-old British rider Finlay Tarling at the Volta race in Portugal, UCI "stressed the urgent need to put in place, as quickly as possible, a dedicated safety system allowing the real-time location of riders and vehicles to be tracked at all professional road cycling events."
The statement also noted that "in discussions on safety, stakeholders need to move past any disagreements on certain issues and act together."
Muriel Furrer's legacy
GPS trackers for pro cycling were introduced at the UCI Road World Championships in Rwanda last year following the death of Muriel Furrer.
The 18-year-old Swiss cyclist lay critically injured for an hour and 20 minutes after she careened off the wet, leaf-strewn road into a secluded wooded area during the 2024 championships in Zurich. She was airlifted to hospital and later died.
Woods, who was at that competition, recalls how the race continued even after Furrer's death.
" The sport's wild in that sense," he said. "When a rider passes away, it's sad. Everyone's impacted by it, but they didn't cancel the event.
"It's the same with other incidents ... where I've raced where professional riders have died [where] maybe we took things a bit easier the next day, or had a moment of silence — but the race continued."
Woods retired from professional cycling last year, because he no longer felt he could race safely. In March 2020, he broke his right femur during the Paris-Nice race. Last year, he woke up in an ambulance with a broken collarbone and a severe concussion after crashing out at the Milano-Torino race.
He's decided, however, to race one last time at the Road World Championships this week so he can end his career in Canada instead of abroad.
Airbags
While GPS trackers can ensure riders will get faster medical attention following a crash, they don't prevent injury itself. Airbags, meanwhile, might help.
In January, UCI put out a call for airbags that could be part of a bike frame and for those that could integrate into a cyclist's clothing.
The latter can be part of bike pants, said Hansen, and has straps around the shoulders.
"When it goes off, it actually puts a ring around your neck area, and it actually covers your collarbone," he said. "It really protects your spine, protects your neck ... [and] goes almost up to your helmet."
Several prototypes are in development, he said. The challenge in the past has been creating something light enough that it won't hinder a rider's speed or their movement.
At least two World Tour teams (Picnic PostNL and Visma-Lease a Bike) are testing out the Aerobag, according to Cycling News. It's not yet on the market nor has it been approved for UCI races; it's unclear exactly when such a measure might be adopted.
Other sports have adopted similar airbags, both in downhill skiing and recreational motorcyclists.
Bike lanes can be dangerous for the pros
Speed isn't the only factor in these crashes.
Woods says UCI has been studying the design of cycling courses, and found that the same elements that make recreational cyclists safer — such as bike lanes with bollards, speed bumps or roundabouts — can be hazardous in a race.
Canadian cyclist Alex Volstad says that when she's in a tight group of riders, known as a peloton, she has limited visibility and may be slower to react.
"Sometimes if it hits you by surprise, then you can get a bit, like, bucked off your bike, like you're riding a horse," she said.
In 2026, for example, a bottleneck of riders approaching a roundabout in the Tour of Oman created a major pileup before the final sprint, knocking some off their bikes.
It's one of the reasons race organizers often favour rural areas, like Saint-Georges, Que., where nationals were held this year, because there's less infrastructure on the road to endanger competitors.
Sometimes, though, it's the simple things that can make a difference, says Michael Barry, a retired professional road racer — like your eyesight.
Just a simple eye test would make a fairly big difference.- Michael Barry, retired cycling racer
Early in his career, he raced without his glasses, because he had a light prescription and the rain, dirt and other debris that could collect on the lenses might slow him down or worsen visibility.
Then, he missed some gravel when he was flying down the French Alps in the ‘90s. He broke his femur in the ensuing crash.
After that, he got custom racing glasses. Soon, some of his teammates did the same, which was uncommon at the time.
It's why he thinks riders should have to get their eyes tested. With riders going as fast as cars, he said it's critical that they have perfect eyesight.
"They're testing for every other physical attribute the riders have," he said. "So just a simple eye test would make a fairly big difference."

Filmmaker and educator Subhash Ghai has congratulated actor Ishita Deshmukh following the selection of Gondhal as India’s official entry for the Oscars. Subhash Ghai celebrates Ishita Deshmukh as Gondhal becomes India’s official Oscar entry

Health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced Thursday a new effort to improve autism diagnoses, arguing that the current model is outdated, too time-intensive, and overreliant on professionals with limited availability.
“We are not satisfied simply for describing autism and managing its consequences. We are asking what drives the different forms of autism, and why developmental trajectories differ, why some children regress, and which interventions work for them,” Kennedy said during his keynote address at a conference for Children’s Health Defense, an anti-vaccine organization he previously led.
The initiative calls for organizations to submit “solutions” — tools and technologies that will not only speed up assessments but also improve autistic people’s quality of life. The program will be administered by the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, which funds novel health research. The announcement does not provide financial details for these grants.
“It’s exciting that ARPA-H is focusing on autism, and I think the idea of exploring ways that technology can transform aspects of diagnosis, interventions, and support is timely,” said Helen Tager-Flusberg, director of the Center for Autism Research Excellence at Boston University, in a text. “We can only hope that the review process will lead to an unbiased selection of projects!”
Autism care is facing some headwinds right now. Wait times to receive an assessment can stretch months or even years as prevalence has increased in recent decades. Health insurers have started pulling back from covering the main therapy used to treat kids after the field was rocked by allegations of fraud.
The autism community has also had to contend with Kennedy’s repeated use of dehumanizing language to describe the condition — he called autistic kids “damaged” during Thursday’s keynote — and his insistence that autism is correlated with vaccines, though there is no scientific evidence for the link. Kennedy and President Trump have also asserted, without evidence, that autism is connected with Tylenol use during pregnancy.
Many autism researchers have been wary of the federal investigations of autism launched by Kennedy, though they remain cautiously optimistic about the Autism Data Science Initiative, which awarded $50 million to 13 projects through the National Institutes of Health in June.
SPECTRA — or Systems for Phenotypic Evaluation, Clinical Trajectories, Response, and Agency — is a bet that greater understanding of interactions among genetic, environmental, microbiome, and other factors will provide advances in the field.
It will be overseen by ARPA-H Program Manager Russell Shilling, who has two kids with autism and used to sit on the Medical and Science Advisory Committee at the influential nonprofit Autism Speaks.

Flock Safety announced a voluntary employee separation program on Friday, offering a “generous” severance package to those who want to leave amid growing backlash against the surveillance technology company, according to an internal email shared with WIRED.
Applications for Flock’s voluntary severance program opened Friday, and employees have until October 2 to decide whether to leave the company. Flock expects to grant buyouts to the majority of workers who apply, according to the email. People familiar with the program but not authorized to discuss it publicly say they believe that a significant number of the startup’s roughly 1,500 employees may try to depart.
Flock is making the severance offers as it continues to lose customers amid growing frustration across the US about its sprawling network of license plate readers, which have raised concerns about privacy and misuse. In the last month, WIRED has documented officers allegedly abusing Flock to track former romantic partners and colleagues, exposed how widely some agencies share access to the system, shown how little is known about the manufacturing of the devices, and revealed in new detail how much information Flock’s cameras collect based on data from a dismantled Flock device.

Founded in 2017, Flock raised money at a valuation of more than $8 billion in a funding round that closed in April. The company has had many of its contracts either not extended or dropped this year, which could leave it short of revenue goals, according to two of the people. A wave of vandalism targeting its cameras has unexpectedly increased expenses. Without buyouts, Flock almost certainly would have to lay off some staff, one of the people believes.
In an internal announcement, Flock said the separation program provides “greater agency” for its workers and “treats employees with transparency, respect, and choice.” It also described the package as the “most generous” ever offered by the company, roughly double its previous severance offers.
Flock did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Some Flock employees have said they have received buyout offers in the range of tens of thousands of dollars, one of the people said. The package also gives employees several months of health care coverage and the ability to exercise stock options within two years after separation, a longer period than the company typically offers resigning employees, according to the email and people familiar with the offer.
Flock employees are expected to learn whether their applications were accepted on October 9, according to the email. Most accepted employees would leave the company by October 29, though in some cases Flock may ask employees to remain for another one to three months.
People familiar with Flock’s severance plan tell WIRED that some employees may take the offer amid speculation that the company, which has raised about $1.2 billion in venture capital, might resort to selling off parts or all of its business to stay afloat. “When you see enough of the vandalism” targeting Flock cameras this year, one of the people says, “you know the writing is the wall” that something has to change.
Flock CEO Garrett Langley said on the All-In podcast last month that “the biggest damage” caused by the backlash against the company had been “internal morale.”
“Because you go on to X or you go on to Reddit and you go, why are people so mad at us when we've been doing the same thing for nine years?” Langley said. “And why are they so mad at us for things we don't do? And we just want people to be safe.”
One advocacy group identified 93 city and county governments that cut ties with Flock in August alone. Overall in 2026, roughly three times as many local governments have dropped Flock compared to the previous five years.
Flock has recently been building products that extend the company beyond its core license plate reader offering. WIRED reported last month that the company has developed AI-powered investigative software to identify drivers, find potential associates based on patterns of movement, and search across police records and other data.
A separate WIRED analysis of Flock’s software found tools designed to continuously search camera feeds for people matching written descriptions. WIRED’s analysis of Flock’s code also found potential integrations with drones and other surveillance systems.

Over 30 people across four states have been poisoned by bacterial toxins after getting intravenous (IV) drips at wellness clinics, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Food and Drug Administration.
The people had received IV drips containing glutathione, which is sold—without evidence—for purposes like detoxification, immune support, increased energy, and skin brightening. Glutathione is an antioxidant that’s found naturally in the body. It has been studied as a potential treatment for various ailments, but so far there is little to no evidence-backed use for the tripeptide; there are no FDA-approved glutathione products in the US.
Nevertheless, it’s commonly used as a supplement and promoted as having various benefits. It’s most often used in supplement pills, taken by mouth. But popular wellness clinics offering IV drips of vitamins and other supplements have also been offering glutathione. According to the CDC and FDA, the problem is that specialty drug makers, called compounding pharmacies, are making these IV drips using glutathione powders that are graded for dietary supplements taken orally. This grading is critically different from that of purified products graded for use in sterile injectable drugs.
In an announcement late last month, the FDA said it had learned that at least two compounding pharmacies had been doing this and that people were getting sick. At the time, the FDA had gotten reports of at least 30 sickened people.
Illnesses
The IV glutathione products involved appeared to be made from glutathione provided by Medisca Inc., headquartered in Plattsburgh, New York. “The glutathione was labeled as dietary supplement grade, which is not an appropriate ingredient to make injectable drugs,” the FDA said. Medisca told the FDA that it had informed its pharmacy customers not to use the product for injectable drugs.

US President Donald Trump said on Saturday (September 19) he will create an “AI Force” to oversee artificial intelligence and plans to appoint an AI “czar” in the near future, as his administration seeks to maintain US leadership in the rapidly developing technology.
Trump made the announcement in a lengthy post on Truth Social, comparing the proposed initiative with the Space Force, which he established during his first term. He did not provide details on the structure, membership or legal authority of the proposed AI Force.
Trump said his administration would not “hinder or stifle” the growth of the AI industry. Instead, he said the government would support and monitor the sector while using existing criminal and civil laws to address harmful activity.
“We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry,” Trump wrote.
He also said the AI initiative would focus on identifying what he described as “BAD” uses of artificial intelligence, arguing that existing legal systems could be used to address such conduct.
Trump described AI as the next “Industrial Revolution, or Internet”, saying he expected its economic impact to be even greater.
He claimed AI could eventually account for as much as 25% of US GDP, although he did not provide supporting data for that projection.
Trump also said the United States was currently leading China and other countries in AI and that he intended to maintain that position.
Trump said he would announce an AI czar “in the near future” to oversee the new initiative. He added that people with high intelligence should apply for the role.
The announcement did not identify a candidate or specify whether the AI czar would lead a new federal agency, coordinate existing agencies or serve in another capacity.
The announcement comes after Trump has repeatedly criticised calls for slowing AI development and concerns about the expansion of data centres.
Earlier this week, Trump dismissed what he described as a conspiracy against AI and data centres and argued that the United States should not impose measures that could slow the industry's growth. Reuters reported that he has previously rejected calls for additional federal AI regulations, saying strong presidential leadership was sufficient.
The announcement also comes as Washington and Beijing prepare to discuss AI during upcoming high-level talks.
US and Chinese officials view artificial intelligence as strategically important to their economic and military competitiveness. The two countries remain divided over advanced semiconductor access, technology transfer and how AI should be regulated.
Trump is scheduled to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington on September 24, with AI expected to be among the issues discussed in the broader US-China relationship.
Trump has so far provided few details about what the proposed AI Force would actually do.
His reference to the Space Force suggests a formal government structure, but the administration has not yet explained whether the AI Force would be a new agency, an interagency task force or another type of federal initiative. The White House had not issued further details.

Attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia undermine regional security: MEA
Reiterating India’s condemnation of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s economic facilities and attempted strike on the holy city of Makkah, EAM spokesperson said
Attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia are unacceptable to India, as they undermine regional security and imperil freedom of navigation in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the external affairs ministry said on Friday.
Reiterating India’s condemnation of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s economic facilities and the attempted strike on the holy city of Makkah, external affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal told a regular media briefing that New Delhi is “deeply concerned” about the escalation in the security situation in the Red Sea.
“We have expressed our condemnation of the attacks on Saudi sovereign territory, including on civilians and economic assets. You would have also seen our statement which we issued following the attempted attack on the holy city of Makkah,” he said while responding to questions on the matter.
“Such attacks, I need not elaborate or reiterate, vitiate regional security, undermine regional peace and security and also threaten freedom of navigation in the Bab el-Mandeb,” he said. “Obviously for various reasons, this is totally unacceptable to us. We hope that there is early restoration of peace and stability in the region.”
Jaiswal said all Indian nationals currently in Yemen are safe, and the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia is in contact with them to ensure their welfare.
The drone attack targeting Makkah is being seen as a major escalation in renewed hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, who have taken control of key territories close to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in recent days.
The importance of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait for energy supplies has grown for India following Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz. India has repeatedly opposed attacks on merchant shipping and civilian infrastructure amid the West Asia conflict and said strikes on Saudi Arabia’s economic infrastructure by the Houthis undermine regional stability.
The issue of Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia figured in a meeting between external affairs minister S Jaishankar and his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud, on the margins of the Brics Summit on September 13.

Two withdrawals, one U-turn: TMC chaos ahead of Bengal bypolls
Rabiul Alam Chowdhury on Saturday said he would withdraw his nomination, but backtracked within two hours.
An intense political drama unfolded in West Bengal on Saturday after Mamata Banerjee's Rejinagar bypoll candidate, Rabiul Alam Chowdhury, announced to withdraw his nomination – only to make a U-turn in less than two hours.
At around 10:50 am, Chowdhury, a former TMC MLA from Rejinagar, told media persons in Murshidabad that he had a discussion with Banerjee on Friday and was likely to withdraw his nomination on Saturday afternoon. He cited the threat of arrests as the reason for his move.

But within two hours, he backtracked, saying that he was not quitting and would start campaigning for the by-elections.
“I had a word with Banerjee. I will start campaigning. Senior leaders of the party will come to Rejinagar to campaign for me. Banerjee may also come,” he said around 12:30 pm.

Nandigram shocker
After Dey withdrew her nomination, Banerjee announced that the TMC would support Milan Pradhan, the Congress candidate in Nandigram. Hours later Milan Pradhan was arrested by the police in 2007 murder cases.

“Milan Pradhan was arrested in connection with four pending non-bailable arrest warrants pending at Nandigram police station. The cases involve serious offences including murder, attempt to murder, abduction with intent to murder, causing disappearance of evidence, house trespass, rioting with arms and deadly weapons,” East Midnapore police said in a statement on Saturday.
The Congress, however, hit back questioning the timing of Pradhan’s arrest and said that the party won’t back down even if Pradhan is sent to jail.
“All the cases against Pradhan were registered during the anti-land acquisition movement in 2007. Similar cases were registered against several other persons. Suvendu Adhikari and his father Sisir Adhikari were also among the leaders during that movement. Why was Pradhan arrested after so many years and that too when he has filed the nomination? If our candidate is sent to jail, thousands of Milan Pradhans will take to the streets in Nandigram and campaign. They will distribute leaflets,” Subhankar Sarkar, state Congress president told the media.
The police, however, said that Pradhan has bene absconding all these years. A senior official said that Pradhan stands chargesheeted in the cases as an absconder. “There’s an epidemic affecting our nation’s young people. The epidemic is fear.”
As I scrolled through Instagram on my ride downtown to the Snapple Island Ferry Comedy Show, a reel from The Free Press popped up. Professor Arthur Brooks was making the case that “Gen Z is perhaps the most risk-averse generation in history.”
Now, I’m no psychologist. I’m a social media editor. And I theorize that some of that fear Brooks describes comes from our overexposure to a digital world that, seemingly, has all the answers. And when someone makes a decision outside the purview of algorithmic logic — like buying an abandoned ferry for $280,000 at a city auction — they are at the mercy of, well, being completely clowned.
Popular on Variety
	That’s exactly what the news cycle did to Pete Davidson and Colin Jost after they joined a group of investors to buy the decommissioned John F. Kennedy in 2022. Built in 1965, the JFK was the oldest ferry in the Staten Island fleet when it was retired last August due to mechanical failures. Davidson and Jost intended to transform the vessel into a floating entertainment venue.
“Davidson, who’s no longer with SNL, might need to call his agent to book those gigs — turning the 57-year-old ship into a nightspot is likely to cost millions,” The New York Daily News reported. The headline read: “Retired NY Ferry Bought by Pete Davidson and Colin Jost Is Full of Asbestos, Roaches, Say Ex-Crew Members.”
The social media hate laid on thick, too: “Have you heard of the hottest club in the city?” one person tweeted (per the LA Times). “It’s called ‘Tetanus’ and it’s located in the rusted belly of a decommissioned Staten Island Ferry. You’ll dance the night away while also always being just moments away from drowning.”
Years had passed without hearing about the ferry until I got an unexpected email in my inbox: “EMBARGOED: Invite to NYC’s Most Unexpected Comedy Club From Pete Davidson and Colin Jost.”
	As it turned out, the “SNL” comedians partnered with Snapple to give New Yorkers an “unexpectedly refreshing break from the daily grind,” transforming their vessel into the Snapple Staten Island Ferry for a free, one-night-only floating comedy show.
	Could the comedians have listed tickets for $200 a pop and still packed the ferry? Undoubtedly. Instead, they dropped a limited batch of free tickets at 3 p.m. each day (Sept. 3-8). The resulting buzz and scramble among young New Yorkers to secure tickets (not totally unlike the IMAX 70mm frenzy surrounding “The Odyssey”) was much more valuable than the low six figures a sold-out show might have grossed at the door.
Those lucky enough to make it aboard became a test audience for two brand comebacks, each fiercely looking to win over a younger generation before betting on a much bigger, more calculated swing.
The first is Snapple, which started phasing out its signature glass bottles in 2017, replacing them with plastic (the transition was complete by 2021). The company justified the brand’s “massive makeover” as a decision made “with the evolution of sustainability in mind.” The operational savings from slashing the cost of manufacturing a bottle to roughly a third of what it once was probably looked pretty savory to the big-wig execs at Keurig Dr Pepper. Consumers weren’t as quenched.
Snapple eventually budged in the fall of 2025, launching a limited glass-bottle revival at select bodegas and retailers across New York, citing a “demand for nostalgia from an OVERWHELMING number of consumers.” The brand has yet to commit to a wider or permanent return, but it was clearly testing the waters with this major brand activation.
Hosting Snapple’s revival party was Davidson and Jost’s own comeback project to replenish the New York comedy scene, taking the form of a floating, popsicle-orange vessel. They once played the purchase off as a joke on “SNL,” with Jost quipping, “We thought the whole thing through” (sarcasm implied). But four years later, this one-night-only comedy show offered them a real opportunity to float their idea.
The main room was packed. Because the ferry, naturally, didn’t have one big corridor, an overflow room projected a live feed of the main stage (shaped like a blocky ‘T’).
	“You’re media, right?” an event coordinator asked me. “Yes!” I had zoned out. “Then we better put you up here.” She whisked me straight to the front and pointed at two young women, who immediately jolted to their feet and shuffled toward the far end of the bench running parallel to the stage.
“I, uh, I’m sorry I took your seats,” I told the two women as I sidestepped past them. They glanced at each other and giggled. “It’s okay,” one of them said. “Trust me.”
	
It took me a couple of minutes to figure out what she meant. Then I pulled out my phone to take a picture of the stage: a black barstool, a (glass!) Peach Tea Snapple and a mic stand. I wasn’t just in the front row. I was in the hot seat. The very hot seat, directly under the mic stand. Stage lights beamed down on me, and the ferry cabin itself was extremely muggy. (I guess in Davidson and Jost’s master plan, A/C hit the cutting room floor.)
The room skewed younger millennials and older Gen Z. Most toward the front looked like (or probably were) influencers who’ll look good on camera. Usually, I’ll recognize at least a few media friends in a crowd like this. Not here. I tried making friendly banter with the dude sitting next to me. He was cordial, but his energy read: Nope.
At nine o’clock sharp, the lights went dark. Davidson and Jost emerged from beneath the neon Snapple Island Ferry sign to rapturous applause. This would be the first and last time we’d see the two co-hosts all night.
I’ve encountered Davidson and Jost in the wild before, but this tight vantage point popped any illusion of celebrity. Picture sitting in the front row of a movie theater.
“This is something we’ve wanted to do for like five years, so thank you guys for coming out,” Davidson opened. “And thank you to our sponsor, Snapple.” After holding a beat for the applause, Davidson exclaimed, “The glass is back, baby!”
Jost added: “I also feel like we should acknowledge our former sponsor: my accountant’s suicide note.” He smirked. “Snapple asked me to say this.”
	They then turned to the first of three lingering storylines from the news cycle they clearly wanted to address. First, the aforementioned clowning.
“The amount of shit that people have talked,” Davidson said. “Well, suck it!”
“Everyone feeling hot and nauseous? That’s a good feeling,” Jost asked the crowd before moving on to news topic numero dos. “Obviously we’ll get going soon. We’re gonna stop at the Strait of Hormuz.” But when Jost looked over at Davidson to tee up the next punchline, it became clear the geopolitical reference sailed right over his head.
“I like how you thought I would know what that is,” Davidson quipped back. He glanced down at the shot clock. 8:17 remaining. The sweat was palpable.
“I love that this is our body language,” Davidson said, leaning into their candid awkwardness as he and Jost stood marooned on opposite ends of the oversized T-shaped stage. “It’s truly like we’re waiting for someone to start a fight.”
Laughing along with the crowd, Jost admitted, “We don’t know exactly what to do.” The audience roared. That unvarnished honesty, the willingness to take themselves down a notch, clearly resonated with the audience of young people accustomed to spending hours each day swiping through content engineered to mask imperfection.
“We have an incredible show. There are so many great comedians here,” Jost said. “Macklemore is here tonight.” The crowd erupted. Jost stalled on a few uhs, his eyes scanning the room as he debated whether it was worth taking the joke any further.
Davidson took advantage of the moment. “You wanted to make a stance tonight, right?” he poked. “Colin was talking mad shit backstage, dude. He was like, ‘Macklemore doesn’t have shit on what I’m about to say.’”
Red in the face, Jost quickly rowed back to safer waters. “So, in other news…” From there, the remainder of their opener centered on Davidson’s recent concussion. But the lineup of fierce rising comics (with considerably less to lose) didn’t shy away from the insecurities and taboos their Gen Z audience might be too anxious to confront.
Matt Richards, who served as emcee for the night (effectively filling the role many of us presumed Davidson and Jost would play), set the tone for the night by chugging an entire Snapple in one go and then telling a story of how he tried to suck his own penis as a teenager. “Happy to say it didn’t work out,” Richards said. “If it did, I wouldn’t be here.” In an alternate timeline, he’d “live under a bridge and suck my own dick all day.”
As the crowd observed Richards, he gauged their reactions, taking the temperature of how far he could push them. The other comics were about to dive into some risqué material — he was just warming them up.
Richards wiped a bulk of sweat from his forehead. The humidity was becoming hard to ignore. Playfully, he advised Davidson and Jost to sort out the A/C situation before the next show. That’s what I was thinking.
When Chris Rock sat down with Variety’s Selome Hailu for his first in-depth interview since “The Slap,” he recalled “dying a death” during a stand-up set in Oakland in ’96. He was workshopping his controversial “Black People Versus N—s” bit, which would eventually appear in his landmark HBO special “Bring the Pain” that helped catapult Rock into rock-star comic status.
“People wanted to fight because I didn’t have it right yet,” Rock explained in his cover story interview. “You gotta go over the line to find the line. That’s what people don’t understand. When a comedian gets in trouble for saying something at the club, it’s like, ‘Dude, that’s what the club’s for.’”
Overcoming the fear of vulnerability, on both sides of the stage, is what makes the club special. A physical vessel where smartphones, despite the event’s plea for ample social coverage, were repeatedly told to stay tucked away.
At one point, a Staten Island photographer named Sean lowered his camera to snap a portrait on his phone of “Impractical Jokers” star Sal Vulcano mid-set. Vulcano immediately stopped. “No cellphones, sir,” he said. “It’s right up in my face.” Sean held up his DSLR, cutting Vulcano’s budding rant short.
“This guy’s just like- oh, you work here?” Vulcano said, his tone instantly changing. “Okay, you’re not fired. You’re great. I love you.”
Even an Impractical Joker, after hundreds of public challenges and punishments designed to push the limits of embarrassment, could still tense up when a cellphone camera caught him experimenting with a new bit. “That was the ending,” he told the crowd after telling a story about buying health insurance for his newborn. “I thought that would get a bigger laugh.”
The crowd loved it. He was hyper-fixated on grading his performance.
	Perhaps that’s why crowd work is so effective. Is there any other setting better designed to experience a flash of public humiliation?
“I like this guy,” Richards said, pointing at me. “You look like a Disney villain.”
“Gaston!” He belted out a Disney song.
Caitlin Peluffo stormed the stage with material in the — let’s call it — advanced workshopping stages. After boldly announcing to the crowd that she was “dropping eggs,” she turned to ask if I knew what ovulating was.
I responded with a sarcastic “Ehh!” and bobbed my head. “Go figure,” she said. “I wouldn’t expect anything less from a man wearing khakis.”
After another minute or two of hyper-sexual jokes, she circled back to me.
“Do you like pussy?”
The camera whipped in my direction.
I froze. Then hit her with the same ambiguous emote.
Why did I just do that? I literally-
“You’re really wishy-washy on the answer, sir.”
“You gotta leave a little mystery.”
“Leave a little mystery?”
Gulp.
“Those pants aren’t leaving any mystery, I’ll tell you that,” she fired back. “You’re not circumcised, I can tell.” The crowd woo-ed. “That’s okay. I like me a full-body boy,” she continued. “I’m not an easy cum. You better crack your knuckles.”
I cracked my knuckles on both hands. She smiled. Peluffo got what she needed from me. Mercifully, she moved on to her next victim.
“Are you a tough cum or an easy cum?” she asked an attractive, reserved young woman. “Which one are you?” I had never seen a face more red in my entire life. “ANSWER THE FUCKING QUESTION!”
“I’m easy!” she finally blurted out.
“Fuck!” Peluffo shot back. “You’re probably cumming right now.”
On the way out, ferry workers dressed in sailor uniforms were handing departing guests free Snapple. I grabbed a glass peach tea and popped a squat on the pier. It really does taste better.
As I sat there taking in the night, the sound of clinking glass got louder and louder. Sure enough, I spotted a small procession bolting away from the boat with entire cases of Snapple.
I walked over and asked a few of the workers why they were giving them away. A woman with a dyed-blonde bob leaned toward me, lowering her voice.
“Please, take one now and leave before anyone sees you,” she said. “We need to get rid of all of these before the end of the night.”

UPDATE, with CAA statement: The Motion Picture Editors Guild is praising California’s bill offering tax incentives for productions that shoot outside the state but bring their post work to California.
The bill, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom yesterday, expands the state’s film and television tax credit program and creates a new tax credit to support workers in all areas of post-production, including picture editorial, sound, music, visual effects, and finishing.
“This is a historic day for Editors Guild members and for California’s film and TV workers more broadly,” said Editors Guild National Executive Director Scott George in a statement today. “AB 186 ensures that the California Film and TV Tax Credit Program continues to drive the recovery of our industry in its historic home, while AB 2319 will complement the program by making sure that even projects shooting outside of our state can come back to California to employ Editors Guild members in post-production.
George also praised Assemblymember Nick Schultz and “all the legislators who recognize the value of entertainment industry workers to our state’s economy, to the California IATSE Council for its powerful advocacy, and, of course, to our partners in the California Post Alliance.”
Watch on Deadline
Newsom signed the bill AB2319 into law Friday, also signing AB186, which exempts certain productions from caps on tax credits.
The post-production bill was overwhelmingly passed the Assembly and Senate at the end of the legislative session, receiving broad, bipartisan support. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass advocated for the measure, as did other local leaders in Southern California. Initial funding of $10 million will be allocated to get the program started
The Editors Guild and the California Post Alliance co-sponsored the bill, which they say is “a necessary step to level the playing field for editors, assistant editors, mixers and other post-production workers who have seen their work lured away to other states and countries with powerful tax incentives.”
“We owe this victory not only to lawmakers and, of course, to Gov. Newsom, but also to the activism of our members and partners,” said F. Hudson Miller, President of the Editors Guild. “Post-production professionals work behind the scenes in dark rooms, unseen, to craft entertainment that dazzles. But for months our union has asked members to get out there and make some noise in order to save our industry. They absolutely delivered.”
The post-production bill complements California’s Film and Television Tax Credit Program 4.0, passed last year, which provides $750 million to incentivize in-state filming and address runaway production to other areas.
Newsom said in a statement, “California is the nation’s entertainment capital. It is the home of storytellers, dreamers, artists, entrepreneurs, and creators who define culture for the rest of the world. This legislation protects the extraordinary people who make this industry possible and makes it unmistakably clear: California is still the future of film and television. We have the talent. We have the infrastructure. We have the creative community. And we have an ecosystem that simply cannot be replicated anywhere else.”
This afternoon, Bryan Lourd, CEO and Co-Chairman, Creative Artists Agency, weighed in, saying in a statement, “We commend Governor Newsom, Senate President Pro Tempore Limón, Assembly Speaker Rivas, and the bipartisan group of legislators for taking action on AB/SB 186. Accelerating refunds and protecting independent film put much-needed money back into production and into the communities that depend on this industry. But the $5 million cap remains a ceiling on potential. Hollywood was born in California, and we must work together to keep it at the forefront of the global entertainment industry.
“At the same time,” he continued, “we welcome the President’s and federal lawmaker’s focus on revitalizing the entertainment industry in America. Federal production incentives, layered on top of state programs like California’s AB/SB 186, are a meaningful step toward making the United States competitive and bringing production back home. This is not a partisan issue. It’s about American jobs, creative output, and economic competitiveness.”

- A rumor circulated online in September 2026 alleging several images show the moment immediately before an Israeli "double tap" airstrike reportedly killed a Gazan child attempting to help a wounded person.
- Research on this subject concluded the images were enhanced, likely with artificial intelligence. However, further examination found an authentic video served as the reference point for the enhanced images.
- According to news reports, the video shows a boy named Muhammad al-Zinati dying in an airstrike that took place moments after an earlier strike injured or killed a man in the Sheikh Radwan neighborhood in Gaza City on Sept. 15. Getty Images hosts authentic photos that appear to match the same neighborhood, date and story.
- We contacted Palestinian news agencies reporting on the matter, as well as the Israeli government, Israeli military, Pentagon and White House, to ask about the incident. The Pentagon referred us to the Israeli military. We will update this article if we receive further information.
In September 2026, people shared various images online allegedly showing the moment immediately before an Israeli "double tap" airstrike reportedly killed a Gazan child who was attempting to help a wounded person. The images show one adult lying on the ground and the child, a boy, reacting to an incoming missile or other type of aerial weapon about to strike the ground.
A Snopes reader emailed an X post attachment, asking, "Very curious to understand if this picture posted to X is real. Stating it's a missile about to hit a child in Gaza."
(@mhdksafa via X)
A reverse image search found users sharing the same image (archived), as well as a slightly different image on Facebook (archived) and X (archived) — featuring differences in the appearance of the purported missile, debris from a destroyed building and a person lying on the ground.
(@PalPress24 via X)
The same reverse image search located posts of a third image showing the same scene, including on Instagram (archived) and X (archived) — also with differences in the appearance of the aerial object, the building debris and the person lying on the ground.
(@hasoonmasre via X)
In sum, the images provided a cropped and enhanced look at a real moment sourced from an authentic video, likely achieved with the help of artificial intelligence. One low-quality, blurry frame of that same genuine video, highlighted in other posts, truly appears to show a missile or other aerial weaponry right before a fiery explosion. For example, this post (archived) shows the authentic, unaltered moment:
(@Hakeam via X)
Two comparisons of the enhanced and original (blurry) frames confirm they were shot from the same perspective, ruling out the idea a photographer also separately captured a still picture at the exact same moment.
A Threads post hosts the authentic (and graphic) video. That post also displays one of the altered and enhanced images to the left of the genuine clip. The video itself doesn't display any signs of AI. The clip's one-minute length serves as a credible indicator of its authenticity (most AI-generated videos on social media are extremely short, lasting only seconds).
Snopes emailed the Israeli government (including the Israeli military) to pose questions about its purported participation in the airstrike. We also emailed the Pentagon, whose spokesperson referred us to the Israeli military, and emailed the White House, as well as news media outlets reporting out of Gaza, for comment. We will update this story if we receive further details.
More about the airstrike deaths
The Arabic-language Al Jazeera and Turkish state-run Anadolu Agency, as well as Palestinian outlets Al-Resalah and Shehab News Agency, all reported the news of the airstrikes.
Some of these outlets shared the enhanced images without making note of the alterations, reporting the location of the incident as the Sheikh Radwan neighborhood of Gaza City, the date as Sept. 15 and the identity of the young victim as Muhammad al-Zinati (الل محمد الزيناتي), a boy described as "no more than 15 years old" who was reportedly walking from a Quran memorization circle. According to the outlets, the video shows him approaching the man lying on the ground, identified as Sharif Shadi Labd (شريف شادي لبد), who was injured by an Israeli airstrike moments earlier.
The Shehab article and that publication's Telegram feed host other videos of al-Zinati's death, including clips reportedly showing his body covered in blood at the scene of the airstrike, as well as several moments with his father crying over him (longer video).
Getty Images hosts photos of the purported father, identified as a relative in several of the pictures, crying over a body, possibly al-Zinati. Its caption and other images match the neighborhood and date. The media-licensing company credited the pictures to photographers Ahmed Younis and Saeed M. M. T. Jaras.
Some of Shehab's still-image content appear to feature AI editing, for example the overly smooth look of an image showing the two victims posing together, possibly created from two authentic photos. The Al Jazeera (Palestine) Facebook page also featured (archived) one of the enhanced images, as well as other video clips allegedly from the same scene.
Via Messenger, we contacted Al-Resalah (archived) and Al Jazeera (Palestine) (archived) to inquire about the altered images in their Facebook posts, as well as Shehab News Agency via X to ask about another enhanced image in one of its posts (archived) — mainly whether the images were edited with AI or reposted from elsewhere. Al-Resalah and Shehab are both affiliated with the militant and political group Hamas, according to The New York Times and BBC News. We will update this article if we receive further information.

Fisheries Minister A. Srinath on Saturday stressed the need for greater awareness and sensitive communication about dementia, saying the way the condition is portrayed could shape how society perceives and treats persons living with it.
Speaking at the valedictory session of DEMCON 2026, organised by the Dementia India Alliance in collaboration with the Department of Health and Family Welfare, Tamil Nadu, Mr. Srinath said awareness should go beyond posters and programmes and help families find answers to practical questions on identifying symptoms, seeking help and supporting a loved one.
“Awareness must begin with understanding,” he said, pointing out that forgetfulness or confusion in an elderly person was often dismissed as a natural part of ageing. “But ageing and dementia are not the same,” he said.
He also underlined the role of the media, cinema, writers and other communicators in changing perceptions of dementia. He said he would facilitate the making of a short film on dementia to create greater awareness about the condition. “We need more sensitive storytelling, more responsible conversations and less stigma,” Mr. Srinath said.
The Minister stressed the need for collaboration between the government, healthcare institutions, civil society, media, families and communities to take awareness and support beyond conference halls and into neighbourhoods and households.
Dementia India Alliance co-founders Radha S. Murthy and Shyam Viswanathan and executive director Ramani Sundaram were among those present.

George Osborne has said he thought no one would find out about a private viewing of the Bayeux tapestry he organised for the tech billionaire Peter Thiel at the British Museum.
The former chancellor, who is chair of the museum, told the Big Brue festival in Somerset that he had been on holiday when the Thiel was shown the medieval artwork.
Thiel, who supports Donald Trump, is the founder of PayPal and Palantir, a software company that builds data integration, analytics and artificial intelligence platforms for government agencies and large corporations.
Palantir has a swathe of British public contracts, including, most controversially, a £330m deal with the NHS, which it has held since 2023.
The company also works for the US, Israeli and UK militaries. Its use of its AI-powered software to support military strikes in Gaza and Iran, US ICE immigration raids and its access to NHS data has stoked concern.
Of the viewing, Osborne said: “It wasn’t like we expected anyone to know about it.” The museum’s director of development, Charlotte Appleyard, hosted Thiel at a VIP viewing of the tapestry before it opened to the public on 18 August.
The visit was revealed in the Guardian shortly after the visit.
When asked what the museum might have got in return, Osborne said: “The short answer is he hasn’t offered any money, and were he to offer money, the board would consider it and have to take into account the pros, you know, receiving more income, and the reputational risks.”
Osborne, who lives in Bruton, near where the festival is taking place, complained that people treat the British Museum like the Foreign Office when they protest about donors who are thought to support the Israeli government.
He said: “The critique was that [Thiel] was a supporter of the Israeli government … I mean, this is the most difficult, and almost all the protests that happen at the museum … When I started five years ago, they were climate protests, Just Stop Oil and that kind of thing. Now they’re almost universally Gaza.
“You know that is the moment I would say the most sensitive, difficult political issue for the museum, and you know we try and navigate it, and I keep trying to point out we’re not actually the Foreign Office.”
He said the museum has to take money from companies such as BP to be able to operate.
“You cannot say we want museums to be free, and then one of the biggest British companies offers us £50m, BP, and we go, oh, don’t, because we object to oil exploration. Where is the money going to come from?
“You’d shut down the British Museum. People do say this. They say you shouldn’t take tech money, you shouldn’t take oil money. You can’t take any money from the banks. We want the museum to be free. The museum would shut down.”

When my husband, a doctor, went in for his first routine colonoscopy at 45 years old, he said nonchalantly, "I'll be done by noon. Then we can grab lunch." He recommends that his patients be screened on time, so he was simply following his own advice.
He had no symptoms suggesting anything was wrong, so when they found a few polyps — the largest one measuring 55 millimeters — we were caught off guard. A second procedure was necessary to remove the larger polyp, and when the biopsy came back showing cancer, our lives crumbled in an instant.
The right portion of his colon was removed, and three weeks later, our whirlwind nightmare began to settle. Luckily, having his screening on time saved his life. Now, we're focused on preventive care.
We're changing our diets, and what our kids eat, too
An average person has about a 4% to 5% lifetime chance of developing colorectal cancer — but having one affected parent raises that risk to roughly 5% to 15%. Someone with a first-degree relative who had colon cancer should have their first screening at 40 or 10 years younger than their family member was diagnosed, whichever comes sooner — for our kids, that means being screened at 35.
With double to triple the risk, I want to be as proactive as I can for my children — now ages 15 and 11 — and that means altering their diet (and ours!) to limit foods that may increase risk. We've read through current research and determined which changes are worth making.
We don't plan to restrict them completely from all foods associated with higher risk because we realize that's unrealistic (and we want them to enjoy eating), but we'll teach them to savor these foods in moderation.
We're limiting how often we eat some foods
First, processed meats will largely be eliminated from their diet. Our bacon-loving sons have only enjoyed this delicacy as a treat during vacations, and that plan will continue. They'll only indulge in other processed meats like hot dogs or ham when served at a barbecue or other social gathering. And cold cuts have been eliminated from our home, except for sliced turkey from our local market, which they prepare in-house without additives like sodium nitrites or nitrates.
Secondly, our kids love a medium-rare steak, and we don't plan to take that from them. But we will limit red meat to once a week or less, filling our other dinner menus with healthier protein like salmon, chicken, or turkey.
In our home, sugary drinks have never been a staple. We don't keep soda in the house, and that's not going to change. Aside from Gatorade during workouts or sporting events, we'll continue focusing on increasing water intake for hydration.
Fast food and other ultra-processed foods have no place in our home. Will my children have McDonald's once or twice a year? Perhaps they will, because my husband is easily persuaded by their happiness! But luckily, I have the time and ability to prepare home-cooked dinners most nights, and I don't plan to stop.
Finally, we've talked with our kids about the dangers of alcohol since they were little, but that conversation will now include the fact that alcohol intake is a risk factor for several types of cancer, colorectal cancer included.
We're also increasing how much we eat other things
We're limiting consumption of some things but increasing how often we eat others. There are certain foods that promote colon health, and we'll make sure they know which ones do. We'll aim for a diet including calcium-rich dairy products, whole grains, fish, and fruits and vegetables.
While our kids may not be receptive to every healthy option now (we struggle with vegetable intake just like many parents!), my hope is that the more we offer these foods and talk about a healthy diet with them, the likelier they are to adopt these eating habits as they grow.
Our kids aren't thrilled that some of the foods they love are being limited — and they likely won't follow every suggestion when they're older — but it's our job to guide them down a healthy path and provide them with the necessary information, especially given their increased risk. Thankfully, my husband's story had a happy ending, and we were given the chance to change the trajectory for our kids.

'Enough is enough': Women protest after string of murders near Johannesburg
Runners gathered in South Africa to pay tribute to Elizabeth Moselakgomo after her body was found east of Johannesburg.
She is one of nine women found in the Kempton Park area, since July.
The jogger, known as "Tsontso", went missing during a routine run.
Runners organised an event in city of Centurion to honour her and defend women's right to run freely.
"This is for her - we just want to live and go running and come back home without having to think that it may be one of us", said Nonhle Mpohlo.
In Cape Town, people gathered in a vigil to honour the victims and called on the government to act.
The police have since set up a task team to investigate the murders and have urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone "particularly in isolated areas".

Alina B.K. should have been preparing for her end-of-year university exams, but news of devastating floods along the Nepal–Tibet border kept pulling her back to a troubling question: what kind of future awaits her?

The world is bracing for a “super” El Niño, and its effects are already being felt in India, where the monsoon has brought less rain than average but more intense downpours.
Meteorologists predict that the current El Niño, which is developing over the Pacific, could be one of the strongest in living memory. India is likely to be heavily affected, particularly later in the monsoon, when El Niño’s influence tends to strengthen.
But, as Ligin Joseph of the University of Southampton explains in The Conversation, its effects on India’s monsoon are not straightforward. A previous study in Science found that El Niño tends to bring more extreme summer monsoon rainfall to India.
This year, the southern state of Kerala has felt the brunt of the building super El Niño, with about a fifth less rain than normal. Yet intense downpours in the first week of August triggered flash flooding and landslides, killing 26 people.
The super El Niño is expected to peak after India’s monsoon season, but Indians are already keeping an anxious eye on the skies, wondering where and when the next deluge may come.
