The Jehovah’s Witnesses have partly eased their long-standing prohibition on the medical use of donated blood, allowing members to receive products derived from blood but maintaining a ban on transfusions of whole blood.
The policy, announced Friday, is the second revision this year in what has long been one of the most controversial and distinctive teachings of the religious organization.
The new policy says that individuals can receive products derived from blood donated by other people. It says they can receive medical treatments that involve the use of the four main components of whole blood: plasma, platelets, and red and white blood cells.
“Each Christian must make his own personal decision about the use of these four primary components in all medical and surgical care,” said Geoffrey W. Jackson, a member of the Governing Body of the organization, based in New York State.
The new announcement also allows members to decide as a matter of individual conscience whether to donate blood to be used for blood products for the medical treatment of others.
But the organization continues to oppose members receiving transfusions of whole blood or donating blood for that purpose.
In March, the Governing Body also announced a revised policy, authorizing members to have their blood stored for their own future medical treatment, but not for others’.
Critics have faulted the organization for prohibiting the use of a proven treatment that can be lifesaving in replenishing blood lost in surgeries, accidents, or violence. Critics, including former church members, say that the teaching has led to deaths that could have been prevented.
The Jehovah’s Witnesses’ longtime opposition to blood transfusions derives from their interpretation of Bible passages requiring believers to “abstain” from blood. While Jewish and other Christian religious traditions have interpreted this as a dietary law, Jehovah’s Witnesses have extended that prohibition to transfusions.
Blood components are often used for specific treatments.
Plasma, the liquid component of blood, is often used for those suffering from trauma or certain diseases, according to the American Red Cross. Red cells can be used to treat conditions such as anemia and white cells to treat certain infections. Platelets are used in some cancer and other treatments.
Members shouldn’t make the decision on using blood products lightly, Paul Gillies, international spokesperson for the Jehovah’s Witnesses, said in an interview.
“What we’re saying is you have to pray about it, you have to study it, you have to see what the Bible has to say about it, because blood in the Bible represents life,” Gillies said. Members need to consider all these factors before reaching “a decision that you feel happy about with your God.”
Jehovah’s Witnesses, who emerged in 19th century America, share many Christian beliefs with other churches but diverge on key theological issues, such as the nature of Jesus and biblical prophecy. They are almost alone in their beliefs about blood transfusions. Jehovah’s Witnesses reported a U.S. membership of 1.3 million in 2025, with a worldwide membership of 9.2 million in more than 200 countries and territories.

Emily Wilson Wanted to Like Nolan’s Odyssey
The translator of Homer’s epic is done talking about her harsh movie review—but eager to translate the poem again.
Emily Wilson has become the most famous living translator of the Homeric epics. Her 2017 The Odyssey, the first major translation of the poem into English by a woman, has sold more than 1 million copies. (Her Iliad translation came in 2023.) And this summer, she found herself right at the center of cultural discourse after she drew her sword and published a scathing review of Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster adaptation of the ancient work. She didn’t anticipate that she would become part of a pop-culture controversy, and she was reluctant to revisit the episode when we sat down for an interview at this year’s Atlantic Festival. “I really wanted to like the film,” she said, but “it seems to me that criticism has a responsibility to tell the truth.” Her strong convictions animate a new book of essays, Crossing the Wine-Dark Sea, which dissects translations of ancient work with unsparing rigor.
Wilson, who is now working on a second translation of The Odyssey, entertained the idea that there might be something “compulsive” in her art and her approach. Her new essays reveal a translator’s difficult balancing act—between fidelity and originality, and between accessibility and strangeness. In the course of our wide-ranging conversation about the pleasures and blind spots of translation—and, yes, the backlash to her now-notorious movie review—she spoke about the imperative she feels to get that balance exactly right.
The following conversation was condensed and edited for clarity.
Gal Beckerman: You take a pretty hard line in this book about when a text should be retranslated, but you’re translating The Odyssey again. It’s interesting that you should want to go back in again. Have you learned something new about the text or come to see it in a new way that makes it exciting for you to tear it all up and start it from scratch?
Emily Wilson: It’s not tearing it up to do a new one, right? Partly it’s that I’m kind of addicted; I can’t stop doing this. I have several other projects I’m supposed to be doing. I did The Odyssey really prioritizing pacing, because my students would very often show up to class saying, Oh, it was so boring. And I would be like, How can The Odyssey be boring? And then I would realize it’s because the translation was twice as long as the original. Then, with my Iliad translation, I was a little bit looser about not confining myself to the exact same number of lines as the original. I thought there were advantages to doing that. So as soon as I’d finished The Iliad, I wanted to go back to The Odyssey and start all over again to produce one that matches my Iliad. So it’s not that I think there’s anything wrong with my current translation, and I think that there will be readers who will like that one better. It will be snappier and all that.
Beckerman: Do you think that translators have a kind of a compulsion to continue to play with the words, to work this Rubik’s Cube?
Wilson: Yeah, I think it is compulsive, maybe that’s right, but I don’t think that’s just me. I think that is very common, especially for a very long project like this. You’re constantly thinking about, How might I be able to get closer to whatever the vision is?
Beckerman: One of the things I love that you do in the book is demystify translation, and make us understand that these are human beings and that they have biases, that they’re in a specific cultural moment—a certain gender, a certain kind of life experience—and that it shows up in the word choices. When your translation of The Odyssey came out, a lot of the excitement about it was that you were the first woman who was translating The Odyssey in English. And I wonder if you feel like being a woman has affected your translation?
Wilson: I think some of those headlines were kind of bogus, right? I mean, they were suggesting this really simplistic set of ideas about gender: And of course gender will be the only factor that will contribute to how someone writes. And of course all women write in iambic pentameter, just naturally, and all men don’t. Some of it was really silly, I thought.
Beckerman: But do you feel like you understand the particular worldview that you’re bringing to it? None of us fully know the water we’re swimming in, of course, but when you’re translating, are you like, Oh, I think that I’m reading this way or I’m making these choices because I’m a woman of a certain age living in the 21st century in America?
Wilson: You know, I honestly never think that. I mean, I think that when I’m talking to people like you. Well, I don’t mean “people like you”—
Beckerman: Nosey journalist.
Wilson: Exactly. It’s only very belatedly that I feel that I have to prepare an answer for things like this. When I’m actually wrestling with it, I do quite often think, Okay, I’m putting the stress on that, and that syllable and that name; is that because I’m British? To what extent is my approach to the passage informed by that critical study or this critical study? That kind of thing comes into my thinking all the time. But the question is about my lived experience, and do I have this particular relationship to this banquet scene because I don’t eat meat? No.
Beckerman: Right. I mean, meter is important to you, that the sound of the poem or the text in another language have some relationship to the original. For translators 200 years ago, they wouldn’t necessarily care in the same way.
Wilson: Yeah, this is a very old-fashioned choice on my part. I see myself as super retro. I see myself very much as taking a sort of mid-19th-century approach to translation.
Beckerman: How do you think film adaptation is different or similar to literary translation? When you think about a director approaching a text like The Odyssey—wanting to adapt it and making very definite choices about the value system that is underlying the plot that he’s created—is that the same type of thinking through interpretation that a translator does when they approach a text?
Wilson: I would say no. I think it’s a very different kind of thinking. What I’m trying to do as a translator is to get to something equivalent to the experience of the original. I think a good adaptation tries to do the opposite of that. Virgil was certainly doing that in rewriting The Odyssey as The Aeneid. It’s on some level the same story; it’s also the opposite story. So I think the more the adaptation pushes against it, in many cases the more successful it is artistically.
Beckerman: There is this interesting sort of tension through a lot of these essays in your new book, where you want these ancient texts to be popular, to get out there, to have people engage with them and to make new things with them. But on the other hand, that often leads to a kind of a reductive quality. And I feel like it’s a tension that came out around Nolan’s movie. You wrote a very critical review of the film, and I had a moment as I read that when I wondered, Is she trying to distance herself from it as something that has reductive qualities, and is it popular in a way that doesn’t engage with the full texture of the text?
Wilson: I wish I would have liked the film more. I went in hoping to like it and thinking I was going to like it. And it turns out I didn’t. It seems to me that criticism has a responsibility to tell the truth. There’s another kind of responsibility: that you shouldn’t actually lie about your actual feelings and thoughts. And there’s also a question about: what does it mean to spread the word that everyone should read ancient literature? Everyone should take some kind of interest in history. Everyone should engage with long, difficult books. I really believe in those things, and I don’t believe that the best way to engage with history and to grapple with the essential questions of art and cinema and plays and music and literature is to sort of say, Yay, we love it all.
Beckerman: But what lenses did you put on to critique the film? As a translation or as an adaptation?
Wilson: No. I mean, I say at the start of the review that very often the best adaptations are the ones that are most resistant to the original. The ways that I was critiquing the film were in terms of pacing and characterization and narrative. A satisfying cinematic experience needs to follow through on its own premises. And so if you set us up to think this is going to be the kind of film where we’re supposed to care about the characters, then you need to follow through on that promise.
Beckerman: What did you make of the response to your response—the backlash of sorts? I’m just curious what it told you about people’s relationship to these stories, because there was this real defensiveness about the film, about this effort to make a popular piece of art around The Odyssey. Were you surprised?
Wilson: Yeah, I thought it was really weird. Many people reviewed this film, including other Odyssey translators, and there was no discourse about anyone except for me, which is really weird, I thought. So I’m not sure that I can really comment on what weird people thought. But I feel like this is taking us a bit far from the book? Because I don’t discuss the film in the book. I discuss theater and ancient literature.
Beckerman: I know, I understand. It’s just that it was an interesting cultural moment. It is not every day that my Twitter feed is full of people wanting to debate the finer points of The Odyssey. So I can imagine, for somebody who’s as immersed in it as you are, that it must be unsettling but also exciting.
Wilson: I think it’s wonderful insofar as it is actually substantially about either the film or about the poem, or some combination of the two. I felt that some of the discourse wasn’t about either of those things. I’m, on some level, interested in it because it’s a symptom of some kind of bad stuff in our culture, but I’m not that interested in it, and I’m not going to celebrate it.
Beckerman: Right. So my last question: I’ve thought a lot about the limits to how much we can understand people’s lived experience so far in the past, and as a translator of these texts, you come the closest—you walk right up to that edge—and I’m curious for your thoughts about that. Is it never going to be possible for us to get at what it meant to be living in the time when The Iliad or The Odyssey were written? Or do you see a kind of universality that connects us to the people who wrote those texts?
Wilson: That’s a great question and such a difficult one. I mean, part of my reason for focusing so much on literary form and poetic form is that even if we can’t get the lived, embodied experience of what it means to be going around in your chitons and eating your ancient Greek olives—I’m not sure that we can get to that through texts—I do think we can get quite close to something like the experience of being a fluent listener or reader. I don’t think that means universals, but I think it means we can get to a kind of multicultural imagination that includes going back in time as well as going to different places in space. And if we can do that, there’s a kind of magic in that in itself.

India continued its winning run in the Open section of the Chess Olympiad 2026 with a 3-1 victory over Spain in the fourth round in Samarkand on Saturday.
D. Gukesh and Arjun Erigaisi delivered the two wins for India, beating Alexei Shirov and Maksim Chigaev, respectively. Gukesh, playing on Board 4, defeated the experienced Shirov in 42 moves, while Arjun overcame Chigaev in 36 moves.
On the other two boards, R. Praggnanandhaa and Nihal Sarin held their opponents to draws. Praggnanandhaa shared the point with David Anton, while Nihal drew against Jaime Santos, completing another 3-1 win for the defending champion.
India had entered the fourth round after victories over Thailand, Indonesia and Italy in its opening three matches.
Women’s matches

Divya defeated Khishigbaatar Bayasgalan in 47 moves to return to winning ways after her draw against Greece in Round 3. She had earlier beaten Johanna Paasikangas of Finland in the second round.
Savitha continued her outstanding start to her maiden Chess Olympiad, defeating experienced Mongolian International Master Batkhuyag Munguntuul in 50 moves. The result took Savitha to four wins from four games, having also won against the Dominican Republic, Finland, and Greece in the first three rounds.
The two victories put India 2-0 ahead against Mongolia at that stage, with the remaining boards still to be decided in the images you sent.

Live music fans raise $1m to save beloved Alice Springs venue after landlord flags sale
It might seem unlikely that a volunteer-run venue in one of the country's most remote towns could inspire people from across Australia and the world to help raise $1 million to save it.
But it did.
Over the past month, the founders of popular Alice Springs live music venue The Black Wreath have been fundraising to buy the building and turn the whole block into a creative hub after their landlord put the property up for sale.
Artists and music industry figures came on board, including Amyl and the Sniffers, who played at The Black Wreath's Blacken Open Air festival in 2022, as well as donors who matched pledges dollar for dollar.
The Black Wreath hosts local gigs and offers artists a recording and rehearsal space, helping kick-start the careers of some of the most remote bands in the world.
Before he launched the campaign on August 4, the Black Wreath's founder, who goes by the mononym Pirate, hardly used social media.
But by the end of the appeal, he was posting daily videos, pushing as hard as he could to save one of the creative heartbeats of Alice Springs.
"It's a massive milestone, I'm really proud of the community achievement and everyone that's gotten behind this," he said.
The fundraisers gave themselves until September 13 to reach their $1 million funding goal, but hit the target two days early before a massive weekend of coordinated gigs across the country in solidarity with the cause.
It wasn't until the day after the Alice Springs gig, headlined by South East Desert Metal, that Pirate had his first day off in months.
He said the whole town "became a metal head for the night".
"The last month it's been 12 to 15 hours every single day, it hasn't been healthy, but it's been necessary," Pirate said.
"And yesterday I just absolutely collapsed, couldn't do a bloody thing."
However, Pirate said there was a long road still ahead.
As part of the fundraising campaign, people from across the country made pledges for something in return, which ranged from T-shirts, records, rings and hats to an entire festival, Blacken Open Air, to be held on April 30 next year.
"I'm not celebrating yet just yet; I'm getting back to work," Pirate said.
Loading...
"It's just the beginning of the process, we've raised some money and now we need to negotiate with the owners.
"There's a lot more to do."
Pirate said the grand vision was to turn the entire property into a creative precinct.
"My big hopes and aspirations and dreams are that it's run as a foundation and the income generated goes into local music and arts," he said.
"And touring Central Australian artists outside of here, [as well as] bringing artists to Alice Springs and putting them on stages here as well.
"Fifteen years of doing this, I find that the travel aspect has been the biggest hindrance to connecting us with a wider community."
Ltyentye Apurta/Santa Teresa musicians South East Desert Metal describe themselves as the most isolated touring band in the world, and credit The Black Wreath for success that's seen them perform on the steps of the Sydney Opera House.
The band's lead vocalist and guitarist, Chris Wallace, said there was nothing else like it in Alice Springs.

Lawsuit accuses Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and SpaceXAI of illegal agreement to slow AI
Anthropic CEO acknowledged potential antitrust hurdles, writing that it would assist if the US government were to mediate ‘or at least enable’ cross-lab discussions
Major artificial intelligence developers face legal action over claims they entered an unlawful pact to intentionally slow down the momentum of their technical advancements.
The lawsuit, submitted Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, alleges that Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceXAI violated federal antitrust laws by colluding on deceleration strategies.
The filing contends that this arrangement ultimately diminishes the value provided to customers paying for AI service subscriptions.
Central to the complaint is an event on Sept. 12, when Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei issued an essay calling for collective industry efforts to curb rapid progress in favor of enhanced safety measures.
Later that day, Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis, OpenAI's Sam Altman, and SpaceXAI's Elon Musk publicly endorsed Amodei's proposals.
The filing maintains that mutual pledges among dominant industry rivals ensuring their timeline "should be slower than competition would otherwise produce has an anticompetitive effect on consumers."
Lawyers representing four named plaintiffs, who pay for subscriptions to ChatGPT, Claude, Grok or Gemini, are bringing the suit on behalf of a proposed nationwide class of other paid subscribers to those services.
"AI will quickly spin out of human control and could kill us all if we allow AI safety and protocol ... to be controlled by private self-serving agreements between the world’s most powerful ‘for profit’ technology companies," stated Nick Rowley, the lead attorney for the plaintiffs.
Representatives for OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and SpaceXAI did not immediately respond to requests for comment Saturday.
In his essay proposing the slowdown, Amodei acknowledged potential antitrust hurdles, writing that it would assist if the U.S. government were to mediate "or at least enable" cross-lab discussions.
Federal officials would not have to participate, he noted, but would need to "issue a narrow waiver for certain kinds of safety conversations."
Replying on social media, Altman stated OpenAI supports a "federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements," while adding "we do not believe we need to wait for an anti-trust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence."
Although recent conversations regarding pacing development stem from growing fears over artificial intelligence escaping human control, industry leaders have long discussed developing shared standards to maintain safety.

‘But why now?’ Mamata questions arrest of Congress’ Nandigram bypoll candidate, calls it ‘BJP's vendetta politics’
Mamata Banerjee alleged that the BJP was using an “old case” against Pradhan and described it as party’s politics of “vendetta and atrocities”.
Former chief minister and TMC founder Mamata Banerjee on Friday questioned the arrest of Congress candidate Milan Pradhan, saying it came ‘minutes’ after her party extended support to him for the Nandigram bypoll.
Banerjee alleged that the BJP was using an “old case” against Pradhan and described it as part of what she called the party’s politics of “vendetta and atrocities”.

“Minutes after we extended our support to the Congress candidate for the bypoll in Nandigram, the Congress candidate Milan Pradhan was arrested. The timing raises serious questions and is the usual BJP formula: dig out an old case. But why now? Just after we announced support to the Congress!” Banerjee said in a X post.
“The BJP’s politics of vendetta and atrocities show a clear pattern. With manipulation, with vote loot, with intimidation the Election Agency-BJP partnership is killing democracy every day,” the post added.

Pradhan's arrest

"In Nandigram, we are going to give our support to the Congress party. It is for the greater interest of the country. Rejinagar, I will decide later. In Assam, we are not contesting," Banerjee said at a press conference in Kolkata.

A fungus that can cause severe pneumonia in people with weaker or weakened immune systems appears to have become resistant to a drug that never intended to kill it, according to the findings of a study by researchers from around the world published in Science Translational Medicine.
The study focused on mycophenolic acid (MPA), an immunosuppressive drug used with people who have received solid-organ transplants. MPA helps keep the immune system from rejecting the organ — but it was also found to affect Pneumocystis jirovecii fungi.
The team analysed 163 P. jirovecii samples from China, Denmark, Germany, Japan, Switzerland, and the U.S., of which 96 came from recipients of transplanted organs, most of whom were also involved in pneumocystis pneumonia outbreaks from 2005 to 2019. The remaining samples were controls.
MPA works by inhibiting an enzyme called IMPDH in human immune cells. The fungus possesses a similar enzyme, and the researchers believe this could be the link. The team found six relatively common mutations in the fungal gene that produces IMPDH. Some 86% of samples from transplant recipients contained a mutation in that gene, versus 13% in the non-transplant samples.
The researchers also produced normal and mutated versions of the fungal IMPDH enzyme in the lab and exposed them to MPA. Depending on the mutation, considerably more MPA was required to inhibit the mutated enzymes than the normal enzyme.
The mutations also appeared in at least 11 fungal strains and varied between countries and over time. That is, rather than resistance arising once and spreading from that source, P. jirovecii seem to have evolved similar adaptations as different populations encountered the same selective pressure.
The researchers have acknowledged that they have only established resistance at the enzyme level, rather than in infected patients, and that their cohort sizes and clinical data were limited.
Nonetheless, researchers understand antimicrobial resistance as microorganisms evolving to resist antibiotics, antifungals or other medicines. But in the study, a drug intended to act on the human body was found unintentionally exerting pressure on a pathogen as well. And mutant fungi that could better tolerate MPA may have enjoyed an advantage among transplant recipients taking the drug, allowing them to survive and spread.
The “results challenge the current status quo on P. jirovecii’s unknown resistance,” the study authors wrote, “calling for reevaluating immunosuppressive strategies and infection control measures and highlighting the broader potential for other pathogens to evolve under selective pressures imposed by human-targeted therapies.”

In September 2026, a rumor circulated online that the footwear company Converse had allegedly released an advertisement that some social media users believed evoked Ku Klux Klan and lynching imagery.
The advertisement that Converse purportedly published showed the bottom half of a person in white holding Converse shoes. The shadows and lighting in the ad create an optical illusion that looked, to some, like a Ku Klux Klan hood and the feet of a hanging person.
Much of the online discourse related to the ad took place on Threads, although posts on Reddit, X, Facebook (screenshotted) and Instagram (screenshotted) also expressed outrage or shared thoughts about the ad's imagery.
Snopes readers asked us if the ad was real and searched the website for "racist Converse ad" and if there was a "Nike Converse commercial" that "looked like a lynching." (Nike owns Converse.)
Converse did, in fact, publish the advertisement (archived) in question as part of its campaign with singer Karina, a member of the K-pop girl group Aespa, to promote the "Chuck 70 X," a newer version of the company's classic Chuck 70 shoes. As such, we have rated this claim as true.
The footwear company did not immediately return an inquiry for more information about its design and approval process, as well as whether Converse plans to pull the ad following online backlash.
A spokesperson for Converse sent the following statement over email when we asked about the ad:
We're sorry. We understand why this image is deeply upsetting and recognize that we got this wrong. We removed it from our channels and are working to remove it everywhere it appeared. This should not have happened, and we will do better.
As of this writing, a link connected to Converse's official Threads account still shows the image in a Sept. 3 post. However, the post does not show up on Converse's main Threads page (archived), suggesting the company may have archived the post to hide it from viewers.
(Converse on Threads)
Per the Wayback Machine archive, an earlier, Aug. 22 version of Converse's U.S. page advertising the Karina and Chuck 70 X collaboration showed that the company had at one point used the image in question on its website. It has since been removed and replaced with a clip of Karina modeling the shoes while wearing a white skirt — presumably the same skirt shown in the controversial picture.
An Aug. 22 version of the Converse page promoting Chuck 70 X shoes in collaboration with Karina. (Converse/Wayback Machine)
Was the campaign created outside US?
Some of the claim posts also said the campaign was created in Malaysia, and thus the team behind it might not have had the cultural and historical context necessary to understand why
Social media users shared screenshots indicating that the image may have initially been posted on the Converse Malaysia Instagram page.
Without more information from Converse, it was not possible to verify whether any members of the creative team were based in or from the U.S. That image was not on Converse Malaysia's Instagram account. A search of the Converse Malaysia website for "Chuck 70 X" returned an error message.
Some posts also shared another advertisement showing a person on a ladder holding Converse shoes, which some social media users similarly thought evoked lynching imagery.
That image is a real Converse ad, too, as evidenced by the fact that was still on Converse Chile's account (screenshotted) as of this writing.
However, the image of the person on the ladder came from a separate campaign that was shot in Italy, according to a LinkedIn post from the founder of Palmes, a tennis and menswear company that collaborated with Converse on it.

AI will be the death of me. And you. And everyone we know.
The AI threat keeping scientists up at night
Claude, design a doomsday bioweapon. Make no mistakes.
At least, this is what a growing number of technologists and policymakers fear.
Last week, a lead researcher at Anthropic declared that there was a greater than 10 percent chance of AI “killing all humans” within the next decade. This nerve-racking forecast, combined with recent AI-initiated cyberattacks, have fueled calls for slowing the progress of artificial intelligence — a proposal that Anthropic and OpenAI subsequently embraced.
Not all prophets of AI doom agree about precisely how this apocalypse would come about. Many focus on scenarios reminiscent of The Terminator films, in which superintelligent machines conspire to exterminate humanity — perhaps in the same not-quite-intentional way that humans laid waste to the dodo, or passenger pigeon.
Key takeaways
- Synthetic pandemics are among the biggest existential risks facing humanity.
- AI could make bioweapons more powerful and easier to build.
- Governments can make us safer from both natural and artificial pathogens by investing more into pandemic preparedness.
But there is another, arguably more intuitive way that AI could bring about mass death, if not human extinction: by making it easier for people to develop and deploy catastrophic bioweapons.
Importantly, this hypothetical doesn’t require AI models to become conscious or superintelligent; it merely requires them to accelerate preexisting trends in biotechnology.
For those alarmed by this hypothetical, the threat AI poses is essentially twofold. First, when combined with technological progress in gene editing and DNA synthesis, chatbots could vastly increase the number of people capable of assembling dangerous viruses already known to medical science. And the more potential bioengineers there are in the world, the higher the odds that one will prove to be a diligent psychopath.
Second, AI could help highly trained biologists to discover — or engineer — a custom supervirus, which could then fall into the wrong hands.
Recent headlines have lent some credence to both of these fears.
Earlier this year, biologists warned that, with a few simple prompts, they’d gotten chatbots to dispense detailed instructions for engineering a treatment-resistant strain of an infamous pathogen, step-by-step protocols for recreating a once-pandemic virus, and advice on dispersing biological payloads via weather balloon.
In August, a team of scientists revealed that an AI model trained on DNA sequences had generated blueprints for deadly viruses unseen in nature (albeit, viruses deadly to bacteria, not animals). And last week, Anthropic announced that it had thwarted several suspected attempts by state actors to use Claude for bioweapons research.
Precisely how much AI is increasing the risk of an artificial pandemic is unclear. Even before ChatGPT, advances in synthetic biology were already making bioengineering tools more potent and accessible. And even after four years of rapid AI progress, the technical barriers to engineering novel superviruses remain formidable.
Regardless, there is a great deal more that governments can — and should — be doing to protect us from synthetic pandemics, both manmade and natural. No matter what AI’s ultimate impact on biosecurity proves to be, now is the time to both prepare for the worst-case scenario and, ideally, preempt it.
Why synthetic superviruses are scary
Before we dig into how AI could raise the risk of a man-made pandemic, it’s worth spelling out why that prospect is so unnerving.
Put simply, few things could more credibly destroy civilization — and/or, the human species — than a synthetic supervirus.
Infectious diseases have killed more humans than any other force on Earth. The Black Death wiped out at least 30 percent of all Europeans in the 1300s, while the 1918 flu killed 50 million people worldwide. You don’t need me to tell you what things were like in 2020 (or how much worse they could have been, if vaccines hadn’t been rolled out in record time).
And nature kicked off these catastrophes without even trying. A bioterrorist consciously seeking to maximize human death could theoretically improve on evolution’s handiwork. If biotech continues to advance — and scientists identify viral genomes that reliably yield high transmissibility and lethality — a malicious actor might one day be able to manufacture a virus that’s both as contagious as measles and as deadly as Ebola.
Natural selection generally disfavors viruses that are both highly transmissible and profoundly fatal; bugs that kill their hosts too reliably often have difficulty spreading. Yet a virus with a long asymptomatic period could escape this tradeoff. For example, HIV can live in a person’s body for a decade before generating noticeable symptoms. In theory, a highly contagious respiratory virus could similarly lie in wait for many weeks, months, or even years.
If bioterrorists ever managed to unleash an easily transmitted, highly fatal virus, they could shake the foundations of modern existence. In that scenario, reliably showing up for work might require accepting a 50-50 chance of getting yourself — and your family — brutally killed. Covid never required essential workers to assume risks anywhere near this high (the virus had a less than 1 percent case fatality rate among prime-age workers, before vaccines became available). Although there are many heroes among us, plenty of doctors, nurses, warehouse workers, power plant technicians, delivery drivers, and other essential laborers might not tolerate a coin flip’s chance of wiping out their loved ones. And if enough sheltered in place, systems for producing and distributing healthcare, food, water, and power could swiftly break down.
Humanity’s “Joker” problem
All this invites the question: Who would ever want to do this?
After all, viruses are terrible weapons: They’re difficult to make, impossible to control, and jeopardize the lives of those who cultivate and distribute them. Partly for these reasons, biological weapons have hardly ever been used; the last fatal bioterror attacks were the anthrax mailings of 2001.
To this, anxious biosecurity experts might reply, to quote the former British intelligence officer Alfred Pennyworth: “Some men just want to watch the world burn.”
Mass shooters regularly forfeit their lives to the cause of killing others at random. And brilliant iconoclasts periodically develop murderous ideologies; Ted Kaczynski, the Harvard mathematician turned Unabomber, wished to bring about the collapse of industrial civilization.
And every once in a while, an aspiring supervillain gets graduate training in virology. In the 1990s, the Kyoto University-educated genetic engineer Seiichi Endo joined Japan’s Aum Shinrikyo death cult. Drawing on the group’s $1 billion in funds, Endo sought to weaponize Ebola, Q fever, botulinum, and anthrax — with the aim of killing as many nonbelievers as possible.
Of course, Endo failed. And lone wolf psychopaths have never gotten their hands on anything more lethal than an assault weapon, bomb, or airplane.
But some scientists believe that technological advances — including generative AI — may provide the Endos and Kaczynskis of tomorrow with catastrophic power.
How AI and biotech could democratize bioterrorism
MIT biologist Kevin Esvelt is among his field’s most prominent Cassandras. And he has voiced two fundamental concerns. The first is that breakthroughs in synthetic biology and AI are rapidly expanding the pool of people who can engineer known viruses.
Over the past 15 years, the cost and difficulty of editing genomes have plummeted. In 2012, to modify a specific site in a genome, you often needed access to custom-engineered proteins that cost upward of $5,000 and still tended to work poorly, according to Olivia Scharfman, a biotechnology fellow at the Institute for Progress. Thanks to the gene-editing tool CRISPR, a scientist with minimal lab training can execute such a modification for as little as $30. Meanwhile, DNA synthesis has also grown radically more affordable.
This might not be such a big deal, if dangerous biological materials were hard to legally access. But Esvelt and his colleagues recently demonstrated that this isn’t the case. As an experiment, they had a student place orders for pieces of the 1918 influenza genome using a pseudonym and fake position. Thirty-six of 38 DNA synthesis companies shipped the genomes without asking whether the applicant had government permission or sound intentions. Together, these fragments were enough to create the virus many times over.
Crucially, in Esvelt’s account, reverse engineering known viruses using modern tools does not require elite skills. Any random biology graduate student may be up to the job.
And AI may be making such rudimentary viral engineering even easier.
In theory, a chatbot can help you plan a bioweapons attack in much the same way that it can walk you through fixing a dishwasher: By finding and synthesizing the internet’s vast trove of information, offering step-by-step instructions for navigating unfamiliar challenges, and fielding all troubleshooting queries that might subsequently arise.
And there’s evidence that AI models will in fact provide would-be bioterrorists with precisely this kind of assistance.
In a 2023 study, MIT researchers asked students to seek guidance on engineering a pandemic from that era’s chatbots. Within an hour, the AI models had suggested four promising pathogens, offered detailed protocols for manufacturing them with with synthetic DNA, provided a list of DNA synthesis retailers with low screening standards, and advised that — if users still found themselves unable to make the virus, even with all this help — they could purchase the assistance of a contract research organization to do some of the bioengineering for them.
And of course, frontier models have gotten a lot better since 2023. Last year, SecureBio, Esvelt’s biosecurity nonprofit, found that one OpenAI model outperformed 94 percent of expert virologists on troubleshooting complex laboratory problems.
Anthropic’s internal research has produced similar results. In one experiment, the company tasked amateurs with drafting a bioweapons acquisition plan. It gave some participants access to basic internet resources and others the assistance of Claude models (with the safeguards turned off). Those working with AI developed far more viable blueprints, according to the biodefense experts who scrutinized the proposals for critical errors.
Thus, there’s reason to think that the number of people with the skills and resources necessary for reverse engineering a virus from genomic blueprints is sharply rising — and with it, the risk that a bloodthirsty nihilist or ideologue gets their hands on a dangerous pathogen.
AI might help scientists learn too much
What’s even worse than bringing back smallpox? Esvelt’s second concern is that these same technological forces — combined with top scientists’ often reckless ambitions — will lead to the discovery or development of a supervirus, a new or custom-designed pathogen even more dangerous than what nature has come up with in the past.
Today, some scientists are actively trying to discover — and publicly identify — novel viruses circulating in nature that could theoretically trigger the next pandemic. Others conduct so-called gain-of-function experiments, altering pathogens to discern which mutations make them more transmissible, lethal, or difficult to detect (some have alleged that Covid-19 emerged from precisely this kind of research, though that theory is widely rejected among epidemiologists). This work is generally intended to anticipate future epidemiological threats, so that we can develop vaccines before they arrive. But their work could inadvertently provide bad actors with recipes for reverse engineering mass-casualty bioweapons.
Separately, advances in gene editing and AI may enable breakthroughs in viral engineering that yield apocalyptic pathogens.
A recent study from researchers at Stanford and the Arc Institute fed such fears. The scientists trained an AI called “Evo” on the DNA sequences of bacteriophages, the simple viruses that infect bacteria. They then used this “genomic language model” to generate blueprints for hundreds of bacteriophages found nowhere in nature. Sixteen of these designs yielded viable pathogens, some of which were better at killing bacteria than their natural ancestors.
What is clear, however, is that novel pathogens are among the greatest security threats our species faces.
Theoretically, scientists may one day be able to engineer novel human viruses using the same basic techniques. What’s more, even if genomic-language models fail at that task, they might still be able to help users tweak existing viruses in ways that render them more transmissible, deadly, or vaccine-resistant.
These discoveries could theoretically filter down to amateur bioterrorists or well-funded extremist groups like Aum Shinrikyo. Alternatively, a state-sponsored weapons program could develop a catastrophic supervirus, then unleash it on the world through a lab leak or (perhaps, more improbably) a deliberate attempt at genocide.
There is some precedent for the former scenario: The Soviet Union tried to weaponize smallpox and the Marburg virus, despite the considerable hazards and dubious military utility of such bioweapons. In the process, Soviet scientists accidentally triggered a smallpox outbreak during testing, while also letting anthrax leak from a laboratory, killing at least 64 people.
Bioweapons ain’t easy
All this said, there are reasons to question whether AI is truly making a synthetic pandemic more likely.
Chatbots may solve some of the challenges facing an amateur biologist with omnicidal aspirations. But it doesn’t necessarily clear the biggest obstacles in that person’s path.
Viral engineering is a complex, difficult, and physical undertaking. Performing it successfully requires what scientists call “tacit knowledge” — practical skills and understandings that are difficult to explain in words: knowing how to suppress the hand tremors that could rip delicate DNA strands, or how to recognize when the DNA in your solution has reached the proper concentration, or how to smell when a sample has been contaminated.
And these are things that Claude still can’t reliably impart. In studies, amateurs with access to a large language model tend to perform better on written biological challenges — but not on actual lab work. In a 2026 randomized study, non-scientists working with frontier AI systems were no more likely to complete a multistep laboratory assignment than those relying on the internet alone.
Of course, tacit knowledge wouldn’t necessarily be a problem for aspiring bioterrorists in the mold of Seiichi Endo — graduate-trained scientists with extensive lab experience. But at a minimum, chatbots don’t appear to have turned every malcontent who once took AP Bio into a competent virologist.
And while AI will likely help top biologists advance their field’s frontiers, the barriers to custom engineering doomsday viruses remain formidable. The “Evo” experiment is arguably a case in point. Although the model did generate working blueprints for a few novel bacteriophages, nearly all of its suggested genomes didn’t work. Researchers had to arduously test hundreds of DNA sequences to arrive at 16 viable strands. And engineering slightly modified versions of an extremely small, well-known bacteriophage capable of infecting E. coli in a lab — and creating a novel virus more fearsome than any nature has yet devised — aren’t especially similar tasks.
To offer a strained analogy: The fact that I can dunk on Victor Wembanyama in NBA 2K26 does not imply that I’m making progress toward being able to dunk on him in real life.
Even in the age of CRISPR and ChatGPT, biology remains an exceptionally difficult discipline that resists reliable modeling. The effects of modifying a single gene can often yield unpredictable and inconsistent results, varying with host biology, immune responses, and environmental conditions that scientists only partly understand. AI may help us overcome these complexities. It also might not.
We need to be preparing for the next pandemic
Scientists disagree about how serious a risk synthetic pandemics pose — and how much AI is magnifying it.
What is clear, however, is that novel pathogens are among the greatest security threats our species faces. Even if synthetic biology and artificial intelligence did not exist, natural selection would keep churning out new viruses — and periodically hitting upon ones that befuddle human immune systems.
For this reason, there would be an urgent need to make our societies less vulnerable to future pandemics, irrespective of AI’s implications for viral engineering. In a world where chatbots and CRISPR are plausibly making bioterrorism easier, failing to invest aggressively in public health is all the more reckless.
The good news is we already know — from hard-earned experience — many steps that we can take to reduce the risk of a new pandemic and prepare to respond to one if needed.
Governments can limit the destructive power of novel contagions by investing in vaccines that protect against entire families of viruses (or ideally, all of them) and broad-spectrum antivirals; raise our odds of catching outbreaks early by funding meticulous wastewater and clinical surveillance; ensure that essential workers don’t have to choose between staying alive and keeping civilization going amid a pandemic by developing and then stockpiling foolproof personal protective equipment; make indoor spaces less hospitable to airborne viruses by upgrading ventilation and filtration systems; and reduce the the threat of bioterrorism by mandating rigorous screening of synthetic-DNA orders.
Fears that humanity will be done in by superintelligent machines are currently galvanizing media attention and political concern. And this may be warranted. But we should pay at least as much attention to our species’ age-old, organic adversaries as we do to our hypothetical, robot ones — and not just because the latter could start teaching the former new tricks.

Asian governments are rushing preparations for the most severe El Niño weather event on record, with hundreds of millions of people bracing for multiple crises at once as extreme heat, heavy rain and food shortages hit the region.
Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to grow to a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027.
The World Food Programme has warned that about 50 million people will probably be pushed into acute hunger due to the exceptionally intense weather system, while UN secretary-general António Guterres said this month that El Niño was “being supersized before our eyes”.
Here are the steps countries in Asia are taking to prepare for El Niño:
‘Climate risk maps’ in China
In Hong Kong, authorities have already been forced to revise workplace policies, after the city experienced its hottest day on record on 9 August. During times of extreme heat, companies are expected to reschedule work, provide cooling equipment and rest breaks for their employees.
Employers in the international financial hub could even face prosecution if they fail to provide staff with support at times of sweltering heat.
In mainland China a 100-day campaign has been launched to prepare for extreme weather and help safeguard harvests against the opposing extremes of drought and intense rainfall.
Beijing has plans to upgrade early warning monitoring systems, and in July, it launched a national plan encouraging cities to draw up ‘climate risk maps’ to help identify areas most vulnerable to flooding and severe heat.
Taiwan, meanwhile, is treating the predicted extreme weather as an emergency situation, and preparing using methods similar to what it would do to train for a terrorist attack or earthquake. In early September, the island nation held a mass exercise simulating three consecutive days of temperatures above 40C. Hundreds of people took part in the field exercises, which simulated power and water disruption, rail problems, air conditioner failure and mass heatstroke.
The government has also been testing its “Cool Map” online platform, which helps to direct vulnerable people to airconditioned and cool spaces.
Sri Lanka plans to process salterwater
El Niño is already wreaking havoc across south Asia; in parts of India there has been a shortfall of monsoon rainfall of almost 50% in September, with knock-on effects on key crops such as rice, pulses, cotton and maize. Concerns are mounting that there could be a diminished harvest in the coming months, likely driving up food prices – already crippling for poor and lower middle class families.
The Indian government has taken a hyper-vigilant approach to establish what the agriculture minister, Shivraj Singh Chouhan, described as a “protective shield for farmers”.
In more than 350 vulnerable districts authorities are boosting water conservation infrastructure and water harvesting, and are encouraging farmers to plant low-water, short duration crops – such as pulses and millets.
But the most intense impact of El Niño in the area is in Sri Lanka, where the absence of rainfall and high temperatures have become so severe that the country is experiencing its worst drought in a decade. More than 160,000 people are now facing a drinking water shortage as several key reservoirs run dry.
Officials have been forced to close the tourist areas of the Yala national park, home to leopards, elephants, crocodiles and spotted deer, and have been bringing in tankers of water to fill the ponds to make sure the animals do not die. In Mullaithivu lagoon, in the north-east of Sri Lanka, thousands of fish were found dead due to the lack of fresh water.
The country’s disaster management centre is preparing for a situation in which freshwater supplies could vanish. “If water sources dry up, there will be no alternative means of obtaining water,” an official said. Colombo would then be forced to process salt water from the sea, although relying on the country’s one desalination plant is not considered workable.
Tackling an agriculture crisis in south-east Asia
In south-east Asia, El Niño is compounded by a series of ongoing crises. The Iran war has already disrupted global energy and supply chains and inflated fertiliser costs, disproportionately hitting the region. At the same time, severe haze from seasonal fires across Malaysia and Indonesia has choked cities and is damaging plants and trees.
During the 2023–2024 El Niño, south-east Asian governments successfully cushioned agricultural impacts by adjusting planting calendars and managing water, but those strategies will be insufficient to deal with the scale of the crisis, experts warn. Regional rice yields are already projected to fall by 8 to 10%.
“We can’t just assume that this El Niño is going to be the same as the last because there are so many challenges that have been stacking on top of each other,” says Elyssa Kaur Ludher, a climate and food security expert based in Singapore.
The Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia are particularly vulnerable to food price changes, says Kaur Ludher, a visiting fellow with the Climate Change for Southeast Asia Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.
“In Singapore, most of our income is not spent on food. It’s under 10%. But for Indonesians, it can be up to 50% or even more as a proportion of income spent on food. So any price rise affects them disproportionately.”
With the potential for price rises to leave people desperate and angry, Kaur Ludher has argued for food security to be reframed as a national security issue. In Indonesia and the Philippines in particular, she said, social stability depends a lot on food prices. “Rice is a lifeline to this region,” she says.
To prepare, south-east Asian governments and farmer cooperatives are promoting regenerative agriculture and shifting toward biofertilisers.
“We have come to a stage where climate change is putting so much pressure on us – on our existing, already crumbling or structurally unsound, systems,” say Kaur Ludher. “Nature will force us to have a reckoning.”
South Korea overhauls its heatwave alert system
South Korea saw the driest July on record in the country’s south-east. Weeks later came a freak reversal, as a weakening storm system dragged in a deluge that dumped some of the heaviest rainfall ever recorded at a Korean weather station. The heat was so intense that farmers described spoilt potatoes as being “boiled” in the ground.
The country’s weather agency has overhauled its heatwave alert system for the first time in 18 years, adding a top tier that triggers official guidance to stop non-emergency outdoor work once feels-like temperatures hit 38C. Nationwide, phones have buzzed for weeks with government alerts urging people to stay indoors during the hottest hours.
Officials are watching out for a rough autumn, with seas around the Korean peninsula remaining unusually warm for the season and forecasters expecting the north-west Pacific to produce far more powerful storms than usual this year, since a strengthening El Niño is weakening the high pressure that has so far kept them away.
Japan prepares for ‘cruelly’ hot days and typhoons
Japan is also bracing for the arrival of so-called super-typhoons, which experts attribute to a combination of El Niño and human-induced global heating.
El Niño was once associated with slightly cooler summers in Japan. But rising sea surface temperatures mean it is having the opposite effect, blanketing many parts of the country in record-breaking heat and humidity in 2023-4, the last time the weather pattern materialised.
Japan recorded its first official “cruelly hot day” – or kokushobi – in July, just after the start of the current El Niño event. The Japanese term, introduced in April to underscore the threat to health posed by rising temperatures, refers to days when the mercury exceeds 40C.
Now, as the summer heat dissipates, the country is bracing for the arrival of potentially destructive typhoons.
The public is encouraged to take measures to protect themselves and their homes, such as heeding official evacuation warnings and stocking up on food and water. People living in apartments are urged to secure or bring inside flower pots and furniture – anything that could become a dangerous flying object during a storm.
This month the infrastructure ministry said it had identified several high-risk underpasses on national highways that would be closed preemptively during heavy rain. Underpasses – which allow cars to travel beneath other roads or railway lines – became a focus of concern last month after two trapped motorists drowned during record-breaking rain in Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo.

The U.S. FDA is holding a public hearing on Monday to gather feedback on the potential therapeutic use of psychedelic drugs, the latest step in a months-long push by President Donald Trump's administration to speed up development of the treatments for serious mental illnesses.
The hearing is part of a broader push launched in April, when Trump ordered the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to focus on qualifying psychedelic drug programs for its priority-voucher program.
The order also directed the FDA to work with the Drug Enforcement Administration on a pathway for some patients to obtain investigational treatments under a law, which allows certain seriously ill patients to seek experimental therapies, and to increase collaboration with the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Since then, the FDA has issued priority vouchers to three companies developing psychedelic-based treatments, one for psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression, another for psilocybin for major depressive disorder and a third for methylone for post-traumatic stress disorder.
The hearing focuses on practical issues that could shape how psychedelic therapies are tested and delivered, including provider training and credentials, patient screening and monitoring, access and reimbursement, clinic capacity and the collection of long-term safety data.
The FDA said it was not seeking views on individual drug applications, the scheduling of controlled substances or the legalisation of psychedelics.
Doctors, veterans, pharmacists and therapists during the hearing urged the regulator to establish clear safety and access standards for psychedelic-assisted therapies.
Experts said any approved psychedelic treatment must include trained staff in the room during sessions, along with proper screening, follow-up care and community support.
Robert Barrow, CEO of Definium Therapeutics, which is developing an LSD-based therapy, told Reuters that the hearing offers "a nice opportunity for that continuing public dialogue" among regulators, clinicians and patients.
He said regulators and industry should treat psychedelics "like it's normal drug development, normal science, normal medicine," rather than as an unusually novel category requiring special treatment.
Just days before the hearing, senior FDA officials, including Michael Davis, head of the agency's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, published a paper in the New England Journal of Medicine outlining a framework for developing and approving psychedelic drugs and saying the agency was "meeting this moment" on hard-to-treat conditions such as major depressive disorder and PTSD.
The American Psychiatric Association said it "appreciates the FDA's public hearing and coordination with federal partners on the potential therapeutic use of psychedelics."
"The FDA's determination of safety and effectiveness... must remain the foundation for any future clinical use."
Jefferies analysts said the framework suggested the FDA was willing to consider flexible trial designs to address challenges including "functional unblinding," when a drug's noticeable psychoactive effects reveal to participants which treatment they received.
The administration's support has stirred fresh investor interest in the sector, with industry executives telling Reuters it could improve coordination between the FDA and the Drug Enforcement Administration and help reduce regulatory delays, even as researchers noted that approved treatments were still likely years away.
Continued alignment among regulators, clinicians and developers on a safe, supervised rollout should benefit AtaiBeckley, Compass Pathways, Definium Therapeutics, Helus Pharma and GH Research, analysts said.
Helus CEO Michael Halstead said "the science continues to advance, and continued thoughtful engagement among regulators, researchers and clinicians is critical to advancing these promising new treatments."

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian visited New Delhi on 11 September 2026 to attend the 18th BRICS Summit. During his visit, he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi and participated in several engagements on the sidelines of the summit. On 11 September 2026, Iran’s Ambassador to India, Dr Mohammad Fathali, hosted an event in New Delhi where Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met religious leaders, intellectuals and other dignitaries, including Jain monk Acharya Lokesh Muni and Jagadguru Swami Satishacharya Maharaj.
In this context, a video of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian bowing down is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows him touching the feet of Jagadguru Ramanandacharya Swami Satishacharya to seek his blessings. Several news outlets, including Times Now Navbharat and ABP News, also reported that Pezeshkian touched the feet of Swami Satishacharya during the event. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian touching Swami Satishacharya’s feet for blessings.
Fact: The video does not show Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian touching Swami Satishacharya’s feet to seek his blessings. Pezeshkian bent down to pick up something that had fallen to the ground, while Satishacharya also bent down at the same time. The Iranian Embassy and people present at the event confirmed that the video does not show Pezeshkian seeking blessings from Satishacharya. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords and found reports published by News18 Hindi and Moneycontrol, citing sources from the Iranian Embassy, which reported that Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian bent down to pick up a piece of paper. According to News18 Hindi, the Iranian Ambassador and diplomats organised a special reception and interaction programme at The Oberoi Hotel in New Delhi, attended by Jagadguru Satishacharya Maharaj, along with several prominent Indian interfaith leaders, intellectuals and businesspeople. During the event, Pezeshkian bent down to pick up a letter that had fallen to the floor, rather than touching anyone’s feet. Moneycontrol also reported, citing Iranian Embassy sources, that the letter had been handed to Pezeshkian by another leader and accidentally fell from his hand, prompting him to bend down and pick it up.
We then conducted a reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video, which led us to social media posts by INN News (archived) and Ismat TV (archived). An INN News post featuring Sahil Naqvi, who was present at the event, addressed the viral video, claiming that Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had bowed to touch the feet of a Hindu priest in India. According to the post, Pezeshkian had bent down to pick up a pen that had fallen to the floor, while the priest also bent down at the same time, creating the impression that the President was touching his feet. The post described the viral portrayal as misleading and said the footage was being presented out of context.
Ismat TV shared a video from another angle, showing both Pezeshkian and Swami Satishacharya bending down to pick up the pen. According to the account, Pezeshkian first attempted to pick it up, followed by Satishacharya. The post said that the incident was a gesture of respect and courtesy and did not show Pezeshkian bowing to anyone.
We then contacted Ismat TV and spoke to Hussain Mehdi, a photographer employed by the organisation. Speaking to Factly, he said that the channel’s staff were present at the event and that the claim that Pezeshkian touched Satishacharya’s feet is false. He also shared another video shot from a different angle, showing both Pezeshkian and Satishacharya bending down to pick up a paper.
We found a Facebook post by Acharya Lokesh Muni, who shared pictures of himself at the event standing next to Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. In the post, he said that he had invited Pezeshkian to host a first-of-its-kind peace summit in Iran, which the Iranian President accepted. He added that religious leaders and peace-loving groups from around the world would gather to promote peace through dialogue and discussion.
We contacted him, and speaking to Factly, he stated that the claim that the Iranian President touched the feet of a Hindu religious leader is false. He said that while he was showing Pezeshkian his magazine, Aahwaan, which is published by the World Peace Centre, an organisation he founded, the magazine fell from his hands. According to him, the video shows the Iranian President bending down to pick up the magazine for him as a courtesy, which was later circulated widely on the internet with a misleading claim.
We also contacted Maulana Taqi Haider Naqvi through the Iran Culture House, New Delhi, via WhatsApp. Naqvi, who was present at the event, also rebutted the claim that Pezeshkian touched Satishacharya’s feet. He also forwarded an Iranian Embassy statement regarding the matter, which reads, “The President bent down to pick up a letter that one of the leaders had given him and that had fallen to the ground.”
To sum up, this viral video shows Iranian President Pezeshkian bending down to pick up something, not to touch a Hindu religious leader’s feet.

England crush Sri Lanka to top T20 world rankings
- Published
Third T20 international, Old Trafford
Sri Lanka 124 all out (18.5 overs): Nissanka 36 (24), K Mendis 35 (28); Baker 2-17, Archer 2-23, Jacks 2-31
England 126-2 (9.4 overs): Buttler 62* (32), Brook 33 (21)
England won by eight wickets, won series 3-0
England steamrollered Sri Lanka in the third T20 to complete a 3-0 series clean sweep and return to number one in the world rankings.
Watched by new Test coach Stephen Fleming, England once again outclassed the tourists to conclude a one-sided series played on the fringe of autumn.
England's pace bowlers were outstanding in dismissing Sri Lanka for a paltry 124, then the home side chased the target in 9.4 overs.
Jamie Overton conceded only 15 runs in his four overs, including taking a wicket. Sonny Baker's improvement continued with 2-17 and Jofra Archer recovered from an expensive start to return 2-23.
England's fielding was sharp, best demonstrated by Liam Dawson's direct hit to run out Eshan Malinga.
The target was never likely to pose a challenge to an England batting line-up that remains powerful despite Phil Salt and Jacob Bethell being absent injured.
Though opener Aneurin Donald was out for 13, Jos Buttler and Harry Brook strolled the pursuit with a second-wicket stand of 85.
Brook was run out for 33, leaving Buttler to wrap it up with a six that left him unbeaten on 61.
The victory by eight wickets was concluded with 62 balls to spare - the most for England in a home T20 international.
The success was England's 23rd win in 26 completed T20s since Brook took charge in the summer of 2024. They have reclaimed their number one ranking from India.
The pity for this group is a rare lengthy wait until the next global T20 tournament. The next men's T20 World Cup is not until 2028, the same year T20 cricket makes its debut in the Olympics.
England are instead building towards a 50-over World Cup in southern Africa in the autumn of 2027. Three one-day internationals against the Sri Lankans begin in Durham on Tuesday.
Seamers another sign of England's versatility
A feature of England's success in this format has been captain Brook's heavy use of spin bowling. On this occasion the spinners took a backseat – Adil Rashid and Dawson sent down only four overs between them.
Instead, it was the seamers to the fore, even without the variations of Sam Curran, another England player absent injured.
Baker endured difficult debuts in all three international formats, yet in this series has started to show his potential.
After Archer's first over went for 15, Baker had Lahiru Udara sky to wicketkeeper Buttler. He later returned to wrap up the innings, taking the final wicket when Dilshan Madushanka skied to Brook.
Archer was a spectator for some time after his initial struggle. When he returned, he got the dangerous Kamindu Mendis to pull to deep mid-wicket for 35.
Archer's second wicket was curious – Wanindu Hasaranga out hit-wicket attempting a slog, his bat almost placed on top of the bails.
Overton was the pick, returning his most economical figures when bowling his full allocation of four in a T20 international.
Though Tom Banton dropped a catch slipping on the greasy outfield, England's fielding was otherwise exceptional.
Brook took a sharp catch at mid-wicket to remove Pathum Nissanka for 36, Rashid was alert enough to run out Charith Asalanka and Dawson's direct hit was the coup de grace.
Donald misses chance before Buttler-Brook show
At the age of 29, Donald has been given an international opportunity in this series as a replacement for Salt.
He has shown only glimpses of his excellent domestic form, returning a high score of 21. On this occasion, he tried to wallop the spin of Tharindu Rathnayake over long-on and was stumped by a distance.
In Buttler and Brook, the captains past and present, England have two men in supreme form. Buttler is England's best white-ball batter of all-time, while Brook is on the way to being one of their greats.
Such is their quality, the second-wicket pair turned the remainder of the chase into little more than a glorified net.
Sri Lanka were scruffy – they conceded 17 runs in wides. The hapless nature of the visitors' display was epitomised when Brook should have been caught off Madushanka, only for keeper Kamil Mishara and point fielder Nissanka to look at each other as the ball dropped to the ground.
There was no need for Brook to attempt a single that Hasaranga fielded in his follow-through, the bowler hitting direct with a throw at the non-striker's end.
Buttler won it in the following over, clubbing 18 from four Malinga deliveries, with two maximums hammered over the leg side.

MCD action continues after Satya Niketan tragedy: 397 properties face demolition in 13 days
MCD data shows that between September 6 and 18, the civic body carried out demolition at 397 properties and sealed 152 properties.
The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) has stepped up its action against unauthorised and unsafe buildings in the national capital, continuing its crackdown following the deadly collapse of a building housing a paying guest (PG) facility in the Satya Niketan area.
MCD data shows that between September 6 and 18, the civic body carried out demolition at 397 properties and sealed 152 properties. During the same period, it issued 310 show-cause notices for unauthorised construction, 178 sealing show-cause notices and 80 demolition orders.
On September 18 alone, MCD carried out demolition at 41 properties, sealed 10 properties, issued 42 show-cause notices for unauthorised construction, 44 sealing show-cause notices and seven demolition orders.
The September 6 collapse of a five-storey building in Satya Niketan killed at least seven people, including five students. MCD subsequently announced a series of steps, including the suspension of officials and a survey of PG facilities, amid criticism from opposition parties.
The MCD crackdown against unauthorised construction had begun before the PG collapse, following recent incidents in Saket and Malviya Nagar. The campaign intensified after the Satya Niketan tragedy.
From June 1 to September 3, the civic body demolished 983 properties, sealed 464 and issued 1,516 show-cause notices over unauthorised construction. It also issued 708 show-cause notices for sealing and 726 demolition orders.
The MCD has also completed a three-month survey of residential areas to detect the commercial use of residential properties. The exercise covered around 300,000 properties across 404 colonies and 168 wards.
The survey found more than 8,000 cases of commercial activity in residential areas. The civic body has started action against activities deemed impermissible under the Master Plan for Delhi. Around 30-40 properties had already been sealed, while proceedings against several others were underway.

Alice Augusta Ball lived a very short life. In 24 years, she had remarkable achievements, and was predictably forgotten for a while, until the world was shaken up to her brilliance. Her work on distilling chaulmoogra oil for use as effective treatment for leprosy brought hope to a number of patients globally.
An African American woman born into middle class in the late 1800s, Alice Ball benefitted from an early exposure to chemical processes as her family was involved in photography. She went on to shine in science at school, and could hope to move on to university, a rare opportunity for a woman and a person of her race at that time. She lived up to her potential and at the University of Washington, racked up her skills in chemistry and pharmacy. She finished two degrees – a bachelor’s in pharmaceutical chemistry and a bachelor’s in pharmacy – thus arming herself for a career –short lived, but so sparkling, people are still talking about her, though subsequent innovations have transformed care for leprosy.
With a full scholarship, another rarity for the times, Alice moved to the College of Hawai‘i, and became the first woman and the first African American to earn a master’s degree in chemistry. We mention it because it is an achievement, but also because it was an achievement that attracted the kind of attention a career flourishes on. It is said that Harry T. Hollmann, a public health officer, thought her thesis research on extracting active compounds from the kava (awa) root might have implications for his passion – finding cures for leprosy.
Leprosy or Hansen’s disease is caused by Mycobacterium leprae, and was discovered by Norwegian physician Gerhard Armauer Hansen in the 1870s. While it is prevalent in people living in tropical regions, leprosy which affects the nervous system, also has the moniker of being the world’s oldest disease. Evidence of leprosy has been found in skeletons from back in 2000 BCE. Those affected develop visible skin lesions and extremities including fingers and toes malformed and misshapen fingers. Sometimes amputations were also performed on limbs that could not be salvaged. As a result of the disfiguration, the stigma surrounding the disease was so high, those with leprosy had to be sequestered in camps and asylums outside the community.
Alice did accept Hollman’s invitation and what she managed to achieve was to revolutionise the field of leprosy care in the very near future. Described as the Ball Method, Alice devised a method that would “convert the oil’s fatty acids into water-soluble ethyl esters that could be injected into patients. Until then Chaulmoogra oil was promising as treatment for leprosy, but it was thick, not soluble in water, besides difficult to inject and swallow. Soon the world adopted the Ball Method and the landmark contribution changed life for the better for people who were battling leprosy across the world, without hope until then. Alice was in her early 20s at the time of this achievement.
Records of the time say, since the new formulation dispersed in the bloodstream instead of pooling under the skin, patients for the first time celebrated as earlier, there was none of the severe local reactions and oozing oil that the injections caused. Used on patients at Kalihi Hospital in Hawai‘i, researchers managed to show that patients administered the new formulation, became ‘bacteriologically negative, their lesions resolved, and many were discharged from isolation to rejoin their families, without fear of infecting them.’ This injectable preparation remained the best available treatment worldwide until sulfone antibiotics, Dapsone, in combination with other drugs, replaced it in the 1940s, facilitating a future unimaginable until then, for those who were diagnosed with leprosy and condemned to social isolation.
However, Alice’s contribution never made it to the headlines thanks to a set of factors – her gender, age and race were primary. She died young, it is speculated that it could be a result of a laboratory accident, a senior male colleague, her department head Arthur L. Dean appropriated and published her work without sharing any credit, in fact, promoting it as the ‘Dean method’, accounts of that period list.
It went unchallenged until decades later, when researcher Harry Hollmann revisited the archives and credited Ball. Finally, the historical records were righted, and Alice Ball’s name was affixed to the method she had painstakingly developed. By 24, despite the disdvantaged circumstances she worked in, Alice Ball had changed the world, it is a matter of speculation how much she would have achieved had she lived longer, but a safe bet to say she would have left a deeper impact. For the punch she packed in her short life, and the revolution she managed in that life, it’s time we say her name, say “Alice Augusta Ball.”
